his system, a voter is in effect given two votes for the House of Representatives – one to elect a district congressman; the other, a party-list representative. In *Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec,*99 the Court ruled that, to determine the winners in the Filipino party-list system, the Constitution and RA 7941 required four parameters, as follows:
“First, ***the twenty percent allocation*** – the combined number of *all* party-list congressmen shall not exceed twenty percent of the total membership of the House of Representatives, including those elected under the party list.
“Second, ***the two percent threshold*** – only those parties garnering a minimum of two percent of the total valid votes cast for the party-list system are ‘qualified’ to have a seat in the House of Representatives.
“Third, ***the three-seat limit*** – each qualified party, regardless of the number of votes it actually obtained, is entitled to a maximum of three seats; that is, one ‘qualifying’ and two additional seats.
“Fourth, ***proportional representation*** – the additional seats which a qualified party is entitled to shall be computed ‘in proportion to their total number of votes.’”
In the 1998 elections, the Commission on Elections did not follow these parameters, particularly the two percent threshold.  It proclaimed 39 political parties as winners, despite their failure to gather the minimum two percent of the total valid votes cast for the party-list system during the 1998 elections.  Thus, the Court invalided the assailed Comelec Resolution.100

Said the Court: “The Niemeyer formula, while no doubt suitable for Germany, finds no application in the Philippine setting, because of our three-seat limit and the non-mandatory character of the twenty percent allocation.  True, both our Congress and the Bundestag have threshold requirements — two percent for us and five for them.  There are marked differences between the two models, however.  As ably pointed out by private respondents,103 one half of the German Parliament is filled up by party-list members.  More important, there are no seat limitations, because German law discourages the proliferation of small parties.  In contrast, RA 7941, as already mentioned, imposes a three-seat limit to encourage the promotion of the multiparty system.  This major statutory difference makes the Niemeyer formula inapplicable to the Philippines.”
“Just as one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines or Guimaras mangoes in the Arctic because of fundamental environmental differences, neither can the Niemeyer formula be transplanted in toto here, because of essential variances between the two party-list models.”

**Protection of the**
**Environment**
Another constitutional paradigm, one that could even qualify as an ideology104 of the new age, is the protection of the environment.  As early as 1993, then Associate Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. stressed in *Oposa v. Factoran*105 the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology,106 which carried with it “the correlative duty to refrain from impairing the environment.”  Accordingly, timber licenses, not being property or property rights protected by the due process clause, may be revoked or rescinded by executive action.  Similarly, in *Tano v. Socrates,*107 the

**Epilogue**
In closing, let me now summarize. 1.  In the profession of law and in the magistracy, a combination of general education and specialized knowledge is essential.  In fact, I believe that in no other profession is this more critical.  Lawyers and magistrates must not only be experts in the law and its myriad twists and turns, but must also have a well-rounded knowledge of history, literature,
philosophy, and the humanities in general; psychology, sociology and other social sciences; ethics; mathematics; information technology; and economics, medicine, biogenics, physics and other natural sciences.
2.  In the e-age, there is an unmistakable shift of power from the state to the private sector.  This is very evident in the new global paradigms of globalization, deregulation, liberalization and privatization.  And even on the national level, the defanging of centralized state control is manifest in the clamor for more political and fiscal autonomy for local government units.  Bottom line: In the 21st century, the role of the state will be reduced.
3.  Following the collapse of totalitarianism and colonialism and the victory of freedom worldwide, the focus of the new economy, the cyber age and the technological revolution is the individual person and whatever exalts individual dignity, liberty and rights.

he focus of the new economy, the cyber age and the technological revolution is the individual person and whatever exalts individual dignity, liberty and rights. 4.  The Philippines, its judicial branch especially, has been able to meet the challenges of the new economy, the new modes of free expression like exit polls; the loosening of citizenship rules; the advances in people power as expressed in the systems of initiative, referendum, recall, the party-list method of representation and, most recently, the EDSA II People Power paradigm; and the advances in science and medicine.
I respectfully submit, however, that in two major areas – namely, the death penalty and due process for our workers — the Supreme Court has yet to catch up
116  *Ramos v. Court of Appeals,* supra.
117  “Whether or not a physician has committed an ‘inexcusable lack of precaution’ in the treatment of his patients is to be determined according to the standard of care observed by other members of the profession in good standing under similar circumstances bearing in mind the advanced state of the profession at the time of treatment or the present state of medical science.”  *Cruz v. Court of Appeals,* 282 SCRA 188, 200, November 18, 1997, per Francisco, J.
118  The Supreme Court justified the use of this old doctrine of *res ipsa loquitur* in this medical malpractice case because the damage to the patient’s brain was caused by the improper administration of anesthesia, and not a consequence of the cholecystectomy, which had actually not been performed.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms
heading: Chapter 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms
text:
Chapter 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms (cont.)

he patient’s brain was caused by the improper administration of anesthesia, and not a consequence of the cholecystectomy, which had actually not been performed. with the cyber age.  It has ignored the international trend to abolish the death penalty.  And by ruling that due process is available only against the government and not against private power, it has turned a blind eye to the fact that, under the policy of globalization and deregulation, the role of the state has been reduced and some of its powers ceded to “market forces” that transcend boundaries and sovereignties.  Hence, corporate behemoths and private individuals may now be sources of abuses and threats to constitutional rights.
Having said that, I am still happy and satisfied that, at bottom, the Philippine Supreme Court has been able to meet satisfactorily the challenges of the Third Millennium through the use of old but reliable doctrines.  And above that, for all the criticisms leveled against it, our 1987 Constitution has proven to be a beacon of light and a rock of stability in the maelstrom of political, social and economic storms that have lashed our country.
I end this lecture with a paean to our Constitution, as I quote from my *ponencia* in *Tañada v. Angara:*119

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 2 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Centenary Lecture Series lecture CJP delivered on February 13, 2001 in the SC Session Hall, surveying how the Court used 'old but reliable doctrines' to meet new e-age paradigms across four domains.
His premise, anchored in Judge Learned Hand, is that judges need both liberal education and legal expertise -- 'it is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of the Constitution.' On the new economy (globalization, liberalization, deregulation, privatization): Tanada v.
Angara upheld WTO membership on grave-abuse deference, holding the 'Filipino First' provisions non-self-executing and the Constitution interpretable for 'future and unknown circumstances'; Manila Prince Hotel was distinguished as a self-executing exception; Tatad v.
Secretary of Energy voided the Oil Deregulation Law (RA 8180) 9-2 for entrenching the Petron-Shell-Caltex oligopoly ('the Constitution mandates this Court to be the guardian not only of the people's political rights but their economic rights as well'), while Garcia v.
Corona upheld the corrected RA 8479; and Pimentel v.
Aguirre affirmed LGU fiscal autonomy.
On constitutional and political law he canvasses free expression (ABS-CBN v.
Comelec protecting exit polls; Vasquez's actual-malice libel standard), the death penalty (his Dissent in People v.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

law he canvasses free expression (ABS-CBN v.
Comelec protecting exit polls; Vasquez's actual-malice libel standard), the death penalty (his Dissent in People v. Echegaray that the 1987 Constitution abolished rather than suspended capital punishment and that executions are 'nightmarishly irreversible'), due process for workers (his Serrano Dissent that due process binds private power, not just government) and extraditees (Lantion), privacy (Ople v.
Torres), citizenship (Frivaldo; Mercado on dual citizenship; the 'reluctant hinges'), automated elections (Loong; Bush v.
Gore), initiative/referendum/recall (Santiago and PIRMA finding RA 6735 inadequate to amend the Constitution), the party-list four parameters (Veterans Federation Party v.
Comelec -- 'the Philippine style party list system is a unique paradigm,' rejecting the German Niemeyer formula because 'one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines'), and the environment (Oposa; Tano).
He treats the Court's role in swearing in President Arroyo on January 20, 2001 only guardedly under the sub judice rule, and closes on medical-malpractice res ipsa loquitur (Batiquin; Ramos).
His epilogue concedes the Court has yet to catch up on the death penalty and private-power due process, but credits the 1987 Constitution as 'a beacon of light and a rock of stability,' ending on his Tanada paean that a Constitution 'can withstand the assaults of bigots and infidels but at the same time bend with the refreshing winds of change.'

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

The 36-volume reading: CJP notes in a footnote that to write the Tanada v. Angara ponencia he had to read the entire 36-volume Uruguay Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations plus treatises on globalization -- a concrete illustration of his liberal-education-plus-expertise thesis.

Anecdote 2

Washington apples and Guimaras mangoes: rejecting the German Niemeyer party-list formula, CJP wrote that 'one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines or Guimaras mangoes in the Arctic,' because the Philippine three-seat-limit, non-mandatory-20% model differs fundamentally from the German Bundestag's.

Anecdote 3

The Echegaray irreversibility: CJP contrasts Leo Echegaray -- executed February 5, 1999 -- with Gallo and De los Santos, whose death sentences were reopened and corrected after the Court found the qualifying relationship had not been alleged in the Information; 'human reversals do not affect the graveyard.'

Anecdote 4

The 'reluctant hinges' lineage: CJP recalls his political-law professor, former CA Justice Delfin Fl. Batacan, teaching 'more than forty years ago' that the doors to Philippine citizenship must open on 'reluctant hinges' -- a phrase he carries into his own jurisprudence.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra

*[**One of the most enduring centenary projects of the Court was the publication of the *Centenary Reader* consisting of three volumes entitled (1) *Supreme Court Decisions as Literature*, (2) *Supreme Court Decisions as Philosophy*, **and (3) *Supreme Court Decisions as History.*  This trilogy contains the most quotable excerpts from the best decisions of the Court during the last 100 years.  While judicial pronouncements are intended mainly to settle litigations, these three volumes demonstrate that they are also sources of literature, philosophy and history.  Because they constitute selections from the best judicial writings of the highest magistrates of the land, Justice Panganiban calls them **obra maestra** in the Prologue he wrote for the anthology.  This Prologue is reproduced in the following pages.]*
**E**ssentially, the Supreme Court has a twofold responsibility: *first,* to review lower court decisions and correct any “reversible errors”; and *second,* in appropriate cases, to pass upon the acts of *any* branch or instrumentality of government in order to determine whether these have been done with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.1
The first constitutes the traditional duty of the judiciary:  to settle actual controversies involving the enforcement of rights, the vindication of wrongs, and the regulation of relationships among the people as well as between individuals and the government.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

ng the enforcement of rights, the vindication of wrongs, and the regulation of relationships among the people as well as between individuals and the government. The second refers to the High Court’s more sensitive, if sometimes controversial, role.  On the one hand, the doctrine of separation of powers, upon which our system of government hinges, decrees that its three great branches — the executive, the legislative and the judicial — should be independent and separate; each one is supreme in matters falling within its own constitutionally allocated sphere.  Thus, no department can or should interfere with the exercise of the rights and the powers of the other two.
On the other hand, when one branch of government abuses the exercise of its powers or crosses its constitutional limits, what remedy may be availed of to vindicate the abuse or excess?  Equally as important, which agency or mechanism would be imbued with the power and the authority to correct the
1 §1, Article VIII, Constitution of the Philippines.  In addition, the Court also exercises administrative supervision and disciplinary authority over all courts and all lawyers.
wrong:  The military?  The police?  An armed revolution?  People Power?2

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

administrative supervision and disciplinary authority over all courts and all lawyers.
wrong:  The military?  The police?  An armed revolution?  People Power?2 The United States Supreme Court, from which we borrowed much of our constitutional wisdom, has long answered this question by placing that responsibility upon itself.  During the first few years of its illustrious history, it voided a law enacted in contravention of constitutional provisions.  It thereby “interfered” in the exercise of the lawmaking prerogative, even in the absence of any *express* constitutional authority to do so.
In the Philippines, this American theory of the supremacy of the Constitution, with the Supreme Court as its guardian, has solidified into a granite doctrine.  Thus, whenever the Constitution is violated by a political branch of government — be it by the Presidency or by Congress — the Supreme Court shall, upon proper petition, come in to strike down the transgression.  It shall do so, not because it has any superior-inferior relationship with the violator, but because the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount.
The doctrine of separation of powers as a stumbling block to the judicial review of governmental actions has been refined further into the “political question” theory.  Such proposition bars courts from looking into matters that, under the Constitution, “are to be *decided by the people* in their sovereign capacity, or in regard to which *full discretionary authority* has been delegated to the legislative or executive branch

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

cided by the people* in their sovereign capacity, or in regard to which *full discretionary authority* has been delegated to the legislative or executive branch 2  Recently in *Estrada v. Desierto* (GR No. 146710-15, March 2, 2001, per Puno, J.), the Court described EDSA People Power II as “an exercise x x x of the freedom of speech and freedom of assembly to petition the government for redress of grievances,” an exercise that caused the resignation of the sitting President and the constitutional ascension of the Vice President.
of the government.  It is concerned with issues dependent upon the *wisdom,* not legality, of a particular measure.”3
The 1987 Constitution, however, has narrowed the reach of the political question.  It has expanded the prerogatives of the judiciary by expressly vesting it with the power to determine grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of government.  This *express*  authority finds its roots in *Avelino v. Cuenco,*4 in which the Supreme Court — after some hesitation — decided that it had the duty and the corollary power to settle the question of who was the duly elected president of the Senate,  a matter normally within the exclusive realm of that chamber of the legislature.  Waxing both literary and philosophical, Justice Gregorio Perfecto, with courage admirable in those days of judicial restraint, boldly declared:

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

he legislature.  Waxing both literary and philosophical, Justice Gregorio Perfecto, with courage admirable in those days of judicial restraint, boldly declared: “Judicial ‘hands-off’ policy is, in effect, a showing of official inferiority complex.  Consequently, like its parallel in the psychological field, it is premised on notions of reality fundamentally wrong.  It is an upshot of distorted past experience, warping the mind so as to become unable to have a healthy appraisal of reality in its true form.”5
In *Santiago v. Guingona,*6 a case decided under the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court ventured even
3  *Tañada v. Cuenco,* 103 Phil 1051, 1067, February 28, 1957, per Concepcion, J. (later, CJ).
4  83 Phil 17, March 4, 1949, per curiam.
5  Concurring Opinion of J. Perfecto, ibid. at p. 77.
6  298 SCRA 756, November 18, 1998, per Panganiban, J.
deeper than it had in *Avelino.*  In the light of allegations in the Petition that the Senate had violated a specific provision of the Constitution regarding the selection of its minority leader, the Court took jurisdiction over the controversy.  Roundly accused of interfering in an *internal* act of the Senate, a political question over which it allegedly had no authority, the Court clarified in *Santiago:*  “[J]urisdiction over the subject matter of a case is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition, regardless of whether the plaintiff or petitioner is entitled to the relief asserted.”

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

of a case is determined by the allegations of the complaint or petition, regardless of whether the plaintiff or petitioner is entitled to the relief asserted.” In exercising its collegial power to uphold the rule of law, the Supreme Court deals not only with the “why,” the “what” and “to what extent.”  It also deals with the “how” in formulating its decisions which, under our Constitution,7 shall state “clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which [they are] based.”  In my lectures on “How to Write Decisions,” delivered during seminars sponsored by the Philippine Judicial Academy for lower court magistrates, I have always emphasized the need to observe the “4 Cs” of effective legal writing:  *correct, complete, clear* and *concise.*  The Supreme Court itself has expressed in the following words its exasperation over “extraordinary verbiage”:
“Kilometric decisions without much substance must be avoided, to be sure, but the other extreme, where substance is also lost in the wish to be brief, is no less unacceptable…  The ideal decision is that which, with welcome economy of words, arrives at the factual findings, reaches the legal conclusion,
7  §14, Article VIII.
renders its ruling and, having done so, ends.”8

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 3: Obra Maestra
heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

h welcome economy of words, arrives at the factual findings, reaches the legal conclusion,
7  §14, Article VIII.
renders its ruling and, having done so, ends.”8 By its nature, decision-writing is aimed mainly at settling a controversy at hand.  It is usually done by simply reciting the facts and then applying the relevant law.  But let it not be forgotten that many decisions are stories of our people’s life and faith, written not just for information; but also for refreshment, upliftment of spirit, and wisdom in many fields of human endeavor.  Sometimes, cases involve life-and-death issues, the interest of the entire country, or the crossroads of pulsating national events.
Thus, they cannot simply be disposed of in a cut-and-dried fashion.  Here, the intellectual and literary talents of the justices are summoned, and their writing skills put to a test.  The Supreme Court itself9 extols “pride of authorship” and exhorts its members to use a “little style” to “help liven the opinion trapped in the tortuous lexicon of the law with all its whereases and wherefores.  A judicial decision does not have to be a bore.”
Indeed, this three-volume publication of the Supreme Court’s *obra maestra* during the past 100 years demonstrates that far from being “bores,” not only are court judgments written in inspired and readable prose; they are also veritable sources of history, philosophy and literature.
Truly, the excerpts contained in this trilogy capture the transformation of the Supreme Court from a passive, laid back, generally cautious and conservative

heading: Chapter 3: Obra Maestra
text:
Chapter 3: Obra Maestra (cont.)

re.
Truly, the excerpts contained in this trilogy capture the transformation of the Supreme Court from a passive, laid back, generally cautious and conservative 8  *Nicos Industrial Corporation v. Court of Appeals,* 206 SCRA 127, February 11, 1991, per Cruz, J.
9  *Francisco v. Permskul,* 173 SCRA 324, 336, May 12, 1989, per Cruz, J.
evaluator of past dramas; to a proactive, interacting and courageous mover and moulder of current and future events.  In both roles, it explains itself in elegant and spirited prose, which would pass for literature of the era.
While each of these three books is classified as literature or philosophy or history, there are many decisions that encapsulate all three essences — and more — in their hallowed pages.  The recent Decision upholding the legitimacy of Mrs. Gloria Macapagal Arroyo’s ascension to the Presidency and the Resolution denying the Motion for Reconsideration, as well as the various Separate Opinions therein, are leading examples of all three.10  The Court’s consciousness of the past, the present and the future is immortalized in *Morales v. Enrile*11 in these words:
“When the judgment of history is written, as leaders of our people, we shall be asked to account not only for what we did, not only for what we did not do, but also for what visions we have today of our tomorrow.”

of our people, we shall be asked to account not only for what we did, not only for what we did not do, but also for what visions we have today of our tomorrow.” In celebrating its 100 years of service to the nation, the Supreme Court has lined up more than 50 projects.  But in presenting to its various publics these three volumes which profile its finest “products,”  it cannot be prouder.  These books aim to prove that Supreme Court decisions qualify, not only as the final words in the settlement of disputes but also as gems of literature, philosophy and history.

heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 3 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Prologue CJP wrote for the Court's centenary anthology, the three-volume 'Centenary Reader' -- Supreme Court Decisions as Literature, as Philosophy, and as History -- which he calls the Court's 'obra maestra.' He frames the Court's twofold responsibility under Article VIII: the traditional duty to review 'reversible errors' and settle controversies, and the 'more sensitive, if sometimes controversial' duty to strike down any branch's act done with grave abuse of discretion.
Posing the question of who corrects a branch that abuses its powers -- 'The military?
The police?
An armed revolution?
People Power?' -- he answers that the US Supreme Court 'long answered this question by placing that responsibility upon itself,' a doctrine that in the Philippines 'solidified into a granite doctrine': the Court strikes transgressions by the Presidency or Congress 'not because it has any superior-inferior relationship with the violator, but because the Constitution must be upheld as truly paramount.' He traces the political-question theory (Tanada v.
Cuenco -- matters of 'wisdom, not legality') and how the 1987 Constitution narrowed it by expressly vesting grave-abuse review, rooted in Avelino v.
Cuenco, where Justice Gregorio Perfecto branded the 'judicial hands-off policy...
a showing of official inferiority complex'; and his own Santiago v.
Guingona, taking jurisdiction over the Senate's minority-leader selection because 'jurisdiction...

ing of official inferiority complex'; and his own Santiago v.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age

*[Justice Panganiban — along with Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing and Philja Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera — was granted a judicial scholarship to attend a “Working Conversation” on biosciences and biotechnology.  Held in Kona, Hawaii, from June 30 to July 4, 2001, the conference was sponsored by the Einstein Institute for Sciences, Health and the Courts (Einshac).  Although not a direct project of the SC Centenary Celebrations, this encounter among a hundred learned men and women of law and science was held to assess the readiness of the world’s judiciaries to tackle the upcoming legal questions posed by DNA, human cloning, stem cells, genetic engineering and other aspects of biosciences and biotechnology.  In this sense, the **avant garde** discussion ushered the bio-age into the Philippine judiciary during the SC’s centenary.  The following were the remarks delivered by Justice Panganiban on July 1, 2001, during a plenary session of the conference.]*
**J**ustice Claire L’Heureaux-Dube (of the Canadian Supreme Court) spoke eloquently of judicial and constitutional globalization.  Indeed, this phenomenon is brought about by many new paradigms that face the judiciaries of the world as the new century beckons.
*Various Challenges*
*to Courts*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

deed, this phenomenon is brought about by many new paradigms that face the judiciaries of the world as the new century beckons.
*Various Challenges*
*to Courts* For a start, in economics and trade, the new policies of deregulation, liberalization and privatization are breaking down traditional sovereign borders and are shrinking the world into a borderless global village.  The world’s judiciaries have had to adjust their attitude towards the old modes of protectionism like tariffs, import quotas, currency controls, tax havens and tax incentives – all of which are giving way to free trade as espoused by the World Trade Organization.
So, too, the new information highway — the third wave of microchips and modems, the Internet and broadband fiber optics — have altered and continue to alter traditional concepts of accumulating vast wealth.  New paradigms of commercial and political preeminence have emerged:  from the manufacture and sale of products to the rendering of services, and from the exploitation of natural resources to the exploration and use of knowledge.
But perhaps the most daunting of these 21st century challenges is the one brought about by the new sciences of genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology, which will all affect not just our material concerns, but also the more intimate and more

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

y the new sciences of genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology, which will all affect not just our material concerns, but also the more intimate and more challenging concepts of health, longevity, human wellness, ethics, morality and the very essence of life itself.  In turn, these new sciences will cause — as in fact they are now causing — mega-shifts in the ways of discovering and processing truth, matters that will profoundly and radically affect judicial dispensation.
The critical question therefore is this:  are the judiciaries of the world ready to tackle these new, interesting phenomena?
Justice Dube articulated the Canadian response, and in the process gave two concrete case samples: the Harvard mouse and Monsanto’s canola.
*The Philippine Response*
*to the Challenges of Biosciences*
Initially, I hoped to respond to this question by giving a survey of the possible answers of the various judicial authorities in my part of the world — Asia.  However, limitations of time do not allow such extended discussion.  It is, on the other hand, more than a consolation that another member of our panel, Judge Clifford Wallace — a member of the US Court of Appeals and consultant of more than 40 judicial authorities worldwide — would probably take this up when he speaks after me.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

llace — a member of the US Court of Appeals and consultant of more than 40 judicial authorities worldwide — would probably take this up when he speaks after me. Let me then answer the query from the point of view of the Philippine judiciary.  I will begin  by relating that three weeks ago, on June 11, 2001, the Philippine Supreme Court celebrated its centenary.  A hundred years ago, the Second Philippine Commission in our country established this Court, as well as the lower tribunals — the Courts of First Instance and the Justice of the Peace Courts.  This Commission had been
tasked by the US government with the mission of setting up a civil government to replace a military group that took control after the Philippine Islands were ceded by  Spain to the US through the 1898 Treaty of Paris, which ended the  Spanish-American War.
Even before 1901, however, there had been courts existing in our  country, like the ones that were established by the US military and the Spanish *conquistadores,* and that lasted for almost 400 years.  But we reckon the founding of our Supreme Court only in 1901, because it was only in that year that a tribunal which enjoyed judicial independence, as we know it today, was set up.  Since then, the Court has functioned independently of the other branches of government, like the executive and the legislative.  I must add, though, that its decisions were appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946, when the US completely withdrew its sovereign claims over our country.
By *independent* I mean the following:

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

ere appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946, when the US completely withdrew its sovereign claims over our country.
By *independent* I mean the following: 1.  Our Court exercises powers and makes decisions that are not reviewable by any other entity or agency of government.
2.  Its financial stability is guaranteed by our Constitution.  Thus, Congress is constitutionally prohibited from reducing judicial appropriations given the previous year.
3.  Members of the judiciary enjoy security of tenure (up to age 70) and security of compensation, both of which cannot be reduced by Congress or by the President.  Members of the Supreme Court may be removed from office only by impeachment.
*Powers of the*
*Supreme Court*
Our Constitution has granted our Supreme Court and our judiciary not just independence, but also vast powers and heavy responsibilities, which I classify into five:
1.  Review of ordinary appeals from judgments of lower courts
2.  Extraordinary review — by writ of certiorari — of the act of
*any* agency of government, including the Presidency and Congress, on the ground of grave abuse of discretion which may consist of the following:
a.  Violation of the Constitution, the laws or judicial doctrines
b.  Whimsical or arbitrary action arising from manifest bias or personal animosity, of such gravity as to deprive the losing party of due process
3.  Administrative supervision of all lower courts, with the sole power to discipline and dismiss judges
4.  Control of admission to the practice of law and discipline of erring lawyers

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

ision of all lower courts, with the sole power to discipline and dismiss judges
4.  Control of admission to the practice of law and discipline of erring lawyers 5.  Preparation and promulgation of rules of procedure and evidence in all courts (Congress cannot increase the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court without the latter’s consent.)
*Readiness of the*
*Philippine Judiciary*
On the basis of these powers and responsibilities, let me now discuss the extent of preparedness of the
Philippine judiciary, especially the Supreme Court, in meeting the challenges of biosciences and biotechnology.
*First,* by its certiorari and ordinary review powers, the judiciary is able, in appropriate cases, to pass upon the actions of all government agencies involved in science, health and technology like the Department of Health, the Department of Agriculture, the Bureau of Patents, and the Food and Drug Administration.  It can, on constitutional grounds, void laws and executive orders like those dealing with abortion, cloning, genetic testing, privacy and confidentiality concerns, and the consequences of biotechnology.
*Second,* by its rule-making power, the Supreme Court can promulgate rules on DNA fingerprinting, the use of genes as evidence, and the admission of biotechnology and genetics as evidence.  Already, our Court is drafting rules on electronic evidence.  Soon, it will also prepare rules of procedure in cases involving genetics and biotechnology.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

nce.  Already, our Court is drafting rules on electronic evidence.  Soon, it will also prepare rules of procedure in cases involving genetics and biotechnology. *Third,* by its administration of bar examinations, it influences directly the curricula of law schools.  It also directly provides — through its education arm, the Philippine Judicial Academy — continuing legal education for judges and quasi-judicial officers.
*Fourth,* through its power to discipline lower court magistrates, the Supreme Court assures uniform application of genetic and bioscientific principles to ethics, as well as to legal and social doctrines.
*Fifth,* because it enjoys judicial independence, it can enter into bilateral and international agreements with the judicial authorities of other countries, as Justice Dube is proposing, without need of approval of any other agency of government.
*Epilogue: New Ways of Discovering Truth*
Let me conclude by saying that *Time* magazine, in its November 13, 2000 issue, reported that in the United States, 80 convicts by final judgments have later on been exonerated, because subsequent DNA evidence showed that they were completely innocent of the crimes attributed to them.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
text:
Chapter 10: Ready for the Bio-Age (cont.)

ts by final judgments have later on been exonerated, because subsequent DNA evidence showed that they were completely innocent of the crimes attributed to them. If this has happened in the US, the most technologically and economically advanced nation in the world, then it has probably happened in the Philippines and other countries.  I shudder to think that during the last five years, our trial courts have imposed on more than 1,500 persons the penalty of death — a penalty which, incidentally, I personally oppose on constitutional and philosophical grounds.
The availability of new breakthroughs in science and technology and the positive response of the judicature should make us more confident that in the future, mistakes in the discovery of truth can be minimized, if not totally avoided.
I thank you.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 10 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's plenary remarks of July 1, 2001 at the Einstein Institute (Einshac) 'Working Conversation' on biosciences and biotechnology in Kona, Hawaii -- a conference of about 100 leaders of law and science he attended on a judicial scholarship with Justice Leonardo A.
Quisumbing and PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A.
Melencio Herrera, framing it as ushering 'the bio-age into the Philippine judiciary' during its centenary.
Building on Canadian Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube's account of judicial and constitutional globalization (with her 'Harvard mouse and Monsanto's canola' examples), he surveys the new paradigms confronting the world's courts: economic deregulation, liberalization and privatization dissolving sovereign borders under the WTO; the information highway shifting wealth 'from the exploitation of natural resources to the exploration and use of knowledge'; and -- 'most daunting' -- genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology reshaping health, ethics and 'the very essence of life itself.' Answering for the Philippines, he restates that the SC is reckoned from 1901 (after the 1898 Treaty of Paris) because only then did an independent tribunal arise, with decisions appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946, and defines judicial independence as non-reviewable decisions, constitutionally guaranteed funding, and security of tenure (to age 70) and compensation.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

l 1946, and defines judicial independence as non-reviewable decisions, constitutionally guaranteed funding, and security of tenure (to age 70) and compensation. He then enumerates the Court's five powers -- ordinary review; certiorari review of any agency, including the Presidency and Congress, for grave abuse of discretion; administrative supervision and discipline of judges; control of the bar; and rule-making -- and maps each to bioscience readiness: reviewing the DOH, DA, Bureau of Patents and FDA, voiding laws on cloning, genetic testing and privacy, promulgating rules on DNA and electronic evidence, shaping curricula through bar exams and PhilJA, ensuring uniform ethical application, and entering international judicial agreements unaided.
He closes on truth: Time magazine's report that 80 US convicts were later exonerated by DNA leads him to 'shudder' that Philippine trial courts had imposed death on more than 1,500 persons in five years -- 'a penalty which, incidentally, I personally oppose on constitutional and philosophical grounds' -- concluding that scientific breakthroughs can ensure 'mistakes in the discovery of truth can be minimized, if not totally avoided.'

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers

*[“E-Values for Lawyers” is a carryover from the three fundamental principles which, in the professional and personal life of Justice Panganiban, have become cornerstones — excellence, ethics and eternity.  He expounded on these quite extensively in three chapters of his book last year, *Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity.*  He found the occasion to apply them to lawyers, in a speech before the Calamba City Lawyers League on August 24, 2001, at the Monte Vista Social Hall, Calamba City.]*
**M**ay I begin by congratulating your new president, Atty. Emilio C. Capulong Jr., and the other officers of the Calamba City Lawyers League on their induction tonight.
It is said that Supreme Court justices are better read than heard.  For this reason, I try to limit my public appearances.  But I cannot turn down this invitation of *Compañero* Capulong, because I want to encourage him in his crusade to use his legal knowledge, not for personal honor or profit, but for the benefit of the underprivileged and the oppressed.  A leading light of *Bantay Katarungan* and *Kilosbayan,* Atty. Capulong equates his being a lawyer to his being a servant of the Lord.  His dual loyalty to the law of humans and to the commandments of the Lord is, in fact, the inspiration for my address tonight.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

his being a servant of the Lord.  His dual loyalty to the law of humans and to the commandments of the Lord is, in fact, the inspiration for my address tonight. Truly, it has been said that the legal profession may be likened to a religious vocation.  I believe that the adage “Many are called, but few are chosen” has relevance to lawyers and clergy alike.  Indeed, the road to that elusive title “Atty.” is no easy path to traverse.  For it demands patience, perseverance  and prayer, much like the virtues required of men and women of the Church.  The stringent training in law school, the extensive preparation for the bar exams, and the agonizing wait for the bar results all form part of that one great experience every lawyer must inevitably go through.  Similarly, priests, pastors, ministers, rabbis, imams and other religious ecclesiastics must pass through rigorous stages of education, training, sacrifice and soul-searching, in order to become worthy leaders of their faiths.
Allow me to pursue the parallelism even further by saying that lawyers, just like their religious
counterparts, should be looked upon with respect, veneration and esteem.  Or are they?  Can we possibly equate the status of lawyers with that of holy men and women?  Does the apparent symmetry between the legal and the religious professions crumble against the realization that lawyers are not exactly an admired, adored or adulated lot?

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

parent symmetry between the legal and the religious professions crumble against the realization that lawyers are not exactly an admired, adored or adulated lot? In his book *Happiness Is A Serious Problem,*1 Dennis Prager says:  “Many people who graduate from law school are worse human beings than they were prior to enrolling.  Why?  Because law school teaches students to stop thinking in moral terms and to start thinking in legal terms — to ask ‘Is it legal?’ rather than ‘Is it right?’”
Closer to home, former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, a legal giant and highly esteemed statesman, buttresses this observation.  In a speech2 before the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, Rizal Chapter, he observed: “There is widespread cynism about lawyers in general and the prevailing belief is that there are too many lawyers for the public good.”  He rues that, whereas “before martial law, most presidents [in our country] were lawyers, no lawyer has been chosen president since Ferdinand Marcos” — a barometer of how low public esteem for our brethren has sunk.
Admittedly, the depreciative perception of lawyers has always been a cause for concern.  Yet it seems to be a perennial problem with no forseeable solution.  Indeed, many lawyers are looked upon with cynicism, consternation and even contempt, especially when they are depicted as scheming, insidious and

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

ble solution.  Indeed, many lawyers are looked upon with cynicism, consternation and even contempt, especially when they are depicted as scheming, insidious and unscrupulous professionals, whose primary concern is winning battles merely for the sake of possessions, power or prestige.  Worse, they appear to thrive on this preconceived notion and actually live the derogatory stereotype to the hilt.  Be it in the arena of politics, business, law practice or other fields of endeavor, the image of a lawyer is certainly far from exemplifying the quintessential man or woman of the Church.  And so you ask, why the comparison?
This seemingly “irreverent and irreconcilable” analogy, although initially hard to comprehend, will be relevant to those who, like Atty. Capulong, consider the legal profession as a vocation or a calling in itself.  In any case, we may as well treat our work with as much conviction and passion, as religious clerics cherish theirs.  More important, I am sure that there are many of us who wish to venture into the journey of life not only in the ways of the *law,* but in the ways of the *Lord* as well.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

tant, I am sure that there are many of us who wish to venture into the journey of life not only in the ways of the *law,* but in the ways of the *Lord* as well. Certainly, it would be unfair, if not impossible, to impose the priestly vows of obedience, poverty and chastity on lawyers.  I can enumerate and expound on some of the reasons, but I am sure you already have a million and one answers to why we just cannot embrace such vows.  Let me instead share with you three fundamental principles that have come to be the cornerstones of my professional and personal life.  These rudiments have consistently underscored my speeches, because I believe that they are timeless and indispensable in this brave new world of technological advancement, modernization and globalization.  Allow me then to discuss the important values, which I refer to as the three *E*’s; namely, excellence, ethics and eternity.
1  Harper Collins, 1998 ed.; see “Here’s an Idea:  Let’s Bean All Lawyers,” *Today,* August 19, 2001, p. 7.
2  *Kilosbayan* Magazine, August 2001, p. 57.
*Excellence*
Excellence in the context of the legal profession means more than just knowledge of the law, mastery of legal procedure, and talent in maneuvering courtroom battles.  It connotes not merely professional competence or the ability to develop legal skills to an optimum level.  More than these, it involves taking responsibility for the consequences of our actions, being sincere in our intentions, and making a difference in the lives of others.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

n these, it involves taking responsibility for the consequences of our actions, being sincere in our intentions, and making a difference in the lives of others. In our line of work, we are faced with difficult questions and controversial issues requiring not only the application of the law, but the discernment of what is right, so that justice in its truest sense may be realized.  In our quest to defend or prosecute, we find ourselves in an introspective examination of our beliefs, principles and morals vis-à-vis the goal we seek to attain.  Ultimately, our motivation should be directed to the end that our conscience can rest easy in knowing that  genuine justice has been rendered.
To many, this attitude may seem like a virtual surrender of the “astutely assertive attitude” commonly possessed by the typical success-driven lawyer.  On the other hand, let me just say that we can never truly achieve the success we aspire for unless our minds, our hearts and our souls are at peace.  For when the days are done and all is gone, we will come to realize that short-lived gains in this earthly existence cannot compare with the rewards that await us yonder.
Another attribute of excellence is devotion to work.  Lawyering has always been viewed as a dignified, prestigious and lucrative vocation.  As a matter of fact, many lawyers will readily admit that honor, prestige and money were the most influential

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

a dignified, prestigious and lucrative vocation.  As a matter of fact, many lawyers will readily admit that honor, prestige and money were the most influential factors that led them to pursue a career in law.  Sad to say, very few are in it for the altruistic feeling of being able to help in the administration of justice, which should be the foremost responsibility of every lawyer.  Such distorted perception of the legal profession has led many of our professional brethren astray and, consequently, paved the way for the proliferation of the so-called “rotten few” among our ranks.
Indeed, there is no substitute for hard work and determination, which characterize all successful men and women of ages past and present, in the Philippines and around the world.  But these efforts should be infused, not with a desire for power or wealth or acclaim.  Rather, lawyers should find inspiration in the very nature of their profession and adopt a sincere outlook towards settling disputes, providing legal services and upholding the rule of law.
Geared towards this end, some pertinent guidelines are provided by the Code of Professional Responsibility.3  For instance, lawyers should not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral or deceitful conduct.4  Neither should they be part of any activity aimed at defiance of the law or at lessening confidence in the legal system.5  Moreover, they must always try to encourage a fair settlement of controversies as

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

aimed at defiance of the law or at lessening confidence in the legal system.5  Moreover, they must always try to encourage a fair settlement of controversies as 3  This Code was promulgated by the Supreme Court on June 21, 1988.  It had initially been drafted by the Integrated Bar of the Philippines’ Committee on Responsibility, Discipline and Disbarment composed of Dean Irene Cortes as chairman; and Justice Carolina Griño-Aquino, Attys. Gonzalo W. Gonzalez, Marcelo B. Fernan, Camilo Quiason, Jose F. Espinosa and Carmelo V. Sison as members; with former Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion and former Justice Jose B. L. Reyes as consultants; and Prof. Myrna S. Feliciano and Atty. Concepcion Lim-Jardeleza as resource persons.
4  Code of Professional Responsibility, Canon 1; Rule 1.01.
5  Ibid., Rule 1.02.
would admit of a proper dispensation of justice for all parties.6  Indeed, the practice of law is a privilege granted only to those who possess the strict intellectual and moral qualifications required of those who would be instruments for the effective and efficient administration of justice.7  This privilege is bestowed by the State on those who show that they possess, and continue to possess, the qualifications required by law for the conferment of such privilege.8

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

is bestowed by the State on those who show that they possess, and continue to possess, the qualifications required by law for the conferment of such privilege.8 No less than dedication, fervor and passion should characterize our attitude towards the profession.  More than the egoistic motivation of personal achievement, the dignity of the legal profession should be the primordial consideration in all our undertakings.  Indeed, the Code of Professional Responsibility mandates that a lawyer shall at all times uphold the integrity and the dignity of the legal profession.9
As lawyers, we are given so much opportunity to make a difference in our community, in our country and in the world.  Indeed, there is so much that can be done and there is so much we can do.  Unfortunately, our idealism and exuberance as young lawyers to “make a difference in society” soon dwindle into nothingness.  This happens when our concerns suddenly shift to climbing the corporate ladder, making “big bucks,” and getting ahead in our chosen career.  These aspirations, although well-meaning and justified, should not, however, be a convenient subterfuge to renege on our duty to help
the underprivileged, champion the cause of the oppressed, and ensure proper observance and respect for the law by all – rich or poor, nobility or commoner, renowned or nameless.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

ed, champion the cause of the oppressed, and ensure proper observance and respect for the law by all – rich or poor, nobility or commoner, renowned or nameless. Accordingly, lawyers should make their legal services available in an efficient and convenient manner compatible with the independence, the integrity and the effectiveness of the profession.10  Except for valid reasons, they must not reject the cause of the defenseless or the oppressed11 or withhold their services from the needy.12  The blessings we share with others and our good deeds that make a better world will live in the memories of those we have helped, long after our personal gains and triumphs shall have already been lost and forgotten.
*Ethics*
A discussion of the value of *ethics* would appear to be out of place in this speech, considering that we are all aware of the Code of Professional Responsibility.  After having taken up legal ethics in law school and in the bar exams, we are, in fact, presumed to know the contents of the Code (at least its essence) by heart.  A perusal of its important provisions will provide sufficient guidelines on how to conduct ourselves as lawyers or jurists.  Be that as it may, let me just emphasize the hierarchy of responsibilities that should be observed at all times by all lawyers in the performance of their duties.
It must always be remembered, *first and foremost,* that lawyers are officers of the court with the primary
6  Ibid., Rule 1.04.
7  *In Re: Al Argosino,* 270 SCRA 26, March 19, 1997.
8  *Arrieta v. Llosa,* 282 SCRA 248, November 28, 1997.
9  Ibid., Canon 7.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

he primary
6  Ibid., Rule 1.04.
7  *In Re: Al Argosino,* 270 SCRA 26, March 19, 1997.
8  *Arrieta v. Llosa,* 282 SCRA 248, November 28, 1997.
9  Ibid., Canon 7. 10  Ibid., Canon 2.
11  Ibid., Rule 2.01.
12  Ibid., Canon 14.
duty to see to it that justice is served.  To be sure, they should exert every effort and consider it their duty to assist in the speedy and efficient administration of justice.13  Thus, the interest of their clients comes in a far *second,* ever subservient to that of justice.  In this connection, it is important to note that lawyers should always be faithful to their clients’ cause and be mindful of the trust and confidence reposed in them.14  Also, they should observe candor, fairness and loyalty in all their dealings and transactions.15  Competence and diligence should characterize the kind of work they do for their clients,16 whom they are expected to represent with utmost zeal within the bounds of law.17  Coming in even a farther *third* are the personal interests of the lawyers, which at all times must bow to the demands of fiduciary relations with the clients and, more important, to the exacting standards of justice as administered by the courts.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

l times must bow to the demands of fiduciary relations with the clients and, more important, to the exacting standards of justice as administered by the courts. Frankly speaking, I seriously doubt whether this threefold responsibility is still being observed by every one of us.  I have come across several cases involving lawyers who seem to have understood the hierarchy of responsibilities the other way around.  As a matter of fact, some of them have come to believe that their interest comes first; next is the interest of their clients; and lastly, if at all, the interest of justice.
For the guidance of the bench and the bar, let me just clarify that the Supreme Court has not issued any circular or memorandum reversing the lawyer’s
hierarchy of responsibilities.  I hope this serves as a reminder to all, lest we be deluded by the actuations of some of our misguided colleagues.  Suffice it to say that the Code and the Canons have been formulated and promulgated for the good of the legal profession and its members; and are there for the convenience, the protection and the service of all lawyers.  Accordingly, compliance therewith we owe not only to ourselves and our peers, but to the profession and the country as well.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

on and the service of all lawyers.  Accordingly, compliance therewith we owe not only to ourselves and our peers, but to the profession and the country as well. The value of *ethics,* which proceeds from personal integrity, motivates us to act in accordance with what is true and honest regardless of personal consequences.  To act with integrity is to act with moral courage.  In these times of materialism and self-aggrandizement, it would be encouraging to know that there are still some who have such integrity to rise above the perverted norms and distorted structures that have degraded our noble profession.  Undoubtedly, this transformation requires not only a change of philosophy but, more important, also a change of heart.  Only one who is clear of mind and pure of heart can act with integrity.
Still, there is no better yardstick to gauge proper adherence to ethical standards than one’s sense of right and wrong.  As beings brought into this world by the grace of God, we are inherently possessed of a general discernment of what is good and what is bad.  Although variable influences like education, experience and exposure may have affected this discernment through the course of our lives, we remain essentially good, God-fearing and just.  And if we remain true to the reality that we are mere creatures of a God who is infinitely good, maintaining ethics in our professional undertakings would entail no effort at all.
13  Ibid., Canon 12.
14  Ibid., Canon 17.
15  Ibid., Canon 15.
16  Ibid., Canon 18.
17  Ibid., Canon 19.
*Eternity*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

undertakings would entail no effort at all.
13  Ibid., Canon 12.
14  Ibid., Canon 17.
15  Ibid., Canon 15.
16  Ibid., Canon 18.
17  Ibid., Canon 19.
*Eternity* Finally, let me share with you the third *E* of the 3E-values formula: *eternity.*  No matter how the world turns or how civilizations progress or how events affect our very existence, never for a moment think that our lives on earth are the only ones we have.  Rather, believe that there is life after death, that there is eternity where our final destiny lies.  I dare say that the sincere acceptance of this reality will dramatically transform our entire value system, alter our behavioral patterns and bring us to a renewed enlightenment of who we really are.
Just as there are human and physical laws, so are there spiritual laws also.  And just as there are consequences for violations of human and physical laws, so are there penalties as well for the transgression of God’s commands.  Regardless of color or creed, we are all bound by a common faith in a Supreme Being who watches over us, silently listens to everything we say, and quietly witnesses everything we do.  Our recognition of a transcendental omniscience will keep us ever so vigilant, cautious and mindful of the fundamental teachings of wisdom, righteousness and justice, which are essentially common to all faiths.  Thus, only when we place God at the center of our lives can we truly achieve  a complete understanding of what is true and just.  In everything we say, everything we do and everything we are, He must always be there.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

can we truly achieve  a complete understanding of what is true and just.  In everything we say, everything we do and everything we are, He must always be there. Let me assure you, ladies and gentlemen, that God is present with us today, here and now in this very place.  He is amongst us to embrace us, above us to inspire us, before us to lead us, beside us to guide us, behind us to protect us, and within us — in our hearts
and our spirits — to bring us to His Everlasting Kingdom.
*Epilogue*
On the whole, the values I have discussed may serve as guideposts in your search for success and fulfillment in your respective careers.  I do not claim to have all the answers to the perplexing questions and mind-boggling issues inherently involved in your work as lawyers.  The method of your practice and the manner in which you conduct your business may be as effective and reliable as you think.  But then, you can never tell if a *little change can make a big difference.*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers
text:
Chapter 11: E-Values for Lawyers (cont.)

in which you conduct your business may be as effective and reliable as you think.  But then, you can never tell if a *little change can make a big difference.* As for my initial proposition of comparing the vocation of lawyers with that of faith leaders, I stand firm in my belief that the legal profession can be on a level with any other pontificate insofar as EXCELLENCE, ETHICS and ETERNITY are concerned.  Just as there are great and noble men and women of the faith, so are there great and noble men and women of the law.  As long as we uphold the dignity of the profession, pursue the cause of justice and promote respect for the rule of law, with God at the center of it all, we can be holy in a “not-so-holy” profession.  Hence, if there is truth to the aphorism that “saints are sinners who keep trying,” then I say unto you all:  let us begin our journey to sainthood!  With God’s grace and with our habitual practice of excellence, ethics and eternity, we may just make it after all.
Thank you and good day!

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 11 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's August 24, 2001 address to the Calamba City Lawyers League, inducting Atty.
Emilio C.
Capulong Jr.
-- a Bantay Katarungan and Kilosbayan figure who 'equates being a lawyer with being a servant of the Lord.' CJP develops the parallel between law and the religious vocation ('many are called, but few are chosen'), confronting the low public esteem for lawyers -- Dennis Prager's charge that law school teaches students to ask 'Is it legal?' rather than 'Is it right?,' and Jovito Salonga's lament that no lawyer has been president since Marcos.
Against this, he offers his three personal cornerstones, the '3 E-values.' Excellence is more than competence; it is responsibility, sincerity and 'making a difference,' pursued not for 'power, wealth or acclaim' but in service of the underprivileged, as the Code of Professional Responsibility requires.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

nd 'making a difference,' pursued not for 'power, wealth or acclaim' but in service of the underprivileged, as the Code of Professional Responsibility requires. Ethics is fidelity to a threefold hierarchy of responsibilities -- the interest of justice first (lawyers are officers of the court), the client's cause a 'far second,' and the lawyer's personal interest a 'farther third' -- a hierarchy some have inverted but which, he stresses, the Supreme Court has issued no circular to reverse; ethics flows from integrity, which is moral courage, and 'only one who is clear of mind and pure of heart can act with integrity.' Eternity, the third E, is the belief that life on earth is not all there is: just as there are human and physical laws, there are spiritual laws, and placing God at the center transforms one's entire value system and reveals 'what is true and just.' He closes that lawyers can stand 'on a level with any other pontificate' through excellence, ethics and eternity -- and that 'if there is truth to the aphorism that saints are sinners who keep trying,' then 'let us begin our journey to sainthood,' becoming 'holy in a not-so-holy profession.'

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 11: E-Values for Lawyers
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

The 'Is it legal?' indictment: CJP cites Dennis Prager's 'Happiness Is A Serious Problem' -- that many people 'are worse human beings' after law school because it teaches them to ask 'Is it legal?' rather than 'Is it right?' -- as the cynic's case against the profession he means to rebut.

Anecdote 2

Salonga's barometer: he quotes Jovito Salonga's observation that whereas before martial law most Philippine presidents were lawyers, 'no lawyer has been chosen president since Ferdinand Marcos' -- a measure of how far public esteem for lawyers has fallen.

Anecdote 3

The inverted hierarchy: CJP says he has encountered lawyers who understood the order of duties 'the other way around' -- their own interest first, the client's next, and justice last, if at all -- and pointedly notes the Court has issued no circular reversing the proper hierarchy.

Anecdote 4

Capulong as living text: the address is inspired by inductee Atty. Emilio Capulong Jr., who 'equates his being a lawyer to his being a servant of the Lord,' embodying the dual loyalty to the law of humans and the commandments of God that CJP holds up as the model.
