in order to disabuse the minds of the supporters of the past regime of any and all unfounded notions, or ill-perceived attempts on the part of the present dispensation, to ‘railroad’ the instant criminal cases against x x x Former President Joseph Ejercito Estrada.”2

*Constitutional Rights* By a vote of 8-6,3 the Court denied the Petition in *Perez v. Estrada*4 and maintained the absolute prohibition against *live* radio and TV coverage.  Although conceding that “the press is a mighty catalyst in awakening public consciousness, and x x x has become an important instrument in the quest for truth,” Justice Jose C. Vitug’s majority ruling opted, nonetheless, to support the argument of former President Estrada.  The latter had contended that his constitutional rights as an accused were impinged by the Perez proposal. *The US Federal Courts’* *Ban on Live Coverage*
The Philippine Supreme Court cited *Estes v. Texas,*13 in which its US counterpart held in 1965 that live television coverage of judicial proceedings was “an inherent denial of due process of an accused.”  The Philippine Court supported the position of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines that such live coverage negated “the rule on exclusion of witnesses”
and allowed the “hooting throng” to arrogate unto itself the task of judging the accused.  The Philippine Supreme Court also expressed concern about possible delays in the trial.  Finally, it said that “the United States Supreme Court and other federal courts do not allow live television and radio coverage of their proceedings.”  So then, why should our own courts do?  It concluded:
“Unlike other government offices, courts do not express the popular will of the people in any sense [in] which, instead, [the courts] are tasked to only adjudicate justiciable controversies on the basis of what alone is submitted before them.  A trial is not a free trade of ideas.  Nor is a competing market of thoughts, the known test of truth in a courtroom.”14

*The Gutierrez Opinion* Like Justices Vitug and Kapunan, Justice Gutierrez put a premium on the constitutional rights of the accused by focusing especially on the equal protection clause.  Media sensationalism, according to the neophyte justice, was not compatible with the “judicial serenity and calm which due process of law guarantees.”  She cited several American decisions that had all backed up freedom from “intensive and hostile news coverage.”  Summing up, she averred:
“In sum, the theory that televising the trial ensures that justice is served is not true.  With intense coverage, the media becomes less of a defensive force against injustice and more of an offensive force by intimidating witnesses, distracting the lawyers and distorting the unfolding drama in the courtroom.24  It gives rise to prejudiced opinion and publicity and creates bias and sometimes confusion among the people.  All these factors definitely render the accused’s right to a fair and impartial trial illusory.  Thus, until and unless the media can secure the rights of the accused and eliminate all the adverse effects, specifically on the general
public, the television should remain outside the courtroom.”

He closed with a warning that the “majority will bring about new Rip Van Winkles in this age of electronic media — We.” *My Dissenting View*
In justifying my Dissent I said that, historically, the Court’s ban on live media coverage had first been promulgated in 1991.  “Today, in 2001, I respectfully submit that it is technologically possible to uphold the right of the people to public information without violating the right of the accused to due process and without impeding the orderly administration of justice.”  I explained:
“The basic premise of this Dissent is that, as a general rule, everyone has a right to attend and witness a trial or hearing, especially if criminal in nature, under the constitutional principles of transparency, and
of free, open and public hearings of cases.  However, given the limitations of time and space in a courtroom, it is not always possible to physically accommodate all persons interested in witnessing a court hearing.  That is why court salas have been enlarged.  Moreover, microphones equipped with electronic amplifiers, and sometimes with closed circuit television, have in the past been used to project the proceedings to the immediate vicinity of the courtroom via radio speakers, TV monitors and projection screens.  *In this manner, people outside have been able to listen to and watch the proceedings, as if they were inside the courtroom.*

monitors and projection screens.  *In this manner, people outside have been able to listen to and watch the proceedings, as if they were inside the courtroom.* “*As the 21**st** century dawns, it is now possible to use even more advanced technology to enable more people to watch judicial proceedings in the privacy of their homes and offices without causing prejudice to the rights of the accused or to the integrity of orderly justice.”*  (emphasis in the original)
Thus, I proposed the use of “a single fixed camera under the control of the court.  x x x.  The audio-video output of the camera could be flashed on big, wide TV monitors or projection screens inside and outside the courtroom.  This will also enable TV and radio crews *outside the courtroom* to beam the output to their respective stations for broadcasting to the public, without the ubiquitous and intimidating wiring, lights or media cameras inside the courthouse.”
The video camera would be placed in the rear of the courtroom, its position locked to wide angle, to attain only a “stationary audience view.”  There would
be no other cameras, lights or other media equipment that could cause nervousness or anxiety to witnesses, lawyers and other personalities directly involved in the judicial trial.
Needless to say, this method would prevent editorializing or sensationalism, which the Court in 1991 feared.  In this manner, there would be no unwelcome camera focusing, probing, angling, panning or other kinds of manipulation.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 17: Perez v. Estrada -- Live Radio-TV Coverage: Bane or Boon?
heading: Chapter 17: Perez v. Estrada: — Live Radio-TV Coverage – Bane or Boon?
text:

onalism, which the Court in 1991 feared.  In this manner, there would be no unwelcome camera focusing, probing, angling, panning or other kinds of manipulation. Radio and TV reporters, by patching their connectors to the distribution amplifiers, would be able to do live broadcasts of the proceedings without hassling the judges, lawyers, parties or witnesses.  They would be able to broadcast only such matters as a spectator in the courtroom could see and hear.
After a long and serious reflection on this matter, I thought that the setting up of a single fixed camera inside the courtroom, to which broadcast stations could connect, was the answer to the opposing positions of the parties and the intervenors in the present matter.
To repeat, *this single fixed camera would give its viewers the chance to be similarly situated as a spectator inside the court – one who can see, watch and hear the unfolding drama of the court proceedings.*  Surely, the recipients of the TV signals beamed by broadcast stations cannot interfere in or prejudice the fair and orderly administration of justice, for the simple reason that they are outside the vicinity of the courtroom.  Thus, they cannot by any means be the “hooting throng” that the IBP scorned and feared, thinking they would destroy the constitutionally recognized judicial atmosphere and decorum.
I concluded my Opinion with this Epilogue:

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 17: Perez v. Estrada -- Live Radio-TV Coverage: Bane or Boon?

IBP scorned and feared, thinking they would destroy the constitutionally recognized judicial atmosphere and decorum.
I concluded my Opinion with this Epilogue: “A new world order brought about by the information highway and the influx of new technology in communications is dawning.  And yet the Court, by its Decision today, has turned its back and refused to march in cadence with the music created by the chimes of changing technology.  Our people, long awakened from the dark ages in Philippine history, are now clamoring to be veritable witnesses to the truth, and this clamor can be answered technologically by giving them a firsthand view of how the justice system operates.  To keep public trust and esteem, transparency and accountability were cornerstones of this Court’s avowed policies as it celebrated its centenary on June 11, 2001.  What better proof that it is sincere in realizing its goal of judicial renaissance than by opening up its proceedings without, however, compromising the rights of the accused and the integrity of orderly justice.
“Indeed, in a free society where transparency and accountability are the desirable standards of public office,29 this Court can no longer totally prohibit live media coverage of trials and hearings, given the reality that the technology of modern communications has adequately overcome the obsolete reasons for the ban.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 17: Perez v. Estrada -- Live Radio-TV Coverage: Bane or Boon?
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 17 of 'A Centenary of Justice' analyzes Perez v.
Estrada (AM No.
01-4-03-SC, June 29, 2001), in which the Court, by 8-6, denied a petition to allow LIVE radio and TV coverage of former President Estrada's plunder trial before the Sandiganbayan and reaffirmed its absolute 1991 prohibition (rooted in Estes v.
Texas and US Federal Rule 53).
The request came from the Kapisanan ng mga Brodkaster ng Pilipinas and was formalized by a petition of Justice Secretary Hernando Perez invoking the public's right to know and to dispel 'railroad' suspicions.
Writing for the majority, Justice Vitug held that in balancing press freedom and the public's right to information against the accused's right to a fair and impartial trial, 'the right of the accused must be preferred': a 'public trial is not synonymous with publicized trial,' television 'can work profound changes' in witnesses and judges, and requiring proof of actual prejudice would ignore 'the subtle threats to justice.' Justice Kapunan concurred ('the balance is never weighed against the accused'; televising could reignite the EDSA II/EDSA III divide), as did Justice Gutierrez (media sensationalism as an 'offensive force').

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 17: Perez v. Estrada -- Live Radio-TV Coverage: Bane or Boon?
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

r weighed against the accused'; televising could reignite the EDSA II/EDSA III divide), as did Justice Gutierrez (media sensationalism as an 'offensive force'). Justice Puno dissented -- Estes had been modified by later cases and most US states now allow cameras -- favoring the trial judge's discretion under detailed standards and warning of 'new Rip Van Winkles.' CJP also dissented, arguing that 2001 technology could satisfy the people's right to information without prejudicing the accused via a single fixed, court-controlled camera at the rear of the courtroom, fed to outside broadcast stations, so home viewers would be no more disruptive than courtroom spectators; he lamented that the Court 'refused to march in cadence with the music created by the chimes of changing technology' and urged that 'the light of truth be beamed to all the people through the advances of science and technology.' In a Postscript, the Court on reconsideration kept the live-coverage ban (9-6) but, by 8-7 (per Mendoza), ordered an audio-visual RECORDING of the entire trial for documentary purposes only -- released after judgment and deposited in the National Museum -- over Vitug's view that even recording would prejudice the accused.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 17: Perez v. Estrada -- Live Radio-TV Coverage: Bane or Boon?
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

The single fixed camera: against intrusive courtroom media, CJP proposed one stationary camera locked to a wide-angle 'stationary audience view' at the rear of the room, fed to outside broadcast stations -- so viewers at home would be 'similarly situated as a spectator inside the court,' never the 'hooting throng' the IBP feared.

Anecdote 2

EDSA II and EDSA III as cautionary tales: Justice Kapunan's concurrence argued that the televised collapse of Estrada's impeachment trial triggered EDSA II and the broadcast of his arrest sparked EDSA III, so televising his Sandiganbayan trial 'would only ignite the spark... and resurrect the division between these groups.'

Anecdote 3

'New Rip Van Winkles': dissenting, Justice Puno warned that by clinging to a 1965-era ban while most US states had moved to allow cameras, the majority risked turning the Court itself into 'new Rip Van Winkles in this age of electronic media.'

Anecdote 4

'Let the light of truth be beamed': CJP closed his dissent with the image of beaming court proceedings to people's homes 'through the advances of science and technology in the 21st century,' lamenting that the Court had 'turned its back' on 'the chimes of changing technology.'

Anecdote 5

The film in the museum: the eventual compromise allowed an audio-visual recording of Estrada's trial -- for documentary use only, shown after judgment -- with the master film deposited in the National Museum and the Records Management and Archives Office 'for historical preservation and exhibition.'

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship

**R**epatriation is a mode of reacquiring Philippine citizenship as provided under Republic Act No. 2630.  What is reacquired in repatriation?  Is it the “original” citizenship that was previously lost, or is it an entirely “new” one?  In the present case, private respondent lost his *natural-born* citizenship when he served in the US armed services and was naturalized as a US national.  By his repatriation, did he reacquire his *natural-born* Philippine citizenship?
The Court en banc answered this question in the affirmative in *Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal.*1
*The Facts*
Teodoro C. Cruz was born of Filipino parents on April 27, 1960 in San Clemente, Tarlac.  Thus, under
1  GR No. 142840, May 7, 2001.
the 1935 Constitution,2 he was a natural-born citizen.  On November 5, 1985, however, he enlisted in the US Marine Corps, took an oath of allegiance to the United States, and thus lost his Philippine citizenship as a consequence.  Under Section 1(4) of Commonwealth Act No. 63, citizenship may be lost by, among others, “rendering service to or accepting commission in the armed forces of another country.”  On June 5, 1990, he was naturalized as an American.
On March 17, 1994, Cruz was repatriated under Republic Act No. 2630.  During the 1998 national elections, he was elected representative of the Second District of Pangasinan, with a convincing margin of 26,671 over Antonio E. Bengson III, who was then running for reelection.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

lected representative of the Second District of Pangasinan, with a convincing margin of 26,671 over Antonio E. Bengson III, who was then running for reelection. Dismissing a Petition for *Quo Warranto* filed by Bengson, the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET) declared Cruz as fully qualified to sit in the House of Representatives.  Bengson elevated the matter to the Supreme Court via a Petition for Certiorari, charging the HRET with grave abuse of discretion in ruling that Cruz had reacquired his original (natural-born) citizenship.
Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez, to whom the case had originally been assigned, recommended the grant of the Bengson Petition.  But during the deliberation, Justice Kapunan and I filed separate Dissents.  By majority vote,3 the Dissents were upheld.  I deferred to Justice Kapunan, who was the more senior member of the Court; thus, he wrote the *ponencia,* while my Dissent was converted to a Concurring Opinion.  In turn, the erstwhile Gutierrez draft became the Dissenting Opinion.
*The Ruling*
In junking the Petition, Justice Kapunan explained the two ways of acquiring citizenship: (1) by birth and (2) by naturalization.  These correspond to two kinds of citizens: the natural-born and the naturalized.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

the two ways of acquiring citizenship: (1) by birth and (2) by naturalization.  These correspond to two kinds of citizens: the natural-born and the naturalized. Natural-born citizens, according to the Constitution, are “those who are citizens from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect such Philippine citizenship”; while naturalized citizens are “those who have become citizens through naturalization, generally under Commonwealth Act No. 473 and Republic Act No. 530.”  On the other hand, citizenship may be reacquired by a former citizen under Commonwealth Act No. 63 (1) by naturalization, (2) by repatriation and (3) by a direct act of Congress.  Since he did not reacquire his Philippine nationality by naturalization or by a direct act of Congress, then Cruz must be natural-born.
2  §1 of Art. IV of the 1935 Constitution provides: “The following are citizens of the Philippines: 1) Those who are citizens of the Philippine Islands at the time of the adoption of the Constitution; 2) Those born in the Philippine Islands of foreign parents who, before the adoption of this Constitution had been elected to public office in the Philippine Islands; 3) Those whose fathers are citizens of the Philippines; 4) Those whose mothers are citizens of the Philippines and, upon reaching the age of majority, elected Philippine citizenship; and 5) Those who are naturalized in accordance with law.”

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

re citizens of the Philippines and, upon reaching the age of majority, elected Philippine citizenship; and 5) Those who are naturalized in accordance with law.” 3  Chief Justice Davide and Justices Bellosillo, Puno, Kapunan; Panganiban, Pardo, Reyes and Santiago voted to deny the Petition; only Justice Gutierrez opted to grant it.  Being members of the HRET, Justices Melo, Vitug and Mendoza took “no part”; while Justices Quisumbing, Buena and De Leon were on leave.
Debunking petitioner’s contention that Cruz could not be considered natural-born because he had to perform an act to regain his citizenship, Justice Kapunan wrote:
“x x x.  As correctly explained by the HRET in its decision, the term ‘natural-born citizen’ was first defined in Article III, Section 4 of the 1973 Constitution, as follows:
‘Sec. 4.  A natural-born citizen is one who is a citizen of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect his Philippine citizenship.’
“Two requisites must concur for a person to be considered as such: (1) a person must be a Filipino citizen from birth and (2) he does not have to perform any act to obtain or perfect his Philippine citizenship.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

sidered as such: (1) a person must be a Filipino citizen from birth and (2) he does not have to perform any act to obtain or perfect his Philippine citizenship. “Under the 1973 Constitution definition, there were two categories of Filipino citizens which were not considered natural-born: (1) those who were naturalized and (2) those born before January 17, 1973,4 of Filipino mothers who, upon reaching the age of majority, elected Philippine citizenship.  Those ‘naturalized citizens’ were not considered natural-born obviously because they were not Filipinos at birth and had to perform an act to acquire Philippine citizenship.  Those born of Filipino mothers before the effectivity of the 1973 Constitution
were likewise not considered natural-born because they also had to perform an act to perfect their Philippine citizenship.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

effectivity of the 1973 Constitution
were likewise not considered natural-born because they also had to perform an act to perfect their Philippine citizenship. “The present Constitution, however, now considers those born of Filipino mothers before the effectivity of the 1973 Constitution and who elected Philippine citizenship upon reaching the majority age as natural-born.  After defining who are natural-born citizens, Section 2 of Article IV adds a sentence: ‘Those who elect Philippine citizenship in accordance with paragraph (3), Section 1 hereof, shall be deemed natural-born citizens.’  Consequently, only naturalized Filipinos are considered not natural-born citizens.  It is apparent from the enumeration of who are citizens under the present Constitution that there are only two classes of citizens: (1) those who are natural-born and (2) those who are naturalized in accordance with law.  A citizen who is not a naturalized Filipino, i.e., did not have to undergo the process of naturalization to obtain Philippine citizenship, necessarily is a natural-born Filipino.  Noteworthy is the absence in said enumeration of a separate category for persons who, after losing Philippine citizenship, subsequently reacquire it.  The reason therefor is clear: as to such persons, they would either be natural-born or naturalized depending on the reasons for the loss of their citizenship and the mode prescribed by the applicable law for the reacquisition thereof.  As respondent Cruz was not required by law to go through
4  The date of effectivity of the 1973 Constitution.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

the applicable law for the reacquisition thereof.  As respondent Cruz was not required by law to go through
4  The date of effectivity of the 1973 Constitution. naturalization proceedings in order to reacquire his citizenship, he is perforce a natural-born Filipino.  As such, he possessed all the necessary qualifications to be elected as member of the House of Representatives.
*My Concurring Opinion*
My Concurring Opinion listed five reasons why the Petition should be dismissed, and why Cruz should be deemed a natural-born Filipino citizen, as follows.
*“1.  Repatriation Is Recovery*
*of Original Citizenship*
“*First,* repatriation is simply the recovery of *original* citizenship.  Under Section 1 of RA 2630, a person ‘who ha[s] lost his citizenship’ may ‘reacquire’ it by ‘taking an oath of allegiance to the Republic of the Philippines.’  Former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga, a noted authority on the subject, explains this method more precisely in his treatise *Private International Law.*5  He defines repatriation as ‘the recovery of the *original* nationality upon fulfillment of certain conditions.’6  Webster buttresses this definition by describing the ordinary or common usage of *repatriate* as ‘to restore or return to one’s country of origin, allegiance, or citizenship; x x x.’7  In relation to our subject matter, *repatriation* then means restoration of citizenship.  It is *not* a grant of
a *new* citizenship, but a recovery of one’s former or original citizenship.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

tter, *repatriation* then means restoration of citizenship.  It is *not* a grant of
a *new* citizenship, but a recovery of one’s former or original citizenship. “To ‘reacquire’ simply means ‘to get back as one’s own again.’8  *Ergo,* since Cruz, prior to his becoming a US citizen, was a natural-born Filipino citizen, he ‘reacquired’ the same status upon repatriation.  To rule otherwise – that Cruz became a nonnatural-born citizen – would not be consistent with the legal and ordinary meaning of repatriation.  It would be akin to naturalization, which is the acquisition of a new citizenship.  ‘New,’ because it is not the same as that with which he has previously been endowed.
“In any case, ‘the leaning, in questions of citizenship, should always be in favor of [its] claimant x x x.’9  Accordingly, the same should be construed in favor of private respondent, who claims to be a natural-born citizen.
*“2.  Not Being Naturalized,*
*Respondent Is Natural Born*
“*Second,* under the present Constitution, private respondent should be deemed natural-born, because he was not naturalized.  Let me explain.
“There are generally two classes of citizens: (1) natural-born citizens and (2) naturalized

6  Ibid., p. 165; cited in the assailed HRET Decision, p. 13.  (italics ours)
7  *Webster’s Third New International Dictionary: Unabridged,* 1993 ed.
8  *Webster’s,* ibid., defines *reacquire* as “to acquire again”; and *acquire* as “to get as one’s own.”
9  *Roa v. Collector of Customs,* 23 Phil 315, 338 (1912), per Trent, J.; citing *Boyd v. Thayer,* 143 US 135.

e again”; and *acquire* as “to get as one’s own.”
9  *Roa v. Collector of Customs,* 23 Phil 315, 338 (1912), per Trent, J.; citing *Boyd v. Thayer,* 143 US 135. citizens.10  While CA 63 provides that citizenship may also be acquired by direct act of the legislature, I believe that those who do become citizens through such procedure would properly fall under the second category (naturalized).”
“Naturalized citizens are former aliens or foreigners who had to undergo a rigid procedure, in which they had to adduce sufficient evidence to prove that they possessed all the qualifications and none of the disqualifications provided by law in order to become Filipino citizens.  In contrast, as stated in the early case *Roa v. Collector of Customs,*12 a natural-born citizen is a citizen ‘who has become such at the moment of his birth.’
“The assailed HRET Decision, penned by Mr. Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, explains clearly who are considered natural-born Filipino citizens.  He traces the concept as first defined in Article III of the 1973 Constitution, which simply provided as follows:
‘Sec. 4.  A natural-born citizen is one who is a citizen of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect his Philippine citizenship.’

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

natural-born citizen is one who is a citizen of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect his Philippine citizenship.’ “Under the above definition, there are two requisites in order that a Filipino citizen may be considered ‘natural-born’: (1) one must be a citizen of the Philippines from birth, and (2) one does not have to do anything to acquire or perfect one’s Philippine citizenship.13  Thus, under the 1973 Constitution, excluded from the class of ‘natural-born citizens’ were (1) those who were naturalized; and (2) those born before January 17, 1973, of Filipino mothers who, upon reaching the age of majority, elected Philippine citizenship.14
“The present Constitution, however, has expanded the scope of natural-born citizens to include ‘[t]hose who elect Philippine citizenship in accordance with paragraph (3), Section 1 hereof,’ meaning those covered under class (2) above.  Consequently, only naturalized Filipino citizens are not considered natural-born citizens.  Premising therefrom, respondent — being clearly and concededly not naturalized — is, therefore, a natural-born citizen of the Philippines.15
“With respect to repatriates, since the Constitution does not classify them separately, they naturally reacquire their *original* classification before the loss of their Philippine citizenship.  In the case of Congressman Teodoro C. Cruz, upon his repatriation in 1994, he reacquired his lost

Ledesma, *An Outline of Philippine Immigration and Citizenship Laws,* 1999 ed., p. 354.  See also 14 CJS §1, 1128; 3A Am Jur 2d Aliens and Citizens, §1411.
11  See Ledesma, ibid., p. 355.

citizenship.  In other words, he regained his original status as a natural-born Filipino citizen, nothing less.
*“3.  No Grave Abuse of Discretion*
*on the Part of HRET*
“*Third,* the HRET did not abuse, much less gravely abuse, its discretion in holding that Respondent Cruz is a natural-born Filipino citizen who is qualified to be a member of Congress.  I stress that the Court, in this certiorari proceeding before us, is limited to determining whether the HRET committed grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction in issuing its assailed Decision.  The Court has no power to reverse or modify HRET’s rulings, simply because it differs in its perceptions of controversies.  It cannot substitute its discretion for that of HRET, an independent, constitutional body with its own specific mandate.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

s in its perceptions of controversies.  It cannot substitute its discretion for that of HRET, an independent, constitutional body with its own specific mandate. “The Constitution explicitly states that the respective Electoral Tribunals of the two chambers of Congress ‘shall be the *sole* judges of all contests relating to the election, returns, and *qualifications* of their respective members.’16  In several cases,17 this Court has held that the power and the jurisdiction of the Electoral Tribunals are original and exclusive, as if they remained in the legislature, a
coequal branch of government.  Their judgments are beyond judicial interference, unless rendered without or in excess of their jurisdiction or with grave abuse of discretion.18  In the elegant words of Mr. Justice Hugo E. Gutierrez Jr.:19
‘The Court does not venture into the perilous area of trying to correct perceived errors of independent branches of the Government.  It comes in only when it has to vindicate a denial of due process or correct an abuse of discretion so grave or glaring that no less than the Constitution calls for remedial action.’

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship
text:
Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship (cont.)

it has to vindicate a denial of due process or correct an abuse of discretion so grave or glaring that no less than the Constitution calls for remedial action.’ “True, there is no settled judicial doctrine on the exact effect of repatriation.  But, as earlier explained, the legal and common definition of repatriation is the reacquisition of the *former* citizenship.  How then can the HRET be rebuked [for] grave abuse of discretion?  At best, I can concede that the legal definition is not judicially settled or is even doubtful.  But an *interpretation* made in good faith and grounded on reason one way or the other cannot be the source of grave abuse amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.  The HRET did not violate the Constitution or the law or any settled judicial

doctrine.  It was definitely acting within its exclusive domain. “Be it remembered that our Constitution vests [in] the HRET the power to be the *sole* judge of the qualifications of members of the House of Representatives, one of which is citizenship.  Absent any *clear* showing of a manifest violation of the Constitution or the law or any judicial decision, this Court cannot impute grave abuse of discretion to the HRET in the latter’s actions on matters over which full discretionary authority is lodged [in] it by our fundamental law.20  Even assuming that we disagree with the conclusions of public respondent, we cannot ipso facto attribute to it ‘grave abuse of discretion.’  Verily, there is a line between perceived error and grave abuse.21
“By *grave abuse of discretion* is meant such capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment as is equivalent to lack of jurisdiction.  Mere abuse of discretion is not enough.  It must be *grave* abuse of discretion as when the power is exercised in an arbitrary or a despotic manner by reason of passion or personal hostility, and must be so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or to a virtual refusal to perform the duty enjoined or to act at all in contemplation of law.’22

*Popular Will Prevails*
“*Fourth,* the Court has a solemn duty to uphold the clear and unmistakable mandate of the people.  It cannot supplant the sovereign will of the Second District of Pangasinan with fractured legalism.  The people of the District have clearly spoken.  They overwhelmingly and unequivocally voted for private respondent to represent them in the House of Representatives. *“5.  Current Trend Towards*
*Globalization*
“*Fifth,* the current trend, economically as well as politically, is towards globalization.29  Protectionist barriers are being dismantled.  Whereas, in the past, governments frowned upon the opening of their doors to aliens who wanted to enjoy the same privileges as their citizens, the current era is adopting a more liberal perspective.  No longer are applicants for citizenship eyed with the suspicion that they merely want to exploit local resources for themselves.  They are now being considered potential sources of developmental skills, know-how and capital.
“More so should our government open its doors to former Filipinos, like Congressman Cruz, who want to rejoin the Filipino community as citizens again.  They are not ‘aliens’ in the true sense of the law.  They are actually Filipinos by blood, by origin and by culture, who want to reacquire their former citizenship.

*The Dissent* Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez’s Dissent traced the historical evolution of our law on citizenship and opined that “the status of being a natural born citizen at its incipient is a privilege conferred by law directly to those who intended, and actually continued, to belong to the Philippine Islands.  Even at the time of its conception in the Philippines, such persons upon whom citizenship was conferred did not have to do anything to acquire full citizenship”
Since Cruz had to perform certain acts, like taking an oath of allegiance to the Republic of the Philippines, registering his oath with the Local Civil Registry, renouncing his American citizenship and executing an
affidavit of reacquisition, he did not reacquire his natural-born citizenship.
The constitutional definition of a natural-born citizen must be applied according to its natural sense.  She concluded:
“For sure, the framers of our Constitution intended to provide a more stringent citizenship requirement for higher elective offices, including that of the office of a Congressman.  Otherwise, the Constitution should have simply provided that a candidate for such position can be merely a citizen of the Philippines, as required of local elective officers.

**Appendix A** **A Salute to My Mentor**
**I** would like to begin by calling attention to and elucidating my own knowledge of an incident mentioned on page 75 of the book being launched today, *A Journey of Struggle and Hope.*
I was a freshman at the Far Eastern University Institute of Law in 1956, the school year barely a few weeks old, when suddenly the law students, who were a thousand strong, declared a “strike” in protest of what they perceived was the precipitate and unjustified retirement of the well-loved and venerable dean of the law school.  As a new law student, I did not personally know our old dean, but I went along with the strikers as they filled the FEU auditorium with chants, slogans and anguished cries of “Persecution!”
Then, a youngish 36-year-old bespectacled professor, a Yale and Harvard graduate and bar topnotcher, walked to center stage, approached the microphone, and singlehandedly faced the hostile

Salonga, spoke with a forceful tremolo and held the rowdy and rambunctious crowd spellbound.  In thirty minutes flat, the huge crowd of activist students trooped back to their classrooms, convinced of the error in their mass action; and of the wisdom, the honesty, the sincerity and the good faith of their new dean.  Thus did I, along with many others, find the guru who would become my role model not only in my chosen career but, more important, in my life as a whole.
As a student, I was very active in extracurricular activities, having become president not only of the university student council, but also of the National Union of Students of the Philippines.  Because of these activities, I tended to give secondary importance to my academic studies.  But Dean Salonga constantly reminded me that my first duty was to excel in academics.
As my professor in evidence and corporation law, he would call me to recite when student activities were at their height — perhaps to test me whether I was adhering to my promise never to forget my academic preparation in the midst of the adulation of my leadership activities not only in FEU, but even in the wider arena of national student politics.  Because of his constant monitoring of my grades, I managed to graduate with Latin honors and as “most outstanding student.”

first-day performance, I wanted to quit the examinations for the remaining days.  But Dean Salonga would not hear of it.  With his constant encouragement, I still managed to pass, copping the 6th highest place.
He invited me to join his prestigious law firm, which included as partners some of the best legal minds in the country like Sedfrey A. Ordoñez, Pedro L. Yap and Neptali A. Gonzales.  He taught me the rudiments of law practice; more significantly, he demonstrated the life-defining values of integrity, prudence and fairness.  My admiration and awe of Dr. Salonga grew even more.
Then and up to now, he is a living model of his teachings.  He taught by example, not by words.  He is a dedicated husband, a caring father, a faithful friend and a devoted man of God.  Never compromising his principles and values in exchange for friendship, kinship, relationship, wealth or power, he lives an almost ascetic life.  He does not smoke, does not drink, and does not gamble.  Money, worldly pleasures, titles and honors hold no fascination for him.

This is probably because we never discuss what separates us, but only what truly binds us.
Prior to my appointment to the highest court of the land, Senator Salonga accorded me — unconsciously, I am sure — the greatest honor in my
career as a practising lawyer, not by awarding me a plaque of gold or conferring on me an honorary degree.  Rather, he did so by asking me to be his personal legal counsel during his incumbency as Senate President and to be concurrently chief legal counsel of the Liberal Party which he then headed.  Nothing is more fulfilling, more exhilarating, than the honor of being counsel to one’s mentor and former boss!

As some of you may know, my ascension to the Supreme Court was not easy.  From 1992 to 1995, there were seven vacancies in the Court due to the compulsory retirement of incumbents.  For each of those seven vacancies, my name was submitted to the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for screening.  I failed the JBC test because of the alleged insufficiency of my professional competence and my alleged transgressions and sins.  But in all those trying three years, Senator Salonga was beside me, behind me, and even above me, cheering me up, tirelessly uplifting my sagging spirit and praying for me.  He would call me up frequently, assuring me of his support and unfailing faith and urging me never to lose trust in the faithfulness of God.  And whenever I felt really low and hopeless, he would patiently remind me of Romans 8:28.
*God makes all things work together*
*For the good of those who love Him*
*And are called according to His purpose.*
When finally I was nominated by the JBC and eventually appointed by President Ramos, he was the first to congratulate me not only for the appointment, but also for my keeping faith in the grace and bounty of the Lord!

APPENDICES In my conduct and work in the Supreme Court, I am proud to say that I have tried my best to follow and express my mentor’s ideas and ideals.  Those who read my decisions in the Court, as well as my writings and speeches elsewhere, will surely detect the legal philosophy and life values of Senator Salonga imbedded in them.  I try to echo, even faintly, his teaching that law cannot be separated from life, that it should be used as a brick in building the social edifice and as a means of fulfilling the deepest aspirations of man.
But his most significant teaching is not really about the law, as it is about life.  And if my presence today must have any relevance at all, I now would like to summarize the one teaching of my guru which I will always treasure, and it is this: While it is desirable to have some of the necessities that money *can* buy, like adequate food on the table, sufficient clothing and shelter for the family, sports and recreation for the body, and even a car and a house, I should never never forget that it is far more important to aspire for the things that money *cannot* buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God as the Source of all that is true, good and beautiful.
*Maraming salamat po.*

**Justice Is God’s Work** **T**en days ago, I received an invitation from the Philippine Judicial Academy (Philja) to deliver the closing address today to end formally the Second Pre-Judicature Program.  I would like you to know that a Philja invitation partakes of the nature of a summons, which cannot be refused or ignored not only on pain of default but, worse, of contempt.
It is said that Supreme Court justices are a courageous lot.  They have braved the onslaughts of lynch mobs, screaming headlines and even presidential tyrants and dictators.  Let me, however, tell you that if there is *anyone* over whom high magistrates sweat bullets, that singular one is Justice Ameurfina Aguinaldo Melencio Herrera, the venerable chancellor of Philja.  Not that she is fearsome, but that she is respected and loved.  When she calls, we answer; when she invites, we consider it a command and we

As I contemplated my message to you today, memories of my own entry into the judiciary, direct to the Supreme Court in 1995, streamed into my mind.  As I began to brush shoulders with the most exclusive brethren in the country, I was filled not only with awe and anxiety at what lay ahead, but also with some intellectual and spiritual soul-searching.
Let me explain that from 1986 to 1995, my wife and I underwent a spiritual rebirth as we joined the *Bukas Loob sa Diyos,* a charismatic community of renewed Catholics.  During those nine years, we embarked on a new journey of faith through a marriage encounter, a “Life in the Spirit” seminar, retreats and various other programs to relearn and reexperience our faith.  We read and reread the Bible several times over, discussed volumes — nay, libraries — of commentaries thereon.  Later on we shared our experiences by speaking in seminars and conferences, and we even became servant-leaders of this community.
In the process, we had a most fulfilling encounter with our Lord Jesus Christ.  We can truly claim that we came to know Him and to experience His love in many ways.
On my part, I have learned to trust Him and to depend on Him for *all* my needs, aspirations and wants.  Many times I would pray.  Even if I do not get what I want, still, I continue to repose my full faith and

*And my ways are not your ways,*

*So high are my ways above your ways*

Let me assure you that in all my life, my struggles, my frustrations, my victories, God has never failed in His promise, as heralded also in Scriptures, in the book of Romans (8:28):
*“God makes all things work*

*and who are called according*

Let me repeat: “God makes *all* things work for the good of those who love Him and who are called according to His purpose.”
The most basic of our Lord’s teachings is love.  When He was asked which commandment of the law was the greatest, He replied, “The first is: love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength.  The second is: Love your neighbor as yourself.”1

1  Mt 22:34-40; Mk 121:28-31. On another occasion, our Lord was preaching on a mountainside, and among other things, he said, “My command to you is: love your enemies, pray for your persecutors.  This will prove that you are sons of your heavenly Father, for His sun rises on the bad and the good.  He rains on the just and the unjust.  If you love only those who love you, what merit is there in that?  Do not tax collectors do as much?  And if you greet your brothers only, what is so praiseworthy about that?  Do not pagans do as much?  In a word, you must be made perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.”2
In the face of this core teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, I asked myself several times: “If God is the very personification of love, why does He punish His people?  At the very least, why does He allow calamity, cruelty, poverty and affliction to assault and damn them?  Why does He not just satisfy all of their needs and wants, something that is definitely within His infinite power and authority?  Why does He not just eradicate poverty, hunger and pain?  He is God; He certainly can do all that.”

that is definitely within His infinite power and authority?  Why does He not just eradicate poverty, hunger and pain?  He is God; He certainly can do all that.” It is with this background of incisive theological questions that, upon my appointment to the Supreme Court, I asked myself: “Our Lord’s greatest commandment is to love God and His people; why am I being called to impose penalties for crimes, enforce difficult obligations and sanction burdensome laws?”  I was baffled by the seeming contradiction between love and punishment, between affection and affliction, until I came upon this little story.
A demure young lady was brought before a traffic court for over-speeding.  In the courtroom, the judge
APPENDICES
asked her: “Young lady, this police officer tells me that you were racing at 100 kilometers per hour in a 50-kilometer zone.  What can you say about that?”
“He’s correct, your Honor.  I am truly sorry I broke the law, but I promise not to do it again,” replied the repentant miss.
“Because of your confession and promise to reform, the law will be lenient on you.  I will just fine you P300 instead of the usual P500,” the judge solemnly decreed.
After adjourning the court session, the judge removed his black robe, went straight to the cashier, pulled out his wallet and paid the P300 fine.  He paid the penalty out of love, because the lawbreaker was his daughter.  *Justice* was served — and so was *love.*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal -- Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship

led out his wallet and paid the P300 fine.  He paid the penalty out of love, because the lawbreaker was his daughter.  *Justice* was served — and so was *love.* In a larger and real sense, the judge in our little story is our Lord Jesus Christ.  And the young lady represents each one of us, all of us in this hall.  His Honor is our Divine Judge and we are His unworthy children.  We, His people, sinned.  We violated the law of God.  And so the justice of God requires our punishment.
Because justice is in the nature of God, He — even if He is the most powerful Being in the universe — cannot refuse to impose the sanction of His own law.  Otherwise, He would be violating His own nature.
But Jesus is also love personified.  So, out of His great love, He became man, came down to earth, suffered, was crucified, died and gloriously resurrected.  He atoned for our sins and owned the punishment meant for us.  He did this because of His great love for us.
2  Mt 5:44-48.
Let me stress it again.  Just as our Lord is a God of love, He is also a God of justice.  Just as it is in His nature to love, it is also in His essence to see that justice is done.  Just as He cannot refuse to love, neither can He decline to render justice.  Both love and justice are in His very nature and essence.  He cannot contradict himself by refusing to fulfill both love and justice.
By sending His only Son and by His Son’s suffering, death and resurrection, He saved humankind from eternal damnation.  In this manner, His justice and His love were both fulfilled.

on and by His Son’s suffering, death and resurrection, He saved humankind from eternal damnation.  In this manner, His justice and His love were both fulfilled. Ladies and gentlemen, if my fifteen-minute talk today is worth anything, it is this: the rendition of justice is not only a human necessity; it is a divine essentiality.  When we give people their due, impose penalties for crimes, uphold liberty, enforce obligations and compel obedience to duties — fairly and speedily, without fear or favor — we really do the work of the Lord.  In short, to dispense *quality* justice is to do God’s work.
To all the graduates, welcome to the divine work of rendering quality *justice* to our fellowmen and to the world!
I thank you.
**Appendix C**
**A Prelude to Paperless Courts**
**T**he third millennium and the twenty-first century ushered in new paradigms, technologies and biosciences.  As a macro consequence of these paradigms, the struggle for world preeminence has shifted from a battle of ideologies and weapons of mass destruction to one of trade dominance.  In the economic and political fields, the strategy has shifted from government control to deregulation, from state ownership to privatization, from national sovereignty to globalization, and from protectionism to trade liberalization.

On the other hand, new computer technologies have accelerated both the obsolescence of the industrial era and the advent of the Information Age.  Indeed, the possession and the distribution of information through instant, lightning-quick electronic data transmission, via the Internet and fiber optics, have become as valuable as oil resources, gold mines, heavy industries and agricultural products.
*  Opening Remarks of Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the Centenary Lecture entitled “Paperless Courts: The Australian Experience,” delivered by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia on September 26, 2001 in the Session Hall of the Philippine Supreme Court.
Meanwhile, the emerging field of biosciences has made it possible to clone living organisms and to replicate or reproduce human organs through the extra-womb development of stem cells.  DNA testing, genetic engineering and other new scientific discoveries promise healthier and longer lives even if, at the same time, they raise ethical and moral concerns.  Given these breakthroughs, our children and grandchildren can look forward to much longer life spans of 150 or even 200 years.

aise ethical and moral concerns.  Given these breakthroughs, our children and grandchildren can look forward to much longer life spans of 150 or even 200 years. These massive economic, political, technological and scientific developments are challenging and transforming not only the geographic and demographic face of the world, but also everything else that matters — political systems, lifestyles, work habits, philosophies, religious beliefs, leisure times, family lives and, yes, even the normally reclusive and exclusive judicial enclaves.
This afternoon, as a consequence also of these new technologies and sciences, we are journeying into one specific transformational shift in our legal realm — the elimination of paper.  At first blush, this proposition seems imponderable, if not totally impossible and absurd.  How can paper be eliminated from our profession?  Indeed, the law is said to be the most paper-dependent discipline in the world.  In no other field is the advice “Put it in writing” more prevalent than in the law.  Whenever a statute or a contract states that something “shall be in writing,” the unsaid assumption is that it shall be written on paper.  So, too, our present procedural rules like those on parol evidence, statute of frauds, best evidence, and many others show a definite bias in favor of documentation.

APPENDICES And whenever the law speaks of documentation, we always assume that it refers to something written on paper.  While the Ten Commandments may have been engraved in stone and Confucian wisdom in wooden tablets, until recently we have always thought of paper as the medium of written communication.
In line with the passage on June 11, 2000, of Republic Act No. 8792 (otherwise known as the Electronic Commerce Act or ECA), the Supreme Court has recently promulgated the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence, which took effect less than two months ago on August 1, 2001.
Together, the ECA and the new Rules on Electronic Evidence eliminate the “disparity of treatment between data messages and paper documents.”  Also, an electronic document is regarded as the functional equivalent of a paper-based document; and an electronic or a digital signature, the functional equivalent of a traditionally penned “John Hancock.”  In brief, the new Rules we have just adopted makes it possible to admit in evidence electronically produced documentation or data messages.
The Supreme Court feels honored and proud of being one of the first tribunals in Asia to produce these Rules and, thereby, to keep in step with the electronic age.  Let me, however, stress that there is as yet no intention in the said law and Rules to eliminate paper as the primary medium of communication in the bar or the bench.

Today, during the lecture and the open forum that will follow, we shall assess whether paper can indeed be expunged from legal practice, and whether
paperless courts are possible in our country.  We are singularly honored to have with us as centenary lecturer and resource speaker the Honorable Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia, who will discuss the Australian experience in this bold new venture.  It is with this mixed feeling of anticipation, awe and anxiety that I welcome all of you today to what may historically be the epochal prelude to paperless legal proceedings in our country.
Thank you and good day.
**Appendix D**
**MPGR**
**T**oday is Justice Minerva Perez Gonzaga-Reyes’ last day as an incumbent member of the Supreme Court and the Philippine judiciary.  On behalf of her and of the Court, I welcome all of you to this commemorative program and dinner in her honor.  On this occasion, I ask all of you to relax; endure the short remarks I will now deliver; and later be rewarded with an enjoyable musicale and, still later, with the delicious food and drinks that Minnie, Johnny and their children — Alda, Edwin Romualdo and Johann Michael — are happily offering for our degustation.

I consider myself lucky for having been assigned, along with Justice Minnie as we fondly call her, to the Third Division of the Court during the past thirty-two months.  During that period, I had the rare but ample opportunity to really know her and to learn from her insights on the many litigations and concerns that confronted our five-member group.  Looking back at our more than two and a half years of working
*  Opening remarks of Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the Retirement Program in honor of Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes held on September 24, 2001 at the Manila Hotel.
together, I think I can summarize my impression of her in four words.
The first word is MODESTY.  By this I do not mean she is timid or bashful.  Rather, I believe she is humble, self-effacing and unpretentious.  Although highly successful in her career and in raising her children to be equally successful, she retains a restrained opinion of herself and of her accomplishments.

gh highly successful in her career and in raising her children to be equally successful, she retains a restrained opinion of herself and of her accomplishments. A good example of her evident modesty is the very program we are holding tonight.  As most of you know, the Supreme Court honors its retiring members with a formal program held in our Session Hall, during which the justices, in their majestic ceremonial robes, individually eulogize their many achievements.  However, Justice Minnie made it plain to all of us in the Court that she would not have such grand eulogy.  She expressed a preference for just hosting a modest get-together with her family and very close friends.  But the justices would not let her go unnoticed.  And tonight’s dinner and short program is a sort of compromise between a grand ceremony and a sparse family gathering.
When she asked me to deliver the opening remarks, it was with the caveat that I should not praise her.  She does not want me to mention this but, as a jurist, I must be faithful to the truth.  And the plain, unvarnished truth is that whoever may be her successor will be very lucky, because Justice Minnie leaves a docket that has “zero backlog.”  She has, in point of fact, decided every ripe controversy assigned to her.  In other words, all the cases in her docket are current, because she has promptly, judiciously and properly resolved every suit therein that had been submitted for resolution.  This is her legacy to the

Court, to her successor, as well as to the expectant and oftentimes demanding public. The second word I associate with Justice Minnie is PERSPICACITY.  Being perspicacious does not merely mean being intelligent or wise.  It also refers to having a clear understanding of every matter and situation on hand; and then acting with delicacy and serenity, confident that her position is the product of purposeful reflection on what is best under the circumstances.
Perspicacity, our honoree has an abundance of.  She never speaks out of turn.  Rather, she speaks rarely — only when she feels her opinions would make a difference.  She explains her views in cadenced, well thought out words calculated to bring home the message without boasting of herself or denigrating anyone else.  She is completely objective and cerebral in her approach; more than that, she never imposes her views as if she were the only knowledgeable person around.  She meticulously writes her thoughts in a straightforward and an unaffected manner.  Indeed, she quietly puts forth her opinions with no braggadocio or exhibitionism of any sort.
The third word that I think best describes her is GENTILITY.  She is not merely polite or respectful towards others.  To use the language we learned more than half a century ago in grade school, she has good manners and exhibits right conduct at all times.  She never loses her temper, never uses obscene words, and never displays tantrums.  Verily, she is always prim, proper and balanced.

ight conduct at all times.  She never loses her temper, never uses obscene words, and never displays tantrums.  Verily, she is always prim, proper and balanced. The final word I associate with Justice Minnie is RECTITUDE, which means she is a person of integrity, uprightness and high moral correctness.  During her many years of public service, she has shrouded herself
with an unassailable reputation, not only for being honest in her dealings, but also for not betraying friends or revealing secrets.  In fact, she is super-discreet and totally trustworthy.
In her decisions and actions, she fights not only for what is legally possible but, in fact, for what is ethical and moral.  She listens patiently to both sides of a controversy but, once she makes up her mind, she is firm and unbending in her judgment.  She leans on her deep spirituality and believes in the innate goodness of humans and their ability to rise above themselves when the occasion calls for it.
To recapitulate, the four words that in my opinion best describe our honoree are MODESTY, PERSPICACITY, GENTILITY and RECTITUDE.  To easily remember these four words, I have coined a key word: *MPGR.*  Come to think of it, the letters *MPGR* are the initials of Justice Minerva Perez Gonzaga-Reyes.
*Maraming salamat po.*

The succeeding seven chapters afford the reader an insider’s first-person retelling of the ‘Judicial Jousts’ which take place in the *sanctum sanctorum* of the Highest Court in the land.  It is a testimony to the author’s literary and journalistic skills that he can instill in the reader a vicarious involvement in what is ordinarily expected to be prosaic prose.”

*A Book Review by ***Justice HILARION L. AQUINO**
*Court of Appeals* In the repertoire of a concert artist, there is usually a *piece de resistance,* and all that comes before builds towards its sterling rendition as a powerful climax.  Like a concert artist, Justice Artemio V. Panganiban has rendered one masterpiece after another: his *ponencias* and separate opinions are examples of artfully written and forcefully argued judicial literature, and his books — of which this is the fifth — dissect, with clinical accuracy, often tangled legal problems while affording the reader the pleasure of unpretentious prose and a warm glimpse at the High Court’s seldom-seen side!  Unlike a concert artist, however, Justice Art does not keep in reserve his juristic acumen and his literary artistry for a *piece de resistance,* because everything he offers either as a magistrate or a writer (and it is not easy to distinguish when he is one or the other) is a masterpiece, not really because he is set on creating an impression, but because he shares of himself without reserve in all that he writes.  What one then has from him is always a piece of his soul and a privileged view of his spirit — and that is always worth any reader’s while!

all that he writes.  What one then has from him is always a piece of his soul and a privileged view of his spirit — and that is always worth any reader’s while! In *Old Doctrines and New Paradigms,* a paper he read for the Centenary Lecture Series of the Supreme Court, the author selects decisions of the Court which, to him, break new ground insofar as they rest on new paradigms.  He announces, for example, that “there is an unmistakable shift from the state to the private sector.”  This is a persuasion shared by contemporary social analysts, and the French philosopher Francois Lyotard is among them.  The center of gravity, many are persuaded, will no longer be the state but individuals and corporations.  This of course provokes the question about what the role of the State will be even as the inexorable trend appears to be towards “decentralization, deregulation.”  Some have gone so far as to suggest that State interference will be like “static” that garbles communication, a thesis Justice Art obviously will not share.  When one reads further on in his disquisition however that the collapse of totalitarianism and the bankruptcy of collectivist societies have led to greater protection of individual rights and liberties, then it should not be too difficult to infer that the author suggests that the proper role of State power will be the protection and enhancement of individuals’ capacity to agree among themselves and to decide.

the author suggests that the proper role of State power will be the protection and enhancement of individuals’ capacity to agree among themselves and to decide. The author is unabashed about admitting his biases.  Bias is one more concept that contemporary thought has vindicated.  In the past, one had to apologize for his biases.  Today, it is common teaching that all knowledge is possible because of that mass of background information and conviction we call bias.  Among the biases of Justice Panganiban is his consistent position against the death penalty, a position we already know of from his separate and dissenting opinions in the death penalty cases.  In fact, the author devotes an entire chapter to the issue, Chapter 14; and while he underscores such considerations as the insouciance of the defense counsel, if not of the judge who ought to proceed in such cases with great circumspection, he also rightly invokes the strength of growing global opposition to the death penalty.

With candor, but without being offensive, Justice Art likewise takes issue with what he considers the erosion of the protection due laborers, when the Court maintained that the requirement of due process is a limitation on state power but not on private action.  One can understand that the author would like labor better protected, but not a few will take issue with him on this point, for there is good reason to distinguish — as recent jurisprudence has done — between those limitations the fundamental law institutes against state power and those that it sets up against the actions of private individuals.

ce has done — between those limitations the fundamental law institutes against state power and those that it sets up against the actions of private individuals. The advance of the sciences in the genome project and in DNA analysis must be exciting to lawyers and jurists.  One will not fail to catch the refrain of Justice Art’s position: The judge cannot be a spectator to the progress in other human disciplines with nonchalance and a noncommittal posture.  Already, scholars have asked whether or not the Philippine judiciary is prepared to cope with such questions as relate to the presentation of DNA test results and matching procedures.  The author suggests the course of the future: “By its rule-making power, the Supreme Court can promulgate rules on DNA fingerprinting, the use of genes as evidence, and the admission of biotechnology and genetics as evidence.”  While, of course, it is always possible for the Supreme Court to settle such issues when it hears and decides cases involving them, it can take a more pro-active stance by issuing rules providing for admissibility or exclusion, and thus anticipate what could be very difficult questions left to the devices of the individual judge.

issuing rules providing for admissibility or exclusion, and thus anticipate what could be very difficult questions left to the devices of the individual judge. One very charming piece in the book is “E-Values for Lawyers.”  Even if he was addressing lawyers, Justice Art started by echoing the humbling but telling observation that more are more cynical about the legal profession.  Lawyers will not welcome this broadside from laypersons, but from a member of the highest court of the land, it was a necessary wake-up call.  He proposes his three values: Excellence, Ethics and Eternity.  E-values, for an E-age.  There is nothing “e” about them, except their first letters, because they do not depend on intricate and sometimes unfriendly e-technology, but they are enduring values even, and maybe particularly, for an e-age.  The legal profession has a noble lineage and a venerable ancestry.  It should not be indifferent to public cynicism and distrust, and the task of redeeming the profession falls squarely on the shoulders of lawyers themselves.  Justice Art’s e-values may help them discern the work that needs to be done.

of redeeming the profession falls squarely on the shoulders of lawyers themselves.  Justice Art’s e-values may help them discern the work that needs to be done. While neither the Chief Justice nor the author took part in the deliberations of the Court leading to its doctrinally innovative decisions in *Estrada v. Macapagal-Arroyo,* Justice Art explains the reason for his recusal or inhibition (taking care, at the same time, to distinguish between *disqualification and inhibition or recusal*).  He makes clear that the petitioner had failed to make a case to disqualify him from participating in the proceedings, even as he insists that all such motions must be firmly anchored in law.  However, he thought it the more prudent course to inhibit himself so that there would be no doubt at all on the integrity of the proceedings and on the fairness of whatever decision the Court would render.  No justice would have relished the prospect of being excluded from the crafting of a decision that would surely be studied by generations of law students and jurists to come, and of leaving one’s mark in the form of a concurring or a dissenting opinion.  The personal decision Justice Art had to make, and which he recounts, calls attention to that dilemma that will, on various occasions, confront a judge: while his voluntary inhibition will be the safer and the more comfortable option — as it will often provide him with the excuse to keep as far away as possible from a tinderbox — a too frequent recourse to the expedient of a voluntary inhibition may in fact be a form of dereliction of one’s duty!

s far away as possible from a tinderbox — a too frequent recourse to the expedient of a voluntary inhibition may in fact be a form of dereliction of one’s duty! Everywhere in the world, the claim of indigenous peoples to land occupied and cultivated since time immemorial has provoked very interesting and trying legal issues, has engendered novel jurisprudence and spurred the emergence of ingenious legislation.
Canada and Australia are examples of jurisdictions that have evolved a body of substantive and procedural law to deal with the problem of what is often called “native title.”  It was then with bated breath that the Philippine legal community awaited the Supreme Court’s verdict on the constitutional challenge to the validity of the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act (IPRA), and many shared the disappointment of petitioner — Mr.
Justice Isagani Cruz — when, because the court was evenly split, the petition was dismissed.
The author discusses the legal theories invoked by his colleagues and explains his own position that was adverse to the law.
In sum, the author’s objection to the law was that considerable portions of Philippine territory would be effectively placed outside the reach of the Philippine Constitution and of the State power it established were one to maintain the theory of the law’s advocates that these were never in fact lands of the public domain.
In fact, what concerned the author was that the claim covered — and potentially included — huge tracts of land.
This is an issue that blurs the already blurred line between law and policy.

author was that the claim covered — and potentially included — huge tracts of land.
This is an issue that blurs the already blurred line between law and policy. Orthodox teaching has it that justiciability goes only so far as law, and that policy is left to the Legislature.
The fact, however, is that when a judge adjudicates due and demandable rights, the law is applied according to its policy.
And when the
validity of a law is impugned, consistency with national policy as this is reflected in the fundamental law of the land will not be an irrelevancy.

And when the
validity of a law is impugned, consistency with national policy as this is reflected in the fundamental law of the land will not be an irrelevancy. What makes for engaging reading is literature that engages the reader in the struggles, pains and disappointments of the author’s soul.  This is a quality one will not find wanting in the author’s book.  In discussing the decision of the Court in *Perez v. Estrada* that reiterated the prohibition against live television coverage of the criminal trials of the erstwhile President, Justice Art could barely conceal his profound disappointment with the majority position when he wrote: “And yet, the Court, by its decision today, has turned its back and refused to march in cadence with the music created by the chimes of changing technology.”  He sided very strongly with the proponents of live coverage in the name of transparency and accountability.  Unfortunately for Justice Art, he was opting for the reversal of a well-entrenched and long-established tradition, not only in the Philippines but elsewhere.  It might not be amiss to add that a more generous allowance demands maturity on their part.  In large measure, the reticence of the Court about media coverage was also a statement of its wariness about the sensationalism and, yes, irresponsibility that have unfortunately marred media’s image.

heading: Chapter 19: Bengson v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal: — Repatriation Restores Original Citizenship

ourt about media coverage was also a statement of its wariness about the sensationalism and, yes, irresponsibility that have unfortunately marred media’s image. True to his cherished belief, the author endeavors to keep the public informed, for it can only be helpful to the Supreme Court — and to the judiciary as a whole — for the public to be educated about its constitutionally apportioned task as well as its role in a democratic state.
The piece on the Supreme Court Justice Panganiban renders for us in *A Centenary of Justice* is one that gives us its *pianissimos* and its *fortissimos,* in tempo that is at times *allegro,* at other times *adagio.*  He invites respect and esteem for the Court on the occasion of its centenary, not because of any pretension at infallibility, but because of its consecration to the often painful and contentious struggle for that measure of justice under the law that is *supremely* available to us who must labor under the vagaries of changing times, circumstances and shifting opinions and philosophical persuasions.
And even as we applaud yet one more masterpiece from this consummate artist of juridical and legal literature, we wait with undiminished excitement for his next rendition!  *Abangan!*
