Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (cont.)

arena of national student politics.  Because of his constant monitoring of my grades, I managed to graduate with Latin honors and as “most outstanding student.” A few days prior to the 1960 bar examinations, I got sick.  To aggravate the situation, a rainstorm hit the city, and I had to wade across knee-deep waters on R. Papa Street from the FEU Hospital where I was confined, to the University of the East where the exams were being held.  After what I thought was a lackluster
APPENDICES
first-day performance, I wanted to quit the examinations for the remaining days.  But Dean Salonga would not hear of it.  With his constant encouragement, I still managed to pass, copping the 6th highest place.
He invited me to join his prestigious law firm, which included as partners some of the best legal minds in the country like Sedfrey A. Ordoñez, Pedro L. Yap and Neptali A. Gonzales.  He taught me the rudiments of law practice; more significantly, he demonstrated the life-defining values of integrity, prudence and fairness.  My admiration and awe of Dr. Salonga grew even more.
Then and up to now, he is a living model of his teachings.  He taught by example, not by words.  He is a dedicated husband, a caring father, a faithful friend and a devoted man of God.  Never compromising his principles and values in exchange for friendship, kinship, relationship, wealth or power, he lives an almost ascetic life.  He does not smoke, does not drink, and does not gamble.  Money, worldly pleasures, titles and honors hold no fascination for him.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (Jovito R. Salonga)
heading: Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor
text:
Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (cont.)

lives an almost ascetic life.  He does not smoke, does not drink, and does not gamble.  Money, worldly pleasures, titles and honors hold no fascination for him. That we are of different religious faiths — he being a devout Protestant, a respected leader of the Cosmopolitan Church; and I, a fledgling Catholic — has not diminished at all our more than four decades of enriching friendship; or my own admiration, esteem and affection for him.  This is probably because we never discuss what separates us, but only what truly binds us.
Prior to my appointment to the highest court of the land, Senator Salonga accorded me — unconsciously, I am sure — the greatest honor in my
career as a practising lawyer, not by awarding me a plaque of gold or conferring on me an honorary degree.  Rather, he did so by asking me to be his personal legal counsel during his incumbency as Senate President and to be concurrently chief legal counsel of the Liberal Party which he then headed.  Nothing is more fulfilling, more exhilarating, than the honor of being counsel to one’s mentor and former boss!

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (Jovito R. Salonga)
heading: Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor
text:
Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (cont.)

nsel of the Liberal Party which he then headed.  Nothing is more fulfilling, more exhilarating, than the honor of being counsel to one’s mentor and former boss! As some of you may know, my ascension to the Supreme Court was not easy.  From 1992 to 1995, there were seven vacancies in the Court due to the compulsory retirement of incumbents.  For each of those seven vacancies, my name was submitted to the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for screening.  I failed the JBC test because of the alleged insufficiency of my professional competence and my alleged transgressions and sins.  But in all those trying three years, Senator Salonga was beside me, behind me, and even above me, cheering me up, tirelessly uplifting my sagging spirit and praying for me.  He would call me up frequently, assuring me of his support and unfailing faith and urging me never to lose trust in the faithfulness of God.  And whenever I felt really low and hopeless, he would patiently remind me of Romans 8:28.
*God makes all things work together*
*For the good of those who love Him*
*And are called according to His purpose.*
When finally I was nominated by the JBC and eventually appointed by President Ramos, he was the first to congratulate me not only for the appointment, but also for my keeping faith in the grace and bounty of the Lord!
APPENDICES

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (Jovito R. Salonga)
heading: Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor
text:
Appendix A: A Salute to My Mentor (cont.)

President Ramos, he was the first to congratulate me not only for the appointment, but also for my keeping faith in the grace and bounty of the Lord!
APPENDICES In my conduct and work in the Supreme Court, I am proud to say that I have tried my best to follow and express my mentor’s ideas and ideals.  Those who read my decisions in the Court, as well as my writings and speeches elsewhere, will surely detect the legal philosophy and life values of Senator Salonga imbedded in them.  I try to echo, even faintly, his teaching that law cannot be separated from life, that it should be used as a brick in building the social edifice and as a means of fulfilling the deepest aspirations of man.
But his most significant teaching is not really about the law, as it is about life.  And if my presence today must have any relevance at all, I now would like to summarize the one teaching of my guru which I will always treasure, and it is this: While it is desirable to have some of the necessities that money *can* buy, like adequate food on the table, sufficient clothing and shelter for the family, sports and recreation for the body, and even a car and a house, I should never never forget that it is far more important to aspire for the things that money *cannot* buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God as the Source of all that is true, good and beautiful.
*Maraming salamat po.*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work

**T**en days ago, I received an invitation from the Philippine Judicial Academy (Philja) to deliver the closing address today to end formally the Second Pre-Judicature Program.  I would like you to know that a Philja invitation partakes of the nature of a summons, which cannot be refused or ignored not only on pain of default but, worse, of contempt.
It is said that Supreme Court justices are a courageous lot.  They have braved the onslaughts of lynch mobs, screaming headlines and even presidential tyrants and dictators.  Let me, however, tell you that if there is *anyone* over whom high magistrates sweat bullets, that singular one is Justice Ameurfina Aguinaldo Melencio Herrera, the venerable chancellor of Philja.  Not that she is fearsome, but that she is respected and loved.  When she calls, we answer; when she invites, we consider it a command and we
*  Closing address delivered by Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the graduation ceremonies of the Pre-Judicature Program of the Philippine Judicial Academy held at the Supreme Court Centennial Building on March 9, 2001.
APPENDICES
always respond.
Let me add that the summons for today’s meeting was personally served on me, not by an ordinary sheriff, but by my esteemed former colleague in the Supreme Court, Justice Antonio M. Martinez.  Let me just recall a bit of what I said of Justice Tony on the occasion of his retirement from the Court on February 1, 1999:

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

urt, Justice Antonio M. Martinez.  Let me just recall a bit of what I said of Justice Tony on the occasion of his retirement from the Court on February 1, 1999: “Regrettably, Mr. Justice Martinez has had a stint in the Court that was too brief.  We his colleagues shall miss him and his cadenced responses to the challenges that faced us.  We shall pine for his scholarly *ponencias,* his industry and his passion for truth and fairness.  His stint may have been too brief, but he has certainly enriched jurisprudence in our land.  He has definitely left his unmistakable imprint in my memory of great jurists.”
What has made the invitation even more compelling is the presence of the chairman of the Pre-Judicature Program, Justice Ricardo C. Puno.  He is held in high regard in the Court and is invariably invited to appear as *amicus curiae* whenever the High Tribunal is faced with novel and difficult questions — invitations he has never turned down, even if he has never been paid for his appearance.
Let me begin by congratulating all of you, dear graduates.  You are the first batch to finish this Pre-Judicature Program in the *first* year of the *first* century of the *new* millennium, a distinction that happens only once every one thousand years!  Today, indeed, marks the opening of a major door to the exclusive and
reclusive world of the men and women in black robes.  As you all know, the Philja Pre-Judicature Program is now a prerequisite to a Judicial and Bar Council recommendation for membership in the Philippine judiciary.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

s you all know, the Philja Pre-Judicature Program is now a prerequisite to a Judicial and Bar Council recommendation for membership in the Philippine judiciary. As I contemplated my message to you today, memories of my own entry into the judiciary, direct to the Supreme Court in 1995, streamed into my mind.  As I began to brush shoulders with the most exclusive brethren in the country, I was filled not only with awe and anxiety at what lay ahead, but also with some intellectual and spiritual soul-searching.
Let me explain that from 1986 to 1995, my wife and I underwent a spiritual rebirth as we joined the *Bukas Loob sa Diyos,* a charismatic community of renewed Catholics.  During those nine years, we embarked on a new journey of faith through a marriage encounter, a “Life in the Spirit” seminar, retreats and various other programs to relearn and reexperience our faith.  We read and reread the Bible several times over, discussed volumes — nay, libraries — of commentaries thereon.  Later on we shared our experiences by speaking in seminars and conferences, and we even became servant-leaders of this community.
In the process, we had a most fulfilling encounter with our Lord Jesus Christ.  We can truly claim that we came to know Him and to experience His love in many ways.
On my part, I have learned to trust Him and to depend on Him for *all* my needs, aspirations and wants.  Many times I would pray.  Even if I do not get what I want, still, I continue to repose my full faith and
APPENDICES

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

for *all* my needs, aspirations and wants.  Many times I would pray.  Even if I do not get what I want, still, I continue to repose my full faith and
APPENDICES confidence in Him.  I know that God is infinitely more intelligent and powerful than I or anyone else.
Indeed, He always knows my needs better than I do.  And I am confident He will provide all things good for me and my family — in His own time and in His own way.  When I am baffled by events that I do not understand, I always remember the book of Isaiah (55:8-9), in which God exclaimed:
*“My thoughts are not your thoughts,*
*And my ways are not your ways,*
*As high as the heavens are above the earth,*
*So high are my ways above your ways*
*And my thoughts above your thoughts.”*
Let me assure you that in all my life, my struggles, my frustrations, my victories, God has never failed in His promise, as heralded also in Scriptures, in the book of Romans (8:28):
*“God makes all things work*
*for the good of those who love Him*
*and who are called according*
*to His purpose.”*
Let me repeat: “God makes *all* things work for the good of those who love Him and who are called according to His purpose.”
The most basic of our Lord’s teachings is love.  When He was asked which commandment of the law was the greatest, He replied, “The first is: love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength.  The second is: Love your neighbor as yourself.”1
1  Mt 22:34-40; Mk 121:28-31.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

ord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your strength.  The second is: Love your neighbor as yourself.”1
1  Mt 22:34-40; Mk 121:28-31. On another occasion, our Lord was preaching on a mountainside, and among other things, he said, “My command to you is: love your enemies, pray for your persecutors.  This will prove that you are sons of your heavenly Father, for His sun rises on the bad and the good.  He rains on the just and the unjust.  If you love only those who love you, what merit is there in that?  Do not tax collectors do as much?  And if you greet your brothers only, what is so praiseworthy about that?  Do not pagans do as much?  In a word, you must be made perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.”2
In the face of this core teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, I asked myself several times: “If God is the very personification of love, why does He punish His people?  At the very least, why does He allow calamity, cruelty, poverty and affliction to assault and damn them?  Why does He not just satisfy all of their needs and wants, something that is definitely within His infinite power and authority?  Why does He not just eradicate poverty, hunger and pain?  He is God; He certainly can do all that.”

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

that is definitely within His infinite power and authority?  Why does He not just eradicate poverty, hunger and pain?  He is God; He certainly can do all that.” It is with this background of incisive theological questions that, upon my appointment to the Supreme Court, I asked myself: “Our Lord’s greatest commandment is to love God and His people; why am I being called to impose penalties for crimes, enforce difficult obligations and sanction burdensome laws?”  I was baffled by the seeming contradiction between love and punishment, between affection and affliction, until I came upon this little story.
A demure young lady was brought before a traffic court for over-speeding.  In the courtroom, the judge
APPENDICES
asked her: “Young lady, this police officer tells me that you were racing at 100 kilometers per hour in a 50-kilometer zone.  What can you say about that?”
“He’s correct, your Honor.  I am truly sorry I broke the law, but I promise not to do it again,” replied the repentant miss.
“Because of your confession and promise to reform, the law will be lenient on you.  I will just fine you P300 instead of the usual P500,” the judge solemnly decreed.
After adjourning the court session, the judge removed his black robe, went straight to the cashier, pulled out his wallet and paid the P300 fine.  He paid the penalty out of love, because the lawbreaker was his daughter.  *Justice* was served — and so was *love.*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

led out his wallet and paid the P300 fine.  He paid the penalty out of love, because the lawbreaker was his daughter.  *Justice* was served — and so was *love.* In a larger and real sense, the judge in our little story is our Lord Jesus Christ.  And the young lady represents each one of us, all of us in this hall.  His Honor is our Divine Judge and we are His unworthy children.  We, His people, sinned.  We violated the law of God.  And so the justice of God requires our punishment.
Because justice is in the nature of God, He — even if He is the most powerful Being in the universe — cannot refuse to impose the sanction of His own law.  Otherwise, He would be violating His own nature.
But Jesus is also love personified.  So, out of His great love, He became man, came down to earth, suffered, was crucified, died and gloriously resurrected.  He atoned for our sins and owned the punishment meant for us.  He did this because of His great love for us.
2  Mt 5:44-48.
Let me stress it again.  Just as our Lord is a God of love, He is also a God of justice.  Just as it is in His nature to love, it is also in His essence to see that justice is done.  Just as He cannot refuse to love, neither can He decline to render justice.  Both love and justice are in His very nature and essence.  He cannot contradict himself by refusing to fulfill both love and justice.
By sending His only Son and by His Son’s suffering, death and resurrection, He saved humankind from eternal damnation.  In this manner, His justice and His love were both fulfilled.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
heading: Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work
text:
Appendix B: Justice Is God’s Work (cont.)

on and by His Son’s suffering, death and resurrection, He saved humankind from eternal damnation.  In this manner, His justice and His love were both fulfilled. Ladies and gentlemen, if my fifteen-minute talk today is worth anything, it is this: the rendition of justice is not only a human necessity; it is a divine essentiality.  When we give people their due, impose penalties for crimes, uphold liberty, enforce obligations and compel obedience to duties — fairly and speedily, without fear or favor — we really do the work of the Lord.  In short, to dispense *quality* justice is to do God’s work.
To all the graduates, welcome to the divine work of rendering quality *justice* to our fellowmen and to the world!
I thank you.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix D: MPGR (a tribute to Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes)
heading: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix D: MPGR (a tribute to Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes)
text:
A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix D: MPGR (a tribute to Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes)

Appendix D of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's tribute 'MPGR,' delivered September 24, 2001 at the Manila Hotel retirement program for Justice Minerva Perez Gonzaga-Reyes, his colleague of thirty-two months in the Court's Third Division (joined by her husband 'Johnny' and children Alda, Edwin Romualdo and Johann Michael).
He distills his impression of her into four words.
MODESTY -- not timidity but humility: she declined the Court's customary grand Session-Hall eulogy, where robed justices individually eulogize a retiree, for a modest family gathering, and even asked CJP not to praise her -- a caveat he gently overrode as a jurist bound to the truth, since 'her legacy' is a docket with 'zero backlog,' every ripe controversy decided and every case left current for her successor and 'the expectant and oftentimes demanding public.' PERSPICACITY -- a clear understanding acted on 'with delicacy and serenity'; she 'speaks rarely -- only when she feels her opinions would make a difference,' in 'cadenced, well thought out words' free of 'braggadocio or exhibitionism.' GENTILITY -- 'good manners and right conduct at all times,' never losing her temper, never using obscene words, 'always prim, proper and balanced.' And RECTITUDE -- integrity and uprightness, an 'unassailable reputation' for honesty and for 'not betraying friends or revealing secrets,' fighting 'not only for what is legally possible but...

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix D: MPGR (a tribute to Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes)
heading: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix D: MPGR (a tribute to Justice Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes)

rightness, an 'unassailable reputation' for honesty and for 'not betraying friends or revealing secrets,' fighting 'not only for what is legally possible but... for what is ethical and moral,' leaning on 'deep spirituality' and a belief 'in the innate goodness of humans' and their capacity 'to rise above themselves.' He then reveals the device: the four words -- MODESTY, PERSPICACITY, GENTILITY, RECTITUDE -- spell MPGR, the initials of Minerva Perez Gonzaga-Reyes.

MODESTY -- not timidity but humility: she declined the Court's customary grand Session-Hall eulogy, where robed justices individually eulogize a retiree, for a modest family gathering, and even asked CJP not to praise her -- a caveat he gently overrode as a jurist bound to the truth, since 'her legacy' is a docket with 'zero backlog,' every ripe controversy decided and every case left current for her successor and 'the expectant and oftentimes demanding public.' PERSPICACITY -- a clear understanding acted on 'with delicacy and serenity'; she 'speaks rarely -- only when she feels her opinions would make a difference,' in 'cadenced, well thought out words' free of 'braggadocio or exhibitionism.' GENTILITY -- 'good manners and right conduct at all times,' never losing her temper, never using obscene words, 'always prim, proper and balanced.' And RECTITUDE -- integrity and uprightness, an 'unassailable reputation' for honesty and for 'not betraying friends or revealing secrets,' fighting 'not only for what is legally possible but...

title: Justice and Faith -- Front Matter: Foreword (by CJ Andres R. Narvasa)
heading: Justice and Faith -- Front Matter: Foreword (by CJ Andres R. Narvasa)
text:
Justice and Faith -- Front Matter: Foreword (by CJ Andres R. Narvasa)

**Foreword**
*Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa*
The collection of writings and speeches of the author’s own choice and excerpting, modest as it is in volume thought not in quality, nonetheless suffices to give the serious reader an insight into what may be called the twin beacons that have guided the professional and personal life of Mr. Justice Artemio Panganiban – those with which he has chosen to title this offering: Justice and Faith.
Particularly impressive are the frankness and humility with which, in one address, he acknowledges his much-cherished ambition for a seat in the High Court and describes the long and difficult road to its fulfillment. That culmination, when it came, he celebrated with exemplary industry in his work as a jurist; by his own reckoning, he has written no less than 230 ponencias in the two years following his elevation. His account of how he developed his decision-writing style as well as his words of advice to would-be lawyers make absorbing reading and should prove useful to those who aspire for the profession.
The writer does not forget the sitting judge when he expounds on the mental skills and disciplines he feels that official should possess and put to use in seeking out the crucial issues in a case, analyzing the evidence and arguments, determining the applicable law and, finally, expressing his conclusions in clear, precise and logical manner; it is pithy advice he gives that judges would do well to follow.

e applicable law and, finally, expressing his conclusions in clear, precise and logical manner; it is pithy advice he gives that judges would do well to follow. The book leaves the reader looking for more in the same vein – which is the least that can be said in praise of it – and the hope that the author will not disappoint him.
**ANDRES R. NARVASA**

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 5: Profiles of Supreme Court Justices
heading: Profiles of Supreme Court Justices
text:
Profiles of Supreme Court Justices

(Remarks made by Justice Panganiban - who was master of ceremonies during the retirement rites held in honor of Justice Justo P. Torres Jr. on October 22, 1997 - in his introduction of the justices of the Supreme Court, as each one of them, in accordance with a hallowed tradition, formally presented to the honoree a memento of his term, something he had used to discharge his function as a jurist. Only ten members of the Court were mentioned, because two - Justice Teodoro R. Padilla and Justice Regino C. Hermosisima Jr. - had retired by then; and two others - Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa and Senior Justice Florenz D. Regalado - were on official business abroad. The introductions are arranged according to the order in which the justices participated in the program. The introduction for Mr. Justice Torres is the longest, because he was the honoree.)
Mr. Justice Reynato S. Puno
Like a trained surgeon, he uses his pen with laser-like precision to separate and excise fabrication from truth and pretension from reality. In the process, he gives life to populist causes and libertarian ideals. Daring, gutsy and erudite, he -  like Justice Holmes - oftentimes wages lonely battles against conventional wisdom with his stirring dissents and insightful opinions.
Mr. Justice Jose C. Vitug
An icon of the academe, he is the ultimate teacher and compassionate friend, in whose restrained language the subtlety and rationality of the law find cadenced expression.
Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero

teacher and compassionate friend, in whose restrained language the subtlety and rationality of the law find cadenced expression.

The essential magistrate to whom law is a jealous master, who never winces or falters in upholding the majesty of the law, regardless of personal consequences and possible public disapproval, always justifying his actions and decisions with only one standard - the quiet comfort of a disciplined conscience.

The classic jurist, molded in the ivy-league traditions of Yale, where he still hobnobs annually with the best and brightest legal minds of the world. His ponencias are always scholarly, well-researched, cerebral, lofty and impeccable.

Bellosillo The paragon, the pith and soul of the career magistrate; quick to spot lesions and mischiefs in the judicial hierarchy, but equally adept at defending and promoting the uprightness and welfare of lower court judges. Diligent, assiduous and methodical, he is single-minded about his work and his mission.
Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.
The epitome of the Filipino jurist, makabayan, maginoo, marangal, matapang, masipag, mapagkakatiwalaan, may mabuting asal at diwa, may pagpapahalaga sa kapwa at may paniniwala sa Pilipino at sa kanyang kakayahang maging malaya, maunlad at mapayapa.
Justice Justo P. Torres Jr.
Plucked out from the Court of Appeals where he was then the thirteenth most senior member, he was appointed to the Supreme Court by President Ramos on March 13, 1996,. Now, upon his retirement, he also ranked thirteenth among the fifteen members of the Supreme Court. Incidentally, his father, Jus to Sr., ranked thirteenth in the bar examinations of 1925. Yes, thirteen is the lucky number of Justice Tito. The only important place where he is not Number Thirteen is in the heart of Rose, where he is Number One and only!

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 5: Profiles of Supreme Court Justices
heading: Profiles of Supreme Court Justices
text:
Profiles of Supreme Court Justices (cont.)

thirteen is the lucky number of Justice Tito. The only important place where he is not Number Thirteen is in the heart of Rose, where he is Number One and only! Mr. Justice Torres' stint in the Court has been regrettably short, spanning only a period of 1 year and 7 months, but he has definitely left his mark in the annals of Philippine jurisprudence. Although senior in chronological age, he is nonetheless very young in mind and in spirit. Verily, he is a head-on activist, who is canalized neither by tradition nor by precedent. He looks at each case with enthusiasm and freshness, ever mindful of its vigor, effect on society in general. Without discounting the relative safety of well-entrenched jurisprudence, he is nonetheless an irrepressible visionary and an ebullient reformer who does not hesitate to try new solutions to resolve recurring problems. God-loving, egalitarian and congenial, he is a connoisseur of fine language. He will now deliver his valedictory address which may give us an opportunity to explore the labyrinth of his vibrant mind and indomitable spirit in the judicial cosmos. Friends, may I invite you to rise and welcome Mr. Justice Justo P. Torres Jr.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 6: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
heading: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
text:
Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court

My brothers and sisters in Christ; you all know that I was recently appointed Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines. I took my oath only a week ago. Let me now tell you how God’s Word guided me in my journey to the Court, how He humbled me in the process and how, eventually, He rewarded me. Let me also tell you how my prayers and faith in Jesus Christ combined to lead me to victory and fulfillment.
Being elevated to the Supreme Court is the highest aspiration and dream of every lawyer. Like any lawyer, I thus aspired to have a place in this Court. My serious quest began some three years ago.
The formal process of getting into the highest court begins in the Judicial and Bar Council or JBC. This council is empowered by our Constitution to screen and then recommend a list of nominees from which the President of the Philippines eventually chooses the appointee. Once appointed, the justice holds office during good behavior until he reaches the age of seventy. The screening process is rather rigid - man’s personal life, professional career and lifelong activities are minutely scrutinized.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 6: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
heading: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
text:
Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court (cont.)

e reaches the age of seventy. The screening process is rather rigid - man’s personal life, professional career and lifelong activities are minutely scrutinized. 	From 1992 to 1994, at least seven vacancies in the Supreme Court were created due to the retirement of incumbent members. In each of these vacancies, my name was submitted to the JBC for screening. But in all seven, I failed the test. Many objections were raised against me - the alleged insufficiency of my professional competence and my alleged sins and wrongdoings. At one time, a former client suddenly surfaced to complain about my alleged mishandling of a case that happened 25 years ago. And after I was able to answer and explain the charges against me, I was bypassed anyway because career appellate justices were given priority over practising lawyers. It was also pointed out that I might be qualified, but that there were others who were even more qualified. In other words, these past three years of screening were one long story of frustration and defeat. Many times, I would sob and ask the Lord: "How long, O Lord, must I bear this frustration and embarrassment of being rejected? Why must I suffer for charges and accusations which are absolutely baseless and misleading? I have repented my sins and reformed my life; why do You still allow me to be humiliated and chastised?"
In all these instances, however, and in spite of such hard rhetorical questions I asked the Lord, I never lost faith in His wisdom and providence. I always took comfort and consolation in Romans 8:28:
God makes all things work together

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 6: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
heading: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
text:
Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court (cont.)

ions I asked the Lord, I never lost faith in His wisdom and providence. I always took comfort and consolation in Romans 8:28:
God makes all things work together for the good of those who love Him and are
called according to His purpose.
In January 1995, after having been bypassed seven times, and convinced that the Lord did not want me to be in the Supreme Court, I humbled myself and bowed to what I thought was God's will for me. My spirit was shattered and my heart bled, but I uplifted my ambition to God with a solemn prayer:
Take, O Lord, all that I am, all that I will ever be. Take my personal ambition, my liberty, my career. Do what You will with them and I will follow whatever it is You want me to do.
In July of the same year, another vacancy in Court occurred with the retirement of Justice Camilo Quiason. A close friend who was and is still a member of the High Court asked me, "Why don't you try again? Don't pass up the opportunity because the next vacancy will be in late 1997 already." At first, I did not take my friend's suggestion seriously, because at the time I had already given up my ambition.
However, about 1 a.m. on Saturday, July 29, 1995, I woke up and could not sleep. My friend's words kept bothering me, kept reverberating in my ears. So I decided to pray for over two hours. I told the Lord that I had already surrendered my quest to Him, that I had already given up. Why was I still bothered? I fell asleep about 4a.m., waiting for a sign from the Lord. None came that night.
But the following morning, he spoke loud and clear to me. Let me explain.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 6: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
heading: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
text:
Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court (cont.)

ed? I fell asleep about 4a.m., waiting for a sign from the Lord. None came that night.
But the following morning, he spoke loud and clear to me. Let me explain. Brothers and sisters, it is my faith that God speaks to us through the Bible. Though written some two thousand years ago, the Scriptures are still sources of God's personal messages. For Jesus Christ is the same today, yesterday and forever. I believe that if we read or listen intently and prayerfully — in full faith and confidence — God will speak to us personally as we are struck by a verse in the Good Book that comes alive and answers our questions.
The following morning, Sunday, July 30, 1995, I served as a special minister of Holy Communion in our parish. As was my habit, with eyes closed and with an ascending Jesus in my mental vision, I intently listened to our parish priest as he read the gospel for the day. I was struck by the following verses he read from the gospel according to Luke 11:1-11:
Ask and you shall receive, seek and you shall find, knock and the door shall be opened to you. For whoever asks, receives; whoever seeks, finds; whoever knocks, is admitted.
I had cold perspiration and my body hair stood up as I gasped, "My Lord, are you asking me to persist in my quest?" But I was not satisfied. I told God in my prayer, "Lord, I may just be deluding myself, hearing things I want to hear. Please give me another sign to confirm this message."

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 6: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
heading: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court
text:
Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court (cont.)

t satisfied. I told God in my prayer, "Lord, I may just be deluding myself, hearing things I want to hear. Please give me another sign to confirm this message." The Lord's confirmation came after one week in the same Church as the same priest was reciting the gospel reading. The following Sunday, August 6, the reading was on the transfiguration of our Lord Jesus as related in Luke 9:28-36. The gospel relates that as our Lord was transfigured,
. . . a cloud came and overshadowed them and the disciples grew fearful. . . . Then from the cloud came a voice which said, "This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him."
"Listen to Him . . . " These three words struck me And once again my heart pounded madly as my body hair stood up and cold sweat oozed from all over my skin. I became sure of what the Lord wanted me to do. After all, it was our Lord Jesus who said the week before, "Ask and you shall receive, seek and you shall find, knock and the door shall be opened to you." And now our Heavenly Father commanded me: "Listen to Him!" So I followed Him. I submitted my name again to the JBC for screening.

door shall be opened to you." And now our Heavenly Father commanded me: "Listen to Him!" So I followed Him. I submitted my name again to the JBC for screening. I felt so sure of the Lord's two messages for me that I shared them with my family. On August 9, Wednesday, Leni (my wife) and I were prayer leaders during the prayer meeting of Bukas Loob ng Diyos (South Sector) held in St. James School in Sucat, Paranaque. During my reflection in that prayer meeting, I spoke of God's two messages for me even at the risk of being ridiculed should the discernment turn out to be false. I boldly proclaimed my discernment and publicly claimed God's will for me. I declared my determination to pursue God's will in my career by quoting a favorite Jesuit saying:
I will work as if everything depended on me, and I will pray as if everything depended on God.
This did not mean, however, that my trials and tests were over. I had to undergo more of them. But I clung to God's word and never lost my faith in His promise. Let me continue my story.
During the meeting of the JBC on September 13, there was a serious attempt to exclude me from the list. I would have been excluded from right then, had it not been for one member, who I believe was guided by the Holy Spirit. He pleaded: "I think we should let Panganiban's name stay in the list in the meantime. We are meeting next week anyway and, if you still insist on deleting him, so be it."

Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court (cont.)

"I think we should let Panganiban's name stay in the list in the meantime. We are meeting next week anyway and, if you still insist on deleting him, so be it." This member told me two days later that, unless a miracle happened, I would surely be out of the list. So I prayed again and told the Lord that human forces, however exalted and powerful, could not prevail against His will. I reaffirmed my full faith in and dependence on His word.
And, true enough, during the JBC meeting one week thereafter on September 20, no one, by some mysterious reason, objected to my name, and for the first time in over three years, I passed the screening. A miracle!
Thereafter, a list of the five JBC recommendees including my name was sent to the President of the Philippines. After being informed that finally I was on the JBC list, President Ramos called and asked me pointblank, "How did you do it?" "Do what, sir?" I asked back. "How did you get the JBC to nominate you? How did you do it?" he repeated.
"Well, sir," I replied, "I did not do it. The Lord did it!"
It took the President another two weeks to make his appointment known. All this time, I had asked our Community during all our prayer meetings and during all intercessory sessions — and Leni asked the Carmelites and the Pink Sisters - to storm the heavens with supplications and sacrifices. And not just I but also Leni and my whole family clung to God's discern ed word and never doubted that He would be faithful and would make His will prevail.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 6: Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court

Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court (cont.)

es. And not just I but also Leni and my whole family clung to God's discern ed word and never doubted that He would be faithful and would make His will prevail. Exactly two weeks after the JBC included me in the list of nominees, the President called me by phone, saying in effect, "I am the Lord's instrument. He has chosen you, and I therefore appoint you justice of the Supreme Court."
I answered, "Alleluia, praise be the Lord God Almighty."
Since then, I have never ceased to praise and thank God for this display of His might and power in my career.
Our God took His time because He wanted me to learn some lessons in humility and purification - to acknowledge my powerlessness. He wanted me to recognize His power over all things, to cling to Him, to have steadfast faith in Him. He wanted me to know that on my own, I could do nothing; but with Him, I can do anything.
Truly, brothers and sisters, when we discern His will, when we surrender our ambition to Him, when we show our obedience and faith - I repeat, OBEDIENCE AND FAITH - He responds mightily in His own time. And because it is my faith that it was God who made this appointment possible, I hereby declare before this Assembly that all my actions and all my decisions will only be in accordance with His commandments and His gospel. I hold office by God's grace and I pledge to serve Him and our people with fortitude, integrity, competence and prudence. I dedicate all that I am, all that I will ever be to Him who is the Source of everything.
Praise to You, Lord Jesus Christ.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves

I would like to thank  your President, Congressman Alberto J. Lopez, my long-time friend and generous former client, for inviting me as your commencement speaker and for conferring upon me the degree of Doctor of Laws (honoris causa). My wife Leni, a professor at the Asian Institute of Management - who is with us now - and my children can at last be proud of me! You see, my wife and my five children - four daughters and one son - each has at least one postgraduate degree from a leading university abroad. Until today, I was the only one in my family who had no master’s or doctor’s degree. But, finally and at last, thanks to Congressman Lopez and the University of Iloilo, I now have a postgraduate degree - a doctor of laws at that!
Since my wife and I were not moneyed, we thought that the best legacy we could leave our children was a good solid education. Education gives fulfillment not only in term provide for our daily needs, but ins of being able to terms of being equal to anyone else in the world, and being useful not only to our fam in terms of as well. That is why I congratulate all of you graduates who will now pass from being students to being active participants in your chosen careers and in the mainstream of our nation.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

congratulate all of you graduates who will now pass from being students to being active participants in your chosen careers and in the mainstream of our nation. I especially greet the honor graduates for their extraordinary achievements. Special maligayang bati to cum laude graduates Noli Barcelona, Maricel Gange, Jonalyn Geroy and Feliza Tanalbon; and honor graduates Maryann Gimoto and Rosalie Malacapo. I am sure their parents stand proud and feel fully rewarded in their long struggle to help their children. Like them, I am impressed by excellence in school work.
After I received Congressman Lopez's kind invitation, I began thinking about what topic I could discuss with you today. I thought that perhaps many of you graduates were like me when I finished my law course thirty-seven years ago - poor, struggling but full of energy and ready to battle life’s challenges. So, instead of delivering a pompous lecture, I decided just to tell you my story, my experiences; to share with you my life, its ups and downs, its victories and frustrations, its ebb and flow; and to extract therefrom a few lessons you may find useful as you begin your own careers.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

, its ups and downs, its victories and frustrations, its ebb and flow; and to extract therefrom a few lessons you may find useful as you begin your own careers. Like many of you, my parents were poor. My father was a lowly government employee and my mother a dutiful housewife. Due to poverty, I studied in public schools during my elementary and secondary years. I had to peddle cigarettes to jeepney drivers, hawk newspapers in the streets of Sampaloc, Manila, and shine shoes to support my studies. After graduating with honors from Mapa High School, I was given a scholarship in U.P., but I could not enrol there because my father did not have enough money to pay for the fifteen-centavo bus fare then from C atalura Cataluña Street in Sampaloc, Manila, where we lived to the U.P. campus in Diliman, Quezon City. I envied my classmates who all enrolled at U.P. In my case, I had to make do with FEU which was walking distance from our house.
While on scholarship at FEU, I sold bibles to my professors and the university officials for my pocket money. I also sold textbooks to my classmates in the Institute of Law to be able to get a book as m y commission. I engaged in extracurricular activities and, during my sophomore year, became the youngest president of the Central Student Council. I co-founded the National Union of Students of the Philippines where I met and fell in love with a cloistered colegiala, Leni Carpio, who is now my wife. She was then editor of their college newspaper in St. Scholastica's College in Manila.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

ell in love with a cloistered colegiala, Leni Carpio, who is now my wife. She was then editor of their college newspaper in St. Scholastica's College in Manila. At the FEU Institute of Law, I was fortunate to meet and be taught by a brilliant lawyer who had just been appointed dean — Jovito R. Salonga who later on became, as you know, a major leader of our country. Although I was active in extracurricular activities, I did not forget my academic studies, because Dean Salonga took a liking for me and monitored my grades all the time. During the bar examinations, Dean Salonga told me that he expected me to be one of the topnotchers. I was pressured so much by his expectations that I got sick. On the first day of the exams, I was confined at the FEU Hospital and had to get special permission from my doctor to walk over flooded streets to the nearby University of the East where the exams were being held.
After taking the bar examinations and, by the grace of God, landing in the top ten, I was invited by Dean Salonga to join his prestigious law firm. His law partners at the time included Pedro L. Yap who later became Chief Justice, Sedfrey Ordonez who later on became Secretary of Justice and Neptali Gonzales who is now senator and former senate president.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

ap who later became Chief Justice, Sedfrey Ordonez who later on became Secretary of Justice and Neptali Gonzales who is now senator and former senate president. At the recommendation of Dean Salonga who was an alumnus of both Yale and Harvard, I was admitted to the Yale Law School, but again I did not have enough money for my transportation fare. I could not enjoy the privilege of education at an ivy league school because of my lack of means. I was embittered. I envied the rich and the powerful, those who seemed to have no problem buying what they wanted and wanting nothing that could not be bought.
But I continued doing my best and striving for excellence in practising and teaching law. I also engaged in business and vowed to myself that travel and education would never be a problem for my children. Many years after my graduation, I witnessed the ultra-rapid amassing of incredible wealth in Hongkong. As a lawyer, I participated in transactions involving billions of Hongkong dollars. For many years, I enjoyed first-class travels, private yachts, five-star hotels, Rolls Royce limousines, Piaget watches and mansions of the rich and famous. But during the stock market crash of 1982 in Hongkong, I lost all that I had earned abroad. I was heart-broken. What I lost was enough to cause me a heart attack. In fact, many were reported to have committed suicide because of losses due to that devastating stock market crash of 1982.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

s enough to cause me a heart attack. In fact, many were reported to have committed suicide because of losses due to that devastating stock market crash of 1982. Forlorn and poor again, I decided to concentrate on my law practice in the Philippines. In 1983, I joined the Rotary Club of Manila where I met then chief of the Philippine Constabulary, Gen. Fidel V. Ramos who — as fate would have it - became our President in 1992 and appointed me to the Supreme Court in 1995. This is not to say that my appointment to the Court was easy. In fact, it was extremely difficult. You see, before the President can appoint members of the judiciary, including those of the Supreme Court, the candidates need to pass meticulous screenings by the Judicial and Bar Council. From 1992 to 1995, there were at least seven vacancies in the Supreme Court by reason of the compulsory retirement of its members who reached the age of 70 years. Given priority to these vacancies were career justices of the Court of Appeals. Only once in a while are outsiders nominated and appointed to the Court. For three years in all these seven vacancies, I was bypassed by the Judicial and Bar Council, because either I was thought to be unqualified; or even if I was qualified, there were others who were thought to be even more qualified.
What lessons can we learn from this short narration of my life experiences? There are at least three:

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

re were others who were thought to be even more qualified.
What lessons can we learn from this short narration of my life experiences? There are at least three: **Lesson Number One.** Sometimes, adversities and misfortunes in life really preludes to greater victories and successes. I had thought that my poverty during my childhood was a curse because I could not enroll in a school of my choice, namely, UP. But because of that, I grudgingly studied at FEU, not knowing that I would encounter a very brilliant mentor - Dean Salonga. I was embittered because I could not enjoy my scholarship at Yale University; I could not raise enough money to pay for my air fare. But because of that, I organized Baron Travel Corporation which enabled me to provide transporation for all our five children who went on to finish graduate degrees at some of the best schools in the world - our eldest, Maria Elena, finished her Master in Business Administration (MBA) at the University of California; another girl, Maria Jocelyn, obtained also an MBA at the University of Chicago and the University of Navarre in Barcelona; a third girl, Maria Theresa, finished her MBA at the University of Michigan and Erasmus University in Holland; our youngest girl, Maria Evelyn, her Master in Economics at Boston University, and her Master in Public Policy at Harvard; while our only son finished his Master in Music in Munich, Germany, and his Master in Operations Research "with distinction" in Stanford. Right now, he is taking his Ph.D. in Engineering Economic System - whatever that is - also at Stanford.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

r in Operations Research "with distinction" in Stanford. Right now, he is taking his Ph.D. in Engineering Economic System - whatever that is - also at Stanford. The point is, while I did wallow in self-pity when I could not study at Yale, I feel more triumphant now that my children have accomplished five times over what I had failed to do. Also, I shed tears of self-pity as I slept on the sidewalks to await the morning newspapers which I sold to our neighbors in Sampaloc, Manila. I wrote in my diary: "Today, I am a newsboy. But someday, I'll be president of a major newspaper." I thought that was just a pipe dream of an ambitious poor boy, but in March 1991, by the grace of God, I became president of the Philippine Daily Inquirer. Finally, I was devastated when I lost my worldly earnings and investments during the Hongkong stock market crash of 1982. But God had other plans for me. I settled back home and was later on rewarded with a membership in the Supreme Court - the fulfillment of every lawyer's dream, an achievement that money cannot buy nor can any stock market crash take away.
**Lesson Number Two.** Whatever happens, do not lose heart. Keep on working, keep on doing your best. There is no substitute for devotion to excellence. Believe in yourself and your infinite capacity to ride over tragedy and defeat. Some of us lose heart with a few disappointments and failures: a failed subject in school, a failed love affair, a lost job, a missed opportunity. Author Anthony Robbins reminds us of the story of a famous American hero who:
At age 31, failed in business

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

ailed love affair, a lost job, a missed opportunity. Author Anthony Robbins reminds us of the story of a famous American hero who:
At age 31, failed in business At 32, was defeated in a legislative election
At 34, failed again in business
At 35, was overcome by the death of his sweetheart
At 36, had a nervous breakdown
At 43, 46 and 48 lost in three successive congressional elections
At 55, was defeated in a senatorial race
At 56, failed in his attempt to become Vice President
At 58, ran for the Senate and lost again
But at the age of 60, was elected President of the United States.
The man's name is Abraham Lincoln, one of the greatest American presidents.
Remember, no matter what happens, continue working hard, continue doing good; persevere in your faith, in your power to conquer any past mistake. Believe in yourselves. Believe in your ultimate victory.
**Lesson Number Three.** Have faith in God. Many times we pray and ask God for what we want: for a good career, for a passing grade, for a reciprocated love, for a healing of some illness, for a car and even for a house. Sometimes when we do not get what we want, we feel embittered and doubt God's power and providence. But our God is an infinitely intelligent and powerful God. He knows our needs better than we do. He will always provide all things good for us —in his own time and way. As God good for has himself said in the Bible, in the book of Isaiah (55:8-9):
My thoughts are not your thoughts,
And my ways are not your ways;
As high as the heavens are above the earth,
So high are my ways above your ways,

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

iah (55:8-9):
My thoughts are not your thoughts,
And my ways are not your ways;
As high as the heavens are above the earth,
So high are my ways above your ways, And my thoughts above your thoughts.
So we trust God. As long as we have faith in Him, He will answer all our prayers in His own way, not our way, and in His own time, not our time. Let me assure you that in all my life, all my struggles, my frustrations, my victories, God has never failed in His promise, as heralded also in Scriptures, book of Romans (8:28):
God makes all things work for the good of those who love Him and who are called according to His purpose.
Let me repeat that "God makes all things work for the good of those who love Him and who are called according to His purpose."
These three lessons for today can be summed up in one sentence: Work as if everything depended on you, and pray as if everything depended on God.
To help you remember today's three lessons, let me in closing relate a little story.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

s if everything depended on you, and pray as if everything depended on God.
To help you remember today's three lessons, let me in closing relate a little story. During the Middle Ages, there lived a farmer, his wife, and his only son who was twenty years old. One day, the farmer's horse ran away to the nearby mountains. So, his neighbors went to him and told him, "Bad luck for you, your horse is gone. Now your family will starve because you cannot till the fields." The farmer replied, "Good luck, bad luck, who knows?" Three days later, the horse returned with nine wild horses from the mountain. The villagers again went to the farmer and said, "Good luck for you. Now you have ten horses." The farmer replied, "Good luck, bad luck, who knows? A few days later, the farmer's son mounted one of the wild horses. But the horse threw him out and he broke his left leg. Again, the villagers told the farmer, "Bad luck for you. With a broken leg, your only son is useless." The farmer replied, "Good luck, bad luck, who knows?" A week later, the kingdom went to war and the king conscripted all the able-bodied young men in the village except, of course , the disabled son of the farmer. The kingdom lost the war and all the young men from the village died. And so the villagers again went to the farmer and chorused, "Good luck for you. You are the only villager with a son to inherit your farm." And the farmer replied, "Good luck, bad luck, who knows?"

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 7: Faith in God and in Ourselves
heading: Faith in God and in Ourselves
text:
Faith in God and in Ourselves (cont.)

e farmer and chorused, "Good luck for you. You are the only villager with a son to inherit your farm." And the farmer replied, "Good luck, bad luck, who knows?" Graduates, parents, ladies and gentlemen, the farmer in our little story is asking, "Good luck, bad luck, who knows?" Who indeed really knows? Only God knows! And if I must leave you anything to remember today, it is this: Regardless of anything that happens, whether it is victory or defeat, fulfillment or frustration, sadness or joy, let us always have faith in God and in ourselves. Every day we shall move on, exclaiming: "We will work as if everything depended on us. And we will pray as if everything depended on God." I thank you.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid

In the gospel reading last Sunday, February 5, 1995, the Evangelist Luke tells us that Jesus was preaching to the crowd from a fishing boat belonging to Simon Peter. When he finished speaking, he noticed that the boat was empty of any catch. So, he told Simon Peter, “Bring the boat into deeper water and lower your nets for a catch.” To this, Peter responded, “Master, we have been hard at it all night long and caught nothing: but if you say so, I will lower the nets.
Peter’s reply must have been a mixture of frustration and weariness. He and his fellow fishermen had searched the sea all night and caught nothing. At the time, fishing was normally done at night. Peter must have told himself, “What is the point of fishing by day when we caught nothing at night?” But Peter, though tired and sleepless, had faith in the Master. So he said, “If you say so, I lower the nets.”
Although the fishermen were weary, although Jesus was not an expert in fishing, although it was obvious that daylight was the wrong time for fishing, and although he knew as a fact that there were no fish around, Peter and his fishermen - in obedience - lowered their nets. It was purely out of faith and out of trust in Jesus that they did so. Peter set aside his own human knowledge, experience, instinct and "better" judgment and simply obeyed and trusted the Master.
**Faith and Obedience Are Indispensable **

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

t aside his own human knowledge, experience, instinct and "better" judgment and simply obeyed and trusted the Master.
**Faith and Obedience Are Indispensable ** In our own journey with Jesus, faith and obedience are indispensable. "Of what use are our efforts, our human resources, our wakeful vigils or even our mortifications if they are separated from any supernatural sense? Without obedience, everything is useless in God's eyes. It would be of no use starting to work if we did not intend to count on our Lord. Even our most worthwhile endeavors would be fruitless if we did not have the desire to carry out God's will." (Fr. Francis Fernandez, On Conversation with God, Vol. Three, p. 235) As St. Crysostom teaches, "God does not need our work. He needs our obedience."
Because Peter obeyed, the Lord rewarded him. In fact, he and his men caught so many fish that their two boats were filled to almost sinking capacity.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

bedience."
Because Peter obeyed, the Lord rewarded him. In fact, he and his men caught so many fish that their two boats were filled to almost sinking capacity. The miracle related in this story tells us of our own uselessness and of the utter necessity of putting our total trust in the Lord. In Him and Him alone. "This miracle shows a great clarity: that God will make possible what for man is impossible. Like Peter, we should all throw ourselves at the feet of Jesus and tell Him, 'Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man? This is our way of acknowledging the loftiness of Christ’s dignity and our own wretchedness and inability to carry out our mission without Him.” Then our Lord will take away our fear and will reveal to us, like Peter, the real purpose of our life: "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching me."
In jest, may I relate a translation joke, if only to emphasize the need to banish fear. A politician actor was before a cheering crowd when he addressed them in all seriousness. "Mga kapatid, mga kababayan. Ito po ang aking samo. Huwag kayong matatakot. Tibayan ninyo ang inyong dibdib. Sa haba ng panahon, magtatagumpay rin tayo. Uulitin ko po: Huwag kayong matatakot. Tibayan ninyo ang inyong dibdib. Sa haba ng panahon magtatagumpay rin tayo. Iingglesin ko po para tayo magkaintindihan: Do not afraid. Strengthen your inside. For in the long of time, we will success!"
**Be Not Afraid Has Biblical Roots **
Brothers and sisters, that may have been a joke. But it will serve to remind us in all seriousness to banish all fear in our lives.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

Afraid Has Biblical Roots **
Brothers and sisters, that may have been a joke. But it will serve to remind us in all seriousness to banish all fear in our lives. "Be not afraid." This is the same exhortation that Pope John Paul II resounded as the theme of his ministry in the See of St. Peter. He repeated this message several times during his last visit to the Philippines. Indeed, "Be not afraid" is mentioned many times in the Scriptures. When the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary to tell her of her impending pregnancy, he said to her: "Be not afraid." (Lk. 1:30) The same truth was proclaimed to Joseph when, upon learning of Mary's pregnancy, he decided to separate from her. The angel solemnly advised him, "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife into your home. For it is through the Holy Spirit that this child has been conceived in her." (Mt. 1:20) In other parts of the Scriptures, Ch ng exhorted His disciples with the same message rist various circumstances. He kept telling them, "Be not afraid." This was because the apostles were full of fear when Jesus was arrested , when he died and even more so after His resurrection.
In his book Crossing the Threshold of Hope (1994) our Supreme Pontiff tells us to put our faith in Jesus and not to be afraid of what men may say or do. He writes (p.219):

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

Crossing the Threshold of Hope (1994) our Supreme Pontiff tells us to put our faith in Jesus and not to be afraid of what men may say or do. He writes (p.219): Have no fear of that which you yourselves have created, have no fear of all that man has produced, and that every day is becoming more dangerous for him. Finally, have no fear of yourselves. Why should we have no fear? Because man was redeemed by God. From pronouncing these words from St. Peter's square, I already knew that my first encyclical and my entire papacy would be tied to the truth of the redemption. In the redemption we find the most profound basis of the words "Be not afraid."
… The power of Christ's Cross and Resurrection is greater than any evil which man could or should fear.
**Be Not Afraid to Be Holy **
"Be not afraid." Place your complete faith and unbending obedience in the Lord, and He will make all things possible. This is the unmistakable message of the Sacred Book. "Be not afraid." This is the resounding cry of John Paul II. "Be not afraid." This is also the Lord's special Word for us today. From this word, there are three directions to each of which I shall address the reflections I want to share with you tonight.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

Lord's special Word for us today. From this word, there are three directions to each of which I shall address the reflections I want to share with you tonight. First, do not be afraid to be holy, to be different, to lead a personal life of chastity, honesty and obedience to God's commandments and beatitudes. In concluding His sermon on the mount, Jesus Christ exhorted us: "Be perfect, just as Your heavenly Father is perfect." (Mt.5:48) By this message of Christ, Christians are called to be holy. The 1987 Synod of Bishops stated that through baptism "a person is called to a life of holiness." That is why in BLD (Bukas Loob sa Diyos), holiness is the first and foremost community value.
It is easy to think of the Pope as holy. That is why over four million people came to see him. It is easy to think of a bishop, of a priest or of a nun as holy. However, is it equally as easy to call Raffy or Willy or Josie holy? You would probably say so. This is because holiness is usually associated with men and women of the cloth.
But it should not be so. As the Bible, the Second Vatican Council and the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines proclaim, the call to holiness is universal; it is for everyone.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

so. As the Bible, the Second Vatican Council and the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines proclaim, the call to holiness is universal; it is for everyone. Many people look at holiness in terms of piety only. Holiness is more than that. In his book, The Filipino Laity: Called to Be Holy (1988), Bishop Teodoro Bacani, Jr. (on page 97) defines holiness as "simply intimate union with God by loving Him above all things and by loving our fellowmen as ourselves. Hence, the holy person is not necessarily the one who does many acts of piety but the loving person." Bishop Bacani continues (page 98):
The general rule is: what one is obliged by one's state of life to do is certainly God's will, and the performance of it helps us to grow in holiness. The important thing is to desist from identifying growth in holiness with the performance of acts of piety, and (instead) to identify growth in holiness with the loving accomplishment of whatever it is God wills for me here and now. . . . We grow in holiness through the loving performance of our ordinary tasks and obligations, and through seizing the many and oftentimes monotonous opportunities of doing good to others.
Hence, our way to holiness consists in doing our assigned tasks in the way God wants us to do them: honestly, effectively and productively. "One grows in holiness as one tries to be a good father or mother, a businessman or a politician, a student or a laborer, a farmer or a fisherman." (Cf. Bacani, op.cit., p.99)
**Holiness Is Fulfilling Our Commitments**

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

mother, a businessman or a politician, a student or a laborer, a farmer or a fisherman." (Cf. Bacani, op.cit., p.99)
**Holiness Is Fulfilling Our Commitments** In BLD, our way to holiness is doing what we have committed ourselves to do, like faithfully following The our eight-point covenant, or serving as auxiliaries during ME (Marriage Encounters) or as shepherds hop during LSS (Life in the Spirit Seminars) or simply faithfully attending and actively participating in our prayer meetings.
Mother Teresa was once asked whether she was embarrassed to hear people calling her a living saint. She replied, "What is so extraordinary about that? Are we not all called to holiness?"
Yes, we are called to holiness — lay people as well as bishops, priests and nuns, charismatics or Opus Dei members, Cursillistas or Focolares. Remember that the first Filipino Catholic saint was a lay person: San Lorenzo Ruiz.
Brothers and sisters, it is said that our transportation vehicle in heaven is determined by the depth of our holiness on earth. Three friends — Juan, Paolo and Segundo - knocked at the pearly gates one day, and they were asked by St. Peter, "How holy were you as husbands?"
This was Juan's reply: "I was a teacher and I was a very good husband. I had eyes only for my dear wife whom I served and loved faithfully."
St. Peter responded, "Excellent. Excellent. I will reward you with a brand-new Mercedes Benz so that you can travel around heaven in style."

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

loved faithfully."
St. Peter responded, "Excellent. Excellent. I will reward you with a brand-new Mercedes Benz so that you can travel around heaven in style." When his turn came, Paolo said, "I was a lawyer. And to be honest, I had a few flings but I always went home to my wife to whom I always denied my unfaithfulness."
"Well," St. Peter answered, "I will give you the benefit of the doubt for your honesty this time. So I will give you a jeep.”
The third caller placed his arms around the shoulders of St. Peter, and with moist eyes said, "Pete, I was a politician. Since I had to get as many votes as I could, I kept a wife and several mistresses. But I provided abundantly for all of them and their relatives. And they were all happy."
St. Peter replied: "Pati ba naman ako binobola mo pa? Basta, bisikleta lang ang wheels mo rito."
The three friends merrily went their separate ways traveling in their assigned vehicles. One day they met again. The last two were surprised that the Mercedes-riding Juan was sobbing. "Why are you so sad when you travel around heaven in a Chedeng? they asked.
Juan lifted his dejected face and tearfully said, "I am not complaining about my Mercedes. I am sad because I just saw my wife merrily moving about in a bicycle!"
**Be Not Afraid to Go into Mission**
Our second direction tonight is "Be not afraid to go into mission." During his visit, Pope John Paul II repeatedly exclaimed: "As the Father has sent me, so I send you!" And our response is Isaia's unconditional acceptance in the second reading: "Here I am Lord. Send me."

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

ly exclaimed: "As the Father has sent me, so I send you!" And our response is Isaia's unconditional acceptance in the second reading: "Here I am Lord. Send me." The Vicar of Christ looks to the Philippines and the fifty-five million Catholic Filipinos to lead the drive for the "new evangelization" of Asia. The world is now populated by 5 billion people but only 1 billion are Catholics. China and India alone have about 2 billion people who do not know Christ. Add Japan, Indonesia and the rest of Asia, and you have about 2.5 billion non-Catholics, about half of the world's population. US President Bill Clinton said that the Asia-Pacific area will be the center of the highest economic growth rate in the world in the coming millennium. Pope John Paul II says that this same region will witness the most miraculous movement of the Holy Spirit in fulfilling the mission that Christ entrusted to His believers: "Go the ref ore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always until the end of the age." (Mt. 28:19-20)
This command of the Lord is echoed by the Second Plenary Council of Philippines (PCP II). In words of the PCP II President, Archbishop Leonardo Z. Legaspi in his "Message of the Council to the People of God in the Philippines" (Feb. 17, 1991):
The Council's thrust is toward a New Evangelization, based not on human expectations and wisdom but on the preaching of Christ crucified to today's Filipinos and Asians.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

il's thrust is toward a New Evangelization, based not on human expectations and wisdom but on the preaching of Christ crucified to today's Filipinos and Asians. But you might say that these are big words and big plans for Asia. What can we do in BLD? Well, I say we have already started this evangelization even ahead of the Pope's visit. For two years, from 1992 to 1993, we prayed and discerned our new mission. And in 1994 we announced this mission as follows:
**Mission **
The Lord calls us to be servants of the pilgrim Church in its efforts at renewed evangelization through the following:
Restoring the Filipino family in Christ
Forming basic communities of faith (Basic Ecclesial Communities or BECs)
Strengthening the Filipino parish
Breaking the yokes of poverty and oppression
Raising an army of prayer warriors for the Church and for national renewal
BLD looks outward to the larger Philippine Church. And it is asking its members to participate actively in restoring the family, in strengthening parishes, in forming an army of prayer warriors and in breaking the yokes of poverty and oppression in our land.
Brothers and sisters, be not afraid to undertake this mission of BLD. For we have the Lord's promise: "I am with you always until the end of this age."
**Be Not Afraid of Failure **
Our third direction tonight is "Be not afraid of failure." Many times we are overwhelmed by the magnitude of our mission. We are awed by the difficulties we perceive before us.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

ion tonight is "Be not afraid of failure." Many times we are overwhelmed by the magnitude of our mission. We are awed by the difficulties we perceive before us. For example, some of our members are truly impressed by our plans for the Covenant House. At the same time they are awed by its this magnitude, its size and its cost. They ask: Why are we attempting to build the largest retreat house in the country? Can we really raise enough funds — over P60 million — to construct it?
As chairman of the BLD Foundation, I have this stock answer: "You know, BLD has been discerning this project since 1988. It has received various prophecies on it. These prophecies have been confirmed in our discernment sessions. We know in faith that our Lord wants us to build this House. His House. Since He wants it built, He will provide us with the means and funds for it. He will use our lips, our hands, our businesses, our professions as conduits to provide the funds and the means. The Lord does not directly hand out money or land. He uses His faithful ones as His instruments to implement His will. Brothers and sisters, the Lord wants us to build the Covenant House. Amen? Be not afraid! It will be built. It will be done. For our God is with us."
**If You Say So, Lord, We Will Have the Victory **

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 8: Be Not Afraid
heading: Be Not Afraid
text:
Be Not Afraid (cont.)

to build the Covenant House. Amen? Be not afraid! It will be built. It will be done. For our God is with us."
**If You Say So, Lord, We Will Have the Victory ** Yes, brothers and sisters, be not afraid of failure. Whatever we do, be it in our home, in our office or in our community, we first pray and discern. Then, we ask for confirmation of our discernment . Then and only then do we go forward boldly and bravely. Never mind the obstacles; never mind the problems. Truly, difficulties there will always be. Our Lord never promised us an easy life. He has sufficiently warned us of persecutions and trials. But we believe that for every problem, the Lord will provide a solution. For every trial, a victory. For every death, a resurrection. This is our faith. And on this faith, we place our trust.
Like Peter, we may be weary, tired and frustrated. Our human experiences, instincts and wisdom may tell us otherwise. But like Peter we say, "If you say so, Lord, we will lower the nets. If You say so, Lord, we will build Your Covenant House. If You say so, Lord, we will not fear. If You say so, Lord, we will have victory."
Praise to You, Lord Jesus Christ.

Summary
