title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time

The gospel reading last Sunday was quite short. Jesus talked about His sheep hearing His voice, knowing him and following him. Because of his, he gives them the best gift of all: eternal life. This exhortation from John 10, verses 27 to 30, is a continuation of Jesus’ famous discourse on the Good Shepherd. My reflection tonight should therefore necessarily relate to these passages on the Good Shepherd. For Jesus is our Shepherd, our Lord and Leader of all time and for all time.
These readings were intended for last Sunday, one day before the election of our new government or for our Church. There is really only one standard of leadership, as there is one leader truly worthy of emulation. And that is Jesus Christ. As we welcome our newly elected officials - senators, congressmen, governors, mayors, etc. - it is good to remind them of the standard leadership we expect of them, which are the standards of Christ himself. Jesus, our Good Shepherd, is the perfect leader whose leadership q u a l i t i e s every other leader should aspire to approximate as closely as possible. In a prayer meeting last year before (where the North Sector was not included), I had the occasion to deliver a reflection on this subject in connection with the celebration of the Feast of Christ the King.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time (cont.)

e North Sector was not included), I had the occasion to deliver a reflection on this subject in connection with the celebration of the Feast of Christ the King. Brothers and sisters in Christ, let me start by saying that Jesus is an unusual leader. His throne is a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven through His palm. His constituents betrayed Him, chanting, "Crucify Him, Crucify Him." And yet He is the only King who resurrected from the dead and by such resurrection conquered sin, not just in His own time but in all eternity. Having said that, let us reflect this evening on what kind of Jesus was a leader and is.
**Leader with a Clear Vision and Mission **
First, Jesus is a leader with a vision and mission. He made it absolutely clear who He was, what His objectives were and how He intended to accomplish them. Jesus incessantly articulated His vision and ideas. To His disciples He spoke loftily, assertively and authoritatively. His mighty sermon on the mount is the greatest teaching of all time and for all time. He leaned heavily in favor of the poor, the sorrowing, the simple-hearted and the peacemakers. He opposed the hypocrite, the arrogant, the proud and the selfrighteous. He forgave the repentant and the simplehearted.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time (cont.)

the simple-hearted and the peacemakers. He opposed the hypocrite, the arrogant, the proud and the selfrighteous. He forgave the repentant and the simplehearted. To those who were not His disciples, to the Jew ship and the Gentiles, to His opponents, he taught through parables. The parables were intended "to enable the ayer ctor listener to discover something for himself." They awakened faith and made the listener discover the truth without being told directly. That is why most of His parables ended with questions. "Which of these three, in your opinion, was neighbor to the man who fell in with the robbers?" was the by question He asked in the parable of the good Samaritan (Lk ins, 10:36); "Which of them was more grateful to him" nail in the parable of the forgiven debtors (Lk 7:42); or "What fate do you suppose the owner of the vineyard yet has in store for them?" in the parable of the tenants (Lk 20:16).
Indeed, Jesus knew who He was, what He was supposed to do and how He was to achieve His mission. He knew He would suffer and die, but also knew He would be victorious! As a great teacher, . He proclaimed His salvific mission in different ways to different listeners.
**A Leader of Courage and Conviction **

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time (cont.)

would be victorious! As a great teacher, . He proclaimed His salvific mission in different ways to different listeners.
**A Leader of Courage and Conviction ** Second, Jesus was a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction. When He walked the earth 2,000 years ago, there was no freedom of speech, and no freedom to dissent. Group conformity — particularly with the religious leaders of the time — was the only measure of truth and virtue. But Jesus did not conform. Albert Nolan, in his book Jesus Before Christianity, describes Him as "a man who has the courage of his convictions. No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted . . .  No assumption was too fundamental to be changed."
He mixed with sinners, tax collectors, a Samaritan woman, a prostitute and an adulteress. He soon acquired a "badö" reputation of being a" glutton and a drunkard." No matter. He did not seek anyone's approval but avowedly denounced sin, repeatedly called for repentance and boldly proclaimed the kingdom of God, a kingdom which is the opposite of that preached by the Jews and the Romans; a kingdom where the weak is strong and the strong is just and the just is compassionate.
He did not mince words in identifying His opponents and in denouncing their sins. He exclaimed (Mt. 23:25-27):

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time (cont.)

the strong is just and the just is compassionate.
He did not mince words in identifying His opponents and in denouncing their sins. He exclaimed (Mt. 23:25-27): Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, you frauds! You cleanse the outside of cup and dish and leave the inside filled with loot and lust! Blind Pharisee! First, cleanse the outside of the cup so that its outside may be clean. Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, you frauds! You are like whitewashed tombs, beautiful to look at on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones.
**An Exemplary Servant-Leader**
Third, Jesus was a servant-leader who led by example. In the gospel according to Mark, Jesus told His disciples:
You know how among the Gentiles those who seem to exercise authority to lord it over them; their great ones make their importance felt. It cannot be like that with you. Anyone among you who aspires to greatness must serve the rest; whoever wants to rank first among you must serve the needs of all. The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve - to give His life in ransom for the many. (Mk. 10:42-45)

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time (cont.)

ank first among you must serve the needs of all. The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve - to give His life in ransom for the many. (Mk. 10:42-45) True it is indeed, among the Gentiles, among the non-disciples: The leaders lord it over their followers. In our country, it is no different. Although our leaders are elected by the people and call themselves public servants, the sad fact is that they arrogate unto themselves power and authority over de by the life and death of our people. Hence, they allocate s told unto themselves huge discretionary funds, so they could dispense patronage and favors. So people will personally owe them the building of roads, the repair of public markets or the construction of water systems. Our leaders make themselves the center of authority such that no business can be opened without their blessings; no employment can be secured without their recommendation; and no wedding or baptism will be complete without a politician as a sponsor. Indeed, our leaders make their importance felt — not by reason of their wisdom or their service - but by the authority and the power they clothe themselves with.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
text:
Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time (cont.)

ndeed, our leaders make their importance felt — not by reason of their wisdom or their service - but by the authority and the power they clothe themselves with. Quite the opposite, Jesus did not come to be served but to serve. He gave of Himself freely and fully, not wanting or needing anything for Himself. And more than that, He led by example. To show that He was ready to perform the humblest of service, He washed the feet of His apostles telling them,, "You address me as 'Teacher' and 'Lord' and fittingly enough for that is what I am. But if I, who am Teacher and Lord, have washed your feet, then you, too, must wash each other's feet. What I did was to give you an example: as I have done for you, so you must do." (Jn 13:14-16)
**A Leader of Prayer and Faith **
Fourth, Jesus was a leader of intense prayer and unbending faith. The Bible is replete with stories of Jesus praying to His Father. Just before Jesus walked on the water, the evangelist Matthew related that He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray, remaining there alone as evening drew on." (Mt 14:23-24). In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed so intensely that His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground (Lk 22:44). And while He was nailed to the cross, He prayed aloud several times: "Father, forgive them for they know not what they do" and "Father, into Your hands I commend my spirit."
And to emphasize the great importance of pra He Himself taught His disciples the best prayer, of all, the Lord's Prayer.
**A Leader of Justice and Love**

irit."
And to emphasize the great importance of pra He Himself taught His disciples the best prayer, of all, the Lord's Prayer.
**A Leader of Justice and Love** Finally and most importantly, Jesus was a leader of justice and love. Romans, Chapter 14, Verse 17 says that "(t)he kingdom of God is not a matter of eating or drinking, but of justice, p e a c e d and the joy that is given by the Holy Spirit." Justice, f. peace and joy. These are hallmarks of Christ.
When the bible speaks of justice, it really refers to righteousness — being "right" with God. We are right with God when we obey His commandments and follow His ways. We can be right with God when we heed Jesus who said: "He who will not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me." Jesus emphasized the importance of righteousness by concluding His sermon on the mount with these words: "Seek ye first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added r unto you." (Mt. 6:33)
The Scriptures describe Jesus as the ultimate judge of all. He will come in glory with His royal angels and will pass judgment on the basis of whether f we His creatures gave food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, and comfort to the S imprisoned (Cf Mt. 26:35-40). In announcing the imminent arrival of Jesus into the world, the prophet Isaiah declared:
Here is my servant whom I uphold,
my chosen one in whom I am pleased,
Upon whom I have put my spirit;
he shall bring forth justice to the nations.
Isa. 42:1;6

:

my chosen one in whom I am pleased,
Upon whom I have put my spirit;
he shall bring forth justice to the nations.
Isa. 42:1;6 But Jesus is not only just. More than anything, He is compassionate and loving. In many parts of the gospel, Jesus showed His compassion for the crowds who followed Him. Though He was at times tired and weary, still He taught them, fed them and healed them. He never turned them down. On the contrary, He showed overwhelming love for the weak, the sick, the poor, the marginalized, the outcast and the sinner.
A good illustration of the supremacy of His love is shown in the story of the adulteress (Jn. 8:1-11). Jesus was confronted by the scribes (or canon lawyers) with a woman caught in flagrante with adultery. "Teacher," the scribes mischievously said to Him, "this woman has been caught in the act of adultery. In the law, Moses ordered such women to be stoned. What do you have to say about the case?"
You know, brothers and sisters, this was a difficult situation, for really the law, as known by the Jews, imposed the penalty of death by stoning every woman who committed adultery. If Jesus had not imposed it, He would have violated the law; and if He did, He would have virtually authorized the killing of a human being. In the face of this dilemma, Jesus replied, "Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone at her." At this, the men dispersed, for they realized that Jesus knew their many sins.

lied, "Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone at her." At this, the men dispersed, for they realized that Jesus knew their many sins. Indeed, to be just is to be wise. But justice is not the most valued virtue in the kingdom of God. It is love. As St. Paul said (1 Cor. 13):
If I speak with human and angelic tongues but do not have love, I am a noisy gong, a clanging cymbal... if I have faith great enough to move mountains, but have no love, I gain nothing... If I give everything I have to feed the poor and hand over my body to be burned but have no love, I am and nothing.
There are in the end three things that last: faith, hope and love, and the greatest of these is love.
In our modern day and age, it is difficult to imagine a leader who is just and loving at the same time. For justice is seen as aloof and objective, while e r y. love is perceived as intimate and subjective. Indeed, how can a judge impose the law as justice requires and at the same time waive the penalty as love pleads? In other words, can justice be satisfied while at the same time express the t r u e s t and dearest of icult love? The answer is YES. Let me illustrate.
There was this young lady-driver who was brought before a judge for speeding. "Young lady," solemnly intoned His Honor, "this police officer says you were driving at 100 kms. per hour in a 50-kilometer zone. What do you have to say?"
"Your Honor," grieved the young lady, "I admit my mistake. I am truly sorry and I solemnly promise I will not do it again."

eter zone. What do you have to say?"
"Your Honor," grieved the young lady, "I admit my mistake. I am truly sorry and I solemnly promise I will not do it again." "For speeding, you are hereby sentenced to pay a fine of P500," concluded the judge.
After adjourning the court session, the judge removed his black robe, went straight to the court cashier, pulled out his wallet and paid the five hundred-peso fine. He paid the penalty out of love because the law-breaker was his daughter. Justice was served — and so was love.
And this is really the story of Jesus: He is justice personified. We, His people, sinned. We violated the law of God. And so the justice of God requires our punishment. Because justice is in the nature of God, He — even if He is the most powerful being in the universe - cannot refuse to impose the sanction of the law. Otherwise, He would be violating His own nature. But Jesus is also love personified.
So, out of His great love, He came into the world and atoned for our sins. He saved us from the fury of hell. He made it possible for us to experience the never-ending joy of heaven. Jesus is the judge in our little story. He had to impose the penalty so justice could be served. But because He loves us, He bore our guilt and paid the penalty. Such is the love of Jesus.
Such is the Leader in Jesus. Such is the Shepherd that is Jesus. Such is the Shepherd of my soul.
Praise to you, Lord Jesus Christ!

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 9 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's BLD reflection on John 10:27-30 (the Good Shepherd discourse), delivered the night before the 1995 Philippine elections and offered to newly elected officials -- senators, congressmen, governors, mayors -- as the leadership measure.
He opens with an unusual-leader catalogue (wooden cross, thorns crown, reed scepter, rusty-nail ring, 'Crucify Him' constituents) before naming the only King who resurrected from the dead, then expounds five leadership qualities of Jesus as the chapter's spine.
First, clear vision and mission -- the Sermon on the Mount as 'the greatest teaching of all time,' preference for the poor and peacemakers, parables designed to make listeners 'discover something for themselves' (Lk 10:36, 7:42, 20:16).
Second, courage and conviction -- Albert Nolan's 'Jesus Before Christianity' on the courage to question tradition, sinners-and-tax-collectors company, the searing Mt 23:25-27 woes against Pharisees as 'whitewashed tombs.' Third, servant-leadership -- Mk 10:42-45 ('Anyone among you who aspires to greatness must serve the rest') is set against Filipino patronage politics in which leaders 'arrogate unto themselves power...allocate huge discretionary funds...dispense patronage and favors'; the foot-washing (Jn 13:14-16) is the example.
Fourth, prayer and faith -- the mountain retreat (Mt 14:23-24), the Gethsemane sweat 'like drops of blood' (Lk 22:44), 'Father, forgive them' and 'into Your hands I commend my spirit' from the cross, the Lord's Prayer as the model.

He closes with a judge-pays-the-fine analogy -- the speeding lady-driver case in which the judge imposes a P500 fine then removes his robe, walks to the court cashier and pays it himself because the law-breaker is his daughter ('Justice was served -- and so was love') -- and reads the atonement as the cosmic instance of this convergence: Jesus the judge imposed the law of God for sin, then bore the guilt and paid the penalty Himself.

Such is the Shepherd that is Jesus.
Such is the Shepherd of my soul.'

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 10: Offering to the Father
heading: Offering to the Father
text:
Offering to the Father

“Father, into your hands, I commend my spirit.” With these last words, Jesus died on the cross. Since then and for two thousand years - up to today and till the end of time - these eternal words will reverberate in the whole universe. Countless homilies and reflections have been written and delivered on these famous last words. The common message is that Christ’s perfect obedience to the Father in heaven led him to the cross and to His death, a death He, as the perfect human servant of the Father, freely and happily chose. As His loyal disciples and followers, we are asked to do no less, we are asked to imitate Jesus, to put ourselves in His place, to commend our spirit, and in every manner of speaking, to die for the eternal Father.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 10: Offering to the Father
heading: Offering to the Father
text:

do no less, we are asked to imitate Jesus, to put ourselves in His place, to commend our spirit, and in every manner of speaking, to die for the eternal Father. 	Two weeks ago, my six-year-old grandson Miggy proudly showed me a certificate and an academic award as an outstanding pupil given him by Southridge School, showing that he successfully passed preschool and was then qualified to enroll in Grade I. I congratulated him and asked him how he did it. He beamed and replied, “Lolo, I studied hard, did not watch television except during holidays, woke up early during school days, and did my homework every day." Then he got back his certificate and award and placed them at our little altar at home. My grandson, in his own innocent way, deprived himself of his little pleasures like watching his favorite TV shows and waking up late, studied hard and then offered his reward to the Lord. Yes, he commended his work to the Father. And by enrolling in Grade I and by promising to study even harder and thus depriving himself of more playful pleasures, he - in his own small way - intensified his personal sacrifice to be able to commend to God a greater part of himself and his work.

Each of us must bring Christ to our workplaces, to the board rooms, to schools, to the streets and every place where we are. title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 10: Offering to the Father
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 10 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's Holy Friday reflection on Luke 23:46 ('Father, into your hands, I commend my spirit'), the last words of Jesus on the cross, framed as a paradigm of perfect obedience that every disciple is invited to imitate in daily work and decisions.
He opens with a vignette of his six-year-old grandson Miggy, who told him he earned a preschool outstanding-pupil award at Southridge School by studying hard, watching no TV except during holidays, waking early, and doing his homework every day -- then placed the certificate at the home altar, a child's complete sacrifice-and-offering.
CJP then catalogues the plural Christian imitations of Christ -- contemplative hermits, priests and nuns, missionaries who 'sail the seven seas,' even flagellants -- before turning to the most ordinary form, citing Mother Teresa: 'We are all called to be Christ to others so that others may become Christ to still many others.' He develops this with a litany of ordinary vocations: a student offering his grades, a policeman patrolling honestly, a housewife preparing meals lovingly, a husband working faithfully, a businessman selling quality at reasonable prices, a government functionary discharging duties in integrity -- each lifts work to the Lord as Christ did on the cross.
Augustine's 'our hearts are restless until they rest in God' anchors a walking-wounded image of humanity; CJP supplies his own confession -- a restless young man chasing fame, fortune, power, position and possession that produced no peace and no fulfillment ('Who am I?
Why was I born?

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 10: Offering to the Father
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

n confession -- a restless young man chasing fame, fortune, power, position and possession that produced no peace and no fulfillment ('Who am I?
Why was I born? Where am I headed for?').
Only when he committed to the Father, acknowledged the Holy Spirit, and proclaimed Jesus as 'Lord and Savior, Healer and Friend' did the dual-citizenship orientation arrive: a resident of earth, truly a citizen of heaven.
He closes with a dedicatory pledge in oath form -- 'I hold my present office -- as indeed my life and my time -- by God's grace' -- and a closing prayer: 'O, Heavenly Father, into Your hands we commend our work, our minds, our lives and our spirits.
Amen.'

title: Justice and Faith -- Appendix A: A Man of God and of the Law
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Appendix A of 'Justice and Faith,' titled 'A Man of God and of the Law,' is the book-jacket-style biographical profile that organizes CJP's pre-bench identity around six topical headings -- Top-Notch Catholic Lay Leader, Well-Known Civic Leader, Former Business Leader, Popular Youth Leader, Outstanding Family Man, and Legal Philosophy -- and closes with five press blurbs from 1995-1997.
The Catholic-lay spine names CJP's 1996 appointment by Pope John Paul II to the Pontifical Council for the Laity (the only Filipino among 30 international members), his national vice chairmanship of PPCRV, secretaryship of the Council of the Laity of the Philippines, servant-leadership of the Bukas Loob sa Diyos Covenant Community, lay delegation to PCP II (Jan-Feb 1991), and parish ministry as special minister of Holy Communion.
The civic-and-business sections record CJP as founder of NUSP, president of FEU Central Student Organization, 'most illustrious knight' of Kappa Gamma Phi, president of the Rotary Club of Manila (1990-1991, the largest in Asia), president of Philippine Daily Inquirer (1991-1992), vice president of PCCI, international chairman of ASTA (first Asian to head it), president of the Organization for Tourism of the Philippines for ten years, governor of MAP for four, chief legal counsel to PPCRV, MAPSA, and the Liberal Party, and chair of the Multi-Sectoral Conference on the Administration of Justice (June 13 and October 17, 1992) that drew up the first-1,000-days program for President Ramos.

title: Justice and Faith -- Appendix A: A Man of God and of the Law
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

PCL singularity: CJP was the only Filipino among the 30 members of the Pontifical Council for the Laity at the time of his 1996 appointment by John Paul II -- a fact stated plainly in the appendix as both honor and responsibility.

Anecdote 2

Multi-Sectoral Conference on the Administration of Justice (June 13 and Oct 17, 1992) -- CJP as chair -- produced the first-1,000-days program for the Ramos presidency, an exercise in civil-society policy convening that prefigured his later reform work on the Bench.

Anecdote 3

Newsboy-to-justice arc: PDI's Oct 14, 1995 blurb names CJP as 'a former newsboy and bootblack who rose to become a prominent lawyer' -- the same biographical material CJP himself uses in the C07 honoris-causa commencement speech.

Anecdote 4

ASTA International chairmanship as first-Asian distinction: presiding over the largest travel association in the world while still in private practice in the late 1980s.

Anecdote 5

Rotary Club of Manila presidency (1990-1991) -- the largest rotary club in Asia -- and the inaugural-speech adoption of 'Love God Serve Man' as life motto, later made the title of CJP's earlier PDI-published speeches volume.

Anecdote 6

PDI 1991-1992 presidency: matches the 'someday, I'll be president of a major newspaper' line CJP records in the C07 commencement speech (he was sleeping on Sampaloc sidewalks as a newsboy when he wrote that diary line).

title: Justice and Faith -- Appendix A: A Man of God and of the Law

Anecdote 7

Children's-credentials catalogue: five children all with master's degrees from leading universities abroad -- Maria Elena (UC MBA), Jose Artemio III (Stanford MS 'with distinction'), Maria Jocelyn (Chicago MBA), Maria Theresa (Michigan MBA), Maria Evelyn (Harvard MPP) -- a deliberate counterpoint to CJP's own missed Yale opportunity recounted in C07.

Anecdote 8

Divestiture-on-elevation: CJP resigned business, professional, and most civic positions on SC appointment, keeping PCL, Rotary Manila, and Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation -- a public ethic of single-minded judicial focus stated as fact in the appendix.

Anecdote 9

Rotary inaugural pledge as closing line of CJP's self-frame: 'I shall be judged ... in my whole unworthy life here on earth' -- a self-imposed eschatological standard, characteristic of CJP's faith-anchored register.

Anecdote 10

Press-blurb dating: the Bas, Farolan, and Sison blurbs all date from late October/early November 1997, within the same fortnight as the book's publication; the PDI and Manila Bulletin blurbs date from October 1995, the week of CJP's SC oath -- bracketing the book between his appointment and his second anniversary.

The back matter of 'Justice and Faith,' titled 'From the Men of Justice and Faith,' is a short anthology of accolades from six named figures across ecclesiastical, judicial, academic, and legal-press vantage points -- Chief Justice Andres R.

The composition is itself the argument: by closing the book with six independent institutional voices -- Cardinal Archbishop of Manila, former CBCP Vice President, Chief Justice, retired Justice, legal-press publisher, and public-university president -- the back matter triangulates the man-of-God-and-of-the-law identity that the Appendix has just stated as fact, and brackets CJP's first two SC years between two clusters of endorsements (September-November 1995 around his oath; October-November 1997 around the book's publication and his second anniversary).
Reprinting Narvasa's 'twin beacons' formula at the back matter closes the volume on the same integrative frame with which it opened -- a deliberate compositional move that makes Justice and Faith the keystone of CJP's self-presentation as a debut author.

title: Justice and Faith -- Back Matter: From the Men of Justice and Faith (accolades)
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

Cardinal Sin hosted a dinner in CJP's honor on October 20, 1995 -- only ten days after CJP's SC oath -- and there delivered the line about CJP being 'a very dear friend and lay collaborator' and 'a truly Catholic lawyer, faithful to the magisterium' -- the timing makes the endorsement an early public welcome from the Cardinal Archbishop of Manila to the new SC justice.

Anecdote 2

Bishop Abaya's Sept 8, 1995 endorsement predates CJP's Oct 10, 1995 oath -- meaning the Church's recognition of CJP as 'a man of God and of our Church' was in place before the JBC's final list was confirmed; the dating implicitly hints at the spiritual-discernment process CJP himself describes in C06 ('Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court').

Anecdote 3

Tayabas's Nov 2, 1995 endorsement (in the third week of CJP's tenure) anchors the academic-civic vantage point: a public-university president identifying CJP as 'an exemplary model' immediately after his arrival on the Bench.

Anecdote 4

Cruz's Oct 15, 1997 letter and Syquia's Oct 31, 1997 attestation come at the very moment of CJP's second anniversary on the Bench and the book's publication -- the late-1997 endorsements close the temporal arc the early-1995 endorsements opened.

title: Justice and Faith -- Back Matter: From the Men of Justice and Faith (accolades)
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 5

The Syquia line is the only accolade that explicitly engages a potential criticism (the quality-vs-quantity tradeoff) and rebuts it: 'despite the quantity of his decisions, they are also 'quality' as well as clear and readable' -- the 'despite' word is doing the rhetorical work, acknowledging that the criticism could be raised and then refuting it.

Anecdote 6

Six independent institutional vantage points -- Cardinal, Bishop, Chief Justice, retired Justice, legal-press publisher, public-university president -- are arranged in the back matter so no single endorsement carries the whole weight; the strategy is plural attestation, not amplification.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.)
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.)
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.)

Foreword
FROM THE CHAMBERS OF
Hilario G. Davide Jr.
CHIEF JUSTICE
Innovations and new discoveries in science and technology have been occurring at virtually the “speed of thought," to adopt Bill Gates’ colorful phrase. That statement is not entirely an exaggeration when one ponders the wonders of the human mind’s creativity and inventiveness. Our laws and judicial doctrines would, sooner rather than later, be tested to the limits in adapting to a rapidly changing world. The Judiciary must be on its toes to keep in step with these developments so that it can successfully grapple with complex scientific and technological issues. Unfortunately, there is, as yet, no body of legal literature which addresses  this looming challenge to the knowledge and skills of our brethren in the Bench and Bar. Happily, however, this is the subject of Justice Artemio V. Panganiban’s latest book, The Bio-age Dawns on the Judiciary.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.)
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.)
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.) (cont.)

of our brethren in the Bench and Bar. Happily, however, this is the subject of Justice Artemio V. Panganiban’s latest book, The Bio-age Dawns on the Judiciary. The uneasy relationship between science and jurisprudence is immediately juxtaposed in the very first chapter of this book when Justice Panganiban tackles the role of the courts in the dawning of the bio-age with its myriad of legal, technological, and ethical problems and consequences. Dissecting a fictional case framed by Dr. Franklin M. Zweig on  "human cloning, genetic engineering, cell-line development, and patenting of genes,” Justice Panganiban  "Filipinized" the case and discusses its legal mutations and possible implications in the administration of justice and the rule of law. It may easily be overwhelming to be confronted by the unfamiliar argot of the bio-sciences and their novel repercussions on the body politic.
As in his previous books, Part II (consisting of eight chapters) is a first person account of what this jurist had previously termed as the “judicial jousts” in which he has played a prominent, if not the leading, role. Evoking the image of white knights in their shining armor, the justices are also portrayed as dragon-slayers of the evils that bedevil our country and people.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.)

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Foreword (by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.) (cont.)

. Evoking the image of white knights in their shining armor, the justices are also portrayed as dragon-slayers of the evils that bedevil our country and people. Indeed, the Supreme Court recently promulgated its landmark decision in the impeachment case against the Chief Justice. The decision is a tribute to the strength and fortitude of our democratic institutions and their leaders who have reaffirmed their faith and confidence in the Supreme Court as the sole arbiter of constitutional questions. Still following the months of incessant assault on the independence and integrity of the Supreme Court, the publication and release of Justice Panganiban’s book is timely, and reading it provides a welcome diversionary pre-occupation.
As Justice Panganiban’s seventh book as a sitting magistrate, The Bio-age Dawns on the Judiciary faithfully chronicles the events in the immediately preceding twelve months of his eighth anniversary in the Supreme Court. It has been a source of amazement to me and our colleagues how he has managed this while writing many ponencias and separate opinions, plus hundreds of minute resolutions. We are grateful for his energy as we benefit from his display of his prolificacy and mental dexterity in this legal treatise which extricates the possible from the hypothetical, the emerging from the established, the literature in science, and the law in art.
Hilario G. Davide Jr.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface

PREFACE
As my small contribution to transparency, I try to report on my work as a member of the Supreme Court yearly, in book form. The present volume covers the salient events during my eighth year in office, from October 10, 2002 to October 10, 2003.
As its title suggests, this book aims to call attention to the new biosciences and biotechnologies, especially how they affect the judiciary's work of decision-making.
It has often been said that law is a jealous mistress that demands constant attention and continuous study. It requires understanding and appreciation, not only of its own disciplines and rules, but also of every facet of life and learning. Consequently, jurists and lawyers should not be merely walking computers of the Constitution, the codes and jurisprudence; they should also have a working knowledge of all branches of human endeavors, including the arts, economics, accounting, mathematics, finance, health, computers, political science, medicine, history, and the latest sciences and technologies.
In the distant past, the preoccupation was feeding and sheltering the population. Hence, the main concern of the world during the agricultural age was land and food production. As a consequence, law and jurisprudence also concentrated on these two subjects.
On the other hand, during the industrial revolution, the world's attention shifted to factories, machineries and tools that were used in the production of wealth. Thus, the judiciary had to adjust to new norms in commercial transactions, corporate structures, taxation, economic indicators and labor requirements.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface (cont.)

f wealth. Thus, the judiciary had to adjust to new norms in commercial transactions, corporate structures, taxation, economic indicators and labor requirements. The third wave of civilization - the information age revolutionized the world through computerization, miniaturization, digitization, satellite communications, fiber optics and the Internet. All these developments, taken together, integrate knowledge on a worldwide scale. As I said in my book Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity, these massive technologies "changed not only the economic face of the globe, but also everything else that matters - political systems, lifestyles, work habits, sciences, philosophies, and yes, even the normally reclusive and exclusive enclave of decision-making."
And now, while still trying to adjust to the transformational shifts of the information age, the world is once more buffeted by a new phenomenon - the completion of the human genome sequence on April 14, 2003. This is a momentous scientific achievement of far-reaching consequence to all of humankind, including the men and women of the judiciary.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface (cont.)

nce on April 14, 2003. This is a momentous scientific achievement of far-reaching consequence to all of humankind, including the men and women of the judiciary. The term "genome" refers to the totality of genetic information in a human being. Because of the completion of the sequencing project, scientists now have a complete list of the relevant parts of the human gene. It is as if all the parts of an airplane have been inventoried, thereby presaging the inevitability of assembling them into a new flying machine or - if such machine has already been assembled - of scientifically repairing a worn-out one. The completion of the project makes it possible for scientists to study, experiment on, modify or alter genetic structures to prolong life" and hasten the pace of evolution.
In our Supreme Court, the awareness of these momentous scientific developments heightened on November 14, 2000, when Dr. Franklin M. Zweig delivered a paper on "Life Technologies and the Rule of Law" as part of the Centenary Lecture Series conducted in 2000-2001 to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Court.
For the Philippine judiciary as a whole, I believe that the defining event that ushered the dawn of the bio-age was the Conference-Workshop on Bioscience and Biotechnology held on August 26-29, 2003 in Tagaytay City, because it involved not only the Supreme Court but also selected lower court judges nationwide. It was during this event that the backbone of the judicial system - the trial courts - learned of the impact of the new sciences on decision-making.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface (cont.)

nationwide. It was during this event that the backbone of the judicial system - the trial courts - learned of the impact of the new sciences on decision-making. My personal participation in this seminar is discussed in Chapter 1, "Enter the Bio-Age." This initial part of the book assesses the intricacies of the new sciences and the applicability, the relevancy and the adequacy of current laws and jurisprudence to meet their challenges.
For those interested in a more in-depth discussion of the new sciences and technologies and their impact on jurisprudence, I have included as Appendices to this book - with the permission of the authors - selected papers submitted during the Tagaytay Conference by Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing, Dr. Pacifico A. Agabin and Fr. Ranhilio C. Aquino. I have also reprinted an Appendix of Dr. Franklin M. Zweig's paper entitled “Life Technologies and the Rule of Law," delivered during the Supreme Court Centenary Lecture Series. These dissertations, I believe, are essential to a well-rounded understanding of the bio-age as it dawns on the Philippine judiciary.
Chapter 2 was my lecture during the First Australasia Judicial Educators Forum. It speaks of paradigm shifts in law brought about by the gigantic strides in other fields of human knowledge, especially the informational and technological revolution, unfolding in the world. Here, I tried to interrelate the information age with the incoming bio-era. I also discussed the many Supreme Court Decisions issued in response to new questions raised by the information age.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Preface (cont.)

information age with the incoming bio-era. I also discussed the many Supreme Court Decisions issued in response to new questions raised by the information age. The rest of Part I speaks of the relevance of legal education and legal practice in the evolution of knowledge in various fields. It also contains "A Primer on the APJR" to keep the readers informed of developments in this major program of the Davide Court.
Part II, on the other hand, discusses the controversial cases rendered by the Court during this same one-year period (2002-2003), in which I took an active part as ponente or as the writer of a separate, concurring or dissenting opinion. It also includes my Dissenting Opinion in the Resolution of the Court promulgating the new "Rule on Declaration of Absolute Nullity of Void Marriages and Annulment of Voidable Marriages."
May I also report in all humility that I was able to write over 100 full-length decisions and six separate opinions during this one-year period, thus bringing my grand total during all of my eight years in office, as of October 10, 2003, at more than 860 ponencias (full-length, signed decisions) and 74 separate opinions. This count does not include the thousands of unsigned minute resolutions I have also penned during those eight years.
The net effect of this production is that all the cases assigned to me have been decided within the two-year constitutional mandate. In other words, I have no backlog.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 3: How the SC Decides Cases
heading: How the SC Decides Cases
text:
How the SC Decides Cases

Date:       2009-06-21
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Without asking for comment, the Supreme Court correctly threw out the petitions assailing the validity of House Resolution 1109. However, the Court still gave them special treatment by issuing a signed resolution extensively explaining its action. Normally, to show its disdain for utterly unmeritorious and "cerebrally deficient" petitions, it simply dismisses them via one-sentence resolutions. To explain, let me write a primer on how the Court decides cases in the normal course.
**Review court**
As a rule, the Supreme Court does not take initial cognizance of controversies. It merely reviews decisions of other tribunals;its work consists mainly of affirming, modifying or reversing decisions or orders of lower courts; and of determining whether a lower court, or an agency of the government including the president and Congress), acted without or in excess of its jurisdiction or committed grave abuse of discretion.
On its own, the Supreme Court does not initiate such review. Its authority must be triggered by the filing of a petition by a proper party. In this sense, the Court (and the entire judiciary) is a "passive branch" of the government. It cannot act on a controversy unless asked to do so.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 3: How the SC Decides Cases
heading: How the SC Decides Cases
text:
How the SC Decides Cases (cont.)

proper party. In this sense, the Court (and the entire judiciary) is a "passive branch" of the government. It cannot act on a controversy unless asked to do so. In trial courts, the proceedings are open to the public. But in the Supreme Court the internal deliberations are confidential; only their net results, written in the form of decisions, resolutions, orders, and opinions (concurring, dissenting, and separate), are released to the public. Emphasizing the sacredness of. Regalado said, collegial deliberations, retired Justice Florenz D "In trial courts, the rule is transparency; but in the Supreme Court, it is confidentiality."
**Collegial decisions**
The justices debate and vote independently of each other but they decide collegially. Thus, all court actions are determined during sessions. Except in emergencies, no justice can act individually to bind the Court. Even simple motions for extension of time are calendared and acted upon by the Court as a collegial body.
The agenda of the Court (whether en banc or in division) usually consists of about 150 to 250 items per session. The Court disposes each of them speedily, but the backbreaking job is done in chambers and at home, when the justices study, read, reflect, pray, and write on the matters assigned to them.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 3: How the SC Decides Cases
heading: How the SC Decides Cases
text:
How the SC Decides Cases (cont.)

hem speedily, but the backbreaking job is done in chambers and at home, when the justices study, read, reflect, pray, and write on the matters assigned to them. Of course, prior to the session, they also need to study the reports of their fellow justices, so they can express concurrence or dissent to, or at least intelligently discuss, the items in the agenda. Nothing is more embarrassing than to be caught unprepared or to be unable to answer questions on matters being reported on.
Verbal discussions are very limited. Contrary to popular impressions, justices do not talk too much. Rather, they write a lot. Arguments, reflections, and position papers are exchanged every day. When the verbal discussion of a case exceeds five minutes, the chief justice normally postpones further discussions, with the suggestion that members write their opinions, pro and contra, to be distributed a few days prior to the next calendar. Oral arguments are usually held in the cavernous and rather intimidating hearing hall of the Court on Padre Faura Street.
Oral arguments, which are rare, are usually held only in cases involving difficult and complicated questions.
The Court delineates the issues; and the lawyers for each side, who are expected to come extensively prepared, dwell on these issues within the allotted time, normally 20 minutes each. However, the justices may, and usually do, ask questions on any topic or issue. Hence, the allotted time is usually extended.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 3: How the SC Decides Cases
heading: How the SC Decides Cases
text:
How the SC Decides Cases (cont.)

ed time, normally 20 minutes each. However, the justices may, and usually do, ask questions on any topic or issue. Hence, the allotted time is usually extended. During oral arguments, the Court sometimes appoints amici curiae (friends of the court) to assist the justices in resolving difficult questions. An invitation to act as amicus curiae is a rare privilege granted only to lawyers of unquestioned stature, competence, and lucidity. After the oral arguments, the lawyers are usually required to file written memoranda.
**En banc or in division**
The Court regularly sits en banc (all members of the Court) and in division (five members each). To grant a motion or petition and to approve a decision or resolution, the concurrence of a majority of those taking part is sufficient. The distribution of the justices to the three divisions is determined by the chief justice, who usually spreads the senior and the junior justices more or less evenly among the three groups.
Seniority based on the date of appointment is strictly observed in seating arrangements. En banc, the chief justice sits at the head of the table, with the most senior justice on his right next to the first, the fourth most senior sits next to the second, and so on down to the fifteenth who sits at the foot of the table on the chief justice's left. The seniority rule is observed also in the divisions, with the chairman sitting at the head of the table.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 3: How the SC Decides Cases
heading: How the SC Decides Cases
text:
How the SC Decides Cases (cont.)

at the foot of the table on the chief justice's left. The seniority rule is observed also in the divisions, with the chairman sitting at the head of the table. The foregoing seating arrangement is followed also during oral arguments, except that instead of sitting around a table, the justices sit on an elevated crescent-shaped rostrum facing the audience.
The most senior member usually chairs each division. A-l though the chief justice is also a division chairman, his functions as chair are actually performed by the "working chairman," who is the next most senior in the division. (June 21, 2009)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 5: Chief Justice of the Philippines
heading: Chief Justice of the Philippines
text:
Chief Justice of the Philippines

Date:       2009-12-27
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
In times of turmoil and crisis, our people have learned to depend on the Supreme Court for direction and salvation. Normally, they should really look to their elected leaders, the president and the members of Congress. Ironically, however, the abusive and illegal acts complained of by our people come mainly from executive officials. Under these circumstances, our people inevitably turn to the chief justice to lead the Supreme Court in protecting their rights. What are the CJ's functions?
1. Primus inter pares. Among the 15 members of our Supreme Court, the CJ is the primus inter pares (first among equals) who presides over its sessions, controls the flow of its proceedings, shapes its agenda, summarizes the discussions, and influences the direction and pace of the Court's work. Nonetheless, the CJ has only one vote. Thus, the CJ relies on moral ascendancy and persuasive skill, not on a boss-subordinate relationship, to sway the Court.
2. Leader of the entire judiciary. The CJ is not just the primus in the highest court. He is also the chief executive officer (or CEO) of the entire judiciary composed of 2,000 lower court judges and 26,000 judicial employees nationwide. He is the leader who inspires, motivates, and moves them to work unceasingly, to rise above their puny limitations, to excel beyond themselves, and to achieve collectively their loftiest dreams and highest aspirations.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 5: Chief Justice of the Philippines
heading: Chief Justice of the Philippines
text:
Chief Justice of the Philippines (cont.)

o work unceasingly, to rise above their puny limitations, to excel beyond themselves, and to achieve collectively their loftiest dreams and highest aspirations. While the jurist in him impels the CJ to follow tradition, to uphold precedents and stabilize judicial thought, the leader in him requires him to innovate, to re-engineer, and to invent new and better ways of moving forward the judicial branch.
3. Passionate reformer and action person. Because the judiciary, like the two other branches of government, must cope with the fast changing judicial, social, economic, and technological environment, the CJ must have a passion for reforms to assure speedy and equal justice for all.
This mission requires not only knowledge of law but also interaction with other offices, agencies, persons-both public and private and even with foreign governments and international institutions. Also, to keep up with the Information Age, the judiciary must automate and computerize.
How to interact with officials and citizens, some of whom may have pending cases in the courts, without arousing public suspicion is a really sensitive balancing act. To be able to do this, the CJ, more than any other official, must rely on deep public trust in his personal integrity and independence.
4. Leader of the bar. Because supervision over the practice of law is vested in the Supreme Court by the Constitution, all lawyers look up to the CJ for guidance in their profession. This is why all bar associations want to listen to the CJ, especially a new one, for direction and inspiration.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 5: Chief Justice of the Philippines
heading: Chief Justice of the Philippines
text:
Chief Justice of the Philippines (cont.)

k up to the CJ for guidance in their profession. This is why all bar associations want to listen to the CJ, especially a new one, for direction and inspiration. 5. Academic and maestro. As ex-officio chair of the Philippine Judicial Academy, the CJ is viewed as a guru, who is expected to make the continuing education of judges a passion and vocation. For this reason and because of lack of government resources, the CJ, without compromising judicial independence and integrity, is often constrained to turn to outside assistance.
6. Mover and shaker. As chairperson of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), the CJ is expected to find new and better ways of searching for, screening, and selecting applicants for judgeships. This job is critical. The need for quality judgments begins with quality judges.
This imperative impels the CJ to move into non-judicial endeavors, like working for better compensation, better security, and better working conditions and facilities for judges. Only by securing better pay, better security, and better facilities will the JBC be able to entice the best and the brightest attorneys to join B the judiciary.
7. Administrator, manager, and financial wizard. The Constitution vests in the Supreme Court "administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof," as well as the appointment of its officials and employees.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 5: Chief Justice of the Philippines
heading: Chief Justice of the Philippines
text:
Chief Justice of the Philippines (cont.)

on vests in the Supreme Court "administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof," as well as the appointment of its officials and employees. This means that the CJ must be a visionary administrator, efficient manager, and sensible financial wizard all at the same time. Several laws, like the Administrative Code and the General Appropriations Act, place on the CJ the responsibility for steering the entire judicial department. The Judiciary Development Fund Law (PD 1949) and the Special Allowance for the Judiciary (SAJ) Law (RA 9227) give the CJ the "exclusive sole power" to disburse the JDF and SAJ funds.
8. Role model and exemplar of public service. Our people especially the young, look up to the CJ as an exemplar and role model. Because of our inquisitive media and open society, every public official is subjected to minute scrutiny. In their search for heroes, our people often look up to the CJ as their choice of an upright public servant.
Especially during these periods of political wrangling, civic groups and non-partisan organizations turn to the chief justice to grace their seminars and inductions. They find solace and peace in his quiet persona.
In sum, the CJ is expected to lead our highest court in its critical role as the last bulwark of democracy. Beyond that, he a tends to many sensitive, non-judicial leadership duties that take him to the farthest corners of the country. That is why he is mor accurately addressed as the , not just Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. (December 27, 2009)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 7: Demystifying the Court
heading: Demystifying the Court
text:
Demystifying the Court

Date:       2010-07-04
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
The recent controversy on the power of the president to appoint a chief justice during the ban on midnight appointments focused public attention on the Supreme Court. Yet, the Court remains the most mysterious among major government agencies. Save in a few high-profile cases, the public discovers a case only after a judgment is issued. Unlike the trial courts where the litigants and the public can monitor hearings, the high court's processes are not generally known.
**Codifying the secrets**
For this reason, I made it my self-imposed duty, during my more than 1 years in the Supreme Court, to write a book each year to demystify the judicial processes and to report to the public the Court's work for that year. Recently, the Court did even better. On May 4, 2010, it issued Resolution A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC that codified its little known processes and published them as “The Interna Rules of the Supreme Court”
Right from the beginning, the Internal Rules emphatically provide a generally caveat: “Nothing in these Rules shall be interpreted to preclude or limit the exercise of the power and authority of the Court as provided in the Constitution, the applicable laws, and the Rules of Court." This simply means that, at any time, the Rules may "be amended, revised, deleted, suspended or dispensed with in particular cases, upon such terms as the Court en banc may decide to be just, fair and proper."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 7: Demystifying the Court
heading: Demystifying the Court
text:
Demystifying the Court (cont.)

ay "be amended, revised, deleted, suspended or dispensed with in particular cases, upon such terms as the Court en banc may decide to be just, fair and proper." In fulfilling its tasks, the Court acts either en banc (where all its members participate) or in three divisions, each composed of five members. A decision rendered by any of the three divisions is deemed a decision of the Court itself, as valid, binding, effective, and final as any judgment rendered by the Court en banc.
Which cases are to be heard and decided by the Court en banc to be heard and decided by the divisions, except the very important ones enumerated in Section 3, Rule 2, which include cases questioning the constitutionality or validity of a treaty, law or executive order; imposing the death penalty or reclusion perpetual raising novel questions of law; reversing earlier jurisprudence; or involving a huge financial impact on business.
**Not appealable to the banc**
Controversial but well settled is the rule that the Court en banc does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the divisions. Otherwise stated, the banc—as a rule does not reverse or modify decisions and actions made by the divisions. Moreover, a denial by a division of a motion to refer a case to the banc is "final and not appealable" to the banc. And the banc may "in the absence of sufficiently important reasons, decline to take cognizance of a case referred to it" by a division.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 7: Demystifying the Court
heading: Demystifying the Court
text:
Demystifying the Court (cont.)

appealable" to the banc. And the banc may "in the absence of sufficiently important reasons, decline to take cognizance of a case referred to it" by a division. Despite these stringent pronouncements, which are not new but merely codified in the Internal Rules, several division judgment s have in the past been elevated to and reversed or modified by the banc. These extraordinary actions of reviewing division decisions by the banc have all been done under the all embracing power, mentioned earlier, to amend, revise, delete, suspend or dispense with the Internal Rules, as the Court en bane "may decide to be just, fair and proper."
Yearly, our Supreme Court receives about 6,000 new cases which it acts on, either by means of unsigned minute resolutions denying due course immediately, or by unsigned extended resolutions, or by full-blown signed decisions or resolutions, commonly called ponencias.
In comparison, available statistics reveal that the US Supreme Court receives about 10,000 petitions each year. Of these, it selects and accepts about 100 cases to be granted plenary review with oral argument, and another 50 to 60 to be resolved without plenary review. Everything else is rejected and dismissed. With a smaller membership of nine and a lighter caseload, the US Supreme Court always acts en banc.
**Raffle system**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 7: Demystifying the Court
heading: Demystifying the Court
text:
Demystifying the Court (cont.)

Everything else is rejected and dismissed. With a smaller membership of nine and a lighter caseload, the US Supreme Court always acts en banc.
**Raffle system** About 30 new cases are raffled monthly to each justice in our high court, to be added to his or her existing caseload of from 300 to over 1,000 cases. Still, our Court manages to render, on the average, anywhere from 1,200 to 1,500 full-length decisions a year (not counting thousands of unsigned minute and extended resolutions).
Under the Internal Rules, as in past practices, the assignment of a new case via raffle occurs almost immediately after the case is filed. Every initiatory pleading (that commences the case), after being docketed at the Judicial Records Office and given an identification number, is raffled among the 15 justices.
The difference is that in the past, the justice to whom a case is raffled automatically became the ponente. Now, per Section 1 of Rule 7 of the Internal Rules, the justice to whom a case is raffled becomes the "Member-in-Charge" who oversees the case's progress and disposition, prepares the initial and final reports, and leads the deliberations throughout; but may or may not become ponente.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 7: Demystifying the Court
heading: Demystifying the Court
text:
Demystifying the Court (cont.)

oversees the case's progress and disposition, prepares the initial and final reports, and leads the deliberations throughout; but may or may not become ponente. Section 5 of Rule 13 provides that immediately upon arriving at a conclusion regarding the issues in the case, the Court shall assign a member to write the opinion of the Court (but does not say how the designation of the ponente will be done). Should a majority of the justices vote affirmatively, this becomes the ponencia or decision. However, if it does not get the necessary votes, the majority will appoint a new ponente, usually the main dissenter. Then, the erstwhile ponencia may be converted into a dissenting opinion. (July 4, 2010)

He recalls making it his 'self-imposed duty' to write a book each year to explain the Court's work, and notes that the Court itself did better on May 4, 2010 by codifying its processes as 'The Internal Rules of the Supreme Court' (A.M.
No.

He explains that the Court sits en banc or in three five-member divisions, that 'a decision rendered by any of the three divisions is deemed a decision of the Court itself,' and that the most important cases (constitutionality of a treaty, law or EO; the death penalty; novel questions; reversals of jurisprudence; huge financial impact) are reserved to the banc.
He lays out the 'controversial but well settled' rule that the banc does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the divisions -- a division's denial of a referral motion is 'final and not appealable' -- while candidly noting that the banc has at times still reviewed and reversed division judgments under its power to suspend the Rules.

nal and not appealable' -- while candidly noting that the banc has at times still reviewed and reversed division judgments under its power to suspend the Rules. On workload, he contrasts the Court's roughly 6,000 new cases and 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year with the US Court's ~10,000 petitions and ~100 acceptances, and describes the raffle system (about 30 cases a month per justice) and the new 'Member-in-Charge' role, which oversees a case but may not become its ponente -- so that if a draft ponencia loses the vote, the main dissenter writes the decision and the old draft becomes a dissent.

text:

A book a year: CJP recounts making it his 'self-imposed duty,' over his years on the Court, to write a book annually 'to demystify the judicial processes and to report to the public the Court's work for that year.'

Anecdote 2

6,000 vs. 10,000 -- but 100 accepted: he contrasts the Philippine Court's roughly 6,000 new cases and 1,200-1,500 full decisions a year with the US Court's ~10,000 petitions, of which only about 100 are accepted for plenary review.

Anecdote 3

30 cases a month: he reports that each justice is raffled about 30 new cases monthly atop a backlog of 300 to over 1,000 -- a vivid measure of the workload behind the robes.

Anecdote 4

Ponente becomes dissenter: under the new Rules, he explains, if a draft ponencia fails to win a majority, the would-be ponente's opinion 'may be converted into a dissenting opinion,' and the main dissenter writes the decision.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 1: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
heading: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
text:
Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets

Date:       2007-05-27
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
At present, the fewer than 2,000 incumbent judges are saddled with about a million pending cases. This means that, on the average, each judge has to shepherd over 500 cases, a horrendous task by any standard. Moreover, the loads are not uniformly distributed; some judges have as many as 6,000 cases while others have a more manageable 200.
**Alternatives to litigation**
Despite best efforts, the case congestion worsens every day due mainly to the avalanche of new filings. Besides, the rendition of a judgment by a lower court may not necessarily reduce the total backlog. It may merely mean a shift of the burden to an appellate court.
To move the wheels of justice faster, the Supreme Court, via the on-going Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), is undertaking several measures, like getting more judges appointed, making them work harder, computerizing the judicial system, streamlining the Rules of Court, and promoting the use of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) methods. I will focus on mediation.
A full-blown litigation has many disadvantages. It is tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive, and often ends up in broken relationships and permanent animosities. Instead of healing controversies, judgments sometimes inflict deeper social wounds and engender vengeance as well as new cycles of violence.
**Win-win solutions**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 1: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
heading: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
text:
Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets (cont.)

stead of healing controversies, judgments sometimes inflict deeper social wounds and engender vengeance as well as new cycles of violence.
**Win-win solutions** On the other hand, mediation solves disputes speedily, conveniently, peacefully, and less expensively. Being less confrontational, it conforms to the Filipino way of ending problems sans loss of face. It produces "win-win" solutions. Since it is conducted diplomatically by professional mediators, it can even improve relationships among the parties after the problem is solved. It may be used prior to, or concurrent with, an actual court litigation.
Mediation is not a newly minted technique. It is as old as civilization itself. In the past, however, it has been frowned upon by the judicial establishment on the theory that it ousts the courts of their jurisdiction. But now, the e-age trend is to welcome all methods to end disputes speedily and conveniently so the judiciary can focus on public interest cases that can neither be mediated nor compromised.
To test the effectiveness of mediation, the Supreme Court T asked the Philippine Judicial Academy (Philja) in early 2001 to train initially about 400 mediators. After finishing their training, the mediators worked on actual cases pending in the National Capital Region, Cebu, and Davao. Voila! In less than two weeks, they were able to settle 80 percent of the 1,000 cases referred to them, some of which were more than 10 years old!

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 1: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
heading: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
text:
Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets (cont.)

u, and Davao. Voila! In less than two weeks, they were able to settle 80 percent of the 1,000 cases referred to them, some of which were more than 10 years old! The Supreme Court was so impressed with this pilot program that it institutionalized court-annexed/referred mediation as a tool for decongesting court dockets. It mandated the Philja to prepare a curriculum to educate mediators and it established the Philippine Mediation Center (PMC), with units all over the country, as their home. A mediation fee is now collected for eveyr new case filed. And all new cases, with the exception of the "non-mediatable" ones, are subjected to mandatory mediation as an essential part of the pretrial proceedings.
**Second phase of court-annexed mediation**
If the mediation is unsuccessful, the pretrial will then proceed. However, a "phase two" mediation, called "Judicial Dispute Resolution" or JDR for short, has been successfully piloted in the San Fernando, Pampanga and Bacolod regional trial courts (RTCs). Here, the pretrial judge (to be called the JDR judge) tries to resurrect the failed process conducted by the professional mediators. This is an innovation proposed by the National Judicial Institute of Canada.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 1: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
heading: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
text:
Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets (cont.)

dge) tries to resurrect the failed process conducted by the professional mediators. This is an innovation proposed by the National Judicial Institute of Canada. Using their moral ascendancy, the previously trained JDR judges act as "conciliators" and reconcile the differences of the parties. The JDR judges may also take the role of "neutral evaluators" and make non-binding assessments of the parties' claims and arguments. If the JDR judges still fail to persuade the parties to settle, the case is then re-raffled to a new judge for trial and judgment. The JDR judge is prohibited from discussing with the new trial judge anything taken up during the failed mediation. And any offer or admission made during the JDR is not admissible in evidence during the trial. A knowledgeable JDR pioneer is Executive Judge Adelaida Ala-Medina of the San Fernando RTC.
**A new profession**
Mediation has become a new profession. Court-annexed mediators are now screened and trained professionally by the Philja. After passing an internship program, they are accredited by the Supreme Court. Mediators need not be lawyers, but they are required to have a four-year bachelor's degree. Like attorneys, they are deemed "officers of the courts."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 1: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
heading: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
text:
Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets (cont.)

eme Court. Mediators need not be lawyers, but they are required to have a four-year bachelor's degree. Like attorneys, they are deemed "officers of the courts." I was so convinced about the need for ADRs to solve our festering backlog problem that, prior to my retirement as chief justice, I convened a two-day "National Conference on Court annexed ADR Mechanisms" on November 27 to 28, 2006. During this confab, which was funded by the United States Agency for International Development and The Asia Foundation, court annexed mediation was singled out for some amazing results. For instance, of the 35,223 cases mediated from 2002 to October 2006, about 24,983 were settled, translating to a 71-percent success rate! (May 27, 2007)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 3: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Role of the Judicial and Bar Council

Date:       2007-09-09
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Congress makes the laws and the president enforces them. Sometimes, these laws collide with the fundamental rights of our people, either in the way they are crafted by Congress or in the manner the president and other officials enforce or "apply" them.
**Importance of judicial independence**
In a constitutional democracy such as ours, political issues are settled by popular or majoritarian ways. However, unelected judges decide legal questions by applying relevant laws to a proven set of facts. When a court upholds the rights of a citizen, or acquits a person accused of a crime by the "People of the Philippines," the winner becomes a majority of one against the whole government.
This awesome power to decide even against the "people" is granted to the judiciary by the Constitution, which, in turn, was approved overwhelmingly by the electorate. But citizens obey judicial verdicts not only because of the authority given to judges by the Constitution but also because of their implicit trust in the wisdom and fairness of these decisions.
To help retain public confidence in our judicial system, magistrates should be chosen prudently. I believe that they must possess four "nis"— independence, integrity, industry, and intelligence, and must be impervious to the "plague of ships" — kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 3: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Role of the Judicial and Bar Council (cont.)

"nis"— independence, integrity, industry, and intelligence, and must be impervious to the "plague of ships" — kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship. Of these qualifications, independence and integrity are probably the most vital, especially in litigation involving actions of the president or of other executive officials. A judge who does not possess independence and integrity does not deserve to be in the judiciary, in the same manner that a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.
**How magistrates are chosen**
In the past, the President was given maximum latitude in appointing any lawyer who meets the minimum length of law practice imposed by law. However, before they assumed office, the appointees needed confirmation by the Commission on Appointments (CA), that was (and still is) composed of members of Congress.
In those days, judicial appointees were subjected not only to intensive questioning by the CA but also to various personal demands for favors by its members. Congressmen required the loyalty of judges assigned to their districts. Those promoted to higher courts were publicly ridiculed for their alleged erroneous decisions. In short, the appointees' integrity and independence were unnecessarily diminished by reckless imputations and political power plays.
To remedy the problem, the 1987 Constitution—at the suggestion of former Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion- created the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) with the "principal function

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 3: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Role of the Judicial and Bar Council (cont.)

lem, the 1987 Constitution—at the suggestion of former Chief Justice Roberto Concepcion- created the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) with the "principal function of recommending appointees to the Judiciary." True, the new Charter still empowered the President to appoint all magistrates, including those on the Supreme Court, but the presidential choices were limited to a JBC-prepared list containing at least three nominees for every vacancy. Magistrates no longer needed A confirmation; thus, they were liberated from undue congressional inquisitions.
**Composition of the JBC**
Under the new Constitution, the JBC is composed of (1) the Chief Justice as chairman, (2) the secretary of justice, (3) a representative of Congress, (4) a representative of the Integrated Bar, (5) a professor of law, (6) a retired Supreme Court justice, and (7) a representative of the private sector. The first three are referred to as "ex-officio members" while the last four, "regular members."
True, the Constitution specified "a representative of Congress." But, in practice and consistent with the bicameral nature of our legislature, two members of Congress—a senator and a JBC. Thus, there are, in fact, congressman—actually sit in the B eight sitting JBC members, each of whom casts one vote. This increase in composition has some implications; for example, the vote needed to approve actions is five (out of eight members), Instead of only four (out of seven). Also, the legislative branch has now two votes in the Council while the two other branches of government retained only one each.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 3: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Role of the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Role of the Judicial and Bar Council (cont.)

ad of only four (out of seven). Also, the legislative branch has now two votes in the Council while the two other branches of government retained only one each. During my watch as Chief Justice, there was a proposal to limit the congressional vote to only one, but the suggestion was abandoned because, to resolve the issue, an "adversarial proceeding" was needed. On the other hand, the four regular, fulltime JBC members are appointed by the President "for a term of four years with the consent of the Commission on Appointments," and could be reappointed.
In sum, under the present system, judicial appointees are shielded from direct congressional influence, but JBC members are not. Further, nothing except the highest form of statesmanship prevents a politically minded President from suggesting, directly or subtly, to the Council— especially to his or her appointees— the nomination of those he or she intends to appoint. Verily, the President could still "pack" the courts, despite the Concepcion-inspired constitutional innovation.
Apart from structural concerns, the JBC has also been criticized for the ways it has conducted its work: (1) its alleged lack of transparency and lackluster nomination process, (2) its supposed inability to fill up the many judicial vacancies, thereby aggravating delays; and (3) the inclusion in its recommended list of some unworthy nominees who unfortunately get appointed and eventually taint the whole judiciary. (September 9, 2007)
