He begins with why independence matters: where Congress makes laws and the President enforces them, 'unelected judges' decide legal questions by applying law to facts, so a court that upholds a citizen's rights becomes 'a majority of one against the whole government' -- a power obeyed because of constitutional authority and 'implicit trust' in the courts' fairness.
Magistrates must therefore be chosen for the four 'nis' (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence) and be immune to 'the plague of ships' (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), with independence and integrity most vital -- 'a judge who does not possess independence and integrity...
has no place' on the bench, 'in the same manner that a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.' Under the old system, he recalls, the President had wide latitude but appointees faced Commission on Appointments confirmation that subjected them to 'intensive questioning' and 'personal demands for favors,' diminishing their independence -- so the 1987 Constitution, at Chief Justice Concepcion's suggestion, created the JBC to recommend appointees, limiting the President to a list of at least three per vacancy and abolishing CA confirmation.

Concepcion's suggestion, created the JBC to recommend appointees, limiting the President to a list of at least three per vacancy and abolishing CA confirmation. He details the JBC's seven seats (three ex-officio, four regular) and the practical wrinkle that two members of Congress sit, giving the legislature two of eight votes and raising the approval threshold to five.
Yet the reform is incomplete: appointees are shielded from Congress, but JBC members are not, and 'nothing except the highest form of statesmanship' stops a President from steering the Council -- so a President 'could still pack the courts.' He closes by listing the JBC's standing criticisms -- opacity and a 'lackluster' process, unfilled vacancies that aggravate delay, and 'unworthy nominees' who get appointed and 'taint the whole judiciary' -- setting up his follow-up column on reforming it.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 4: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council

Date:       2007-09-16
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Last Sunday, I discussed the role of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) in assuring a credible judiciary. Because of deficiencies in the JBC's structure, and alleged defects in its nomination process, some critics have proposed its abolition and a return to the old system of confirming judicial appointments by the Commission on Appointments (CA).
**Reforming systemic deficiencies**
As I have explained, the present system has shielded justices and judges from direct congressional interference, but not the four regular JBC members who need CA confirmation. JBC members are vulnerable to the same political pressures foisted on judges under the old system. Furthermore, judges—as presidential appointees-are still subject to executive influences. This is especially true of magistrates who seek promotion to higher courts (or to other jobs), and of JBC members who aspire for reappointment.
With due respect to the critics, I believe in strengthening the anti-political shield of the judiciary, not in shoving it back to the partisan mud. To accomplish this goal, the Supreme Court should be empowered to appoint the JBC regular members representing (1) the retired Supreme Court justices, (2) the Integrated Bar, and (3) the legal academe. The President may appoint the representative of the private sector, without need of CA confirmation.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 4: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council (cont.)

ustices, (2) the Integrated Bar, and (3) the legal academe. The President may appoint the representative of the private sector, without need of CA confirmation. Under this proposal, the President will have two JBC representatives (the secretary of justice and the private sector appointee); Congress will also have two (a senator and a congressman); and the Supreme Court, four (the chief justice three others named by the Court). In this way, the nomination process will be further depoliticized and judicial independence better assured.
The JBC was created 20 years ago by the 1987 Constitution. Since then, the creation of similar councils has become a favorite global judicial reform project. It has been adopted, in one form or another, in more than 25 countries, especially in Europe and Latin America. This worldwide trend has been "heralded as a way of depoliticizing appointments, guaranteeing the selection of better judges, and advancing judicial independence."
A study, made by Judge Sandra Oxner of the Commonwealth Judicial Institute of Canada, shows this unmistakable direction. In some countries like France, Italy, Portugal, and Spain, the councils-which are much larger in composition, averaging about 20 members—not merely nominate but in fact appoint the president of the country, as in France and Italy. More often, however, the chief justice chairs the council. In Japan, the system l. is simpler: the Supreme Court performs the work of the council
**Reforming JBC processes in the past**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 4: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council (cont.)

chief justice chairs the council. In Japan, the system l. is simpler: the Supreme Court performs the work of the council
**Reforming JBC processes in the past** Systemic changes require a tedious process of constitutional amendment. In the meantime, the JBC has tried its best to confront criticisms of the conduct of its business. When it started operating in 1988, the JBC did not have any rules or personnel to assist it. Even the four regular members worked on a part-time basis only.
On October 10, 2000, the "Rules of the Judicial and Bar Council" were promulgated. The Rules were intended to implement the constitutional mandate that members of the judiciary must embody "proven competence, integrity, probity, and independ- . Pimentel Jr. (when he ence." At the instance of Sen. Aquilino Q was a B JBC ex-officio member), the Rules were amended to allow a single member to veto the nomination of an applicant who has "questionable integrity."
Later on, the B JBC required full time service from-and paid regular compensation (no longer just per diems) to-the four regular members so they could actively help in steering the council. In late 2005, the B JBC hired a full time staff, led by an executive officer, to assist it in its administrative work, especially in verifying the candidates' "reputation for honesty, incorruptibility, irreproachable conduct and fidelity to sound moral and ethical standards."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 4: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
heading: Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council
text:
Reforming the Judicial and Bar Council (cont.)

k, especially in verifying the candidates' "reputation for honesty, incorruptibility, irreproachable conduct and fidelity to sound moral and ethical standards." To be more transparent, the JBC opened its interview of candidates to the media. However, it has refrained from mimicking legislative-type investigations, on the justification that, precisely, the JBC was created to shield judges from abrasive and insulting inquisitions that tend to diminish their dignity. As Chief Justice, I launched on April 21, 2006 the JBC website (jbc.supremecourt.gov.ph), showing information about the council, its work, and its processes.
**Reforming the JBC further**
Critics lament that, despite the above reforms, some unworthy candidates are still able to sneak into the JBC nomination list and get themselves appointed. Until the council is completely liberated from political influence, its members will simply have to work more heroically to nominate only the best and the brightest.
To help achieve this, I have some humble suggestions: (1) T the names of the JBC members voting for candidates who make it to the nomination list should be made public, in the same manner that the votes of justices are made known; (2) the reguJBC members should observe, by analogy, the judges' code lar B of ethics; for example, they should avoid socializing with candidates; and (3) the regular members-as the full-time vanguards of the judiciary-should, like judges, perform their work with the same standard of "proven competence, integrity, probity and independence." (September 16, 2007)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 5: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
heading: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
text:
How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams

Date:       2008-04-20
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Last Sunday, I commented on the dismal results of the 2007 bar exams. I said that it was high time the Supreme Court, the Philippine president, and the law schools collaborated to produce better lawyers. "We concur," chorused many readers. But the more pressing query of law students and reviewees for the 2008 test is: "Can you give us tips on how to pass the 2008 tests?
Having taken the exams eons ago, I feel inadequate answering the question. Besides, I placed only sixth. So I called someone more qualified, 2005 topnotcher Joan de Venecia. In turn, she summoned help from two other numero unos, Arlene Maneja (2002) and Mercedita Ona (2007). Incidentally, Arlene comes from UST, Joan from UP, and Mercedita from Ateneo de Manila. Here are their common tips.
Believe that you deserve to take the test. Forget the times you botched up a recitation or failed an exam. You're past that. Believe that you have been allowed to sit for the bar because you have a fighting chance to pass it. Cultivate composure with that
thought. You'll need it.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 5: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
heading: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
text:
How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams (cont.)

hat. Believe that you have been allowed to sit for the bar because you have a fighting chance to pass it. Cultivate composure with that
thought. You'll need it. Make time for serious self-evaluation. Have an honest assessment of the subjects you are good at, and those you feel you have an inadequate foundation on. If you sincerely believe that you do not have sufficient knowledge of a particular subject, accept it humbly and know that you still have a number of months to study for it. Adjust the number of days devoted to each subject according to the results of your self-assessment. A schedule is recommended to serve as a guide as to how many days you can allot for every subject.
Have a study plan and be realistic about it. At the start of the bar review, set aside all the materials you want to cover—all the books, reviewers, and notes for each subject. Make it your guide and pace yourself. People without a plan either underestimate the workload or get swamped with available materials; either way, they don't finish everything. So, too, organize your review materials. Time is of the essence during the bar review. You cannot afford to waste time by looking for misplaced review materials. Maintain eight separate boxes or drawers for each of the subjects. This will help you sort through your materials and decide which to read during your pre-week.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 5: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
heading: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
text:
How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams (cont.)

Maintain eight separate boxes or drawers for each of the subjects. This will help you sort through your materials and decide which to read during your pre-week. Be realistic about your capabilities. People say they will "start afresh" during the bar review-study more, play less. That's nice but it rarely happens. So, in setting astudy plan, be kind to yourself. Give yourself time to attend review lectures, to wake up late, to be lazy, to go out and to have fun. The bar test is difficult enough without making yourself sick because of unrealistic expectations.
Do not compare yourself with other reviewees. We all have our own rhythm. Listen to yours. Bar preparation is an -individual task. It is ultimately your understanding of the law l and its varied nuances, not how many readings you do, or the laws that you memorize verbatim that makes the difference.
Be physically fit. Try to get regular exercise. Eat nourishing meals. Get enough sleep every day. Take vitamins and supplements. Manage your stress. Remember, all your efforts will be wasted when your body bogs down.
Use your time wisely. Sit in a review class or do personal reading. If you know the subject well enough, refresh yourself by attending review classes. If not, read up first. Review classes assume a certain level of knowledge and, without it, you'll be lost during the discussion and waste valuable time. Know that you still have the pre-week review for all those "bar tips" that most reviewers give.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 5: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
heading: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
text:
How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams (cont.)

t, you'll be lost during the discussion and waste valuable time. Know that you still have the pre-week review for all those "bar tips" that most reviewers give. Abandon all emotional problems. Inform your family and friends about what you are going through in preparing for and in taking the exam. Ask for their understanding and support. The last thing you need is an additional source of stress when preparing for the bar is draining enough. Avoid all distractions. Keep your focus.
Perfect your handwriting and grammar. Bar examiners have to go through thousands of exam booklets, and they are only human. As would any other normal person, they appreciate, and understand more, an answer that is at the very minimum, readable and logical. All three topnotchers have good handwriting, and believe that their passing, nay topping, the bar was in large part due to this. So, practice writing neatly, legibly, and fast.
If you are a visual person, write down your notes. This exercise will aid your quest for a beautiful penmanship, and help you retain the facts and the law that may be difficult to retrieve as you store more information in your brain bank.
Study smartly. Streamline. Codal provisions, a good reviewer for each subject, and updates on jurisprudence should suffice.
Master the basics. Understand the substance of the law and how to apply it to given situations. Recall legal provisions during your spare time. Listen to audio codals when you travel.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 5: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
heading: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams
text:
How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams (cont.)

rstand the substance of the law and how to apply it to given situations. Recall legal provisions during your spare time. Listen to audio codals when you travel. Ask for updates. Doctrines that you have studied in school may have already been overturned or modified by the Supreme Court or by Congress. Request your bar operations team to include abbreviated facts in the updates, because bar questions are often facts-based.
Pray. Pray. Pray.
A final reminder. There is no shortcut to passing the bar. If you want to pass on the first take, you have to put in the hours, and get yourself in the mood to study. Do not focus on things you cannot control (e.g., bar examiners, kinds of questions). Devote all your energies to studying and positive thinking. Good luck! (April 20, 2008)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 5: How to Pass, Nay, Top the Bar Exams

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 6: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
heading: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
text:
Responsibility for Selecting Justices

Date:       2008-10-12
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
I am glad that the members of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) are preparing to face the challenge of nominating only the best and the brightest to the seven Supreme Court vacancies to be created by the retirement of an equal number of justices in 2009. Never in the normal history of the Court has almost one-half of its membership changed within just one year. (I say "normal" to exclude extraordinary events like the judicial cleansing undertaken by the Aquino revolutionary government in 1986.)
**Scrutinizing the JBC**
The Constitution provides that members of the Supreme Court (and the entire judiciary) shall be appointed by the president from a list of at least three individuals nominated by the JBC for every vacancy. The president's power to appoint justices is severely limited; the field of choice is restricted only to those nominated by the council. Having been pre-screened by the JBC, judicial appointments are no longer passed upon by the Com- mission on Appointments.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 6: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
heading: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
text:
Responsibility for Selecting Justices (cont.)

nly to those nominated by the council. Having been pre-screened by the JBC, judicial appointments are no longer passed upon by the Com- mission on Appointments. Clearly then, the primary responsibility for choosing worthy justices falls squarely on the JBC. If the council nominates only the most qualified as it should, and expunges politics and favoritism from its selection, then every appointment made by the president would be unquestionable. However, even if just one undeserving candidate is smuggled into the list, the whole selection process tumbles because the president could then appoint that unworthy one. For this reason, the JBCs' process of searching for, screening, and selecting nominees (I call them the three "s functions) cannot afford a single mistake.
Yes, the task of the JBC is not easy. The Constitution specifies three quantifiable requirements for Supreme Court members: natural-born citizen, at least 40 years of age, and practice of law or judgeship in a lower court for at least 15 years. More significantly, the Charter requires all jurists to possess four nonquantifiable qualities: "proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence." Of these, I believe the most important are independence and integrity. How to find these most elusive but most essential qualities is the JBC's ultimate task.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 6: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
heading: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
text:
Responsibility for Selecting Justices (cont.)

" Of these, I believe the most important are independence and integrity. How to find these most elusive but most essential qualities is the JBC's ultimate task. The selection process for the first vacancy that will occur when Justice Ruben T. Reyes retires on January 2, 2009 has already begun. The JBC set October 13 as the deadline for the filing of applications. This early deadline is not generally known. I think it should be extended.
**Monitoring the JBC**
Relevantly, the initiative of Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, the Senate's representative in the JBC, to convene the "Bantay Korte Suprema" is laudable. He is inviting the legal community, -ac deme, civil society, and business groups to organize themselves and participate actively in the selection process and to make sure that the public understands it.
The Pangilinan initiative dovetails with an existing method of checking the background of candidates. Authored by Dean JBC member representing the academe, Amado L. Dimayuga, B the system was derived from the Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission, the JBC's equivalent in the state of California.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 6: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
heading: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
text:
Responsibility for Selecting Justices (cont.)

ting the academe, Amado L. Dimayuga, B the system was derived from the Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission, the JBC's equivalent in the state of California. Under this method, the applicant is required to fill up a personal data questionnaire that asks for a list of courts in which he or she has appeared as counsel during the last two years as well as the names of prosecutors, private attorneys, court personnel, and other references in the legal community. If the applicant is an incumbent judge, he or she must list colleagues in the judiciary. Then, survey forms are sent to randomly picked references. From the responses (at least 20 must be received), the JBC makes an evaluation of the candidate. This system has been piloted and has produced some good results.
**Judging the JBC**
Also praiseworthy is the proposal of J. Conrado P. Castro, JBC member representing the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, that the votes cast by JBC members be recorded and made public. At present, the voting for Supreme Court nominees is done by secret ballot. Hence, there is no way of knowing who voted for whom.
However, the Castro proposal will make the process more transparent and the JBC members more accountable for their actions. When magistrates misbehave and are sanctioned, the natural question is: who were responsible for the appointment of the errant jurist? At present, there is no way to divine who among the eight JBC members voted for the penalized magistrate. The Castro plan will pinpoint responsibility for bad choic86.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 6: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
heading: Responsibility for Selecting Justices
text:
Responsibility for Selecting Justices (cont.)

ent, there is no way to divine who among the eight JBC members voted for the penalized magistrate. The Castro plan will pinpoint responsibility for bad choic86. The votes of individual justices in all Supreme Court decisions, including the most controversial, are made known. Thus, I see no reason why the votes of JBC members should be hidden from similar scrutiny. Transparency translates to that in turn breeds public confidence in our institutions and officials.
Obviously, the JBC is expected to nominate only and the brightest from among the most eminent, not who barely qualify. To select the finest for the s is a monumental task. The JBC members will be praised or condemned by the quality of all their choices. Will they pass the test?
Aside from Pangilinan, Dimayuga, and Castro, members are Chief Justice Reynato S. Puno (chair), Justice Secretary Raul Gonzalez, Rep. Matias Defensor Jr., re Court Justice Regino Hermosisima Jr., and retired Court of Appeals Justice Aurora S. Lagman. (October 12, 2008)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 10: Small Claims Court
heading: Small Claims Court
text:
Small Claims Court

Date:       2010-12-12
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
To the poor, justice is elusive, distant, and expensive. The courts smack of intimidating technicalities, procedural complexities, bottomless lawyers' fees, and inexplicable delays. Rather than bring their woes to the system, they simply bear the injustice. In all, the poor become prey to the importuning of extremists and rebels, who promise instant vindication without the intricacies of due process.
**Simple procedure**
To solve or minimize this perennial problem, our Supreme Court turned a page in judicial reform and implemented a system of filing and prosecuting small claims, involving no lawyers, no formal pleadings, and no strict legal rules of evidence. What's more, the judge is encouraged to issue the decision after just one hearing! Previously unheard of in this country, it's the dream of the legally illiterate.
No new courts were created and no new judges were specially appointed. The Supreme Court simply promulgated "The Rule on Small Claims Cases" which authorized the first level courts Metropolitan Trial Courts, Municipal Trial Courts in cities, Municipal Trial Courts and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts-to act concurrently as the s or SCC. (I call them the Poor Man's Courts.)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 10: Small Claims Court
heading: Small Claims Court
text:
Small Claims Court (cont.)

ipal Trial Courts in cities, Municipal Trial Courts and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts-to act concurrently as the s or SCC. (I call them the Poor Man's Courts.) The Rule on Small Claims covers suits in which the claim does not exceed P100,000, excluding interests and costs. It includes (a) purely civil cases, or (b) the civil aspect of criminal actions, or (c) actions to enforce barangay amicable settlements, or arbitration awards involving money claims. o take advantage of this simple, lawyer-less system, the T plaintiff merely files a "Statement of Claim," using ready-made forms provided in the Rule. In turn, the defendant must answer the claim, within 10 days from receipt of summons issued by the SCC, by filing a verified "Response," also using ready-made forms.
Both parties may ask the assistance of the court staff in accomplishing the forms. Litigants must attached certified copies of the documents upon which they base their suits, affidavits of witnesses, and other evidence to support their allegations or defenses. Evidence not submitted together with the Claim or the Response will not be accepted at the hearing.
**No lawyers please**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 10: Small Claims Court
heading: Small Claims Court
text:
Small Claims Court (cont.)

support their allegations or defenses. Evidence not submitted together with the Claim or the Response will not be accepted at the hearing.
**No lawyers please** To prevent delays and minimize legal technicalities, the Rule prohibits certain pleadings, like motions to dismiss, or for postponement, or for extension of time to file pleadings, or for new trial, or for reconsideration of a judgment, or for reopening of the trial; and petition for relief from judgment, third-party complaints, and interventions, and the like. Significantly, even petitions for certiorari, mandamus, and prohibition are disallowed. At bottom, the Rule emphasizes the summary character of the procedure and the finality of the judgment.
Also prohibited is the appearance of lawyers at the hearing unless the lawyer is one of the parties. However, both the plaintiff and the defendant may consult legal counsel, if they so desire, before or after the hearing, especially if there are legal Issues like lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, prescription (claim is time-barred), or improper venue (claim is filed in the wrong place).
If no Response is filed on time and the defendant fails to appear at the hearing, the SCC shall render judgment on the same day, as may be warranted by the facts proved by the plaintiff. Likewise, on the date and time set for the hearing, the parties must appear in court, either personally or through a representative (not a lawyer) authorized via a special power of attorney.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 10: Small Claims Court
heading: Small Claims Court
text:
Small Claims Court (cont.)

set for the hearing, the parties must appear in court, either personally or through a representative (not a lawyer) authorized via a special power of attorney. If the plaintiff fails to attend the hearing, his/her claim will be dismissed without prejudice to its re-filing. The defendant's failure to appear will have the same effect as the failure to file • Response, unless there are two or more defendants pleading a common defense and one happens to appear at the hearing.
**Principal purpose**
The hearing involves few legal technicalities, the principal purpose being to encourage the parties to reach an amicable settlement. At the hearing, the judge first conducts "Judicial Dispute Resolution," which is essentially a method of persuading the parties to settle the litigation via the known techniques of mediation, conciliation, early neutral evaluation, and the like.
If no settlement is reached, the case moves into the "Judicial Decision Phase." The judge conducts the proceedings in an informal and expeditious manner aimed at rendering substantial justice. Unlike ordinary cases in which the judge is passive and allows the parties to do most of the talking, the judge here takes an interventionist role by actively eliciting evidence from the litigants.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 10: Small Claims Court
heading: Small Claims Court
text:
Small Claims Court (cont.)

dge is passive and allows the parties to do most of the talking, the judge here takes an interventionist role by actively eliciting evidence from the litigants. The judge is expected to lend a helping hand, but must rei main strictly neutral. Looking for common grounds between the parties, the magistrate must ensure a level playing field while protecting the weak, so each party has a fair opportunity to present his or her case and to challenge that of the adverse party, thus making it easy for the parties to accept the judicial decision that would eventually be rendered
The hearing is to be terminated in one day, and a judgment issued on the same day. Once rendered, the decision is immediately entered by the clerk of court in the court docket, and copies are immediately given to the parties. The decision is final and unappealable.
The SCC should substantially declog court dockets and, more important, dispense swifter justice to the poor and powerless. (December 12, 2010)

heading: Summary
text:

Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol.
3), CJP's December 12, 2010 Inquirer column, hails the Supreme Court's small-claims reform as a remedy for the poor, 'to [whom] justice is elusive, distant, and expensive' -- deterred by 'intimidating technicalities,' 'bottomless lawyers' fees' and 'inexplicable delays,' so that they 'simply bear the injustice' and risk becoming 'prey to the importuning of extremists and rebels' who promise 'instant vindication without...
due process.' The Court, he writes, 'turned a page in judicial reform' with a system that needs 'no lawyers, no formal pleadings, and no strict legal rules of evidence,' with the judge encouraged to decide 'after just one hearing' -- 'the dream of the legally illiterate.' No new courts or judges were created: 'The Rule on Small Claims Cases' lets the first-level courts (MeTC, MTCC, MTC, MCTC) sit concurrently as Small Claims Courts -- 'the Poor Man's Courts' -- for money claims not exceeding P100,000 (purely civil cases, the civil aspect of criminal actions, or the enforcement of barangay settlements and arbitration awards), begun by a ready-made 'Statement of Claim' and answered within 10 days by a verified 'Response,' with court-staff help.
To keep things summary and final, the Rule bars most motions and 'even petitions for certiorari, mandamus, and prohibition,' and forbids lawyers from appearing at the hearing (though parties may consult counsel before or after).

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 10: Small Claims Court
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

en petitions for certiorari, mandamus, and prohibition,' and forbids lawyers from appearing at the hearing (though parties may consult counsel before or after). The hearing has two phases: the judge first conducts 'Judicial Dispute Resolution' (mediation, conciliation, neutral evaluation) and, failing settlement, a 'Judicial Decision Phase' in which -- unlike a passive ordinary-case judge -- he takes an 'interventionist role,' 'actively eliciting evidence' while staying 'strictly neutral,' ensuring 'a level playing field while protecting the weak.' The hearing must end in one day, with a same-day, 'final and unappealable' judgment immediately furnished to the parties -- a reform meant to 'substantially declog court dockets' and, 'more important, dispense swifter justice to the poor and powerless.'

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
heading: Chapter 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
text:
Chapter 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary

*	[The sixth year of Justice Panganiban’s incumbency in the Supreme Court — October 11, 2000 to October 10, 2001 — was highlighted by the Court’s observance of its centenary.  Although the exact 100**th** birthday of the Court was on June 11, 2001, the celebrations were started one year before that day.  And recently, Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. has even extended the celebrations one year more — until June 11, 2002.  Lined up to mark the centenary are more than 50 activities and projects, which are being superintended and monitored by the Centennial Executive Committee chaired by Justice Panganiban.  Of these, none has attracted more attention and appreciation from the judiciary’s intellectual public than the Court’s Centenary Lecture Series.  It was hailed by Justice Panganiban as the fulcrum of the celebrations when, on June 11, 2001, right after the last lecture of Phase 1 of the Series, he delivered the Closing-Statement, which is reproduced as Chapter 1 of this book.]*
4          A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
heading: Chapter 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
text:
Chapter 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary (cont.)

he last lecture of Phase 1 of the Series, he delivered the Closing-Statement, which is reproduced as Chapter 1 of this book.]*
4          A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE **T**he Centenary Lecture Series is one of more than 50 activities and projects that the Supreme Court is sponsoring to celebrate its 100th anniversary.  And today’s event marks the final lecture of Phase I in this monthly intellectual pursuit which began on July 11 last year, when former Chief Justice Andres R. Narvasa delivered the first one entitled “The Chief Justices in Philippine History.”  The lectures that followed discussed the achievements of the Philippine judiciary during the last one hundred years.  Thus, retired Chief Justice Enrique M. Fernando spoke of “A Century of Constitutionalism: The Mission (per Malcom, J.) and Its Fulfillment (per Laurel, J.).”
	During the past one hundred years also, the women on the bench were not to be deprived.  They, too, contributed their well-deserved share of the judiciary’s glory.  Though outnumbered, the lady justices were never out-written, out-argued or out-achieved by the men.  This outstanding fact was spelled out by Madame Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera in her lecture entitled “Feminine Grace, the High Court and Jurisprudence.”
	Our Muslim brothers and sisters were not forgotten.  In his lecture on September 12, 2000, Professor Michael O. Mastura, a former member of the House of Representatives, explained the relations between the “Shari’ah Law and the Philippine Legal System.”

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
heading: Chapter 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary
text:
Chapter 1: A Renaissance in the Judiciary (cont.)

ofessor Michael O. Mastura, a former member of the House of Representatives, explained the relations between the “Shari’ah Law and the Philippine Legal System.” 	Law is territorial in its scope.  Nonetheless, its basic principles — especially those on human rights and civil liberties — are universal.  On this verity, we listened most auspiciously to two foreign legal luminaries: first, Justice Dorit Beinisch of the Israeli Supreme Court who, even in the midst of disruption and violence in her country, spoke fervently of “Protecting Civil Liberties in a State of Continuing Emergency”; and second, Dr. Pal Solt, President of the Hungarian Supreme Court who eloquently explained the “Function of the Supreme Court of Justice in Hungary,” a state that had emerged triumphantly from political and economic crises not too long ago.
	The current trends in jurisprudence were dissected in four well-attended lectures entitled (1) “Contracts and Transactions in E-Commerce” by Congressman Leandro B. Verceles Jr.; (2) “Life Technologies and the Rule of Law” by Dr. Franklin M. Zweig of the Albert Einstein Institute for Science, Health and the Courts; (3) “Old Doctrines and New Paradigms” by an incumbent member of the Court whose name need not be mentioned; and (4) “The Impact of People Power on Our Legal System” by a panel composed of Dean Raul Pangalangan, Atty. Katrina Legarda and Professor Randy David.

ntioned; and (4) “The Impact of People Power on Our Legal System” by a panel composed of Dean Raul Pangalangan, Atty. Katrina Legarda and Professor Randy David. 	As I said earlier, today marks the culminating lecture in our pre-anniversary series.  It is significant that, while the lecture round was started by the immediate past Chief Justice, it is now closed by the incumbent Chief; and while the first lecturer spoke of the past, and those in between extolled the present, the last one dwelt largely on the future — on his vision of “a judiciary that is independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence; and on a legal profession that provides quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal service to our people.”
	Indeed, the “Davide Watch” — a brushwork of the judiciary at the threshold of the new millennium,
6          A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE
announced by the Chief Justice immediately upon his assumption of office on November 30, 1998— was inspired by Scripture, born of idealism, but grounded on the reality of the possible.

ustice immediately upon his assumption of office on November 30, 1998— was inspired by Scripture, born of idealism, but grounded on the reality of the possible. 	The Davide program for the judiciary and the legal profession is not meant to be merely a broad statement of intent and principles.  It is complemented by a definite development plan implemented day by day, pursuant to an ongoing Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR).  Notably, the Program is actively supported not only by the Philippine government and local donor groups, but also by international development bodies like the United Nations Development Fund, the World Bank, the Asia Foundation, UNICEF, the Asian Development Bank and government-to-government assistance from several countries including Japan, Canada, Australia, the United States and the Netherlands.
	The entire centenary celebrations are focused not only on the contributions of the judiciary in nation-building during the last one hundred years but, more significantly, on the reforms that Chief Justice Davide has spoken about so enthusiastically in his lecture.  Indeed, a celebration as momentous as a centenary cannot be justified by a mere rehash of past successes or by an overextended gloating over the present.  Verily, it must set forth our collective dreams of the future — a future that glories in the well-earned achievements of the past and builds on the bright hopes for posterity.

set forth our collective dreams of the future — a future that glories in the well-earned achievements of the past and builds on the bright hopes for posterity. 	By his long-term vision, commitment to excellence and ethics, untiring dedication to duty, unquestioned integrity, as well as simple and transparent life and work style, Chief Justice Davide has unleashed the long-dormant will of everyone in the judiciary.  I am confident that under his leadership, we will all transcend our puny limitations and achieve far greater success than we all are capable of imagining.
	I cannot close our program today without thanking Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera and her co-workers in the Philippine Judicial Academy — specially retired Justice Antonio M. Martinez, Dr. Purificacion V. Quisumbing, and the others who are responsible for this highly successful lecture series.  Although we have more than 49 other centennial activities, none has probably whipped up more attention and appreciation from the Court’s intellectual public than the Centenary Lecture Series.
	For today’s lecture, I also thank our co-sponsors; namely, the Court of Appeals, University of Sto. Tomas, International Law Association and Lawasia.

e Series.
	For today’s lecture, I also thank our co-sponsors; namely, the Court of Appeals, University of Sto. Tomas, International Law Association and Lawasia. 	Ladies and gentlemen, “the trouble with hello is goodbye” – so goes the familiar strains of a song popularized many years ago.  It philosophizes about all things on earth having to come to an end.  It rhapsodizes on an unsaid tragedy woven by time and space on this finite earth.  It teaches that every novel must close, every journey must end, and every theater must draw its curtains.
	I say, however, that while our pre-centenary lecture series must conclude today, its influence, its reach and its memory will not end.  In this sense, this final lecture will live on as a testament to the long-term vision of our great Chief and the common dream of this august Court.  Indeed, today, no curtain will be drawn; our journey will not screech to an end.  Our judicial reform program, which speaks boldly of hope,
shall not just be for the nonce — engraved as it is in the granite edifices we are building and in the hearts and minds of a grateful people, fulfilled in the rule of law and strengthened by the agelessness of ongoing inspiration.
Indeed, the end product of our encounter today and during the whole lecture series will be a well-remembered renaissance in the judiciary, brought about by the vision of our leader and by the labor of his inspired colleagues.
I thank you.

Chapter 4: The Centenary and the Academe

*[**A majority of the more than 50 centennial projects and activities are dedicated to the improvement of the judiciary.  However, there are at least four programs that are intended to address the academe — law schools and law students.  These were explained by Justice Panganiban in a speech he delivered during the Centennial Debate between Ateneo de Manila and Silliman University on February 9, 2001, at Dumaguete City.*
*Although that debate was noncompetitive (no winner was adjudged), the competitive ****National Speech Festival**** referred to by the good justice in this speech actually took place.  During the finals of the ****National Oratorical Contest,**** held on June 7, 2001 in the Supreme Court Session Hall, the following won: Claude Albert Morales, University of the Philippines, overall champion; Andre A. Fornier, Ateneo de Manila University, first runner-up; and Cynette Lovelyn Mirasol, University of San Agustin, second runner-up.  In the ****National Debate,**** Xavier University in Cagayan de Oro (represented by Marlowe Selecios, Jo-Shancy Bermudez and Nueva Tagarda) emerged as the national champion; while the University of the Philippines (represented by Arnell Uychoco, Michael Mejia and Diane Desierto) was runner-up.  The ****Essay Contest**** produced the following winners: Margarita Eugenio F. Victorino, (FEU), first place; Jan Kendrick Z. Velasco (FEU), second place; and Adrian R. Montemayor (UST), third place.*
*Justice Panganiban’s speech at Dumaguete, reproduced hereunder, explains these centenary projects for the academe.]*

Do you agree?  And the audience, too, is excellent and responsive!  This is the first time I find people — 800 strong here in Luce Auditorium — who paid an admission fee (P50 each) to be able to witness a debate.  I thought such an aberration would happen only during PBA basketball games or during concerts of Regine Velasquez!
For a change, I am glad that I did not have to act as judge, but only as guest speaker.  Otherwise, I would have had to make a choice and thus disappoint some of the debaters.  Happily, I leave that difficult chore to the very capable Board of Judges composed of Sen. I will just await these excellent debaters when, after they pass — nay, top — the bar examinations, they will appear as lawyers in the Supreme Court.  Until then, I reserve the opportunity to judge them.

To commemorate its 100th anniversary which falls on June 11, 2001, the Supreme Court has lined up over fifty programs and activities for a period of one year
starting June 11 last year.  The centenary celebrations include all types of activities — intellectual, cultural, historical, educational, physical and structural — participated in by all sectors of society including educators, students, media persons, judges, lawyers, court employees and the general public in all regions of the Philippines.
Our goals are, *first,* to communicate to the whole country the role of the judiciary in nation-building; and *second,* to focus on and encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program of the Supreme Court.  Our overall theme is “*Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman.*”  By this, we emphasize our allegiance to one cause,  justice; and to one entity, the nation.

But I would like to call your attention to four programs that have immediate impact on law schools and law students.
*First,* the Supreme Court, through its Centenary Executive Committee, inspired the formation of the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education, chaired by Atty. Ricardo J. Romulo.  The Court has committed itself to contributing the seed fund of P10 million; for its part, the Foundation will raise P40 million, for a total initial fund of P50 million, which will be used as an endowment for the establishment of national professorial chairs in law, as well as fellowships and scholarships for deserving but poor law students.
With the help of this Foundation, the Court hopes to elevate the standards of legal education by providing adequately paid, competent, full-time

With the help of this Foundation, the Court hopes to elevate the standards of legal education by providing adequately paid, competent, full-time professors to law schools that cannot afford to hire them on their own meager resources.  Schools like Ateneo and Silliman may not have as much need for these national professors, because such schools can more than adequately afford their own full-time mentors.  But in the rest of the country, there are many schools that need assistance to enable them “to teach law in a grand manner,” as do Ateneo and Silliman.  The idea is to encourage academic professionals to have a full-time career in teaching law, for which they will be adequately paid — as much as, for example, professors at the Asian Institute of Management.
Also, we know that there are several poor but bright students who need assistance to pursue their legal studies both here and abroad.  The Foundation will assist them in realizing their dreams.
*Second,* the Court has created a Special Committee on Legal Education — chaired by Justice Jose C. Vitug — which is looking into the law school curriculum with a view to making it more responsive to the needs of the new century.  Corollary to this is another group headed by retired Justice Ameurfina Melencio A. Herrera, which aims at reforming the bar examinations to attune them to new requirements.

of the written and the spoken varieties.  A student who does not have a singular command of communication skills has no place in the noble profession of law. Language is a time binder.  It is responsible for the success of humanity and ensures its superiority to all other creatures on this planet.  Humans have built a civilization of prosperity and technological might, because they have been able to communicate their discoveries and wisdom to their successors and heirs through the medium of language.  It took Gregor Mendel a lifetime to discover the law of dominant and recessive characteristics; and Albert Einstein, the theory of relativity.  But because Mendel and Einstein recorded their knowledge in clear, precise language, their discoveries can be explained to and known by the rest of mankind in just a matter of hours.  Indeed, language binds time and enables humans to dominate the beasts of the earth and the forces of nature.
By the same token, through the mastery of forensic and writing skills, men and women of the law are able to discover the truth, prove their legal theories, formulate legal principles and render justice to all.  In no other profession is the mastery of language more critical than in law.
It is in this spirit of binding time and of advancing truth and justice that I congratulate both the Ateneo de Manila and the Silliman University debating teams for their excellent forensic skills.  May you never tire of developing your talent to even higher standards, and may you become the competent and ethical lawyers that you aspire to be.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 5: Mediation, an Old Method with a New Twist
heading: Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist
text:
Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist

*[**One of the major problems of the judiciary is its clogged dockets.  It seems that Filipinos are a litigious people.  The number of cases filed are more than those decided by the courts.  The net result is delayed justice.  Thus, the Supreme Court has proposed various reforms to address this basic complaint of our people.  These solutions were essayed in Chapters 1 and 2 of Justice Panganiban’s earlier book, *Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity* (2000 ed., pp. 3-45).  One solution mentioned was to encourage our people to avail themselves of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) methods, especially mediation.  The Supreme Court’s policy on mediation is explained in this chapter, which is taken from Justice Panganiban’s speech during the “Advocates’ Forum for Media” held on March 16, 2001, at the Linden Suites, Ortigas Business District, Pasig City.]*
**D**uring the ancient days, men settled their disputes by subduing their opponents with the use of superior muscles, swords or guns.  The stronger person, clan, tribe or nation prevailed and dominated the weaker ones.  Sheer force decided conflicts.  Might dictated right.
Nowadays, there are still those who settle their conflicts in similar ways; in fact, people have crafted more sophisticated weapons of destruction and invented subtler modes of coercion — short of actual force — like bribery, blackmail and even sorcery.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 5: Mediation, an Old Method with a New Twist
heading: Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist
text:
Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist (cont.)

ave crafted more sophisticated weapons of destruction and invented subtler modes of coercion — short of actual force — like bribery, blackmail and even sorcery. But gentility and civilization have taught us that in the long term, right is better than might; the pen, more powerful than the sword; and reason, more reliable than aggression.  Hence, humankind created constitutions, codes and courts to spell out more civilized ways of governing, regulating, acting and settling disputes.
In our country, we believe in our Constitution.  From grade school, we are taught that our individual rights and liberties are inviolable.  Laws and ordinances have been enacted to regulate relationships and interactions.  And to resolve conflicts and vindicate rights peacefully and civilly, courts have been created.  Litigation has become the standard method of resolving disputes.
To be sure, however, litigation has many disadvantages — it is tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive, and most often, ends up in broken relationships and permanent animosities among the parties, even after a final judgment has been rendered.  Instead of healing controversies, judgments sometimes inflict deeper wounds and engender vengeance as well as new cycles of violence.
The e-age trend is to avoid litigation and to find alternative solutions to resolve disputes — solutions that are less time-consuming, less tedious, less confrontational and more productive of goodwill and lasting relationships.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 5: Mediation, an Old Method with a New Twist
heading: Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist
text:
Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist (cont.)

ions to resolve disputes — solutions that are less time-consuming, less tedious, less confrontational and more productive of goodwill and lasting relationships. Ever inventive, human beings have crafted several substitutes to litigation.  The most popular of these are negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration.  These are collectively referred to as ADRs — Alternative Dispute Resolution methods.
ADRs are by no means novel.  Some of them are even older than litigation itself.  But lately, they have been refined and polished to become more effective and acceptable methods of settling controversies.  The present effort to promote their use in our country is indeed new and fresh.  In brief, they are old methods with a new twist.
Verily, they form an integral part of the judicial reform program of the Supreme Court.  During its centenary celebrations, the Court would like to popularize them and promote their use.  We believe that the proper and extensive recourse to these alternative methods would not only decongest court dockets, but also result in better and more civilized solutions to human disputes.
Rule 18 of the Rules of Court requires trial courts to consider, during the pretrial stage, the possibility of submitting a controversy to ADRs.  The very new Interim Rules on Corporate Rehabilitation (Rule 4) also impels such referral as a mandatory step during a pretrial conference.  Even the new Electronic Commerce Act and the Retail Trade Liberalization Law encourage the use of ADRs.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 5: Mediation, an Old Method with a New Twist
heading: Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist
text:
Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist (cont.)

erral as a mandatory step during a pretrial conference.  Even the new Electronic Commerce Act and the Retail Trade Liberalization Law encourage the use of ADRs. In a very recent case, *Purefoods Corporation v. Court of Appeals* (GR No. 128066, June 19, 2000), the High Tribunal grieved that the “simple case” between the parties “could have been resolved through mediation and conciliation during its infancy stage, had the parties been earnest in expediting the disposal of this case.  They opted, however, to resort to full court proceedings and denied themselves the benefits of alternative dispute resolution, thus making the process arduous and long drawn.”  The dispute involved the purchase and the installation of generators to alleviate the effects of the power crisis in 1992.  The case was finally decided only in the year 2000, when the crisis was already over and the generators no longer needed by the buyer.
Of the ADRs I mentioned, mediation is what we are focusing on today.  Armed with a grant from the Asia Foundation, the Supreme Court and its education arm, the Philippine Judicial Academy, have conducted several workshops and seminars on this topic.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 5: Mediation, an Old Method with a New Twist
heading: Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist
text:
Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist (cont.)

from the Asia Foundation, the Supreme Court and its education arm, the Philippine Judicial Academy, have conducted several workshops and seminars on this topic. To direct and conduct the Court’s training program for mediators and mediation advocates, the Court and its co-sponsors are proud to have retained the services of Mrs. Annabelle T. Abaya, a Boston-based Filipino mediator.  She has prepared herself in this field, not only with graduate studies at the University of Massachusetts and Harvard, but also with success stories in her handling of actual cases.  She has proven the value of mediation in solving various potential litigations ranging from small family problems to mind-boggling international disputes.
Mediation, as an alternative method of settling legal controversies, is encouraged by the Supreme Court.  We know that, more than litigation or
arbitration, it will bring solutions to disputes speedily, conveniently and peacefully.  Being much less confrontational, mediation conforms with the Asian and Filipino ways of solving problems without loss of face to the claimants.  More significantly, because it is conducted tactfully and diplomatically, it can even improve relationships and interactions between parties after the problem is solved.  Mediation is especially important in cases of continuing relationships like family disagreements, labor and tenancy problems especially in special economic and freeport zones, commercial disputes, consumer controversies and *barangay* level disagreements.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 5: Mediation, an Old Method with a New Twist
heading: Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist
text:
Chapter 5: Mediation, an Old Method  with a New Twist (cont.)

s, labor and tenancy problems especially in special economic and freeport zones, commercial disputes, consumer controversies and *barangay* level disagreements. As will be explained at greater length later on in this program by Ms Abaya and Dean Eduardo D. de los Angeles, mediation will henceforth become part of our ordinary vocabulary and will be as popular as “your Honor,” “objection sustained,” “irrelevant and immaterial” – phrases which the public learned during the Senate impeachment trial.  Its effectivity and timeliness in resolving conflicts will be shown ten days from now during our celebration of “Settlement Week” from March 26 to April 6.
During this period, over 300 regional trial courts in Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao will simultaneously refer actual court cases to 300 trained mediators.  The latter will demonstrate from a few hours to a maximum of a few days that mediation, properly used, can resolve conflicts speedily, conveniently and peacefully.
Indeed, mediation resolves controversies.  Beyond that, it ushers in better harmony and improved relationships in the future.  Hence, its promotion and more extensive use is fully encouraged by the Supreme
86    A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE
Court.  I close this message with an appeal to our friends in media to help the Philippine Judicial Academy (Philja) and the Supreme Court in informing the public about this old method with a new Philja twist.
I thank you.

Chapter 5 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's speech at the 'Advocates' Forum for Media' (March 16, 2001, Linden Suites, Ortigas), explaining the Supreme Court's centenary push for mediation as a remedy for clogged dockets and delayed justice -- a problem he had earlier addressed in 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' (2000).
He opens with a civilizational arc: ancient disputes were settled by 'superior muscles, swords or guns' where 'Might dictated right,' until gentility taught that 'right is better than might; the pen, more powerful than the sword; and reason, more reliable than aggression,' giving rise to constitutions, codes and courts.
But litigation, he notes, is 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive,' and often ends in 'broken relationships and permanent animosities,' sometimes inflicting 'deeper wounds' and 'new cycles of violence.' The e-age alternative is Alternative Dispute Resolution (negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration) -- 'old methods with a new twist,' some older than litigation, now refined into an integral part of judicial reform.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary

*[The Supreme Court centenary is commemorated not only in Manila, but also in all judicial regions and by all courts and court personnel all over the Philippines. Under the direct supervision of the court administrator and the executive judges in the regions, the trial courts and their employees gathered by the thousands and celebrated by means of motorcades, cultural programs, convocations and rallies. In most of the regional celebrations, Justice Panganiban, as overall chair, flew in to deliver messages. He exhorted his audience to celebrate not just with “temporary merriment,” but also with a pledge to implement the judicial reforms the Supreme Court was espousing. Typical of these speeches was the following address he delivered in the Baguio City Convention Center on April 4, 2001, during the joint celebration of Judicial Regions 1 and 2.]*
88    A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE
**O**n behalf of the Supreme Court and the Centenary Executive Committee, I welcome all of you today. I am pleased to see the many radiant faces — at least three thousand — in this Hall, a sign, I take it, that all the officials and employees in Regions 1 and 2 are happy and contented.
I realize that most of you who live and work outside Baguio have come here today at great effort and expense. I appreciate your attendance and cooperation in making our regional centenary celebrations a rousing success.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

have come here today at great effort and expense. I appreciate your attendance and cooperation in making our regional centenary celebrations a rousing success. At the outset, let me just clarify that the judiciary reckons its founding on June 11, 1901, because it was on this date that Act No. 136, otherwise known as the Judiciary Law, was enacted by the Second Philippine Commission. This law “vested judicial power xxx in the Supreme Court, Courts of First Instance and Justice of the Peace Courts and such other courts as may be authorized by law.”
A year earlier, on May 29, 1899, the then American military governor, Gen. Elwell Otis, issued General Order No. 20 which created a “Supreme Court” and designated its members. However, the said Order was “really nothing more than an extension of the military authority of the United States Army.”
On the other hand, Act No. 136 was approved by a civil government; equally important, it established an independent judicial hierarchy, with the Supreme Court as the apex. Since we treasure independence as a basic feature of our judicial system, we have chosen June 11, 1901, as our foundation date. Thus, on June 11, 2001, the Supreme Court and the judiciary will be 100 years old.
A MEANINGFUL CENTENARY    89
To properly celebrate this once-in-a lifetime occasion and to fittingly remember the many great and heroic men and women who have graced the bench, the Supreme Court formed the Centenary Executive Committee, which I have the honor of chairing.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

e many great and heroic men and women who have graced the bench, the Supreme Court formed the Centenary Executive Committee, which I have the honor of chairing. The Committee has lined up more than 50 projects and programs. They involve all types of activities — intellectual, cultural, historical, educational and physical. Participants include different sectors of society, especially judges and other judicial personnel, lawyers, educators, students, media persons, other government officials and employees, and the public at large in all regions of the country, from the Ilocos area to the islands of Sulu and Tawi-tawi.
Our goals are, *first,* to communicate to everyone the role of the judiciary in nation-building during the last 100 years; and *second,* to focus on and encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program of the Supreme Court. Our overall theme is “Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman.” By this, we stress our allegiance to only one cause, justice; and to only one entity, the nation.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

t. Our overall theme is “Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman.” By this, we stress our allegiance to only one cause, justice; and to only one entity, the nation. While our centenary celebrations involve all types of activities and include not only the judiciary, but also the general public throughout the country, the Executive Committee is keenly proud of our regional centenary celebrations like that which we are having today. After all, the judiciary is composed of not only the Supreme Court and the other appellate courts, but also the trial courts all over the Philippines. In fact, trial courts really constitute the backbone of the judicial branch of government. If I may compare the judiciary with the military, I would say that trial judges, clerks of court, sheriffs, process servers and other judicial
90    A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE
personnel are equivalent to the marines and the foot soldiers in the front line of the battlefield. Indeed, it is you who encounter, face to face, the weary litigants, their sometimes arrogant lawyers, the critical media and the expectant general public. Indeed, to the masses of our country, you are the sparkling representatives of the judiciary and the veritable symbols of justice itself.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

ectant general public. Indeed, to the masses of our country, you are the sparkling representatives of the judiciary and the veritable symbols of justice itself. In this context, I am very happy to note the extensive and all-out participation of all front liners in Regions I and II, as shown by the massive audience of 3,000 warm bodies we have today. Truly, it is exhilarating to get together and celebrate our centenary with sports contests, parades, merriment, fellowship, as well as cultural and educational programs. On this occasion, however, we should also remind ourselves of and participate in the judicial reforms the Supreme Court is pushing forward. Of the many changes the High Court is sponsoring, perhaps none is more visible and important to the public than the speedy dispensation of quality justice.
Delay in the disposition of court cases has been a longstanding complaint not only in the Philippines, but also in many other countries around the world. The International Herald Tribune, in its June 2, 2000 issue (p. 12), reports that in one Asian country, “[a]bout 25 million cases are pending, a breathtaking pile up of untried accused and unsatisfied aggrieved. By one calculation, even if no new actions were filed, 324 years would be needed to clear the dockets.”
Fortunately, the problem of clogged dockets in our country is not as bad as that reported in the *Herald Tribune.* For one thing, the Supreme Court has worked hard to reduce its own backlog. By *backlog* I refer to
A MEANINGFUL CENTENARY    91

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

ported in the *Herald Tribune.* For one thing, the Supreme Court has worked hard to reduce its own backlog. By *backlog* I refer to
A MEANINGFUL CENTENARY    91 cases that were deemed submitted for the decision of the Court more than twenty-four months after the last pleading had been filed. Twenty-four months is the period mandated by the Constitution for the highest Tribunal; for the trial courts, three months. Five years ago, when I joined the Court, we had about 2,000 overdue cases. As of today, April 4, 2001, we have been able to reduce this to about 300 only. We hope to resolve most, if not all, of these and thus completely eliminate our backlog or reduce it to an insignificant number by June 11, 2001, our 100th anniversary.
Without meaning to splash cold water on our warm celebrations today, let me add, however, as a measure of transparency, that the picture in the lower courts is not as good. In my latest book, *Transparency, Unanimity **&** Diversity* (2000 ed.), I reported that in the Court of Appeals (CA), for the five-year period 1995-1999, with a yearly average of 8,907 new cases filed and 8,290 decided, there were more than 3,000 (3,088) cases newly filed (8,907) than those decided.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

od 1995-1999, with a yearly average of 8,907 new cases filed and 8,290 decided, there were more than 3,000 (3,088) cases newly filed (8,907) than those decided. In the second-level courts, which include the Regional Trial Courts (RTC), the Court of Tax Appeals (CTA) and the Shari’ah District Courts (SDC), the case inflow for the same five-year period (1995-1999) was nearly 850,000 (848,329), while the case outflow was only about 815,000 (814,354). The total increase, then, was almost 35,000 for the said period. Now, that’s a lot of piled-up cases!
The situation is no better in the first-level courts, which include Metropolitan Trial Courts (MeTC), Municipal Trial Courts in Cities (MTCC), Municipal Circuit Trial Courts (MCTC), Municipal Trial Courts (MTC) and Shari’ah Circuit Courts (SCC). During the same period (1995-1999), there was an increase of
92    A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE
almost 65,000 cases per year or a humongous total of almost 325,000 (324,174) for the last five years.
I mention these statistics not to condemn you, but merely to remind you, our esteemed partners in the judiciary, of one persistent public complaint, which is delay in case adjudication. I know that many problems, sometimes outside our control, caused this huge increase in pending cases. For one thing, one third of all trial courts are vacant, due largely to the fact that there are not enough qualified applicants. Indeed, the low salaries, coupled with the unfavorable peace and order conditions in outlying areas, have discouraged many capable lawyers from joining the judiciary.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

, the low salaries, coupled with the unfavorable peace and order conditions in outlying areas, have discouraged many capable lawyers from joining the judiciary. For another, we need better judicial tools and facilities. To partially solve this problem, the Supreme Court has already authorized the purchase of computers for *all* regional trial courts and selected metropolitan and municipal courts all over the Philippines. These computers will be distributed soon, together with up-to-date software, to enable judges to access all decisions of the Supreme Court from 1901 to the present.
Then, of course, we know that because of *Batas Pambansa Bilang* 22, first level courts are swamped with bouncing checks cases. This is why the Supreme Court has issued a Circular giving trial courts some guidelines in imposing penalties for the violation of this law. We would like to discourage the use of the court system as a collection agency for rubber checks. Certainly, the banking system should find some other ways of solving the problem of unpaid checks. For instance, habitual bad check writers could be banned from opening and maintaining checking accounts.
A MEANINGFUL CENTENARY    93
This is the practice in the United States and many other developed countries.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

anned from opening and maintaining checking accounts.
A MEANINGFUL CENTENARY    93
This is the practice in the United States and many other developed countries. Aside from our effort to eliminate delays in court cases, there are many other reforms being highlighted during our centenary celebrations. Many of these reforms aim to improve legal and ethical standards. Some intend to recruit and properly pay “national professors of law” who will be assigned to various law schools, which otherwise cannot afford to pay them socially relevant compensation. Still some other reforms aspire to provide continuing education for judges and other judicial personnel; to construct Halls of Justice in all judicial regions, consistent with the dignity and high office of judges; to raise the salaries of judges and other judicial personnel by exempting the judiciary from the clutches of the Salary Standardization Law; to improve the judicial disciplinary process; and to encourage the use of alternative dispute resolution methods. I do not have the time to explain all of these reform measures, but soon you will be hearing, seeing and, I hope, participating in many of them.
But let me take this occasion to appeal to all of you to help the Supreme Court in its effort to institute these much needed reforms. You can start by helping reduce, if not eliminate, your own roster of delayed cases. If the Supreme Court can eliminate its own backlog, I know the lower courts will be able to follow suit.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

ce, if not eliminate, your own roster of delayed cases. If the Supreme Court can eliminate its own backlog, I know the lower courts will be able to follow suit. One way to do this is for judges to individually attend to their own backlogs, to hold hearings regularly and diligently or otherwise to get the parties to settle their controversies amicably, and to render judgments and orders within the reglementary period.
94    A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE
I know that if we have the will and the determination, we will all be victorious in the battle for swift, transparent and quality justice in our country.
As we celebrate our centenary, we have every reason to be proud of the excellent record of the judiciary during the last 100 years. It has been a dynamic, active and independent institution that has an enviable record of competence and integrity. It now enjoys unprecedented public attention. Because of the well-publicized Senate impeachment trial, our people have become very much aware of the importance of judicial proceedings. Legal phrases like “Your Honor,” “Immaterial and irrelevant,” “Objection sustained” and “Objection overruled” have become part of the lay person’s vocabulary.
Equally important, we have a Chief Justice whose integrity, ability and sterling performance as presiding officer of the impeachment trial has been universally acclaimed. Today, he is rated as the most credible Filipino; and the institution he represents — the Supreme Court — enjoys the highest approval rating in all public polling surveys.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

s rated as the most credible Filipino; and the institution he represents — the Supreme Court — enjoys the highest approval rating in all public polling surveys. Indeed, as members of the judiciary, we stand proud and honored during our centenary. But we cannot rest on these laurels. We must continue to work hard, improve our performance even more, and meet the high expectations of our countrymen.
As I close my little message today, let me recite one of my favorite prayers composed by the late Bishop Benny Tudtud, entitled “Disturb Us O Lord.” I believe it is relevant to all of us, who have persevered in our work and achieved some success in our careers, to remind us not to be complacent with our minuscule
A MEANINGFUL CENTENARY    95
achievements or satisfied with the adulation and esteem accorded us. Let us remember that reforming the judiciary and elevating our standards of performance are never complete. Let us bear in mind that the reward for good work is more work. Here is the inspiring prayer of Bishop Tudtud:
*Disturb us O Lord,*
*When we are too well-pleased with ourselves,*
*When our dreams have come true because we*
*dreamed too little,*
*When we have arrived in safety because we*
*sailed too close to the shore.*
*Disturb us O Lord,*
*When with the abundance of things we possess,*
*We have lost our thirst for the water of life,*
*When having fallen in love with time,*
*We have ceased to dream of eternity,*
*And when in our efforts to build the new earth,*
*We have allowed our vision of the new heaven*
*to grow dim.*
*Stir us O Lord,*

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary
text:
Chapter 6: A Meaningful Centenary (cont.)

ceased to dream of eternity,*
*And when in our efforts to build the new earth,*
*We have allowed our vision of the new heaven*
*to grow dim.*
*Stir us O Lord,* *To dare more boldly to venture on wider seas,*
*Where storms shall show your Majesty,*
*Where losing sight of land we shall find the*
*stars,*
*In the name of Him who pushed back the*
*horizons of our hopes*
*And invited the brave to follow Him.  Amen.*
*Maraming salamat po.*
EMPLOYEE PARTICIPATION DURING THE CENTENARY   97
**⚖**

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 6: A Meaningful Centenary
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

The rejected founding date: a year before Act 136, US military governor Gen. Elwell Otis issued General Order No. 20 (May 29, 1899) creating a 'Supreme Court' and naming its members -- but the judiciary declined to date itself from that order because it was merely an extension of US Army authority, choosing instead the independent, civil-government Act 136.

Anecdote 2

The 324-year docket: CJP cites an International Herald Tribune report that in one Asian country about 25 million cases were pending, so that 'even if no new actions were filed, 324 years would be needed to clear the dockets' -- a foil that makes the Philippine backlog look comparatively manageable.

Anecdote 3

The lower-court candor: in a 'measure of transparency,' CJP discloses unflattering numbers -- a Court of Appeals net pile-up of 3,088 and a first-level-court increase of roughly 324,174 cases over 1995-1999 -- even amid a celebration, refusing to let the festivities obscure the problem.

Anecdote 4

Bouncing checks and vacant courts: he notes that first-level courts are 'swamped' with Batas Pambansa 22 cases and that one-third of all trial courts sit vacant because low salaries and poor peace-and-order conditions deter qualified lawyers.

Anecdote 5

The 'Disturb Us O Lord' close: CJP recites a favorite prayer he attributes to the late Bishop Benny Tudtud -- a plea to be disturbed 'when our dreams have come true because we dreamed too little' -- to remind a proud audience that 'the reward for good work is more work.'
