title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 7: Employee Participation During the Centenary
heading: Chapter 7: Employee Participation During the Centenary
text:
Chapter 7: Employee Participation During the Centenary

*[Not only magistrates but also ordinary employees participated in the 100ᵗʰ birthday celebrations of the Supreme Court. The Court officials and staff were themselves deeply involved in various projects. In this chapter, Justice Panganiban pays tribute to them in a speech he delivered on February 14, 2001, in the Court of Appeals Auditorium.]*
**M***agandang hapon po sa inyong lahat. Binabati ko kayo ng isang Maligayang Araw ng mga Puso!  Happy Valentine!  Itinapat po nating talaga ang ating pagdiriwang para sa ating mga pinuno at mga manggagawa ng Kataastaasang Hukuman, Hukuman ng Apelasyon at Kagawaran ng Katarungan ngayong araw ng Valentine, upang idiin na ang mga pinakamalapit sa puso ng Supreme Court ay ang mga kawaning naglilingkod sa hustisya.  Alam na po nating lahat na ang ika-sandaang anibersaryo ng Korte Suprema ay sa ika-labing isa ng Hunyo ng kasalukuyang taon.  At ang ating pagdiriwang ngayon ay isang pagpapasinaya sa anibersaryong iyan.*
The centenary celebrations include all types of activities — intellectual, cultural, historical, educational and physical — participated in by all sectors of society including judges, lawyers, students, educators and all court employees in all regions in the Philippines.

After all, without our employees, we cannot speak of the judiciary and the justice system. We all know that an office, however exalted or however lowly, can be effective only when it has the support and the cooperation of the people composing it. In the final analysis, therefore, the most important components of judicial dispensation and thus of our centennial celebrations are the men and women who compose the judicial branch of government; namely, all of us in this hall today.

Chapter 9: A Benchbook for Judicial Excellence

*[One of the more visual projects completed during the centenary is the *Benchbook*, which contains in one single volume all the relevant information a judge needs to know while presiding during a trial. This book was formally launched on January 20, 2001, during a simple program held at the new SC Centenary Building. Here are Justice Panganiban’s short Closing Remarks during that occasion.]*
	108            A CENTENARY OF JUSTICE	A BENCHBOOK FOR JUDICIAL EXCELLENCE   109
**T**he Supreme Court, as many of us know, is celebrating its 100th anniversary on June 11, 2001. To commemorate this historic event, more than 50 projects and programs have been lined up from June 11, 2000 to June 11, 2001.1 They include all types of activities — intellectual, cultural, historical, educational and physical — participated in by all sectors of society especially judges and other judicial personnel, lawyers, educators, students and the public at large in all regions of the country.
Our goals are, *first*, to communicate to everyone the role of the judiciary in nation-building during the last 100 years; and, *second*, to focus on and encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program of the Supreme Court. Our overall theme is “Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman.” By this we emphasize our allegiance to one cause, justice; and to one entity, the nation.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 9: A Benchbook for Judicial Excellence
heading: Chapter 9: A Benchbook for Judicial Excellence
text:
Chapter 9: A Benchbook for Judicial Excellence (cont.)

eme Court. Our overall theme is “Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman.” By this we emphasize our allegiance to one cause, justice; and to one entity, the nation. Essentially, the Judicial Reform Program aims to uplift the judges themselves, their judicial tools and their working environment. The reforms are designed to enhance what I call the four “Ins” of a great magistrate; namely, integrity, intelligence, independence and industry.
Indeed, we need ethical and competent magistrates who will rise to the high standards demanded by our people. To achieve this, we need a program of continuing legal education; and, in particular, a handy reference book that can be instantly used by judges to resolve, on the spot, issues and questions that may be raised in the course of a trial. Verily, the
*Benchbook*, which Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. calls the judicial bible, is a necessary component of our Judicial Reform Program and a major part of our centenary activities.
This book is a much-needed tool of the men and women in black robes, because it assures them of up-to-date, reliable and dependable information to back up their decisions and actions. It gives them strength and confidence in making their rulings and, generally, in dealing with their work.

Our Constitution requires judges to render written decisions in which the facts and the applicable law are correctly, clearly, completely, and concisely explained. This *Benchbook* — whether in print, CD ROM, disc or webpage version — is an indispensable guide for the speedy dispensation of quality justice. Indeed, it is a necessary tool to enhance judicial excellence.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations

*[“This chapter is taken from the keynote address of Justice Panganiban during the Anvil Awards sponsored by the Public Relations Society of the Philippines (PRSP) on February 23, 2001, at the Hotel Intercontinental in Makati City.  Although delivered during an event not directly connected with the centenary, it is nonetheless included in this book, because it explains the present Supreme Court policy of transparency.  It also discusses Justice Panganiban’s role as chair of the centenary celebrations.]*
**O**n behalf of the board of judges, which I have the honor of chairing, I congratulate all the winners of the Anvil Awards sponsored by the Public Relations Society of the Philippines (PRSP).  To be sure, all the entries were unquestionably of very high quality.  But choices had to be made, and the judges carefully and meticulously chose the winners.
The judges are particularly proud of the Grand Anvil winner — the Intel Philippines Science Fair.  I believe that it vividly demonstrates corporate selflessness.  As a nationwide competition to discover and recognize our best student-scientists, it focuses on the country’s need to orient our young people to science and technology, which are essential to our individual and national prosperity in the new century.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

es on the country’s need to orient our young people to science and technology, which are essential to our individual and national prosperity in the new century. This does not necessarily mean that the others which rated second best were less than outstanding.  Quite the contrary, all the finalists for the Grand Anvil were truly excellent models of responsible corporate citizenship.  Most of the entries did not directly promote the products or the services of the sponsors, but were aimed more at inculcating civic consciousness and developing the potentials of our people and of our country as a whole.
Our task as judges was not easy.  We had to individually read, view and evaluate over a hundred entries.  Then we met and deliberated collegially in all seriousness during three long evenings.  At one time, I remarked that with the dedication, the focus and the passion displayed, the deliberations of the board of judges were comparable to those of the Supreme Court en banc except that, during the Anvil sessions, there were more jokes and relaxing one-liners interjected than during the more somber sessions of the High Tribunal.
In any event, let me recognize the judges, whom I am requesting to stand as I call their names alphabetically:  Ms Corazon S. Alvina, Ms Luchi Arguelles, Ms Candace T. Giron, Mr. Philip R. Ives, Mr. James S. Ong, Mr. Gary Z. Pimentel, Mr. Winston A. Marbella, Atty. Melvyn S. Martin, Mr. Edgar S. San Luis, Ms Victoria Segovia and Amb. Bienvenido A. Tan Jr.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

. James S. Ong, Mr. Gary Z. Pimentel, Mr. Winston A. Marbella, Atty. Melvyn S. Martin, Mr. Edgar S. San Luis, Ms Victoria Segovia and Amb. Bienvenido A. Tan Jr. May I also congratulate the PRSP, especially its president — the hard-working and well-liked Gen. Honesto M. Isleta, APR; as well as  the Anvil Awards Committee headed by the indefatigable Evelyn M. del Rosario, APR.  *Palakpakan po natin sila.*
Aside from heading the Anvil board of judges, I was also requested by Ms Evelyn del Rosario to deliver a few remarks tonight as guest of honor and speaker.  I accepted this added responsibility for three reasons.
*First,* my wife, Leni, who is the real chief of this justice and who is present tonight, is the daughter of the late Jose A. Carpio Sr., the founding father and first president of the Public Relations Society of the Philippines.  He was also the first Filipino to be elected to active membership in the Public Relations Society of America.  As most of you probably know, he is credited with having elevated public relations to a profession on the same level as law, medicine, engineering and the priesthood.  He espoused corporate social consciousness as a vital function of public relations.  His crusade for responsible corporate citizenship culminated in the organization of Philippine Business for Social Progress, the acknowledged leader of corporate social responsibility in our country.  Best of all, his family will always be grateful for the grant to

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

or Social Progress, the acknowledged leader of corporate social responsibility in our country.  Best of all, his family will always be grateful for the grant to him of the first1 “Gawad Panday,” the highest honor conferred by PRSP, in recognition of his being the “Dean of Filipino PR Practitioners.”
On a personal basis, I should add that Mr. Carpio nearly succeeded in convincing me during my fledgling years, while still an underpaid and overworked law practitioner, to join his public relations firm as executive vice president.  Looking back, I could have followed in his footsteps in this profession, had it not been for my *Kapampangan* stubborness that made me want to stand on my own two feet, instead of relying on the generosity of my kind father-in-law.
*Second,* my fascination with public relations did not end with the demise of Mr. Carpio in 1989.  Even now, the many PR concepts and principles I learned from him serve me in good stead as a member of the Supreme Court.  Two years ago it organized, for the first time in its 100-year history, a Committee on Public Information which I was asked to chair.
Until recently, the Supreme Court was probably the most inscrutable government institution in this country.  It was regarded as a fortress, a Mount Olympus where the gods dwelt far above and removed from the teeming crowd.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

table government institution in this country.  It was regarded as a fortress, a Mount Olympus where the gods dwelt far above and removed from the teeming crowd. Our Code of Judicial Ethics limits the public appearances of justices, who are expected to socialize mainly among themselves only.  They are viewed as beings who are apart and removed from the mundane concerns of daily living.  And yet, they are called upon
1  Together with President Fidel V. Ramos, Mr. Carpio was posthumously given this Award on August 31, 1998, at the Social Hall of the Development Bank of the Philippines.
to decide questions and issues that involve the lives, the liberties, the properties and the relationships of the people at large.  Certainly, both the Court and its members could not forever resist the intrusion of the Information Age or the curiosity — not to say the prying and preying eyes and ears — of an awakened, technology-driven and people-powered citizenry.
I must add that the need for the judiciary to be better understood and appreciated is not merely a Philippine phenomenon.  It is a worldwide trend.  Most judicial authorities in Europe and America realize the need for public information to improve their relationship with their various publics.  Even the very conservative Supreme Courts of the United States and of Great Britain have found the need to properly inform the public of their actions and pronouncements.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

ery conservative Supreme Courts of the United States and of Great Britain have found the need to properly inform the public of their actions and pronouncements. While its specific decisions are nonpolitical and thus not subject to popular vote, much less to referendums, the Supreme Court nonetheless realizes that it can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public.  Indeed, a litigation is won, not because one side gets more cheers from the gallery, but because it is upheld by the law through a process of reasoning.
At the same time, we know that public acceptance of the Court’s actions and decisions — especially those that go against public opinions and perceptions — is possible only if the Tribunal enjoys the people’s residual respect and esteem, which are engendered when people know enough of its members and their work.  To be appreciated and defended, the Supreme Court realizes that it must first be understood by our people.  And this is possible only if it adheres to a policy of
transparency by systematically enabling the people to know its actions, programs and work.  In short, even the Supreme Court needs public relations.
*Third,* I asked the Court to create a Public Information Office and summoned professional full-time help, first by inviting Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr. to head it.  Then there was the effort to orient the justices themselves on the need for transparency, for issuing decisions in simpler language with less legalese, and for more openness to public scrutiny without losing the mystique and the respect due our offices.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

issuing decisions in simpler language with less legalese, and for more openness to public scrutiny without losing the mystique and the respect due our offices. I would like to report very briefly on what the Supreme Court’s Committee on Public Information has done during the last two years.  As soon as I was appointed Public Information chair, I defined our objective as simply “to tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work.”  It is not to “sanitize” or to “angle” stories.  Neither is it to “proselytize” and “propaganize,” much less to spin tales or embroider the Court’s work.  Our goal is simple: to tell our various publics the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.
Further, I thought the Court was an abstract institution that needed a human face.  So I looked upon the Chief Justice as the representation or human symbol of the institution.  To make that symbol known, I wrote a book about him shortly after his assumption of office in 1998.  I entitled it *Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard,* 3,000 copies of which were distributed to decision-makers, government officials, media personalities, libraries, business leaders, non-government organizations and civic groups.  In November 2000, I followed this up with another

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

t officials, media personalities, libraries, business leaders, non-government organizations and civic groups.  In November 2000, I followed this up with another volume, *Transparency, Unanimity **&** Diversity,* which dwelt on the judicial reform program of the Supreme Court.  We also opened a web page that contained up-to-date information about the Court, its members and their work.  In early December 2000, during many radio-TV interviews in which there were questions on Hilario G. Davide Jr., I simply pointed to these publications and web site, adding, “I assure you that Chief Justice Davide will preside over the impeachment trial in a manner all of us Filipinos will be proud of.”
It is not really difficult to speak or write about our Chief Justice, because he personifies what I call the four “Ins” of an ideal magistrate; namely, integrity, intelligence, independence and industry.  In short, he is the model judge.  His irreproachable conduct during proceedings of the recent Senate Impeachment Court made him, according to poll surveys of SWS and Pulse Asia, the most trusted Filipino today.  Indeed, the cautious and choosy *Philippine Daily Inquirer* has named him “Filipino of the Year 2000.”  In the process, the Supreme Court, which he heads and represents, has grown in public esteem as the most credible public institution in the country today.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
text:
Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations (cont.)

00.”  In the process, the Supreme Court, which he heads and represents, has grown in public esteem as the most credible public institution in the country today. But having a great leader is not enough.  The institution itself must meet public expectations for speedy quality justice.  Hence, we have availed ourselves of various public relations programs and tools to push the judicial reforms the Supreme Court is sponsoring.  We view the 100th anniversary of its founding on June 11, 2001 as a fitting occasion to focus on the role of the judiciary in nation-building and to push our reform agenda.  This reform program has caught the attention and the support not only of our countrymen, but also of multinational and foreign
developmental agencies like the World Bank, UNDP, USAID, Canadian CIDA, the Dutch and the Belgian governments, Australian AID, Asian Development Bank, Asia Foundation and many others.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Chapter 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations

Summary

Chapter 12 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's keynote at the PRSP Anvil Awards (February 23, 2001, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati), included in the book because it lays out the Supreme Court's transparency policy.
After congratulating the Grand Anvil winner (the Intel Philippines Science Fair) as a model of corporate selflessness, CJP gives three reasons for speaking.
First, family: his wife Leni is the daughter of the late Jose A.
Carpio Sr., founder and first president of the PRSP and 'Dean of Filipino PR Practitioners,' who once nearly recruited CJP into his PR firm.
Second, the PR concepts he learned from Carpio now serve him at the Court, which had organized 'for the first time in its 100-year history' a Committee on Public Information that he chairs.
Third, he created the Public Information Office under Atty.
Ismael G.
Khan Jr.

Third, he created the Public Information Office under Atty.
Ismael G.
Khan Jr. His governing thesis is that the once-'inscrutable' Court -- 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus' -- must embrace transparency because, though its rulings are nonpolitical, it 'can be effective only insofar as it retains the long-term support of the public,' which is possible only if the institution is understood; hence the PIO's objective is simply 'to tell others the truth about the Supreme Court and its work,' not to 'sanitize,' 'angle,' 'proselytize' or 'propagandize.' To give the Court a 'human face,' he wrote 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' (3,000 copies) and 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity,' opened a web page, and presented CJ Davide -- personifying the four 'Ins' (integrity, intelligence, independence, industry) and named 'Filipino of the Year 2000' -- as the model judge.
He notes the reform program's broad support (World Bank, UNDP, USAID, CIDA, the Dutch and Belgian governments, AusAID, ADB, the Asia Foundation) and closes with a call for PR practitioners to help, since 'public relations and judicial dispensation have a basic commonality -- the search for truth.' A long photo section documents the centenary, from President Arroyo's launch of the Centenary Reader to the Centennial Dinner with visiting foreign chief justices.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 12: Even the Supreme Court Needs Public Relations
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

The PR career not taken: CJP recalls that his father-in-law Jose A. Carpio Sr. nearly convinced him, 'while still an underpaid and overworked law practitioner,' to join his PR firm as executive vice president -- but his 'Kapampangan stubbornness' made him want to stand on his own rather than rely on his kind father-in-law.

Anecdote 2

The Court as Mount Olympus: CJP describes the pre-reform Supreme Court as 'probably the most inscrutable government institution,' regarded as 'a fortress, a Mount Olympus where the gods dwelt far above and removed from the teeming crowd' -- the image transparency was meant to dispel.

Anecdote 3

Giving the Court a human face: to make the institution known, CJP wrote a book about CJ Davide ('Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard,' 3,000 copies distributed), then 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity,' and opened a Court web page -- telling interviewers in December 2000 simply to consult these about Davide before the impeachment trial.

Anecdote 4

PR judging vs the Court en banc: CJP quips that the Anvil board's three evenings of deliberation were 'comparable to those of the Supreme Court en banc' -- except there were 'more jokes and relaxing one-liners' than in the High Tribunal's 'more somber sessions.'

heading: Chapter 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals: — Sauce for the Poor Goose — a Postscript
text:
Chapter 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals: — Sauce for the Poor Goose — a Postscript

**C**hapter 22 of my last book — *Transparency, Unanimity **&** Diversity*1 — discussed what I thought (and still think) was the inappropriate elevation of a Decision of the Third Division to the full Court.  It was inappropriate because the movants who lost in that Decision “had utterly failed to adduce any legal reason for such referral.”  However, by a vote of 8 to 7,2 the Court en banc “decided to yank the cases out of and against the will of said Division and treated [them] as en banc cases.”
*Reconsideration*
*Unanimously Overruled*
Let me now write on how the full Court ruled on the Motion for Reconsideration filed by the petitioner-
1  2000 ed., pp. 413-433.
2  The 8 were CJ Davide and JJ Bellosillo, Kapunan, Mendoza, Purisima, Buena, Santiago and De Leon; while the 7 dissenters were JJ Melo, Puno, Vitug, Panganiban, Quisumbing, Pardo and Reyes.
movants, who had challenged the Third Division’s Decision.  After hearing oral arguments from the parties, the full Court, on January 30, 2001, issued a Resolution3 *unanimously* denying the Motion for Reconsideration and upholding the Third Division’s equally unanimous original Decision, on the following grounds:
1.  “Petitioner’s arguments have been squarely discussed and x x x fully considered in [the Third Division’s] Decision and we reiterate that the Court of Appeals did not err in denying the petition to annul judgment in view of the decision of this Court in the *Margolles* case.”  Explained the Court:

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals -- Sauce for the Poor Goose: A Postscript
heading: Chapter 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals: — Sauce for the Poor Goose — a Postscript
text:
Chapter 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals: — Sauce for the Poor Goose — a Postscript (cont.)

the Court of Appeals did not err in denying the petition to annul judgment in view of the decision of this Court in the *Margolles* case.”  Explained the Court: “Petitioner’s contention that it was never a party to the *Margolles* case is not decisive of the issue.  We have stated that absolute identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity of parties for the application of the rule on res judicata.  We agree with the respondent Court of Appeals that although petitioner was not a party in the *Margolles* case, its claim in the instant case and that of the losing parties in the *Margolles* case raised exactly the same argument and relied on the same evidence to justify invalidation of OCT No. 4216[;] namely, that said title supposedly covers unclassified public land (forest land) so that the CFI of Rizal, sitting as a land registration court in 1929, did not acquire jurisdiction to adjudicate the subject property in favor of the original applicants, the Gana spouses.  Such
a shared identity of interest as shown by the identity of the relief sought by one person in a prior case and the second person [in] the subsequent case, i.e., to declare the nullity of Oct No. 4216, is sufficient to make them ‘privy in law’4 for purposes of the operation of the rule on res judicata or conclusiveness of judgment.”

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals -- Sauce for the Poor Goose: A Postscript

Chapter 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals: — Sauce for the Poor Goose — a Postscript (cont.)

he nullity of Oct No. 4216, is sufficient to make them ‘privy in law’4 for purposes of the operation of the rule on res judicata or conclusiveness of judgment.” 2.  “While it may be true that an applicant for original registration of a parcel of land bears the burden of overcoming the presumption that the land sought to be registered forms part of public domain, compliance with this burden should [have been] proven in the original proceedings instituted by the Gana spouses in 1927, and must [have been] legally presumed to have been satisfied as a decree was issued in favor of the petitioners-spouses.  Thus, where a petition is filed to annul the said judgment on the ground that it is fatally void, the burden of proving the nullity rests with the petitioner.”
3.  “Contrary to the Republic’s posture” in its Motion for Reconsideration, the State was in no danger of being “deprived of its patrimony” by reason of the Third Division’s Decision.  If the Motion is granted and the disputed land is reverted in favor of the government, the parcel recovered “would not [have been devoted] to public use, but [would have been reserved] for eventual disposition to other private persons,” particularly to the private petitioner, Firestone Ceramics, Inc.
3  In this Resolution, Justices Santiago and Gutierrez took “no part.”
4  *Valencia v. RTC of Quezon City,* 184 SCRA 80, April 3, 1990; *Comilang v. Buendia,* 21 SCRA 486, October 25, 1967; *Santos v. Gabriel,* 45 SCRA 288, May 31, 1972; *Widows and Orphans Associations v. CA,* 212 SCRA 360, August 7, 1992.

Buendia,* 21 SCRA 486, October 25, 1967; *Santos v. Gabriel,* 45 SCRA 288, May 31, 1972; *Widows and Orphans Associations v. CA,* 212 SCRA 360, August 7, 1992. “Indeed, to annul the existing torrens titles derived from OCT No. 4216 which was issued seventy years ago, only to enable the government to dispose anew the lands covered thereby to new or subsequent applicants would betray a subservience to technicality that will not be in the public interest [or] serve our declared national land policies any useful purpose.  *This is a simple matter of equity and good sense.*”
*Rationale for*
*Inclusion in This Book*
I decided to include the foregoing short discussion in this book to complete and put to rest Chapter 22 of *Transparency.*  I thought that the unanimous Resolution dated January 30, 2001 also showed the folly of failing to heed the maxim “Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander.”  As it is, the banc’s inappropriate (in my humble opinion) takeover of *Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals* merely resulted in a waste of precious time and attention; at bottom, it uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court’s dockets.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals -- Sauce for the Poor Goose: A Postscript
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 18 of 'A Centenary of Justice' is a short postscript completing a critique CJP began in Chapter 22 of his earlier book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity': that the Supreme Court en banc, by a one-vote 8-7 margin, had inappropriately pulled the Firestone Ceramics v.
Court of Appeals cases 'out of and against the will of' its Third Division and treated them as banc cases, even though the losing movants 'utterly failed to adduce any legal reason for such referral.' He now reports the sequel: on January 30, 2001 the full Court UNANIMOUSLY denied the movants' Motion for Reconsideration and upheld the Third Division's own unanimous original decision.
On the merits, the Court reaffirmed that the Court of Appeals correctly refused to annul the title -- res judicata applied through the Margolles case because 'absolute identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity,' Firestone and the Margolles losing parties having raised the same argument against OCT No.

heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

e identity of parties is not required but only substantial identity,' Firestone and the Margolles losing parties having raised the same argument against OCT No. 4216 (that it covered forest land so the 1929 registration court lacked jurisdiction over the Gana spouses), making them 'privy in law'; the burden of proving a 70-year-old decree void rests on the petitioner; and the State faced no real loss of patrimony, since reverted land 'would not be devoted to public use' but reserved for disposition to private persons, including Firestone itself -- 'a simple matter of equity and good sense.' CJP's purpose in including the piece is institutional: the unanimous outcome showed 'the folly' of ignoring the maxim that 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander,' since the banc's needless takeover 'merely resulted in a waste of precious time' and 'uselessly and imprudently clogged the Court's dockets.'

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 18: Firestone Ceramics v. Court of Appeals -- Sauce for the Poor Goose: A Postscript
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

The case that was 'yanked': CJP recounts that the en banc, by a one-vote 8-7 margin, pulled the Firestone Ceramics cases 'out of and against the will of' the Third Division and treated them as banc cases -- even though the losing movants had given no legal reason for the referral.

Anecdote 2

Vindication of the Division: the same full Court that took over the cases ended up unanimously denying reconsideration and upholding the Third Division's own unanimous original decision -- the outcome CJP cites to show the takeover changed nothing but the docket load.

Anecdote 3

The poor goose and the rich gander: CJP frames the whole episode around the maxim 'Sauce for the poor goose should be the same sauce for the rich gander,' arguing that special banc treatment for a well-resourced litigant's case, absent any legal ground, is exactly the inconsistency the saying warns against.

Anecdote 4

Reversion that helps no one public: the Court noted that if the disputed land were reverted to the government it 'would not be devoted to public use' but reserved for disposition to private persons -- indeed to Firestone itself -- so annulling 70-year-old titles would be 'subservience to technicality,' not service of the national patrimony.

text:
A Centenary of Justice -- Front Matter (Cover, Centennial Prayer, Contents, Foreword, Preface)

Front matter of 'A Centenary of Justice' (December 2001), the annual chronicle of Justice Artemio V.
Panganiban's sixth year on the Supreme Court (Oct 11, 2000 - Oct 10, 2001), published during the Court's 1901-2001 centenary under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan Magpakailanman' (Justice and Country Forever).
The opening pages reproduce the SC Centenary Logo and Justice Leonardo A.
Quisumbing's exegesis of it -- purple scales for equality and majesty, and an equilateral triangle that doubles as the Greek letter delta, meaning 'change,' to signify the Court's openness to reform -- followed by the Centennial Prayer for the Courts.
In his Foreword (15 October 2001), CJ Hilario G.
Davide Jr.
calls the launch 'an unfailing annual ritual' and the book 'the fifth book in a series that chronicles the preceding twelve months of his magistracy,' produced amid the Estrada-Arroyo succession crisis; Davide records that he and Panganiban voluntarily inhibited themselves from the unanimous succession decision (Chapter 13) and that 'our recusal has further served to strengthen the independence of the judiciary and the rule of law.' CJP's Preface explains the Court's founding rationale -- June 11, 1901 (Act 136, the Judiciary Law of the Second Philippine Commission) is reckoned the SC's birthday because it established an INDEPENDENT judicial hierarchy, unlike the executive-attached Royal Audiencia and the American-era court.

s reckoned the SC's birthday because it established an INDEPENDENT judicial hierarchy, unlike the executive-attached Royal Audiencia and the American-era court. He describes chairing the Centenary Executive Committee (50-plus projects across 13 judicial regions, June 2000 to June 2002), his sixth-year output (over 100 ponencias and 10 separate opinions; a six-year total above 650 ponencias and 60 separate opinions), and the book's two-part design mirroring his dual duties: Part I (Centenary Celebrations, Chapters 1-12) and Part II (Judicial Jousts, Chapters 13-20, covering Estrada v.
Desierto/Arroyo, the death penalty, Cruz v.
Secretary of Environment, Ang Bagong Bayani, Perez v.
Estrada, Firestone Ceramics, Bengson v.
HRET, and Social Weather Stations v.
Comelec).
Two governing achievements close the preface: the zero-backlog program that cut the SC backlog from ~6,000 cases in 1986 to fewer than 50 ('I am not clapping yet...
zero backlog is a continuing effort'), and his simple-language writing philosophy -- against pedantic legalese and aimed so 'even high school graduates would comprehend me,' echoing how Christ reduced the Ten Commandments to two while humans complicated them into countless laws.
The matter also logs court-composition changes (Purisima→Sandoval-Gutierrez; Gonzaga-Reyes→Carpio; the new U-shaped conference table) and international engagements with the chief justices of China, Hong Kong, and New Zealand.

Quisumbing's exegesis of it -- purple scales for equality and majesty, and an equilateral triangle that doubles as the Greek letter delta, meaning 'change,' to signify the Court's openness to reform -- followed by the Centennial Prayer for the Courts.
In his Foreword (15 October 2001), CJ Hilario G.
Davide Jr.
calls the launch 'an unfailing annual ritual' and the book 'the fifth book in a series that chronicles the preceding twelve months of his magistracy,' produced amid the Estrada-Arroyo succession crisis; Davide records that he and Panganiban voluntarily inhibited themselves from the unanimous succession decision (Chapter 13) and that 'our recusal has further served to strengthen the independence of the judiciary and the rule of law.' CJP's Preface explains the Court's founding rationale -- June 11, 1901 (Act 136, the Judiciary Law of the Second Philippine Commission) is reckoned the SC's birthday because it established an INDEPENDENT judicial hierarchy, unlike the executive-attached Royal Audiencia and the American-era court.

Anecdote 1

The zero-backlog turnaround: the SC backlog fell from about 6,000 cases in 1986 to ~2,000 in 1998, ~1,000 in 2000, and fewer than 50 by 2001 -- achieved by redistributing all cases docketed 'GR 120000' or lower to senior justices who had no backlog. CJP refuses to celebrate prematurely: 'I am not clapping yet... zero backlog is a continuing effort.'

Anecdote 2

The Greek-delta logo: the equilateral triangle supporting each disc of the balance in the SC Centenary Logo doubles as the Greek letter delta, the mathematical symbol for 'change' -- encoding the Court's openness to reform directly into its centennial emblem.

Anecdote 3

The mutual recusal: both CJ Davide and Justice Panganiban voluntarily inhibited themselves from the landmark unanimous decision on Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's succession to the presidency (Chapter 13), turning what could have read as absence into a deliberate strengthening of judicial independence.

The robe and wig in Wellington: after the Christchurch conference, NZ Court of Appeals President Ivor Richardson invited Panganiban to try on the gala robe and wig worn by New Zealand magistrates -- one of several international-engagement vignettes preserved in the book's photo captions.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
heading: Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
text:
Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts

**T**he third millennium and the twenty-first century ushered in new paradigms, technologies and biosciences.  As a macro consequence of these paradigms, the struggle for world preeminence has shifted from a battle of ideologies and weapons of mass destruction to one of trade dominance.  In the economic and political fields, the strategy has shifted from government control to deregulation, from state ownership to privatization, from national sovereignty to globalization, and from protectionism to trade liberalization.
On the other hand, new computer technologies have accelerated both the obsolescence of the industrial era and the advent of the Information Age.  Indeed, the possession and the distribution of information through instant, lightning-quick electronic data transmission, via the Internet and fiber optics, have become as valuable as oil resources, gold mines, heavy industries and agricultural products.
*  Opening Remarks of Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the Centenary Lecture entitled “Paperless Courts: The Australian Experience,” delivered by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia on September 26, 2001 in the Session Hall of the Philippine Supreme Court.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
heading: Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
text:
Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts (cont.)

Experience,” delivered by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia on September 26, 2001 in the Session Hall of the Philippine Supreme Court. Meanwhile, the emerging field of biosciences has made it possible to clone living organisms and to replicate or reproduce human organs through the extra-womb development of stem cells.  DNA testing, genetic engineering and other new scientific discoveries promise healthier and longer lives even if, at the same time, they raise ethical and moral concerns.  Given these breakthroughs, our children and grandchildren can look forward to much longer life spans of 150 or even 200 years.
These massive economic, political, technological and scientific developments are challenging and transforming not only the geographic and demographic face of the world, but also everything else that matters — political systems, lifestyles, work habits, philosophies, religious beliefs, leisure times, family lives and, yes, even the normally reclusive and exclusive judicial enclaves.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
heading: Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
text:
Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts (cont.)

ms, lifestyles, work habits, philosophies, religious beliefs, leisure times, family lives and, yes, even the normally reclusive and exclusive judicial enclaves. This afternoon, as a consequence also of these new technologies and sciences, we are journeying into one specific transformational shift in our legal realm — the elimination of paper.  At first blush, this proposition seems imponderable, if not totally impossible and absurd.  How can paper be eliminated from our profession?  Indeed, the law is said to be the most paper-dependent discipline in the world.  In no other field is the advice “Put it in writing” more prevalent than in the law.  Whenever a statute or a contract states that something “shall be in writing,” the unsaid assumption is that it shall be written on paper.  So, too, our present procedural rules like those on parol evidence, statute of frauds, best evidence, and many others show a definite bias in favor of documentation.
APPENDICES
And whenever the law speaks of documentation, we always assume that it refers to something written on paper.  While the Ten Commandments may have been engraved in stone and Confucian wisdom in wooden tablets, until recently we have always thought of paper as the medium of written communication.
In line with the passage on June 11, 2000, of Republic Act No. 8792 (otherwise known as the Electronic Commerce Act or ECA), the Supreme Court has recently promulgated the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence, which took effect less than two months ago on August 1, 2001.

title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
heading: Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
text:
Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts (cont.)

t or ECA), the Supreme Court has recently promulgated the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence, which took effect less than two months ago on August 1, 2001. Together, the ECA and the new Rules on Electronic Evidence eliminate the “disparity of treatment between data messages and paper documents.”  Also, an electronic document is regarded as the functional equivalent of a paper-based document; and an electronic or a digital signature, the functional equivalent of a traditionally penned “John Hancock.”  In brief, the new Rules we have just adopted makes it possible to admit in evidence electronically produced documentation or data messages.
The Supreme Court feels honored and proud of being one of the first tribunals in Asia to produce these Rules and, thereby, to keep in step with the electronic age.  Let me, however, stress that there is as yet no intention in the said law and Rules to eliminate paper as the primary medium of communication in the bar or the bench.
Today, during the lecture and the open forum that will follow, we shall assess whether paper can indeed be expunged from legal practice, and whether
paperless courts are possible in our country.  We are singularly honored to have with us as centenary lecturer and resource speaker the Honorable Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia, who will discuss the Australian experience in this bold new venture.  It is with this mixed feeling of anticipation, awe and anxiety that I welcome all of you today to what may historically be the epochal prelude to paperless legal proceedings in our country.

heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Appendix C of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's opening remarks, 'A Prelude to Paperless Courts,' delivered September 26, 2001 to introduce a centenary lecture by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia on the Australian paperless-courts experience.
CJP surveys the new-millennium paradigms reshaping the world -- the contest for preeminence shifting from ideologies and weapons to trade dominance, and strategy moving 'from government control to deregulation, from state ownership to privatization, from national sovereignty to globalization, and from protectionism to trade liberalization' -- alongside the Information Age (where data via the Internet and fiber optics is 'as valuable as oil resources') and the biosciences (cloning, stem cells, DNA, lifespans of 150-200 years).
These forces, he argues, transform even 'the normally reclusive and exclusive judicial enclaves.' He then turns to the provocative idea of eliminating paper from 'the most paper-dependent discipline in the world,' where 'Put it in writing' assumes paper and rules like parol evidence, the statute of frauds and best evidence carry 'a definite bias in favor of documentation.' The concrete milestone is legal: with RA 8792 (the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000) and the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence (effective August 1, 2001), an electronic document becomes the 'functional equivalent' of a paper one and a digital signature the equivalent of a penned 'John Hancock' -- making the Supreme Court 'one of the first tribunals in Asia' to keep step with the electronic age.

**JUSTICE**
**On Developing My Decision-Writing Style**
**Prologue** To commemorate my second year as a member of the Supreme Court, I thought of setting down the main features of the decision-writing style I have been developing. Being a non-career jurist – my appointment to the Supreme Court being my first full-time government job – I took my oath before President Fidel V. Ramos on October 10, 1995, without having authored a single judicial decision. Hence, I had to put together and evolve rather speedily my own decision-writing style and format. It did not take long, however, for me to produce my first opinions and decisions. My first extended opinion was my Dissent from the court’s en banc Resolution (denying the Motion for Reconsideration) in Imelda Marcos vs. Comelec promulgated 15 days after I assumed office. My first ponencia, on the other hand, was the unanimous en banc case of Ty vs. Trampe, promulgated 52 days after my said assumption. This case is significant not only because it was the first decision I penned, but also because it nullified an unreasonable increase in real estate taxes. Since then, I have written over 230 full-blown signed ponencia, 11 separate opinions (including dissenting and concurring ones), about 140 extended resolutions and some 675 minute resolutions disposing of cases. The ponencias and opinions have been bound into 11 volumes consisting of about 500 pages each or a total of 5,500 pages. Each ponencia averages 25 pages and each opinion, 12 pages. The unsigned extended resolutions constitute another volume. The minute resolutions, each consisting of only a few sentences, have not been collected and bound.

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style
heading: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style

The unsigned extended resolutions constitute another volume. The minute resolutions, each consisting of only a few sentences, have not been collected and bound. —--------------
I started preparing unsigned extended and minute resolutions right after my assumption into office.
An inventory by my staff showed I "inherited" over 700 pending cases from my predecessor. An additional 280 cases were "unloaded" to me by the other incumbent members of the Court when I assumed office. Thus, I was initially assigned about one thousand cases, excluding administrative matters and complaints against lawyers numbering about 100 more. Every month, each member of the Court, including me, receives, by raffle, about thirty-five (35) new judicial cases plus about 10 administrative cases (Because of their other responsibilities, the Chief Justice, the two senior justices who are Division chairmen and the next senior justice who is a "working chairman" receive about 50% less).
The longest is 72 pages, Tañada vs. Angara, G.R. No. 118295, May 2, 1997; while the shortest is four (4) pages, Cruz vs. Correctional Institute for Women, 262 SCRA 552, September 27, 1996.
The longest is 32 pages - Separate Opinion in People vs. Echegaray, G.R. No. 117472, February 7, 1997; and the shortest is three (3) pages - Separate Dissenting Opinion in Manila Prince Hotel vs. Government Service Insurance System, G.R. No. 122156, February 3, 1997.
Most of them consist of one or two pages. The longest is 12 pages.
—--------------

—-------------- Even though my decisions are written primarily to resolve legal issues and are thus emblazoned with a considerable amount of endeavored to write in sim legalese, I have ple English, comprehensible as much as possible to a high school graduate. I want to be understood not only by the legal profession but also by the parties themselves, especially by persons accused of crimes, and by the public at large as regards cases involving interpretation of the Constitution. As I wrote in my Dissenting Opinion in Marcos:
"The Constitution is the most basic law of the land. It enshrines the most cherished aspirations and ideals of the population at large. It is not a document reserved only for scholarly disquisitions by the most eminent legal minds of the land. The Constitution is not intended for lawyers to quibble over, nor to define niceties and articulate nuances legal about, in the ascertainment of its import. Its contents and words should be interpreted in the sense understood by the ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense and who pin their hopes for a better life on its fulfillment."

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style
heading: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style
text:
Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style (cont.)

e sense understood by the ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense and who pin their hopes for a better life on its fulfillment." More than lingual elegance and even legal pugnacity, I strive for simplicity, clarity and precision in nuances and shades of meanings. I believe that the trend in all professions and occupations - be they medicine, theology, science or music - is to be understood not just by the members of a particular discipline but by the public at large. While specialization cannot be avoided, generalization of public understanding is at the same time demanded in this age of mass communication, globalization and universal education. Indeed, no principle is so complicated and no mystery so deep that cannot be explained in clear and simple language to be capable of general understanding.
In my decisions, I also endeavor to answer and settle all relevant issues and questions raised by the parties. As a former practicing lawyer, one of my worst nightmares was to read a decision disposing of a case I argued based merely on one or two of the many issues I raised - or worse, on issues other than those raised. Sometimes, courts would narrate facts not backed by the records or the evidence. To avoid these — now that I am on the backside of the judicial bench - I strive to state facts as accurately as I can, in the words of the parties if possible, and to resolve all issues raised.

the backside of the judicial bench - I strive to state facts as accurately as I can, in the words of the parties if possible, and to resolve all issues raised. The features of the writing style presented here are progressive and cumulative. Thus, some of them may not be found in my first writings. They are collected and used gradually and increasingly as time goes by. The perceptive reader will find, for instance, that in my earlier ponencias, I did not capitalize the "R" in "Respondent Court,” or the “A” in "Appellant Juan dela Cruz.” Neither did I separate a topic under the title "Statement of the Case” or “The Case” as much as I did toward the latter part of the two-year period. Prospectively, I shall use much, if not all, of the features described here. In fact, it is possible that in the future I shall use more features than what are now included here. Thus, an update of this work may be needed from time to time.
—---------------
I must concede, however, that there are technical fields, like remedial law, which laymen may find difficult to comprehend. See, for instance, Arcelona vs. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 102900, October 2, 1997, dealing on the grounds for voiding a final judgment; and Mondonedo vs. Court of Appeals, 252 SCRA 28, January 18, 1996, reiterating the doctrine that certiorari is not a substitute for a lost appeal.

Court of Appeals (251 SCRA 391, December 19, 1995) and Yu vs. Court of Appeals (251 SCRA 509, December 26, 1995) , I did not use many of the features explained in this article. These ponencias were originally intended as unsigned extended resolutions but my colleagues in the Third Division thought the Resolutions merited the signatures of the justices who unanimously concurred with them.
By “style," I do not refer to a distinctive form of prose or literary expression, as in "the style of Mark Twain," or “the style of St. Paul.” Rather, it is my own preference of subject presentation, typographic arrangement and display, use of tenses, punctuation, abbreviation, capitalization, etc., which I have adopted in writing my decisions.
—--------------
Each justice and judge in the Philippines or elsewhere has his/her own style of writing which characterizes pathways in his/her mind. By and large – except for glaring lapses in grammar, sentence construction, tenses, numbers, or typing - I believe there is no right or wrong style. And any claim of superiority or dominance in writing style by anyone would be pure hubris.

**PART I. FEATURES OF MY DECISION-WRITING STYLE**

**PART I. FEATURES OF MY DECISION-WRITING STYLE** A distinct visual feature of my decisions is the use of topical titles or nomenclatures for their different parts. In general, the main parts of these decisions consist of: (1) an introduction or prologue, (2) the statement of the case, (3) the statement of facts, (4) the issues or assignment of errors, (5) the Court ruling in which each issue is separately considered and resolved, followed finally by (6) the dispositive portion. In cases in which controversial issues are involved or where new principles are introduced, an epilogue is included just prior to the disposition. In discussing my decision-writing style, however, I differentiate between criminal and noncriminal cases.
A. CRIMINAL CASES
**1. Introduction, Prologue or Opening Statement **
Decisions involving criminal cases usually open with a concise statement of the principal factual or legal issue/s of the case. For example:
"In seeking acquittal, appellant insists that the complainant was his sweetheart who willingly consented to the sexual congress.
or
"The appellant admits to having sexually molested the ten-year-old victim in this case, but claims that he merely used his fingers and is thus guilty only of acts of lasciviousness and not of rape."
or

molested the ten-year-old victim in this case, but claims that he merely used his fingers and is thus guilty only of acts of lasciviousness and not of rape."
or "The accused-appellant admits having killed his wife but insists that he did so only after surprising her in the very act of sexual intercourse with another man. However, he fails to substantiate the stringent elements required by law to absolve him of criminal responsibility. His defense appears no more than an amalgam of confusion, contradiction and concoction.”
In some instances, the opening statement is an iteration of a legal maxim or principle most relevant to the resolution of the case. Thus, in People vs. Quinao, et al.," I wrote:
"In resolving this appeal, this Court once more stresses these general rules: alibi and denial are weak defenses which cannot prevail over the prosecution witnesses' unhesitating, positive and firm identification of the accused as the persons responsible for the crime; and conspiracy, like any element of the offense, must be proved as clearly and as convincingly as the crime itself."
In People vs. Binamira, I said:

the crime; and conspiracy, like any element of the offense, must be proved as clearly and as convincingly as the crime itself."
In People vs. Binamira, I said: "In acquitting the accused, this Court stresses two doctrines: (1) a violation of the accused's right to retain a counsel of his own choice during custodial investigation renders his extrajudicial confession inadmissible even where such confession was extracted on October 3, 1985, i.e., before the effectivity of the 1987 Constitution, and (2) to sustain a conviction anchored on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must convincingly prove an unbroken chain of events from which only one fair and reasonable conclusion can be inferred - that of the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. Where such circumstances can be the subject of two possibilities, one of which is consistent with innocence and the other with guilt, then such evidence has not fulfilled the test of moral certainty and the constitutional presumption of innocence must be upheld." In other instances, I state my view on the nature and implications of the crime involved, such as in People vs. Julian:
"Rape is chilling, naked sadism. It is marked by the savagery and brutality of the assault on the helpless victim's privacy. Thus, a severe penalty is meted out by the State, as parens patriae, for this abhorrent crime, revealing the clear legislative intent to protect clear legislative women against the bestiality of persons who cannot controlled their libidinous proclivities."

The objective in placing an introduction to my ponencias is to show concisely but comprehensively the decisive point that disposes of the case. It also serves to acquaint readers with the specific nature of the controversy and the issues involved. With it, readers can determine right away whether further reading is useful or helpful to them.
However, the introduction or opening statement is not indicated by a title since it often consists of only a single sentence or paragraph.
**2. Statement of the case or The Case**
The introduction or opening statement is followed by a legal statement of the nature of the action. Criminal cases elevated to the Supreme Court normally involve ordinary appeals from trial court decisions imposing the penalty of reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment, and automatic review of decisions imposing the death penalty. The following are contained in this part of my ponencias:
a. the specific charge against the appellant/s and his other co-accused, if any (Thus, the accusatory portion of the information filed in court by the public prosecutor is always quoted in full).
b. the court of origin, the name of the judge who penned the decision, and the date of the appealed decision (Where the ponente is other than the judge who tried the case, both are named, usually in a pertinent footnote).
c. the criminal case number in the trial court
d. the plea of the accused

Sometimes there are decisions of the Court of Appeals or the Sandiganbayan which impose the same penalties. They are thus reviewed in general like those of trial courts. Where the penalty involved is less than life imprisonment, the proper remedy is a petition for review under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court. These latter cases are included in the topic, “Non-Criminal Cases.”

In some instances, I likewise indicate the names of the public prosecutor and the counsel de oficio or de parte. Naming the judge and the lawyers involved serves to encourage our public and private legal officers to render their best in the performance of their duties and functions in the administration and dispensation of justice. Their competence (or incompetence) is often demonstrated or evaluated, wittingly or unwittingly, in the disposition of the appealed case. Such competence refers not only to knowledge of substantive legal matters or procedural techniques, but also to their command of language or lack of it) as can be observed from the transcripts, pleadings and the assailed decision itself.

The verbatim reproduction of the criminal information guides this Court on the nature and the gravity of the offense for which said accused may be found culpable. As a rule, courts cannot convict an accused of a crime different from or graver than that charged. Unless for an "offense proved included in that which is charged" (Section 4, Rule 120 of the Rules of Court).
Mentioning the court of origin and the case number originally assigned to the particular case helps in facilitating the consolidation of the records of the case in both the trial and the appellate courts after entry of final judgment.
The plea of the accused is important to ensure that due process was accorded him. Absence of or irregularity in the arraignment may render the judgment void, and further consideration by this Court would be futile. In some instances, I may refer to the conduct of a preliminary investigation because this is a right granted by the Rules to the accused,  without forgetting of course that the failure of the accused to question defects in the proceedings may mean a waiver thereof. Also, in some instances I mention the fact of appellant's detention in order to dispose of the preliminary query in appealed cases not subject to automatic review: whether or not the appellant has abandoned his appeal by escaping from detention.

**3. Statement of Facts or The Facts**
The versions, of both the prosecution and the defense, of the facts of the case are usually presented in my ponencias. If they have been written clearly, accurately and sufficiently in the parties' respective pleadings or in the assailed decision itself or in the solicitor general's brief, I simply reproduce them verbatim. Otherwise, I restate them for better comprehension and appreciation.

Both the version of the prosecution and that of the defense are presented in the interest of fairness and due process. The resolution of most appealed criminal cases, unlike in civil and other cases, depends to a large extent on factual issues and the appreciation of evidence. The plausibility or incredibility of each version can sometimes be initially gleaned from a reading of the facts. The Court’s detailed evaluation of the contentions of the parties appears in the discussion of our ruling at the latter part of the decision.
The bases of the trial court in arriving at its findings and conclusions are also presented. Again, this apprises the reader of the reasons why the trial judge gave credence to the prosecution evidence while discounting that of the defense or vice versa. The fact that the assailed decision fully, intelligently and correctly resolves all factual and legal issues involved may partly explain why this Court finds no reason to reverse the lower court’s findings and conclusions. Conversely, a patent misappreciation of the facts or misapplication of the law by the trial court would aid in a better understanding of the reversal or the modification of its ruling.

The appellant's assignment of errors as contained in his brief is usually copied verbatim. By stating the assigned errors, the Court is guided on what specific issues to delve into. The purpose in reproducing in toto the appellant's words is to avoid motions for reconsideration of the final decision on the ground that the Court failed to consider all assigned errors that could affect the outcome of the case.

**5. The Court's Ruling **
This part begins with a single sentence stating how the Court disposes of the case under review. Examples are: "We affirm the judgment of the trial court”; “The appeal is not meritorious”; or “The appeal is bereft of merit.”

**6. The Disposition or Dispositive Portion ** The dispositive portion is the essential part of the decision. It states whether the appeal is granted, denied or modified; whether the appealed decision is affirmed, reversed or modified; whether the accused is convicted or acquitted. Sometimes the trial court may be correct in finding the guilt of the accused but may err in imposing the proper penalty. A common error is the lower court's occasional equation of life imprisonment with reclusion perpetua. These are different. So, too, the proper designation of the penalty — like prision mayor or reclusion temporal — is stated because each carries specific accessory penalties. Finally, to guide penal officers in case of acquittal, the clause "x x x his [the appellant's] RELEASE from confinement is immediately ORDERED, unless he is being detained for some other legal cause,"or words to the same effect, are added bearing in mind that a judgment of acquittal is unappealable and immediately executory.

**2. Statement of the Case ** The nature of the petition is indicated here. Generally, they are either petitions for review under Rule 45 or certiorari under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court or other original actions within the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. Where the public respondent is the Court of Appeals, the National Labor Relations Commission or the Sandiganbayan, the particular division which decided the case elevated for review is mentioned and the members thereof named, with the ponente specified. This is for the same purpose as mentioning the trial judge and lawyers concerned in a criminal case.
Quoting the dispositive portion of the appealed decision also serves the same purpose as that in criminal cases. In instances where the appealed decision is a reversal or a substantial modification of the trial court’s, the disposition of the latter is also quoted in full.
Where the petitioner filed a motion for reconsideration in the lower tribunal, this is also mentioned, including a reference to the order or resolution denying the motion. This is important in certiorari proceedings where, as a rule, the filing of a motion for reconsideration is a condition precedent to a petition before this Court.

**3. The Facts ** Unlike in appealed criminal cases, the opposing sets of facts are, generally, no longer presented here. Issues for resolution usually involve questions of law, grave abuse of discretion or want of jurisdiction; hence, the facts of the case are often not disputed by the parties. With a few exceptions, factual issues are not entertained in noncriminal cases. Consequently, the narration of facts by the appellate body, when exhaustive and clear, is reproduced; otherwise, the material factual antecedents are reconstructed by the Court.
As in criminal cases, the ratio decidendi of lower court or body whose decision is under review is laid out for the same reasons. It aids the reader in understanding why the lower court ruled in a certain way and why this Court either finds no reason to reverse it or concludes otherwise.
**4. Issue/s**
The issues raised by the petitioner are often also quoted in full, unless they are verbose, in which case they are restated in plain and more comprehensible language. A lone and simple issue to be resolved, as most often in administrative cases is directly stated . A summary of the respective contentions of the parties and an evaluation of the same in the Court's ruling follow.

**6. Dispositive Portion**
Finally, I lay down the fallo of the case, which is the real judgment in a litigation. It states whether the petition is granted or denied, and/or whether the appealed decision is affirmed, modified or set aside. Where the appealed judgment is nullified or set aside, the new judgment rendered by the Court is set down herein. In administrative cases supported by substantial evidence, the fallo indicates the liability of the private respondent and also the penalty imposed (whether dismissal from the service with its accessory penalties, suspension, reprimand, fine, etc.) Where the penalty is lower than dismissal, the warning clause "the commission of the same or similar acts in the future shall be dealt with more severely by this Court” or words of similar import.

C. SEPARATE OPINIONS The format of my separate opinions differs from that in my ponencias. In my separate (as well as concurring and dissenting) opinions, I state directly either the holding of the Court majority or the issues of the case. Then I briefly express my view thereon (whether agreeing or not) before proceeding to discuss fully the reasons behind such stance. I no longer state the nature of the case and its factual antecedents since these are already laid down in the main decision. Generally, the only topical titles in my opinions are the different issues presented for resolution. In some instances, particularly where a novel subject involving the public interest is at issue, I also add an epilogue. Finally, I normally cast my vote on whether to grant or to deny the petition or the appeal; or to affirm, reverse or modify the lower tribunal's judgment.

I can write on and on about improving my decision-writing style and about topics like the use of punctuation marks, the positioning of participial phrases, the use of more vivid and compelling words and the shades and meanings of commonly used expressions. Perhaps, on another occasion, I will do so. But for now I must end.
**Epilogue **
My first two years in the Court have been very challenging and engaging. I had to do my share in reducing the case backlog of the Court. I worked day and night, even on weekends. I have never been absent or late from any Court session. In fact, I cannot remember ever having preoccupied in all my life. But I am not complaining. I must quickly add that I enjoyed and will always cherish all those full days and long nights. And I look forward with more relish and intensity to the remaining years of my term.

that I enjoyed and will always cherish all those full days and long nights. And I look forward with more relish and intensity to the remaining years of my term. When I joined the Court, I sold completely and absolutely my interests in my law firm, resigned from my business involvements and cut off memberships in professional, civic, religious, charitable and other non-judicial associations, with the exception of three. I also severely limited my presence in social functions, attending only when there were special reasons like family get-togethers, weddings or anniversaries of very close friends, sports competitions (golf and tennis) with members of the judiciary or close relatives and friends with whom I was already playing prior to my appointment or who, in any event, have no known litigations before the Court.

diciary or close relatives and friends with whom I was already playing prior to my appointment or who, in any event, have no known litigations before the Court. Some of my relatives and friends must be disappointed with me - a burden I must bear - because I refuse to receive visitors and telephone calls, and I shun any conversation regarding my work. In fact, I have given written instructions to the Supreme Court security force not to allow any visitor in my chamber without my prior express permission. And when people write to me about the Court matters, even those marked "personal," I always include them in the Court's agenda for proper notation. I feel there is nothing "personal" about matters pending before the Court, and fairness demands that every item involving litigations must be brought to the Court's or, at least, the Chief Justice's attention and, when appropriate, also to the opposing side. Whenever the opportunity is present - particularly during the few speaking engagements I accept — I make it a point to tell my audience to do me the favor of not writing or calling me up or discussing with me any matter pending before the Court.
I cannot close this anniversary piece without thanking our Lord Jesus Christ for the graces and blessings He has mercifully showered me. In trying to help render justice in our sinful world, my prayer is that I may be granted wisdom, discernment and courage to do His will. "Your will be done, oh Lord, not mine."
—--------

—-------- If the 6000 pages of ponencias, opinions and extended resolutions I penned for the Court are divided by the two years or 731 days I have served, that would mean I produced an average of 8.2 pages everyday including Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. In addition, I had to report on an average of about 35 items assigned to me during Division sessions of the Court on Mondays and Wednesdays and the about 12 items during en banc meetings every Tuesday, aside from reading and studying the proposed ponencias and recommendations of the 14 other members of the Court.
Under Art. VIII, Sec. 11 of the Constitution, members of the Court shall serve, during good behavior, or until the age of seventy (70) years.
After my first two years, I will have a lessened caseload, not only because of my foregoing dispositions but also because I would have the privilege of "unloading" old cases to incoming appointees to the Court. As a rule, these old cases - meaning, more than two years from submission of the last pleading — may no longer be penned by more than two-year incumbents, per the Constitution. Perhaps, now I can look forward to "smelling the flowers" on workless Sundays.

Prior to my appointment, I was active in more than 15 organizations from all of which I had to resign, except in three: (a) Pontifical Council for the Laity, (b) Rotary Club of Manila, and (c) Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation. There are precedents allowing incumbent justices to be members of these organizations like Feria, *J. *in PCL; Malcolm, Paras and Padilla, *JJ.* in RCM; and Yap, *C.J. *and Sarmiento, *J.* in Bantayog. In addition, I serve as a Special Minister of Holy Communion when I attend masses in my parish, where there is likewise a precedent - Vitug, J. serves as SMHC in his parish.
In moments of solitude and personal prayer, I contemplate my nothingness, my unworthiness before my Lord and Savior, and I always break out with a thanksgiving, reminiscent of St. Paul’s First Letter to Timothy (1 Tim 1:12-17).

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 1 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's October 10, 1997 second-anniversary self-account of how he, a non-career jurist whose Supreme Court appointment was his first full-time government job, evolved his decision-writing style from zero -- having taken his oath on October 10, 1995 'without having authored a single judicial decision.' He reckons the output: 230 full-blown signed ponencias, 11 separate opinions, ~140 extended resolutions, ~675 minute resolutions, bound into '11 volumes of about 500 pages each or a total of 5,500 pages' -- 8.2 pages per day for 731 days including weekends.
His first Dissent (Imelda Marcos v.
Comelec, 15 days after oath) and first ponencia (Ty v.
Trampe, 52 days after, nullifying an unreasonable real-estate-tax increase) anchor the chronology; Tañada v.
Angara (WTO, 72 pages) is the longest ponencia.
The thesis: 'simple English comprehensible as much as possible to a high-school graduate' so the Constitution is read 'in the sense understood by the ordinary men and women who place their lives on the line in its defense' (Marcos Dissent).
'More than lingual elegance and even legal pugnacity, I strive for simplicity, clarity and precision in nuances and shades of meanings.' Part I lays out a six-part ponencia anatomy (introduction → statement of the case → statement of facts → issues → Court ruling → disposition, with optional epilogue), distinguishes criminal from noncriminal cases, codifies the present-tense convention ('the drama of each case becomes more vivid...

title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 1: On Developing My Decision-Writing Style
heading: Summary
text:
Summary (cont.)

on, with optional epilogue), distinguishes criminal from noncriminal cases, codifies the present-tense convention ('the drama of each case becomes more vivid... as if the parties or their counsel are actually and presently arguing'), and demands disciplined penalty designation and an acquittal-clause RELEASE language.
The Epilogue records the monastic discipline of chambered work -- completely sold his law-firm interests, resigned all business, cut civic memberships with three exceptions (Pontifical Council for the Laity, Rotary Club of Manila, Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation), bars visitors and personal phone calls, and includes letters marked 'personal' in the Court agenda because 'there is nothing personal about matters pending before the Court.' He closes with a Lord's-Prayer echo: 'Your will be done, oh Lord, not mine.'
