"At balance, the question really boils down to a choice of philosophy and perception of how to interpret and apply laws relating to elections: li or liberal, the letter or the spirit, the naked provision or its ultimate purpose, legal syllogism or substantial justice, in isolation or in the context of s conditions, harshly against or gently in favor of the voters' obvious choi In applying election laws, it would be far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms. Indeed, to inflict a thrice rejected candidate upon the electorate of Sorsogon would constitute unmitigated judicial tyranny and an unacceptable assault upon this Court's conscience ."
Extradition:
Global Cooperation in
Criminal Law Enforcement
A matter that has long gripped the attention of the world legal community is cooperation in criminal law enforcement. Recently, there has been a surge of interest in this field, and judicial cooperation has been invoked in pursuing the extradition of fugitives who escape the jurisdiction of one state and hide in another. Due to the principles of territoriality and state sovereignty, an order of arrest issued by a foreign court cannot automatically be enforced in the forum, absent a treaty authorizing it.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization (cont.)

erritoriality and state sovereignty, an order of arrest issued by a foreign court cannot automatically be enforced in the forum, absent a treaty authorizing it. In the Philippines, the subject of extradition captured national attention when the United States government, citing the US-Philippine Extradition Treaty, sought the return of Mark Jimenez to its custody. He is a Filipino congressman, for whom an order of arrest was issued by the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida. The arrest order was occasioned by indictments for conspiracy to defraud the United States, tax evasion, wire fraud, false statements and illegal campaign contributions.
Specifically, the question raised was whether Congressman Jimenez, as a prospective "extraditee," was entitled to bail while the extradition proceedings in the Philippines were pending. In Government of the United States v. Purganan, the Supreme Court answered that, in general, persons sought to be extradited were not entitled to bail and provisional liberty because of the flight risk involved. Having had a track record of avoiding the judicial processes of the requesting state, the prima facie presumption was that they would escape again if granted bail.
That the offenses for which Jimenez was sought to be extradited were bailable in the United States was not deemed to be an argument to grant him bail while the extradition proceedings in the Philippines were pending. He should apply for provisional liberty before the US court trying the extradition court.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization (cont.)

ail while the extradition proceedings in the Philippines were pending. He should apply for provisional liberty before the US court trying the extradition court. That Jimenez was a congressman whose arrest would allegedly disenfranchise his constituency and deprive it of representation in Congress was also debunked by the Court on the ground of equal constitutional protection for all regardless of position in government or station in life.
Apart from the specific issue of entitlement to bail, this case is significant because it also laid down hallmarks of international judicial cooperation — the so-called "five postulates of extradition" as follows:
1. Extradition is a by-product of the "era of globalization," because states need "to cooperate with each other to improve [their] chances of suppressing crime."
2. An extradition treaty presupposes that "both parties thereto have examined, and both accept and trust, each other's legal system and judicial process." A state's capacity and willingness of the other state to protect the b rights of the person sought to be extradited."
3.   Extradition proceedings are not criminal in nature thus, the constitutional rights of the accused are not applicable. "Extradition is merely a measure of international judicial assistance through which a person charged with or convicted of a crime is restored to a jurisdiction with the best claim to try that person."
4. Fulfilling obligations under an extradition treaty promotes comity. Thus, the principle of pacta sunt servanda binds the contracting parties.

4. Fulfilling obligations under an extradition treaty promotes comity. Thus, the principle of pacta sunt servanda binds the contracting parties. 5. Persons sought to be extradited are presumed to be flight risks. Having fled once, what is there to stop them, given the opportunity, from fleeing a second time?
In a related case, Cuevas v. Muñoz, the Supreme Court ruled that a lower court judge had not erred in ordering the provisional arrest of the person sought to be extradited, on the basis of the Hongkong government's outstanding warrant that contained a summary of the facts of the case against respondent; as well as the documents required by the Extradition Treaty and appended to the application, his showing probable cause for the issuance of the warrant.
The Internationalization of Labor:
Equal Pay for Equal Work
Let me now discuss some other Decisions of our highest Court expressing adherence to globalization in labor relations.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization (cont.)

zation of Labor:
Equal Pay for Equal Work
Let me now discuss some other Decisions of our highest Court expressing adherence to globalization in labor relations. In International School v. Quisumbing, the Court ruled that, by the doctrine of incorporation, the Philippines adopts the generally accepted principles of law that proscribe discrimination of any sort, as embodied in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination; the Convention Against Discrimination in Education; and the Convention (No. 111) Concerning Discrimination in Respect of Employment and Occupation. Thus, it required the employer to give equal pay to locally hired teachers who had performed work equal in value to that performed by foreign hires. In short, equal pay for equal work finds support not only in our own laws, but also in international covenants.
Bayan v. Zamora bravely opined that, "as a member of the family of nations, the Philippines agrees to be bound by generally accepted rules for the conduct of its international relations. x x x. Hence, we cannot readily invoke the Constitution as a convenient excuse for non-compliance with our duties and obligations under international law."
Protection of the
Environment

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization

eadily invoke the Constitution as a convenient excuse for non-compliance with our duties and obligations under international law."
Protection of the
Environment Another paradigm, one that would even qualify as an ideology of the new age, is the protection of the environment. As early as 1993, Oposa v. Factoran stressed the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology, which carried with it "the correlative duty to refrain from impairing the environment." Accordingly, timber licenses, not being property or property rights protected by the due process clause, may be revoked or rescinded by executive action. Similarly, in Tano v. Socrates, the Court upheld the City of Puerto Princesa and the Province of Palawan, which had issued Ordinances to protect the environment. It emphasized the duty of the State "to protect the nation's marine wealth" by upholding local measures "imposing appropriate penalties for acts which endanger the environment, such as dynamite fishing x x x.
Validation of
DNA Testing
Finally, let me bring your attention to a bio-age decision. In many countries, DNA has become a routine method of identification; for that purpose, it is considered to be more reliable than fingerprints. In People v. Vallejo, promulgated last year, our high court expressly acknowledged the scientific soundness of DNA. Said the Court for the first time:
"DNA is an organic substance found in a person's cells which contains his or her genetic code. Except for identical twins, each person's DNA profile is distinct and unique.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization (cont.)

rganic substance found in a person's cells which contains his or her genetic code. Except for identical twins, each person's DNA profile is distinct and unique. "When a crime is committed, material is collected from the scene of the crime or from the victim's body for the suspect's DNA. This is the evidence sample. The evidence sample is then matched with the reference sample taken from the suspect and the victim.
"The purpose of DNA testing is to ascertain whether an association exists between the evidence sample and the reference sample. The samples collected are subject to various chemical processes to establish their profile. The test may yield three possible results:
'1) The samples are different and therefore must have originated from different sources (exclusion). This conclusion is absolute and requires no further analysis or discussion;
'2) It is not possible to be sure, based on the results of the test, whether the samples have similar DNA types (inconclusive). This might occur for a variety of reasons including degradation, contamination, or failure of some aspect of the protocol. Various parts of the analysis might then be repeated with the same or a different sample, to obtain a more conclusive result; or
‘3) the samples are similar, and could have originated from the same source (inclusion). In such a case, the samples are found to be similar, [and] the analyst proceeds to determine the statistical significance of the similarity.

source (inclusion). In such a case, the samples are found to be similar, [and] the analyst proceeds to determine the statistical significance of the similarity. "In assessing the probative value of DNA evidence, therefore, courts should consider, among others things, the following data: how the samples were collected, how they were handled, the possibility of contamination of the samples, the procedure followed in analyzing the samples, whether the proper standards and procedures were followed in conducting the tests, and the qualification of the analyst who conducted the tests."
Epilogue
When the e-age was just dawning and the consequences of what we now call information technology were initially being analyzed, George Orwell authored a book entitled 1984. He predicted that the computer would presage a vast totalitarian empire, where a device called a telescreen would be put up in every home and public place. This huge two way TV network would centralize social life, and privacy would be abolished because computers would be used to monitor every word and every act of everyone. Thus, there was considerable anxiety that the computer would end human freedom and phase out liberal democracy as the prevailing governmental system in the globe.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization (cont.)

us, there was considerable anxiety that the computer would end human freedom and phase out liberal democracy as the prevailing governmental system in the globe. Now, as the e-age matures, we are realizing that such dire predictions have not and would not happen. Instead of becoming an instrument of centralization and oppression, the personal computer, linked to the Internet and the ubiquitous cell phone, has led to just the opposite: the facilitation of more information to the people, resulting in their greater participation in governance. Instead of Big Brother watching everyone, people have in fact more effectively used the computer to demand more transparency in governance.
As discussed earlier, the 21st century beaconed a new age - the bio-age. Again, many are uncertain about the future because of the many changes that biotechnology is bringing: the conception of children no longer in wombs but in vitro; surrogate motherhood; genetic engineering not only for the manufacture of spare human organs, but for the creation of made-to-order babies; and, eventually, the abolition of disease and social conflict, thereby guaranteeing life without depression or loneliness, a world where religion would become irrelevant, because wonder drugs would make everyone feel happy and contented; sex would always be good and available; and poverty would practically be abolished.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 2: Judicial Globalization (cont.)

relevant, because wonder drugs would make everyone feel happy and contented; sex would always be good and available; and poverty would practically be abolished. Indeed, as Dr. Francis Fukuyama explains in his new book, Our Posthuman Future, biotechnology could make our grandchildren's lives longer, healthier and happier. But it could also make them cease to be human beings because they will "no longer struggle, aspire, love, feel pain, make difficult moral choices, have families, or do any of the things that we traditionally associate with being human. They [will] have the characteristics that give us human dignity.
In the face of all these, however, I am unfazed. Just as Orwell has been proven wrong in his 1984 prediction of the death of human freedom, I am confident that the human spirit will emerge triumphant, as humankind - the judiciary in particular - tackles the challenges posed by the bio-age.
As I have mentioned earlier in my lecture, paradigms, perspectives and philosophies of the computer age have merged with traditional concepts of governance and judicial dispensation. This merging has happened - perhaps not in one seamless package but, just the same, in a manner that permits human rights, dignity and honor not merely to survive, but in fact to flourish.

Let me add that aside from issuing decisions that rule on computer age paradigms, our Supreme Court is now in the process of finalizing a five-year (2003-2007) Information System Strategic Plan or ISSP for short. Under this program, our entire judiciary would be totally computerized to deliver more speedily what I term "quality" justice. Specifically, the ation of          Supreme Court, with the help of Sen. Aquilino Pimentel Jr., is in the process of setting up four pilot e-courts in the country.
And to prepare our judges for the dawning bio-age, the Philippine Judicial Academy is sponsoring next month (March 2003) a seminar on the judicial uses of DNA. In October, also this year, Philja - with the assistance of the Einstein Institute for Sciences, Health and the Courts (EINSHAC) of Washington, DC - will hold a more extensive national seminar on the wider reaches of biotechnology including genome mapping, stem cells, cloning and germ line engineering.

As I end, let me finally articulate my hope that during the last one hour or so, I have demonstrated the capacity and the ability of the judiciaries of the world to keep pace with our economically, politically, technologically and scientifically shrinking world; and that judicial globalization has not stifled nationalism and individualism. It is my firm belief that the growing trend toward judicial globalization in my country has united us with the judiciaries of the rest of the world in our common aspirations to strengthen the rule of law and to uphold human dignity and human rights worldwide, without sacrificing our quest for national interest and our unique identity as a nation.
Thank you.

Summary

Chapter 2, 'Judicial Globalization,' is CJP's lecture at the First Australasia Judicial Educators Forum (Philja; judges from 21 countries) on 'Paradigm Shifts in Law and Changing Philosophical Perspectives.' He argues the informational and technological revolution is transforming law and doctrine, surveys numerous Supreme Court decisions responding to new questions (from Echegaray to election-law and treaty cases), and frames judicial globalization as the cross-border exchange of judicial ideas.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR

Chapter 3
A Primer on the APJR
The Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006 (APJR) is the concrete response of the judiciary to the challenge of improving its quality of service and, accordingly, enhancing its image and status as an efficient, trustworthy and accountable dispenser of justice. Founded on Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.'s vision and mission as expressed in the "Davide Watch," the APJR seeks to build a strong foundation for the long-term development of the judiciary.
The details of the program are found in a 156-page document entitled "Action Program for Judicial Reform 2001-2006." Updates on its reform components were recently incorporated as a supplement. In my book Reforming the Judiciary, I have written about the general framework of APJR. However, due to the length of the latter, I reprinted only its "Executive Summary," which I used as an introductory chapter in the book. In the present volume, I have decided to present a more detailed summary of policies and strategies, projects and accomplishments, and key targets of the AlJR. The following discussion is taken from pertinent documents prepared by the Program Management Office (PMO), the lead office that handles the APJR's day-to-day implementation. I will be intentionally following the presentation format that the PMO used.
Vision and Mission
As mentioned earlier, the APJR operates for the attainment of the judiciary's vision and mission as advocated by Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. in the "Davide Watch," according to which the judiciary is committed to the following vision and mission:

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

on as advocated by Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr. in the "Davide Watch," according to which the judiciary is committed to the following vision and mission: "VISION
"A judiciary that is independent, effective and efficient, and worthy of public trust and confidence; and a legal profession that provides quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal service to our people and is willing and able to answer the call to public service.
"MISSION
"In pursuing the stated vision, the Davide Watch articulates the following goals: (1) delivery
of speedy and fair dispensation of justice to all; (2) judicial autonomy and independence from political interference; (3) improved access to judicial and legal services; (4) improved quality of external inputs to the judicial process; (5) efficient, effective and continuously improving judicial institutions; and (6) a judiciary that conducts its business with dignity, integrity, accountability and transparency."
Reform Challenges and Issues Facing the APJR
Designing a reform program for the judiciary necessarily entailed the evaluation of present conditions affecting its delivery of services. Exhaustive consultations with various stakeholders across the country were conducted in order to identify the issues confronting the judiciary and the needs of all those involved in its administration.
Nine Critical Issues
Addressed by APJR
The result of various consultations revealed nine critical issues, which are now being addressed by the APJR.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

nistration.
Nine Critical Issues
Addressed by APJR
The result of various consultations revealed nine critical issues, which are now being addressed by the APJR. First, there is case congestion and delay in the resolution of cases filed. This problem is the most prevalent concern faced by our magistrates. For instance, statistics show that in 2002, there were only 67 metropolitan trial court judges working on 179,449 cases. And while the average output per judge was 871, a total of 121,0834 cases were still pending at the end of the year.
This problem may have resulted from a number of reasons like the increase in the cases filed, inadequacies of judges and trial lawyers, deficient case management systems, loopholes in the law, and procedural rules that invite delay.
Second, there is budget deficiency. In the past three years, the share of the judiciary in the national budget has declined from 1.13 percent in 1999 and 1.20 percent in 1998 to 1.07 percent in 2000. As the bulk of its budget is devoted to expenditures for personnel services, there is thus little flexibility in satisfying the needs for maintenance and other operating expenses and outlays.
Third, there is a need to improve the appointment process for justices and judges and to further insulate it from political influence. A more transparent system is likely to result in the recruitment and promotion of the more qualified and capable ones.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

her insulate it from political influence. A more transparent system is likely to result in the recruitment and promotion of the more qualified and capable ones. Fourth, there is a need to strengthen judicial autonomy as mandated by the Constitution. In practice, however, the executive and the legislative branches assume administrative and fiscal powers over the judiciary, thus making it vulnerable to political interference.
Fifth, there is a need for re-engineering the human resources development system to support continuing capacity improvement of human resources that are involved in the provision of legal and judicial services. Among the concerns that must be addressed are the uneven quality of         legal education institutions, uncompetitive judicial remuneration, hierarchical and inflexible staffing structure, deficient career pathing, and continuing training and capacity building for nonjudicial employees.
Sixth, the dysfunctional administrative structure and operating systems and inadequate court technologies gravely affect the efficiency and the accountability of the judiciary. There is a need to update these structures and systems in order to respond to the demands of                      decentralization and modernization.
Seventh, public information and collaboration with civil society must be improved and strengthened in order to facilitate people empowerment.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

and modernization.
Seventh, public information and collaboration with civil society must be improved and strengthened in order to facilitate people empowerment. Eighth, the growing perception of corruption in the judiciary must be eliminated by addressing such issues, not only within its ranks but also in other government agencies, through court cases filed against public servants.
Finally, there is a need to improve the poor's access to quality judicial services.
Reform Program Components of the APJR
The APJR recognizes that the issues faced by the judiciary are caused by factors that overlap. Thus, reform efforts are directed not only at a particular issue in isolation of other issues, but as a comprehensive set of solutions that simultaneously and holistically address the concerns.
To this end, the APJR responds through its six-point program of sectoral reforms: [1] judicial systems and procedures, [2] institutions development, [3] human resources development, [4] reform support systems, [5] institutional integrity development and [6] the poor's access to justice.
Judicial Systems and Procedures

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

resources development, [4] reform support systems, [5] institutional integrity development and [6] the poor's access to justice.
Judicial Systems and Procedures Judges have high productivity outputs, considering their volume of work. Despite their efforts, however, they are still saddled with a high number of pending cases. This problem is caused by a number of reasons that include the enactment of different laws redefining the jurisdiction of courts, the variety in the rules of procedure, the increasing number of cases being filed, and the inadequate capability of lawyers and jurists. These factors lead to delay in the delivery of justice, which in turn breeds graft and corruption. And an environment of graft and corruption destroys the people's trust and confidence in the judiciary.
In order to address this concern, the APJR aims to improve court management systems, procedural rules, jurisdictional structures of courts, and alternative dispute settlements.
A milestone pilot project dealing with this problem of delay is the implementation of Case Flow Management (CFM) in the Pasay City trial courts. CFM is the court's supervision of the management of time and case events or of stages in the movement of a case through the court system, from the filing to the disposition of the case. This project aims to provide a systematic tracking system that enables the efficient monitoring of the status of each case. The implementation of CFM began on July 1, 2003 for all cases filed on the same day and onward.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

hat enables the efficient monitoring of the status of each case. The implementation of CFM began on July 1, 2003 for all cases filed on the same day and onward. Projects introducing technology intended to modernize the court systems are also underway. The system design for electronic courts was completed in 2001 and will be piloted in five local government units in Metro Manila and Cebu. In line with this project, the installation of new transcription and recording technology is ongoing.
The APJR is also committed to conduct a comprehensive review of the Rules of Court. Of particular concern is the integration of the rules and procedures in the law on e-commerce (RA No. 8792 or the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000).
Another major aspect of this component is the strengthening of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms. These mechanisms refer to several formal and informal processes for the settlement of conflicts, outside of or on the periphery of institutional judicial processes such as arbitration, mediation and conciliation. The promotion of ADR to all the stakeholders is being done through various education and training activities nationwide.
Institutions Development
The institution development component of the APJR is independent of the other branches of government. The judiciary seeks to attain full autonomy while respecting the existing powers and jurisdictions of the executive and the legislative branches.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR (cont.)

of government. The judiciary seeks to attain full autonomy while respecting the existing powers and jurisdictions of the executive and the legislative branches. As an initial step, the full fiscal autonomy of the judiciary, as provided for in the Constitution, is being advocated by the APJR." The current financial management system being adopted in approving the budget of the judiciary limits its freedom to reprioritize and allocate that budget according to its needs. For instance, its annual budget, like the budgets of the other government agencies, undergoes the same revisions by the Department of Budget and Management (DBM). Congress, on the other hand, adopts the revised budget approved by the DBM. The result is a reduced and reconfigured budget that leaves very little room for the judiciary to program its resources.
Moreover, certain matters relating to the internal operations of the judiciary are subject to the DBM's evaluation and approval. These involve modifications in its staffing pattern, position classification and description system, salary grades and rates of positions and tion the incumbents thereof, and the manner in which it may use its income.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: A Primer on the APJR

tion classification and description system, salary grades and rates of positions and tion the incumbents thereof, and the manner in which it may use its income. Under these circumstances, the lack or absence of judicial autonomy creates a system that is inherently vulnerable to political pressure. Thus, the APJR responds by aiming to improve the organizational capacities and internal management operations of the judiciary. This move will require major shifts in its approaches to planning, budgeting and performance management systems and better internal control and accountability mechanisms.
A study of the proposed improved systems procedures had already been completed. A "Detailed Design Report," which had resulted from various consultations and roundtable discussions, was presented to key officials of the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals, the Sandiganbayan, the Court of Tax Appeals and the Philippine Judicial Academy. The Report is currently being revised, taking into issues raised and the recommendations made during the presentation. Once completed, the Report Final will be endorsed to the Supreme Court en banc for approval.
Also, an information system using the latest technology will be enhanced in order to achieve the desired operational efficiency and organizational effectiveness. Projects include the automation of case management systems, judicial libraries and judicial archives; and their integration into an enterprise-wide network, with the Office of the Court Administrator as operator of oversight management applications.

Another element of the institutional development reforms is the judicial infrastructure program. It focuses on the creation of an integrated master plan for the construction of new halls of justice and the maintenance of existing ones. The Committee on Halls of Justice (CHOJ) takes the lead in implementing this program. Directly under the supervision of the Chief Justice, it is a committee tasked to ensure tha basic utility services are adequately delivered to the halls of justice.
Human Resource Development
The success of the reform efforts of the judiciary depends largely on the people who will implement them. Thus, human resource development (HRD) has been made an integral component of the APJR.
HRD aims at improving and strengthening the capacities of those who are responsible for performing the various component operations of the judiciary. They include justices, judges, internal personnel of the judiciary, and those in the law profession. HRD also involves the cooperation of institutions like personnel management units and appointing authorities in the judiciary, the Philippine Judicial Academy (Philja), the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), formal legal institutions, and the continuing legal education service providers.
HRD reforms will focus on judicial education, capacity building and training of nonjudicial personnel, judicial appointments, career development, and position classification and remuneration.

ial education, capacity building and training of nonjudicial personnel, judicial appointments, career development, and position classification and remuneration. 1.     Judicial Education
The institution responsible for programming judicial education is the Philippine Judicial Academy or Philja. It was first organized in 1996 and later granted legislative charter in 1998. It has been tasked with providing a systematically planned and structured regimen of courses to judicial officers as well as to candidates for judicial office.
The APJR is committed to enhance the institutional capacity of Philja. As a first step, the latter has already completed an assessment of the environment or conditions of directions for change. Reform efforts will be directed at improving the profile of Philja's educators, changing the method of instruction from law-school type to adult professional instruction, regionalizing training programs,  and improving the curricula to respond to current trends and emerging perspectives.
Another area of concern is the improvement of legal education. The APJR recognizes that many problems in the profession can be traced to the system of basic legal education and the quality of learning derived from law schools. There is thus a need to review today's law curriculum to make it responsive to changing cultures and legal trends. Specific projects under this sector include the incorporation into the curriculum of a public internship program for law students in order to promote public interest in lawyering, as well as the review of the conduct of bar examinations.

The APJR is committed to develop not only judicial but also nonjudicial personnel, who are key components in an efficient and  effective judicial organization. The program aims to design a comprehensive human resource development plan that will identify the training needs of the personnel in the context of a reforming judicial organization.
3.   Judicial Appointments and Career Development
The JBC is responsible for screening, assessing and positions of justices and judges. It was created to insulate the appointment process from political pressure and thus ensure that the appointees are the most qualified.
Reforms in judicial appointment will be directed toward the re-engineering of the appointment process for better transparency and accountability. To be pursued are steps for clarifying, simplifying and publicizing procedures for screening, selection and nomination; as well as results of evaluations by the JBC and, if possible, by the President.
4. Judicial Remuneration
Advocacy for adequate and competitive compensation for justices and judges is the core of this reform.

4. Judicial Remuneration
Advocacy for adequate and competitive compensation for justices and judges is the core of this reform. Remuneration, particularly basic salaries in the Philippine Civil Service, is governed by Republic Act No. 6758, otherwise known as the "Compensation and Position Classification Act of 1989." The basic salaries of judges and justices are set in accordance with this law. Compared with remuneration in the private sector, that for the justices and judges is low. It is thus difficult to attract qualified professionals to positions in the judiciary.
Various schemes have been attempted to increase the overall take-home pay of justices and judges, but these have not been satisfactory. However, a strong advocacy to remedy this problem has recently generated a concrete solution. The Twelfth Congress of the Philippines passed on second reading bills granting "[a]ll justices, judges and all other positions in the judiciary with the equivalent rank of justices of the Court of Appeals and judges of the Regional Trial Court" a "special monthly allowance equivalent to one hundred percent (100%) of the basic monthly salary specified for their respective salary grades under Republic Act No. 6758."

Taking into consideration the financial limitations of the government, the proposed law seeks to provide that special allowances be given in four equal installments over a period of four years. The first 25 percent of the compensation package is to be drawn from national government funds, while the succeeding installments are to be sourced from the collections of new fees imposed after the law's effectiveness."
Reform Support Systems
The Reform Support Systems component of the APJR involves efforts that harness the symbiotic relationship of the various stakeholders in the judiciary's reform program in order to sustain its smooth, timely and effective implementation.
This reform component requires advocacy work and consensus-building activities. The target areas of development are organizational culture, public information, education and communication, and networking and collaboration with other branches of government, civil society and the business sector.
1. Organizational Culture
Organizational culture is the system of shared meanings that are held by the members and that distinguish their organization from other organizations. The judiciary has defined its desired organizational culture and provided directions for its attainment through its vision and mission as expressed in the "Davide Watch," which is supported by the Blueprint of Action for the Judiciary.

The reform projects that are aimed at strengthening the judiciary's organizational culture involve the conduct of dialogues and orientation seminars for all court officials and employees, the development of a court identity manual, and the establishment of a performance awards system for judicial and nonjudicial employees.
2.   Public Information, Education and Communication (IEC)
A system of public information, education, and communication is a key component of a well-functioning system of justice and judicial process. Such system is mutually beneficial to the judiciary and the public, for it is a significant factor in organizational improvement and people empowerment.
Efforts at public lEC aim to achieve a consensus among the judiciary's external stakeholders such as the executive department - particularly agencies in the criminal justice system - the legislative department, local government units, the legal profession, business and industry, civil organizations such as nongovernmental organizations and local communities, as well as the mass media.

Specific projects under this sub-component are the production and the dissemination of information materials regarding the APJR, the creation of a manual of court processes and of a mass media-judiciary manual, surveys of awareness and opinion, the establishment of a speakers bureau, legislative tours of legal schools, and multi-sectoral conferences on critical judicial issues.
3.  Networking and Collaboration
Networking is the establishment of working relationships with other sectors and organizations for collaborative and coordinated IEC activities. Networking and collaboration facilitate information exchange, lities, co technology transfer, sharing of equipment and facilities, cost sharing, access to other types of manpower (expertise), and reinforcement and maximum dissemination of messages. They promote better understanding of the problems confronting the judiciary and produce various alternatives for addressing issues and generating commitment to the  resolution of those issues.
The thrust of this reform component, therefore, is to establish strong linkages and to organize community-based or multi-sectoral groups in order to remove any communication gaps and thereby build trust and confidence in the judiciary. Specifically, this component endeavors to assist in the creation of watchdog organizations, multisectoral support groups and inter-agency bodies.

With regard to media relations, friendly and formal contacts with media organizations have been initiated nationwide. Formal relations with media practitioners s assigned to judicial beats have also been established. News bulletins and backgrounders on Court decisions and activities have been issued to the media on a regular basis Such information is also available through the Court's website, www.supremecourt.gov.ph.
Integrity Infrastructure Development
The level of the people's faith and confidence in the judiciary is a gauge of how well it performs its functions or how effectively it attains its purpose in society. For this reason, the judiciary makes it a major component of its reform program to aggressively address the issues that affect people's trust in the justice system.
Thus, the thrust of this component is to eradicate graft and corruption, not only within the ranks of the judiciary, but also in other government agencies through the court cases filed against public servants. This effort is in line with the national government's drive to improve governance, build public trust and confidence locally and internationally, and strengthen the global competitiveness of the economy.

The judiciary recognizes, however, that addressing graft and corruption requires a comprehensive approach. This approach involves not just the strengthening of the disciplinary system or the policing mechanism but, more importantly, removing the institutional weaknesses that render the system and its personnel vulnerable. In the judiciary, the operational areas where opportunities for graft and corruption may arise include the appointment of judges, litigation practices of lawyers, adjudication practices of judges, the procurement and disposal of assets, revenue administration, auditing, and resource support from the local government units.
The implementation of the integrity infrastructure development program necessarily involves institutional and procedural reforms, civil society education and information, and public sector inter-agency collaboration.

The Poor's Access to Justice One of the goals of the judiciary is to ensure the accessibility of the judicial system to everyone, especially the marginalized and disadvantaged sectors, which are vulnerable to injustice and to diminished access to basic services. Thus, the APJR explicitly addresses this issue by ensuring that the poor have equal access to and treatment under the law, within a judicial system that ensures impartiality.
Access has several dimensions. It includes convenience (level of ease in physically reaching the starting point of service, as well as level of ease and speed in receiving the necessary service), as well as availability (presence of the service and its geographical proximity and accessibility) and affordability of several services in the justice system. The APJR aims to respond to the requirements of each dimension.
As an initial activity, a survey was conducted to evaluate the sufficiency of existing programs and to establish preliminary indicators to be used in a baseline study of the poor's access to justice. Baseline studies on inmates, private legal practitioners, the Public Attorney's Office and expanded caseloads have also been completed.

Projects are likewise being directed at reviewing substantive laws and their impact on the access to justice by the poor and disadvantaged. The areas of concern include gender mainstreaming, strengthening of the legal protection of children, and responsiveness of the Code of Muslim Personal Laws.
The APJR also recognizes the need for collaborative work with other agencies involved in providing improved access to justice. Specifically, it is committed to assist in the design and the implementation of the Department of Justice's own reform agenda. Likewise, it will endeavor to strengthen investigative, prosecutorial and legal assistance services rendered by the Department of Interior and Local Governments; and the legal or quasi-legal services provided by other national government agencies.

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education

Chapter 4
The Essentials of Legal Education
There are a few things in life that senior citizens in their mid-sixties like me relish and enjoy. One of them is the opportunity to relate with young, promising and talented people like all of you tonight. In this light, I wish to thank your affable and illustrious Dean Antonio H. Abad Jr. for inviting me to this gathering. Dean Abad and I finished our legal education in the same University - the best law school on Quezon Boulevard, Manila!
Many, many years ago when most of you were not yet born, we were law partners. I can therefore attest to the brilliance and the high ethical conduct of Dean Abad, whose one and only lifetime inspiration is my comadre, Atty. Marina Dalena-Abad.
Having thus personally known Dean Abad for almost half a century, I can openly tell you that my fervent wish is for him to be a member of the Supreme Court! But he would not hear of it, because his sense of delicadeza would not allow him to sign the usual application forms required by the Judicial and Bar Council from judicial applicants. Indeed, Dean Abad is so sensitive about judicial ethics that avoids talking with me. I attest to and truly appreciate the fact that in spite of our lifetime close professional, personal and family ties, he has never - at any time, anywhere - spoken with me about any matter pending in the courts, especially the Supreme Court. He is someone special who needs no reminder that a magistrate's independence and confidence should always be respected and preserved.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

ecially the Supreme Court. He is someone special who needs no reminder that a magistrate's independence and confidence should always be respected and preserved. Tonight, we are gathered in this elegant ballroom of the Hyatt Hotel to break bread and to celebrate the 61st anniversary of the Adamson University College of Law. On this occasion of warm felicitations and glorious jubilation, allow me to share with you a few thoughts on a subject matter that constitutes the very cornerstone of every law school in this country - legal education.
In preparing this address, I reviewed the statement of vision, mission and values of Adamson University in general and your College of Law in particular.
I must say that I admire your University's express devotion to be a "leading center for quality education particularly for the socially disadvantaged." I identify most avidly with this philosophy, because during my school days I belonged to the socially disadvantaged. To support myself in elementary and high school, I hawked newspapers, shined shoes and peddled cigarettes to jeepney drivers while they waited for the green light at traffic intersections. During my law school days, I sold bibles to my professors and textbooks to my classmates so I could own one myself as my sales commission.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

raffic intersections. During my law school days, I sold bibles to my professors and textbooks to my classmates so I could own one myself as my sales commission. But let me go back to my topic tonight. In its most simplistic sense, legal education can easily be defined as the teaching of the law. Moreover, it is the formal training that law students undergo in preparation for the bar examinations and their eventual induction to the legal profession. Indeed, the standard by which any law school is judged is the "quality" of legal education that it offers.
To achieve this standard, many law schools have adopted educational frameworks that are geared largely, if not entirely, to the mastery of the law. They emphasize the need to memorize the constitution, the codes and the statute They stress the necessity of repeating judicial doctrines and many times, of Latin maxims they hardly understand.
To my mind, such overzealous focus on pure legal craftsmanship, although advantageous in some respects, tends to neglect the other essential aspects of a legal education. It is important to note that its primary purpose is to turn law students into great lawyers, not into mere walking encyclopedias or computer chips of statutes and decisions.
On this note, let me briefly discuss with you what I consider as the three fundamental paradigms in the training and development of every law student. For convenient reference and recall, I have labeled them as the three Ls of legal education: language, law and life.
Language

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

development of every law student. For convenient reference and recall, I have labeled them as the three Ls of legal education: language, law and life.
Language First, let me talk about language. It has been said that "knowing the law" is one thing and "speaking the law" is quite another. In my experience as a law practitioner, law professor and jurist, I have encountered many lawyers who, despite their exemplary knowledge of the law, are unable to express themselves in plain and simple English.
A lawyer's deficiency in "linguistic aptitude," so to speak, can easily be detected in poorly drafted pleadings as well as in dismal oral arguments. Effective legal communication requires the mastery of four Cs = correct, complete, clear and concise. "Correct" refers not only to proficiency in law, but also to accuracy in grammar. Nothing is more frustrating than to read or hear ungrammatical presentations of misplaced law. "Complete" means that all relevant issues and aspects of a problem are presented and addressed. "Clear" refers to the use of simple but elegant words, phrases and sentences to express an idea and to make it understandable. We must avoid the use of hackneyed, highfalutin language that merely calls attention to itself and       not to the subject being discussed. "Concise" requires the use of as little time and as few words as we can to express an idea.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

ls attention to itself and       not to the subject being discussed. "Concise" requires the use of as little time and as few words as we can to express an idea. The basics of oral and written communication ought to have been learned by law students in their pre-law courses or even as early as in high school. Still, it would be advisable that some relevant reminders in this regard be included in the teaching of every law subject by requiring the use of these four Cs at every opportunity - during classroom recitation, discussion and examination.
Law
As mentioned earlier, mastery of the law is not the endall and be-all of legal education. The ultimate objective is not so much to know the law but to understand its rationale and application. Certainly, there is a vast difference between merely stating the law with utmost precision on the one hand and comprehending its purpose and meaning on the other. Thus, law students should be trained to look into the history and the rationale of statutes, to study the development of jurisprudence on important legal issues, and to think and argue logically on the basis of their analysis of the law as applied to specific factual situations.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

f jurisprudence on important legal issues, and to think and argue logically on the basis of their analysis of the law as applied to specific factual situations. Indeed, the measure of the talents of lawyers is how they can invoke a favorable rule of law in one case and provide a substantially meritorious exception in another. To be able to do this, their grasp of the law should transcend mere memory work. It should involve the ability to analyze the interaction of different, yet related, legal provisions as well as their implications to a case under consideration. Clearly then, it is not simply a matter of how much you know about the law but rather how you decipher, interpret and apply it to a given factual milieu.
Indispensably, it is both the duty and the function of law professors to sharpen the minds of their students by asking incisive and probing questions that involve more than just a cursory appraisal of legal principles and concepts. Whether it is a change in the school curriculum or the teaching styles of professors, what is important is for law students to be trained to think critically and independently. By providing them with training modules that test their analytical techniques and logical reasoning more than just the reading comprehension and memory capacity, we can be sure that they will be better prepared for the many different challenges that they may encounter in their profession.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

mprehension and memory capacity, we can be sure that they will be better prepared for the many different challenges that they may encounter in their profession. Hence, aside from the typical Socratic method of conducting recitations in class, I would suggest that a free-flowing or an open-forum type of discussion be conducted from time to time. In this way the students will be encouraged to speak their minds freely on legal issues and case studies without the pressure and the fear of humiliation or low recitation grades. This method will evoke creativity and analytical thinking on their part and will certainly build their confidence in intellectual discourse and public speaking.
Life
Finally, we should remember that in any field of study or specialized discipline, the purpose is not only to prepare the student for a professional career, but also for the journey of life itself. To realize this goal, every institution of learning should promote more than just academic excellence or scholastic aptitude in its students. It should aim to develop their full potentials so that they will become noble members of society, country and humanity.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

or scholastic aptitude in its students. It should aim to develop their full potentials so that they will become noble members of society, country and humanity. Law students are, first and foremost, human beings who pursue their respective dreams amidst the many realities of life. Some of these realities may not be as appealing as one might wish, and they may demand more than just technical expertise in the law. Mere intellectual capabilities may not be sufficient to enable a law student to survive the trials and tribulations of life. Certainly, there are many questions in this world that cannot easily be answered solely by the finite expanse of the mind.
Long ago, I thought that success in one's profession and in life in general is assured for people with high intelligence quotients. Later on, however, I observed that there were many summa cum laudes and bar topnotchers who could not hack the jungle of life and the rigors of the profession, and they ended up as mere clerks in large corporations or as also rans and wannabes elsewhere. On the other hand, I also noted that there were many students of average intelligence who rose to become great advocates, jurists, educators, business entrepreneurs and government leaders. So I kept on asking myself this question: why is it that some people with high IQ flounder, while many with modest 1Q do surprisingly well?
Two years ago, my wife Leni, who was associate dean at the Asian Institute of Management asked me to read Daniel Goleman's Emotional Intelligence.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

isingly well?
Two years ago, my wife Leni, who was associate dean at the Asian Institute of Management asked me to read Daniel Goleman's Emotional Intelligence. This book explains that to succeed in life, we must rely not merely on our intelligence quotient or IQ; we must also develop our emotional intelligence or EQ. EQ is the proper development of emotions - the ability to express the proper emotion with "the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right purpose and in the right way." It includes self-control, zeal and persistence, and the ability to motivate oneself.
Mr. Goleman says that new scientific discoveries about the brain's emotional architecture offer an explanation of those baffling moments in our lives when feeling overwhelms rationality. Understanding the interplay of brain structures that rule our moments of rage and fear or passion and joy - reveals a lot about how much our emotional habits can undermine our best intentions, and what we can do to subdue our more destructive or self-defeating emotional impulses.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

t about how much our emotional habits can undermine our best intentions, and what we can do to subdue our more destructive or self-defeating emotional impulses. Just recently, my wife again showed me a book entitled Spiritual Intelligence by Danah Zohar and Ian Marshall. This book explains that apart from IQ and EQ, there is a third aspect: spiritual intelligence or SQ, which is our ultimate intelligence. It says that human beings are essentially spiritual creatures who are driven by a need to ask "fundamental" or ultimate questions, like why was I born? What is the meaning of life? Why should I go on when I amit so tired or depressed, or when I feel beaten? What makes all worthwhile? In short, human beings are driven by a longing to find meaning and value in what they do and experience.
Let me quote directly from the book. "SQ gives us our ability to discriminate. It gives us our moral sense, an abi to temper rigid rules with understanding and compassion and an equal ability to see when compassion and understanding have their limits. We use SQ to wrestle with questions of good and evil and to envision unrealized possibilities - to dream, to aspire, to raise ourselves out of the mud."

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

limits. We use SQ to wrestle with questions of good and evil and to envision unrealized possibilities - to dream, to aspire, to raise ourselves out of the mud." This book on Spiritual Intelligence was first published in the year 2000, but it became an instant hit in the United States after the 9/11 terrorist attacks at the World Trade Center and the Pentagon building. All of a sudden, Americans were awakened from their complacency and sense of security when so many thousands could be killed so brazenly in their favorite sanctuaries. Hence, they started to ask: What is the meaning of all these? Why is human life so brittle? What is the purpose of life? Raising these questions does not mean that Americans are becoming religious or liturgical. Spiritual quotient is not measured or enhanced by plain religiosity. Going to church regularly or mumbling repetitive prayers is not the equivalent of high SQ.
All in all, these new readings on EQ and SQ tell me that we need to develop three kinds of intelligence: intellectual, emotional and spiritual. The intellectual gives us vast academic knowledge; the emotional allows us to judge what situation we are in and then to behave properly within it through the discrete use of our knowledge; the spiritual enables us to ask if we want to be in this particular situation in the first place and to dare us to create a better one.
In short, IQ deals with the mind, EQ with the heart, and SQ with the spirit.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

this particular situation in the first place and to dare us to create a better one.
In short, IQ deals with the mind, EQ with the heart, and SQ with the spirit. Indeed, our schools should prepare us not only for the present life, but also for the hereafter and forever. No matter how the world turns or how civilizations progress or how events affect our very existence, never for a moment think that our lives on earth are the only ones we have. Rather, believe that there is life after death, and that there is eternity where our final destiny lies.
Just as there are human and physical laws, there are also spiritual laws. And just as there are consequences for violations of human and physical laws, so are there penalties for the transgression of God's commands. For example, civil laws protect contracts, and a party who breaks them may be liable for damages. In the same manner, one who injures another violates criminal laws and is jailed as a consequence. So, too, a violation of the laws of physics impels consequences; hence, one who jumps out of a window falls in accordance with the law of gravity.
By the same token, spiritual laws operate on our spirits, whether we like it or not. When we transgress the Ten Commandments or the beatitudes proclaimed by our Lord Jesus, our spirits suffer the necessary consequences by being damned in eternity. Just as there are reparations for violations of human and physical laws, there is also salvation from our sins - by repentance, restitution and reformation.

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 4: The Essentials of Legal Education (cont.)

ty. Just as there are reparations for violations of human and physical laws, there is also salvation from our sins - by repentance, restitution and reformation. Even as we feast and celebrate on this beautiful evening, isn't it wonderful to know that God is present with us, here and now, in this beautiful ballroom? He is amongst us to share our joy, above us to inspire us, before us to lead us, beside us to guide us, behind us to protect us, and within us - in our minds, our hearts and our spirits - to possess us and bring us to His everlasting Kingdom!
Epilogue
To close this address, let me summarize. I believe that every great school of law must teach its students the three Ls of legal education; namely, language, law and life. Looking over your school brochure, I see that these triple Ls have already been taken into account. Furthermore, Adamson University is committed to the core values of, first, academic a excellence which involves the IQ; second, social responsibility which your school defines as the "building of a society based on justice, peace, respect for human dignity and the integrity of creation" - all of which are really encompassed by EQ; and third, inspiration of St. Vincent de Paul in pursuing  gospel values, a pursuit that develops the SQ.
In short, let me again congratulate all of you tonight on the 61st anniversary of the College of Law of Adamson University - an institution of higher learning that inculcates in its students the three Ls of quality legal education.
Mabuhay ang Adamson University!
