title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice

Chapter 5
Excellence and Ethics
in Appellate Practice
It is said that justices are better read than heard. Upon their enrolment in the magistracy, they are expected to cut all social, personal and professional ties and become virtual recluses in their sensitive work of deciding litigations. This ode of honor requires them not only to be pure, but also to appear pure before their critical public. It is perhaps for these reasons that Supreme Court justices are sometimes referred to as "the gods of Padre Faura.”
Indeed, as most of you know, I have tried my best to avoid unnecessary public and even private audiences have refrained from entertaining visitors in my chambers and avoided telephone calls and conversations regarding ending matters in the courts, especially the Supreme Court.
Every year, I receive about thirty speaking invitations, but because of the foregoing reasons, I have accepted only a few. Tonight is one of those exceptions. I regard the Philippine Trial Lawyers Association as a special forum for reaching out to the legal profession with minimal risk of undue public criticism. After all, I know that you understand and appreciate the necessity of preserving the independence and the integrity of our black-robed men and women.
Furthermore, I could not turn down the invitation of your distinguished president, former Assemblyman and former Deputy Education Minister Salvador B. Britanico. Buddy and I have known each other since our student leadership days at Far Eastern University.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

lyman and former Deputy Education Minister Salvador B. Britanico. Buddy and I have known each other since our student leadership days at Far Eastern University. In your general assembly in this elegant ballroom of the Traders Hotel, I would like to offer you some insights or tips, to use a colloquial term, on how to be more effective appellate court practitioners. I realize that you are the country's most experienced litigation lawyers, who therefore know how to win their cases.
Let me, however, give you an insider's window on how to win not only your cases, but also - and perhaps even more important - how to gain the esteem and respect of the Supreme Court. After all, justice - not necessarily victory - in all litigations is the ultimate aim of our profession. Tonight, therefore, let me discuss two sure ways to gain the esteem and even the admiration of our Supreme Court, in the process, win your cases and render justice to all.
A Reputation
for Excellence

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

sure ways to gain the esteem and even the admiration of our Supreme Court, in the process, win your cases and render justice to all.
A Reputation
for Excellence First, cultivate a reputation for excellence. This means that you must know by heart the many special rules observed in and by the Supreme Court. As you all realize, the preparation of pleadings to be filed in the Supreme Courts is much more complicated than that in the lower courts. Many petitions are denied due course at sight, simply because the lawyers have overlooked certain elementary procedural requirements, like the failure to attach an affidavit of service, a no-forum-shopping certification, or a clear duplicate original or certified true copy of the judgment or order contested. In my book Battles in the Supreme Court published in 1998, I listed at least 21 procedural errors, any one of which would be sufficient to justify the outright dismissal of a case.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

n the Supreme Court published in 1998, I listed at least 21 procedural errors, any one of which would be sufficient to justify the outright dismissal of a case. Those aspiring to be appellate law practitioners should avoid those errors. Otherwise, their petitions would have very slim chances of being granted due course. At this point, I would like you to know that the names of the lawyers of the parties are always listed in the agenda of the court. Thus, when petitions are dismissed because of lapses in elementary procedure, the lawyers are known immediately, and questions about their competence and thoroughness immediately crop up. And when petitions prepared by the same lawyers are repeatedly denied because of simple e technical lapses, they acquire a reputation for sloppiness. Justices invariably comment that, for the sake of their clients, these advocates should stop appearing in the Supreme Court.
Ire of the Court
and of Their Clients

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

stices invariably comment that, for the sake of their clients, these advocates should stop appearing in the Supreme Court.
Ire of the Court
and of Their Clients Many times also, some lawyers - either due to negligence or laziness or both - fail to comply with simple resolutions to file a comment, a reply or other pleadings. When the Court threatens them with disciplinary actions, these lawyers often pass the blame on their hapless associates or meek secretaries who have allegedly neglected to remind them of the deadlines for filing those pleadings. I would like you to know that we frown on this hackneyed buck-passing            technique and almost always admonish or fine counsels who habitually do so. Worse, when it is the petitioner's counsel who fails to comply with these simple resolutions, the Court not only disciplines the lawyer, but it also dismisses the petition altogether. As you all know, once a petition is thrown out due to procedural or other lapses, it is quite difficult to have it reinstated. Invariably, the lawyer gets the ire not only of the Court, but also of their clients!

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

o procedural or other lapses, it is quite difficult to have it reinstated. Invariably, the lawyer gets the ire not only of the Court, but also of their clients! Then, there is the even more pressing need for excellence in presenting the substantive aspects of your case. Except for a few instances like criminal cases, in which the lower courts have imposed the death penalty or reclusion perpetua, the acceptance of an appeal is purely discretionary on the part of the Supreme Court. The High Tribunal is even more discriminating in giving due course to original actions for certiorari and similar petitions that attribute lack of jurisdiction or grave abuse of discretion to other offices and officials of our country.
Poorly prepared pleadings and difficult-to-understand language inevitably spell denial for many petitions. Since the grant of due course in the High Court is discretionary, it behooves lawyers to write pleadings that are clear, correct, complete and concise. It is not enough to allege ultimate facts; it is equally important to back up your allegations with citations of authorities showing that the lower court has indeed committed reversible errors that should be corrected on appeal.
Overworked Justices

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

ations with citations of authorities showing that the lower court has indeed committed reversible errors that should be corrected on appeal.
Overworked Justices Please remember that justices of the Supreme Court are quite overworked. They have to attend to some 6,000 pending cases, and additionally, to shepherd about 5,000 new cases every year. These figures mean that each justice has an average case load of about 400 pending cases plus 25 new ones per month. You can understand why magistrates dismiss at sight unreadable, illogical, ungrammatical and legally shaky pleadings.
In my more than seven-year experience as a sitting justice, I believe that about 60 percent of all new petitions are denied at sight, either because of procedural lapses, or because of the failure of the petitioner to demonstrate clearly any reversible error or grave abuse of discretion on the par of the lower court. A further 20 percent are thrown out after the comment and the reply are filed. In other words, less than 20% of the 5,000 new filings are given due course and mature into full-blown, written ponencias.
Remember that appellate advocates are measured on the basis of how they can invoke a favorable rule of law in one case and provide a substantially meritorious exception in another. Those who are able to decipher, analyze and synthesize nuances of the law eventually get the nod of the Court.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

a substantially meritorious exception in another. Those who are able to decipher, analyze and synthesize nuances of the law eventually get the nod of the Court. If you are new in appellate practice, it is worthwhile to read slowly and deliberately how decisions are written, how justices analyze legal provisions and applicable jurisprudence, and how carefully distinctions are laid out in given factual milieus. As an illustrious US justice once said, cts; general propositions do not decide specific problems; each case has its own peculiarities that must be ruled upon based on the unique factual circumstances obtained. A great lawyer is able to craft a theory that addresses the issues without offending settled doctrines and yet is able to propose a meritorious exception to the prevailing jurisprudence on the matter. It is also suggested that you read petitions, comments and memoranda of respected appellate court practitioners. Study how excellently they present their cases, and why they succeed in persuading the Court to adopt their presentation. They do not merely repeat doctrines or blindly rely on copied quotes; they explain in elegant prose and unbendable logic why their cases and causes deserve to be upheld.
Pleading with
Distinction

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

or blindly rely on copied quotes; they explain in elegant prose and unbendable logic why their cases and causes deserve to be upheld.
Pleading with
Distinction Indeed, I have not always agreed with the briefs, memoranda and other pleadings submitted by distinguished advocates like Estelito Mendoza, Mario Bautista, Agustin Benitez, Eduardo de los Angeles, Simeon Marcelo, Theodore Te, Rene Saguisag, Pacifico Agabin, Antonio Abad Jr., Lorna Kapunan, Katrina Legarda, Roberto Abad and, of course, your president Buddy Britanico. But I have always found great pleasure in reading them, especially during weekends when I cram to write my ponencias.
To encourage lawyers to prepare their pleadings with distinction, Isomètimes quote them in my ponencias. Always, I indicate their names in an appropriate footnote. As some of you know, since I joined the Court more than seven years ago, I have been working seven days a week including Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. The dreariness of routine work is occasionally broken by the spirit-uplifting and free flowing prose of these practitioners. Their pleadings are structured, well-researched, logic-driven and yet simply written. They avoid highfalutin and bombastic language. Moreover, they are respectful in tone even if emphatic in their arguments.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

, logic-driven and yet simply written. They avoid highfalutin and bombastic language. Moreover, they are respectful in tone even if emphatic in their arguments. More than all these, I especially urge you to reserve your best performance for occasional oral arguments called by the Court. Study minutely the facts of your case, stick by your theory, and prepare to answer probing questions on every little detail. I assure you the justices do their homework. They read the pleadings, study the law and applicable jurisprudence, and are always ready to pounce on your case theory. Sometimes, they ask questions because they do not know the answers, but more often, they ask questions to test the lawyers' grasp of their arguments. Many years ago, there was a solicitor general who appeared during oral arguments with less than ideal preparation. Thus, he stumbled from question to question. He would change his theory of the case with each hostile interrogation. Worse, he would contradict justices who were trying to help him, but whom he suspected were against him. Up to this day, he is a favorite topic of private jokes amongst the magistrates.
High Ethical
Conduct
My second suggestion on how to win the respect of our justices is for you to develop a reputation for high ethical conduct. Ethics embraces, among others, fairness, candor and integrity in your professional and personal lives.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

for you to develop a reputation for high ethical conduct. Ethics embraces, among others, fairness, candor and integrity in your professional and personal lives. Fairness means not merely fighting for even-handed treatment of one's cause and case. It extends to a refusal to take undue advantage of the other side, of being honorable in battle and of being scrupulous in the choice of legal weapons.
Immediately after passing the bar examinations in 1960, I became an associate in the law office of our then law dean, Dr. Jovito R. Salonga. One early morning, Dean Salonga called me up at home to say that he was indisposed and could I substitute for him in that morning's trial at the then our   Court of First Instance of Pasay. Even if I knew very little about that inheritance case he was directly handling, I stood up gallantly when the case was called that morning and mumbled, "Ready for the defense, Your Honor."
Judge Angel Mojica, who was presiding, looked askance at me and asked suspiciously, "Where is Atty. Salonga? And young man, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of the plaintiff?"
"He called me up early this morning to say that he was indisposed, Your Honor. He told me that I should not ask for a postponement because there is a standing agreement not to delay the case," I nervously replied.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

s indisposed, Your Honor. He told me that I should not ask for a postponement because there is a standing agreement not to delay the case," I nervously replied. "Your Honor," butted in Atty. Jose W. Diokno, the counsel for the plaintiff, “It is true that we agreed not to defer today's hearing. But in fairness to our young compañero, and knowing that Atty. Salonga would not tell a lie about his health, I myself am now moving to postpone the hearing.
Anyway, this case is also scheduled to be heard two more times during the next two weeks." Addressing me, Judge Mojica boomed, "What do you say to that motion, counsel"?
"No objection, Your Honor," I quickly answered.
This may have been a little incident in the checkered life of the late illustrious Atty. Jose W. Diokno, but it was a major one of mine. It showed me how a great advocate could demonstrate fairness to a young inexperienced lawyer, who hardly knew the pending case; and who, at that point, would probably not have been able to cross-examine the plaintiff adequately. Atty. Diokno earned my immediate admiration and awe, not only for his vaunted competence, but also for his genial sportsmanship in refusing to take undue advantage of a young, nervous lawyer. I am certain that Judge Mojica, who is now in the Great Beyond, was impressed, too.
Candor and
Integrity
Candor refers to straightforwardness or forthrightness in admitting a weakness or even an error. Some lawyers are so proud they would not admit a mistake. Matitigas ang mga ulo.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

straightforwardness or forthrightness in admitting a weakness or even an error. Some lawyers are so proud they would not admit a mistake. Matitigas ang mga ulo. There are also lawyers who insist on equating the ratio decidendi of a decision with a mere obiter dictum. Credibility goes up when a lawyer frankly admits that a statement in a decision is a mere obiter and may not be binding. And respect rises even more when the learned counsel explains why the obiter makes sense and should anyway be adopted as a doctrine.
But nothing erodes a lawyer's credibility more than the deliberate misquoting of a decision or, worse, the omission of certain words or sentences that qualify or restrict the sense of a ruling. Remember that the eagle-eyed magistrates can easily detect misquotations, out-of-context statements and misleading arguments.
A candid lawyer is a humble person - not only one who is not afraid to admit an error or a shortcoming, but also one who rises from a mistake and more than makes up for it the  next time around.
Finally, by integrity I refer to honesty and truthfulness. A person of integrity acts in accordance with what is true and honest regardless of personal consequences. To act with integrity is to act with moral courage. This involves not only theoretical bravery in battle but, a priori, purity of spirit and clarity of conscience. For only one who is pure of heart and d u e clear of mind can act with integrity.
Assistance in
Reforming the Judiciary

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

ity of spirit and clarity of conscience. For only one who is pure of heart and d u e clear of mind can act with integrity.
Assistance in
Reforming the Judiciary The Supreme Court, as you know, has embarked on a comprehensive reform program to address the many complaints of corruption, incompetence and delay in the delivery of justice. Many times these problems are brought about, or at least aggravated, by members of the bar.
I now take this occasion to call for your cooperation and assistance in eradicating these ills. As active practicing lawyers, you know who are the corrupt and the incompetent among the magistrates. You know who do not deserve to wear their majestic black robes.
Lawyers of integrity will never bribe judges. Remember, corruption will take place only if it is abetted or tolerated by the bar. Integrity demands not only moral courage in denouncing the corrupt and the incompetent but also the initiative in defending the decent and the competent from malicious, unreasonable and scurrilous attacks.
Just as there are some dishonest judges, there are also some unscrupulous lawyers who want to win at all costs. Worse, in an effort to earn more, there are lawyers who ask money from clients, allegedly to line the pockets of magistrates. Whether they actually bribe magistrates or merely increase their earnings unethically, such practice is reprehensible and should be condemned by all lawyers of integrity.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Excellence and Ethics in Appellate Practice (cont.)

ey actually bribe magistrates or merely increase their earnings unethically, such practice is reprehensible and should be condemned by all lawyers of integrity. I also denounce most vehemently some lawyers' habit of terrorizing decent and competent judges with threats of administrative complaints. Thus, the promotion of deserving magistrates are sometimes stymied or delayed. The mere pendency of these baseless charges is enough to hinder the Judicial and Bar Council from processing their otherwise deserving promotions.
To summarize, if my presence tonight will have any lasting significance and if you are lending me twenty minutes of your precious attention and time will have any worth, please remember this. To win the hearts and the esteem of the Supreme Court, there are two "E" words to live by: excellence and ethics. If you develop these two values to perfection, I assure you of success, not just in winning cas in the Supreme Court, but also in gaining the respect and the admiration of the justices.
Maraming salamat po.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate

Chapter 6
Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
On behalf of the Supreme Court, I welcome all of you to this newly renovated, awesome, serene and majestic temple of justice in our country. You may be pleased to know that this Session Hall where we are holding our program has just been reopened last Tuesday, April 1, 2003 after being refurbished under the direction of our honoree, Mr. Justice Vicente V. Mendoza. The renovations of this Hall and several other parts of our building, including the construction of a new Division Hearing Room on the ground floor, are part of our honoree's legacy to the Court.
I am greatly honored at being chosen by Mr. Justice Vicente V. Mendoza to deliver the Opening Remarks in today's program commemorating his retirement from the Supreme Court. To fulfill my delicate task of setting the proper theme, tone and cadence of this afternoon's proceedings, I decided to speak from the heart and to relate my personal impressions of our honoree. After all, the official appreciation of the entire Court is elegantly expressed in a Plaque that will be read later on during these ceremonies.
Initial Impressions

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

er all, the official appreciation of the entire Court is elegantly expressed in a Plaque that will be read later on during these ceremonies.
Initial Impressions Prior to my joining the Court in 1995, Mr. Justice Mendoza was a distant star. True, I had telescoped him from afar and learned of his solid reputation as a respected Court of Appeals justice, a hardworking assistant solicitor general and a scholarly professor of constitutional law. But we  had no personal dealings or close friendship to speak about. However, a few months into the Court, I quickly learned to look up to him as a model of how a magistrate of  the High Court should comport himself in public and in private. In my esteem, he has become one of the brightest, calmest, most diligent and most trustworthy jurists I have ever met.
True to his humble, almost self-effacing nature, Mr. Justice Mendoza does not actively volunteer his views on every question placed on our agenda. But he is always ready, when asked, to render an in-depth and a well-studied advice. He speaks in a slow, modulated baritone that exhibits a natural sense of order emanating from a logic-driven mind. The deliberate manner in which he delivers his carefully d, chosen words inspires confidence and concurrence. Indeed, he explains with the methodology of a teacher, the clarity of a savant, the finesse of an artist and the passion of a love all of which he is.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

currence. Indeed, he explains with the methodology of a teacher, the clarity of a savant, the finesse of an artist and the passion of a love all of which he is. On the other hand, his written opinions, whether representing those of the majority or of the minority, are always carefully phrased, grammatically precise, and minutely calibrated to express as accurately as possible the principle expounded and the limitation within which they can be used.
He is always mindful of the advice of his fellow scholar and co-author, Professor Paul A. Freund of the Harvard Law School, who said: "Judging is a high art, and the judge, like the artist, must feel that the shoddy is an offense against his medium, as a lie is a sin against language.” Indeed, in his judicial pronouncements, Mr. Justice Mendoza is always prudent, never shoddy; and in his language, always precise, never tentative. He is moved, never by pique and spite, never by prejudice and vindictiveness, but always by deliberate and well-studied choice.
The Private Person
In contrast to his distant, majestic and almost stoic public image, he is in private a very friendly and congenial person. During our informal lunches and meetings, he would freely exchange jokes and repartees with us. He would begin a conversation with an almost wry affability but would eventually break out into a beaming, infectious and disarming smile.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

nd repartees with us. He would begin a conversation with an almost wry affability but would eventually break out into a beaming, infectious and disarming smile. To his own assistant and staff, he is known to be a caring elder who is always interested in their mundane problems and concerns. He leads them by his example of extensive research, thorough study, and long working hours even during weekends and holidays. A natural mentor, he likes to needle his subordinates for their less than perfect reports; but at the same time, he is informal enough to break bread with them at lunchtime. In short, he is a demanding disciplinarian when it comes to work, but a sensitive and considerate elder with regard to personal relations.
As a young bachelor, Mr. Justice Mendoza was shy and reserved. It took him five long years to court his wife, Thelma. She finally said "yes" only after he had repeatedly but very privately crooned to her his favorite ballad popularized in the 1950s by his tocayo, Vic Damone, entitled "In My Own Quiet Way." I will quote portions of the song that capture the winning, wooing style of Justice Vic:
"I am not the kind who sighs
Every time you wander by
Or weep when you are gone for just a day
But still and all my dear
I really love you in my own quiet way.
"I admit I'm absentminded and forgetful
Does your birthday come in April or May?
There are times when I am likely to be fretful
Or I'll pick darndest moments to be shy
But with all my faults you'll find
I'm the true and steady kind
And it's no lie believe me when I say

kely to be fretful
Or I'll pick darndest moments to be shy

And it's no lie believe me when I say Deep down inside I know I'll always love you
In my own quiet way!"
Here are a few more tidbits about the private Mr. Justice Mendoza:
1. Every year during the last 39 years since their marriage in 1963, Justice Vic and Professor Thelma always visited at least 7 churches every Maundy Thursday.
2. Every New Year's Eve, he always relished biringhe, the Capampangan version of arroz valenciana, and nilagang baka with chorizo, as well as hot chocolate drink - no, not instant variety, but that which is beaten in a batirol from round chocolate balls.
3. Whenever a birthday is celebrated, there has to be a pancit to celebrate a long life.
4. His favorite dishes are pesang dalag with buro, inihaw na hito with atsarang kamias, alige ng talangka, tinolang palaka and adobong camaro or crickets. His idea of heaven on a Sunday morning is salted fresh carabao milk mixed with hot steamed rice, scooped with his bare fingers.
In his early years as a father to two sons and one daughter, he tended to be protective, strict and distant, but not confrontational. He had long ago laid down the household rules and expected all of them to observe them strictly. He exacted simple values: respect for elders, honesty, responsibility and observance of the golden rule. He was the stern padre de familia, not a back-slapping barkada to his children. He preferred to talk to them indirectly by asking Thelma to "tell them this" or "tell them that."

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

padre de familia, not a back-slapping barkada to his children. He preferred to talk to them indirectly by asking Thelma to "tell them this" or "tell them that." Still and all, behind the tough veneer is the soft-hearted father. Up to now he uses his children's childhood pictures as bookmarks and fusses over their juvenile drawings and sketches. He keeps an album of every picture and letter they had sent him until they left the family residence many years ago.
Indeed, underneath his stoic expression is a sentimental father who sheds tears of joy every now and then over a child's great achievement, or tears of compassion over a crushing failure or disappointment. But if there is anyone who can make this giant jurist dance on a rope, it is his eldest granddaughter, the apple and orange of his eye. No one, but no one, dares to interrupt his work - certainly not his Supreme Court session - except this little girl. So, when he is really in a bad mood, when he is under insurmountable stress, there is only one sedative and therapy: a hug or even just a phone call from little Allyn.
The Disciplined Jurist
As a jurist, Justice Mendoza may be characterized as traditional and conservative in the sense that he is a stickler for rules. His mind is very disciplined, methodical and deliberate. His every word and action always carries the authority or backing of some law or precedent. He does not invent or second-guess. He always moves with certainty, predictability and finality. That is why it is easy to concur in his ponencias, but difficult to dissent from them.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

econd-guess. He always moves with certainty, predictability and finality. That is why it is easy to concur in his ponencias, but difficult to dissent from them. From every petitioner and pleader, he demands proof of standing. He does not heed a person who cannot show  any direct and viable interest in a judicial undertaking. He wants to be sure that no interloper or pretender would dilute the purity of judicial proceedings.
By the same token, he ardently believes that "the power of judicial review is premised on the existence of an actual case or controversy." To buttress this belief, he often cites Justice Felix Frankfurter and Professor Alexander M. Bickel, who both said that the concepts of standing and case and controversy tend to ensure that the "hopes and prophecies expressed in legislation [would be] tested in the actual workings of our society."
For these reasons, he rules narrowly - ever careful to excise obiters, extravagance and bravado from his ponencias. Justified by a passion for unfettered fairness, he follows to the letter the wise advice of one of his favorite American magistrates, Mr. Justice Benjamin Nathan Cardozo, who explained:

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

r unfettered fairness, he follows to the letter the wise advice of one of his favorite American magistrates, Mr. Justice Benjamin Nathan Cardozo, who explained: "The judge, even when he is free, is not wholly free. He is not to innovate at pleasure. He is not a knight-errant, roaming at will in the pursuit of his own ideal of beauty or of goodness. He is to draw his inspiration from consecrated principles. He is not to yield to spasmodic sentiments, to vague and unregulated benevolence. He is to exercise a discretion informed by tradition, methodized by analogy, disciplined by system and subordinated to the primordial necessity of order in social life. Wide enough in all conscience is the field of discretion that remains.”
Unlike our honoree, I do not always abide by Cardozo. I do not always follow tradition. Neither am I methodized by analogy or imprisoned by precedent. Sometimes, I like to blaze new trails, to be eclectic, to be daring, to be revolutionary. However, that does not lessen my admiration and awe of Mr. Justice Mendoza. Strangely enough, it is this very difference in legal philosophy and methodology that attracts me to and causes my unbending esteem for him. I admire his tenacity, consistency and insistence on the welltrodden path, on jurisprudential principles tested by time and opportunity.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

bending esteem for him. I admire his tenacity, consistency and insistence on the welltrodden path, on jurisprudential principles tested by time and opportunity. Although I do not always concur in all his ponencias, and although he does not always agree with mine, I always - without exception - seek his views on all important issues deliberated upon by the Court. And even during those occasions when I suspect beforehand that his opinion may be opposite mine, I still consciously seek it anyway. And he never withholds it, because we both realize that the Supreme Court thrives in a kettle of free ideas where truth, fairness and justice can be distilled only after all sides, including the most outlandish ones, have been poured out and percolated.
Indeed, we discuss and debate animatedly, even ardently. Although we disagree on ideas, philosophies and other matters of the mind, we never carry those difficulties on a personal plane, much less on an emotional level. In short, our differences are focused on the arguments, never on the person. While our minds may clash some of the time, our friendship is robust and pleasant all the time.
The Greatest Accolades
Verily, I believe that the greatest accolades to Mr. Justice Mendoza comes not from those who always agree with him, but from those who, from time to time, disagree with him honestly and sincerely; yet have no doubt of his single-mindedness of purpose, his unflinching honesty of opinion and his clarity of thought. His most prized commendations come from his erstwhile critics who have become his new converts.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Veracious and Venerable Magistrate (cont.)

, his unflinching honesty of opinion and his clarity of thought. His most prized commendations come from his erstwhile critics who have become his new converts. Deeply ensconced among his cherished mementos is the award given to him two months ago by Bantay Katarungan or "Justice Watch" headed by former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga and former Justice Secretary Sedfrey A. Ordoñez. Extolled the former critics and now admirers of our distinguished honoree:
"In April this year, Supreme Court Justice Vicente Mendoza retired without any taint or blemish after forty one (41) years in public service. During the almost nine (9) years when he served on the Supreme Court, the High Court had to draw on his wisdom, his integrity, and independence of mind, in resolving many difficult, controversial cases. He responded with masterful craftsmanship, relying on his deep knowledge of the law and his conscience as his guide. Through his majority and dissenting opinions, he defined the place of judi power in a constitutional democracy, always striking the delicate balance between political majorities that make for popular democracy, on the one hand, and the transcendental claims enshrined in the Constitution on the other."
Today, Mr. Justice Mendoza retires. Now freed of backbreaking workload in the Court, he will no longer bear the heavy yoke of pulling the judicial cart. I am happy for our friend, but sorry for us who will be orphaned. He was a fountain of wisdom that always refreshed us. Now, with neither fountain nor water, how will his orphans quench thirst?

rry for us who will be orphaned. He was a fountain of wisdom that always refreshed us. Now, with neither fountain nor water, how will his orphans quench thirst? I can talk on and on, all day long, about Mr. Justice my Mendoza until the spoken words are erased from vocabulary. But if my address today is to have any significance, I must in closing leave you two words Justice in my opinion, define the very essence of Mr. Justice Mendoza. These words are veracious and venerable: veracious to mean that he is credible, dependable, truthful and upright; and venerable to mean that he is dignified, knowledgeable, respectable and sagacious.
Friends, ladies and gentlemen, join me in remembering and applauding Mr. Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, the veracious and venerable magistrate of the Supreme Court of the Philippines.
I thank you.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 1: GMA's Legacy
heading: GMA's Legacy
text:
GMA's Legacy

Date:       2007-08-12
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
How will President Macapagal-Arroyo be remembered in history? Will the Philippines be better off on June 30, 2010 when she ends her term than on Jan. 20, 2001 when she began it? The President's State of Nation Address gives her own answer. But is her hoped-for legacy doable?
**GMA' Sona**
In her Sona, GMA focused on her three priorities for "the past three years.. First, investments in physical, intellectual, legal and security infrastructure to increase business confidence. Imprastraktura para sa negosyo at trabaho. Isang milyong trabaho taon-taon.
"Second, investments in a stronger and wider safety net—murang gamot, abot-kayang pabahay, eskwelang primera klase, mga gurong mas magaling at mas malaki ang kita, mga librong dekalidad, more scholarships for gifted students, and language instructions to maintain our lead in English proficiency. Dunong at kalusugan ang susi sa kasaganaan.
Third, investments in bringing peace to Mindanao; in crushing terrorism wherever it threatens regardless of ideology; and putting a stop to human rights abuses whatever the excuse."
It is difficult to fault GMA's investments. Mainly, her critics merely ask: Where will she get the trillions to fund her grandiose dreams? Borrow again? Raise taxes again? Sell off the nation's patrimony? Or just let the people salivate now and despair later?
**Regain credibility first**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 1: GMA's Legacy
heading: GMA's Legacy
text:
GMA's Legacy (cont.)

se dreams? Borrow again? Raise taxes again? Sell off the nation's patrimony? Or just let the people salivate now and despair later?
**Regain credibility first** Even if she finds the money to fund these quixotic quests, the first priority-as I see it-is to earn the trust of our people. Without trust, no leader can succeed. Last week, I wrote on Cardinal Gaudencio B. Rosales' exhortation that "it is treason to lead without a vision, supported by core values. And as I have often said, visionary leadership by example is the best way to lead.
As for core values, may I paraphrase former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga: It is good to aspire for the many things that money can buy, like roads, skyways, bridges, airports, piers, schools, houses, power plants, transmission towers, and computer technologies but it is better to have, first and foremost, the things that money cannot buy, like integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy, and credibility.
Over the years, GMA has, rightly or wrongly, been vilified for many alleged wrongdoings, thereby pushing her public acceptance ratings down to record lows. The big question is: Can she still regain her credibility to enable her to achieve her Sona dreams? I believe so. I hope so. As a citizen of this Republic, I want the President to succeed and foster democracy and development; freedom and food; nay, liberty and prosperity for all.
How?
**Lead internal transformation**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 1: GMA's Legacy
heading: GMA's Legacy
text:
GMA's Legacy (cont.)

want the President to succeed and foster democracy and development; freedom and food; nay, liberty and prosperity for all.
How?
**Lead internal transformation** First, if I were in her place, I would call all my close relatives, officials, and cronies and tell them that I would forget in the meantime whatever sins and wrongs they might have done in the past. But henceforth, they must strictly follow the Constitution, anti-graft law, ethical standards law, public bidding laws, and similar codes. Woe to those who don't.
To start off, I would personally lead the example by being skills needed to achieve the legacy, not those employed to win elections. "A President is always as strong as she wants to be." Yes, but I will use presidential strength to be transformational, no longer transactional.
**Fortify democratic institutions**
Second, I would fortify our democratic institutions by naming trustworthy officials, especially to the Supreme Court and the Commission on Elections. Between now and June 30, 2010, eight justices will retire (Cancio C. Garcia on Oct. 15, 2007; Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez, Feb. 28, 2008; Ruben T. Reyes, Jan 3, 2009; Adolfo S. Azcuna, Feb. 16, 2009; Dante O. Tinga, May 11, 2009; Consuelo Ynares Santiago, Oct. 5, 2009; Leonardo A. Quisumbing, Nov. 6, 2009 and Minita Chico Nazario, Dec. 5, 2009). Moreover, Chief Justice Reynato Puno will end his term on May 17, 2010. Let me caution, however, that the Constitution bans appointments "two months immediately before the next presidential elections and up to the end of (her) term."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 1: GMA's Legacy
heading: GMA's Legacy
text:
GMA's Legacy (cont.)

et me caution, however, that the Constitution bans appointments "two months immediately before the next presidential elections and up to the end of (her) term." In view of her many debacles (like EO 464, CPR, PP 1017 and People's Initiative), GMA will be tempted to fill up the Court with "loyalists." With due respect, I say banish the thought. Dwight Eisenhower tried to "pack" the US Supreme Court, but his own choices, led by Earl Warren and William Brennan, voted down his cases. Ferdinand Marcos produced a compliant Court that, ironically, aggravated the discontent that eventually toppled and disgraced him. Change tactics. With prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law!
In the Comelec, there is now one vacancy. On Feb. 7, 2007, Chair Benjamin Abalos and Commissioners Rex Borra and Florentino Tuason will retire, thereby giving GMA the opportunity to appoint a new chair(Like Romulo Macalintal) and commissioners (like Leila de Lima and Howard Calleja). Without credible officials, it is useless to talk of electoral reforms or to expect an orderly 2010 election.
Before she exited in 2010, GMA would have named all 15 justices and all seven commissioners. Will she bequeath a Supreme Court and a Comelec that are credible and fortified, or arrant and spineless?
Transforming the internals of GMA's leadership now and fortifying the Court and the Comelec will constitute a lasting legacy that requires no funding. Moreover, such selfless actions will elevate her credibility to new heights; and propel her Sona legacy into a 2010 reality. (August 12, 2007)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 2: For or Against GMA
heading: For or Against GMA
text:
For or Against GMA

Date:       2007-09-30
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
My August 12 column, titled “GMA Legacy,” continues to draw reactions. One was quite pointed, even sarcastic: “After the Supreme Court-under your leadership last year-dealt successive blows to GMA, how can you say that, as a Filipino, you still want the President to succeed and foster democracy and development; freedom and food; nay, liberty and prosperity for all.’ I thought all along that you have joined us in the anti-GMA movement.”
**For or against actions, not persons**
I write for or against causes, actions and principles, not pro or contra persons and personalities. As a retired jurist, I am used to deciding in favor of or against petitions or complaints, not pro or contra the parties in the controversy. I am interested in what wins, not in who wins. I impugn the crime, but I do not detest the criminal. As Christian theology goes, we hate sin but not the sinner. And we do not just criticize; we also help find solutions.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 2: For or Against GMA
heading: For or Against GMA
text:
For or Against GMA (cont.)

crime, but I do not detest the criminal. As Christian theology goes, we hate sin but not the sinner. And we do not just criticize; we also help find solutions. My column stated that it is difficult to fault the President’s aspirations for an infrastructure-laden legacy. However, I also cautioned that while it is good to aspire for the many things that money can buy-like roads, bridges, airports, and school houses-it is better to have, first and foremost, the things that money cannot buy, like integrity, public esteem, character, moral ascendancy, and credibility. Without credibility, no leader can succeed. And visionary leadership by example is the best way to lead and to gain credibility.
**GMA's worst failing**
I think that GMAs worst failing is in transparent and accountable governance, resulting in her massive loss of credibility. For too long, her trust rating has been miserably low. According to the most recent SWS survey, issued on September 24, it is now a dismal minus 11. Our people have a deep-seated impression of widespread graft in her government. Worse, she is not doing enough to abate or even minimize it. In fact, the Philippines fell from 121st to 131st place, out of 180 countries, in the corruption rating of the Berlin-based Transparency International (Inquirer, 9/27/07).

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 2: For or Against GMA
heading: For or Against GMA
text:
For or Against GMA (cont.)

e Philippines fell from 121st to 131st place, out of 180 countries, in the corruption rating of the Berlin-based Transparency International (Inquirer, 9/27/07). To regain her credibility, I have suggested that she (1) direct all her close relatives, officials and cronies to "follow strictly the Constitution, anti-graft law, ethical standards law, public bidding laws, and similar codes;" and (2) fortify "our democratic institutions by naming trustworthy officials, especially to the Supreme Court and the Commission on Elections." I added, "With prudent legal advice, goals can be attained under the rule of law".
**The rebounding economy**
On the other hand, the most bright-lined area of her governance is the improved economy. Though not an economist, I can feel the effects of economic indicators. The budget deficit has been arrested, thus reducing foreign borrowing; the interest and inflation rates are at an all-time low, enabling consumers to stretch their buying power especially in durables like homes and condos; the peso has risen in value, enhancing the people's ability to enjoy their income.
Many say that the economy is propelled by the sweat of the overseas Filipino workers, not by the genius of GMA. They argue that the OFWs who remitted a hefty $14 billion last year—double that sent five years ago-are the real heroes. Of that, there is no doubt.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 2: For or Against GMA
heading: For or Against GMA
text:
For or Against GMA (cont.)

ius of GMA. They argue that the OFWs who remitted a hefty $14 billion last year—double that sent five years ago-are the real heroes. Of that, there is no doubt. But GMA's Herculean effort in pushing for the expanded Value Added Tax (EVAT), the privatization program especially of the power sector, foreign investments in large-scale mining, the major rise in tourism arrivals, and the resurgent stock market cannot be brushed aside. New investments mean more jobs, more production, and more income.
Certainly, the OFW remittances are a major reason for our economic upturn, measured at a record 7.5-percent annual rate in the second quarter this year. But GMA deserves equal credit (or discredit?). In fact, consumers are still pillorying her for the higher EVAT they pay, especially for oil products that used to be VAT-exempt. Indeed, the defeat in the last senatorial election of GMAs' candidates, like Ralph Recto and Mike Defensor, has been attributed invariably to the perceived evils of EVAT.
Her critics further lament that the rebounding economy is a myth, a statistical hocus-pocus, because the poor do not feel its effects. Maybe so, but we must begin with the first of a thousand steps. The resurgence of Korea, Singapore, and now of China needed several years of spectacular growth before the benefits reached the masses.
**Credibility, first and foremost**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 2: For or Against GMA
heading: For or Against GMA
text:
For or Against GMA (cont.)

nce of Korea, Singapore, and now of China needed several years of spectacular growth before the benefits reached the masses.
**Credibility, first and foremost** Which brings me back to GMA's basic problem of low credibility. A cancer patient who trusts a physician will not resent the debilitation of chemotherapy. Similarly, a people who have confidence in their 1 leader will willingly suffer transitory torment, in exchange for the eventual healing of their malady.
In contrast, the leader who is not trusted will be mocked not only for the real economic malaise but also for the temporary pain caused incidentally by the remedy. The applause of the world media (Wall Street Journal, Clinton Global Initiative, etc.) confirms G GMA's work to the converted, but not to the non-trusting locals who remember only the agony of her reign.
That was what happened in India. The leaders who prescribed the painful medicine were booted out of power, and the politicians who opposed them were voted in to revel in the prosperity started by the hated reformers. The moral lesson: aspire for credibility, first and foremost. (September 30, 2007)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 3: Rage for Truth
heading: Rage for Truth
text:
Rage for Truth

Date:       2008-03-02
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
The people’s confidence in the Arroyo government is deteriorating daily as the corruption scandals hounding it escalate in number and gravity. As President Macapagal-Arroyo’s credibility continues to plunge, even well-meaning citizens who several months ago wanted to give her a last chance at good governance are now growing pessimistic about her redemption.
**Unlikely possibilities**
What are the ways of confronting or solving this fast deteriorating scenario? The “least disruptive” is voluntary resignation as demanded by Cory Aquino. But GMA has rejected this option outright. “I am President and no one else,” she bellowed after hearing Mass in Malacanang last February 25.
A second way is a snap election, which Ferdinand Marcos chose in 1986. But there is no vacancy in the presidency. Furthermore, a law is needed to authorize a special election. Besides, under the Constitution, “in case of death, permanent disability, removal from office, or resignation of the President, the Vice-President shall become President to serve the unexpired term.” In 1986, there was no incumbent vice-president.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 3: Rage for Truth
heading: Rage for Truth
text:
Rage for Truth (cont.)

office, or resignation of the President, the Vice-President shall become President to serve the unexpired term.” In 1986, there was no incumbent vice-president. A third option is impeachment a la Joseph Ejercito Estrada. But an impeachment should be initiated in the House of Representatives. After witnessing how easily the Kampi Party had defrocked Jose de Venecia, there seems no hope of an impeachment ever passing the bigger house. A fourth possibility is a coup d'etat. A military coup that will install a Burma-type junta would be far worse than GMA. It will obliterate the Constitution, our democracy, our economy, and everything our heroes and martyrs have fought for over the last 100 years.
Martial law under the present Constitution is toothless. But a fifth option of setting aside the Constitution and declaring emergency rule would make GMA a dictator, something our people will fight tooth and nail. GMA I think is smart enough not to want to be remembered in the company of Marcos, Suharto or, worse, Idi Amin.
How about people power? Our country may not be ripe for an Edsa-type peaceful revolution. The economy is still holding up, unlike in 1986 and 2001 when the peso was sinking and prices were escalating, when business was deteriorating and investments were migrating. Too, Jaime Cardinal Sin is no longer around to summon a critical mass of half a million. Moreover, the military is very loyal to GMA. People power would "weaken our democratic institutions," said Archbishop Leonardo Legaspi. Neither did the bishops call for resignation, only for an end to corruption.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 3: Rage for Truth
heading: Rage for Truth
text:
Rage for Truth (cont.)

power would "weaken our democratic institutions," said Archbishop Leonardo Legaspi. Neither did the bishops call for resignation, only for an end to corruption. **GMA's best option**
GMA is an astute politician who carefully weighs all her options. She must be aware that all the above scenarios are unpalatable. She must also know she has two very important aces: (1) the economy is still looking up and the middle forces will not just endanger it unnecessarily; and (2) she has only two more years in her regular term. There are many people of goodwill, who are still willing to wait provided there is credible assurance she would really step down in two years, and provided she abates the corruption engulfing her.
I think that, from GMAs perspective, the best way she can honorably survive this grave crisis of confidence is by convincing the middle forces that she would really relinquish power in June 2010 and stop graft immediately. How? First, halt all moves to amend the basic law. Any proposal to alter the Constitution, regardless of purpose and method, always reeks with suspicion that it is intended to prolong her stay.
Second, strengthen the credibility of the Commission on Elections by filling up the two existing vacancies with independent and competent non-politicians. In the same way, name a no-nonsense chair of the Commission on Audit who will not allow hanky-panky in the disbursements of the people's money. Also, appoint trustworthy justices to the Supreme Court, starting with the seat of just retired Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez.

heading: Rage for Truth

isbursements of the people's money. Also, appoint trustworthy justices to the Supreme Court, starting with the seat of just retired Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez. Third, prosecute immediately and send to jail some big names involved in the NBN-ZTE mess and other corrupt-ridden transactions. B e transparent. Allow the Senate an untrammeled inquiry into these transactions. Cooperate with independent efforts to ferret out t h e truth.
Fourth, take preventive measures to minimize the impact of the receding US economy on our country. (Relevantly, may I just quickly remind her about the laments of our overseas Filipino workers, the backbone of our economy, who are still awaiting her definitive action on their five recommendations as reported in my column last February 10.)
Undertaking in good faith all these steps would result in a win-win solution for her and our people. She might yet save her presidency while satisfying the clamor to abate corruption and reform governance.
**Continue the blitz**
In the meantime, what should the citizens do? I say, rage on! ! Press on with the demos. Make them more massive. Intensify the media blitz. Sharpen the Senate investigations. Hasten the Supreme Court decision that, I believe, would unshackle Romulo Neri. Fill our churches during Masses for truth and justice. Pray with our bishops, priests, and nuns until "communal action" shall lead us to a new type of people power that would liberate us from corruption and restore integrity.

heading: Untrammeled Search for Truth
text:
Untrammeled Search for Truth

Date:       2008-03-16
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
More than just recommending the "abolition of EO 464,"ally wanted a "search for the truth" that is "untrammeled, especially at the present time when questions about the moral ascendancy of the present government are being raised."
**Completing the CBCP's joy**
Thus, by itself, President Macapagal-Arroyo's revocation of Executive Order 464 and Memorandum Circular 108-described by Solicitor General Agnes Devanadera as a mere "symbolic act"-does not satisfy the CBCP's desiderata of a "determined and relentless" way of "Seeking the Truth, Restoring Integrity."
That is why to "complete the joy" of our bishops, I urged the President last Sunday to let former Neda chief Romulo Neri testify freely at the Senate probe. Such loosening will demonstrate the President's sincerity and goodwill in fully responding to the with the middle forces and belie the charge that the revocation was just "another double speak.” joying the applause of our bishops, GMA is now expected to facilitate, not hinder further, the discovery of the truth. But, if the President continues to invoke-improperly in my humble view— executive privilege in lieu of the unlamented EO, the perception that GMA was directly and personally involved in the alleged ZTE bribery will gain more credence. The more Neri is barred from speaking, the worse will GMAs public posture be.
**No direct link to NBN mess**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 4: Untrammeled Search for Truth
heading: Untrammeled Search for Truth
text:
Untrammeled Search for Truth (cont.)

in the alleged ZTE bribery will gain more credence. The more Neri is barred from speaking, the worse will GMAs public posture be.
**No direct link to NBN mess** As it is now, there has been no evidence directly linking GMA to the alleged ZTE-NBN overprice. Other than by innuendo, not even Jun Lozada has testified that GMA was part of the bukol. Neither has Joey de Venecia definitively said that GMA was a direct beneficiary of the supposed $130-million "commission." However, by preventing her subaltern from speaking, GMA is fostering the belief that Neri's putative testimony would directly and personally link her to the mess.
During the Supreme Court hearing, there were three specific questions that the President did not want Neri to respond to: "(1) Did the President have any interest in the NBN project? (2) Did the President order Neri to prioritize the NBN? and, (3) Did she order the continuance of the project despite his allegations of bribery?"
Frankly, I cannot understand why the President did not want Neri to answer these simple questions. If the answers are in the negative, then there is absolutely nothing to worry about. She would not be linked to the alleged bribery. So, the desire to silence Neri must come from the belief that the answers would be in the positive: "Yes, she was interested in the project. Yes, she ordered the project to be prioritized. Yes, she wanted the project to continue despite the allegations of bribery."

Ironically, this insistence on secrecy merely fortifies the claim of the 80 Former Senior Government Officials (FSGO) that GMA was "at the center of the corruption and cover-up" of the NBN deal. If she were innocent, why in the world would she prevent Neri from telling the truth? Worse, by choosing silence, she is unable to explain her perceived complicity in the mess.
**Volcanic communal action**
In my last column, I explained that, based on the parameters laid down in the unanimous decision in "Senate vs Ermita," Neri's plea for silence cannot be granted. However, there have been reports that tremendous pressures are allegedly being exerted on the justices to reverse, or modify, or find some wayward exceptions to the acclaimed Ermita ruling. I believe that such pressures are normal, and that the justices will not cave in to them and will decide according to what becomes of them as jurists. They know that history will ultimately judge them.
However, it is entirely possible that the Court, for some novel reasons beyond my range now, may surprisingly rule in favor of secrecy. Denied an , the Senate may just as suddenly close its investigations. That may be the wish of the avid advisers of the President. But I think that abruptly and inconclusively terminating the Senate probes is not good for her.

ons. That may be the wish of the avid advisers of the President. But I think that abruptly and inconclusively terminating the Senate probes is not good for her. If it must come out, and as sure as the rising sun it will, is it not better for all, especially for GMA, that it should shine forth now while she is still in the best position to contain any possible damage and brighten her side too?
The only independent and credible state institutions that the public still trusts in the search for truth are the Senate and the Supreme Court. Should these two fail to unravel the complete truth, the people, especially the middle forces, those who are still willing to wait for a constitutional change of leaders in mid-2010—may finally lose hope in our normal democratic processes. They may once again take to the streets and the plazas to forge what CBCP President Angel Lagdameo calls a "new type of people power."
Indeed, a sudden halt of the Senate's search for truth caused by a surprise ruling of the Supreme Court could be the tipping point in the present crisis, much like the Enrile-Ramos defiance in Edsa ,I or the prosecutors' walk out in Edsa I. Date:       2008-03-23

By: Artemio V. Panganiban
In her Lenten Message, President Macapagal-Arroyo vowed once more to eradicate corruption. Her mesage was an obvious response to the earlier pastoral statement from the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines (CBCP), that said we face a "crisis of truth and the pervading cancer of corruption."
**Truth, accountability, and reform**
Similarly, in obedience to the CBCP's call "to pray together, reason together, decide together, and act together," the Watch, Pray and Act (WPA) Movement-composed of the leaders of the nation's Catholic schools-committed to fight for a specific, point-by-point action program for "truth, accountability, and reform."
For my part, I have during the past weeks challenged our citizens to rage for truth by amplifying the demos, sharpening the Senate investigations, intensifying the media blitz, and pressing on with their various demands on the President. At the sametime, I wrote that GMA could save her presidency by convincing the middle forces that she would really (1) relinquish power when her term ends on June 30, 2010, and (2) abate immediately the corruption engulfing her.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 7: Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?
heading: Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?
text:
Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?

Date:       2008-07-27
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Last Sunday, I posed two questions… Will our Congress, Supreme Court, Commission on Elections and people allow Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo to stay in power after June 30, 2010? Realistically, can GMA-unlike Ferdinand Marcos (FM)- extend her reign without martial law?
**Marcos precedent**
First, a little history. When FM declared martial law on September 21, 1972, the Constitutional Convention (Con-con) of 1971 was still meeting. But it was obvious that the Con-con was not minded to extend his term, which was ending on Dec. 30, 1973.
However, after FM imposed martial law, the Con-con—with stirring dissents from a courageous few-obligingly approved the 1973 Constitution changing the then presidential system to the parliamentary form. The Charter change (Cha-cha), done under martial law, extended Marcos' rule indefinitely.
FM, the wily lawyer, was a stickler for legalism. He took extreme pride in boasting that his Proclamation 1081 imposing martial law was issued pursuant to the then Constitution. To stress his claim, he labeled his regime "constitutional authoritarianism." He knew that the two anchors of his regime-the military establishment and the international community, especially the United States-would support him as long as he showed a veneer of constitutional legitimacy to his iron fist.
"Oppositors" and issues

l community, especially the United States-would support him as long as he showed a veneer of constitutional legitimacy to his iron fist.
"Oppositors" and issues Now fast forward to the present. To extend her reign beyond 2010 through a parliamentary shift, GMA would probably choose—as I wrote last week—-the constituent assembly (Con-ass), not the tedious Con-con. However, most of the presidential wannabes like (alphabetically) Joseph Estrada, Panfilo Lacson, Loren Legarda, Mar Roxas, and Manuel Villar would surely besiege her. So would the various oppositionists like Jejomar Binay, Alan and Pia Cayetano, Francis Escudero, Jamby Madrigal, and Aquilino Pimentel Jr.
Too, the militants, party-lists, civil society, labor unions, business organizations (like the Makati Business Club), and student groups would escalate their "political noise." Expect print and broadcast media to intensify their attacks.
However, I think that the swing group would be the middle forces, those who, to preserve our democratic institutions (or what's left of them, were willing to wait for GMA to serve her term but who would now be confronted by the specter of her continued stay. These forces will include the bishops, Catholic laity, El Shaddai, and other religious groups.
As vital as the personalities opposing GMA are the bread and butter issues: the soaring prices of food, transportation, petroleum, and energy; deteriorating peace and order; and the corruption scandals. A march of the hungry and the angry, aggravated by their "most corrupt" and "most unpopular" perceptions, would be invincible.

text:
Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War? (cont.)

der; and the corruption scandals. A march of the hungry and the angry, aggravated by their "most corrupt" and "most unpopular" perceptions, would be invincible. **GMA's weapons**
To win the Cha-cha, GMA will probably rely on her two big T weapons: the resources of government and her vast political machinery: the Lakas-Kampi monolith plus her firm grip on the House of Representatives and the governors, mayors, and barangay leaders.
Unlike Marcos, GMA may not be a wily lawyer, but she is a shrewd politician. She has perfected patronage as a political weapon. She adroitly uses the budget, Page or and PCSO earnings and other public money, and personally inaugurates school buildings, housing projects, new roads, bridges, and other infrastructure. She justifies VT as a tax on the rich and dispenses its katas in terms of low-cost NEA rice, lifeline electricity subsidies, and other doles.
During an unprecedented meeting of the controversial Judicial, Executive and Legislative Advisory Council (Jelac) held right in the Supreme Court's inner sanctum, GMA committed a P3-billion largesse for the judiciary next year. To pacify the bishops, she uses her social funds to contribute to their favorite charities.
She has appointed choice candidates to critical offices, like the Supreme Court and Commission on Elections, and has anointed a formidable network of generals, admirals, and superintendents in various levels of the armed services.
**People's victory**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 7: Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?
heading: Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War?
text:
Will GMA Win the Cha-cha War? (cont.)

ion on Elections, and has anointed a formidable network of generals, admirals, and superintendents in various levels of the armed services.
**People's victory** But Marcos too had all these-political sycophants, friendly justices, compliant election officials and fat pork barrels, plus to subdue the opposition and to get an indefinite extension of unlimited power.
Holding the balance now are the middle forces. Once they join Erap's teeming "masa," the opposition and the media, GMA may think of iron rule. However, to prevent a repeat of Marcos, the present Constitution extracted the teeth of martial law. It may be used only to quell "invasion or rebellion" and only for a "period not exceeding 60 days" after which it is automatically lifted. Neither does it suspend the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus nor the operation of the Constitution, the Supreme Court and Congress. Because of these and other limits, martial law may not help GMA the way it did Marcos.
How then will GMA win (or lose) the Cha-cha war? To quote Executive Secretary Eduardo Ermita's mantra to the SWS survey showing his boss as the "most unpopular leader" since 1986, "Let the people be the judge." So be it, provided the Comelec counts the votes accurately.
Should the enraged middle forces pour into the streets and plazas in massive numbers during the Con-ass debates, the Chacha express may not reach the Supreme Court, the Comelec, and the plebiscite. Rather than risk a new type of people power revolt, GMAs' allies may just bugle an early retreat. (July 27, 2008)
