title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 6: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
heading: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
text:
Thunderous Triumph of People Power

Date:       2010-05-16
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Despite the sweltering kilometric queues, technical glitches, carelessness, mismanagement, and other booboos of Comelec and Smartmatic, our people persevered. Human frailties and technological hitches could not stop the thunderous Noynoy landslide.
**New manifestation of People Power**
Our first nationwide automated election is a resounding triumph of People Power of the strict constitutional genre. Our people opted for a peaceful transition of power, no longer by
staging mammoth street rallies, but by pouring a massive electoral m a n d a t e on their new leader.
People Power 1 was "extra constitutional." Cory Aquino succeeded to the 1986 presidency outside the pale of the Constitution then; in fact, her government was "revolutionary" in character. Though the Supreme Court (Estrada vs Desierto, March 1, 2001) ruled that Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo ascended legitimately via the "intra constitutional" People Power 2, many constitutionalists still contest the legitimacy of her ascension in 2001. In contrast, the 2010 People Power 3 catapults Noynoy Aquino with unquestioned constitutionality.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 6: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
heading: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
text:
Thunderous Triumph of People Power (cont.)

nalists still contest the legitimacy of her ascension in 2001. In contrast, the 2010 People Power 3 catapults Noynoy Aquino with unquestioned constitutionality. This new genre of People Power is embodied in the 1987 Constitution of Cory. Fittingly, it ushers the presidency of her son. The thunderous landslide gives him a clear head start to begin his reform program. Noynoy's overwhelming mandate assures public support for his agenda of change. It gives him enormous clout to transform our savaged democratic institutions immediately.
As I anticipated in several columns, the clustering of the precincts precipitated long lines that were caused mainly by the logistical miscalculation of assigning only one Board of Election Inspectors (BEI) and one PCOS machine to 1,000 voters. My wife and I arrived at our voting center before 7 a.m. Yet, there were over 20 voters ahead of us. We lined up patiently and were able to vote after 45 minutes. It turned out we were lucky. Other people, including Noynoy, sweated many hours to cast their ballots. Just how many were actually disenfranchised, how many could not stand the heat or could not wait because of other commitments may never be accurately counted.
Just how many votes were wasted because of PCOS machine malfunction, oval misalignment, ballot rejection, and printing errors may no longer be precisely known.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 6: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
heading: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
text:
Thunderous Triumph of People Power (cont.)

Just how many votes were wasted because of PCOS machine malfunction, oval misalignment, ballot rejection, and printing errors may no longer be precisely known. Similarly, just how the inadequate training of the BEsl, the insufficiency of the Comelec instructions, and the scanty education of voters impacted on the results; just how many were not able to vote because of their exclusion from the voters' list; and just how many candidates have been denied victory due to disenfranchisement may no longer be exactly determined. (I agree though with Sen. Jamby Madrigal that these puzzles must still be investigated.)
**Mis-chief-makers deterred**
No matter, the many who were able to vote gave Noynoy a phenomenal landslide. They prevented mischief-makers from manipulating the results and discouraged cheaters from plying their trade. Our people gave him such a huge margin that it could not be overcome by cheating. Indeed, those who wanted to corrupt our succession rules via the holdover scenario, or worse via military rule, were overwhelmed by the Noynoy tsunami.
True, the Commission on Elections labored under difficult circumstances. It had less than one year to jump from full manual count to full automated count, a feat never attempted anywhere in the world. However, there were, apart from the unfortunate clustering of precincts, other glaring errors and missteps that could have been easily prevented or avoided.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 6: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
heading: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
text:
Thunderous Triumph of People Power (cont.)

ld. However, there were, apart from the unfortunate clustering of precincts, other glaring errors and missteps that could have been easily prevented or avoided. For example, why did Comelec choose small covers measuring only half the size of the ballots thereby violating the secrecy of the vote? The Inquirer front-page photo catching the ballot of former President Joseph Estrada and exposing his failure to vote for a vice president is a picturesque reminder of this violation. The lack of polling booths that provided voter secrecy was also prevalent. The past Comelecs had their faults too, but none of them overlooked voter privacy.
**No transparency of precinct count**
Our result-starved people applauded the instant transmission of the results and their immediate media distribution. The parallel counts of the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting and media outfits like GMA7 and ABS-CBN affirmed the count. Note, however, that all these automated results came from the same election returns spewed out by the PCOS machines at the clustered precincts.
They do not explain how the PCOS machines counted the individual votes. There was no check on how the machines tallied the individual ballots. Remember that the voters were merely told by the machines that their ballots were "scanned" and counted. But there was no proof of how the machines actually tallied them.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 6: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
heading: Thunderous Triumph of People Power
text:
Thunderous Triumph of People Power (cont.)

hat the voters were merely told by the machines that their ballots were "scanned" and counted. But there was no proof of how the machines actually tallied them. Comelec inexplicably disengaged a machine safeguard where a report of the vote would be flashed on the small screen on the PCOS machine. Only after the voters are satisfied that their ballots had been accurately captured would they then press a button for the machine to count them. All in all, I heave a sigh of relief that the worst-case scenarios like a nationwide failure of election, corruption of the source code, holdover presidency, and military rule did not come to pass. I hail this new manifestation of People Power and the miraculous start of a peaceful transition of power. May the miracle continue and guide our new president in reinventing a new and better Philippines. (May 16, 2010)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 7: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
heading: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
text:
Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem

Date:       2010-05-23
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Great victories spawn great expectations instead of massing in our streets to oust disgraced leaders and to install new ones, our people overrode technical glitches and human frailties in our first automated national election to hand Noynoy Aquino the most convincing electoral mandate since the new Constitution took effect in 1987. They want him to use this new genre of People Power to transform our country.
**Prosecution of grafters**
Verily, our people expect Noynoy to solve their gnawing problems. They are hungry for food, for justice, and for peace. They want him to cleanse the cesspools of corruption, poverty, ignorance, criminality, and separatism. For too long they have been deprived. They cannot wait too long. They want immediate action, from Day One of his presidency.
To do this, he needs to choose exemplary subalterns; to expand his congressional base and push necessary legislation; to reform the police and the military; to improve tax collection and local governance; to beef up education and health care; to straighten the bureaucracy; to clean up the environment, and to elevate ethical standards. But the most vexing problem is the prosecution of grafters. His mantra of Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap was the most applauded portion of his campaign. He promise to investigate and prosecute the alleged excesses and ill-gotten wealth of the Arroyos. This is easier said than done.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 7: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
heading: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
text:
Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem (cont.)

auded portion of his campaign. He promise to investigate and prosecute the alleged excesses and ill-gotten wealth of the Arroyos. This is easier said than done. His mother, Cory, had one year of revolutionary rule-undeterred by legal niceties-to dismantle the Marcos machine, to name a new Supreme Court, to change the Constitution, and to reorganize the bureaucracy. Then, she had five more, or a total of six years from 1986 to 1992 (equivalent to Noynoy's own x-is year term), yet these were not enough. Up to now, the chase for the allegedly fabulous Marcos wealth has not ended.
In this sense, Noynoy faces more daunting odds than his mother did because he would not enjoy that one year of free rule to scrape the barnacles of government. Right off, eh has to face the gridlocks of democracy and the many constitutional checks that could be misused and abused to stymie his reforms. President Macapagal-Arroyo carefully selected all the members of the Supreme Court and the Office of the Ombudsman to be sure-s o goes the public perception that she and her cronies would be beyond the reach of our laws.
**Early confrontation**
Noynoy has publicly criticized GMAs' appointment of Chief Justice Renato C. Corona, saying that he would break tradition and refuse to be sworn in by the new chief magistrate. This early confrontation is symptomatic of the difficulties he would be facing.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 7: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
heading: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
text:
Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem (cont.)

he would break tradition and refuse to be sworn in by the new chief magistrate. This early confrontation is symptomatic of the difficulties he would be facing. Noynoy's anti-corruption campaign would surely flounder without the cooperation-worse, with the enmity—of the Supreme Court, which reversed half a century of jurisprudence banning midnight appointments to usher the coronation of its new chief. The creation of a commission to investigate the Arroyos' alleged ill-gotten wealth, similar to that created by his mother for the Marcoses, would amount to nothing without a cooperative Ombudsman and an unbiased judiciary.
Surely, Noynoy's crusade would grind to a halt if he cannot win over the indispensable prosecutor (the Ombudsman) and the final arbiter (the Supreme Court) of corruption cases. The Constitution has given these agencies fixed terms of office and formidable fiscal and administrative independence from the President and Congress.
His problem though is not unique. US President Franklin Delano Roosevelt entered office in 1933 at the tail of the Great Depression. The American electorate gave him an enormous mandate, which he used during his first 100 days to convince the US Congress to grant him carte blanche in bringing America back to its feet. However, the US Supreme Court frowned upon and declared unconstitutional much of his New Deal program.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 7: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
heading: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
text:
Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem (cont.)

t him carte blanche in bringing America back to its feet. However, the US Supreme Court frowned upon and declared unconstitutional much of his New Deal program. Roosevelt retaliated by proposing to increase the number of Supreme Court justices so he could "pack" the Court with members sympathetic to his cause. The proposal generated massive protests and was defeated. But Roosevelt prevailed anyway because one SC justice (Owen Roberts) switched positions and effectively created a liberal majority that carried his initiatives.
**Courage, innovation, passion**
A current example is President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of Brazil. Rising as the leader of the leftist Workers' Party, Lula met strong opposition to his radical reforms. After moderating his ideas, he used his political capital to lift Brazil from the brink of bankruptcy.
His country now belongs to BRIC (Brazil, Russia, India, and China), the most economically progressive nations on this planet. Recently, Time Magazine named Lula one of the most influential leaders of the world. During the G20 Summit in London in April 2009, US President Barack Obama fondly greeted him, "That's my man right there. The most popular politician on earth."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 7: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
heading: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
text:
Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem (cont.)

During the G20 Summit in London in April 2009, US President Barack Obama fondly greeted him, "That's my man right there. The most popular politician on earth." Like in the United States, our media give new presidents 100 days of honeymoon. If Noynoy must succeed in transforming this nation, he must immediately seize the momentum and deftly use his huge political capital, the new form of People Power, to win over the constitutional structures that are dominated by appointees of the predecessor he has promised to bring to us someday the gravitas to be hailed later on by our people (and, maybe, Obama too), "That's our man, our sword of justice and our liberator from poverty"? (May 23, 2010)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 8: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
heading: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
text:
Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty

Date:       2010-05-30
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
Our people handed Noynoy Aquino the most overwhelming mandate since our present Constitution took effect in 1987. They opted for a peaceful transition of power, no longer by staging mammoth street rallies, but by rolling a tsunami of votes that could not be stopped by cheating, computer glitches, human errors, carelessness, and logistical lapses. They invented a new form of People Power to reshape the Philippine landscape.
**Moratorium on amortizations**
This thunderous triumph of People Power so impressed the international community that many ambassadors, led by those of the United States (Harry K. Thomas Jr.), China (Liu Jianchao), Japan (Makoto Katsura), and the European Union (Alistair MacDonald), laid aside legalities and diplomatese to congratulate our new leader even before the formal process of ballot canvassing had begun.
Time Magazine has been sufficiently swayed as to feature Noynoy twice in the span of less than a month, first on its cover on April 26 and second in its May 24 issue. Time led the world's media (from Thailand to Britain to Chile) in focusing on the Philippines, not as much as it did in 1986 celebrating the first miracle of People Power but enough to make our country become the darling of the world again.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 8: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
heading: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
text:
Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty (cont.)

e Philippines, not as much as it did in 1986 celebrating the first miracle of People Power but enough to make our country become the darling of the world again. This is a shining moment we cannot let pass. Let us strategically use it in the war against corruption and poverty. This burst of international goodwill can generate new investments, funding grants (like from the US Millennium Challenge Corporation), and favorable trade agreements.
With innovation and imagination, our new president can negotiate for sovereign debt waivers, whether of the principal or interest or both. At the very least, a moratorium of say three years in the amortizations of our international debt should not be too difficult to obtain. This will give Noynoy the capacity to meet immediate, impatient expectations and the gestation time for his longer-term solutions. Instead of amortizing debt, our meager funds could be diverted to pump-priming and job creation.
**Passion to liberate**
As I wrote last Sunday, it takes courage, innovation, and passion to satisfy the people's hunger for justice and for food. And now, it may be asked: What propelled Noynoy's cry of "kung leader walang corrupt, walang mahirap"? What gave our new the passion to liberate his people from corruption and poverty? The answer may be found in a letter sent to him by his father, Ninoy, a copy of which was given me by retired Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 8: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
heading: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
text:
Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty (cont.)

ption and poverty? The answer may be found in a letter sent to him by his father, Ninoy, a copy of which was given me by retired Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero. Dated August 25, 1973, the letter was written while Ninoy was still in prison during the martial law regime. It advised the young Noynoy about his decision, "after lengthy conference with my lawyers, Senators Jovito R. Salonga and Lorenzo M. Tañada. not to participate in the proceedings of the Military Commission assigned to try the charges filed against me. Inasmuch as [the trial] will be a completely one-sided affair. I expect to be sentenced to imprisonment the rest of my natural life, or possibly be sent to stand before a firing squad. By adopting the course of action I decided upon this afternoon, I have literally decided to walk into the very jaws of death."
Continuing, Ninoy told his teenaged heir the reason for his sacrifice, "You may ask: why did you do it? Son, my decision is an act of conscience. It is an act of protest against the structures of injustice that have been imposed upon our hapless countrymen. Futile and puny, as it will surely appear to many, it is my last act of defiance against tyranny and dictatorship."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 8: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
heading: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
text:
Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty (cont.)

ve been imposed upon our hapless countrymen. Futile and puny, as it will surely appear to many, it is my last act of defiance against tyranny and dictatorship." Regretting his inability to secure his son's and four daughters' financial future, Ninoy wrote, "The only valuable asset I can bequeath to you now is the name I carry. I have tried my best during my years of public service to keep that name untarnished and respected, unmarked by sorry compromises for expediency. I now pass it on to you, as good, I pray, as when my father, your grandfather, passed it on to me."
Then, Ninoy apologized for "passing unto your young shoulders the great responsibility for our family. I trust you will love your mother and your sisters and lavish them with the care and protection I would have given them. I was barely fifteen years old when my father died. His death was my most traumatic experience. I loved and hero-worshipped him so much; I wanted to join him in his grave when he passed away.
"Finally, stand by your mother as she stood beside me through the buffeting winds of crisis and uncertainties, firm and resolute and uncowed. I pray to God, you inherit her indomitable spirit and her rare brand of silent courage."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 8: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
heading: Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty
text:
Destiny and Legacy, Not Dynasty (cont.)

eting winds of crisis and uncertainties, firm and resolute and uncowed. I pray to God, you inherit her indomitable spirit and her rare brand of silent courage." The legacy lives on. Then came Ninoy's parting words, asking Noynoy to bear his legacy of heroic service. "The only advice I can give you: Live with honor and follow your conscience. There is no greater nation on earth than our Motherland. No greater people than our own. Serve them with all your heart, with all you might and with all your strength. Son, the ball is now in your hands." Like his mother, Noynoy had no plans of seeking the presidency. Not at this time, anyway. He was content to support the ambition of his friend, Mar Roxas. But destiny beckoned. The death of his mother on August 1, 2009 altered history and catapulted him.
Time Magazine ascribed his ascension to "dynasty." With due respect, I think it was , that propelled Noynoy to the top and kindled his passion to liberate his people from corruption and poverty. (May 30, 2010)

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 9: Exercise in Courage
heading: Exercise in Courage
text:
Exercise in Courage

Date:       2010-07-18
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
The electoral protest filed by Mar Roxas against Vice President Jejomar Binay is an exercise in courage. To prosecute the suit requires herculean effort, enormous time, and humongous expense that could reach P50 million without any assurance of victory. In fact, no one has won an electoral protest for any national position (president, vice president, and senator) since the 1987 Constitution took effect.
**Past electoral suits**
Miriam Defensor-Santiago protested the election of President Fidel V. Ramos in 1992 but due to her election as senator in 1995, the Supreme Court en banc-acting as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET)-dismissed her protest, reasoning that by choosing to be a senator she had abandoned her claim to the presidency. Similarly, Loren Legarda's protest against Vice President Noli de Castro in 2004 was thrown out after Legarda won a Senate seat in 2007.
Fernando Poe Jr's protest against President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo in 2004 was dismissed for being academic due to Poe's untimely death. Aquilino (Nene) Pimentel Jr. 's challenge against Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile in 1995 was also dismissed due to Pimentel's senatorial victory in 1998. The only pending protest involving a national office (other than Roxas') is that of Aquilino "Koko" Pimentel III, filed in 2007 against Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 9: Exercise in Courage
heading: Exercise in Courage
text:
Exercise in Courage (cont.)

The only pending protest involving a national office (other than Roxas') is that of Aquilino "Koko" Pimentel III, filed in 2007 against Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri. Election protests are time-consuming because they involve the visual examination of the ballots. Electoral tribunals create several teams of "revisors" to pass upon the validity and recount of each contested ballot. Forensic and other experts era employed. The litigants pay for the fees and other expenses of these revisors, experts and, of course, lawyers.
**Essentials of the Roxas protest**
Over 100 pages long, the protest involves about three million ballots. Of these, Roxas claims that 2.6 million have not been counted properly because the PCOS machines classified them as "null/misread votes," meaning that the voter (1) may have voted for other positions but abstained from voting for any VP candidate; or (2) "under shaded" the ovals for VP; or (3) voted for more than one candidate for VP; or (4) the machine omitted counting, for some unknown reason, the vote for VP.
Given that "no human eye saw how the votes were appreciated by the PCOS machine, or whether they were appreciated at all," Roxas argues that the ballot boxes should be opened and the ballots minutely examined and manually counted by revisors appointed by the PET. He explains that this is the only way to prevent the wholesale disenfranchisement of 2.6 million electors. If these ballots are correctly counted, Roxas claims he can overtake Binay's lead of 727,084.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 9: Exercise in Courage
heading: Exercise in Courage
text:
Exercise in Courage (cont.)

prevent the wholesale disenfranchisement of 2.6 million electors. If these ballots are correctly counted, Roxas claims he can overtake Binay's lead of 727,084. Revising Roxas' 2.6 million "null/misread" ballots will probably cost five times more than revising Koko Pimentel's 500,000 protested ballots. Not only that, Binay will probably file a counter protest involving several million votes too. Counter-protests are normal parts of due process. So now, we see why protests are tedious and expensive.
A first in an automated election, Roxas' protest spawns novel questions, which will mean more expenses and delays. For example, Comelec Chairman Jose A. R. Melo told media that automated ballots cannot be manually examined and that only the same PCOS machines which produced the original results will recount them. However, Roxas is precisely contesting the accuracy of the machine count. The best way to do that is to manually check the ballots. Verily, the Rules of Procedure for election contests using the PCOS, decreed by the Supreme Court on April 27, 2010, expressly recognize manual revision of ballots.
**Answers to lingering questions**
Other than the null/misread ballots, Roxas blames Comelec and Smartmatic "for disabling or entirely removing crucial (legally mandated) safeguards that should have prevented the occurrence of system-wide electoral frauds in the vice presidential contest." Some of these disabled safeguards and alleged fraud s are:

The mandated random manual audit "was improperly and irregularly conducted." But I welcome it if only to quiet down many misgivings about our automated election system, to cure its many flaws, and to prevent their repetition in the future.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 10: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
heading: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
text:
How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court

Date:       2010-10-24
Publisher:  Philippine Daily Inquirer (Opinion)
Source:     With Due Respect (2011)
By: Artemio V. Panganiban
If there is an agency or group, whether in the government or elsewhere, that can scuttle the avowed anti-corruption and anti-poverty programs of President Aquino, it is the supreme Court. Being an independent and apolitical branch of government, it is not bound by the election promises or the political agenda of the government. Its fealty is to the Constitution and the rule of law that, per Chief Justice Renato C. Corona in a very recent speech, "will never bend to the ever-shifting political winds and passions of the moment ."
**Crucial Supreme Court cases**
I wrote last Sunday that I was invited to a tête-a-tête with presidential allies, including Sen. Franklin Drilon, Secretaries Cesar Purisima, Butch Abad, Dinky Soliman, PCGG Chairman Andy Bautista, SSS Chairman Johnny Santos, and former Defense Secretary Nonong Cruz.
Among the items we discussed were the crucial cases facing the P-Noy regime: the impeachment of the Ombudsman, the onstitutionality of the Truth Commission, the validity of midnight appointments, and the legality of public-private partnerships (PPP). In reaction, readers asked me to share some ideas on how P-Noy can win these cases.

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 10: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
heading: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
text:
How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court (cont.)

idnight appointments, and the legality of public-private partnerships (PPP). In reaction, readers asked me to share some ideas on how P-Noy can win these cases. Already, the Court has issued two status quo ante (SQA) o-r of ders. The first barred the Committee on Justice of the House Representatives from hearing the two impeachment complaints filed against Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez, while the second stopped the firing of an alleged midnight appointee, Bai Omera Dianalan Lucman of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos. Earlier, it issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) that halted the toll increases in the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX).
SQAs are worded more benignly than TROs so as not to offend co-equal branches of government against whom they era directed. However, by their nature, they have the same effect as TROs. They are effective immediately since they do not mandate the filing of bonds, which the Rules of Court require in TROs, to answer for possible damages the respondents may suffer in case the courts ultimately rule against the petitioners.
**Prima facie meritorious**

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 10: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
heading: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
text:
How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court (cont.)

quire in TROs, to answer for possible damages the respondents may suffer in case the courts ultimately rule against the petitioners.
**Prima facie meritorious** While SQAs and TROs do not necessarily guarantee the success of the petitioners, their issuance implies that the Court has found the petitions to be prima facie meritorious. In simple language, this means that, unless successfully overturned, the petitioners have preliminarily shown they are entitled to the reliefs they are praying for. It thus behooves the respondents (the House of Representatives and the Aquino administration) to e-r but the prima facie case, if they are to win the cases eventually,
And this is precisely what happened in the SLEx case rove which the TRO was issued. Convinced by the cogent arguments of the respondents, the Court lifted the TRO. Moreover, it decided immediately on the consolidated petitions involving the toll ways in Luzon. In Francisco vs. Toll Regulatory Board (October 19, 2010), the Court unanimously upheld the PPP entered into by the government not only with the SLEx but also with North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) and the South Metro Manila Skyway.
Speaking through Justice Presbitero J. Velasco Jr., the Court upheld PPP as a viable mode of economic strategy, thus: "Running through the gamut of our statutes providing for and encouraging partnership of the public and private sector is the paramount common good for infrastructure projects and the equally important factor of giving a reasonable rate of return to private sector's investments."

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 10: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
heading: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
text:
How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court (cont.)

s the paramount common good for infrastructure projects and the equally important factor of giving a reasonable rate of return to private sector's investments." Indeed, the Court answered the exhortation earlier this week of Neeraz Jain, country director of the Asian Development Bank, that investors must be assured that "the judicial system will uphold contractual rights." Indeed, even without P-Noy's criticism of the SLEx TRO, the Court upheld the legality of toll road PPPs.
**How cases are judged**
Without going into the complexities of the other crucial cases facing the P-Noy regime, I shall outline the two main theories on how controversies are decided.
Theoretically, cases are judged by applying the law to the proven facts per this simplified formula: facts times law equals decision F( x L= D). Known as the analytical method, this is the most commonly accepted theory. However, there are many ways of interpreting and applying the law. This is why lawyers argue interminably and justices differ passionately in their opinions. Understandably, the formula sometimes fails to answer the basic question: What is the specific interpretation or application that the court will use?
In turn, the sociological school of legal philosophy holds that to predict how a case would be decided, one must consider the personality of the magistrate and the various stimuli attendant to a case per this formula: personality times stimuli equals decision (P x S = D).

title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 10: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
heading: How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court
text:
How P-Noy Can Win the Supreme Court (cont.)

consider the personality of the magistrate and the various stimuli attendant to a case per this formula: personality times stimuli equals decision (P x S = D). The personality of a magistrate includes intrinsic qualities like upbringing, education, relationships, track record, previous decisions, religious faith, character, skills, habits, personal philosophy, motivations, idiosyncrasies, aptitudes, etc. Stimuli refer to how he or she responds to externals, like public opinion, peer pressure, religious leaders, medical condition, appointing authority, appointment sponsor (if any), close friends, etc.
To win his cases, P-Noy must strategize patiently and properly, using other than his past frontal criticisms-analytical and sociological ways of persuasion and remembering that, in the end, the law is what the Supreme Court says it is. (October 24, 2010)

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age

PART I
Chapter 1. Enter the Bio-Age
Many years ago, Dr. Christian Barnard thrilled the world with the first successful heart transplant. Even before that, however, kidneys had been routinely excised from healthy donors and surgically implanted in patients with renal failures. Only recently, a Filipino senator was the recipient of a liver transplant from his son.
These astounding surgeries, however, are always hounded by the danger of rejection. The human body is naturally conditioned to expel any foreign object artificially embedded in its loins. Whether it be an organ donated from another human or an artifice made of plastic or titanium, the net response of the body is to reject the foreign even if well-intentioned invader.
Healing Miracles
Via the Biosciences
Would it not be marvelous if, instead of transplanting organs and tissues via complicated surgeries and medical procedures, the heart or the pancreas may be coaxed to repair and regenerate itself internally? This is precisely the thrust of new sciences - to enable our body or any of its many organs and tissues to repair itself or to accept new parts made from its own cells. Now, stem cell research shows credible evidence of lasting cures - not only for defective body organs but also for Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and countless other deadly diseases.
Scientists have amply demonstrated "manufacturing" or "repairing" body parts by means of cells from - either embryonic or adult stem cells —"incubated" from the same person is not only possible but is in fact already being experimented on in many places in the world.

r embryonic or adult stem cells —"incubated" from the same person is not only possible but is in fact already being experimented on in many places in the world. Researchers have also shown that hair-width electrodes attached to the motor cortex of the brain can carry electronic signals detectable by a computer? This phenomenon makes it possible for more sophisticated gadgetry to bypass spinal cord injuries and make paralyzed people move their arms and legs again.
Modification of
Human Conduct
But the biosciences extend beyond the healing of physical diseases. Their incursions into the mental faculties are even more dramatic, because they enhance knowledge of and the ability to manipulate the brain - the source of all human behaviors. For this reason, they are able to influence, if not control, social conduct and human relationships.
By healing diseases, prolonging human life, relieving pain and manipulating behavior, the new sciences can change demographics, population densities and economic indicators. Moreover, by tinkering with human behavior through genetics, they may also trigger major societal and political changes. Indeed, intelligence, crime proclivity and sexuality - three higher-level behaviors with genetic roots - may be enhanced or depressed via manipulations of the brain.

d, intelligence, crime proclivity and sexuality - three higher-level behaviors with genetic roots - may be enhanced or depressed via manipulations of the brain. Already, there are brand-name medicines that alter human conduct by re-circuiting neurotransmitters in the brain. Some of these are Prozac, manufactured by Eli Lilly; Zoloft, by Pfizer; and Paxil by Smithkline Beecham. These antidepressants effect miraculous changes in the "most central of political emotions, the feeling of self-worth, or self esteem." In this sense, Prozac is a kind of "happiness pill" for millions of people with aggression or depression syndrome.
Another drug, Ritalin, increases attention span, creates a sense of euphoria and builds up energy levels.' It is useful for restless young people who cannot sit still in classrooms. It nudges them into more socially correct behavior.
I will not exaggerate by advocating that the State should exercise social control through genetic engineering and miracle medicines reminiscent of the Boys from Brazil, but it is equally possible to imagine that mind-altering drugs could be used or even misused by social players other than the State - parents, teachers, employers and others who have an interest in how people behave.

drugs could be used or even misused by social players other than the State - parents, teachers, employers and others who have an interest in how people behave. This is not to say that bio-genetics is the be-all and end-all of the human essence. The perennial debate about which is more potent - nature or nurture - is not settled as yet. Not to be overlooked is the ethical and moral issue of whether genetic modification should be undertaken at all. The point for now, however, is that humankind is able to change itself not only by improving the environment, but also by altering genetic make-up. In other words, our uniqueness as individuals is dictated by our genome (the totality of our genetic information) which in turn is affected by nutrition, upbringing, environment and education.
Enhancement of
Food Production
Moreover, biotechnology makes it possible to enhance agricultural products through genetic modification. Already, this scientific advance is evident in the Philippines through successful experiments on hybrid rice and corn, which are claimed to be superior not only in nutrition but also in their easy and short planting requirements. This mutation translates to benefits for both producers and consumers in terms of lower prices and greater product availability.

nd short planting requirements. This mutation translates to benefits for both producers and consumers in terms of lower prices and greater product availability. I realize that the use of genetically altered organisms and foods is still controversial. One set of advocates rejects these products because of the risks they pose to the health of those who ingest them, whether they are people or livestock. On the opposite camp are those who claim that these genetically modified (GM) foods are the answer to the urgent need to feed the burgeoning world population. In the Philippines as elsewhere, this controversy goes on not only in scientific laboratories but also in street marches, legislative deliberations and even in pulpits.
There are basically three science issues in this debate: allergenicity, gene transfer and outcrossing. The first concerns the possible allergic effects GM foods may bring to consumers; the second involves the possibility of gene transfer from GM foods to the cells of the consumers, particularly if antibiotic-resistant genes used in GMOs are transfused; and the third refers to the mixing of genes from GM plants with those "in the wild," such as when GMOs good only as feeds for livestock appear in products for human consumption.

ers to the mixing of genes from GM plants with those "in the wild," such as when GMOs good only as feeds for livestock appear in products for human consumption. The biotechnological controversy is also relevant to environmental protection. For example, a genetically modified bacterium may be applied to the banks of a river to clean up waste and mining sludge. But after slurping the waste, what would the organisms do to the environment? Will they devastate it and produce a problem more difficult to assess and to solve than the original one?
Judicial Awareness
of the Biosciences
These controversies aside, it is obvious that the gigantic strides in life sciences and life technologies will change human behavior and social interaction. That is certain. These resulting alterations will, in turn, require new modes of governance and, for us in the judiciary, new jurisprudential norms without precedents. For this reason, the Supreme Court has been monitoring these epochal transformations, wrought by biosciences and biotechnologies, and the need to keep our judiciary attuned to them. How has this awareness of the Philippine judiciary come about?
First, the Court invited Dr. Franklin M. Zweig, president of the Einstein Institute for Science, Health and the Courts (EINSHAC), to orient it on the new sciences and how they could affect judicial decision-making. As a participant in the Supreme Court Centenary Lecture Series, Dr. Zweig delivered his talk entitled "Life Technologies and the Rule of Law" on November 14, 2000.

a participant in the Supreme Court Centenary Lecture Series, Dr. Zweig delivered his talk entitled "Life Technologies and the Rule of Law" on November 14, 2000. Our guest lecturer explained a brief overview of the “unprecedented rise, expansion and pervasiveness of biological technologies,” which will demand jurisprudential answers with no precedent or analogy. The study of human genetics may show “significant  limitations to human abilities to exercise free will." Thus, the "variations in the degrees of freedom that chemistry confers upon individuals" are likely to provide new defenses in criminal and civil cases. "My genes made me do it," can scientifically become a "respectable claim in criminal justice proceedings.”
On another level, the distinguished lawyer-scientist added that genetic tests might be used to pre-screen appointees or candidates for public office. The possibility is imminent, considering that the new sciences may arguably show a predisposition to Alzheimer's disease, cancer, diabetes or other defects and illnesses.
On the whole, his lecture opened new vistas that may indeed alter our traditional concepts of dispute settlement.

On the whole, his lecture opened new vistas that may indeed alter our traditional concepts of dispute settlement. Second, at EINSHAC's invitation, several Supreme Court justices participated in two international “conversations” on biosciences and biotechnologies as they affect the courts. One was held in Kona, Hawaii from June 30 to July 4, 2001; and the other, in Ottawa, Canada from June 17 to 21, 2002. As of this writing, there is a more than even chance that one of these international "conversations" may be held in the Philippines in the foreseeable future, perhaps in a year or two.
During these international gatherings, scientists and academicians well-versed in the new sciences freely conversed with jurists and explained how DNA, as the elemental building block of nature, could be altered to change life-styles and societal phenomena, which in turn would necessitate new jurisprudence. In A Centenary of Justice, which came out in 2001, I included as Chapter 10 the talk I delivered during the Kona round entitled "Ready for the Bio-Age." Likewise, in Reforming the Judiciary, published in 2002, I incorporated, as Chapter 7, "Transparency, the Key to Sound Judgments," my remarks during a panel discussion in the Ottawa meeting.
All in all, these two international meetings provided the Supreme Court delegation with sufficient introductory knowledge that excited and enabled it to appreciate the relevance of the biosciences to the work of the judiciary.

Supreme Court
Decisions on DNA Third, in Tijing v. Court of Appeals, the Supreme Court (Second Division) for the first time - even if only as an obiter - said that "we now have the facility and expertise in using DNA tests for identification and parentage test.” It, however, cautioned that "being a novel scientific technique, the use of DNA test as evidence is still open to challenge. Eventually, as the appropriate case comes, courts should not hesitate to rule on the admissibility of DNA evidence. For it was said that courts should apply the results of science when competently obtained in aid of situations presented, since to reject said result is to deny progress. Though it is not necessary in this case to resort to DNA testing, in future it would be useful to all concerned in the prompt resolution of parentage and identity disputes."
A year later, in People v. Vallejo, the Court en banc was more definitive in unanimously acknowledging the probative value of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) testing as a means of identification. "When a crime is committed, material is collected from the scene of the crime or from the victim's body for the suspect's DNA. This x x x evidence sample x x x is then matched with the reference sample taken from the suspect and the victim," the Court added.
Then the Court discussed the possible results of DNA testing and its forensic uses, as follows:

sample taken from the suspect and the victim," the Court added.
Then the Court discussed the possible results of DNA testing and its forensic uses, as follows: "The purpose of DNA testing is to ascertain whether an association exists between the evidence sample and the reference sample. The samples collected are subjected to various chemical processes to establish their profile. The test may yield three possible results:
"1) The samples are different and therefore must have originated from different sources (exclusion). This conclusion is absolute and requires no further analysis or discussion;
"2) It is not possible to be sure, based on the results of the test, whether the samples have similar DNA types (inconclusive). This might occur for a variety of reasons including degradation, contamination, or failure of some aspect of the protocol. Various parts of the analysis might then be repeated with the same or a different sample, to obtain a more conclusive result; or
"3) The samples are similar, and could have originated from the same source (inclusion). In such a case, the samples are found to be similar, the analyst proceeds to determine the statistical significance of the similarity.

In the Philippines, "DNA has been successfully isolated from biological materials such as blood and bloodstains, saliva, semen and seminal stains, vaginal smears/ swabs, tissues and organs, bones and hair with follicles." In trial courts, these specimens have been used in cases - both civil and criminal - involving questioned parentage and identities of suspects.
The Supreme Court
Bioscience Conference
Fourth and more pervadingly, the Supreme Court, the Philippine Judicial Academy and EINSHAC, with a grant from the US Agency for International Development (US AID) co-sponsored the "Conference-Workshop on Biosciences and Biotechnology" for Philippine magistrates on August 26-29, 2003 in Tagaytay City.

Indeed, through lectures, case studies, workshops and discussion groups, the Conference tackled the role of the courts in the genomics age. I will not attempt to summarize and report on the entire conference; I will just concentrate on the subject of human cloning, cell-line development, genetic engineering and patenting of genes - the subject assigned to me. Instead of the usual lecture-open forum, these topics were taken up via a fictional case scenario, printed copies of which were distributed to the attendees in advance. The "facts" of the case were originally prepared by Dr. Zweig, and discussed during the Ottawa round of the EINSHAC "conversations" For the Philippine seminar, I changed the scenario slightly by "Filipinizing" it to make it relevant and interesting to the Filipino judges attending the meeting.
With the aid of "powerpoint" audiovisuals, I discussed the legal issues arising from the scenario. Thereafter, an open forum and a group discussion followed. Here are the "facts" of the case.
Human Cloning, Genetic Engineering,
Cell-Line Development and Patenting of Genes:
A Fictional Case Scenario

Human Cloning, Genetic Engineering,
Cell-Line Development and Patenting of Genes:
A Fictional Case Scenario In 1998, Pedro Santos (a Filipino) and Maria Mancini (an Italian) exchanged marital vows in a well-publicized wedding held at the Santuario de San Antonio in Makati. Pedro was a biological software engineer working for a multinational pharmaceutical firm, while Maria was a jeweler who catered to the rich and famous. They lived in a beautiful house in Forbes Park and enjoyed all the blessings and bounties that money could buy. Everything seemed perfect, until they were told by their obstetrician that Maria was incapable of conceiving a child. The young couple was devastated. The revelation caused a lot of frustration, anxiety and pressure on their relationship as husband and wife. As a result, they decided to separate for a while, although the marriage remained.
After zealously researching on the Internet, Maria learned of a new development in reproductive technology. That innovation was known as somatic cell nuclear transfer, otherwise referred to as reproductive cloning. The technology involves the extraction of a cell nucleus containing virtually the entire cell's DNA from a donor's tissue - for example, skin or mammary tissue. This extracted nucleus is then inserted into an egg cell whose original nucleus has been removed. After chemical and electronic stimulation successfully coaxes the reconstituted cell to divide, it can then be implanted into a human uterus.

has been removed. After chemical and electronic stimulation successfully coaxes the reconstituted cell to divide, it can then be implanted into a human uterus. Amazed and inspired by this new technology, Maria told her husband Pedro of her interest in undertaking this alternative reproductive method. Pedro vehemently opposed the idea and expressed his apprehensions regarding Maria's plan. Wanting so much to have a baby, Maria, accompanied by her best friend, Katrina Bond - a British lady married to Juan de la Cruz, a Filipino physician - went to a fertility clinic in Hong Kong to avail herself of the new reproductive procedure, even against her husband's wishes.
In Hong Kong, Maria submitted herself to pre-implantation genetic tests. The initial testing revealed no known inherited diseases or genetic predisposition for developing any other defects or ailments. After a cell nucleus had been extracted from Maria's skin tissue and inserted into an egg cell that had already been denucleated, the resulting zygote or fertilized egg began to divide. Later, over the vehement objections of Juan, it was transferred to the womb of Katrina who served as a surrogate mother for the developing fetus.
Shortly after the baby was born, Maria and Katrina, together with the cloned child Carmina, returned to the Philippines. They resided in Ayala Alabang, separately from their Filipino husbands. The cloned child was raised jointly by the two women, who decided to live together.

Carmina, now a toddler, was left for a week in the care of Pedro, because Maria and Katrina had to attend a conference in Europe for a work-related convention. There had only been sporadic prior contact between the child and Pedro, and no legal arrangements had been made for custody or child support. On the second morning thereafter, Pedro noticed that the child manifested an unusually large amount of cranial hair loss. He systematically collected hair follicles from the child's bed clothes and pillow during the week that she was in his care. Maria and Katrina returned from their European trip and took the child back from Pedro. They had no idea that he had taken hair and follicle samples from Carmina.

Shortly after this baby-sitting episode, Pedro accepted a position in New Delhi, India, with a major Indian pharmaceutical corporation, IndoPharma. He then relocated to India and immediately assumed the functions of his new job. Working with a computational biologist, a structural biologist and a toxico-geneticist at IndoPharma, he analyzed Carmina's hair follicle cells from carefully preserved samples that he had brought with him from the Philippines. His scientific research team found abundant amounts of a previously unreported protein, which they named Rejectin-1 They demonstrated that it was encoded by a gene located on chromosome 6. This gene had a single-base mutation in Carmina. Private animal studies earlier conducted by IndoPharma had suggested that Rejectin-1 limited progesterone production during pregnancy.

Working with another IndoPharma reproductive technology team, the group found that Rejectin-1 was present in 80 percent of the women tested for spontaneous reproductive rejection. IndoPharma won India and US patents for Rejectin-1 and its gene-precursor. With the drug firm's approval, Pedro and his research colleagues formed an Australian-based company called AustroPharma, the primary business purpose of which was to license Rejectin- 1-producing cell lines for research derived from Carmina's hair follicles, the process for which an Australian patent was granted. AustroPharma was 40 percent owned by IndoPharma; the remaining 60 percent was owned equally by Pedro and Juan.

Two years after its founding, AustroPharma developed a gene therapy procedure to repair Rejectin-1 mutations. The firm obtained from the California Institute of Technology (CalTech) a license for "antisense oligonucleotide," a small piece of DNA that would bind to and neutralize the mutant gene, thereby infecting the cell by means of a lentivirus that carried the DNA "repair kit." CalTech reported this molecule as a successful repair mechanism. With its viral vector in a supportive solution, AustroPharma patented a vaccine named "ARO." The vaccine not only reduced Rejectin-1 levels, but also detected the latter's expression in uterine tissue by micro-array analysis. AustroPharma's confidential laboratory and clinical findings reported that uterine tissues could be fully targeted by one administration of intramuscular ARO. Further research determined that ARO administration substantially reduced implantation rejection among rabbits and mice with induced Rejectin-1 mutations.

On a vacation trip to the Philippines, Pedro decided to visit Carmina. During this visit, he administered the ARO vaccine to the cloned child without the knowledge and consent of Maria and Katrina. A few weeks later, Carmina's hair loss ceased and replacement hair grew. After a year, she was diagnosed by a doctor to be afflicted with B-Thalessemia. Prior to the administration of the ARO vaccine, Maria had secured a life insurance contract for Carmina valued at P50 million, with Pedro as beneficiary.
In the meantime, AustroPharma generated massive income from sales of the cell lines and their derivative products and procedures. With these earnings, it bought Gentox, a laboratory located in the United States and incorporated in the State of Delaware. Gentox had had much experience in applying to the Philippine and the US Food and Drug Administrations (FDAs) for clinical trials of investigational biologics with human subjects. Gentox applied for a phase-one clinical trial permit to test ARO's toxicity on human beings for both infertility treatment and hair restoration purposes. Through Gentox, the Philippine and the US FDAs were provided all of AustroPharma's data. A large number of fertility and in-vitro fertilization clinics at   and dermatologists organizations endorsed the proposal and offered their participation.

In the course of issuing its approval for a phase-one clinical trial, the FDAs posted on their respective websites substantial information regarded by AustroPharma and Gentox to be their trade secrets. Specific, non-patent intellectual property regarding uterine targeting was  disclosed. AustroPharma valued this disclosure at an operating loss of $US 1.5 billion over the next five years. The second disclosure was that a cloned child was the source of the cell line, from which the gene therapy vaccine had been derived. Media frenzy ensued. Legal systems geared up for criminal prosecutions and civil actions, including damage/ injury/liability suits and reviews of administrative decisions by the Philippine and the US FDAs.
The Legal Issues
During the conference, I took up the legal and judicial issues arising from the foregoing fictional case scenario, as follows:
Is a Clone
a "Person"?.
To start with, is Carmina, the cloned child, a "person" in legal contemplation? Or is she merely an "extension" of a human cell and tissue that have evolved into human form?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

, is Carmina, the cloned child, a "person" in legal contemplation? Or is she merely an "extension" of a human cell and tissue that have evolved into human form? Under Article 40 of the Civil Code, "birth determines personality." But this determination seems to refer only to a "conceived child." Is Article 40 then not applicable to one who was not "conceived"; that is, one who was not the result of the normal fertilization of a human egg by a human sperm? Since the human clone is first a fetus before being born, is it not entitled to be accorded "birth" and "personality" - qualities that are "favorable to it" under Article 41?
If Carmina is a "person," when was she conceived? How was her "intra-uterine" life determined? Who is her mother? Maria from whose cell she originated? Or Katrina from whose womb she was physically carried, nurtured and born?
Who is her father - Pedro? Juan? Is she legitimate or illegitimate? How can her filiation be established? Will a DNA test sustain her identity and parentage?
If Carmina is merely an extension of an original person, are we prepared to say that a being that is capable of breathing, thinking, talking and working like any other human can be considered merely as an object? Or is she a sister of Maria and therefore, like her, the daughter of Maria's parents, since she possesses the chromosomes of these forebears?
In view of the new science of cloning, are we prepared to classify parents as legal, biological, surrogate or adoptive? ?
Filiation of a
Human Clone

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

forebears?
In view of the new science of cloning, are we prepared to classify parents as legal, biological, surrogate or adoptive? ?
Filiation of a
Human Clone The Family Code provides that the filiation of children may be by nature or by adoption. It also states that children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate. If the child is conceived through artificial insemination with the sperm of the husband or a donor, the child shall likewise be considered a legitimate child of the husband and the wife, provided that both spouses authorized or ratified the insemination process in a written instrument executed before the birth of the child. On the other hand, it also mandates that children conceived or born outside a valid marriage are considered illegitimate.
In our case study, the means by which Carmina was born - reproductive cloning - can hardly be described as natural. The procedure utilized for the conception of the cloned child was not artificial insemination, as it did not involve the sperm of Pedro or any sperm for that matter. Neither was there a written instrument, ratifying or authorizing such a reproductive procedure, executed by Pedro or Maria prior to the birth of Carmina. In view of the foregoing, was the conception or birth of Carmina within or outside the validly existing marriage of Pedro and Maria? How about Juan and Katrina?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

In view of the foregoing, was the conception or birth of Carmina within or outside the validly existing marriage of Pedro and Maria? How about Juan and Katrina? Another important consideration of the child. Article 15 of the Civil Code states that laws relating to family rights and duties; or to the status, the condition or the legal capacity of persons, are binding upon citizens of the Philippines, even though living abroad. The Philippine law on citizenship adheres to the principle of jus sanguinis. Hence, a child follows the nationality of the parents regardless of the place of birth, as opposed to the doctrine of jus soli which determines nationality or citizenship on the basis of the place of birth. Is Carmina a Filipino? Assuming that both Italy and Britain follow jus soli, may she still be considered a Filipino? Does she possess dual citizenship under our laws?
Parental Authority
Over a Human Clone
After the resolution of these underlying issues come several other civil law questions. Specifically, who should exercise parental authority over Carmina? Who should have custody over her?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

e underlying issues come several other civil law questions. Specifically, who should exercise parental authority over Carmina? Who should have custody over her? Note that under the Family Code, the father and the mother jointly exercise parental authority over their children; but in case of disagreement, the decision of the father prevails. Corollary to this, Article 220 of the Family Code provides that parents exercising parental authority have the right, among other rights, to keep their children in their company.26 Verily, parental authority stands to include the right and the duty to the custody of the child - excepting, of course, only what might otherwise be best for the child's welfare. The paternity issue could become even more complicated if, in a suit for support, the putative father refuses to acknowledge or recognize the child for having been conceived and born without his sperm or his adoption. On the other hand, may the fact of "living together" on the part of Maria and Katrina be characterized as " scandalous" and disqualify them from exercising parental authority over the clone?
Ownership
of Derivatives

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

the part of Maria and Katrina be characterized as " scandalous" and disqualify them from exercising parental authority over the clone?
Ownership
of Derivatives As narrated in the facts, Pedro was able to obtain discarded hair follicle samples from Carmina - samples from which were discovered and developed derivative products and procedures. Given this factual scenario, does Carmina have a cause of action to file a suit for damages against Pedro, Juan, IndoPharma, AustroPharma and Gentox for the conversion of her "property" into cell lines and gene therapy protocols and vaccines? How about Maria and Katrina - can they, instead, sue on the premise that the cell lines derived from Carmina, which were presumably Maria's, were unlawfully converted to commercial use by Pedro and by companies involved in the development of the vaccine and of the gene therapy procedures?
Looking at the other side of the contention, can Pedro argue that he is entitled to the hair follicles, considering that Maria and Carmina are his wife and daughter respectively? In this connection, I refer you to the Family Code provision with respect to legal guardianship of the child’s property - both parents exercise legal guardianship even without a court appointment to that effect. And just like the rule on parental authority, the decision of the father generally prevails.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

legal guardianship even without a court appointment to that effect. And just like the rule on parental authority, the decision of the father generally prevails. There is also the need to determine whether the discarded hair follicles, the cell lines and their derivative products/procedures are susceptible to ownership under our laws. Will the Civil Code provisions on property and ownership apply to the peculiar circumstances in the case study? Will the hair follicles not be considered as abandoned and thus capable of being owned by the finder? How about the cell lines, can they be deemed abandoned also? Your analyses and conclusions on these points will establish the property rights of the protagonists in our story and determine the course of their respective legal actions.
Causes of Action
for Damages
Insofar as entitlement to damages is concerned, the Civil Code provides that actual or compensatory damages may be awarded to any person suffering pecuniary loss. 03 Likewise, compensable damages include not only the value of the loss suffered, but also the profits that were not realized.13 Did Carmina or Maria or Katrina suffer pecuniary loss or compensable injuries from the acts of Pedro and his associates as would warrant indemnification for actual or compensatory damages? Can a cloned child actually suffer compensable personal injury? Can the three ladies singly or collectively sue for violation of their privacy rights or for damages under Article 26 of the Civil Code?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

nsable personal injury? Can the three ladies singly or collectively sue for violation of their privacy rights or for damages under Article 26 of the Civil Code? Assuming arguendo that Carmina does have a cause of action for damages against Pedro, does she have the legal or juridical capacity to sue? Should she be represented by Maria or Katrina, or should Maria or Katrina file the case in their respective personal capacities?
Insurance Subjects
and Beneficiaries
In connection with the insurance policy taken on the life of Carmina, may I pose the following questions: Can a cloned child be the subject of a life insurance policy? Or should the clone be insured as personal property of the donor? Does Maria or Pedro have an insurable interest in the life of Carmina?
One is said to have insurable interest when one has a relationship or connection with the insured; or a concern that one will derive pecuniary benefit or advantage from its preservation and will suffer pecuniary loss or damage from its destruction, termination or injury by the occurrence of the event insured against. Likewise, Section 10 (1) of the interest in one's life and health, spouse and children.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

n, termination or injury by the occurrence of the event insured against. Likewise, Section 10 (1) of the interest in one's life and health, spouse and children. Other questions on the subject of insurance include the following: Was it proper for Maria to designate Pedro as the beneficiary? Can Maria subsequently revoke his designation as such? What if Carmina dies as a result of B-Thalessemia, which she developed after the ARO vaccine was administered to her? Can Pedro still recover the proceeds of the insurance contract? To answer these questions, there is need to consult the Insurance Code.35 Under Section 12 thereof, the interest of the beneficiary may be forfeited if he willfully brings about the death of the insured.
Laws on Patents and
Intellectual Property
Moving on to patents and intellectual property laws, may I pose the following inquiries: Can Pedro apply for a patent to the Rejectin-1 protein, the ARO vaccine and the gene therapy method here in the Philippines? Can Maria, Katrina or Carmina file an action to invalidate or cancel these patents if ever they are acquired? Can Pedro argue that the derivative products and procedures (the ARO vaccine, the gene therapy method, and so on) were merely inspired by the early analysis of Carmina's hair follicles, but were developed mainly through his own industry and scientific research?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

, and so on) were merely inspired by the early analysis of Carmina's hair follicles, but were developed mainly through his own industry and scientific research? Under Philippine law, the right of ownership over intellectual creation is recognized. Specific provisions in the Civil Code and special laws afford the necessary protection against possible infringement thereof. Specifically, Article 721 of the Civil Code provides that scientists and technologists acquire ownership of their discoveries or inventions. Likewise, Article 722 states that such ownership exists even before the patents are granted. On the other hand, Sections 21 and 22 of RA 82933 (the Intellectual Property Code) defines patentable and non-patentable inventions.
Can we now say that ownership of the foregoing patentable products and procedures belongs entirely to Pedro, even when he could not have developed these without the cell lines of Carmina and Maria? Take note that per Section 61 of RA 8293,37 a patent may be cancelled if it is "contrary to public order or morality."
Another related incident with considerable legal consequences is the Philippine Food and Drug Administration's posting on its website of information on the ARO vaccine and its development - information that AustroPharma and Gentox consider trade secrets. Did the disclosure of such secrets amount to an infringement of intellectual property? Can the courts compel the Philippine FDA to compensate AustroPharma and Gentox for their alleged losses?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

ets amount to an infringement of intellectual property? Can the courts compel the Philippine FDA to compensate AustroPharma and Gentox for their alleged losses? To be able to answer these questions, it would be advisable to look into the provisions of the new Intellectual Property Code, which has superseded and / or expanded the coverage, the application and some of the provisions of the Patent Law.
Criminal Liability
We now come to the criminal law aspect of our case study. From the given set of facts, Pedro took hair follicle samples from Carmina without her knowledge and consent.
Did this "taking" constitute theft? Can there be theft of abandoned or discarded hair follicles? Was the alleged theft committed against the clone Carmina or the donor Maria? Who would be the complainant? In the first place, can Pedro commit theft against his "daughter" or his wife?
Before you even begin to identify the elements of the crime of theft, you may want to refer to Article 332 of the Revised Penal Code which exempts spouses, ascendants and descendants from any criminal liability for theft, swindling and malicious mischief.
Relevant to the civil and the criminal actions against Pedro are the rules on evidence. Can Maria, the wife, testify against him, given the prohibitions/ disqualifications in Section 22 of Rule 130 of the Rules of Court? Suppose the case is instituted by Maria as the legal representative of Carmina; will these disqualifications and prohibitions still apply?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

f the Rules of Court? Suppose the case is instituted by Maria as the legal representative of Carmina; will these disqualifications and prohibitions still apply? In administering the ARO vaccine to Carmina, is Pedro liable for physical injuries? Can his act be considered criminal, considering that his intentions were noble, having been done for the benefit of the child? Of particular interest in connection with this inquiry is Article 264 of the Revised Penal Code, which punishes the act of knowingly administering any injurious substance or beverage to another even without any intent to kill.
What if the Carmina dies from the disease developed? Can Pedro be held criminally liable for the resulting death? Would the charge be for murder, homicide or parricide? Is the killing of a clone considered destruction of human life or merely of property?
Even the provisions of our tax laws will be affected. Can cloned children be considered dependents, for which additional exemptions can be claimed by a taxpayer? Can the nucleus derived from a donor's tissue, which is not susceptible of appropriation, be considered as a donation subject to a donor's tax?
Conclusion
Given the wide and deep range of legal issues I have raised, you - the judges-participants - may by now be suffering from an overdose. You may be more bewildered now than when I first started this talk. Consequently, during your group discussions, there will probably be a wide divergence of views and spectrum of theories that you may not be able to reconcile.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

. Consequently, during your group discussions, there will probably be a wide divergence of views and spectrum of theories that you may not be able to reconcile. However, do not despair or be disheartened, for even the Supreme Court may not have ready answers to the legal dilemmas posed by our case study - at least, not yet. Remember that our purpose in this exercise is to be able to understand the intricacies of the new sciences and to be able to assess the applicability of existing laws and jurisprudence as well as the readiness of our courts to meet the exciting challenges of the dawning bio-era.
To this date, I am unaware of Philippine laws or statutes that have been proposed, much less enacted, to address these legal challenges. In some jurisdictions, current legislations refer only to restrictions on the development of cloning technology and the provision of criminal sanctions for violations of declared prohibitions. Moreover, I have yet to find any local jurisprudence that can directly guide us in the resolution of novel issues on human cloning, genetic research and other life technologies.
Dr. Franklin M. Zweig, in his lecture entitled "Life Technologies and the Rule of Law, "41 explained the dilemma in this wise:
"Imposed on our global society by the unprecedented rise, expansion and pervasiveness of biological technologies, we should anticipate, analyze and deliberate on cases and controversies for which historically we have no precedent, [and] no analogy.”

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age (cont.)

biological technologies, we should anticipate, analyze and deliberate on cases and controversies for which historically we have no precedent, [and] no analogy.” Indeed, legal issues involved in cloning and stem cell technology are inherently complex. There are many baffling areas where we may not have firm answers as yet. But we must still grapple with the realities of the new bio-sciences and learn to cope with the long-term and far-reaching effects they will have on our legal system and dispensation of justice. After all, under our Civil Code, the silence, the obscurity or the insufficiency of our laws is not an excuse to avoid rendering judgments in appropriate cases.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Ch. 1: Enter the Bio-Age
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 1, 'Enter the Bio-Age,' surveys the biosciences and biotechnologies — organ transplants (opening with Christian Barnard's first heart transplant), gene therapy, cloning, stem cells, and DNA — transforming society, and the legal and ethical questions they pose for the judiciary. CJP touches on DNA evidence (People v. Vallejo, Tijing v. Court of Appeals) and intellectual property (RA 8293), arguing the incoming 'bio-age' will test the law as profoundly as the information age.
