title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law

Appendix A
Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
Dr. Franklin M. Zweig, Ph.D., JD
President
Einstein Institute for Science, Health & the Courts
Maryland, USA
Please accept my heartiest congratulations on the occasion of the Philippine Supreme Court's 100th Anniversary.
I know I bring the Einstein Institute's concurring best wishes, shared by all men and women of goodwill and caring, that your distinguished Court will independently prosper and rule for many centuries ahead as the protector and guarantor of the rule of law.
Acknowledgment of the role of the Philippine Judicial Academy is also appropriate. As the affairs of nations, laws and economies intermingle to become ever more complex, the continuous education of judges gains in importance. It falls upon the courts' education arms to provide the foundation for judging the 21st century's cases. Only an educated, up-to-date judiciary can retain public confidence and enhance their judicial systems' independent status. In the United States, our Judicial Branch leaders deeply appreciate the Philippine Supreme Court's commitment to the highest quality education and program.
Your decision to memorialize the Supreme Court's centenary anniversary with a Lecture Series is commendable. It is also imaginative.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

lity education and program.
Your decision to memorialize the Supreme Court's centenary anniversary with a Lecture Series is commendable. It is also imaginative. Albert Einstein is reported to have said in a scientific context that "knowledge is important, but imagination is more so." Knowledge, and its academic celebration in the legal context, builds and reinforces institutional memory, imaginatively preparing us all for the future while at the same time observing and honoring your court system's institutional history.
A lecture series is also a bold commemoration of past values presented in such a way to foreshadow the future. It permits an American lawyer who manages a non-governmental judicial science education agency to raise with you the challenges that high courts and trial courts around the world face in the near future. The principal theme I would like to discuss with you tonight is this:
Imposed upon our global society by the unprecedented rise, expansion and pervasiveness of biological technologies we should anticipate, analyze and deliberate cases and controversies for which historically we have not only no precedent, but no analogy.
Let's explore together a few scenarios connecting life technologies and the rule of law.
The Biology of Violent Conduct

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

e not only no precedent, but no analogy.
Let's explore together a few scenarios connecting life technologies and the rule of law.
The Biology of Violent Conduct Our scientific adventures in human genetics, fortified by the use of computer science, may well report in the next few years, for example, significant limitations to human abilities to exercise free will. If scientifically valid studies from Iceland, Sardinia and Estonia, among a growing number of indigenous genetic databases, concur in finding the genetic levers and limiting gradients for conduct, particularly violent conduct or addictive disorders, our global legal institutions may well be required to revisit longsettled principles of jurisprudence.
Among those principles is the foundation concept of individual responsibility for harmful actions freely taken. Many prominent scientists believe that national databases capable of analyzing thousands of genes simultaneously will soon disclose the chemistry of free will. And many expect to find significant variations in the degrees of freedom that chemistry confers upon individuals. In the United States, we have sometimes bantered that criminal and civil cases alike will be geneticized, and provide new claims in matters of criminal conduct and civil liability. "My genes made me do it" seems to be the underlying metaphor.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

ke will be geneticized, and provide new claims in matters of criminal conduct and civil liability. "My genes made me do it" seems to be the underlying metaphor. How knowledgeably and imaginatively national and international jurisprudence will harness such science remains to be seen. Some cases may be less direct, however. "My genes made it impossible for me to prevent myself from doing it" may be a more sophisticated, more scientifically respectable claim in criminal justice proceedings.
In the United States, we have experienced one famous case that may be a harbinger of the future. See Mobley v. State 455 S.E.2d61(ga.) cert denied 516 U.S. 942 (1955). In Mobley, the chemistry of disabled non-violent behavior caused by a genetic mutation was raised in defense of a murder suspect. Let's look at the facts and then review the science.
Defendant Mobley was accused by the State of shooting to death a pizza parlor manager and of armed robbery. The murder was particularly grizzly. Observed by other employees, the manager was forced to a kneeling position following the robbery and shot, execution style, in the back of the head. Mobley was apprehended in a police chase following the suspect's escape from the crime scene by automobile. The gun used in the murder was thrown away during the chase, but later found. Ballistics tests indicated that the recovered weapon had been used in previous robberies, although none of the previous discharges resulted in death.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

ter found. Ballistics tests indicated that the recovered weapon had been used in previous robberies, although none of the previous discharges resulted in death. At trial, defendant Mobley's attorney attempted to introduce scientific evidence reported by Dr. Brunner and associates derived from a large family of Dutch felons apparently predisposed to intergenerational acts of violence. Mobley, his counsel argued, suffered from the absence of an essential brain chemical; that loss rendered Mobley incapable of controlling his murderous rages and murderous conduct. In short, Mobley was unable to exercise reason and control over his impulses and should not have been held responsible legally. Let's look at the scientific background.
Brunner, a well-regarded scientist, noticed that many forms of violent, anti-social behavior ran in a large family he studied in the Netherlands. Dutch authorities recorded the family's violent, criminal history among five generations of males. Using a combination of laboratory tests, Brunner determined that the family exhibited in common a deprivation of an important neurotransmitter, Monomine Oxidase A.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

ng a combination of laboratory tests, Brunner determined that the family exhibited in common a deprivation of an important neurotransmitter, Monomine Oxidase A. Earlier, but relatively recently, studies had demonstrated that that Monomine Oxidase A is an essential protein for the breakdown of serotonin, a primary neurotransmitter whose extended presence in brain synapses can cause hyperactivity, excessive irritability, combative attitude, and may be associated with aggressive, anti-social behavior. One minor change in the gene responsible for Monomine Oxidase A shut off supply of the chemical. As a result serotonin remained in its most powerful form in the brain to excite brain activity for abnormally long time periods and with abnormal behavioral results.
Defendant Mobley's counsel petitioned the judge presiding in the murder trial for genetic tests to determine that Mobley indeed exhibited the genetic mutation that deprived him of Monomine Oxidase A. The petition was denied, accompanied by the judge's reason that such DNAbased genetic tests (in the early 1990s) were too expensive for the State to bear. The defendant's father, a millionaire businessman, volunteered to pay for the tests, and counsel renewed the petition. It was again denied, based on the judges assessment that such tests were too experimental, unproven and unreliable to be used in justice proceedings.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

petition. It was again denied, based on the judges assessment that such tests were too experimental, unproven and unreliable to be used in justice proceedings. The matter moved to trial. The defendant was convicted of murder. He was sentenced to death after the chemically mediated loss of free will argument failed to convince the court that he warranted a lesser sentence.
In a post-conviction remedy motion, habeas corpus, Mobley moved for a new trial based on his contention that he had been ineffectively represented by his counsel at his first trial. Failure to obtain and introduce the genetic tests lay at the foundation of Mobley's motion for a new trial. The motion was denied and the matter was appealed to the Georgia Supreme Court. The court ruled that Mobley's counsel had represented him effectively in requesting genetic and other tests, and that the trial judge properly denied the petition based on the then known validity of gene testing technology. The court opined as well that the MOA theory might well not apply to Mobley at all, since the original Dutch family studied evidenced inherited mental retardation as well as violent tendencies. The court noted that Mobley had been tested and found to possess normal intelligence. An appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court failed to grant a hearing. Mobley is currently incarcerated on death row in Georgia.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

d found to possess normal intelligence. An appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court failed to grant a hearing. Mobley is currently incarcerated on death row in Georgia. The Mobley case is but the tip of the iceberg of new legal arguments that will be based in neuro and behavior genetics. As large databases replicate and combine scientific studies and monitor genetic tests administered in large numbers, gene mutation profiles will emerge. Those profiles hold great hope of identifying genes that predispose people for risk of mental diseases. High among the national genome database projects currently underway, for example, is the search for genes that cause or contribute to the scourge of schizophrenia. The hope is to find candidate genes through tests, and then to perfect the gene therapies that can restore people to full mental vitality. But such medical findings may also disclose the biological basis for personal violent cond If so, violence causation may gain a new paradigm, that is, as a biomedical, rather than a social condition.
From tests alone, courts may well insist that the capacity to form a reasoned action will continue to be the legal standard, but that insistence could relent if new technologies provide cures to inherited violence. Then the courts could be confronted with not only conduct-mitigating biomedical defenses. The demand to treat violence with gene therapies likely would follow. Here the administration of justice could face a simple problem and several complex ones.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

. The demand to treat violence with gene therapies likely would follow. Here the administration of justice could face a simple problem and several complex ones. If reliable gene therapies applied to individuals could "cure" violent conduct, or addictions, or tendencies to embezzle property, for example, courts would be faced merely with the question of sentencing offenders to treatment. Genetic treatments presumably would be enduring and non-obvious. Once the mutations were "repaired," permanent rehabilitation could be expected. In most law-abiding societies, courts would only worry about side effects. Gene therapies might trigger other medical conditions, and a presiding judge would find herself weighing the therapeutic value against side effect's health risks. (Neurotransmitter chemical treatments would be far less reliable as a treatment alternative; courts routinely confront defendants and probationers who have abandoned their medications.)

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

l treatments would be far less reliable as a treatment alternative; courts routinely confront defendants and probationers who have abandoned their medications.) Two kinds of complex problems confront courts from slightly different technologies. The first could be a demand to modify inherited behavioral traits permanently. That is, in addition to treating the individual with genetic technologies, policies could be advocated to prevent the unwanted conduct in future generations. There is every scientific basis to accomplish germ-line gene therapies, although the technologies have not yet moved from laboratory to the clinic. Here body cells are not the treatment target; sex cells are. How should a Constitutional court rule in the face of public demands, say through legislation, to modify the germ line?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

not the treatment target; sex cells are. How should a Constitutional court rule in the face of public demands, say through legislation, to modify the germ line? A second problem concerns the biomedical prediction of violent criminal behavior. Let's assume that computergenerated profiles of thousands of genes indicate the likelihood that a particular family or individual is predisposed to violence. Should they be treated preventively d      for a statistical similarity to dangerousness? How would a court develop laws so as to balance society's predicted benefit against protected personal rights? If behavioral profiles are statistically questionable, should courts endorse universal genetic screening for offensive genetic components? The technologies will soon exist to measure thousands of genes at one time, at birth, for example. Should such screening results be routinely made available to law enforcement? Will a demand surface for biomedical courts?
All such inquiries will provide jurisprudential headaches aplenty by this decade's end. They illustrate the coming clash between life technologies and the law. It is difficult to conceive of a scenario in which independent courts of any nation will be spared a role in adjudicating these high-impact decisions. In fact, some may directly be aimed at judges, the professional core of effective dispute resolution systems.
Genetic Testing of Judges for Dementing Illnesses

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

In fact, some may directly be aimed at judges, the professional core of effective dispute resolution systems.
Genetic Testing of Judges for Dementing Illnesses Judges are public officers, and the public often demands to know their officer's health histories. Judges mediate and adjudicate heated conflicts, and their own deportment is constantly subject to scrutiny. Such observations can be used to justify pre-appointment and pre-election as well as reappointment and re-election genetic tests applied to judges.
The main question that judicial screening commissions and the public clamor to know is whether a candidate is likely to experience a serious dementing condition during service on the Bench. Alzheimer's disease and stroke are the disabling dementias most commonly feared. Both can generate emotional turmoil in opposition to expected judicial temperament. Both rob their victims of memory and language. So if it were possible to estimate a judicial candidate's risk for such conditions, why would it not be in the public interest to predictively diagnose such conditions by simple genetic tests before onset? It is far easier to deny admission to juridical robes than to remove a sworn judicial officer based on disability allegations.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

imple genetic tests before onset? It is far easier to deny admission to juridical robes than to remove a sworn judicial officer based on disability allegations. At present, prediction of dementing illnesses is a flat enterprise. Even though four genes have been found to be linked to Alzheimer's disease, for example, they are predictive only half the time. And 50% of persons actually afflicted with Alzheimer's disease test negatively for the f genetic markers currently available. There are obviously unseen genetic and environmental causes, promoters, and enhancers at work. It is possible that a developmental cascade of 30 genes will be found to play a role. Those pathways will be found by the end of this decade. The court's challenge now is to understand the state and direction of the science, to assess emerging gene technologies, and to determine how these forces should be channeled into legal domains supportive of dispute resolution institutions.
A Science and Technology Primer
With your leave, it might be helpful to take a short break from the judicial policy issues engendered by life technologies. Let us explore a brief overview of the scientific basis for human biotechnology. It is not mystical and is well within the reach of the average person, even lawyers, as I can attest. Science's amazing feature is that the code of life extends across all of nature, and the same basics underpinning human life are relied upon by all animals, plants, and bacteria.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

feature is that the code of life extends across all of nature, and the same basics underpinning human life are relied upon by all animals, plants, and bacteria. Following this primer, I shall outline case scenarios prominently poised to surface in national and international dispute resolution forums. And then I will confide to you a few capacity-enhancing steps I believe court systems - unable to escape the fray in light of legislative fears about genomic policymaking - need to take in this extraordinary age of genetic engineering.
Life technologies underpinning ideas are simple.
A. All life is embodied in and expressed by cells. These are small biochemical factories that build up and break down wed   proteins, the molecules of life. They are numerous; we may each have a trillion cells in our bodies. As we sit in the majesty of this hall of justice, we are elegantly configured masses of our   cells performing different tasks to bring us our humanity.
B. In each cell are all the biological machines - called organelles - to survive, grow, reproduce, communicate and supervise the production of proteins. In (Your Favorite Cell's) YFC's center is an organelle called the Nucleus and within each nucleus are the 46 shipping packages of inheritance, the chromosomes, along which are strung all our genes, about 100,000 of them. The Human Genome. Project has almost completed identification of all our genes
C. What do all these genes do?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

h are strung all our genes, about 100,000 of them. The Human Genome. Project has almost completed identification of all our genes
C. What do all these genes do? They simply instruct organelles in the cell, outside of the nucleus, to make proteins. The basic idea is that one gene sends an instruction to the cell's protein assembly machine, the Ribosome, to assemble a protein from amino acids. Remember the gene that instructs the production of MOA? It is a single protein that works on serotonin breakdown and removal from the brain's firing structures. It takes one gen to instruct the right cells to make that protein.
D. Finally, life technologies are significantly based upon the fact that cells can be engineered in numerous ways using microscopic instruments. Whole animals can be cloned. There is no technological reason why humans cannot be cloned as easily as sheep, cows, mice or pigs.
Judges' Science Tools for Case Management
of a Wide Range of Case Scenarios
I would like to congratulate you for your successful mastery of these life science and technology basics. They are the foundation of evidence that will soon be presented to courts everywhere on our small planet.

tic tests for diseases, predispositions and susceptibilities, including the role of and safeguards for genetic databases.
The Eugenics Shadow for Case Scenarios Mention should be made of eugenics, the last century's discredited social doctrine based on false biological information manufactured for the justification of discrimination and individual and population group harms. I need not catalogue eugenics world-wide, dreary history. It will suffice to note that as we enter the age of the New Biology, all case scenarios are shadowed by the fact that gene technologies provide a new basis for favoring some heritages and eschewing others. Courts must be especially sensitive to elevating our conception of human rights above the formulas that will be advanced by some to deprive people of their humanity based on genetic arguments. While life technologies can be expected to improve the quality of life, the rule of law must trump all enterprises and place in proper context that each human person has equal rights under law.
The International Perspective
for Life Technology Disputes
Biotechnology offers the best hope in human history for cost-effective health care, remediation of degraded and dangerous natural environments, and a sufficient and nutritious food supply for ten billion who will inhabit this planet by the quarter-century mark.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

graded and dangerous natural environments, and a sufficient and nutritious food supply for ten billion who will inhabit this planet by the quarter-century mark. From molecular medicine, we will soon inherit treatments for human illnesses once thought entirely impossible. They include cancers, diseases of combined genetic and environmental causation. From veterinary biotechnology, we may be able to assure biological diversity of the world's species and the conservation of endangered species. From microbial biotechnology, we soon could harness the means to use engineered bacteria for environmental restoration. From agricultural biotechnology, we can expect nutrition supplements and vaccines to be built into health-promoting foods. The economies of many nations are now directed to biotechnology as a hope for future trade, wealth and security. From these hopeful perspectives, there is no better time to be alive and there never has been a better time for children's advent into the world.
At the same time, these life technologies spawn disputes that place courts front and center in the resolutions that will enhance their benefits and contain their risks. Courts could anticipate them in the course of conferencing and judicial education activities without diverting too much time or effort from the normally daunting responsibilities of case processing and management.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

ncing and judicial education activities without diverting too much time or effort from the normally daunting responsibilities of case processing and management. Three life technology issues arise all over the world. They provide a strong reason for courts to develop a global community of discourse. The first is human experimentation. The second is the nature and status of biological property. The third is the release of genetically modified organisms into the environment.
Human experimentation. Courts will hear cases of direct and indirect human experimentation. Direct human experimentation is conducted through clinical trials based upon people. While laboratory and animal studies guide technology development, the only certain way to assess biological tests and therapies intended for humans is to test them on humans. Gene therapy to repair Monomine Oxidase A deficiency, for example, can only be proved safe and efficacious in human clinical trials. But who conducts these trials, and with what ethical safeguards is of paramount importance. Courts will soon get cases in large alleging breach of human subject protections or breach of human rights conventions in the absence of explicit human subject protections. Unless courts understand the scientific and technological basis for these trials, conditions exist for important errors and harms.

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

it human subject protections. Unless courts understand the scientific and technological basis for these trials, conditions exist for important errors and harms. Many nations have laws, regulations and standards governing human clinical trials. Judges must understand the legal causes and biomedical causation in disputes alleged to violate national standards. This matter holds international implications because much human experimentation will be conducted by international teams, especially transnational corporations seeking new drugs, vaccines, and medical technologies. Because the world's legal domain is so varied as to the nature of human subject policies and remedies, it. will be important for judges to know the span of legal doctrines, and what their colleagues in other nations apply as law in such cases.

icies and remedies, it. will be important for judges to know the span of legal doctrines, and what their colleagues in other nations apply as law in such cases. Indirect experimentation is conducted by monitoring the effects upon human populations of life technologies directed initially at environmental remediation and agricultural products. Our interdependent, interactive world assures multiple impacts from intervention intended for one purpose but resulting in several outcomes. Cleaning a waterway from bacteria seeping from agricultural livestock, for example, may result in some unanticipated consequences for humans using it. Fashioning remedies in such complex, indirect cases will be common tasks in law courts as engineered biology is used to promote life. Judges will be asked to rule on evidence generated by new scientific techniques, such as meta-analyses and risk analyses. Public confidence in rulings will depend in large part upon the judiciary's confidence in managing such evidence.
The nature and status of biological property is a matter for international treaty, but some nations or constituencies feel left out of considerations. They will take their cases to court. They will plead for equity and argue to invalidate treaty provisions. To deal with such claims, judges will need to know the various schemes of intellectual property protection.

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

or equity and argue to invalidate treaty provisions. To deal with such claims, judges will need to know the various schemes of intellectual property protection. Finally, food and agricultural disputes can be expected to expand. Changes in the nature of food deeply affect cultural perspectives. Control over food is one of human kind's most dearly protected privileges. We can expect legal attacks upon new technologies that threaten to control. Judges, again, will fortify confidence in the rule of law when their decisions and the opinions supporting those decisions disclose an understanding of the biological elements brought to the Bench as essential ingredients of their disputes.
The Prospects for Effective Adjudication
of Life Technology Disputes
Never in prior human history have we had the ability to plan and engineer our biological future. Life technologies now place that future squarely in our hands. That power used for human good could produce unlimited benefits - cure of disease, remediation of handicaps, supplies of vital replacement organs, extended life spans among them. Never in human history have we had the opportunity to squander our biological resources and distort life technologies for unlawful purposes.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix A: Life Technologies and the Rule of Law (cont.)

e spans among them. Never in human history have we had the opportunity to squander our biological resources and distort life technologies for unlawful purposes. Judicial capacity can be built to apply the rule of law to the optimistic prospects and dispute scenarios promised by life's new technologies. But judicial branches can no longer expect national borders to confine disputes or decisions. Judicial capacity can best be enhanced by establishing and maintaining a community of discourse, an interacting judicial core from every nation boasting an independent judicial system.
To effectively apply and enforce the law under these new, volatile, promising and fear-generating conditions, courts will benefit from collegial consultation and exchange. Effective adjudication never depended so much upon shared jurists' perspectives. Respectful differences in those perspectives can be bridged by the enrichment provided by shared judicial experiences. EINSHAC's International Program will continue in 2001 with a working conversation in Hawaii for Common Law and Pacific Rim courts, in the Hague, and in Rome. We hope that the wonderful knowledge and legacy of the Philippine Supreme Court and its constituent forums can be shared with the world's judiciary.
EINSHAC and its judicial and legal leadership look forward to the Philippine Supreme Court's legacy for the next hundred years, a legacy that will include leadership in harnessing burgeoning life technologies to the rule of law.

text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products

Appendix B
GMO & Food Products: Current & Emerging Issues
Hon. Leonardo A. Quisumbing
Associate Justice, Supreme Court
I.
Risks and the Promise
What Lies Ahead in Asia?
Biotechnology is one field where the law appears to lag behind science. Yet modern biotechnology is now a booming multi-billion dollar industry worldwide. Food biotechnology, in particular, holds the promise of abundance. But it is mired in controversy. Much of it concerns genetically modified organisms and the dangers they pose, when released to the environment or ingested as art of food products for people or feeds for livestock.
Bishop Jesus Varela, an adviser of Biotechnology Foundation, recently underscored the essence of the debate about GMO and food products:
"Society has a moral responsibility to feed the world's burgeoning population. The solution is not population control, but rather food production . . . food biotechnology promises us this is possible though there are risks . . .
"Whether GMO can and will deliver its promise to alleviate world hunger remains to be seen. It has enormous potential. But the risks have to be addressed." (Phil. Daily Inquirer, "Ex-bishop urges caution on GMOs," 12/08/03, p.14, c.6. See also his paper at the Conference on the "Ethics of GMO: Its Application to the Philippines.")

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

uirer, "Ex-bishop urges caution on GMOs," 12/08/03, p.14, c.6. See also his paper at the Conference on the "Ethics of GMO: Its Application to the Philippines.") Last month, Bishop Dinualdo Gutierrez of South Cotabato touched on a current feature of the controversy: ongoing street protests. Streamers in churches and cathedral in Mindanao denounced products containing GMO. This appeared to be part of the struggle against transgenic crops and foods entering the country. The religious sector in Koronadal City launched a campaign to boycott certain staples, particularly Bt corn. A parish priest there, Fr. Bo Parreño, averred the boycott aims "to secure the health of humans from the alleged hazardous effects of genetically altered crops." An advocacy officer of the diocesan justice and peace desk, Gloria Sabit, added that the local church was urging parishioners "to boycott the products containing GMOs because they have not been proven safe to human health and the environment." (Today,'"Boycott of GMO food launched," 22/07/03, p. 3, c.2).
What is happening in Mindanao is not isolated. Violent demos, mass rallies, and hunger strikes have also been staged in Metro Manila, Northern Luzon, and the Visayas, against Bt corn and other GMO crops.

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

ed. Violent demos, mass rallies, and hunger strikes have also been staged in Metro Manila, Northern Luzon, and the Visayas, against Bt corn and other GMO crops. The response of the government to the boycott demanding a moratorium on biotech crops such as Bt corn partakes of a forensic challenge to anti-biotech forces. Secretary Luis "Chito" Lorenzo, Jr., has stated that a moratorium would mean "reversing more than five years of scientific studies by the government and the private sector." The government, he stressed, would consider a moratorium on Bt corn planting in the country only after there is a showing by "overwhelming" scientific evidence that the crop poses health and environmental dangers. This response flies in the face of the assertion of some scientists, including Dr. Chito Medina of U.P., Los Baños, that Bt corn and other genetically altered crops were not yet "scientifically proven to be safe for consumption." The forensic battle of the two "Chitos" is reflected in media debates involving not only activist laymen but highly trained scientists and technocrats, such as a hunger strike leader, Engr. Ben Bersola. It is safe to say that the GMO controversy is not limited to scientific fora and journals abroad. It has now intruded into public decision-making here as well.

heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

It is safe to say that the GMO controversy is not limited to scientific fora and journals abroad. It has now intruded into public decision-making here as well. Yes, GMO is now in Asia. Independent of foreign aid, China has built up its biotechnology capacity. It has been noted that China has done better than most developing countries to promote use of GM crops. (UNU/Intech I:2:2002). The worry in the developing world, according to Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, chairwoman of India Biocon company, "is this: Why has Europe banned it? It must be for " Yet, she believes that India must enhance a reason. biotechnology to overcome widespread poverty, malnutrition, hunger, and disease. (IHT, "From Indian taboo, biotech is born," 8/19/03, p. 11, c.2).

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

nce a reason. biotechnology to overcome widespread poverty, malnutrition, hunger, and disease. (IHT, "From Indian taboo, biotech is born," 8/19/03, p. 11, c.2). At the outset, we must acknowledge the historical contributions of two monks, Mendel and Malthus, to the present debate. GM coincidentally are the initials of Gregor Mendel, 1822-84, the recognized father of the science of modern genetics. It was this Moravian monk who cultivated different kinds of peas and recorded the effect of their crosspollination on hereditary traits. The other clergyman, Thomas Malthus, 1766-1834, is remembered for a theory named after him. His essay, On the Principle of Population, posited a crowded planet where food supply is outstripped by population growth, so that starvation and death result. At the time, 1798, earth’s population was about 800 million only. Now, the same number, if not more, go to bed hungry every night. The world population now exceeds 6 billion, but acreage of arable land actually diminished for various reasons like war, urbanization, climate change, and desertification. It is said that in some southern African countries, e.g. Zambia, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, some 15 million people face starvation yearly because of drought and flood. In northern Asia, a vast expanse of mainland China is being overrun by dust and sandstorm, destroying pastures and croplands, obviously without regard to ideology.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products

The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

northern Asia, a vast expanse of mainland China is being overrun by dust and sandstorm, destroying pastures and croplands, obviously without regard to ideology. Expanding population and dwindling resources, sparking local wars and widespread violence, are not a novelty in our midst. That is why those in government including the judiciary must take heed of what lies ahead. Let me just call attention to one forecast:
"By 5050 or so, the world population could start to level off at about 9 billion. Most of the increase in population will be in the developing w o r l d . . . All the signs point to a future in which the world's poor will not be able to afford enough food to live on and in which the distribution system in undeveloped countries will not improve sufficiently to distribute [food] that is available." (Peter Pringle, Food Inc., p. 20.)
Forewarned is forearmed. Could recombinant DNA technology or bio-engineering (gene splicing or genetic modification) of staple crops and food products come to the rescue? If so, at what risks, and what price?
II.
Patent on a Life Form: Microbes Win in America?
During a round-table conference with judges of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit and patent attorneys in Washington, D.C., this spring, we had a chance to discuss whether a living creature or life form could be the subject of a valid patent. Attention was called to the American case of Diamond v. Chakrabarty, 447 US 303 (1980).

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

r a living creature or life form could be the subject of a valid patent. Attention was called to the American case of Diamond v. Chakrabarty, 447 US 303 (1980). It appears that in 1972, Dr. Ananda Chakrabarty, a GE microbiologist, applied for a U.S. patent on "human-made, genetically engineered bacterium" capable of breaking down multiple components of crude oil, a capability not possessed by ordinary bacteria. The patent examiner denied his application on the ground that "micro-organisms are products of nature" and "living things were not patentable." The Patent Board of Appeals upheld the examiner's decision. But the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals reversed the Board. So Commissioner Diamond went on certiorari before the U.S. Supreme Court.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

e examiner's decision. But the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals reversed the Board. So Commissioner Diamond went on certiorari before the U.S. Supreme Court. In a split decision, 5 to 4, the U.S. Supreme Court in 1980 held that Chakrabarty's bacterium is patentable. The majority reasoned that Congress meant the patent law to be of wide scope, so as to cover anything under the sun made by man's ingenuity. The fact that the applicant's microorganism is alive is without legal significance for purposes of the patent law, said the majority, citing In re Bergy, 563 F2d 1031. What is decisive is the fact that the applicant's microbe bore markedly different characteristics from any found in nature, with the potential for significant utility. The relevant distinction is not between living and inanimate things but between manmade inventions and products of nature. Chakrabarty's claims were upheld; his bacterium passed the triple tests of utility, novelty, and non-obviousness upon which patentability of an invention depends.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

akrabarty's claims were upheld; his bacterium passed the triple tests of utility, novelty, and non-obviousness upon which patentability of an invention depends. This development, according to the minority view, went against the 1970 law known as the Plant Variety Protection Act, which specifically excluded bacteria. The dissenters argued that only the U.S. Congress, not the Supreme Court, could broaden the reach of patent laws. In 1930, it was recalled, the Plant Patent Act covered only species (whether fruits, nuts or flowers) that are asexually propagated. Breeders' monopoly control over staple crops was rejected, particularly over potatoes. The 1970 statute on plant variety protection gave only patent-like protection to food crops that sexually reproduced (eg. corn, wheat and rice). The 1980 decision, from the minority point of view, looked novel indeed. This radical development was further bolstered soon by actions taken by the patent office itself. It granted a series of patents to another microbiologist (Kenneth Hibberd) on a new line of corn, covering the process of creating the new variety as well as the product - namely the DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) sequence, genes, cells, tissue culture, seed, specific parts of the plant, and the entire plant itself.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

as the product - namely the DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) sequence, genes, cells, tissue culture, seed, specific parts of the plant, and the entire plant itself. Dr. Chakrabarty was pleasantly surprised by his victory in court. All he did, according to him, was to make what amounted to a soup of different strains of bacteria hoping they would interact. What he got was a new life form, with a patent to his credit, assigned to GE. At Wall Street, the risk takers were jubilant: stock prices of biotech firms shot up dramatically.
Thereafter, it is said the patent office started granting patents on "products of nature," or functional equivalents. Products of skill rather than invention received patents. Apparently the American biotech industry was in a race against time to assure its pre-eminence globally. Even university researchers, under the Bayh-Dole Act of 1980, could take patents on federally funded projects. Later, colleges and individual academic researchers entered into deals with corporations engaged in biotechnology and related sciences. Companies were created just to buy other companies possessing patent rights.
The result? Fear of US monopolies or oligopolies in the biotech industry, agribusiness and research. Anxious Europeans responded with regulations that apparently built a grand trade barrier against American ingenuity.
III.
Labelling and Traceability:
A "Frankenfood" in Europe?

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

s responded with regulations that apparently built a grand trade barrier against American ingenuity.
III.
Labelling and Traceability:
A "Frankenfood" in Europe? Genetically modified organisms (GMO) may be defined as organisms in which the genetic material (DNA) has been altered in a way that does not occur naturally by mating or natural recombination. The technology of alteration is known as genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, or modern biotechnology. This technology allows selected individual genes to be transferred from one organism into another, as well as between non-related species. (See Brussels, Memo 02/160-Rev., 01/07/03.)
Considering the complexity of GMO debates, care must be taken to make a distinction between scientific questions requiring analysis and ideological questions raised for nonscientific reasons. But pardon me if sometimes I get carried away and forget the distinction.
In 1998, the EU closed its doors to GM crops. The GM controversy devastated the US farm-products from Europe, for instance, halving the sale of soya pro engineered herbicide-resistant soybeans. Recent scare stories like the "mad cow disease," also shook public GMO food products.

nce, halving the sale of soya pro engineered herbicide-resistant soybeans. Recent scare stories like the "mad cow disease," also shook public GMO food products. Antibiotech forces fall into 3 groups: rejectionists, reformists and moderates. For safety and environmental as well as religious and ideological reasons, rejectionists believe plant biotechnology is wrong and dangerous. Reformists dislike new and alien foods for humans as well as feeds for livestock. They believe scientists, business and government mishandled the problem of GMO products. The moderate organic group of growers and consumers wanted immediate labeling of GMO products. GM crops must be isolated, to reduce cross-pollination. Tracers must be significantly used to prevent genetic pollution.
In 1996, the first GM product - a paste of tom bought fish gene - appeared in Britain. The Britons bought it enthusiastically as it was cheaper than usual. But by Christmas 1998, sales of that tomato sauce paste reportedly dropped to almost zero. Large European market chains had joined forces to eliminate GM ingredients from made it clear, product brands. Reason: US companies had made it clear, rather proudly, that if Europeans wanted American soybeans their only choice would be the GM variety. Another reason: Prince Charles of England joined the fray and encouraged protests. The public became fearful and refused to buy GM food. NGOs like Greenpeace succeeded in halting the use or import of biotech crops. "Frankenfood" became a by-word to denigrate GMO and food products as monstrous and dangerous.

In practice, the EC thru Directive 2001/18/EC continues in place a step-by-step process of approval on a case by case assessment of the risks to human health and the environment before any GMO or product consisting of or containing GMO, such as maize and tomatoes, or GMM (microorganisms) can be released to the environment or placed in the market. Directive 90/219/EEC, as amended, regulates the continued use of GMM for research and industrial purposes. Regulation (EC) 258 on Novel Food and Novel Food ingredients sets out rules for authorization and labeling of novel foods/ food products containing, consisting or produced from GMO. There are rules for genetically modified seeds and forestry reproductive material as well as medical and veterinary products. Since 1997, labeling is mandatory to indicate presence of GMO as such in a product. There are proposals now for new regulations on traceability and labeling of GMO and GMO products, including foods and feeds.

Noteworthy is the EC proposal on the regulations of exchange of GMOs with countries outside EU. This proposal appears to be in line with the UN agreement to establish by common rules for transboundary movements of GMOs in order to ensure globally the protection of human health and biodiversity (the UNEP Cartagena Protocol). GMOs for export have to be identified. Notification to those concerned must be made regarding exported GMOs intended for deliberate release into the environment, and even their accidental release. Information must also be provided to international partners of EC concerning Community legislation, decisions and practices on GMOs.
Needless to emphasize, the Europeans have been widely chided for over-regulation as well as for undermining globalization and free trade. Like rallyists before the Seattle WTO meeting, they seem to say loudly "NO, NO to GMO!"
IV.
Randy Rape Seed Case:
A Gandhi in Canada?
Several cases are now on record among the classics of the court battles between opposing forces in biotech/GMO warfare. These include subjects like Bt toxin in transgenic potato; Star Link in taco shells; RiceTec and basmati rice; Delta-Pin eland and cotton; Bt pollen and monarch butterflies. But my favorite court saga is that of a Canadia prairie farmer and the so-called Round-up Ready Canola, also known as the randy rape seed.

monarch butterflies. But my favorite court saga is that of a Canadia prairie farmer and the so-called Round-up Ready Canola, also known as the randy rape seed. Past retirement age, Percy Schmeiser was one of hundreds of farmers in Canada as well as the USA sued by the Monsanto company for illegally using its proprietary seeds. Allegedly, Percy planted in his 1400-acre family farm those seeds without Monsanto's prior consent and without him signing a technical use agreement with Monsanto. At that time, some 20,000 farmers had signed up so that 40% of canola grown in Canada used Monsanto's seeds. Known popularly as Round-up Ready Canola, they contain an alien gene which made them resistant to a herbicide called Roundup, another product of Monsanto company. Monsanto's seed police found that Percy had used its proprietary seeds in 90% of his farm area.
In his defense, Percy contended that he was a victim of Monsanto's new technology which invaded his farm. He claimed the genetically modified seeds of Monsanto were blown by wind and carried by bees from Monsanto's contract farms to his own. Seed trucks of Monsanto trespassed into his land, and Monsanto's seeds fell from those trucks to his land. When the GM seeds sprouted and grew they contaminated his organic rape seeds, his plants and his harvest, he added.

's seeds fell from those trucks to his land. When the GM seeds sprouted and grew they contaminated his organic rape seeds, his plants and his harvest, he added. Percy counter-sued, demanding $4.2 million from Monsanto for defamation, as well as for genetic pollution. According to him, Monsanto's canola plants had spread pollen all over the countryside. They cross-pollinated with conventional plants like his own. Organic farms like Percy's stood to lose their organic certificate, because of contamination by Monsanto's GM seed. These certificates take years to acquire and are prized possession. Once contaminated by GMOs, Percy's produce could no longer n   be sold as "GM-free." While the case was pending in court, Percy traveled to several countries with a message against GMO and Monsanto. India gave him a Gandhi award, and he was considered a folk hero.
The federal court, however, found in favor of Monsanto. It did not matter, said the judge, where in this case the rape seeds actually came from and how they got to be in Percy's farm. The source of the seeds is not decisive in the issue of liability for illegal use of proprietary seeds. Percy ought to know or have known that planting those seeds and growing the genetically modified canola plants without prior leave or license given by Monsanto is an infringement of the company's patent. Hence, Percy is liable to pay royalty as well as damages to the company. (Percy has elevated his case to the Canada Supreme Court, whose decision is now awaited.)

Life Beyond Harvard's Creation?

V.
Of Transgenic Mice and Men:
Life Beyond Harvard's Creation? The last controversial case I would like to bring to the attention of our judges is that of the oncomouse, also known as the Harvard mouse case decided recently by the Canadian Supreme Court. (See Canada Com. of Patents v. Harvard College, 2002-12-05, SCC at http://www.canlii.org/ca/cas/scc/2002/ 2002cc76.html). Debated by that tribunal was the patentability of higher life forms. Could transgenic mammals like mice and even humans be patented?
Previously the USA, Japan, and many European countries have granted a patent on Harvard's mouse, which is used as a platform for the study of cancer cells. But the Canadian Supreme Court in a split decision, 5 to 4, sustained the decision of the Commissioner of Patents which denied Harvard's application to patent the oncomouse in Canada. The majority of the Court reasoned that the words "composition of matter" in the Canadian Patent Act do not the word "manufacture" in the context of said Act as commonly understood denotes a non-living mechanistic product or process, not a higher life form. (By way of distinction, Chakrabarty's patent in the USA involves a single cell microbe, a lower life form.)
Four justices, including C.J. McLachlin, dissented.

title: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
heading: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products
text:
The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary -- Appendix B: GMO & Food Products (cont.)

(By way of distinction, Chakrabarty's patent in the USA involves a single cell microbe, a lower life form.)
Four justices, including C.J. McLachlin, dissented. In their view, the oncomouse is a patentable product or subject matter. "The extraordinary scientific achievement of altering every single cell in the body of an animal which does not in this altered form exist in nature, by human modification of the genetic material of which it is composed is an inventive 'composition of matter' within the meaning of s. 2. of the Patent Act."
It may be noted, for emphasis, that only the claim for the product -oncomouse - was rejected by the Patent Examiner, the Patent Commissioner, and the Supreme Court's ruling. The claims for the process by which the oncomouse was produced won a patent from the Patent Office. This distinction concerning process and product is significant in patent claims.
New Zealand has patented another mouse, one injected with HIV genes. Certainly more news will be heard about mice, if not men, as transgenic mammals. Can we say that genetic modification of life forms continues to advance or desecrate our idea of life itself?

Summary

Appendix D reproduces Fr. Ranhilio Callangan Aquino's essay on the ethics of the 'brave new world' of human cloning and genetic engineering. II, Sec. 12), and calls for serious philosophical reflection on manipulating human life.

Edited copy of the Impromptu Closing Remarks delivered by retired Chief Justice ARTEMIO V. PANGANIBAN at the end of a Professorial Lecture delivered by founding law Dean Jose Manuel "Chel" Diokno held at the De La Salle School of Law on April 6, 2024, sponsored by the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity.
---
Magandang hapon po sa inyong lahat. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.
SALUTATIONS AND GREETINGS
Our esteemed lecturer, Dean Jose Manuel Diokno, is known better as "Chel" Diokno. To me, he's the worthy son of a worthy father. I will elaborate on that a little later after I greet the other personalities here.
Of course, our esteemed host, Dean Gil De Los Reyes of the Tañada-Diokno School of Law of De La Salle University. I was here in 2010 when your school was inaugurated. Since then, 14 years have passed, and you now have a fully matured law school that's the best in BGC.

sity. I was here in 2010 when your school was inaugurated. Since then, 14 years have passed, and you now have a fully matured law school that's the best in BGC. Dean Gil, why did you apologize for rendering the Invocation? I think we should be proud that we pray. To be clear, praying is not disallowed by any law; in fact, it is encouraged by our Constitution and by our Supreme Court. As we all know, the Preamble of our Constitution begins with "We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God . . ." That's an express prayer to God. When I was an associate justice, we celebrated the 100th anniversary of the Supreme Court during the entire year from June 2001 to June 2002. The Supreme Court was born in 1901 and became 100 years old in 2001. I was named chairman of the Executive Committee by Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide, Jr. with the mandate to celebrate our centenary. One of the things we did was to compose a "Prayer for the Courts."
We started praying it in 2001. Up to now, it is still prayed before the Supreme Court begins its sessions. Thereafter, the Court of Appeals and the trial courts followed suit. So, Dean Gil, please don't apologize. Thank you.

He reminds me of one of my three favorite lawyers when I was a young man, up to now. And I'll say them in alphabetical order: Jose W. Diokno, Jovito R. Salonga, and Claudio Teehankee.
I used to be a student of Dr. Salonga at FEU. And when I passed the bar examinations, he took me into his law office for three years. But what is so unique about him? He is sui generis because he did not finish the four-year law course. He was taught by his father who was a justice of the Supreme Court. Inspite of not finishing a four-year course in law, he was given special permission to take the bar examination which he topped, tied with Senator Salonga.
One time, we had a case where he was the opposing lawyer. I was in my first year as a lawyer, as an assistant of Dr. Salonga who was for the plaintiff and Jose W. Diokno was for the defense in an inheritance case. The trial before the old Court of First Instance in Pasay was a delight. For me, it was a spectacle watching them cross swords.
One early morning, Senator Salonga called me over the phone, "Artemio, I'm not feeling well. I have a bad stomach. I have LBM. Please attend the session tomorrow in the sala of Judge Angel Mojica." I was shocked because, you know, I was a new lawyer. I was just his briefcase carrier. I was just a bench warmer in the courtroom drama between two legal eagles. He said, "Don't ask for postponement because we have an agreement that there will be no postponement of the trials."
And so I went to court, knowing practically nothing of the case except what I wrote as a brief for Dr. Salonga.

Jose W. Diokno stood up, "Ready for the defense." And Judge Mojica looked at me, askance (He used to be my professor) and asked, "Where is Attorney Salonga?" I replied, "Your Honor, he called me up early this morning, and told me, 'Please attend the hearing, and do not ask for postponement.'"
"Are you ready, Attorney Panganiban?" asked Judge Mojica. "Ready, Your Honor." I nervously replied. JWD stood up and said, "Your Honor, we have an agreement not to postpone this case; that we will try it until its end, but next week we have another hearing. In fairness to my young compañero, may I ask for a postponement?" Judge Mojica boomed, "Any objection, Attorney Panganiban?"
I STOOD UP AGAIN AND I REPLIED, ****"****NO OBJECTION.****"
I am telling you this incident to show that JWD was a gentleman; he could have taken advantage of me, ran roughshod of me. I was shaking in my boots, although I did not want to show it; after all, he was my idol, along with Salonga and Teehankee.

HUMAN RIGHTS IN THE WORLD
Now, I'm very happy about this lecture, probably one of the best, if not the best, I've heard in our professorial series. We have had 17 lectures and, to repeat, this is one of the best. We are producing a book, an anthology of lectures. Of course, Dean Diokno's lecture will be printed there.
We promote liberty and prosperity under the rule of law. That is the mission of the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity, and it happens to be my own philosophy of law. First, we say, safeguard the liberty of our people. Liberty as a generic term, of course, includes human rights. And this piece of Chel Diokno is a refreshing addition to what we know already of liberty.

The international recognition of human rights as a component of business, as Dean Diokno explained, started from the United Nations, and then, it spread to many countries, and then to Southeast Asia, and then to our country. What we need really is a National Action Plan (NAP) that will be incorporated as part of the laws of our country and then implemented in action formats. He outlined not just the theory, not just the reality, but the needed National Action Plan to implement it.
We safeguard liberty in the FLP – under the rule of law. In authoritarian regimes, they say, "Oh, we also have human rights." I dare object because their human rights, their libertarian rights are not protected by "the rule of law." They are under the rule of one, the dictator, the authoritarian ruler. On the flip side of the FLP coin is the "nurturing of prosperity" for our people. In the FLP, we nurture prosperity by helping those who cannot help themselves through private entrepreneurship.
NOT JUST PROFIT, BUT GROWTH AND THE NATIONAL INTEREST
Now, a question was raised during the open forum about listed companies' reaction to human rights. And someone said that the end of business is profit. That's not necessarily true. Not the ones I know of, because growth is important. The share price of listed company is perhaps the most important factor that investors watch.

The point is that investors, especially the big-time investors look beyond profits. They look for ESG, and in this case they will look for the protection of human rights. What I'm saying is, if we can, we all of us, led by Dean Diokno can imbed this not only with the corporations, but with the big investors, the big investors will require from the companies to honor, respect, and give remedies to human rights.
To stress, my suggestion, or addition to what Dean Diokno already said, is this: Let us convince the investors, not just the companies, to demand the observance of the PRR of human rights and the banks to lend only to companies that observe the PRR.
PEACEFUL SETTLEMENT OF BUSINESS CONFLICTS
Note, however, that the judiciary, starting from the Supreme Court, encourages peaceful settlement. The Rules of Court mandate mediation. Even criminal cases are now settled. The Court encourages peace, isn't it? And even more than that, the Court imbedded the alternative dispute resolution methods as parts of trial court proceedings. Peaceful settlement of disputes is especially mandated in business. Businessmen and businesses do not like long litigations because they are not good for business. Today, in almost every major contract, the parties stipulate what we call "arbitration clauses" in which the decision of the arbitral tribunal is final and unappealable.

Address delivered by retired Chief Justice ARTEMIO V. PANGANIBAN, Chairman of the Philippine Delegation to the General Assembly and Governing Board Meetings of the ASEAN Law Association (ALA) held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia on October 17-22, 2023.
---
The Honorable Sundaresh Menon, Chief Justice of Singapore and President of the ASEAN Law Association, fellow delegation heads, fellow delegates, ladies and gentlemen.
Since we are given only three minutes to address the General Assembly, but five minutes during our Governing Council Meeting on Saturday, October 21, 2023, permit me to limit my talk this morning to two topics only: first, to present my delegation, and, second to thank our kind hosts.
On the first, allow me to introduce the incumbent Chief Justice of the Philippines, the Honorable Alexander G. Gesmundo who is also the honorary head of our delegation and the incoming Chairman of ALA Philippines effective January 1, 2024. Upon my strong, personal request, he was unanimously elected Chairman of ALA Philippines effective immediately.

an of ALA Philippines effective January 1, 2024. Upon my strong, personal request, he was unanimously elected Chairman of ALA Philippines effective immediately. However, when he learned of his election, he fervently asked me to carry on as Chairman because our Supreme Court and he were very busy conceiving and implementing their new reform program called the "Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation" designed to uplift the Philippine judiciary to the "Age of Artificial Intelligence." In turn, I begged him to please take it immediately because I was, and still am, already an ancient relic who has overstayed as ALA Philippines Chairman since 2015. As a compromise, we agreed that I would stay till the end of this year, and that he would take over at the beginning of the new year. May I request CJ Gesmundo to stand up and take a bow. Thank you.

unforgettable Opening Ceremony. Truly, my puny words cannot fully express our humble thanks and appreciation. Again, Mabuhay ALA. Mabuhay "Malaysia Truly Asia!" Your Excellencies, Your Honors, fellow delegates, ladies and gentlemen, before I begin my remarks, let me thank most profusely our President, Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon, for calling for one minute of silent prayers in honor of my dear wife, Leni, who passed suddenly and unexpectedly to the Eternal Kingdom on April 9, 2023. She was the gentle wind beneath my wings and the inspiration of my humble career. She attended all the major events of our Association. Now, I know she is above us in spirit, watching us, listening to us, rejoicing with us, thanking us for remembering her and for praying for her. Thank you, dear friends, and ALA colleagues.
As an ALA member since its founding 40 years ago, I consider myself fortunate to have been a happy witness of its storied history. During all these 40 years, consensus has always dominated our discussions and decisions. This rule of unanimity forged our unity despite our diversity in our national histories, customs, traditions, religions, economies, sociology, and forms of government. True, our countries had differences between and among them especially in their territorial and maritime boundaries. But we have been able to surmount them in peaceful and friendly ways, with consensus as our North star.

title: Consensus, Rule of Law, Liberty, and Prosperity in ASEAN

especially in their territorial and maritime boundaries. But we have been able to surmount them in peaceful and friendly ways, with consensus as our North star. Foremost among these peaceful and friendly ways is our adherence to the rule of law, and our abhorrence of armed, forcible, insidious, and bullying modes of settling disputes. We have never used military arms against each other, not even the so-called "gray tactics" because we believe in the rule of law, NOT in the rule of the mob, NOT in the rule of propaganda and falsehood and NOT in the rule of nuclear weapons. We believe in the sacredness of covenants and treaties, of international and regional bodies like the United Nations, and of judicial and arbitral tribunals like the International Court of Justice, the Appellate Body of the World Trade Organization, and the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague.
Notably, ASEAN's adherence to the rule of law is manifested not only in settling disputes peacefully or in defending territorial integrity, sovereignty, and sovereign rights. The rule of law is also the best way to safeguard liberty and to nurture prosperity.

Since this will be my last address as head of the Philippine delegation, please allow me to bring you back to, and quote partially my address during the 12th ALA General Assembly on February 26, 2015, the year I humbly assumed the chairmanship of ALA Philippines: "…My firm belief is that truth is eternal and limitless; that truth is not bound by sovereignty, or territory, or ideology, or legality; that what is true in America is also true in the Philippines, in the Asean and in the world. And that truth is this: humans need both justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics; peace and development; nay, liberty and prosperity; these twin beacons must always go together; one is useless without the other."
As you may be aware, I have always espoused "Liberty and Prosperity Under the Rule of Law." Even in retirement, I continued my advocacy for these twin and inseparable beacons.
May I report that as of today, the Foundation – together with its like-minded partners and in furtherance of the liberty aspect of its philosophy – has chosen and funded 83 full law scholarships, 16 professorial chairs, and 27 primary winners in its dissertation writing contests. And to promote the prosperity aspect of its philosophy, it granted 10 "ESMEL" fellowships for masters' degrees in entrepreneurship, sustainability, management, economics, and business law.

The second is the establishment of the multi-billion-peso "Prosperity Fund" to help the poor help themselves through private entrepreneurship. Before I leave this earth and enter the Great Beyond, I hope to complete these projects.
As I fade away from my humble leadership position, let me express my valedictory wish and prayer that the ASEAN Law Association will let consensus and the rule of law reign as the methods of attaining liberty and prosperity for the peoples of our region and of our world.
Thank you for your kind attention.

---
The Honorable Chief Justice of Singapore Sundaresh Menon, our esteemed ALA President; the Honorable Chief Justice of Indonesia Mohammad Syarifuddin, our generous host for this momentous Meeting; the Honorable Heads and Members of the various delegations to the 43rd ALA Governing Council Meeting; Honorable Judge Paul Quan, ALA Secretary General; ladies and gentlemen:

title: Thank You to Our Kind Host
heading: Thank You to Our Kind Host
text:

Heads and Members of the various delegations to the 43rd ALA Governing Council Meeting; Honorable Judge Paul Quan, ALA Secretary General; ladies and gentlemen: Good afternoon at magandang hapon po. At the outset, let me apologize profusely to our respected host, the Honorable Mohammad Syarifuddin, for my inability to honor his invitation to attend this meeting of our Governing Council in person. Despite my best effort, I could not be with you in person. I already made reservations on Philippine Airlines flight 539 from Manila to Jakarta that was scheduled to arrive in Jakarta last Saturday, October 1, 2022 at twelve noon. However, several days ago, Philippine Airlines notified us that the flight was "not going to be operational." Thus, we tried to book on Singapore Airlines on the route Manila/Singapore/Jakarta. However, the connecting flight from Singapore to Jakarta was only one hour and ten minutes. I was willing to board the next flight which involved over five hours of waiting at the Changi Airport. Sadly, the flight was super full. Hence, to my extreme regret and utter disappointment, I had to cancel our trip, a cancellation that my staff earlier communicated to Mr. Swandy Halim of ALA Indonesia. I am also sorry to miss the Grand Dinner last night in honor of my good friend, retired Chief Justice Hatta Ali.
