title: The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint
heading: The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint
text:
The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint

Outline of the lecture of retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban at the Columbia University in New York City on April 29, 2008.
---
Introduction: President Dwight Eisenhower and the liberal duo (Chief Justice Earl Warren and Justice William Brennan).
THE MAJOR SOURCES OF PHILIPPINE LAW
A short historical background. Constitutional, political, commercial and remedial law. Civil and criminal law.
THE PHILIPPINE JUDICIARY
The Philippine governmental structure; separation of powers. Scope of judicial power; Section 1, Article VIII, Philippine Constitution: Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of government.
Definition of grave abuse of discretion: Capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment by reason of passion or personal hostility in a manner so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or to a virtual refusal to perform the duty enjoined, or to act at all in contemplation of law. Also, any action done contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence.
Comparison of judicial power in the US and the Philippines. Theory of political question. Conditions, limitations or restrictions of political power. Jurisdiction over political questions.
MEASURES TO GUARANTEE JUDICIAL INDEPENDENCE

title: The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint
heading: The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint
text:
The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint (cont.)

litical question. Conditions, limitations or restrictions of political power. Jurisdiction over political questions.
MEASURES TO GUARANTEE JUDICIAL INDEPENDENCE Fiscal autonomy. Security of tenure and compensation. Protection from removal from office of justices and judges. Non-diminution of powers and jurisdiction. Administrative supervision over lower courts. Continuing judicial education. Freedom from congressional confirmation. Control of admission to the bar. Rule-making power. Protection and enforcement of constitutional rights.
ACID PROBLEMS OF THE JUDICIARY
Access to justice by the poor. Corruption. Incompetence. Delay in the delivery of quality judgments.
Vision: a judiciary characterized by four Ins: Independence, Integrity, Industry and Intelligence; one that safeguards the liberty and nurtures the prosperity of our people.
Conclusion: The might of the judiciary.

heading: Summary

Summary

Published April 29, 2008 as the outline or lecture notes for a presentation titled 'The Philippine Supreme Court: Activism and Restraint,' this document by CJP is structured as topic labels with brief descriptions rather than a full speech transcript.
It begins with the Eisenhower-liberal-duo framing (CJ Earl Warren and Justice William Brennan as Eisenhower's unintended activist appointees).
It covers the major sources of Philippine law (constitutional, political, commercial and remedial law; civil and criminal law), the Philippine governmental structure (separation of powers), and the definition of judicial power under Section 1 Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution: (1) settling actual controversies involving legally demandable rights; (2) determining grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.
The definition of grave abuse of discretion is given in full: 'Capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment by reason of passion or personal hostility in a manner so patent and so gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or to a virtual refusal to perform the duty enjoined, or to act at all in contemplation of law.
Also, any action done contrary to the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence.' The outline compares the Philippine grave-abuse-of-discretion jurisdiction with the US political question doctrine.

the Constitution, the law or jurisprudence.' The outline compares the Philippine grave-abuse-of-discretion jurisdiction with the US political question doctrine. title: Local Solutions to National Problems
heading: Local Solutions to National Problems
text:
Local Solutions to National Problems

Keynote address of retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the opening of the World Bank-sponsored Philippine Development Innovation Marketplace, Panibagong Paraan 2008, held on April 9, 2008 at the SM Megamall, Mandaluyong City.
---
I thank World Bank Country Director Bert Hofman for inviting me to be the Keynote Speaker during the opening of the Philippine Development Innovation Marketplace, Panibagong Paraan 2008. I am very impressed by Panibagong Paraan's search for innovative ideas as well as by the theme of this year's program, Building Partnerships for Local Governance, that I decided to accept the challenge of facing you today.
A COUNTRY IN CRISIS
Let me begin my keynote with an assessment of the present state of governance in our country. The CBCP said that we are in the midst of restlessness and confusion, facing a crisis of truth and the pervading cancer of corruption. We must seek the truth and we must restore integrity. The Catholic Church asked the faithful to go back to circles of discernment at the grassroots level, in our parishes, Basic Ecclesial Communities, recognized lay organizations and movements. From the grassroots will come out a culture of truth and integrity we so deeply seek and build.
GRASSROOTS SOLUTIONS

title: Local Solutions to National Problems
heading: Local Solutions to National Problems
text:
Local Solutions to National Problems (cont.)

recognized lay organizations and movements. From the grassroots will come out a culture of truth and integrity we so deeply seek and build.
GRASSROOTS SOLUTIONS Today in our Panibagong Paraan search for innovative ideas for development, we also turn to local governance for cooperative solutions to our national problems. Instead of using spiritual discernment, prayer and communal action, we look into more secular concepts and processes to promote and perpetuate the same goals of integrity, accountability and transparency in governance.
Also, instead of the usual Filipino method of solving problems from the top down, we invert the organizational pyramid by starting good governance innovations from the base going up to the apex of government. This great innovation of solving the nation's problems from the base up rather than the traditional direction coming from the top going to the grassroots is itself the big innovation in our marketplace today.
PRINCIPLES AND VALUES
Let me now share with you some principles and values that will help us in our search for ideas to solve our nation's ills. First, uphold truth and integrity at all times. Truth is the basis of credibility that in turn is the indispensable ingredient of successful governance. Integrity goes beyond mere honesty or the refusal to tell a falsehood; it is the moral courage to denounce a wrong and to promote the truth.
Second, practice transparency and exact accountability. Those who govern must be ready to endure the sunlight and the scrutiny of their public as well as private lives.

title: Local Solutions to National Problems
heading: Local Solutions to National Problems
text:
Local Solutions to National Problems (cont.)

practice transparency and exact accountability. Those who govern must be ready to endure the sunlight and the scrutiny of their public as well as private lives. Third, strengthen the rule of law. The rule of law reigns when the actions and decisions of government are made and done in accordance with the Constitution and the laws, not pursuant to the wiles and whims of the governors.
Fourth, practice responsible citizenship by being constantly informed of national and community affairs, participating in communal activities, and helping in the transformation of our culture of patronage to a culture of integrity.
Fifth, adhere to and fortify democratic institutions like due process, civilian supremacy, and checks and balances.
VISIONARY LEADERSHIP BY EXAMPLE
Sixth, always start with a vision; have a clear idea of what you want to accomplish and the specific ways of accomplishing them. A vision-mission statement must be specific and quantifiable, not a mere collection of motherhood principles.
EPILOGUE
In those early three days as PLDT's new chief executive, Manuel V. Pangilinan led his subalterns in practising the prudent use of corporate assets, integrity in money matters and on-time office arrival. After a few years of leadership by example, the market worth of the Philippine Long Distance Telephone Company multiplied tenfold, and its corporate ethics a hundred fold.

That, in a sentence, is my keynote message today. Maraming salamat po.

title: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
heading: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
text:
Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan

Lecture delivered on January 29, 2008 by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban at the Malolos Constitution Lecture Series sponsored by the Bulacan State University, Malolos, Bulacan.
---
Magandang umaga po sa inyong lahat. Lubos po akong nagagalak at nakabalik muli ako rito sa Bulacan State University. Itinuturing ko na pung isang tahanan at paaralan ang pamantasang ito. Mula po nuong minarapat ninyong bigyan ako ng karangalang maging isang Doctor of Laws, honoris causa, itinuring ko na po ang aking sarili na isa na ring alumnus ng BSU.
TALAYANG DAPAT IPAGDIWANG
Talagang dapat ipagdiwang ang Malolos Constitution, hindi lamang dahil sa ito ay isang simbolo ng ating kalayaan sa lahat ng mga banyaga, kungdi upang sariwaiin din sa alaala na nuon pa man, mahigit na isang daan taon na ang nakararaan, ang ating bayang Pilipinas ay isa ng constitutional democracy.
We feel proud that our Malolos Constitution has all the earmarks of a good fundamental law. It contains the three basic elements of a model constitution: a Constitution of liberty, a Constitution of government, and a Constitution of sovereignty, all at the same time.
LAYING THE PREMISE
In the recent past, we have read in the newspapers or heard over the radio and television, the men and women of the cloth commenting on how our government has been characterized by rampant corruption, violence, extra-judicial killings, and disappearances. On the other hand, high officials of government have been highly visible in big prayer rallies. Do these activities on either end violate the separation of the Church from the State?

title: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
heading: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
text:
Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan (cont.)

h officials of government have been highly visible in big prayer rallies. Do these activities on either end violate the separation of the Church from the State? EARLY BEGINNINGS
The Spanish Constitution of 1876 ordained Catholicism as the state religion. Under that set-up, there was no dividing line between the Catholic Church, as a religious denomination, and the State as a secular institution. Civil authorities exercised religious functions and the friars exercised civil powers. The Americans altered that cozy relationship. The Treaty of Paris of December 10, 1898 guaranteed religious freedom to the Philippines.
RELIGIOUS FREEDOM UNDER THE MALOLOS CONSTITUTION
On January 22, 1899, the Filipinos guaranteed themselves religious freedom when they adopted the Malolos Constitution. Its Preamble recognized the presence of a Power higher and greater than the State. Article 5 stated: The State recognizes the freedom and equality of all religions, as well as the separation of the Church and the State.
THE NON-ESTABLISHMENT CLAUSE
Cases involving the non-establishment clause have invariably sought to protect the people's choice of religion within the bounds of their conscience and free from the dictates of the State. The purposes are two-fold: one, to encourage voluntarism and two, to insulate the political process from interfaith dissension. Thus, the non-establishment clause demands that government be neutral with regard to religious matters.
THE FREE EXERCISE CLAUSE

title: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
heading: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
text:
Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan (cont.)

ess from interfaith dissension. Thus, the non-establishment clause demands that government be neutral with regard to religious matters.
THE FREE EXERCISE CLAUSE The Free Exercise Clause of the Constitution takes its bearing from the notion that freedom of belief, including religious belief, is as limitless as one's imagination and thought. However, the exercise of religious belief is an altogether different matter. The Philippine Supreme Court is not predisposed to invalidate a law that seems offensive to religious freedom; instead it tries to carve out an exception to accommodate religious exercise when it is justified.
SUMMATION
Sa loob po ng nakaraang oras, tinangka ko pong sagutin ang masalimuot na mga tanong sa ating talakayin ngayon. Masasabi nating mula nuong ipasinaya ang Malolos Constitution hanggang ngayon, nagaruon tayo sa Pilipinas ng isang pananaw sa isyu ng pagiging magkahiwalay ng Simbahan at Estado na iba sa pananaw sa Amerika.
Dito po sa bayan natin, nagdarasal tayo bago magsimula ng pagpupulong. Bago simulan ang sesyon ng Kabinete at ng Kongreso ay nagdarasal muna ng invocation. Pati po ang hudicatura, mula sa Kataas Taasang Hukuman hanggang sa mga Municipal Courts, nagsisimula po ang mga hearing sa pagdarasal ng Centennial Prayer for the Courts.

title: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
heading: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
text:
Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan (cont.)

g hudicatura, mula sa Kataas Taasang Hukuman hanggang sa mga Municipal Courts, nagsisimula po ang mga hearing sa pagdarasal ng Centennial Prayer for the Courts. To sum up, the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic. In fact, it is monotheist; it worships one God. That is why, its concepts and interpretations of the separation of the Church and the State, though originating from the United States, have been evolved over the last one hundred years in a uniquely Filipino manner, as the Malolos Constitution itself is uniquely Filipino.
Maraming salamat po.

title: Ang Pagiging Hiwalay ng Simbahan at Pamahalaan
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Delivered January 29, 2008 at Bulacan State University -- where CJP holds an honorary Doctor of Laws and considers himself a BSU alumnus ('itinuring ko na po ang aking sarili na isa na ring alumnus ng BSU') -- on the occasion of the Malolos Constitution celebration, this bilingual address (Filipino opening and close; English main body) argues that the Malolos Constitution deserves celebration not only as a symbol of independence but because it proves that the Philippines was already a constitutional democracy over 100 years ago.
The speech then tackles whether priests commenting on corruption/EJKs and officials attending prayer rallies violate church-state separation.
The historical context: the 1876 Spanish Constitution made Catholicism the state religion (friars exercised civil powers; civil authorities performed religious functions); the 1898 Treaty of Paris guaranteed religious freedom; on January 22, 1899, the Malolos Constitution's Article 5 declared 'The State recognizes the freedom and equality of all religions, as well as the separation of the Church and the State.' CJP analyzes the non-establishment clause (two purposes: encourage voluntarism; insulate political process from interfaith dissension; government must be neutral on religion) and the free exercise clause (freedom of belief is limitless; exercise can be regulated; Philippine SC carves out exceptions to accommodate religious exercise).

and the free exercise clause (freedom of belief is limitless; exercise can be regulated; Philippine SC carves out exceptions to accommodate religious exercise). In fact, it is monotheist; it worships one God.
That is why, its concepts and interpretations of the separation of the Church and the State...
have been evolved over the last one hundred years in a uniquely Filipino manner, as the Malolos Constitution itself is uniquely Filipino.' Evidence: Cabinet sessions, Congressional sessions, and court hearings all open with invocations.

title: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
heading: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
text:
The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity

Address delivered by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the induction of officers of the Association of Certified Public Accountants in Public Practice, held on January 29, 2008 at the Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City.
---
May I thank your President, Reynaldo S. Altre, for inviting me today to be your inducting officer and guest speaker. Having already retired from active public life, I no longer accept speaking invitations. However, your president was quite insistent. He reminded me that he and his firm have been the auditors of our small group of companies for about 40 years already, since 1968. So, I could not refuse.
I decided to speak on the role of certified public accountants in general, and of your organization, the Association of Certified Public Accountants in Public Practice in particular, in safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people.
Liberty and Prosperity under the Rule of Law — this was my guiding philosophy during my more than eleven years in the Supreme Court from 1995 to 2006; ten years as associate justice and one year as Chief Justice. Now, it is still my favorite clarion call.
THE IMPERATIVES OF LIBERTY AND PROSPERITY
Immediately upon assuming office as Chief Justice, I declared my vow to lead a judiciary characterized by four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence; and one that is morally courageous to stand its ground against the onslaughts of influence, interference, and indifference.

title: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
heading: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
text:
The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity (cont.)

pendence, industry and intelligence; and one that is morally courageous to stand its ground against the onslaughts of influence, interference, and indifference. I envisioned a judiciary that is impervious to the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship. And one that battled what I call the ACID problems of limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay in the delivery of quality judgments.
This vision of a reformed judiciary and a revitalized legal profession was directed towards two loftier goals of safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people under the rule of law.
THE ROLE OF COURTS AS THE GREAT EQUALIZERS
It is easy to see the role of courts as the great equalizers between the citizens and the government. The battle for civil liberties is a never-ending saga of trials and triumphs for the judiciary and for our people.
Ironically, how much lawyers know about protecting civil liberties seems to be negatively correlated with how little they have thus far devoted to nurturing the prosperity of our people. This is the reality that persists despite the Mandates of the 1987 Constitution: to alleviate the plight of the marginalized and the poor; to promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty; and to achieve a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth.

title: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
heading: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
text:
The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity (cont.)

he prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty; and to achieve a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth. I am truly convinced that the prosperity of our people requires as much nurturing in the present century as that accorded to liberty in the past. To be relevant, courts must be constantly attuned to the needs of the present and the vagaries of the future, so that they can respond in a timely and prudent manner to the people's ever-expanding well-being.
ACPAPP****'****S ROLE IN LIBERTY AND PROSPERITY
Professional organizations like the ACPAPP form part of what is broadly referred to as civil society. Civil society has been in the forefront of the fight for liberty. Popular action has brought down a dictatorship; it has also rejected a once populist, but later perceived to be corrupt, administration. Thus has People Power been carved into the consciousness of our citizenry: lying latent while restrained, but deadly when unleashed.
From the foregoing discussion, it is obvious that civil society in general and ACPAPP in particular assist the three great branches of government in their common effort to uplift our people from the plagues of misgovernance, tyranny, poverty and want. Specifically, it can play a significant role in promoting economic development by supporting judicial initiatives along this line.
CONCLUSION

title: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
heading: The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity
text:
The Role of CPAs in Safeguarding Liberty and Nurturing Prosperity (cont.)

poverty and want. Specifically, it can play a significant role in promoting economic development by supporting judicial initiatives along this line.
CONCLUSION ACPAPP as a microcosm of civil society has a big stake in ensuring the liberty and prosperity of our people. The road to attaining the twin objectives of liberty and prosperity may be long and difficult. But with your help and active participation, the vision becomes clearer and our resolve firmer. Please join me in tirelessly searching and fearlessly espousing both jobs and justice, food and freedom, investments and integrity, economics and ethics, development and democracy; in short, Liberty and Prosperity.
Maraming salamat po.

title: Vision and Values
heading: Vision and Values
text:
Vision and Values

Keynote Address delivered by retired Chief Justice ARTEMIO V. PANGANIBAN on the first day of the 36th National Student Congress sponsored by the National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP) held on December 15-18, 2007 in Cebu City.
---
May I thank you, the delegates from NUSP-member schools attending this 36th National Student Congress, for inviting me to deliver the keynote address on the theme NUS at 50: Continuing the Legacy of Passionate Student Leadership, Advancing the Rights and Welfare of Students and the Filipino People, Strengthening the Union Towards Serving Society.
DELIGHTED TO RELIVE CAREFREE YEARS
Though already retired from the judiciary and perhaps old enough to be your grandfather, I am nonetheless delighted to be with you today to relive my carefree days as a young man. I have lived on this planet for over seventy years; have met some of the most important people that populate it during my lifetime; have traveled to all the continents of our earth, except Antarctica. Yet let me tell you very candidly that I would exchange all of that to turn back the hands of time and to relive my years as a student leader.
THREE-FOLD NUS CONFERENCE THEME

title: Vision and Values
heading: Vision and Values
text:
Vision and Values (cont.)

l you very candidly that I would exchange all of that to turn back the hands of time and to relive my years as a student leader.
THREE-FOLD NUS CONFERENCE THEME Your theme is very appropriate during this 50th year of the NUSP. First, you want to look back into the past and connect with the legacy of our Union, its visions and values at its inception. Second, you also seek to improve the future by advancing the rights and welfare of the students and the entire Filipino people. Third, you want to foster the present by strengthening the NUSP so it could continue serving society.
I firmly believe that every person and every organization must have a vision of what he, she or it intends to accomplish, a method of fulfilling them, and a set of immutable values to guide the journey until the destination is reached. Without vision and values, one will be like a ship without a rudder, or an airplane without avionics.
THE COLD WAR: THE US AND THE USSR
At that time, the world was divided into two great camps: the liberal democracies led by the United States, and the totalitarian-communist states headed by the erstwhile Soviet Union. The cold war's long international tentacles crept into the student movements in the Philippines. A congressional investigation showed that the communists infiltrated student organizations. Also, the government tried to muzzle student organizations by corralling them in what was called the Consultative Council of Students.
THE WALK-OUT AND THE BIRTH OF THE NUS

title: Vision and Values
heading: Vision and Values
text:
Vision and Values (cont.)

vernment tried to muzzle student organizations by corralling them in what was called the Consultative Council of Students.
THE WALK-OUT AND THE BIRTH OF THE NUS In September 1957, I rose as the then newly elected president of the FEU Central Student Organization to question these communist and partisan political activities that shackled both the SCAP and the CONDA. Instead of satisfactory answers, the SCAP leaders tried to placate me by unanimously electing me as vice president for international affairs, a much-coveted position that would have entitled me to travel free of charge to many countries with pocket money from Malacanang.
Notwithstanding all these, I chose the more difficult, straight and narrow path by seceding from both the SCAP and the CONDA, rejecting my lucrative position in SCAP, and refusing membership in the President's august Little Cabinet. Luckily, I was not alone in my idealism. Student leaders from UP, UST, San Beda College, St. Theresa's, National University and Sta. Isabel joined in the walk out and formed the nucleus of the NUSP.
THE NUSP VISION AND VALUES
From this rather long narration of the beginnings of NUSP, let me summarize our vision at its inception: The NUS was founded as a positive answer to the decadent state of student leadership in the country. The Union is pledged to unite and reflect faithfully student opinion on current national issues, free the youth from undue political interferences, fight communist infiltration in the campuses, and redirect the youth's thinking and energy to constructive idealism.

title: Vision and Values
heading: Vision and Values
text:
Vision and Values (cont.)

e youth from undue political interferences, fight communist infiltration in the campuses, and redirect the youth's thinking and energy to constructive idealism. Its core values were dignity, integrity, independence, liberty, responsibility and democracy. These ideals were achieved: the communist effort to infiltrate student movements failed; freedom prevailed; and the students were liberated from the political and partisan apron strings of the government.
PRESENT PROBLEMS FACING THE YOUTH
The problems facing the youth today are the very same humongous problems that face our nation: wrenching poverty, declining educational standards, malgovernance, endemic corruption, flagrant election cheating, human right violations, lack of accountability, and assaults on our democratic institutions. Because our country really belongs to the young, the old people merely administer it for them in the meantime. Therefore, during this NUSP Congress, I expect you to tackle these plagues, denounce their perpetrators, and offer some perspectives and solutions.
FULFILLING THE VISION AND CORE VALUES

title: Vision and Values
heading: Vision and Values
text:
Vision and Values (cont.)

SP Congress, I expect you to tackle these plagues, denounce their perpetrators, and offer some perspectives and solutions.
FULFILLING THE VISION AND CORE VALUES Finally, let me end this address with a question for each one of you. Do you each have a vision and values to guide you in the next fifty years of your life? Fifty years from now, you may be invited like me to keynote the 100th anniversary of the NUSP. Can you speak about how you lived your vision and values? For your own recording, please put them in writing and include them in your digital files, so that fifty years from now, in the presence of your children and grandchildren, you may show these mementos and declare before God and man that you have lived your life in accordance with these cherished ideals.
Maraming salamat po.

title: Entering the Legal Profession
heading: Entering the Legal Profession
text:
Entering the Legal Profession

Address delivered by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban as guest of honor and speaker during the 116th Foundation Day Celebration of the Philippine Bar Association, held at the Hotel Intercontinental on April 26, 2007.
---
I am deeply honored to have been invited as your guest of honor and speaker. Although I have already retired from the judiciary and am now a private citizen, the Philippine Bar Association has deemed me still worthy to address this important milestone: the 116th foundation day celebration of the oldest and largest voluntary aggrupation of lawyers in our country.
Born on April 8, 1891 as the Colegio de Abogados de Filipinas, the PBA has a pedigreed tradition dating back to the gloried days of Apolinario Mabini, Felipe Calderon, Cayetano Arellano and Jose Abad Santos, to name a few of its illustrious heroes and leaders.
THE 2006 BAR EXAM
Yesterday, at the Philippine International Convention Center, 1,893 law graduates who passed the 2006 bar examinations were sworn in as new members of the noblest profession in the world. The Supreme Court ended its summer session in Baguio and the justices motored to Manila to attend the solemn rites.
A graduate of the University of the Cordilleras (Noel Neil Q. Malimba) topped the test. For the nonce, the traditional rivals, Ateneo de Manila (Ricardo M. Pilares Jr.) and the University of the Philippines (Deborah S. Acosta) had to content themselves with a tie for second place. Far Eastern University (Gina Lyn R. Rubio) took the fifth place.

title: Entering the Legal Profession
heading: Entering the Legal Profession
text:
Entering the Legal Profession (cont.)

y of the Philippines (Deborah S. Acosta) had to content themselves with a tie for second place. Far Eastern University (Gina Lyn R. Rubio) took the fifth place. The 2006 bar will be remembered for many things. This batch, numbering 6,187, is the largest ever to take the examination. The year 2006 marks the first time that four non-Metro Manila schools copped four of the top ten places: University of the Cordilleras, University of San Carlos, Romualdez Educational Foundation, and University of Cebu.
THE BAR EXAM ILLUSTRADOS
Many bar illustrados have demonstrated enviable track records in the profession and in the government. Four incumbent SC justices are bar placers: Antonio T. Carpio (6th place, 1975), Adolfo S. Azcuna (4th, 1962), Presbitero J. Velasco Jr. (6th, 1971) and Antonio B. Nachura (7th, 1967).
Of the 21 past Chief Justices, nine were topnotchers, including Pedro L. Yap (1st, 1946), Andres R. Narvasa (2nd, 1951) and Artemio V. Panganiban (6th, 1960).
PERFORMANCE OF THE LAW SCHOOLS
In the exams held from 1946 to 2006, a period of 60 years, the University of the Philippines produced 25 number ones; Ateneo de Manila, 17; San Beda, six; Far Eastern University, four. Based on average passing percentages for the period 1991-2005, Ateneo de Manila topped with 87.57 percent; San Beda, 80.38; UP, 76.4.
REFORMS IN THE BAR TESTS

title: Entering the Legal Profession
heading: Entering the Legal Profession
text:
Entering the Legal Profession (cont.)

. Based on average passing percentages for the period 1991-2005, Ateneo de Manila topped with 87.57 percent; San Beda, 80.38; UP, 76.4.
REFORMS IN THE BAR TESTS Over the years, the SC has tried to upgrade the bar examinations. Extensive reforms were approved under Bar Matter 1161 dated June 8, 2004, including: those who have failed five or more times shall be allowed to take only one more exam after finishing a one-year refresher course; candidates who obtain a grade below 50 percent in any subject were disqualified; multiple choice questions have been adopted.
REFORMS IN LEGAL EDUCATION
The Supreme Court did not act on four proposals to improve legal education: the accreditation and supervision of law schools; the inclusion of clinical education in the law curriculum; the imposition of sanctions on sub-standard law schools; and the taking of a national admission test by those entering a law school. These four items were referred to the Legal Education Board. Sadly, although created 14 years ago, the LEB has not been operationalized.
ETHICS AND COMPETENCE

title: Entering the Legal Profession
heading: Entering the Legal Profession
text:
Entering the Legal Profession (cont.)

. These four items were referred to the Legal Education Board. Sadly, although created 14 years ago, the LEB has not been operationalized.
ETHICS AND COMPETENCE As a final note, more than knowledge of the law and competence in its practice, legal ethics should be emphasized both in basic legal education and in the bar exams. To close this address, I would like to paraphrase an oft-quoted Supreme Court decision: the doors to our legal profession must swing on reluctant hinges. Those who want to pass those doors must make a solemn commitment to adhere to an ethical compass. Quality justice always begins with a high standard of ethics. During my term as Chief Justice, I advocated the revitalization of the legal profession by breeding competent and ethical lawyers. Yes, competent and ethical attorneys, code-named EC, that is the legacy I would like to leave our profession.
Maraming salamat po.

title: Urbanity and Integrity
heading: Urbanity and Integrity
text:
Urbanity and Integrity

Keynote address delivered by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the launching of Diokno on Trial: Techniques and Ideals of the Filipino Lawyer, authored by the late Sen. Jose W. Diokno and updated by Atty. Jose Manuel I. Diokno, held on February 26, 2007 at the De la Salle University, Taft Avenue, Manila.
---
I am deeply honored to have been invited to deliver this keynote address in honor of the late Senator Jose W. Diokno — whose book, Techniques and Ideals of the Filipino Lawyer as updated by his son, Compañero Jose Manuel I. Diokno — is now being launched. Today also marks the 85th birthday of Senator Diokno. And tomorrow, February 27, we shall commemorate his 20th death anniversary.
LEARNING FUNDAMENTALS BEFORE ACTUAL TRIAL
Learning trial techniques is like learning how to drive or how to swim. One has to be on the wheels, or in the water to master these skills. By the same token, to become a great trial lawyer, one has to go to court, get immersed in the proceedings, and actually try a case.
Tapping into the wealth of the late Senator Diokno's extensive experience in evidence and trial techniques, the update by Jose Manuel I. Diokno vis-a-vis his father's earlier work is a highly useful repository of valuable lessons on how best to prepare, monitor and handle flesh-and-blood cases. Functionally, according to Senator Diokno, that task is to convince the court that one's client is right.

title: Urbanity and Integrity
heading: Urbanity and Integrity
text:
Urbanity and Integrity (cont.)

to prepare, monitor and handle flesh-and-blood cases. Functionally, according to Senator Diokno, that task is to convince the court that one's client is right. This book aptly opens with the elder Diokno's interesting story on how to win a case. According to him, three things are necessary: a good case, a good lawyer and a good judge. The first two, the lawyer could guarantee; the third, he could not. Having served in the Supreme Court for over 11 years, I can only stress on the significance of the third ingredient. Indeed, good lawyers need good judges who are ready to follow the law and do justice.
DIOKNO****'****S TRIAL TECHNIQUES
Having laid the proper premise, the compilation meticulously discusses the techniques used and tested by Senator Diokno in presenting oral and documentary evidence; in overcoming problems related to the presentation of evidence; and in presenting trial checklists and forms to aid and guide practitioners as they go through the various phases of trial. For all trial lawyers, both the young and the old, the novice and the experienced, this book is a must read.
A GENTLEMAN-LAWYER
Immediately after passing the bar examinations in 1960, I became an associate in the law office of our then dean, Dr. Jovito R. Salonga. One early morning, Dean Salonga called me up at home to say that he was indisposed, and to ask if I could substitute for him in that morning's trial at the then Court of First Instance of Pasay.

title: Urbanity and Integrity
heading: Urbanity and Integrity
text:
Urbanity and Integrity (cont.)

lled me up at home to say that he was indisposed, and to ask if I could substitute for him in that morning's trial at the then Court of First Instance of Pasay. Atty. Jose W. Diokno, the counsel of the plaintiff, generously moved to postpone the hearing in fairness to the young, inexperienced lawyer on the other side. This may have been a little incident in the checkered life of the legendary Atty. Jose W. Diokno, but it was a major one in mine. It showed me how a great advocate could demonstrate fairness to a young, nervous lawyer. Atty. Diokno earned my immediate admiration and awe, not only for his vaunted competence, but also for his genial sportsmanship in refusing to take undue advantage of a young, nervous lawyer.
A DEEPER AND GREATER QUALITY
Apart from his urbanity, there is yet another quality, a deeper and greater one, that Senator Diokno has imprinted on my memory.
During the martial law years, the country was besieged by officials who arrogated absolute power to themselves, plundered the treasury, and used their public offices to amass ill-gotten wealth. There were, however, a handful who kept themselves personally pure. While these few good men and women can be described as honest public servants, they did nothing to stamp out the evil around them, contented as they were with distancing themselves from the evil conspiracy.
Honesty is a virtue taught in grade school. But beyond honesty, the country needed men and women of integrity, who will not merely refuse to tell a falsehood, but who possess the moral courage to denounce a wrong and to promote the truth.

title: Urbanity and Integrity

eded men and women of integrity, who will not merely refuse to tell a falsehood, but who possess the moral courage to denounce a wrong and to promote the truth. Jose W. Diokno twice supported the presidential candidacy of Ferdinand E. Marcos. In fact, he was elected senator under the same party as Marcos. In the beginning, he helped him. But after it became clear that Marcos was veering from the straight and narrow path, Ka Pepe did not hesitate to part from him and to denounce his excesses. He could have kept quiet and tolerated the abuses. Instead, he worked fervently and actively, at the risk of his own safety, health, earthly possessions and career, to restore freedom in our land, to denounce the plunderers, to help the poor and to make truth and justice prevail.
More than being honest, Jose Wright Diokno was a person of moral courage. He was moved by immutable values and principles, not by pettiness or convenience. Indeed, he was a visionary leader of exemplary integrity.
Maraming salamat po.

title: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
heading: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
text:
The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance

Address delivered on February 16, 2007 by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban as resource speaker during a seminar in Cebu City sponsored by the Philippine Judicial Academy and the Values for Development Foundation.
---
At the outset, allow me to thank Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera, chancellor of the Philippine Judicial Academy, for inviting me to be the resource speaker on Democracy and Development: the Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance. This topic is close to my heart. I believe it is a restatement of my own judicial philosophy of Liberty and Prosperity Under the Rule of Law.
SAFEGUARDING LIBERTY
Safeguarding liberty, or democracy, for that matter, has long been a traditional expectation from our courts. Their role is to be the great equalizers when individual freedoms are buffeted by the awesome powers of the State. These epic constitutional struggles between the government and its citizens are written in the annals of our nation's history.
In litigations involving civil liberties, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the people, particularly the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed, and the weak. Laws and actions that restrict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity. This policy is commonly referred to as heightened or strict scrutiny.

title: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
heading: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
text:
The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance (cont.)

ict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity. This policy is commonly referred to as heightened or strict scrutiny. Consistent with this policy, the Supreme Court during my incumbency as Chief Justice promulgated three landmark decisions: one upholding the right of Congress to summon executive officials for investigations (Senate v. Ermita); one scuttling the Calibrated Preemptive Response policy and ruling in favor of the people's right to peaceful assembly (Bayan v. Ermita); and one recognizing the fundamental rights of the people under a state of national emergency (David v. Arroyo).
NURTURING PROSPERITY
While safeguarding liberty is a fairly common task for the judiciary, nurturing prosperity is something even seasoned jurists may not readily understand. Nonetheless, I maintain that the judiciary has a duty to nurture prosperity and to alleviate poverty.
Our 1987 Constitution contains several provisions involving the economic rights of our people. The Constitution commands the State to promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty. The Constitution also mandates a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth.

title: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
heading: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
text:
The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance (cont.)

d independence of the nation and free the people from poverty. The Constitution also mandates a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth. In litigations affecting prosperity, development and the economy, the courts must defer as much as possible to the actions of the political branches of government, namely the Presidency and Congress. This approach is referred to as deferential interpretation of laws and executive actions. In Tanada v. Angara, the Court deferred to the wisdom of the Senate when it upheld that legislative body's consent to the Philippine ratification of the World Trade Organization Agreement. In La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, the Court affirmed the constitutionality of the Mining Law allowing 100-percent foreign investments in large-scale mining.
RULE OF LAW
The safeguarding of liberty and the nurturance of prosperity must always be planned, worked on and carried out in accordance with pre-agreed rules and procedures. What differentiates libertarianism from authoritarianism is the rule of law. No person, no matter how powerful or talented, can be above the law. Everyone, rich or poor, powerful or powerless, must follow pre-agreed rules.
EPILOGUE

title: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
heading: The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
text:
The Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance (cont.)

law. No person, no matter how powerful or talented, can be above the law. Everyone, rich or poor, powerful or powerless, must follow pre-agreed rules.
EPILOGUE To my mind, the peculiar facts and distinct circumstances of the Philippines make the formula Liberty and Prosperity Under the Rule of Law still the most viable economic and judicial philosophy here. After all, during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress. Our 1987 Constitution has imposed upon the entire judiciary the duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion committed by any branch or instrumentality of the government. By prudently exercising this constitutional duty, the 21st century judges are really pursuing their proper roles in the governance of our country.
Maraming salamat po.

title: Visionary Leadership By Example
heading: Visionary Leadership By Example
text:
Visionary Leadership By Example

Keynote address delivered by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban on the opening day of the 9th National Ayala Young Leaders Congress (AYLC 2007) on February 7-9, 2007, at the San Miguel Corporation Management Training Center, Alfonso, Cavite.
---
May I thank Mr. Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala, chairman and CEO of the Ayala Corporation, for inviting me to keynote the 9th National Ayala Young Leaders Congress. May I also commend the Ayala Corporation itself for launching this program in 1998 and for doggedly pursuing it during the past nine years as its strategic investment on the youth, and ultimately, in the future of this country.
I accepted this invitation to dialogue with this year's crop of well-selected campus personalities because I, too, believe that building the confidence and honing the leadership skills of our youth leaders is a worthy investment in national development.
MEMORIES OF MY OWN STUDENT DAYS
My presence here today brings back nostalgic memories of my own student days some 50 years ago, and of my own search for identity, pursuit of excellence, chase for exuberance, and quest for enduring values. I was very poor and orphaned early in life. I had nothing. No worldly treasures to keep, no reputation to protect, no close relatives to defer to.
But I organized and headed the National Union of Students of the Philippines, which was born as a rebellion against a decadent student milieu. The NUSP was founded on the proposition that the best in a person and in society can be attained only in freedom, dignity, equality and shared responsibility.

title: Visionary Leadership By Example
heading: Visionary Leadership By Example
text:
Visionary Leadership By Example (cont.)

. The NUSP was founded on the proposition that the best in a person and in society can be attained only in freedom, dignity, equality and shared responsibility. CLEAR IDEA OF GOALS AND METHODS
Every leader must have a clear idea of what ultimately he or she wants to accomplish, and of the specific ways of how to achieve the declared goals. I refer to this statement of goals, values and methods as the vision-mission of every leader or organization.
TWO ROLES OF THE CHIEF JUSTICE
The Chief Justice has two major roles: first, he is the highest magistrate of the land, the primus inter pares among the fifteen members of the Supreme Court; and second, he is the leader of the entire judicial branch of government.
Upon being inducted into office, I announced my vision: a judiciary that safeguards the liberty and nurtures the prosperity of our people under the rule of law. My mission was to lead a judiciary characterized by four Ins: independence, integrity, industry and intelligence; to reform the justice system by fighting the four ACID problems (limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence, and delay in the delivery of quality judgments); to revitalize the legal profession by breeding competent and ethical lawyers; and to grant all judicial employees maximum benefits, asking for DHL: dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and full loyalty to the Supreme Court.
SAFEGUARDING LIBERTY

title: Visionary Leadership By Example
heading: Visionary Leadership By Example
text:
Visionary Leadership By Example (cont.)

t all judicial employees maximum benefits, asking for DHL: dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and full loyalty to the Supreme Court.
SAFEGUARDING LIBERTY In litigations involving civil liberties, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the people, particularly the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed, and the weak. The Court during my incumbency promulgated three landmark decisions upholding these principles.
NURTURING PROSPERITY
While safeguarding liberty is a fairly common task for the judiciary, nurturing prosperity requires more conscious effort. In litigations affecting prosperity, development and the economy, the courts must defer as much as possible to the actions of the political branches of government.
RULE OF LAW
The safeguarding of liberty and the nurturance of prosperity must always be planned, worked on and carried out in accordance with pre-agreed rules and procedures. The rule of law differentiates democracy from the rule of the mob.
My Vision is not liberty or prosperity; it is liberty and prosperity. These twin beacons of justice must go together; we cannot sacrifice one for the other; they may otherwise be stated as freedom and food, democracy and development, ethics and economics, integrity and investments.
EPILOGUE

title: Visionary Leadership By Example
heading: Visionary Leadership By Example
text:
Visionary Leadership By Example (cont.)

rifice one for the other; they may otherwise be stated as freedom and food, democracy and development, ethics and economics, integrity and investments.
EPILOGUE On his first day in office, the new chief executive of one of the top ten Philippine companies asked how many cars were assigned to his office. He was stunned to learn there were more than five dozens. He retained only one and ordered the immediate sale of the remainder. On his second day, an assistant visited with a briefcase full of cash, his personal share of advertising commissions. He ordered them deposited in the company's bank account. On his third day, he arrived at 8:00 a.m. daily without comment. In those first three days, Manuel V. Pangilinan led his subordinates in practicing prudence in spending, integrity in money matters and on-time office arrival. After a few years, the worth of PLDT multiplied tenfold and its corporate ethics, a hundred fold.
Having a clear vision and mission is an essential beginning. Leading by example is the best, if not the only, way to accomplish the vision and mission. My short answer to AYLC's crucial question of how to lead during these challenging times: visionary leadership by example.
Maraming salamat po.

title: Maraming Salamat Po
heading: Maraming Salamat Po
text:
Maraming Salamat Po

Valedictory address delivered by Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the retirement ceremonies held in his honor on December 6, 2006, 4:30 p.m., at the Supreme Court Session Hall.
---
What does one do when he receives a blessing of enormous value? How does one behave when the heart is full, and words are inadequate? Indeed, what can I do after having been given the very rare chance to serve as our country's highest magistrate? What can I say upon ending this extraordinary opportunity to be remembered beyond my mortal life?
What else can I do but say, Maraming maraming salamat po to everyone who has made this miracle possible. Indeed, in this serene and majestic temple of justice of our country, I celebrate my fervent thanksgiving.
THANK YOU TO TWO PRESIDENTS
Let me say maraming salamat po to Her Excellency, President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, for naming me as the 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines, the first in the 21st century, and for administering my oath of office on the 21st day of December 2005. Let it be on record that President Arroyo had not asked me to do anything in return for that momentous event.
Maraming salamat po to President Fidel Valdez Ramos for initiating me into the Supreme Court on a Double Ten, October 10, 1995. Though I owe my appointment to the Court solely and completely to him, let me add very quickly that he never spoke to me about any case or matter pending in the Court since then. Such is the gentleman that he is.
THANK YOU TO MY COLLEAGUES

title: Maraming Salamat Po
heading: Maraming Salamat Po
text:
Maraming Salamat Po (cont.)

dd very quickly that he never spoke to me about any case or matter pending in the Court since then. Such is the gentleman that he is.
THANK YOU TO MY COLLEAGUES Maraming salamat po to all my colleagues in the Supreme Court. By their own writings, opinions and decisions, as well as discussions during our sessions, they have helped me test and mold my own thoughts. I cherish my work in the Court, because I find our intellectual exchanges, both verbal and written, stimulating, challenging and sometimes humbling.
As the primus inter pares of the Panganiban Court, I am especially appreciative of the individual and collective efforts of my colleagues to help me attain my vow to lead a judiciary characterized by four Ins: independence, integrity, industry and intelligence; one that is morally courageous to resist influence, interference, indifference and insolence; and is impervious to what I call the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship.
I am thankful for their wholehearted cooperation in continuing our Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), especially in focusing on what I refer to as the ACID problems that corrode justice in our country: limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay in the delivery of quality judgments.

title: Maraming Salamat Po
heading: Maraming Salamat Po
text:
Maraming Salamat Po (cont.)

ID problems that corrode justice in our country: limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence and delay in the delivery of quality judgments. To my mind, the battle for the four Ins and against the four ACID problems should lead to the attainment of two loftier end goals: safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people under the rule of law. That we have been successful in spreading this gospel of Liberty and Prosperity is exemplified not only by the decisions and actions of the Court, but also by the testimonials we received during the recent Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity held on October 18-20, 2006.
THANK YOU TO MY TEACHERS
Maraming salamat po to all those who helped me in my education: Candaba Elementary School; Juan Luna Elementary School; Mapa High School; and most especially Far Eastern University, where I learned not only academic excellence and well-rounded education, but also student leadership and the rudiments of my Catholic faith.
Maraming salamat po to the many institutions of learning which granted me honorary doctoral degrees without my having to enroll and to sweat during examinations. Before these doctorates were conferred upon me, I was the only member of my immediate family who did not have a graduate degree. To my wife and children who all hold masteral or doctoral degrees from pedigreed universities here and abroad, I say, we are now equal.
THANK YOU TO MY SHEPHERDS

title: Maraming Salamat Po
heading: Maraming Salamat Po
text:
Maraming Salamat Po (cont.)

o my wife and children who all hold masteral or doctoral degrees from pedigreed universities here and abroad, I say, we are now equal.
THANK YOU TO MY SHEPHERDS Maraming salamat po to the shepherds of my faith and to my spiritual mentors. Towering above them are Fr. Michael Nolan, now in the Great Beyond, who, as chaplain of Far Eastern University in the 1950s, introduced me to our Lord; to Fr. James Sheehy, his successor, who eventually baptized all of my five children.
But the one person outside of my immediate family who has had the longest and perhaps the deepest influence in my life, career and faith is Dr. Jovito R. Salonga. I met him some 50 years ago when he was my professor and dean at FEU. Since then up to the present, he has remained my lifetime guru and model of how to live a life worth living. His foremost teaching: while it is desirable to have some of the necessities that money can buy, we should never ever forget that it is far more important to aspire for the things that money cannot buy, like honor, dignity, ethics, character and excellence.
THANK YOU TO MY FAMILY
Maraming salamat po to my wife Leni, who has showered me with unconditional love, endless devotion, and constant faithfulness during our more than 45 years of married life. She is my anchor in the stormy seas of adversity and the wind beneath my wings during my flights of fantasy.

title: Maraming Salamat Po
heading: Maraming Salamat Po
text:
Maraming Salamat Po (cont.)

ness during our more than 45 years of married life. She is my anchor in the stormy seas of adversity and the wind beneath my wings during my flights of fantasy. Thank you also to my five children — Len, Archie, Celine, Tet and Mabel — each of whom has achieved my impossible dream of graduate education in an eminent institution in the United States. And to my nine lovable, healthy and good-looking apos. To all of you, I dedicate my eleven books.
TO GOD BE THE GLORY
As I end my valedictory, let the choicest gratitude and praise be unto God Almighty who, despite my occasional shortcomings and failures, has been ever faithful to me in all my 70 years of temporary sojourn here on earth.
The Lord is my Shepherd. There is nothing I shall want. He has given me more than I deserve — a happy home, a healthy body, accomplished children over whom I no longer worry, a stable career, a chance to serve our people, an opportunity to be remembered longer than my own life. Other than fulfilling my role in the Court, I have no more earth-bound ambition. I live my life with only one consuming passion: on that inevitable day when I will finally knock at the pearly gates, my Lord and Master will open the door, spread his arms and say: Well done on your earthly sojourn. You have passed the test. Welcome home to my everlasting Kingdom!
To God be the glory!

heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Delivered on December 6, 2006 at the Supreme Court Session Hall as his retirement valedictory, CJ Panganiban structures his thanksgiving in concentric circles -- first the two Presidents who appointed him (Ramos to the Court on October 10, 1995, and Arroyo as 21st Chief Justice on December 21, 2005), then his Supreme Court colleagues, his teachers from Candaba Elementary to FEU, his spiritual shepherds led by Fr. Michael Nolan and Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, and finally his wife Leni and their five children and nine grandchildren. He uses the occasion to crystallize the institutional vocabulary of what he calls 'the Panganiban Court': the 'Four Ins' the judiciary must embody (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence), the four institutional vices it must resist (influence, interference, indifference, insolence), the 'plague of ships' that corrodes impartiality (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), and the 'ACID problems' that the Action Program for Judicial Reform attacks (limited Access by the poor, Corruption, Incompetence, Delay). All of these, he argues, are means toward the twin end-goals of safeguarding liberty AND nurturing prosperity under the rule of law, exemplified by the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity he convened October 18-20, 2006. He closes with a personal Psalm-23 echoing prayer dedicating his life to God.

title: Striking the Right Balance
heading: Striking the Right Balance
text:
Striking the Right Balance

Keynote speech delivered by Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban on November 29, 2006 during the Fourth Conference of Asian Constitutional Court Judges at the Diamond Hotel, Manila.
---
Good morning! I am certainly glad to be part of your two-day conference. The Philippines, unlike your countries, does not have a separate constitutional court. Its functions and duties are discharged by our Supreme Court.
CONFLICTS OF RIGHTS
The theme you have chosen for this conference is extremely interesting and thought-provoking, because it mirrors a number of realities existing in our respective jurisdictions. Notwithstanding skirmishes between different sectors of society, our courts are determined to strike the proper balance between contending rights.
CIVIL, POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC RIGHTS
Our history shows that civil and political rights, particularly those enshrined in our Bill of Rights, have been zealously guarded and upheld. Courts are expected to safeguard liberty. Their role is to be the great equalizers when individual freedoms are buffeted by the awesome powers of the State.
Other parts of our Constitution, however, enunciate economic rights as well. The Article on Principles and State Policies directs the State to promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty. Article XII mandates a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth.
LIBERTY AND PROSPERITY AS STANDARDS OF REVIEW

title: Striking the Right Balance
heading: Striking the Right Balance
text:
Striking the Right Balance (cont.)

e the people from poverty. Article XII mandates a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth.
LIBERTY AND PROSPERITY AS STANDARDS OF REVIEW The equally important demands of liberty and the needs of prosperity have come before the Supreme Court at various times. The Court has adopted two standards of review, which I have referred to as the twin beacons of Liberty and Prosperity under the rule of law.
First, in cases involving liberty, the scales of justice have weighed heavily against government and in favor of the people, especially the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak. Laws and actions of government come to the court highly suspect in their constitutional validity, whenever they restrict the fundamental rights of our people.
Second, in cases involving prosperity and development issues, deference is accorded to the political branches of government, namely the Presidency and Congress. While cases on civil and political freedoms have highlighted the need for strict scrutiny, the High Court has adopted a deferential stance in controversies involving the merits or wisdom of economic policies.
THE RIGHT BALANCE
How to find the right balance between the two paradigms is a continuing endeavor of our courts. What is crystal-clear, though, is that both liberty and prosperity must be pursued hand in hand under the rule of law.

title: Striking the Right Balance
heading: Striking the Right Balance
text:
Striking the Right Balance (cont.)

s is a continuing endeavor of our courts. What is crystal-clear, though, is that both liberty and prosperity must be pursued hand in hand under the rule of law. Finding the right balance is indeed a country-to-country search depending on the history, culture, environment, habits and mores in each jurisdiction. This statement was proven to be a truism during the recently concluded Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity hosted by our Supreme Court on October 18-20, 2006. While there was unanimity on the need to pursue both liberty and prosperity, there was also the caveat that each country must pursue internally its own quest for its own philosophical and jurisprudential identity.
To my mind, the peculiar facts and distinct circumstances of the Philippines make the formula Liberty and Prosperity still the most viable economic and judicial philosophy here. After all, during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.
Finally, I wish the Asian constitutional courts good speed and success in finding and striking the right balance between the sometimes contending demands and jurisdictions of the state, culture and religion; and, if I may add, those of safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our peoples.
Thank you very much. Maraming salamat po.

title: Honoring the Peacemakers
heading: Honoring the Peacemakers
text:
Honoring the Peacemakers

Keynote address delivered by Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the National Conference on Court-Annexed/Referred ADR Mechanisms on November 27, 2006 at the Century Park Hotel, Vito Cruz, Manila.
---
I am pleased to meet all of you during this two-day National Conference on Court-Annexed/Referred Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) Mechanisms. I could not decline the invitation of Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, our esteemed chancellor of the Philippine Judicial Academy. Besides, I am always delighted to be in the company of peacemakers. Just looking at your radiant and smiling faces gives me the assurance that there is always a workable and satisfactory solution to any problem in the hands of able, imaginative, patient and committed mediators like you. Sabi nga ng theme ninyo, Ayusin ang Gusot, Habaan ang Pasensiya.
THREE INCIDENTS
Let me begin by relating three incidents in the life of a fictional character, whom I will call Hukom Juan Suplado. One early morning while our judge was having breakfast at home, he was visited by a lawyer. The lawyer said: Your Honor, I am not giving you the car. I am selling it to you. And how much is the car? His Honor asked. One thousand pesos. In that case, Hukom Suplado said, I will buy two!
These three apocryphal incidents in the life of Hukom Juan Suplado may be funny, but they illustrate the most common complaints against the judiciary: corruption, incompetence and delay.
ACID PROBLEMS IN THE JUDICIARY

title: Honoring the Peacemakers
heading: Honoring the Peacemakers
text:
Honoring the Peacemakers (cont.)

n Suplado may be funny, but they illustrate the most common complaints against the judiciary: corruption, incompetence and delay.
ACID PROBLEMS IN THE JUDICIARY These three problems of corruption, incompetence and delay, along with limited access to justice by the poor, have been the special focus of my chief justiceship. I referred to these problems of the judiciary as ACID: limited access to justice by the poor, corruption, incompetence, and delay in the delivery of quality justice.
THE PROBLEM OF DELAY
The significance of court-annexed or court-referred alternative dispute resolution mechanisms cannot be overemphasized in relation to the problem of delay in the delivery of quality justice. Factors behind this lingering predicament of our courts include both systemic causes arising from our adversarial system of litigation, as well as man-made causes including litigants and lawyers who misuse and abuse the Rules of Court to defeat the very objective of our legal system.
ADDRESSING DELAY THROUGH ADR
To address the problem of delay, resort to alternative dispute resolution methods such as negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration have been made over the years. The Supreme Court is actively behind efforts to institutionalize ADR mechanisms.
The Supreme Court has approved court-annexed mediation as a mandatory component of pretrial at the trial court level. It has also recently approved recourse to mediation at the level of the Court of Appeals.

title: Honoring the Peacemakers
heading: Honoring the Peacemakers
text:
Honoring the Peacemakers (cont.)

diation as a mandatory component of pretrial at the trial court level. It has also recently approved recourse to mediation at the level of the Court of Appeals. I am equally delighted that our PhilJA has also begun to study the feasibility of implementing a court-annexed arbitration. Arbitration would also be less time-consuming, less tedious, less confrontational, and more productive of goodwill and lasting relationships.
PEACEMAKERS
Most of you here are court officials and court employees who are also mediators. Your work is aptly described by the theme of this conference: Ayusin ang gusot, habaan ang pasensya. To be successful peacemakers, you must exude professionalism and practice patience. Accept the difficulty of your work and have the persistence to reach for an amicable settlement.
While the financial rewards may not be too enticing, it is the knowledge of promoting peace that will bring self-worth and true happiness. Remember that your thoughts and actions will continue to live on in the hearts and minds of those who, by your efforts, have been led back to peaceful relations with friends, neighbors, business associates, clients, or erstwhile lovers.

title: Honoring the Peacemakers
heading: Honoring the Peacemakers
text:
Honoring the Peacemakers (cont.)

ts and minds of those who, by your efforts, have been led back to peaceful relations with friends, neighbors, business associates, clients, or erstwhile lovers. I must commend Justice Amor and her office staff for their tireless efforts in advancing alternative modes of settling disputes. I also thank all mediators who have tirelessly worked for the decongestion of court dockets. I am convinced that all of you have helped my chief justiceship in addressing the problems plaguing the judiciary, particularly the D in ACID, or the fight against delay in the delivery of quality judgments.
As I close, let me remind you that the road to peace may be difficult, but you will find comfort in knowing that you are not alone in this worthwhile endeavor.
Mabuhay kayong lahat! Maraming salamat po.

title: Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda
heading: Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda
text:
Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda

Speech delivered by Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the San Beda Alumni Association Homecoming and Fellowship Night, held on November 15, 2006, at the Kalayaan Hall, Club Filipino, Greenhills, San Juan, Metro Manila.
---
At the outset, allow me to congratulate San Beda College for winning the National Collegiate Athletic Association basketball crown after 28 years. From what I hear, a San Beda basketball dynasty is in the making. That should not come as a surprise, because Bedans are said to have been dominating all kinds of courts, including our courts of law.
I thank the San Beda Law Alumni Association for inviting me to this festive gathering and for making me its honorary member. Now, I am not only a Tamaraw, I am also a Red Lion!
DISTINGUISHED BEDANS
Through the years, I have been truly blessed to have the opportunity to meet and befriend many Bedan lawyers, all brilliant and distinguished. In the National Union of Students of the Philippines in the late fifties and when I was a young lawyer in the early sixties, I met talented, up-and-coming men like Raul Roco, Rene Saguisag, Pablo Trillana, Rudy Robles, Vic de la Serna and Boy Brillantes. During my first few years in the Supreme Court, I was equally privileged to discuss and deliberate important issues and cases with Justices Florenz D. Regalado, Justo P. Torres Jr. and Antonio M. Martinez, all red-blooded Bedans.
AIMING FOR EXCELLENCE

title: Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda
heading: Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda
text:
Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda (cont.)

iberate important issues and cases with Justices Florenz D. Regalado, Justo P. Torres Jr. and Antonio M. Martinez, all red-blooded Bedans.
AIMING FOR EXCELLENCE I believe that the professional and public service milestones reached by every Bedan alumnus and alumna present here tonight reveal the seeds of the passion for excellence and the highest Christian virtues planted and nurtured by San Beda's law school.
After graduation, when we faced the real world and dealt with real-life situations, we began to understand that excellence was a value that demanded the best performance from all of us all the time. Excellence connotes not merely competence, but also dedication to duty and hard work put together.
ETHICS: SOURCE OF TRUE SUCCESS
Excellent service, however, is not enough. We must also strive to possess uncompromising personal integrity. Integrity refers not only to honesty, but also to truth. A person of integrity acts in accordance with what is true and honest regardless of personal consequences. Integrity requires the moral courage to stand for one's convictions against all odds.
FIRMLY ROOTED
The third e-value is faith in eternity as our final destiny. My wife Leni and I underwent a spiritual rebirth from 1986 to 1995 after we joined the Bukas Loob sa Diyos. During those nine years, we embarked on a journey of faith. I have learned to trust the Lord and to depend on Him for all my needs, aspirations and wants.
GOOD ROOTS, GOOD FRUITS

title: Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda
heading: Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda
text:
Magkaisa, Pamilyang San Beda (cont.)

years, we embarked on a journey of faith. I have learned to trust the Lord and to depend on Him for all my needs, aspirations and wants.
GOOD ROOTS, GOOD FRUITS To live a life mindful of these three Es is not easy. The attainment of discipline and passion must be prudently begun and continuously nurtured. In other words, for the fruit to be of good quality, the plant must be rooted well. Good roots yield good fruits.
In closing, allow me, on behalf of the Supreme Court, to acknowledge and thank San Beda for its active partnership with us in pushing for continuing reforms in the judiciary. I am particularly happy to note that the San Beda College of Law shares our vision for the improvement of legal and ethical standards, which it emphasizes just as strongly as academic excellence.
Finally, let me end with these excerpts from the various letters of St. Paul: Stand by what you have learned and what has been entrusted to you, remembering from whom you learned it. Run the great race of faith; take hold of eternal life. Let us never tire of doing good, for if we slacken not our efforts we shall in due time reap our harvest.
Ladies and gentlemen, Ut in Omnibus Glorificetur Deus — That in All Things, God May Be Glorified!
Maraming salamat po.
