title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow

Address delivered by retired Chief Justice ARTEMIO V. PANGANIBAN during the TeaM Energy Corporation's Senior Management Session held at the Shangri-la at the Fort Hotel, Taguig City on November 14, 2019.
---
President John Alcordo and esteemed members of the TeaM Energy Management Team.
A beautiful lady-tourist slipped on a ship and fell into the sea. Amid the commotion, a man dived and went on to save the woman from drowning. When the "hero" climbed aboard with all the passengers clapping, he was asked for a speech, and the first thing he said was: "All I want to know is who pushed me?"
By your laughter, you love jokes. Here's one more from Fr. Jerry Orbos. A priest said in his homily: "I have good news and bad news. The good news is that there is enough money to complete our church. The bad news is that the money is still hidden deep in your pockets."
I have also good news and bad news. The good news is that Christmas is just six weeks away and Christmas bonuses 10 times more than last year's will be granted today. The bad news is that the good news is fake news.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

at Christmas is just six weeks away and Christmas bonuses 10 times more than last year's will be granted today. The bad news is that the good news is fake news. One final joke. A naughty teenager climbed atop a very tall tree. No one, not even his father and mother, could make him come down with loud threats to spank him and to stop his school allowance. Finally, his grandfather named Mang Art, ehem, went near the tree trunk and gently told the boy something very softly. And immediately, the boy slid down. When asked to explain how he disciplined the boy, the grand pa said, "Well, I softly told him that I came with a motorized saw to cut down the tree. And immediately, he understood the risks to his limbs and life."
THREE SPEECH TOPICS
Seriously now, I thank our President John V. Alcordo for inviting me today to give my thoughts on what he called the "PESTLE (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environment)" situation of our country now and in the future. Specifically, he requested me to discuss (1) the three branches of our government; (2) the important legal/regulatory/political factors or trends TeaM Energy should consider in the next few years; and (3) in view of the end of the cooperation period, my thoughts on life after retirement.
SEPARATION OF POWERS

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

M Energy should consider in the next few years; and (3) in view of the end of the cooperation period, my thoughts on life after retirement.
SEPARATION OF POWERS On the first item, our Constitution, as you probably know, instituted the doctrine of separation of powers and the American presidential system backed-up by the corollary system of checks and balances. In this way, it recognized and hoped to avoid the evil of concentrating governmental powers in only one person or group of persons which, as world history has repeatedly demonstrated, leads to dictatorships, abuses, corruption and violations of human rights.
Thus, pursuant to this tripartite system, legislative power, or the power to enact laws, is vested in a bicameral Congress composed of (1) the House of Representatives, with 80 percent of its members elected in their respective congressional districts and 20 percent nationally chosen via the Filipino-style party-list system. All of the representatives, whether district or party-list, have a term of three years to sit for a maximum of three consecutive terms or a total of nine consecutive years, and (2) the Senate, composed of 24 members elected nationally with a term of six years each with one consecutive reelection. The term limits were conceived with the laudable aim of preventing political dynasties and lifelong addictions to political power.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

h one consecutive reelection. The term limits were conceived with the laudable aim of preventing political dynasties and lifelong addictions to political power. Executive power, or the power to execute the law, is vested by the Constitution in the President, to be elected for a term of six years without reelection. He is assisted by the Cabinet composed of department secretaries, whom he or she appoints, with the consent of the Commission on Appointments composed of 24 members of Congress, with the Senate President as chairman.
The third branch of government composed of the Supreme Court and the lower courts is vested the judicial power or the power to interpret the Constitution and the laws. They could, upon the filing of the appropriate cases, review and strike down the statutes passed by Congress as well as the executive actions of the President for being unconstitutional or for having been issued with grave abuse of discretion. This power to strike down acts committed with grave abuse of discretion is a distinct and unique power not granted to other judiciaries in the world. It was given to our judiciary to prevent the President from abusing his or her power, as President Ferdinand Marcos had done during his over two decades in office. Moreover, the Constitution did not define the meaning of "grave abuse of power." It left the definition to the Supreme Court itself. This unique anti-grave-abuse power was intended by the framers to enable the Supreme Court to stop the abuses of a corrupt and dictatorial President.
CHECKS AND BALANCES

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

ue anti-grave-abuse power was intended by the framers to enable the Supreme Court to stop the abuses of a corrupt and dictatorial President.
CHECKS AND BALANCES Under the corollary system of checks and balances, each of the three great branches of the government is granted powers to prevent the other two from abusing or exceeding their constitutionally-allocated powers.
For example, the President checks Congress by the power to veto bills that are unwise or inappropriate. Also, the President, through the Budget Secretary, may refuse to release funds allotted for the pet projects of the members of Congress. The President may check the Supreme Court by the power to appoint its members from a list of at least three nominees submitted by the Judicial and Bar Council or JBC. The problem though is that of the seven members composing the JBC, the super majority are appointed or controlled by the President. Thus, the JBC's role in checking the President becomes illusory since he names the four regular JBC members plus the Secretary of Justice, who automatically sits in the JBC as an ex-officio member. Moreover, while the JBC is required to nominate at least three persons for each vacancy, all that the President needs to do is to have his or her favorite candidate included among the nominees.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

ed to nominate at least three persons for each vacancy, all that the President needs to do is to have his or her favorite candidate included among the nominees. On the other hand, Congress may check the President (1) by its power to confirm or reject or by-pass presidential appointees, and to refrain from enacting laws – including the appropriation bills – wanted by the Chief Executive; and (2) by its investigative and oversight powers to pass upon excessive or irregular acts of executive officials. Further, it may check the President and the judiciary by its authority over the budget and by its power to impeach and remove him or her and the Supreme Court justices. However, the budgetary power is limited by the constitutional ban against the reduction of the appropriations for the judiciary to a level below the amount allocated during the prior year, and by the ban to reduce the compensation of justices and judges.
In turn, the Supreme Court, in appropriate cases, may check the President and Congress by declaring executive or legislative actions invalid or illegal or unconstitutional or gravely abusive. However, sometimes this judicial power becomes illusory when members of the Court compromise their independence and integrity by being subservient to the appointing authority.
AUTONOMOUS CONSTITUTIONAL COMMISSIONS

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

ry when members of the Court compromise their independence and integrity by being subservient to the appointing authority.
AUTONOMOUS CONSTITUTIONAL COMMISSIONS In addition to the three great and independent branches of government, the Constitution also created autonomous, non-partisan and independent offices. They are the Commission on Elections, Civil Service Commission, Commission on Audit, Office of the Ombudsman, and the Electoral Tribunals of both houses of Congress. The acts, however, of these constitutionally-created commissions are subject to a review of the judiciary in appropriate cases.
THEORY VERSUS PRACTICE
While in theory the three great branches of the government are equal, in actual fact, however, the Presidency is the most powerful because the Chief Executive is the commander-in-chief of the military and the police. And again, though theoretically, Congress has the sole power to appropriate funds for the government, such power is really limited by the authority of the President to propose the national budget before it is taken up by Congress. Moreover, the Budget Secretary who is a subordinate of the President controls the releases of the funds appropriated by law. Also, he or she has the power to veto entire laws or line items in the budget.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

ordinate of the President controls the releases of the funds appropriated by law. Also, he or she has the power to veto entire laws or line items in the budget. Truly, having control of both the sword and the purse of the government, the Presidency is really the most powerful branch. Moreover, his control is easy to wield because it is singular while the power of Congress is collegial and bicameral, while the power of the Supreme Court is likewise collegial though mercifully unicameral. Hence, being collegial, these two branches – weaker as they already are – need deliberation and majority vote before action could be made. Additionally, being a passive branch, the Supreme Court cannot act unilaterally on its own volition. It needs an appropriate petition to be able to act and decide.
Also, in the real world of politics, the House of Representatives is traditionally easy to sway in favor of the President. This had always been the case since the new Charter took effect in 1987. During elections, there may be many disparate parties vying for popular support, but after the election is over, most of the political parties and the elected members of Congress realign their political loyalties and essentially gravitate around the President.
LEGAL, REGULATORY AND POLITICAL FACTORS

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

es and the elected members of Congress realign their political loyalties and essentially gravitate around the President.
LEGAL, REGULATORY AND POLITICAL FACTORS Let me now turn to the second topic, the important legal, regulatory and political factors that can influence the future of power generation. Essentially, the energy business has been divided into three interdependent areas; namely, generation, transmission and distribution. In the past, both the law and the public focused merely on the distributors of electric energy, especially on Meralco, because they are the ones who deal directly with and bills the consumers. Lately however, the two other components, the generators and the sole transmitter – the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines – have been the subject of controversy and regulation.
Undoubtedly, however, there is a growing trend to lean towards green energy like hydro, river, ocean, geothermal, natural gas, wind, and solar. Even nuclear power has regained some momentum after billionaire Bill Gates devoted several billions dollars researching on why the Chernobyl and Fukushima nuclear plants exploded in disaster and on how to make nuclear energy safe, cheap and available 24/7, unlike wind and solar which need gigantic and expensive batteries to make them available 24/7.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

and on how to make nuclear energy safe, cheap and available 24/7, unlike wind and solar which need gigantic and expensive batteries to make them available 24/7. Anyway, whether it be green or otherwise, the Philippine need for electric power, whether for base load, mid-merit or peaking, is growing rapidly. Statistics revealed by the First Gen Corporation show that the Philippines' power demand has expanded "at a robust 5.3 percent compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) in the last 10 years on the back of the country's strong economic and population growth."
NO RETIREMENT, JUST A CHANGE OF TIRES
I now come to the third topic, what we should expect when the cooperation period ends. To begin with, TeaM Energy, I am sure, would still be around even if the Sual Plant is turned over to the government or to San Miguel. TeaM would still have interests in other generating plants like Pagbilao.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

ll be around even if the Sual Plant is turned over to the government or to San Miguel. TeaM would still have interests in other generating plants like Pagbilao. I do not know why brilliant people, like our President John who is young enough to be my grandson, are now thinking of life after the cooperation period, and even of possible retirement. By my own experience, retirement merely means a change of tires to embark on a new journey. It does not mean the end of work. I retired from law practice and from my active social and civic life in 1995 to embark on my hermetic and ascetic life at the top of the judicial Mt. Olympus as a Supreme Court member, free from the hustle and bustle of my old life in the plains. I worked day and night to write the most number of decisions, about 1,200 full length judgments during my over 11 years in the Court, aside from authoring one book of over 400 pages every year, books reporting on the accomplishment of the high court, especially as they related to me.
Indeed, I thought I would end my career with those unsolicited, heart-warming testimonials. In fact, I bought a small, 350-square-meter lot where I planned to build a small bungalow, and shopped for a two hectare farm in Tagaytay where I could grow a few plants and write my memoires. But lo, and behold, 13 years have passed since then, and my wife and I have not moved from our oversized 7-bedroom house in a 1,500 square meter lot in Makati, abandoned by our five children who have now built their own homes and who left my octogenarian wife and me alone in that rather large family home.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

ot in Makati, abandoned by our five children who have now built their own homes and who left my octogenarian wife and me alone in that rather large family home. Why have I not retired from active work? Simply because right after my judicial term ended, I have been surprisingly offered to join several big conglomerates as an Independent Director and to serve several philanthropic and charitable foundations as an officer and trustee. Yes, after my retirement from the judicial Mt. Olympus, I have been asked to join again the race in the plains below where I enjoyed once more the perks of social life. I travel abroad at least five times a year on corporate meetings and tours of my favorite places in the world from Iceland and Alaska in the North to Chile and Capetown in the South.
From that discussion on the fallacy of complete retirement from work, let me go to the macro level on what young people, like all of you, can look forward to. I think a faster-paced world awaits you because of the advent of the fifth generation technology or 5G in telecommunication which will have giant ripple effects in the life of everyone on earth. The Information Revolution has changed our lives, beginning with the founding of the Internet on October 29, 1969 at the University of California in Los Angeles, and the creation of new wealth that is sometimes invisible to the naked eye.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

of the Internet on October 29, 1969 at the University of California in Los Angeles, and the creation of new wealth that is sometimes invisible to the naked eye. But beyond the Internet and 5G will proliferate in the next five years the wonders of artificial intelligence, crypto currencies and the Internet of Things. And even beyond them also, those of you who are two generations younger than me, those who belong to Generation Z, will witness a revolution in health care that would easily make you live much longer than me, as much as 150 years, because you will have the advantage of growing your own replacement body parts through the marvels of stem cell technology and the conquest of the now-fatal diseases like cancer, heart failure, diabetes and physical disabilities. Indeed, you can grow, exchange or even trade-in spare hearts, spare limbs and spare brains.
In fact, some genetic engineers say that by 2045, death from disease will be "optional" and ageing will be reversed. Humans would no longer die from natural causes or illnesses. Advance medical knowledge will be able to eliminate dead cells from the body, repair damaged cells and regenerate new ones through stem cell replacements.

title: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
heading: Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow
text:
Our Country's PESTLE: Today and Tomorrow (cont.)

sses. Advance medical knowledge will be able to eliminate dead cells from the body, repair damaged cells and regenerate new ones through stem cell replacements. All these lead me to an old favorite joke of mine to end this talk. It is said that in the future, the brains of the dead would be sold and installed to replace those of the living. Publicly auctioned by Sotheby in London would be the preserved brains of Albert Einstein and of Alberto Estan, a Filipino who failed the bar exams three times in a row. The auction started with $1,000 dollars for Einstein's brain and $100,000 for Estan, the bar flunker. When a bidder asked why Einstein's brain was much cheaper than the Estan's, the auctioneer curtly replied: "Einstein's brain is already overused while the bar flunker's brain is almost new and underused."
Thank you, ladies and gentlemen. May we all have underused brains so our heirs may inherit them and fill them up with wit and wisdom we missed in our own carefree lives listening to irreverent speeches and corny jokes like mine.
Mabuhay!

title: Respect for the Chinese Judiciary
heading: Respect for the Chinese Judiciary
text:
Respect for the Chinese Judiciary

Remarks delivered by retired Chief Justice ARTEMIO V. PANGANIBAN during the Testimonial Dinner in honor of Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines LIU JIANCHAO hosted by Dr. and Mrs. George S. K. Ty at the GT Tower on December 15, 2011.
---
During the last 20 years, I have toured at least 20 cities in China. One of the most memorable of them were two trips hosted by President Xiao Yang of the Supreme Peoples Court when I visited not only Beijing, Shanghai, Wuhan and Chongquing but also the Three Gorges Dam, the largest hydro-power project in the world.
Chief Justice Xiao, now also retired like me, whom I consider a close friend and who has visited our country twice at my invitation, showed not just the many interesting Chinese tourist spots but likewise the different judicial courts of China. The Chinese judicial system may be different from ours but it works well and renders justice in accordance with Chinese laws, traditions and history. The Philippine judicial system, which is patterned after that of the United States, may be different from yours. But our people definitely respect and accept the Chinese courts' ability to render justice fairly and objectively.
That we respect the Chinese judicial system is shown by our peoples' acceptance of the judgments rendered by the Supreme Peoples Court convicting and executing some Filipinos for drug offenses. While there were requests for clemency or postponement of the death sentences, our people nonetheless accepted the judgments rendered and executions undertaken by the Chinese authorities.

title: Respect for the Chinese Judiciary
heading: Respect for the Chinese Judiciary
text:
Respect for the Chinese Judiciary (cont.)

or clemency or postponement of the death sentences, our people nonetheless accepted the judgments rendered and executions undertaken by the Chinese authorities. Compare this with the howling, demonstrations and rallies undertaken when Filipinos were convicted and sentenced to death in some other countries. In one instance many years ago, the protests were so virulent that at least two Cabinet members, the secretary of foreign affairs and the secretary of labor, had to resign from their posts to own the responsibility for these death judgments imposed by the foreign tribunals.
In stark contrast, our people accepted and respected the judgments rendered by the Supreme Peoples Court of China. This, I think, is a testament to the close friendly relations between our two countries and peoples, made possible no doubt by the outstanding work of diplomats, like Ambassador Liu.
Mr. Ambassador, I know that you have many achievements in fostering the close and enduring friendship between our two countries. But as a retired Chief Justice of my country, may I salute you in particular for your silent work in earning the admiration and esteem of our people leading to their respect and acceptance of the Chinese judicial system and the final judgments of the Supreme Peoples Court, even if such judgments may have meant the loss of life of fellow Filipinos.

of the Chinese judicial system and the final judgments of the Supreme Peoples Court, even if such judgments may have meant the loss of life of fellow Filipinos. Your Excellency, thank you for your outstanding service in promoting close ties between the Philippines and China. We will certainly lose a great friend but we wish you success in your new post. On a personal level, I will miss you not only in the official diplomatic circles but also in the green links of the Manila Golf Club where I see you tee off in the very early mornings before you begin your official work. title: Automation or Confusion
heading: Automation or Confusion
text:
Automation or Confusion

Outline of the extemporaneous talk delivered by retired Chief Justice ARTEMIO V. PANGANIBAN as Guest of Honor and Speaker during the Makati Business Club meeting, April 20, 2010, Rigodon Ballroom, Peninsula Hotel.
---
DESIDERATA
To have a credible and democratic turnover of power via HOPE: Honest, Orderly and Peaceful Elections, if possible, automated.
REALITY
Automation has many problems: limited time, defective automation system, lack of transparency, spotty Comelec preparations, inadequate testing of PCOS, and inadequate orientation of teachers and voters.
FUNDAMENTALS OF AUTOMATION
Precinct-specific ballots; precinct-specific PCOS machines; automated counting at precincts; automated transmission of results; proclamation based on automated results.
SOME AUTOMATION PROBLEMS
PCOS or ballots are misdelivered; PCOS fail to function at the precincts; PCOS are stolen, disabled or burned; ballots are erroneously printed; election results are transmitted wrongly; massive disenfranchisements due to long queues.
If the foregoing problems happen only in a few towns, the problems would be localized. But if they occur in too many places and involve more ballots than the margin of the leading presidential candidate over the next, no one would be proclaimed winner.
POSSIBLE LEGAL CONSEQUENCES
Failure of elections: when no election is actually held. Failure of proclamation: when no clear winner. Massive disenfranchisement. Massive electoral fraud: retail and wholesale.
POSSIBLE POLITICAL CONSEQUENCES

title: Automation or Confusion
heading: Automation or Confusion
text:
Automation or Confusion (cont.)

held. Failure of proclamation: when no clear winner. Massive disenfranchisement. Massive electoral fraud: retail and wholesale.
POSSIBLE POLITICAL CONSEQUENCES Presidential Succession by July 1, 2010: Vice President, Senate President, Speaker. GMA Holdover: not expressly provided by the Constitution but supported by jurisprudence, the latest of which is Seneres vs Comelec (April 16, 2009).
BRAINS AND BRAWNS
Necessary Elements for GMA's holdover: Supreme Court; Armed Forces; Philippine National Police; Filipino people including Church, INC, and People Organizations; and the International Community, especially the US, to prop up the economy.
WAYS TO AVOID HOLDOVER OR MILITARY RULE
Overwhelming victory by the presidential winner; overwhelming victory and proclamation of the VP winner; vigilance before, during and after election day.
TIMING PROBLEMS
From Election Day, May 10, 2010, to the end of GMA's term on June 30, 2010 is 61 days. Many things can happen during that period.
NOTES

text:
Automation or Confusion (cont.)

ion day.
TIMING PROBLEMS
From Election Day, May 10, 2010, to the end of GMA's term on June 30, 2010 is 61 days. Many things can happen during that period.
NOTES Failure of Elections is distinguished from Failure of Proclamation. Congress, not Comelec, canvasses and proclaims newly elected President and Vice President, to be started no later than 30 days after Election Day. In case of a tie, one shall be chosen by the vote of a majority of all the Members of Congress (Art. VII, Sec. 4). Presidential Succession: if a President shall not have been chosen, the VP-elect shall act as President until a President shall have been chosen and qualified. Where no President and Vice President shall have been chosen or qualified, the President of the Senate, or in case of his inability, the Speaker of the House of Representatives shall act as President until a President or a Vice President shall have been chosen and qualified (Art. VII, Sec. 7).

title: After the Last SONA, GMA's Options
heading: After the Last SONA, GMA's Options
text:
After the Last SONA, GMA's Options

Outline of the extemporaneous talk delivered by retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban during the Inquirer Briefing on July 30, 2009 at the Philippine Daily Inquirer Multi-Purpose Hall, Makati City.
---
1. Prepare to step down from power
Exit gracefully, name transition team and relish legacy. Some SONA bites: The state of our nation is a strong economy. Our reforms gave us the resources to protect our people, our financial system and our economy from the worst of shocks. Since 2001 our economy posted uninterrupted growth for 33 quarters; more than double its size from $76 billion to $186 billion. The average GDP growth from 2001 to the first quarter of 2009 is the highest in 43 years. I never expressed the desire to extend myself beyond my term. I accepted the invitation of President Obama to be the first Southeast Asian leader to meet him at the White House later this week.
Assure a credible 2010 election. Protect her back; strengthen hold on the House of Representatives, Supreme Court and Sandiganbayan, Ombudsman, Commission on Elections, and Military. Choose a viable presidential candidate who would shield her; run for vice-president and team up with Noli or Erap; run for a congressional seat in Pampanga.
2. Extend reign as President/Prime Minister
Charter change via peoples initiative for simple amendments only, not complicated revisions; or via constituent assembly requiring a three-fourths vote of all members of Congress; or via constitutional convention, with no more time before elections.

title: After the Last SONA, GMA's Options
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Published July 30, 2009 as a policy analysis of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's options after her last SONA (July 27, 2009), this document by CJP presents three tracks. Option 1 -- Step down: exit gracefully with a legacy narrative (strong economy, 33-quarter uninterrupted growth, GDP doubled from $76B to $186B, 'highest average GDP growth in 43 years,' imminent White House visit as first Southeast Asian leader to meet Obama); protect institutional back (House, SC, Sandiganbayan, Ombudsman, Comelec, Military); choose a viable presidential candidate or run for VP (with Noli or Erap) or for a Pampanga congressional seat. Option 2 -- Extend reign as PM/President: (a) Cha-cha via people's initiative (for simple amendments only, not revisions), constituent assembly (three-fourths of all Congress), or con-con (no more time before elections); (b) martial law (only for invasion/rebellion; 60 days only; Congress can revoke; SC reviews factual basis within 30 days); (c) emergency rule -- 'no constitutional authority; no international backing; our people will rebel against it; even the military may not support it'; (d) holdover -- 'not expressly provided by the Constitution but supported by jurisprudence.' Option 3 -- Preventions: HOPE elections; vigilant people and media; People Power; CBCP; Twitter revolt; full-scale revolution. (Note: this is a companion to SE103's Automation or Confusion analysis from April 2010.)

title: PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn
heading: PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn
text:
PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn

At dawn on January 20, 2001, the Philippines was no longer governed by certainty.
The night had ended, but the morning refused to arrive cleanly. Manila stirred under a low sky, its streets restless with rumor and anger. Barricades stood at Mendiola. Protesters clustered like unsettled weather. Somewhere between the palace and the people, authority had fractured.
Government, that great machinery of order, had stalled.
Inside this moment — before the oath, before the headlines, before history hardened into verdict — **Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr.** prayed.
He was not a man drawn to drama. He did not court crisis or relish the spotlight of emergency. He had spent his life inside institutions, not outside them — believing, stubbornly, that constitutions mattered even when crowds did not.
But now the Constitution itself trembled.
Joseph Estrada was still, technically, President. Gloria Macapagal Arroyo was Vice President — unable to act while legality remained unresolved. The military watched. The streets waited. A coup was imaginable. Bloodshed was possible. Silence was dangerous.
In the quiet hours before noon, Art reached a conclusion that would follow him for the rest of his life.
If the law waited, chaos would arrive first.
And so, at approximately 5:30 in the morning, he made a call — not as a politician, not as a strategist, but as a jurist confronting the edge of collapse. He called the Chief Justice and proposed something radical in its simplicity: swear her in.
Do it now.
Do it lawfully.
Do it before the Republic fractures beyond repair.

title: PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn
heading: PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn
text:
PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn (cont.)

the Chief Justice and proposed something radical in its simplicity: swear her in.
Do it now.
Do it lawfully.
Do it before the Republic fractures beyond repair. That call — invisible to the crowd, absent from photographs — would become one of the most consequential acts of judgment in modern Philippine history.
To understand how a man could make such a decision, one must return not to the Supreme Court, but to a sidewalk in Sampaloc — where a boy once learned that survival itself requires discipline, and that order, when absent, must be built by hand.

title: PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn
heading: Summary
text:

Art Panganiban Jr., characterized as a jurist who had spent his life inside institutions believing 'stubbornly that constitutions mattered even when crowds did not,' reaches the conclusion that 'if the law waited, chaos would arrive first.' At approximately 5:30 AM he places the call to the Chief Justice with three imperatives -- 'swear her in. Do it now. Do it lawfully. Do it before the Republic fractures beyond repair' -- a call described as 'invisible to the crowd, absent from photographs' yet 'one of the most consequential acts of judgment in modern Philippine history.' The chapter closes with a narrative pivot: to understand how a man could make such a decision, one must return not to the Supreme Court but to a sidewalk in Sampaloc, where a boy once learned that survival itself requires discipline, and that order, when absent, must be built by hand.

title: The Boy Who Slept on Pavement
heading: The Boy Who Slept on Pavement
text:
The Boy Who Slept on Pavement

Sampaloc did not produce future Chief Justices.
It produced workers. Survivors. Children who learned early that hunger was not an event but a condition.
In a cramped rented apartment on Cataluña Street, the youngest of four children grew up listening to adult conversations about money that never stretched far enough. His father, Artemio Sr., had left school early to support seven younger siblings after the death of his own father. His mother, Patricia Villaseñor, had little formal education but possessed the quiet endurance common to women who carry families through scarcity.
For the youngest son, childhood ended early.
He sold newspapers before dawn. He sold cigarettes during the day. He learned which streets produced buyers and which produced trouble. Some nights, it made no sense to go home. He slept on sidewalks — not from neglect, but from calculation. The papers arrived early. He needed to be there first.
Years later, he would recall those nights without sentimentality. He remembered the cold stone beneath his back. The envy he refused to indulge when he imagined classmates sleeping in beds. He remembered telling himself, again and again, that this was temporary — that discipline would outlast deprivation.
It was here, long before law books or Latin maxims, that Art learned his first philosophy: endure first, explain later.

title: The Boy Who Slept on Pavement
heading: The Boy Who Slept on Pavement
text:
The Boy Who Slept on Pavement (cont.)

at discipline would outlast deprivation.
It was here, long before law books or Latin maxims, that Art learned his first philosophy: endure first, explain later. School became refuge. He studied not because teachers praised him, but because excellence was the only escape route he could see. He graduated with honors from public schools — Juan Luna Elementary, Victorino Mapa High — rising in crowded classrooms where obscurity was the default fate.
When he was accepted to the University of the Philippines on scholarship, it seemed that fate had finally cracked open.
Then came the bus fare.
Fifteen centavos.
That was the distance between Sampaloc and Diliman — between promise and possibility.
He never complained. He simply walked to Far Eastern University instead.

The boy sold newspapers before dawn and cigarettes during the day, sleeping on sidewalks not from neglect but from calculation (the papers arrived early), recalling those nights later 'without sentimentality' -- 'the cold stone beneath his back' and 'the envy he refused to indulge' when he imagined classmates sleeping in beds. Here, 'long before law books or Latin maxims,' he learned his first philosophy: endure first, explain later. School became refuge -- he graduated with honors from Juan Luna Elementary and Victorino Mapa High, then was accepted to UP on scholarship, only to be foreclosed by a fifteen-centavo bus fare that was 'the distance between Sampaloc and Diliman, between promise and possibility.' He never complained -- he simply walked to Far Eastern University instead.

title: FEU and the Construction of Ambition
heading: FEU and the Construction of Ambition
text:
FEU and the Construction of Ambition

Far Eastern University was not his second choice.
It became his proving ground.
He walked into FEU carrying more than notebooks. He carried urgency. He studied as if time itself were rationed. He graduated summa cum laude in pre-law, cum laude in law, and in 1959 was named the Most Outstanding Student of the entire university.
Yet the transformation was not merely academic.
He entered FEU with almost no understanding of faith. Catholic by baptism, secular by upbringing, he once failed a scholarship interview because he could not name the persons of the Trinity. It would later become one of his favorite stories — told not for humor, but as testimony.
At FEU, faith arrived quietly.
A chaplain noticed the disciplined student. A priest invited him to Student Catholic Action. Another insisted that integrity was not enough — leadership required moral responsibility for others. Slowly, a boy raised without catechism began to read Scripture not as doctrine, but as instruction.
Leadership followed.
He became president of the FEU Central Student Organization — the youngest ever elected. He co-founded the National Union of Students of the Philippines, discovering that influence required listening as much as command. In student assemblies, he learned how ideals fracture under pressure — and how institutions survive compromise without surrender.
It was also here that he met Elenita Carpio.

title: FEU and the Construction of Ambition
heading: FEU and the Construction of Ambition
text:
FEU and the Construction of Ambition (cont.)

emblies, he learned how ideals fracture under pressure — and how institutions survive compromise without surrender.
It was also here that he met Elenita Carpio. She was thoughtful, precise, intellectually formidable. Where he was urgency, she was balance. Where he pushed, she measured. Their partnership would anchor him through decades of ambition and uncertainty.
But before life offered stability, it would test resolve.

title: The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain
heading: The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain
text:
The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain

In **1960**, as bar candidates across the country arranged their schedules, sharpened their pencils, and rehearsed doctrines late into the night, Art lay flat on a **hospital bed**.
The timing could not have been worse.
The Philippine Bar Examination was not merely an academic hurdle; it was a rite of passage that determined whether years of sacrifice would harden into profession or dissolve into regret. For many, it was the most demanding intellectual trial of their young lives. For Art, it arrived when his body had begun to fail him.
Fever drained his strength. His head throbbed. His limbs felt heavy, unresponsive. Doctors advised rest. Friends urged caution. The sensible choice — the rational choice — was withdrawal. There would be other years, they said. Better to recover fully than to risk collapse.
But withdrawal carried its own cost.
It meant postponement without guarantee. It meant prolonging dependency. It meant risking the erosion of momentum he had fought so hard to build. And, perhaps most painfully, it meant conceding that circumstance — not discipline — would dictate his limits.
Then his dean arrived.
**Jovito R. Salonga**, himself already a figure of moral and intellectual authority, looked at the weakened young man and said words that would lodge permanently in Art’s memory:
“Do not quit.”
There was no lecture. No pep talk. Just conviction.
Salonga understood something essential about the student before him: that quitting now would wound him more deeply than any physical strain. That endurance, once surrendered, is difficult to reclaim.

title: The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain
heading: The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain
text:
The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain (cont.)

about the student before him: that quitting now would wound him more deeply than any physical strain. That endurance, once surrendered, is difficult to reclaim. So, Art rose from the hospital bed and entered the examination hall.
For **four relentless weeks**, he endured the bar examinations while ill. Each day demanded sustained concentration — hours of legal reasoning, careful writing, precision under pressure. The questions were unforgiving. The days were long. The nights offered little relief. His body weakened even as his mind was forced into sustained clarity.
It was an ordeal of balance: pushing hard enough to perform, but not so hard as to collapse.
He finished not with exhilaration, but with exhaustion.
When the results were released, his name appeared among the top ten — **sixth overall**, with a rating of **89.55 percent**.
There was satisfaction, yes — but not celebration.
What marked the moment most deeply was not triumph, but **confirmation**. Proof that pressure did not fracture him. Proof that adversity, when met with discipline, could be absorbed rather than feared. Proof that he could endure without compromise.
It would become a defining trait — one that would surface again and again in courtrooms, committees, crises, and moments when retreat would have been easier than resolve.
Yet even as congratulations arrived and professional doors seemed poised to open, opportunity once again revealed its conditional nature.

heading: The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain
text:
The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain (cont.)

n easier than resolve.
Yet even as congratulations arrived and professional doors seemed poised to open, opportunity once again revealed its conditional nature. A scholarship awaited him at **Yale** — a chance to pursue graduate legal studies at one of the world’s most storied institutions. It was the culmination of academic excellence, the validation of promise.
But validation did not pay for passage.
He applied for financial assistance. He sought a travel grant. He waited.
The answer came back: **denied**.
Without funds for airfare, the scholarship became an abstraction. The door closed — not dramatically, not cruelly, but decisively.
Years later, Art would say this was the moment when the world seemed to collapse around him.
He had done everything right. He had endured illness, excelled under pressure, earned distinction. And still, the horizon withdrew just as he approached it.
The disappointment was profound.
But it was not terminal.
In time, he would come to see this denial not as an ending, but as a redirection — one that forced him inward, toward mentorship instead of credentials; toward institution-building instead of personal advancement; toward a path that would ultimately carry him farther than Yale ever could.
The world had not closed.
It had simply asked him to enter through a different door.

title: The Mentor and the Moral Spine
heading: The Mentor and the Moral Spine
text:
The Mentor and the Moral Spine

The Yale scholarship that never materialized became, in retrospect, one of the most formative disappointments of Art’s life.
He had wanted it badly. Not for prestige — but for completion. He sensed, even then, that law was not merely a profession but a calling that demanded the sharpest tools available. Yale represented the pinnacle.
But money intervened, as it had before.
When the travel grant was denied, frustration gave way to something darker: the feeling that no matter how hard he worked, the ceiling might always descend just before he reached it.
It was at this juncture that **Jovito R. Salonga** stepped fully into his life — not merely as a former dean, but as a moral architect.
Salonga had walked the path Art dreamed of. He had studied at UP, Harvard, and Yale. He had absorbed not only legal technique but the ethical traditions of Western jurisprudence. When Yale became unreachable for his young protégé, Salonga made a quiet offer that would change everything:
*If you cannot go to Yale, Yale will come to you.*
At **Salonga, Ordoñez and Associates**, where Art apprenticed from 1961 to 1963, law was not practiced as transaction. It was practiced as **responsibility**. Cases were dissected for principle as much as outcome. Victory without integrity was considered failure. Political expediency was distrusted. Conscience mattered.
Here, Art learned something more valuable than advanced degrees: **judgment**.

title: The Mentor and the Moral Spine
heading: The Mentor and the Moral Spine
text:
The Mentor and the Moral Spine (cont.)

was considered failure. Political expediency was distrusted. Conscience mattered.
Here, Art learned something more valuable than advanced degrees: **judgment**. Salonga introduced him to a lineage of Filipino legal giants — **Jose W. Diokno**, whose human rights advocacy would become legend; **Claudio O. Teehankee**, whose judicial courage would later define an era. These were not men who merely interpreted law. They *embodied* it.
Art absorbed their example with reverence. He learned that law divorced from morality becomes tyranny by another name. That judges must sometimes stand alone — and accept isolation as the cost of fidelity.
This apprenticeship forged his moral spine.
When he left to establish his own firm in 1963 — **PABLAW** — he carried with him not only legal competence, but a philosophy: **success must never outpace conscience**.

title: Independence by Design
heading: Independence by Design
text:
Independence by Design

Art did not rush into government service.
Offers came early — invitations to become a judge, to join Malacañang as a technical assistant. He declined them all.
The reasons were not ideological. They were practical, even parental.
Public service did not pay enough to shield his family from the kind of insecurity he had known as a child. He was determined that his children would never sleep on pavements — metaphorical or otherwise.
So, he built independence first.
PABLAW grew steadily. He became a respected practicing lawyer, then a senior partner. Teaching followed — at Far Eastern University, Assumption Convent, San Sebastian College. His classrooms were demanding. He insisted on clarity, precision, and ethical reasoning. Law, he told students, was not about cleverness. It was about **trust**.
Beyond the courtroom and classroom, he ventured into business — not for opulence, but for autonomy.
He founded **Baron Travel Corporation** in 1967, then **Arpan Tourism Industries Corporation** in 1974. What began as pragmatic entrepreneurship evolved into leadership at scale. He would eventually lead the Philippine Society of Travel Agents, the Tourism Organization of the Philippines, and even the global **American Society of Travel Agents**, becoming the first Asian to chair it internationally.
This mattered.
By the time he reached his forties, Art had achieved something rare: **freedom from political dependency**. He owed no patron his livelihood. He could say no — and often did.

title: Independence by Design
heading: Independence by Design
text:
Independence by Design (cont.)

reached his forties, Art had achieved something rare: **freedom from political dependency**. He owed no patron his livelihood. He could say no — and often did. He also achieved something quieter but more enduring: the restoration of a childhood dream. The boy who once slept on sidewalks waiting for newspapers now ran travel companies that took him — and later his children — across the world. The Yale degree he never earned would, in time, be eclipsed by something more personal: five children who would graduate from Harvard, Stanford, Chicago, Michigan, and Berkeley.
Scarcity had been defeated — not by luck, but by architecture.

title: Faith Finds Its Voice
heading: Faith Finds Its Voice
text:
Faith Finds Its Voice

For many men of ambition, faith is an accessory — useful in ceremony, silent in decision.

For Art, faith arrived late — and then refused to stay quiet.

His early encounters at FEU had planted questions. Years of reading, listening, and reflection followed. But it was only in the mid-1980s, when he and his wife **Elenita** joined **Bukas Loob sa Diyos (BLD)**, that faith ceased to be theoretical.

BLD demanded vulnerability. It asked professionals to pray aloud, to confess uncertainty, to submit ambition to discernment. It was not comfortable — which is precisely why it reshaped him.

He became a servant leader. A marriage encounter facilitator. A speaker in Life in the Spirit seminars. He read Scripture not as metaphor but as instruction. Leadership, he began to believe, was not granted by election alone — it was **discerned**.

Faith soon pulled him into national service.

He became secretary of the **Council of the Laity of the Philippines**, a delegate to the **Second Plenary Council of the Philippines**, and later — improbably — the **only Filipino appointed by Pope John Paul II** to the **Pontifical Council for the Laity**.

The irony was not lost on him.

The boy who once could not name the Trinity now advised the Vatican on the life of the faithful.

Faith had not replaced law in his life. It had **disciplined** it.

title: Rotary, Earthquake, and the Test of Leadership
heading: Rotary, Earthquake, and the Test of Leadership
text:
Rotary, Earthquake, and the Test of Leadership

In **1990**, Art found himself standing at the threshold of an institution older than the Republic he would one day help steady.
The **Rotary Club of Manila** — the first Rotary club in Asia and among the most influential civic organizations in the Philippines — was not merely a luncheon forum or a professional network. It was a proving ground for leadership, a gathering of Cabinet secretaries and jurists, captains of industry and ambassadors, physicians, educators, and public servants whose conversations often spilled beyond the ballroom and into the national bloodstream.
Its presidency was not sought. It was **conferred**.
Rotary tradition in Manila did not reward ambition. It elevated those who topped the open election for the Board of Directors, an arrangement that made the presidency both inevitable and inescapable. When Art emerged with the highest number of votes, the path ahead was clear — even if he did not wish to walk it.
His first instinct was refusal.
The presidency demanded near-total commitment. Former presidents had taken leaves of absence from their professions to serve properly. Art, at the time, was deeply embedded in multiple worlds: a flourishing law practice, expanding business interests, a growing family, and an intense commitment to **Bukas Loob sa Diyos (BLD)**, where he and his wife were entrusted with leadership roles that required spiritual, emotional, and logistical labor.
This was not a role that could be added casually to an already full life.
And so, he did what had become his reflex in moments of consequence: **he prayed**.

title: LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN.
heading: LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN.
text:
LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN.

The reaction was immediate — and fierce.
Rotarians were aghast. Religion, they warned, had no place in a civic institution built on pluralism and neutrality. The credo was divisive. Unprecedented. Risky. Some feared it would alienate non-Christian members. Others worried it would reduce Rotary’s work to moral exhibitionism.
No one could recall a Rotary president anywhere who had framed his term so explicitly in theological language.
Art listened patiently. He explained calmly. He did not retreat.
He argued that Rotary’s foundational maxims — *Service Above Self*, *He Profits Most Who Serves Best* — were not merely civic slogans but moral truths, deeply consonant with the commandment to love one’s neighbor. His credo, he insisted, was not an imposition of belief but a **clarification of purpose**.
Faith, for him, was not sectarian. It was catalytic.
On **July 12, 1990**, he was inaugurated. He distributed a **76-page Program of Action**, unprecedented in the Club’s history — detailing **178 projects**, a calendar of execution, and a proposed budget of **₱90 million**, an amount that dwarfed anything the Club had attempted before.
Skepticism followed him into the ballroom.
Then, four days later, the earth itself intervened.
On **July 16, 1990**, a **7.7-magnitude earthquake** tore through **Luzon**, flattening communities, burying buildings, and killing more than two thousand people. Baguio lay in ruins. Panic spread faster than information. Suffering arrived before response.
At the next Rotary meeting, there was no prepared speech.

title: LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN.
heading: LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN.
text:
LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN. (cont.)

people. Baguio lay in ruins. Panic spread faster than information. Suffering arrived before response.
At the next Rotary meeting, there was no prepared speech. Art stood and made an appeal — not for ceremony, not for recognition, but for immediate action. He asked the Club to help the poor, the injured, the displaced — the least visible victims of a catastrophe too vast for any one institution to manage.
What followed stunned even him.
Within **thirty minutes**, pledges reached **₱5.5 million**. By the next day, contributions exceeded expectations many times over. Doctors volunteered their services. Businessmen redirected resources. Rotary Anns mobilized clothing and food. A **tent city** rose in **Burnham Park**, sheltering hundreds of families.
Rotary clubs abroad responded as well. The **Rotary Club of Waikiki** organized a massive airlift — over **3,300 kilograms** of relief goods flown in from Hawaii.
This was not charity as gesture.
It was compassion as mobilization.
Standing amid the whirlwind of response, Art understood something fundamental about leadership. Conviction, when aligned with compassion, could move institutions faster than policy, more decisively than procedure, and more enduringly than rhetoric.
His credo had been tested — not in theory, but in catastrophe.
And it had held.
For the first time, he allowed himself to believe that faith, when married to action, was not divisive at all.
It was transformative.

title: The Reckoning of a Year -- and the Quiet Accumulation of Trust
heading: The Reckoning of a Year -- and the Quiet Accumulation of Trust
text:
The Reckoning of a Year -- and the Quiet Accumulation of Trust

When **June 1991** arrived, Art did not speak of legacy. He spoke of **accounting**.
True to his nature, he refused to let the Rotary presidency dissolve into memory without measurement. At his valedictory meeting, he distributed a **94-page Final Report** — a document unprecedented in the history of the **Rotary Club of Manila**. It was exhaustive, almost severe in its precision. Numbers were tallied. Projects itemized. Outcomes measured against promises.
Of the **178 projects** pledged at the start of his term, **185 had been implemented**. Of the **₱90 million** budget once deemed unrealistic, nearly all had been responsibly deployed. Committees had multiplied. Attendance had deepened. Service had expanded beyond rhetoric into reach.
But what mattered most was not arithmetic.
It was **credibility**.
For the first time in years, Manila Rotary was being spoken of not merely as influential, but as **effective**. Not merely prestigious, but **purposeful**. The Club had rediscovered its moral center without sacrificing its civic breadth.
Art did not claim credit.
Instead, he offered confession.
In his closing address, he described himself not as a successful leader, but as an **unworthy servant**, sustained not by talent alone but by grace. It was an unsettling posture for an audience accustomed to triumphal retrospectives. Yet it resonated. His humility did not diminish his authority — it clarified it.
Something had shifted.

Something had shifted. Men who had once regarded him as a capable lawyer now saw him as a **trusted steward**. Business leaders observed how he balanced vision with discipline. Clergy took note of a layman who understood that faith, to be credible, must translate into service. Public officials — watchful, pragmatic — recognized in him a rare combination: decisiveness without arrogance, conviction without cruelty.
He had passed a test few recognized at the time.
Not of popularity, but of **governance**.

title: From Civic Leadership to National Visibility
heading: From Civic Leadership to National Visibility
text:
From Civic Leadership to National Visibility

In the years that followed, Art did not announce ambition.

He returned quietly to his law practice, his businesses, his writing, his work in Catholic lay movements. Yet invitations began arriving — first sporadically, then persistently. He was asked to chair awards committees, to mediate disputes, to speak on governance, ethics, and the rule of law.

He became **Chief Legal Counsel of the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV)** — a role that placed him near the moral fault lines of Philippine democracy. He advised without theatrics. He guarded credibility as fiercely as outcomes.

During elections, when passions flared and accusations multiplied, he insisted on process. When activists demanded instant righteousness, he cautioned patience. When institutions faltered, he argued not for replacement — but for reform.

This was not the language of partisanship.

It was the language of **institutional preservation**.

Presidents noticed.

title: The Call from Malacañang -- and the First Refusal
heading: The Call from Malacañang -- and the First Refusal
text:
The Call from Malacañang -- and the First Refusal

By **1992**, the country stood again at a turning point. A new administration was taking shape. The wounds of authoritarianism had not fully healed; democratic institutions remained fragile, distrusted, incomplete.

President-elect **Fidel V. Ramos** summoned Art for a private meeting.

The offer was direct: **Secretary of Justice**.

It was the kind of appointment that would have thrilled many. For Art, it triggered caution. He had not campaigned. He had not sought office. More importantly, he sensed that politics — even in reformist guise — would exact a cost his family and conscience might not be prepared to pay.

He declined.

Ramos pressed him. Not with flattery, but with reasoning. He spoke of trust. Of observed competence. Of Rotary. Of PPCRV. Of a country that needed steady hands more than loud voices.

Still, Art hesitated.

Then came the alternative.

“If not the Cabinet,” Ramos said, “then the **Supreme Court**.”

It was not a consolation prize.

It was a summons.

title: Seven Rejections
heading: Seven Rejections
text:
Seven Rejections

By the early 1990s, Art had done everything one was supposed to do before entering public service.
He had built professional independence.
He had raised his children into academic excellence.
He had led civic institutions without scandal.
He had deepened his faith into discipline.
When the call to serve finally came, it did not come gently.
It came with rejection.
From **1992 to 1995**, vacancies opened repeatedly in the Supreme Court. Each time, Art’s name was submitted to the **Judicial and Bar Council**. Each time, it was scrutinized. Each time, it was questioned. And each time, it was passed over.
Seven times.
Objections arose from the past — some vague, some petty, some resurrected from decades-old client dissatisfaction. A former case was reexamined. An old grievance was amplified. Others were deemed “more qualified,” usually because they had climbed the judicial hierarchy instead of practicing law.
Each rejection landed heavily.
Art was not naïve. He understood institutional caution. But the cumulative effect was corrosive. Each screening became a public exposure. Each delay, a whisper of doubt. Each rejection, a silent question: *Was this calling real—or self-invented?*
At night, he prayed with increasing urgency.
“How long, O Lord?”
“Why humiliation if the path is Yours?”
“Why surrender ambition only to be tested again?”
The law had taught him patience. Faith demanded more.
In **January 1995**, after the seventh rejection, something broke — and something else was born.
He surrendered completely.
He prayed not for appointment, but for removal of desire.

Seven Rejections (cont.)

He surrendered completely.
He prayed not for appointment, but for removal of desire. “Take all that I am,” he offered.
“My career. My ambition. My will.”
“Do what You want.”
For the first time in years, he stopped hoping.

title: Ask. Seek. Knock.
heading: Ask. Seek. Knock.
text:
Ask. Seek. Knock.

In **July 1995**, when Art had finally convinced himself that the chapter was closed, the past returned quietly—almost apologetically.
A friend from the **Supreme Court** approached him without ceremony, without persuasion, without the urgency that usually accompanies opportunity. It was said almost in passing, as if testing the air.
“Why don’t you try again?” the justice asked.
“There won’t be another vacancy for years.”
The words were simple. The effect was not.
Art dismissed the suggestion almost immediately. He had already surrendered. Months earlier, after seven humiliating rejections by the Judicial and Bar Council, he had made peace with what he believed was God’s answer. He had prayed not for appointment, but for detachment. He had offered up the ambition itself, believing that obedience meant letting go.
To hope again felt like disobedience.
To apply again felt like pride disguised as perseverance.
And yet — the words lingered.
They followed him home. They surfaced in the quiet between conversations. They returned in moments of stillness, unwelcome and unresolved. He could not tell whether they were temptation or invitation.
On the night of **July 29, 1995**, sleep refused him.
Past midnight, he lay awake, staring into the darkness, rehearsing the same question over and over—not aloud, but with the intensity of a cross-examination.
Was he clinging to ambition?
Or resisting obedience?
He rose and prayed. Not briefly. Not casually. For hours.

title: Ask. Seek. Knock.
heading: Ask. Seek. Knock.
text:
Ask. Seek. Knock. (cont.)

Was he clinging to ambition?
Or resisting obedience?
He rose and prayed. Not briefly. Not casually. For hours. He did not ask to be appointed. He did not ask to be vindicated. He asked only for clarity—for the grace to know whether persistence would be faithfulness or defiance. He told God that he had already surrendered the dream. Why, then, would it not leave him alone?
Near dawn, exhausted, unanswered, he slept.
The following morning, **Sunday**, he served as a **Special Minister of Holy Communion**, as he had done many times before. The ritual was familiar. The church was quiet. His role was routine.
Then the Gospel was read.
From **Luke**:
*Ask and you shall receive.*
*Seek and you shall find.*
*Knock and the door shall be opened to you.*
The effect was immediate and physical.
His skin prickled. Cold sweat gathered at his temples. Gooseflesh rose along his arms. The words did not sound ancient; they sounded personal—uncomfortably so.
He whispered inwardly, almost in protest:
“My Lord, is this meant for me?”
But discipline had taught him caution. He had spent too many years in law to trust first impressions, even spiritual ones. He feared mistaking desire for discernment.
That day, he prayed again.
“If this is truly Your will,” he asked quietly, “give me another sign. One more. I do not want to be deceived by my own longing.”
One week later, in the same church, with the same priest, the Gospel was read again—this time the account of the **Transfiguration**.
*A cloud came and overshadowed them… and a voice said:*

*Listen to Him.*
**Listen.**
The word struck him harder than the first reading.
Not *ask*.
Not *seek*.
Not *knock*.
**Listen.**
In that single command, the conflict resolved itself. Listening did not mean ambition. It meant obedience. It meant acting not because he wanted to rise, but because he was being called to respond.
That was enough.
He submitted his name to the Judicial and Bar Council once more.
The resistance returned immediately.
At one meeting, there was a concerted effort to strike his name from the list. Old objections resurfaced. Familiar skepticism hardened. The vote came dangerously close.
Only one member intervened.
“Let us defer this,” the member said. “We are meeting again next week.”
It was a procedural delay. Nothing more.
Two days later, the same member spoke to him privately.
“Unless something extraordinary happens,” he said plainly, “you will be removed next week.”
Unless a miracle happens.
Art did not panic.
He prayed — not defensively, not anxiously, but defiantly in faith. He had reached a strange calm. He no longer argued his merits. He no longer rehearsed rebuttals. He rested entirely on a conviction that had crystallized within him:
Human forces, however exalted, could not override divine will.
At the next meeting, something inexplicable occurred.
No one objected.
The accusations did not resurface.
The arguments did not return.

title: The Bench
heading: The Bench
text:
The Bench

In **October 1995**, **President Fidel V. Ramos** appointed Artemio Panganiban Jr. as **Associate Justice of the Supreme Court**.

When Ramos later asked him how he had finally passed the Judicial and Bar Council, Art answered without irony:

“I did not do it. The Lord did.”

The bench changed him — and revealed him.

He wrote relentlessly. Opinions poured from his chambers. Decisions were not merely rendered; they were *reasoned*. Colleagues soon noticed the pattern: clarity without arrogance, firmness without cruelty.

Justice Antonio Carpio would later call him **“the most prolific writer of the Court.”**

More than a thousand decisions bore his name.

He chaired divisions. Led reform committees. Wrote books — one each year — as if compelled to account for his stewardship. His judicial philosophy crystallized into a simple, audacious premise:

**The judiciary must protect liberty and nurture prosperity.**

Law, he argued, was not merely restraint. It was enablement. Predictable justice encouraged economic growth. Fair courts strengthened democracy. Liberty without order was chaos; order without liberty was tyranny.

Then history intruded.

title: EDSA, Judgment at Dawn
heading: EDSA, Judgment at Dawn
text:
EDSA, Judgment at Dawn

January **2001** was not a legal puzzle to be solved by precedent or procedure.
It was a **moral emergency**, unfolding faster than doctrine could keep pace.
The streets had already rendered their verdict. President **Joseph Estrada** had lost the confidence of the people—his authority eroded not by court ruling, but by public withdrawal. Protesters massed at EDSA. Barricades hardened around Mendiola. The chants grew louder, angrier, less patient. Yet in the cold language of law, he remained President.
On the other side stood Vice President **Gloria Macapagal Arroyo **— endowed with moral authority, buoyed by popular support, but still tethered by constitutional constraint. She could not act without risking illegitimacy. The Constitution, designed to ensure order, now threatened paralysis.
The military hesitated. Each hour of delay increased the danger of miscalculation. A coup — open or disguised — was no longer unthinkable. Government machinery faltered. Authority fractured. The Republic stood exposed, suspended between legality and collapse.
From within the Supreme Court, **Art** watched the situation darken.
He saw the abyss clearly—not as abstraction, but as consequence. He imagined what hesitation could unleash: violence at the barricades, bloodshed justified by confusion, the Constitution rendered irrelevant by force. He understood that once order dissolved, no court ruling could restore it intact.
He feared violence more than controversy.
He feared constitutional collapse more than personal criticism.

title: EDSA, Judgment at Dawn
heading: EDSA, Judgment at Dawn
text:
EDSA, Judgment at Dawn (cont.)

er dissolved, no court ruling could restore it intact.
He feared violence more than controversy.
He feared constitutional collapse more than personal criticism. And so, he did what he had trained himself to do his entire life: he withdrew from noise and turned inward — to reflection, to prayer, to judgment.
In the quiet hours before dawn on **January 20**, he reached a conclusion that would mark him permanently. The Constitution, he believed, had to be **saved from annihilation by inaction**. If the law could not move forward decisively, it would be overtaken by events beyond its control.
There was only one path left.
He placed the call to Chief Justice **Hilario Davide Jr.**.
His words were direct. Unembellished. Grave.
**Swear her in.**
Davide listened.
The proposal was extraordinary — not because it was illegal, but because it was unprecedented. It carried risk. It invited criticism. It would be misunderstood. But it offered one essential thing: continuity of constitutional order without resort to force.
By **noon**, before uncertainty could metastasize into violence, Gloria Macapagal Arroyo took the oath of office.
The immediate crisis passed. The Republic held.
But the argument did not.
The decision would divide opinion for decades. Scholars would debate it. Politicians would weaponize it. Critics would accuse the Court of intervention; defenders would call it constitutional rescue. History would refuse easy consensus.

title: EDSA, Judgment at Dawn
heading: EDSA, Judgment at Dawn

EDSA, Judgment at Dawn (cont.)

iticians would weaponize it. Critics would accuse the Court of intervention; defenders would call it constitutional rescue. History would refuse easy consensus. When the legality of Arroyo’s presidency later reached the Supreme Court, Art did what his conscience and integrity required: **he recused himself**. So did Davide. The Court deliberated without them.
The result was unequivocal. **Thirteen justices voted unanimously** to uphold Arroyo’s ascension to the presidency, and later to deny with finality Estrada’s motion for reconsideration.
The Court spoke.
History continued to argue.
Art did not.
He had not acted to seize power.
He had not acted to choose a president.
He had acted, as he understood it, **to preserve order when order was about to fail**.
In moments like that, he believed, a jurist is not judged by popularity or applause — but by whether, when the Constitution trembles, he chooses courage over comfort and responsibility over silence.

title: Chief Justice
heading: Chief Justice
text:
Chief Justice

On **December 20, 2005**, Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr. ascended to the highest judicial office in the land as **Chief Justice of the Philippines**.
There was no campaign trail behind him. No whispered lobbying. No calculated pilgrimage to political powerbrokers. He had not even sought an audience with the President who would appoint him. His elevation was not the result of orchestration, but of culmination — an acknowledgment, belated yet unmistakable, of a jurist whose life had already been spent in preparation.
For Art, the Chief Justiceship was not a coronation. It was a burden.
He entered the office without triumphalism, keenly aware that the authority of the Supreme Court does not rest in robes or titles, but in public trust — fragile, conditional, easily lost. He presided not as a conqueror of the institution, but as its **custodian**, conscious that he was merely holding the Court in trust for those who would come after him.
From the outset, he framed his leadership around restraint and reform. He championed judicial modernization, transparency, and ethical accountability — not through grand pronouncements, but through steady institutional discipline. Independence of the judiciary, he believed, was not something to be declared loudly; it was something to be **practiced quietly**, day after day, decision after decision, even when it proved inconvenient or unpopular.

title: Chief Justice
heading: Chief Justice
text:
Chief Justice (cont.)

hing to be declared loudly; it was something to be **practiced quietly**, day after day, decision after decision, even when it proved inconvenient or unpopular. Criticism came readily, as it always does to those who stand at the summit of power. He met it without retaliation. He neither belittled dissent nor weaponized authority. In an era where power was often confused with invulnerability, Art insisted on something rarer: **intellectual humility**.
That humility was tested publicly in **2006**, after Congress abolished the death penalty. Reflecting on the now-historical case of **Leo Echegaray**, whose execution in 1999 he had affirmed as an Associate Justice, Art spoke with candor that unsettled many. He suggested that the Court may have committed a **judicial error **— that not all qualifying circumstances required for the ultimate penalty had been conclusively established.
He did not raise the issue to provoke outrage or to rewrite history. He raised it to confront moral consequence.
The reaction was swift. Death-penalty advocates bristled. Critics accused him of undermining the Court’s authority. Others worried that such admissions might weaken public confidence in the judiciary.
Art listened.
Then he clarified — calmly, precisely, without defensiveness. His remarks, he explained, reflected **his personal conscience**, not an institutional pronouncement. Courts speak collectively through decisions; individuals, even Chief Justices, remain accountable to their own moral reckoning.
It was a subtle but profound distinction.

It was a subtle but profound distinction. In making it, he articulated one of his deepest convictions: that **truth is not diminished by humility**, and that the judiciary is not weakened when its leaders acknowledge fallibility. On the contrary, he believed that moral honesty — especially when voiced without compulsion — strengthens the legitimacy of institutions far more than rigid silence ever could.
For Art, the law was not a fortress designed to conceal doubt. It was a living structure, sustained by integrity, reflection, and the courage to confront uncomfortable truths.
That, more than any title he would ever hold, defined his tenure as Chief Justice.

title: Retirement Without Retreat
heading: Retirement Without Retreat
text:
Retirement Without Retreat

When Art stepped down from the Supreme Court in **December 2006**, there was no sense of disappearance.
He did not retreat into silence. He did not retreat into comfort. He did not retreat at all.
The robe came off, but the vocation did not.
Retirement, for him, was not an ending but a repositioning — a shift from judgment rendered behind closed doors to judgment articulated in the open forum of public discourse. He had spent more than a decade shaping jurisprudence through decisions. Now he would shape civic conscience through words.
In **February 2007**, he began writing a weekly column for the *Philippine Daily Inquirer* titled **“With Due Respect.”**
The title was not accidental.
It reflected both tone and posture: firm but civil, critical but disciplined, grounded in law yet attentive to human consequence. He wrote not as a partisan, nor as a scold, but as a former Chief Justice who understood how easily institutions could be weakened — and how slowly they were rebuilt.
Each Monday, readers encountered a familiar voice: measured, precise, occasionally stern, often pastoral. He wrote about governance, corruption, constitutional limits, judicial independence, moral leadership. He wrote as someone who had seen power from the inside and understood how thin its moral margins could be.
It did not take long for the column to find its audience.
Law students dissected it. Policymakers bristled at it. Judges quietly admired its restraint. Ordinary readers trusted it because it did not shout.

title: Retirement Without Retreat

Law students dissected it. Policymakers bristled at it. Judges quietly admired its restraint. Ordinary readers trusted it because it did not shout. In time, the columns were gathered into books — *With Due Respect*, *With Due Respect 2*, *With Due Respect 3* — each volume a ledger of civic conscience, each page insisting that democracy survives not on passion alone, but on restraint.
Even in retirement, Art remained accountable — to history, to faith, to the discipline of thought.

title: The Elder Statesman
heading: The Elder Statesman
text:
The Elder Statesman

Age did not soften Art into ceremonial irrelevance. It sharpened him.
He became a sought-after **independent director**, adviser, trustee, and chairman — not because of prestige, but because of trust. Corporations and institutions did not ask him to decorate their boards; they asked him to **steady** them.
He sat at tables where decisions affected power grids, energy policy, banking stability, telecommunications infrastructure, mass media, ports, hospitals, food systems, and national investment. He chaired audit committees, risk oversight bodies, governance panels. He insisted on process. He insisted on independence.
When asked why he continued to accept such roles long after he could have rested, his answer was consistent:
Institutions matter.
And institutions require guardians.
Beyond corporate governance, he returned again and again to foundations — the quieter arenas of nation-building. He led and advised organizations devoted to liberty, prosperity, judicial education, dispute resolution, the Church, and civic formation.
In **2017**, he was appointed **Chairman of the Philippine National Group to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague**, a role that carried international consequence and symbolic weight. It was fitting: the former Chief Justice, once denied Yale for lack of fare, now represented his country in one of the world’s most venerable legal institutions.
Recognition followed — but he never chased it.

title: The Elder Statesman
heading: The Elder Statesman
text:

enied Yale for lack of fare, now represented his country in one of the world’s most venerable legal institutions.

When he was honored by the **Bantayog ng mga Bayani** as a **Haligi ng Bantayog**, he stood among figures associated with resistance, integrity, and moral courage. He understood the symbolism — and the burden.
And when the Church conferred upon him the papal award **Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice**, he received it not as culmination, but as confirmation: that a faith discovered late could still be lived fully.
