title: EPILOGUE: The Judgment That Endures
heading: EPILOGUE: The Judgment That Endures
text:
EPILOGUE: The Judgment That Endures

In the quiet accounting of a life, titles eventually fall away.
Chief Justice.
Associate Justice.
President.
Chairman.
Columnist.
What remains is judgment — not the kind rendered from a bench, but the kind history renders over time.
Art was not born into advantage. He was born into necessity. His childhood taught him endurance before it taught him law. His poverty taught him discipline before it taught him ambition. His faith arrived not as inheritance, but as discovery — earned slowly, tested often, and embraced finally with conviction.
He learned early that institutions are fragile — that law must be defended not only from enemies, but from apathy; that democracy is not self-sustaining; that liberty decays without stewardship; that prosperity falters without fairness.
When the Republic trembled, he chose order over applause.
When ambition tempted, he chose patience.
When faith demanded obedience, he answered — even when the cost was delay, humiliation, or doubt.
He once wrote that he held office **by God’s grace** — and he meant it not as piety, but as accountability. Power, in his worldview, was never owned. It was borrowed.
Now, as age confers perspective rather than limitation, he stands as a reminder of something increasingly rare: that leadership can be both principled and effective; that judgment can be both firm and humane; that faith and reason, properly disciplined, do not compete — they converge.

title: EPILOGUE: The Judgment That Endures
heading: EPILOGUE: The Judgment That Endures
text:
EPILOGUE: The Judgment That Endures (cont.)

ip can be both principled and effective; that judgment can be both firm and humane; that faith and reason, properly disciplined, do not compete — they converge. From the pavements of Sampaloc to the halls of the Supreme Court, from silence to authorship, from judgment rendered to judgment reflected upon, his life traces a single, unwavering arc:
**Liberty must be protected.**
**Prosperity must be nurtured.**
**And the law, above all, must be worthy of the people it governs.**
When future generations ask what steadied the Republic in moments of peril, they will not find the answer in slogans or speeches.
They will find it in men who chose restraint over power, conscience over convenience, and judgment over noise.
They will find it in the life of **Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr.**

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Chapter 1: Early Years
text:
Chapter 1: Early Years

__Prologue__
__*Dusk was setting in, extending shadows before nightfall\. A man looked at the sky, quietly watching streaks of light fade into the darkness\. He sat in a room full of memorabilia, souvenirs from travel, books he had written, a collection of honors and accolades reaped over a remarkable career\. There were citations framed on the wall and photographs with men of history, leaders and king makers who counted him their equal\. The accomplishments and regard had mattered enough that he commissioned this private museum built to house such glory\. But without discounting the achievements of an extraordinary life, these no longer held his heart\. Something happened that caused him to see the value of things in the light of eternity\. He watched as stars began to flicker in the night sky\. Tomorrow would be another day but he was happy to sit under a heaven bright with a constellation overhead*\.__
__*Artemio V\. Panganiban pondered the events of his life from the vantage point of 89 years\. Though he had not been schooled in catechesis, a confluence of events led to the firm acknowledgement that Divinity had charted his course\. He deemed that circumstances and encounters, people he met, opportunities as well as failures and losses were alliances of destiny\. These led to a faith life that he now valued more than the successes of a career, material gain and the esteem of men\. He saw that all that had been was an orchestration to realize a plan greater than he had envisioned for himself\.*__

He saw that all that had been was an orchestration to realize a plan greater than he had envisioned for himself\.*__ __*There were markers that punctuated the progression to a relationship with God\. Some might have been perceptible, others not as apparent\. Yet when he reflected on his spiritual journey, Artemio believed with certainty that the Christian God he raged against had been with him from the moment he took his first breath\. It may not have seemed so to him then, growing up in humble circumstances, losing a parent, hawking newspapers to pay for his studies and*__

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: EARLY YEARS
text:
EARLY YEARS

__*How does the president of a nation, a pope and a disruptive world situation factor into the life of a newborn who began his existence nondescriptly in a Tondo hospital? Only in hindsight would the interweaving threads of religion, politics, social and economic conditions make apparent the unique tapestry of a remarkable life\. It would scarcely be discernable that a child born in humble circumstances would contribute on a national scale to righting societal ills championed by a commonwealth leader or take up the cause of the Church he nominally knew\.*__
__*His birthplace, where he grew up, what he would become were also affected by decisions and actions taken by his forebears\. There were also the considerations of migration, the social and cultural milieu that would invariably affect his future\. External conditions as*__
__*zeitgeist, environs, events that occurred oceans and continents away, family,	associations	and	the community at large would leave an impression upon him, consciously or otherwise\. to shape his values, outlook and ultimately character\. The distinctive moral and mental qualities arising from these factors formed the compass that would consequently define the person and his chosen path\. Yet beyond all that, there remained a Prime Mover greater than all these\.*__

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: EARLY YEARS
text:
EARLY YEARS (cont.)

formed the compass that would consequently define the person and his chosen path\. Yet beyond all that, there remained a Prime Mover greater than all these\.*__ Artemio V\. Panganiban was born in the year when Manuel L\. Quezon was president of the Philippine Commonwealth, Pope Pius XI was head of the Catholic Church and the world was in the throes of the Great Depression, one of the worst economic downturns in the industrialized world\. The Philippine head of state had mounted a vigorous campaign to institute social justice particularly for the Philippine working class, inspired by the encyclicals of Pope Pius XI’s *Quadragesimo* *Anno *and Pope Leo XIII’s *Rerum Novarum*\. The latter document issued on May 15, 1891 was widely held as a modern Catholic position on the economic, social and political order, addressing the industrial revolution and transitions of governments across Europe\. The progressive tenets aligned the Church with the marginalized and the working man, supporting the rights of labor, rejecting socialism and
communist ideologies and cautioning against unrestricted capitalism\.
Forty years after, Pope Pius XI amplified the ethical considerations for economic justice and the rights of the workers\. He opposed socialist and communist systems, as well as laissez\-faire capitalism\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: EARLY YEARS
text:
EARLY YEARS (cont.)

The spirit of these Catholic documents resonated with President Quezon who introduced executive and legislative measures to benefit the Filipino working class and agricultural workers, people like the family of Artemio V\. Panganiban, who descended from a generation of tenant farmers\. His father, Artemio, Sr\. was the eldest of eight children born to Wenceslao Panganiban and Honorata Pelayo\. The couple actually had another eight offspring who had either died at childbirth or thereafter\. Wenceslao was a farmer whose parents traced their roots to Batangas\. After he married Honorata, they moved to Barrio Mandili, her domicile in Candaba, Pampanga\. Pursuing the occupation of their forebears, the couple tilled land they did not own\. As tenants, they followed the ancient practice of sharing their harvested crops with the landowners\. Farming was a matter of survival and hardly a means to improve one’s station\.
Agricultural laborers apply themselves to months of backbreaking, manual work and then wait till the crops are ready for harvesting\. During their “dead time,” a period known as *tiempo muerto*, they have no income, no other source of livelihood\. It is a cycle of penury for farming
families, who are unable to shore up savings and inevitably rack up

EARLY YEARS (cont.)

families, who are unable to shore up savings and inevitably rack up debts to tide them over till they can gather the yield of their labors\. Even then, what they earn remains insufficient\. There is barely enough for daily subsistence and practically nothing for medical concerns, much less for education\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Temi and Patricia
text:
Temi and Patricia

It was fortuitous that the boy Artemio’s father, known to kin as “Temi,” finished high school\. Education likely opened the mind of the young man to possibilities of a future different from that of his progenitors\. Just as important would be the choice of a life partner who would join him in diverting from the agrarian occupation\. Temi had managed to gain the favor of Patricia, daughter of the *cabeza del barrio, *Señor Igmidio Villaseñor, locally known as “Apong Midio\.”
While her family was a little better off than Temi’s, Patricia’s stern and old\-fashioned father did not believe in education\. Midio’s wife had passed away shortly after Patricia was born\. Agang, as she was called, was the younger of two daughters\. While she was growing up, it became her assigned lot to keep house for the family\. Studying was not a priority and she did not finish elementary school\. However, though she spoke no English and could barely manage Tagalog, Agang was adept in the
culinary language of her province, arguably among the best of Filipino regional cuisine\. She prepared *morcon *or *bulanglang *without the benefit of a cookbook, approximating portions of ingredients and seasonings to produce exact flavors that she would confidently serve without even tasting them\. That no one ever complained was a testament to her culinary skills\. She had been brought up to be a homemaker and that was the path she took when she eloped with Temi to Manila\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Temi and Patricia
text:
Temi and Patricia (cont.)

mplained was a testament to her culinary skills\. She had been brought up to be a homemaker and that was the path she took when she eloped with Temi to Manila\. Relocation to the city effectively embarked the family on a trajectory away from the tenant\-farmer occupation that had sustained generations on both the paternal and maternal sides of their families\. Temi and Agang’s children would consequently be exposed to a life other than farming\.
The young couple established residence on Cataluña Street corner España in the district of Sampaloc\. Cataluña, now known as G\. Tolentino Street, was neither picturesque nor indistinguishable from other low\-income residential areas\. Proximity to a concentration of Catholic churches and learning institutions made it a convenient place to live, albeit congested and teeming with human activity\. This was where they settled and where Temi’s sisters eventually came to reside with them\. It was not an uncommon arrangement for extended family members to live together under one roof\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Temi and Patricia
text:
Temi and Patricia (cont.)

and where Temi’s sisters eventually came to reside with them\. It was not an uncommon arrangement for extended family members to live together under one roof\. Though only a secondary school graduate, Temi found employ as a clerk in the old Bureau of Lands and was able to provide a decent life for his family on a government worker’s salary\. He may have been among the rank and file, but he would go to the office every day wearing a necktie\. The division chiefs and higher officials sported suits with starched wing\-collar shirts, even if the *americana *was too warm for Philippine weather\. American presence in the country would leave an impression on many facets of Philippine life and culture, not the least in the way people dressed\. The more practical *Barong Tagalog, *which had been discarded in the late 1920s, only resurfaced as formal wear when President Ramon Magsaysay began wearing the untucked, loose Filipino men’s shirt to official functions\. Fashion had become an expression of patriotism\.
The political and economic landscape was greatly determined by Americans who replaced the Spanish colonizers in 1898\. Trade agreements provided for tax\-free import of Philippine raw materials, and the US became the primary market for Philippine exports\. When the Great Depression hit America, the Philippines was indirectly affected by America’s diminished economic capacity\. The colonized archipelago had been made economically dependent on the US and the reduced demand stunted the growth of exports, adversely affecting the supply of currency,

Stirrings of nationalism were on the rise as was the movement to become an independent nation\. While there were clusters in the provinces expressing patriotism and advocating freedom, most of the
activities pushing for independence were happening in Manila where the Panganibans had chosen to reside\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Favorite Child
text:
Favorite Child

All the children of Temi and Agang were born in the metropolis\. Their eldest was a daughter named Teresita\. She was followed by Nardo and then Lolita\. The youngest son and namesake, Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr\., was born on December 7, 1936 at the Mary Johnston Hospital in Tondo\. A year prior to the young Artemio’s entry into the world, Manila had just been designated as the capital of the newly formed Commonwealth of the Philippines\. Historically, it had been the seat of power for centuries and an important trading hub\. Access through the Pacific Ocean established it as a center of commerce, bringing worldwide trade particularly during the Spanish era\. Historical notes described the Manila district of Tondo as the Eastern capital, so named by the Chinese for its location southeast of China\. “The polity of Tondo flourished during the latter half of the Ming dynasty as a result of direct
trade relations with China\. The Tondo district was the traditional capital of the empire, and its rulers were sovereign kings, not mere chieftains\.” \(Manila – The Reader Wiki\.com\)

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Favorite Child
text:
Favorite Child (cont.)

na\. The Tondo district was the traditional capital of the empire, and its rulers were sovereign kings, not mere chieftains\.” \(Manila – The Reader Wiki\.com\) The birth of the youngest of the Panganiban brood happened a few weeks before Christmas\. He was born during the holiday season amidst the festiveness anticipating one of the most awaited feasts of the Catholic Church\. Particulars of his arrival are lost memories although relatives recounted that the infant Artemio refused to suck from Agang’s breasts\. Consequently, Temi’s sisters referred to him as “*anac ning baca*” \(son of a cow\) because he drank canned evaporated milk instead of his mother’s milk\.
Family and close relations called the second Panganiban son *Dayunior*, having been christened with the same name as his father\. The appendage “Jr\.” was registered in his birth certificate, school records, marriage certificate and other early documents and became his nickname from childhood through young adulthood\.
While he had a good relationship with his father, Dayunior was attached to his *Ima, *the Capampangan term for mother\. Agang doted on him and turned a blind eye to the mischief of her little boy\. He was a bit of a rascal who felt he could get his way and inevitably got into trouble\. The spirited child terrorized his playmates for sport\. Despite his lean

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Favorite Child
text:
Favorite Child (cont.)

e was a bit of a rascal who felt he could get his way and inevitably got into trouble\. The spirited child terrorized his playmates for sport\. Despite his lean frame, he was said to have bullied the children of poorer neighbors who resided in makeshift houses by a nearby sawmill\. However, before he could grow up into a rogue, a cataclysm suddenly descended upon him and his family, his country and the world a day after his fifth birthday\. Japanese forces bombed Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941\. Ten hours later, they attacked the Philippines with aerial bombardments and ground troop assault\. World War II had begun\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Escape to Mandili
text:
Escape to Mandili

Following the attack on Pearl Harbor, Temi immediately decided that it was best for their family to move back to Barrio Mandili\. The Japanese were arriving and Gen\. Douglas MacArthur declared the capital an “open city” to forestall destruction by ground or air offensive\. Manila was demilitarized and all defensive efforts were abandoned\. Dayunior had just turned five years old\. He would have no memory of life before the war\.
War brought displacement, abrupt relocation and changed circumstances\. The magnitude of any war’s disruption escalates human capacity to adapt, no matter how young or old a person is, although children are among the most vulnerable in a situation of armed conflict\.
Like any parent, Temi’s instinctive response to the news of the attack
was to move his family immediately to safety\. He quickly entrusted the children to his three sisters to take them posthaste to the province away from impending danger\. He and Agang were to follow with whatever they could bring\. The women and their wards traveled in the cover of night, passing through the town of San Miguel in Bulacan, taking an outrigger canoe to reach their destination\. It was a long trip and the very first Dayunior took without his Ima\. He had never been separated from her before that time\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Escape to Mandili
text:
Escape to Mandili (cont.)

canoe to reach their destination\. It was a long trip and the very first Dayunior took without his Ima\. He had never been separated from her before that time\. The boy might not have understood the magnitude of war and its dire implications but the separation was serious enough to convey horrors he had not previously known\. Being whisked from home at a time when he should have been getting ready for bed was bewildering but the absence of his Ima’s comforting presence left him distraught\. He cried throughout the journey, inconsolable in the arms of his aunts who took turns carrying him in their arms trying to soothe him\. Their efforts were no match for his fears\. Unable to calm Dayunior, they resorted to scare tactics and threatened him with stories of a *kapre*, the folkoric giant who would snatch and kill him if he did not stop his sobbing and whimpering\. Huddled in the *banca*, unable to make out forms in the darkness, he became even more terrorized\. The figure of a monstrous creature lurking in the watery blackness added to his distress and
increased his wailing\. By the time they landed, he had lost his voice\.
The exhausted party made their way to the nipa hut of his grandmother Honorata where they waited till Temi and Agang arrived\. Dayunior had been so traumatized by the departure and separation experience that he became psychologically unresponsive and recessive\. It took the comfort, affection and nurturing of his parents to help him recover\. As soon as they were reunited, the family moved to the larger house of Patricia’s father\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Escape to Mandili
text:
Escape to Mandili (cont.)

comfort, affection and nurturing of his parents to help him recover\. As soon as they were reunited, the family moved to the larger house of Patricia’s father\. By this time, Apong Midio had remarried\. The union had produced a son named Frankie, who was about the same age as Dayunior\. Though effectively his uncle, Frankie became Dayunior’s best friend and all seemed well in their world\. They played games together, spent days running around or stealthily clambering up the fruit trees that the stern and taciturn Apong Midio prohibited them from climbing, in fear they would fall or hurt themselves\.
Living in the barrio honed his ability to speak the local dialect reasonably well\. His mother spoke to her children only in Pampango\. He learned to adapt to environs that were different from what he had previously known and likely contributed to building in him an inner capacity to adjust to change\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Hideaway Discovered
text:
Hideaway Discovered

The family stayed in the remote town for a couple of years\. It was located in the middle of the Candaba swamp and was constantly flooded\. The place, like many backwoods in the country, had no running water\. Barrio folk got their drinking water from a hand pump\. They washed and cooked, sourcing water from a nearby stream\. Hospitals or medical facilities were nonexistent\. Health concerns were brought to *herbolarios*, folk healers who chanted prayers and used indigenous plants to medicate ills, aches and pains\. Barrio Mandili also did not have a church or chapel, much less a priest\. The absence of conveniences and services notwithstanding, it offered a sense of security, however tenuous\. Location and distance from the urban center made the residents feel far removed from the conflict and violence raging in the capital\.
The war, however, caught up with them one day and violently intruded into the community\. Japanese soldiers descended upon the remote village and shattered any illusion of being hidden and unreachable\. Armed and threatening, they immediately rounded up all the able\-bodied men and arrested them on suspicion that they were part of the *Hukbong Bayan Laban sa Hapon, *literally translated as “People’s Army Against the Japanese\.” Widely known as the Hukbalahap or by the
abbreviation “Huks,” this socialist/communist guerrilla movement was originally formed by farmers in Central Luzon to resist Japanese invaders\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Hideaway Discovered
text:
Hideaway Discovered (cont.)

lahap or by the
abbreviation “Huks,” this socialist/communist guerrilla movement was originally formed by farmers in Central Luzon to resist Japanese invaders\. Temi was among the victims who were beaten and threatened by the soldiers\. The Japanese who entered the house saw a photograph of a man in full uniform and concluded he had ties with the rebels\. He was, in fact, an active supporter of the guerillas and a good friend of Luis Taruc, the Hukbalahap leader from 1942 to 1950\. Dayunior was terrified as his father was slapped and kicked mercilessly\. It was a horrifying
tableau unfolding before his eyes as Agang fell on her knees and begged the tormentors to stop\. His parents were at the mercy of these strangers with bayonets, and death was not a remote possibility\. Through tears, his mother implored them to spare her husband, pleading in Pampango, the only language she knew\. The Japanese did not know the dialect but they understood her importuning\. Whether they had been moved or decided he was of no consequence to them, Temi was released\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Three Years in Candaba
text:
Three Years in Candaba

The episode with the Japanese soldiers was a harrowing experience that left them feeling exposed and unprotected\. The chance to relocate opened up when Servando Sagcal, the mayor of Candaba,
offered Temi the position of mayor’s secretary\. He accepted and moved his family to the town center\. They lodged in the Home Economics Building of the Candaba Elementary School\.
Just like Mandili, the town had no hospital, clinic, pharmacy or practicing doctors\. When Dayunior contracted dysentery at the age of six, his demise was a foregone conclusion since they had no access to medical help\. It was his Ima who took care of him untiringly, sponging his fevered body and rubbing his aching stomach\. She held him in her arms all through the days and nights, giving him water to keep him hydrated as he drifted in and out of consciousness, that he recovered without medicine or medical attention was regarded as a miracle\.
Dayunior was seven years old when he enrolled in first grade\. One of his teachers was the mayor’s pretty daughter Liling who taught her students to sing nursery rhymes that he enjoyed\. The faculty included enlisted men of the Imperial Army who instructed the students to speak Nihongo\. They learned basic Japanese from these soldiers who were friendlier than the ones Dayunior had first encountered in Mandili\.
He studied at the Candaba Elementary School until the third grade\. The war raged for three years but in 1945, American troops arrived and the tide turned against the Japanese\. US aircraft began dropping bombs

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Three Years in Candaba
text:
Three Years in Candaba (cont.)

the third grade\. The war raged for three years but in 1945, American troops arrived and the tide turned against the Japanese\. US aircraft began dropping bombs which signaled the arrival of liberation forces\. Dayunior witnessed airplanes in a dog fight near their residence\. When an American warplane started a bombing run, he ran with his siblings to the underside of the Home Economics building for shelter\. The small air raid dump was more like a hole in the ground, where he crouched in fear as bombs exploded near them\. When the fighting ceased, they emerged from their hiding place, and onto the threshold of a new chapter in their life as a family and as a nation\.

title: Chapter 1: Early Years
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 1 opens with an 89-year-old Artemio V.
Panganiban in his private museum at dusk, looking back on a remarkable career and concluding that 'Divinity had charted his course' -- the providential thesis that frames the whole biography.
The chapter proper then situates his 1936 birth in Tondo against the Commonwealth presidency of Manuel L.
Quezon, the papacy of Pius XI, the Great Depression, and the Catholic social encyclicals (Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum, Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno) that animated Quezon's social-justice program and would later define CJP's own 'Liberty and Prosperity' motto.
His paternal line -- tenant farmers Wenceslao Panganiban and Honorata Pelayo in Barrio Mandili, Candaba, Pampanga, the eldest of their eight surviving children named Artemio Sr.
('Temi') -- had moved between Batangas and Pampanga in the agrarian *tiempo muerto* poverty cycle; his maternal line through *cabeza del barrio* Igmidio Villaseñor ('Apong Midio') produced Patricia 'Agang,' the Pampango-only-speaking homemaker who eloped to Manila with Temi.
The Pacific War defines the chapter: after Pearl Harbor and MacArthur's 'open city' declaration, the family flees back to Mandili in a night canoe through San Miguel, Bulacan -- five-year-old Dayunior separated from his mother for the first time, terrorized by his aunts' *kapre* tales until his voice fails, arriving 'psychologically unresponsive' for days until reunited with Agang.

heading: Summary
text:

A Japanese raid finds a framed photograph of a uniformed man and beats Temi as a suspected Hukbalahap supporter -- which he was, Luis Taruc being his friend -- until Agang's Pampango plea (which the soldiers could not understand but evidently felt) spares his life.
The family then relocates to Candaba town when Mayor Servando Sagcal offers Temi a secretary post, lodging in the Home Economics Building of Candaba Elementary School where Dayunior begins first grade under Liling Sagcal and Imperial Army instructors.
At six he survives dysentery with no medicine through Agang's continuous nursing -- a recovery 'regarded as a miracle' -- and in 1945 he watches the American liberation bombs from the underside of the Home Economics building.
The chapter ends with the family at the 'threshold of a new chapter,' and with the prologue's claim quietly ratified: that everything that had already happened was 'an orchestration to realize a plan greater than he had envisioned for himself.'

title: Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years
heading: Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years
text:
Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years

CHAPTER 2
__Boyhood Years __
While his occupation as a bootblack was short\-lived, Dayunior pursued another means of earning money by peddling newspapers\. This was something he liked to do, displaying an innovative spirit coupled with hard work and determination\. He thought of ways to outsell other newspaper boys and built a wagon that he loaded with the dailies\. The future president of a national broadsheet distributed them to customers, slipping it under their doors and returning after his paper run to collect the payment\.
“I hawked newspapers in the streets of Sampaloc, running around in quite a big area\. We woke up early in the morning, ready to pick up the fresh delivery of dailies and be first to run to the streets where customers were usually awake by 5 AM to buy their favorite paper\.
“Later on, we decided to sleep on the sidewalk near the newspaper dealer’s apartment so we would get first crack when the delivery trucks from the publishing houses arrived\. Together with Frankie and the other newsboys, we tried to outrun one another to reach the waiting customers who paid cash – 10 centavos, and later 15 centavos per copy\. We would shout at the top of our voices: *“Manila Times\! Manila Chronicle\! Philippine Herald\! Manila Bulletin\!” *And in the afternoon, it would be *“Evening News\! Daily Mirror\! *We made two centavos per copy sold \(three, when the price was increased to 15 centavos\)\.

title: Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years
heading: Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years
text:
Chapter 2: Return to the City - Boyhood Years (cont.)

*And in the afternoon, it would be *“Evening News\! Daily Mirror\! *We made two centavos per copy sold \(three, when the price was increased to 15 centavos\)\. *The Manila Times *was the largest circulated daily, larger than all the others combined and did not accept returns\. When we took the copies, they were considered sold\. Because I could not carry enough copies, I built a wooden *cariton *to deliver them\. And to beat the boys, I initiated a credit system in which I just handed the copies to the customers or slipped them under their doors and then came back later to collect the payments\. In this enterprising way, I became the dealer’s best newsboy\.
“Because I sold the most copies, the news dealer, whom we simply called “Mister,” liked me\. He gave pep talks to the newsboys using me as an example of an innovative seller\. Years later, when I became one of the bar topnotchers, he gave a blow out in my honor, right there in his apartment \(also on Cataluña\), with all his newsboys at the time as guests\.”

me to death, but I was able to lie down flat and clear the high wheelbase of the truck\. I cheated death and swore never to jump from a running vehicle again\.” The near\-death incident did not deter him from peddling newspapers\. Besides providing funds to support his education, hawking dailies was something he liked to do\. Still, when he chanced on other children playing basketball or having fun during school breaks, the boy ached inside\. Discontent over dispossession stirred in his heart\. He was deeply aware of the difference between his lot and those of classmates whose families had the means to send their children to school\. Because of their circumstances, they had the privilege of time for leisure, which was normally part of childhood, but was denied him\. Playtime was an indulgence that had to be foregone, just so he could pursue his schooling and contribute to the family’s meager resources\. Days were spent either studying or working to earn money\.
“I enjoyed selling newspapers even if I sometimes cried my heart out comparing myself to classmates whose parents could afford their education,” AVP recalls\. “Many times, as I lay awake on the cold pavement, waiting for the break of dawn, I had to fight back tears and feelings of self\-pity\. During those times, there was no faith to comfort me\. Although born a Catholic, I did not know my religion\. I had a purely secular education at Candaba Elementary School during the war and later at the Juan Luna Elementary School and then at Mapa High School\.

heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 2 follows the post-war family return from Candaba to Sampaloc, Manila, and the formation of CJP's working-student identity from roughly age 9 to 18.
After a brief stint as a bootblack, Dayunior pursued newspaper-selling on Cataluña Street with the enterprise that would mark his whole life: building a wooden *cariton* to carry more copies, instituting a credit-and-collect system to beat other boys to the doors, and tracking the 2- or 3-centavo commissions on the 10- or 15-centavo dailies (Manila Times, Manila Chronicle, Philippine Herald, Manila Bulletin in the mornings; Evening News, Daily Mirror in the afternoons).
Through years of sleeping on the sidewalk near the news dealer's apartment to get first crack at delivery trucks -- and one near-fatal jeepney fall on España and Lerma Streets that a 6x6 military truck nearly turned terminal -- he supplied his own school money, supported his family in small ways, and built the *alkansya* he would keep into professional life as a trophy.
In a diary on the cold pavement he wrote 'Today I am just a newsboy.
Someday, I will be president of the Manila Times' -- a line redeemed in March 1991 when he became president of the Philippine Daily Inquirer, and again in 2011 when Marixi Prieto invited him back as a regular Sunday columnist; he later donated an entire year's professional fee to the Inquirer Newsboys Foundation.

text:

tire year's professional fee to the Inquirer Newsboys Foundation.
Schooling alternated with the route: Juan Luna Elementary School (where Grade IV's strict Mrs. Isabel Fajardo and her ruler 'could be credited with my being disciplined the rest of my life'), then Victorino Mapa High School from 1950 to 1954 -- one of four Manila public high schools named after Filipino jurists (Arellano, Araullo, Mapa, Torres), the largest with over 6,000 students, with classmates like future Senate President / 9th VP Arturo M.

He earned a UP full scholarship but could not afford the 15-centavo daily bus fare to Diliman; he tried for a UST scholarship but lost it to the third Holy Trinity question, replying 'Jesus, Mary and Joseph' to the old Dominican priest.
FEU sat five minutes and two streets away from Cataluña, the walking-distance fallback that would become the pivot of his life.
The chapter closes with his father's discovery of 'chemical engineer' in the yearbook 'Ambition' entry and the gravely-spoken request: that the son who carried Artemio Sr.'s name pursue law instead -- 'so he would truly live in me.' Dayunior agreed with a two-year escape clause, not knowing that Temi would die during his first pre-law year and that the filial vow would become irrevocable.

__The Rise of the Student Leader __
The Far Eastern University was by no means an inferior choice\. FEU had previously been the Far Eastern College, which was founded in 1919\. Initially offering courses in liberal arts, it expanded with the establishment of the Institute of Accountancy that later became the Institute of Accounts, Business and Finance \(IABF\)\. The learning institution became a university when the liberal arts college merged with the IABF\. Additional course offerings in the coeducational learning institution expanded the curriculum and over the years the school in Sampaloc held its own academically among the leading universities in the Philippines\. President Manuel L\. Quezon was quoted as saying that FEU was “the best non\-sectarian institution in the country\.” Ironically, it was here that Dayunior’s spiritual awakening began\.
Initially the young man was unhappy about enrolling in a school he had not chosen\. The first day at FEU however brought a change of heart\. He stepped in the classroom and felt immediately challenged by the

title: Chapter 3: The Rise of the Student Leader
heading: Chapter 3: The Rise of the Student Leader
text:
Chapter 3: The Rise of the Student Leader (cont.)

ling in a school he had not chosen\. The first day at FEU however brought a change of heart\. He stepped in the classroom and felt immediately challenged by the unusually strict and demanding professors\. His classes were stimulating and intellectually challenging\. The academic environment invigorated him and the student quickly immersed himself in the pursuit of scholastic achievements\. Whatever initial resentments he had over the inability to enlist in the school of his choice were dispelled as satisfaction from the overall learning experience overtook any misgivings\.
His early accomplishments led him to the realization that being in FEU did not make him less than his counterparts from the more prominent learning institutions\. “I was an equal of the UP, the Ateneo or the La Salle student,” he would later reflect\. “I could, in fact, compare and compete favorably with the best and the brightest from any school in the country and in the world\.”
__Marx and the Bible Salesman __
Dayunior was on a scholarship granted by FEU and he studied hard to keep his grant\. Educational subsidy notwithstanding, the pre\-law student continued to earn his keep by selling bibles to his professors and textbooks to classmates\. He applied for work in a company that sold pricey editions of the Douay\-Rheims Bible\. Each copy of the Latin Vulgate translation cost 70 pesos which in 2021 is estimated to be equivalent to 20,000 pesos\.

He strategically targeted a few people of means, approaching the likes of the FEU president, the FEU treasurer and the chairman of the board of trustees of FEU\. From every Bible sold, Dayunior generated pocket money for a whole month\. Commissions from the sales also allowed him to buy his own textbooks which cost 10 pesos each\. Like a sponge absorbing learnings from readings and educators, he soaked in the intellectual richness afforded by the academe\.

A few months into his first semester as a freshman, any remaining thoughts of pursuing other than a law degree were cancelled out by the passing of his father\. Temi had been working two jobs with little time to rest, and the physical exertion took a toll on his health\. Dayunior was walking home from FEU on the bright morning of February 17, 1955, when he caught sight of his father being carried down from the second floor apartment in Cataluña to a waiting taxi\. The son hurriedly jumped into the backseat and joined the others to the emergency room of the UST Hospital\. They sat in the medical treatment facility anxiously waiting for one of the ER staff to attend to them\. Sadly it took five hours before anyone assessed Temi who was obviously breathing with difficulty\. He was having an asthma attack, wheezing and gasping for air as nurses and doctors bypassed him\. Dayunior held his father as the bronchospasms accelerated\. He felt helpless and desperate as Temi’s pulse throbbed slower and slower, the pulsation growing fainter at the neck and temple till the heart stopped beating altogether\. When the dean of the UST College of Medicine finally came, Temi was no longer breathing\. He was 54 years old when he expired\.

art stopped beating altogether\. When the dean of the UST College of Medicine finally came, Temi was no longer breathing\. He was 54 years old when he expired\. Grief and bitterness surged in Dayunior’s heart\. The loss of his father, incomprehensible sadness and an anguished helplessness gnawed at him, stoking his anger over their poverty\. He felt discriminated against in the ER\. It was a busy place with patients coming in succession with different ailments and various conditions\. Dayunior watched as arrivals were attended to by doctors and nurses who bypassed him and Temi even if they had been there ahead\. Once more, the painful realization that being poor relegated them to insignificance\. It seared into his core\. The inequality dealt to the disadvantaged added to his increasing resentment over their station in life\.
It was discontent that reflected on a wider scale in different parts of the world\. Doctrines developed by Karl Marx in the mid\-19th century had spread across the continents and surfaced in the country\. Marxist

title: Chapter 3: The Rise of the Student Leader

text:

different parts of the world\. Doctrines developed by Karl Marx in the mid\-19th century had spread across the continents and surfaced in the country\. Marxist tenets analyzed the economic structure of society and advocated a transformation of the populace and of social consciousness from capitalism to a worker\-driven economic and political system\. It became the foundation of Marxism\-Leninism and Maoism which gave rise to radical labor and socialist movements in western Europe\. Marxist theories also defined communism, which the Soviet Union embraced, to become the first communist government\. Other countries such as China moved towards a society where there was no private property, no state, and every person engaged in the production of goods and services according to individual abilities\. This way of erasing poverty and bringing about economic equality was gradually seeping into the Philippines, particularly into learning institutions in Manila\. It appealed to the poor, struggling student\. The loss of a father could have driven him towards communism, but another father opened him up to another direction\.
__The Sophomore President __
Temi’s namesake felt honor\-bound to make his father’s wish come true\. He embraced the rigorous life of a working student while still fulfilling responsibilities outside the academic requirements of his course\. An unexpected development added to his widening and agreeable experience of college life\. The year was 1955\. Dayunior had

cademic requirements of his course\. An unexpected development added to his widening and agreeable experience of college life\. The year was 1955\. Dayunior had been recruited to run as the freshman delegate in his first year at the FEU Institute of Arts and Sciences, which would be the equivalent to the College of Liberal Arts\. He won the seat and became a part of the winning bloc\. These blocs were like political parties in the student government\. The freshman representative was immediately thrown into the vortex of extra\-curricular activities and became actively involved in the rich, interactive life of the university\.
A whole new horizon opened up as he was thrust into student activism and a position of leadership\. It led to a transformation from being timid and shy to becoming bold and confident\. The war and their family circumstances, the angst and the curtailment of childhood privileges had made him reserved\. As a boy, Dayunior already knew he was unlike other children because he did not have the things they owned\. Other than with his cousin Frankie, he kept mostly to himself\. His growing years were filled with self\-doubt and insecurities that remained all through high school\. University life was the game changer\. His high school classmates, who had known him as an introvert, were surprised by the transformation of the once inhibited boy to a self\-assured university man\.

The academic prerequisites leading up to a law degree required completing two years in the FEU Institute of Arts and Sciences, before four more years in the Institute of Law\. Dayunior proved to be adept at juggling the scholastic demands and his responsibilities as the freshman delegate\. When he completed his pre\-law studies, it was with distinction, graduating as Associate in Arts “With Highest Honors,” equivalent to summa cum laude\.
His leadership abilities had made him recognizable as a campus figure such that when he moved to the Institute of Law, he was once again recruited to run for the position of freshman delegate to the FEU Central Student Organization \(FEUCSO\)\. Effectively, he was a freshman in the Institute, even if it was his third year in college\. By this time he was no longer called Dayunior, but Art\.
His capabilities had been noted particularly by Fr\. Michael Nolan,
SSC, the archdiocesan spiritual director of the Student Catholic Action and FEUCSO president Ronaldo Balboa\. Fr\. Nolan, who was also the university chaplain, encouraged Art to contend for the freshman delegate position at the Law Institute\. The Irish priest went so far as to say that thereafter Art could contend for the presidency of FEUCSO, and that he would convince the SCA bloc to support Art’s bid\.

the Institute of Law\. It was succession planning, as Balboa was in his last year\. He said, “Once you become chairman of the Institute of Law, I can assure you that you will head our bloc in the university and we will support you to get elected president of the FEUCSO\.”
Art calculated his chances\. His first two years at the Institute of Arts and Sciences had given him a fair grasp of what the position entailed\. If he won as freshman delegate of the Law Institute, he would be eligible to run for chairman of the Law Institute and consequently the FEUCSO presidency\. Emboldened by the encouragement of Fr\. Nolan and Ronald Balboa, he threw his hat into the ring and emerged a winner\. Not only was he elected as freshman delegate of the Institute of Law, but he was also voted treasurer, a post normally held by sophomores and juniors\. The next step was to muster support for his bid for chairmanship of the Law Institute\.
What he had to contend with were the upperclassmen who were aghast at the temerity of an upstart to challenge the seniors\. It had never happened before that a sophomore would even aspire for the chairmanship\. Traditionally, hierarchy determined that only seniors and sometimes juniors occupied that position\. It was a status quo that Art

text:

aspire for the chairmanship\. Traditionally, hierarchy determined that only seniors and sometimes juniors occupied that position\. It was a status quo that Art would overturn\. He plunged into the campaign systematically and charismatically, going from classroom to classroom to introduce himself\. Art was able to persuade the freshman and sophomore electorate, and a smattering of juniors and seniors, to vote for him\. When the ballots were tallied, he was short by two votes and lost to a senior\. Going by his instincts, he filed an electoral protest and in the recount was declared the winner by five votes\. The incoming sophomore would sit as chairman of the Law Institute\. The next step would be to present himself as a candidate for the FEUCSO presidency\.
There were seven institutes or colleges and each had five delegates representing the different class years, plus the chairman delegate\. The freshman, sophomore, junior and senior delegates were each elected by their year batch while the chairman delegate was elected by the students of their respective institutes\. The FEUCSO presidency was a battle among the chairmen of the different institutes\.
The recount had caused Art to lose several days of campaigning for the FEUCSO presidency\. He was not deemed a candidate while the electoral protest was in progress\. Only after he was declared the winner of the chairmanship was he able to launch his bid for the top FEUCSO post\. Meanwhile, the other chairman delegates were already deep into an intense contest that was a macrocosm of national electoral campaigns\.

r the top FEUCSO post\. Meanwhile, the other chairman delegates were already deep into an intense contest that was a macrocosm of national electoral campaigns\. The FEUCSO was organized like a parliamentary government\. But only the seven chairman delegates were qualified to be nominated and elected president of the entire student council\. However, the other delegates \(freshmen, sophomores, juniors and seniors\) could vote for the president and the other officers of the FEUCSO\. These voters were offered housing with food to keep them from being present on campus prior to election day to prevent them from being “snatched” by the opposing camps\.
As a member of the majority bloc, Art had good numbers on his side\. When he was finally declared the winner of the Law Institute, he already had Father Nolan in his corner and effectively, the SCA\. The campus\-based organization was committed to the formation of Catholic
student leaders through whom the founders envisioned transformation of schools, parishes and groups through Christian living\. The SCA was founded in 1936 and nurtured by Fr\. Edward McCarthy during the early
years but it was in the late ’50s to the ‘60s that it became invigorated as a force under Fr\. Michael Nolan, who took an active role in safeguarding the faith and spiritual well\-being of the students\. While the SCA was a minority group, its support would add to the numbers needed to install him as student body president\. He already had the support of “Rocky Balboa” and his bloc, plus his own Law bloc\.

rt would add to the numbers needed to install him as student body president\. He already had the support of “Rocky Balboa” and his bloc, plus his own Law bloc\. Art’s strongest opponent was the chairman delegate of the Institute of Accounts or the College of Commerce who already had a sizeable number of supporters\. He expected the SCA’s support to clinch the presidency\. The 10 SCA delegates, however, stood full square behind Art, creating the upset that was nothing less than astounding\. Never in the school annals had there been a student body president who was only a second year law student\. He had made history\.
__Leading the First Student Walk\-Out __
Art’s feverish pace during the campaign did not let up after his victory\. He spent practically whole days at the FEU Central Student Organization office attending to student affairs\. The headquarters occupied the entire second floor of a two\-storey building built by the owners of the university for the exclusive use of the student council on the second floor and the *FEU Advocate, *the weekly student newspaper, on the first floor\. The second floor was divided into three rooms\. One
served as the reception room, another was designated for the president, and the largest was the conference room\. Like all other presidents before him, Art was given a monthly allowance of P50\.00 which was a sizable amount, considering that the tuition fee then was P130\.00 per semester\.

residents before him, Art was given a monthly allowance of P50\.00 which was a sizable amount, considering that the tuition fee then was P130\.00 per semester\. There were a lot of expectations of the young president added to the pressure that went with the position\. He plunged into the groove of weekly meetings with the student council delegates, attended activities of the Central Student Organization, and worked to promote the rights and the well\-being of the students\. These included developing programs and activities within and outside the university\. Two main issues confronting the students then were communist infiltration of the campus and government interference\.
Communism was on the rise in the Philippines with Jose Ma\. Sison and Satur Ocampo eventually leading the extreme left\. When President Carlos P\. Garcia came into office in 1957, a congressional investigation exposed communist infiltration in leading student organizations then, particularly the Student Council Association of the Philippines \(SCAP\) and the Conference Delegates Association \(CONDA\)\. Their leaders were wooed with trips to communist countries where they were accorded special treatment while being indoctrinated\. It was part of the
strategy of the communists to bring young leaders into their fold and thereby gain access to student populations\.

hile being indoctrinated\. It was part of the
strategy of the communists to bring young leaders into their fold and thereby gain access to student populations\. President Garcia had strongly opposed communism even before assuming the presidency\. During his term, he signed the bill outlawing the Communist Party of the Philippines\. Garcia sought to counter the communist efforts by constituting the Consultative Council of Students composed of student council presidents from selected schools\. The aggrupation of student heads at the behest of the chief of state was aligned with measures to counterbalance seeping communist activity on the campuses\. Members of the council received perks like travels abroad to different countries with doles and other benefits\. The expected reciprocity was further rewarded with partisan political favors\. This arrangement did not bode well for student autonomy\. Art deemed that the independence of the students would be compromised by this matter of governmental overreach\. It was a burning issue together with communist penetration of the students that faced Art as FEUCSO president\.
“I later learned that Luis Taruc, the leader of the rebels in Central
Luzon, had been my father’s friend,” Art intimated\. “Taruc noted my student activities and wrote me several encouraging letters from his hiding place in the boondocks\. I was most fortunate that when I was

ated\. “Taruc noted my student activities and wrote me several encouraging letters from his hiding place in the boondocks\. I was most fortunate that when I was elected president of the FEU Central Student Organization, Fr\. Nolan was already my spiritual adviser\. Otherwise, given my reformist streak, I could have joined the extremist groups and who knows where I would be now,” Art reflected in hindsight\.
He found guidance and support from Fr\. Nolan\. The Columban priest and the SCA bloc had delivered the swing votes and Art recognized his debt of gratitude to them\. He said, “In my mind, I was no longer the leader of the dominant group\. We were now a hybrid group\. I became friendly with the SCA bloc and began to veer towards Fr\. Nolan\.”
Fr\. Nolan figured largely in this chapter of Art’s life\. After Art won the elections, the Columban priest provided strong support to the new FEUCSO president to help him address the looming issues of the times\. Art frequented the SCA office and on those occasions, a plan of action evolved to counter the worrisome menaces\.
FEU was a traditional leader in SCAP and CONDA, owing to the large student population of the university and the support from its administration\. When Art was offered the position of Vice\-President for International Affairs of SCAP, it was intended to simmer down his dissent from the communist and partisan political activities of these

n of Vice\-President for International Affairs of SCAP, it was intended to simmer down his dissent from the communist and partisan political activities of these organizations\. Also in the agenda of these groups was to enlist Catholic schools to join them through the FEU connection\. The SCA had gained a foothold in FEU and besides St\. Paul’s College and Sta\. Isabel College, there were no other schools run by religious orders that participated in SCAP and CONDA\.
Accepting the offer would have given Art the opportunity to travel to China and Russia, Moscow, in particular\. All those who previously held the post had been invited\. Fr\. Nolan felt the time was right to break away from these two major groups\. Having gained Art’s confidence, the priest conveyed the idea of dissociating from both SCAP and CONDA, and organizing a new one\. The priest was bullish about the prospect of establishing a student group independent of government maneuverings and free from Marxist influence\. Fr\. Nolan’s SCA counterpart in the University of the Philippines, Fr\. John Delaney, SJ, had also scored a victory over the dominant bloc in the state university\. Coming together with UPSCA, Fr\. Nolan expanded alliances with other Catholic schools, enjoining them to leave the two biggest organizations that were suspected to be communist fronts\.
Art’s respect and fondness for Fr\. Nolan, as well as his debt of gratitude to the 10 SCA delegates who had clinched the win for him factored into his decision to lead the charge in bolting from SCAP and

as well as his debt of gratitude to the 10 SCA delegates who had clinched the win for him factored into his decision to lead the charge in bolting from SCAP and CONDA\. During a Students Council Association of the Philippines convention, he protested government’s interference, arguing that students should be free to criticize the establishment and not be subjugated as an adjunct of the government\. Addressing the concern of communist infiltration, he denounced the trips to Peking, as Beijing was then known, as well as the trips to Moscow, and rejected the vice presidential post offered to him\. After expressing his position, Art turned around and led what might have been the first student walkout in a major national organization in the country, with student leaders from UP, UST, San Beda College, St\. Theresa’s College, National University and Sta\. Isabel joining him\.
Eventually, with the support of Fr\. Nolan, he co\-founded the National Union of Students of the Philippines in 1957, initially composed of 17 of the largest and most prestigious universities and colleges, like UP and FEU\. “Fr\. Nolan egged me on to organize \-\- along with student leaders from the other leading schools like UP, San Beda, and St\. Theresa’s \-\- the National Union of Students of the Philippines \(NUSP\),” Art recalls\.
“To strengthen NUSP, Fr\. Nolan helped me convince exclusive Catholic schools like Ateneo, La Salle, Maryknoll \(now Miriam\), Holy Spirit, St\. Scholastica’s, University of San Carlos in Cebu City,

me convince exclusive Catholic schools like Ateneo, La Salle, Maryknoll \(now Miriam\), Holy Spirit, St\. Scholastica’s, University of San Carlos in Cebu City, University of San Agustin in Iloilo City and others to come out of their sheltered cocoons and join us\.” Art became president of the NUSP\. He stressed in a speech delivered then: “The NUSP was founded to be the
answer to the decadent state of student leadership in the country\. The Union is pledged to unite and reflect faithfully student opinion on current national issues, to free the student from undue political interference, to fight communist infiltration on the campuses, and to redirect the youth’s thinking and energy towards constructive idealism\.”
The SCA worked hard to recruit new leaders\. Its efforts paid off and NUSP grew to become the biggest student organization in the country, a distinction that persists to this date\. “It happened because of the inspiration and assistance of the Student Catholic Action,” Art maintains\.
__Three Prayers __
Fr\. Nolan’s influence over his protégé extended beyond student affairs\. He enlisted the un\-catechized student to join the SCA\. The priest took it upon himself to educate the FEUCSO president on the rudiments of Catholicism\. “I had grown up a Catholic ignoramus until the SCA introduced me to Christ,” Art often said\. “Fr\. Nolan didn’t impose anything\. He didn’t even tell me to go to Mass every Sunday\. He just taught me three prayers: The Our Father, The Hail Mary and

text:
Chapter 3: The Rise of the Student Leader (cont.)

id\. “Fr\. Nolan didn’t impose anything\. He didn’t even tell me to go to Mass every Sunday\. He just taught me three prayers: The Our Father, The Hail Mary and The Glory Be\. And he gave me booklets about Catholicism, not even a book\. He was a nice Irish priest who taught by example more than by words\. A very prayerful person, he would invite me when he had special Masses, simply saying, “Why don’t you attend?”
Art acknowledges with gratitude the significant role of this priest in his life\. “ I was most fortunate to have been recruited by Fr\. Nolan into the SCA\. I was a rebellious young man, but he expertly channeled my personal rebellion into constructive endeavors, like organizing the National Union of Students\.”
The NUSP’s activities then were largely secular, limited to the concerns of students such as improving educational standards, how to become better citizens, and how to enlarge educational outlook through co\-curricular pursuits\.
Art was able to devote three years of his student life to the NUSP, from1957 till he graduated in 1960\. He was vital in organizing, molding and strengthening NUSP during its formative years\. Even after he had graduated and was working as an assistant in the law firm of Dr\. Jovito Salonga, he continued to secure and provide financial assistance by organizing the Institute of Student Affairs, a nonstock, private organization which he set up\. ISA was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission and functioned like a foundation to assist student organizations\.

organization which he set up\. ISA was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission and functioned like a foundation to assist student organizations\. Fifty years later, in 2007, he once again recalled the ideals of the NUSP at its National Student Congress in Cebu City to mark its golden anniversary\. He said in his keynote address: “The NUSP was born as a rebellion against a decadent student milieu that was prostituted and muzzled by the government then…\[it\] was formed out of a vision that the young must be freed from the political apron strings of the old\. We espoused the idea and ideal that the student can think for himself, knows what is best for him and for his future, and thus must be given the freedom to express himself and to pursue his destiny\. It was founded on the proposition that the best in man and in society can be attained only in freedom, dignity, equality and responsibility\.”
These principles of the NUSP, articulated by the founder, reflected values that formed the bedrock of the man Art was becoming\. The timing of seemingly unfortunate incidents and episodes, failures and losses, challenges and triumphs, configured to shape his character and choices\. While it was not one event or person that accounted for his transformation, the school he had not chosen figured largely in his pivot towards an enlightenment that would eventually determine the course of his life\.

text:
Summary

Chapter 3 covers Art's three-year FEU undergraduate stretch (1955-1958), framed by the chapter's epigraph from 1 Timothy 4:12 ('Do not let anyone look down upon you because you are young').
Initially unhappy at the place he had not chosen, Art discovers stimulating professors and discovers he can compete with UP, Ateneo and La Salle students -- and so begins the accidental triumph of FEU, the institution Quezon called 'the best non-sectarian institution in the country.' He supports himself selling Douay-Rheims Bibles (70 pesos each, ~20,000 in 2021 money) to FEU's president, treasurer and devout-Catholic professors, and reselling textbooks to classmates for free copies.
On February 17, 1955, walking home from FEU, he catches sight of his asthmatic father being carried down to a taxi -- and then spends five hours in the UST Hospital ER as nurses and doctors bypass them, until the Dean of the UST College of Medicine arrives too late and Artemio Sr.
expires at 54.
The bypass in the ER sears into Art's core -- an inequality witnessed that the biography presents as the origin of CJP's later 'last sanctuary of the oppressed' jurisprudence.
Grief and rage make communism a real attraction -- Karl Marx's tenets seeping into FEU through Prof.
Primo Tongco, Jose Ma.
Sison and Satur Ocampo leading the extreme left, Luis Taruc (the Hukbalahap leader who had been Temi's friend) writing Art encouraging letters from his hiding place.

title: Chapter 4: The Law Student
heading: Chapter 4: The Law Student
text: Chapter 4: The Law Student __CHAPTER 4__ *Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life\.* __* Psalm 138\.7*__ __ __ __ The Law Student __ Far Eastern University is located in the heart of Manila, but the frenzy of the metropolis quickly dissipates within the premises\. It is a campus of architectural gems, a distinction later recognized by UNESCO in the 2005 Asia\-Pacific Heritage Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation\. The Science Building was an eight\-story structure constructed in 1957 by renowned Architect Felipe Mendoza\. His aesthetic brought together form and function, making the best use of natural light and ventilation\. An earthquake damaged it in 1970, resulting in the scaling down of the building to four floors\. Then there was the Arellano Hall which housed the Institute of Law\. Designed by National Artist Pablo Antonio, it was one of two edifices flanking the Administration Building\. Impressed by Antonio’s work, particularly the Ideal Theater on Avenida Rizal, FEU founder Dr\. Nicanor Reyes commissioned him to design several buildings for the university\. The campus became an assemblage of Art Deco architecture, reputedly the largest ensemble of sleek, linear edifices with curved ornamental forms breaking the geometric lines\.

title: Chapter 4: The Law Student
heading: Chapter 4: The Law Student
text:
Chapter 4: The Law Student (cont.)

ame an assemblage of Art Deco architecture, reputedly the largest ensemble of sleek, linear edifices with curved ornamental forms breaking the geometric lines\. Art spent considerable time on campus, most of his waking hours in these buildings, attending classes and fulfilling his responsibilities as a student leader\. It was, however, in the FEU chapel where he found some quiet moments to pause and reflect\.
The SCA office was situated beneath the consecrated space of Our Lady of Fatima Chapel\. The second building designed by Felipe Mendoza showcased works of three National Artists\. The Crucifix and the Stations of the Cross were painted by National Artist for Painting Carlos “Botong” Francisco, then a young intern\. Art describes from memory the 14 images depicting Christ’s Way of Sorrow: “The paintings were not visibly separate from each other the way they usually were\. They were big and seemed connected to each other in a continuum, like the Sistine Chapel ceiling paintings\.” Botong Francisco also painted the Crucified Christ which dominated the wall behind the altar\. The oil\-on\-canvas rendition hung above the tabernacle and was the focal point of the interiors\.
There were several life\-sized religious statues which the noted Quiapo *santonero* Maximo Vicente had been commissioned to make\. Among these were the Sacred Heart of Jesus, St\. Joseph with Jesus, and Our Lady of Fatima\. Years later, National Artist for Sculpture Napoleon Abueva would donate a fiber\-glass sculpture of *La Pieta,* inspired by Michelangelo’s masterpiece in Rome\.

Years later, National Artist for Sculpture Napoleon Abueva would donate a fiber\-glass sculpture of *La Pieta,* inspired by Michelangelo’s masterpiece in Rome\. The exterior of the chapel was distinguished by the artistry of still another National Artist for Visual Arts, Vicente Manansala\. On the facade he created a tiled mosaic of Our Lady of Fatima in bright blue hues\. It was a rare work, being the only one of a kind that the Filipino
master had ever done\.
The chapel could accommodate a combined sitting and standing capacity of 300 to 500 people\. It was a small space, given the academic population of enrollees, teachers and university personnel\. Mendoza addressed the limitation by keeping three sides of the building open and constructing the altar at an elevation that allowed the students sitting under the trees to see the altar from where they sat, allowing them to participate in the masses being officiated\. Art had not yet gotten his spiritual moorings, but he was drawn to the chapel and to the Lady for whom it was dedicated\. Decades later, he would have an epiphany of the Blessed Mother’s presence at different times of his life\. Times spent in the chapel had a calming effect much like a mother’s embrace\.

__Teachers’ Favorite__ The university’s curriculum provided a well\-rounded education that exposed Art’s inquisitive mind to different disciplines\. In the course of his university life, the young Art developed life\-changing associations that significantly contributed to who he would become\. “FEU taught me that it was not enough to be an expert in one’s profession,” he says\. “One should also have more than an adequate knowledge of the arts, history, literature, ethics and the humanities in general\.”
His appreciation for other disciplines beyond the study of law widened in the classrooms of luminaries like Dr\. Alejandro R\. Roces, who was then the newly appointed dean of the Institute of Arts and Sciences\. Dr\. Roces was highly instrumental in passing on the ideals of a truly educated person, one bred in the humanities, anchored on values and moved by principles\. “His words and example influenced my youthful aspirations for a place in society,” Art intimates\.
There was also Dr\. Teodoro Evangelista, the FEU president whom Art describes as outstanding and single\-minded in his educational policies\. “Dr\. Evangelista believed that education in the right sense of the word aims to prepare for work, not as an end in itself but as a means for the enjoyment of a life of the mind and the spirit\.”

I still use the elementary rules of logic I learned from Dean Africa and those of basic grammar from Professor Melchor\.” Another professor he recalls was Primo Tongco who tried to impress Marxist doctrines on his malleable mind\. Professor Tongco taught in liberal arts and engaged the pre\-law student in thought\-provoking exchanges\.  “He told me communism was Christianity,” Art recalls\. “Of course, at that time I didn’t understand it\.  He said that according to Christianity we must share with our neighbor, we must share everything, as we didn’t own anything\. That was what communism was about, he said\. The proletariat didn’t own anything\. Everything was owned by the State\. He triumphantly proclaimed that the disciples of Christ shared everything, but he twisted that teaching and said the Marxist philosophy of collective ownership was ideal\. He kept on emphasizing, “To each according to his need, from each according to his ability\.”
“I became Professor Tongco’s favorite\. He loved to argue with me and pierce my brain\. He told me, ‘You are bright\. You do your best when you are a professional, but you should not get paid according to your ability\. Because if you are paid according to your ability, you will be paid more and you will become rich\. That’s bad, because you will deprive others\. You should give to others, and you do that by not receiving more than the others\. Everybody should be given the same thing\.’ That was very attractive to me\. I was very poor and what he said appealed to me and sounded true\.”

I could not be a preacher or even a philosopher\. I had to follow my father, who by that time had already died\. He was very impressive\.”
It was the Christian tenets, however, that prevailed under the mentorship of Fr\. Nolan as well as that of another Columban clergyman, Fr\. James Sheehy, SSC\. “Fr\. Sheehy insisted that a good Catholic must not only be personally pure but must also lead others to purity\. In short that meant being Christ to others\. These teachings were enough for me to further my efforts to learn and experience my faith more\. My initial contacts in FEU impelled me to search for God more deeply and passionately all my life\.

__Legal Luminaries__
	Art’s professors in law were legal heavyweights, several of whom would figure in the nation’s political life\. “In the Institute of Law, I was amply armed with a formidable legal arsenal\. At the top of the list was Dean Jovito R\. Salonga, who became my role model in my chosen career and, more important, in my life as a whole\. Through my esteemed guru, I had the privilege of receiving not only UP\-style education, but Harvard and Yale\-type techniques as well\. Dean Salonga shared with us what he learned in those three schools where he finished his bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees\. I am grateful to him for his legal expertise; but more than that, for his moral courage, high\-mindedness and love of country – values that I have aspired to internalize and emulate\.”

Even now, Art holds him in the highest esteem\. “He was not just a good lawyer who topped the Bar exam\. He took his masters at Harvard and his doctorate at Yale\. Not many have finished a masters in Harvard and a doctorate in Yale\. Fewer still are those who can combine the two schools because these are rivals in the United States\. One does not recognize the degrees of the other\. In other words, if you graduate with a Master of Laws in Harvard, Yale will not recognize that for admission to doctoral studies\. But in his case, Dean Salonga was able to convince Yale that he could enroll for his doctorate in that university, even if his masters was from Harvard\. That he was able to do so was quite an achievement\. Indeed, he was a fantastic person, and I am proud to say that he was my professor when I was in law school from 1956 to 1960, and that I became one of his favorite students\.”

__Another Brush with Mortality__ It was a balancing act for the young man who was just as caught up in the NUS as he was in his law studies\. One of the issues that NUS undertook to address was communism\. Responding to the signs of the times, Art organized information campaigns against the political and economic ideologies opposed to democracy\. He himself had listened to persuasive arguments passed on by one of his professors and was aware of the potential sway of that political and economic ideology\. Credit is once again given to Fr\. Nolan for giving him the perspective that strengthened his belief contrary to the communist ideals\. Art made it his responsibility to undertake action informing others similarly situated as himself in the academe\. He recounts, “In 1958, I was leading the NUS delegation to Naga to conduct a seminar for student leaders to help them understand what communism was about and why it was abhorrent\.”

After the talks were done, their group took advantage of some free time to tour the vicinity\. Just as they were climbing Mount Mayon, Art experienced severe abdominal pains\. Some of his friends took him down to Tabaco in Albay for medical treatment\. “The only clinic available at that time was St\. Mary’s Maternity Clinic,” Art recounts\. “They brought me there even if it was for women\.” The doctor who attended to him diagnosed his symptoms as the result of indigestion and gave him castor oil\. That remedy only aggravated his condition and he ended up vomiting the medication\. “In desperation, the doctor gave me a shot of morphine, and I slept for the next 24 hours\.” He felt much better afterwards and rejoined the conference as presiding officer\. That evening, he was on the dance floor as if nothing had happened\.

However, two weeks later, the stomach pains recurred with such severity that his classmates brought him to the FEU Hospital on Morayta Street, which was then adjacent to the university\. It turned out he had appendicitis\. His medical condition put him in a situation that confronted an issue he had been opposing\. As a student leader, Art had taken a position against a six\-peso compulsory hospitalization and medical fee being mandated for all students\. He questioned the additional compulsory charges, arguing it was the duty of the university to provide medical help for all enrollees\.
When Dr\. Ricardo Alfonso who was the surgeon and director of the hospital came to see him, he said, “Artemio, there’s something wrong inside you\. I don’t know what it is, but something is wrong\. I have to open you up because you have poison inside your stomach\. What do you want to do? You want to pay the full hospitalization costs and surgeon’s fees, or do you just want to pay the six\-peso medical fee required for all students?” The point was well\-taken\.  “Of course, I told him I’d rather pay the six pesos,” Art said\. “You win, Doctor\. I will withdraw my opposition\.”

“At that time, I did not understand what he meant,” Art said\. “It took decades before I realized that Dr\. Alfonso was saying the Lord had saved me\. “When I look back now, I believe I survived a war, dysentery as a child, falling from a moving vehicle and being almost run over as a boy, and a ruptured appendix as a student because God had a mission for me and thus delivered me from death\.”

I was young and reckless\. I confronted people, the authorities\. We started rallies long before the demonstrations against Marcos when he imposed martial law in 1972\. As a student leader, I led the demonstrations in FEU\. This took up a lot of my time\. It came to a point when, during my sophomore year in law school, my grades tumbled and disqualified me from continuing as a scholar\. I lost my scholarship and could not enroll anymore for the first semester of my third year\.
 “It was good that my Uncle Ben came to the rescue\. He asked me how much my tuition fee cost\. At the time, it was about 135 pesos per semester\. He said, ‘I will give you 150 pesos to cover tuition for your first semester, your books and your allowance\.’ My books cost only about 10 to 20 pesos\.” His uncle admonished him, “Don’t think of doing anything else other than studying\.  If you don’t get good grades, I won’t support you for the second semester\.” Art took his uncle’s words to heart\. He gave more time to his academics and got his scholarship back for the second semester\.
__The Death of Patricia__
