ter\.” Art took his uncle’s words to heart\. He gave more time to his academics and got his scholarship back for the second semester\.
__The Death of Patricia__ Art had to deal with more than just the academic load, his responsibilities in the student government as well as in the other organizations\. A personal tragedy during his fourth year of studies added to the load he was carrying\. His beloved *Ima *passed away\.
Agang lived in Marulas, Polo, Bulacan, in a house that Art, Nardo and Frankie had constructed with their bare hands\. It was a small place they had toiled on together\. They slept on bare ground at the construction site to guard against possible theft of the materials\. When it was finally done, Art recalls his feeling of accomplishment and pride in what he saw as a beautiful house\.  It became the home he shared with his *Ima*,* *brother and uncle\.
Agang had not been well in her last years, her health diminished by tuberculosis\. When there was money to be spared, she would get injections of streptomycin which Nardo administered\. More often, there were no funds for medication and after four years she succumbed to the disease\. Art grieved the loss that seared into the depths of his heart\.
“I had always blamed God,” he reflects\. “As a child, as a student, as a leader, even as a professional, I blamed Him for the difficulties we experienced\. It was only much later that I realized God does not remove obstacles\. Rather, he gives us the strength to overcome them\.”

He became more immersed in his academics and in preparations for the professional licensure examination for lawyers\. “Dean Salonga told me he expected me to be one of the bar topnotchers,” Art remembers\.  The added pressure of his mentor’s expectation took a toll on his health, and he fell sick with a severe case of gastroenteritis and the flu\.
“On the first day of the exams, I was confined at the FEU Hospital\. Disheartened and discouraged, I thought of giving up and not continuing with the examinations\. Dean Salonga, however, was adamant and emphatic in advising me to continue\. So I persevered and had to get a special permission from my doctor to walk through the flooded streets
to the nearby University of the East where the exams were being held\.”

	Dean Salonga recounted that time in his Foreword to Art’s 2007 book, *A Test of Courage:* “He took the Bar Review seriously, but unfortunately, he was hospitalized during the first Sunday of the 1960 bar exams because of diarrhea and flu\. There was a heavy downpour the night before the exams and he had to walk over flooded water on R\. Papa Street that connected FEU Hospital where he was confined and the University of the East, the venue of the bar tests\. He was discouraged by his performance during the first day which was why he came and asked for my advice\. After shaking and holding hands a little longer than usual, I said, ‘Art, take the exam; you will get well\.’ He followed my advice and placed sixth in the 1960 bar exams\. Later, in talking about the same incident, whether at the FEU or at Kilosbayan Forum or elsewhere, I would take the liberty of saying Art might have placed first or second if he had not been sick\.”
Art graduated with the degree of Bachelor of Laws, cum laude\.

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
text:
Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams

__CHAPTER 5__
*Then the LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone\. I will make a helper who is just right for him*__*\.”    Genesis 2: 18, *__[__*New Living Translation*__](https://biblehub.com/nlt/genesis/2.htm)
__    Keeper of Dreams__
Somewhere in those frenetic years of law school and the pursuit of intellectual and principled ideals, there was a train ride that would take Art on an unplanned route\. The campaign of the National Union of Students to educate student leaders on the abhorrence of communism included a seminar in Naga City\. It was a 10\-hour train ride from the Tutuban Station in Manila to the city in Camarines Sur, a long trip by any standard\. The railway transport was used by all the delegates to the NUS seminar\. Art was traveling with his cousin and best friend Frankie, who was enlisted to help in the preparation and distribution of materials for the conference\.
They arrived at the station together but when the young student leader boarded the compartment, he quickly surveyed the passengers on board and espied a vacancy beside a young *colegiala*\. He instinctively decided it was the best place for the half\-day journey and made his way towards her\. Art stopped when he reached the girl who was seated by the window and asked if the vacant spot was occupied\. He tried to make it appear like a disinterested inquiry, but the sound of his voice came across louder and friendlier than he had intended\. The petite college

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
text:
Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams (cont.)

He tried to make it appear like a disinterested inquiry, but the sound of his voice came across louder and friendlier than he had intended\. The petite college student looked up at the lean man standing in the aisle\. She was slightly built and appeared fragile\. After nodding her head, she moved closer to the side–whether to make room or to keep a distance, it wasn’t clear to him\.
He settled down beside her and cleared his throat\. Politely, he introduced himself and was gratified by a smile\. Elenita Carpio went by the name Leni and was representing St\. Scholastica’s College, the convent school run by German Benedictine nuns\. Founded as a learning institution to provide religious education for the children of Manila, it was primarily a girls’ school, although they accepted male enrollees when the
nuns opened programs for music, fine art and interior design\.
The Benedictine sisters were particularly fond of Leni\. She had expressed an intention to join their congregation and they were anticipating she would be a good addition to their number\. A fine student, she was also the editor of their school paper and had been designated to represent SSC in the Naga seminar\. Their decision to send her did not factor in the meeting with the NUS president and the ensuing friendship that would derail her vocation\.

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
text:
Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams (cont.)

n the Naga seminar\. Their decision to send her did not factor in the meeting with the NUS president and the ensuing friendship that would derail her vocation\. Any thought Art might have had of sleeping through the trip was gone\. They fell into hours of conversation and he was taken by her intelligence and gentleness\. By the time they reached their destination, she had made a deep impression on him\. Frankie noticed that while Art circulated among the delegates, he paid particular intention to her during the conference party\. Later, he intimated to his confidant that she was conservative, a nice person, and that he would like to see more of her\. It was unfortunate that on the day of the organized tour of Mayon Volcano, Cagsawa Ruins and Naga City, Art’s appendix ruptured\. He was brought to a hospital for medical treatment and missed the chance to spend more leisure time with her\.

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: The Suitor
text:
The Suitor

The episode was a mere hiccup in his intentions to get to know her better\. Together with Frankie, he would commute to her residence, get off at the nearest stop and take a cab to her house\. He wanted to make a good impression on her family and felt the appearance of a respectable arrival in a taxi would help to camouflage an economic standing that was far lower than her family’s comfortable station\. It was unnecessary\. The Carpios were decent people who held no social\-status prejudices\. They received the lean law student with cordiality and eventually accepted him when the relationship with their daughter had been formalized\.

It may have helped that he was a known student leader who excelled in his academics and was setting his sights on a career in a well\-regarded profession\. He was respectful, appropriate and clear about his intentions\. The more stringent requirements before accepting

his suit came from Leni herself\. Having been schooled and mentored by the good sisters in her convent school, she was steeped in the teachings 

and practices of the Catholic church\. Before Art began his pursuit, she could already foresee a life in the nunnery\. Any alternative to that future would necessarily also be grounded in a shared faith life\.

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: Winning the Novice
text:
Winning the Novice

So it was that Art found himself attending mass with her every Sunday\. It was her requirement that they would not only participate in the weekly service, but that he would receive holy communion and go to confession every month\. He dutifully accompanied her when the family went to the Eucharistic celebrations, knelt with them, crossed himself and bowed his head\. The man who grew up in nonsectarian schools furthered his education in the ecclesiastical expressions of Christianity\. He became familiar with church practices and while it was mere compliance to push his suit, there was little doubt that the prayers of the future Mrs\. Artemio Panganiban were not going unheard\.
The suitor himself may have learned to go beyond the formulaic recitations of the “Our Father,” “Hail Mary” and “Glory Be” that Fr\. Nolan had taught him\. He was connecting with the Divine in his desire to have her for his wife\. Utterances of the heart raised to the God at the altar are as well received as spoken words\. That the Lord had seen fit to answer him favorably when she accepted his marriage proposal was no small matter\. He had been up against a congregation that disapproved of the match\. The Benedictines of St\. Scholastica deemed she was best suited to join them than to marry an unchurched and uncatechized man\.
They wanted her in the novitiate\. Even the parish priest, Fr\. Anselmo Bustos, was on the congregation’s side and refused to perform the rite of marriage\. The responsibility to officiate the matrimonial was delegated to the assistant parish priest\.

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: Winning the Novice
text:
Winning the Novice (cont.)

congregation’s side and refused to perform the rite of marriage\. The responsibility to officiate the matrimonial was delegated to the assistant parish priest\. They were married in a simple ceremony on the morning of April 8, 1961, in her parish church in Cubao\. The local community church would later become the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception\. It may not have been of particular significance to him then, but on their diamond anniversary decades and five children later, Art would remark that being married in a church dedicated to Our Lady of the
Immaculate Conception was another indication of the Blessed Mother’s presence in his life\.

title: Chapter 5: Keeper of Dreams
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 5 is the shortest in the biography and pivots on a single meeting.
On the 1958 NUS train from Tutuban Station to a 10-hour ride to Naga City -- the same trip on which Art's appendix would burst on Mt.
Mayon -- Art surveyed the compartment, espied an empty seat beside a petite *colegiala* by the window, and 'instinctively decided it was the best place for the half-day journey.' The young woman was Elenita 'Leni' Carpio, editor of the St.
Scholastica's College paper and the German Benedictines' anticipated novice, sent by the nuns to represent SSC at the seminar -- a decision the chapter notes they would come to regret as the friendship with the NUS president 'derailed her vocation.' Frankie, Art's cousin and confidant on the trip, watched Art pay 'particular attention to her during the conference party,' and heard the verdict: 'she was conservative, a nice person, and he would like to see more of her.' On the day of the organized tour of Mt.
Mayon, Cagsawa Ruins and Naga City, Art's appendix ruptured and the chance for leisure time with her was foreclosed by emergency hospitalization.
The courtship that followed had Art commuting with Frankie to her residence by jeepney to the nearest stop and then by taxi to her house, to 'camouflage' his economic standing -- unnecessary, the chapter notes, since the Carpios held no social-status prejudices and received him cordially.
The stricter requirements came from Leni herself: shared faith life as the ground floor, weekly Mass with her family, monthly Communion, monthly Confession.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
text:
Chapter 6: The Lawyer

__                                           Chapter 6__
*“Without counsel plans go awry, But in the multitude of counselors they are established\.” *__*Proverbs 15:22*__
The Lawyer
The world was beginning to look brighter for young Art as developments transpired towards an upward turn\. Graduating from law school with Latin honors, placing among the top 10 in the bar exams, marrying a gem of a woman–it seemed he was finally navigating towards the fulfilment of his aspirations for a better life\. Men on the trajectory to realizing their dreams, however, may find themselves racing ahead without the benefit of pause and reflection\. Pondering is necessary to understand that not everything is a result of one’s efforts\. It opens the possibility of seeing that there could be so much more beyond fulfilling personal ambitions to attain greater than what is imaginable\.
Art now owned his father’s dream, but Temi was no longer around to provide perspective or give him direction\. The newly minted lawyer, however, looked up to certain legal luminaries to whom history would later ascribe places of honor\. They became guideposts whom he sought to emulate\. Foremost among them was Dean Jovito R\. Salonga and,
fortuitously, Art had come under his mentorship while he was still a law student\.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
text:
Chapter 6: The Lawyer (cont.)

m he sought to emulate\. Foremost among them was Dean Jovito R\. Salonga and,
fortuitously, Art had come under his mentorship while he was still a law student\. Following graduation from the FEU, Art was heady over finishing in the top 10\. He was done with the backbreaking work of law school and could finally put the four grueling years behind him\. While he was grateful, not just for the academic education but also for the training and character formation, it had been difficult, challenging and oftentimes exhausting\. Relief and jubilation, however, were followed by apprehension over what to do next\. Tempering the initial euphoria was the uncertainty of the future\. Many opportunities for success lay before him but he was well aware that these could also spell failure\. He had to make careful and deliberate choices\.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Aborted Dream
text:
Aborted Dream

Dr\. Salonga recognized Art’s potential and encouraged him to prioritize his academic studies\. The Dean of the Law Institute recommended that the bar placer pursue further studies and endorsed him for a master’s degree scholarship\. Salonga had the unique distinction of having gone to both Harvard and Yale\. The former awarded him an LL\.M\. degree and the latter a doctorate in law\.
The law dean explained the difference between the approaches

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Aborted Dream
text:
Aborted Dream (cont.)

oth Harvard and Yale\. The former awarded him an LL\.M\. degree and the latter a doctorate in law\.
The law dean explained the difference between the approaches of the two top law schools\. Compared to Yale, Harvard Law School was reputed to be inhospitable\. Faculty members would tell new students to look at the persons beside them because one or the other would no longer be there by Thanksgiving\. Yale, on the other hand, kept the classes small and made every effort to make students feel at home\. “If a lawyer wants to argue a case before the court from the viewpoint of law and jurisprudence, Harvard is an excellent law school,” Salonga said\. “But from the viewpoint of the policy\-oriented approach of Yale, a lawyer is not just an advocate who specializes in rules and doctrines for the sake of his clients\. He should go beyond these and do what would serve the interests of the nation and the world community\.” Art was ignited by the Yale approach and upon the recommendation of Dean Salonga, applied and was awarded a scholarship in the Ivy League school\. The young lawyer never imagined such a door of opportunity opening up for him\. Hope and ambition surged in his heart and he was beside himself, imagining life in the third oldest institution of learning in the US\. It would be a prestigious addition to his resume\.
However, there was the matter of securing money to pay for the trip\. While board, lodging and tuition were included in the scholarship, plane fare was not part of the arrangement\. He pinned his hopes on a

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Aborted Dream
text:
Aborted Dream (cont.)

y to pay for the trip\. While board, lodging and tuition were included in the scholarship, plane fare was not part of the arrangement\. He pinned his hopes on a Fulbright/Smith\-Mundt travel grant from the United States embassy in Manila\. The US government appropriated dollars to support educational exchange and Art hoped to avail himself of the money for a ticket to America\. It was the only thing that stood between him and the realization of a dream he hadn’t even fantasized about\. He submitted his application with eager anticipation and was devastated when the application was denied because of his activist streak as a student leader\. It was a crushing blow\. Once again, he felt the pain of being financially disadvantaged\. Frustration and anger welled up within\. A sense of helplessness replaced the elation and excitement\. He had no access to funds needed for the flight\. It seemed the world was bearing down on him\.
Once again Dr\. Salonga provided a lifeline\. He consoled the dejected lawyer by extending an invitation to be part of his highly regarded Salonga, Ordoñez , Sicat and Associates law office\. “I will thus teach you what I learned from the University of the Philippines, Yale and Harvard\.”

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: The Salonga Tutelage
text:
The Salonga Tutelage

Art accepted the offer and came under the wing of the man he would later refer to as his guru\. He continued his education and

hands\-on training\. “Through him, I had the best of four educational worlds: FEU, UP, Harvard and Yale\.”

The law office was a powerhouse that counted the likes of Sedfrey A\. Ordonez, Pedro L\. Yap and Neptali Gonzales\. Ordoñez would later be appointed Secretary of Justice in 1987 by President Corazon C\. Aquino\. Yap would thereafter be named Chief Justice of the Supreme Court in 1988\. And Gonzales would go on to be elected President of the Philippine Senate from 1992 to 1993, 1995 to 1996, and again in 1998\. Salonga himself would hold the position of Senate President from 1987 to 1992\. With them working together, their law firm flourished and they counted distinguished names among their clientele\.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Eminent Influencer
text:
Eminent Influencer

Art earned his spurs as a junior associate of the law firm from 1961 to 1963\. The exposure and proximity to legal luminaries served to expand his experience and depth of knowledge, but beyond the practice of law, he drew from Dr\. Salonga life lessons that would form his character\.
Dr\. Salonga effectively became his surrogate father, imparting life\-defining values of integrity, prudence and fairness\. The example of
his life offered lessons that Art consciously and subliminally absorbed\. The young man saw and described him as a dedicated husband and caring father, a faithful friend and a devoted man of God who did not smoke or drink or gamble\. A well\-regarded leader of the Cosmopolitan Church, Dr\. Salonga lived a simple, almost ascetic life\. Wealth, power, worldly allurements, titles and honors did not fascinate him\.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Eminent Influencer
text:
Eminent Influencer (cont.)

der of the Cosmopolitan Church, Dr\. Salonga lived a simple, almost ascetic life\. Wealth, power, worldly allurements, titles and honors did not fascinate him\. Art saw him as a model for how to live meaningfully\. His former dean, professor, senior partner, mentor and guru would continue to be a strong presence throughout his career and his life\. Decades later, a very accomplished Art would repeatedly speak about this man’s impact on his values, demeanor and outlook\. During the eulogy for Dr\. Salonga, which he delivered on March 14, 2016, Art said, “I can never adequately acknowledge the pervading influence of former Senate President Jovito R\. Salonga in my life\.” He mentioned the different roles and life lessons imbibed through the years\. “There were countless, undeserved favors he had given me in the course of almost six decades since he was my dean at the FEU Institute of Law and my boss when I was a struggling associate in his prestigious law firm\. He taught me not only the rudiments of the philosophy and practice of the noble profession of law but also the more life\-moving virtues of integrity, prudence, fairness and temperance\. From him I learned that law is not a mere abstract or
syllogism separate from the social milieu\. Experience, not logic, should be the life of the law\. It should be used as a brick in building the social structure and as a means of fulfilling the deepest aspirations of the people\.
“But his foremost teaching is not really about law as it is about life\.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Eminent Influencer
text:
Eminent Influencer (cont.)

e social structure and as a means of fulfilling the deepest aspirations of the people\.
“But his foremost teaching is not really about law as it is about life\. And if my presence today in these necrological rites must have any relevance at all, I would like to sum up now the one teaching of my guru which I will always treasure, and it is this: While it is desirable to have the many necessities that money can buy, like adequate food on the table, sufficient clothing and shelter for the family, sports and recreation for the body and even a car and a house, never ever forget that it is far more important to aspire for, imbibe and live by the values that money cannot buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity, and a reverential regard and love for God as the Source of all that is true, good and beautiful\.”

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: The Understudy to Greatness
text:
The Understudy to Greatness

Another lawyer whom Art also admired was Jose W\. Diokno, regarded as the “Father of Human Rights Advocacy in the Philippines\.” Diokno became Secretary of Justice in 1962 before getting elected to the
Philippine Senate in 1963\. There was one occasion when Art, as Salonga’s briefcase carrier, had to face the formidable Diokno in court\. Salonga was unwell and telephoned Art to be at the Court of First Instance in his stead\. He instructed his junior assistant to be at the hearing presided by Judge Angel H\. Mojica, who had been Art’s professor\. His boss explicitly told him not to ask for a postponement since Salonga had promised the judge there would be no deferment of the proceedings\. It meant that Art was coming up against Diokno, counsel of the plaintiff\.
The confidence of his mentor notwithstanding, the prospect of sparring with a legendary attorney was intimidating\. While he had prepared the case for Dr\. Salonga, his knowledge of the inheritance case was limited and he felt grossly unprepared\. Still, he went to court that morning, an exercise in obedience, and picked up another significant learning\. When the case was called, he gallantly stood up and mumbled, “Ready for the defense, Your Honor\.”
Judge Mojica looked askance at him and inquired where the venerable Attorney Salonga was\. The magistrate sat behind his desk on an elevated platform, eyeing his former student quizzically\. He asked, “Young man, are you ready to continue the cross\-examination of the plaintiff?” Art pulled himself up with as much composure as he

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: The Understudy to Greatness
text:
The Understudy to Greatness (cont.)

udent quizzically\. He asked, “Young man, are you ready to continue the cross\-examination of the plaintiff?” Art pulled himself up with as much composure as he could muster and declared he was ready for the defense\. Nervously he explained that Atty\. Salonga had called early that morning to convey he was unwell but had instructed him not to ask for a postponement because of a standing agreement not to delay the case\.
The presiding justice turned to Diokno who had been observing Salonga’s junior assistant\. “What do you say, counsel?” Mojica asked\. The petitioner’s jurisprudent–who had never completed his degree in law owing to the war but was later given permission by the Supreme Court to take the qualifying tests and went on to top the 1944 Philippine bar examinations–had already assessed an easy victory as did Art and Judge Mojica\. Nonetheless, he did something totally unexpected and declared, “Your Honor, it is true we agreed not to defer today’s hearing but in fairness to my young *compañero *and knowing that Atty\. Salonga would not tell a lie about his health, I myself am now moving to postpone the hearing\. Anyway, this case is scheduled to be heard two more times in the next two weeks\.” Mojica reverted to Art and asked, “What do you say to that motion, counsel?” Recovering quickly from his shock, the defendant’s lawyer replied, “No objections, your honor\.”
He was stunned, relieved and grateful\. Diokno now loomed even higher in his esteem\. The man, who in his mind was a heavyweight

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: The Understudy to Greatness
text:
The Understudy to Greatness (cont.)

, “No objections, your honor\.”
He was stunned, relieved and grateful\. Diokno now loomed even higher in his esteem\. The man, who in his mind was a heavyweight boxer, had chosen not to take advantage of an amateur flyweight\. Art had been given a lifeline\. He felt that by requesting a postponement, the senior lawyer showed both graciousness and humility\. “He did not belittle me but instead gave me respect,” Art reflected\. “This may have been a little incident in the life of the legendary Atty\. Jose W\. Diokno, but it was a major one in mine\. It showed how a great advocate could demonstrate fairness to a young, inexperienced lawyer who hardly knew the pending case\. I would probably not have been able to cross\-examine the plaintiff adequately\.
“Atty\. Diokno earned my immediate admiration and awe, not only for his vaunted competence but also for his gallant sportsmanship in refusing to take undue advantage of a young, nervous lawyer\. I am certain that Judge Mojica was just as impressed\.”

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Libertarian Teehankee
text:
Libertarian Teehankee

Besides Diokno, Art hero\-worshipped another legal luminary, Atty\. Claudio Teehankee, the astute jurist who went on to become the 16th Chief Justice of the Supreme Court\. Teehankee graduated summa cum laude in his preparatory law studies at the Ateneo de Manila in 1938, repeated the feat with an LL\.B summa cum laude two years later,
also at the Ateneo, and topped the bar examinations that same year\. He applied his extensive knowledge to the technicalities of the law, its reach, consequences and limitations, not just as a legal technician serving the causes and interests of his clients but as one interpreting it to fulfill the ultimate ends of justice\. Art described him as a social engineer who saw the law as an instrument to build a just society\. “He reached for the stars to render justice via the all\-encompassing rule of law\.”
Salonga himself looked up to Teehankee\. When they had cases where they had to contend with him, Salonga would tell his young associate, “You better prepare our trial brief very well because we are going to be up against one of the best lawyers in town,” referring to Teehankee\.
Claudio Teehankee was known to stand for his convictions and uphold his beliefs against all odds\. He stood for liberty and pioneered the libertarian philosophy in the Philippines\. He strongly believed in autonomy and political freedom and maintained his position even at the cost of his personal safety and that of his family\.

title: Chapter 6: The Lawyer
heading: Libertarian Teehankee
text:
Libertarian Teehankee (cont.)

hilippines\. He strongly believed in autonomy and political freedom and maintained his position even at the cost of his personal safety and that of his family\. For Art, the example of these legendary practitioners of the law contributed not just to setting the standard for his own practice but just as much to the formation of his belief
Independence, integrity, industry and intelligence would become the hallmarks of his judicial career\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
text:
Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace

__Chapter 7__
*“My thoughts are not your thoughts, And my ways are not your ways;As high as the heavens are above the earth, So high are my ways above your ways, And my thoughts above your thoughts\.”       *__*Isaiah 55: 8\-9*__
Lawyer in the Market Place
Art worked hard and gained much experience in the law office of Salonga\. The demands and responsibilities of providing for a growing family led him, however, to consider setting up his own practice\. Three years after apprenticing in Salonga, Ordoñez, Sicat and Associates, he put up his own firm with the blessings and help of his mentor\. Over the years, theirs would be a long and deep association marked by mutual respect and esteem\. Through different shifts and turns in Art’s career, his former dean would provide perspectives or opportunities that widened his horizon\.
While the realities of economics triggered Art to establish his own practice, there were motivations fermenting in his heart\. He was still an angry man, and the deprivations of poverty remained an unhealed wound\. Sometimes he would remember what he had missed, and the memories would gnaw at him\. He could have gone to a prestigious university abroad or gotten better medical attention for his parents if he had the means\. These thoughts churned in his mind, casting a long, dark shadow that threatened to eclipse the remarkable strides he had made and the uncanny occurrences that had spared his life on different occasions\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
text:
Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace (cont.)

a long, dark shadow that threatened to eclipse the remarkable strides he had made and the uncanny occurrences that had spared his life on different occasions\. He was determined that his children would not experience the deprivations he had gone through\. The goal was to become prosperous and be able to control the lives of other people\. His competence and hard work had given him successes, but these were not enough\. He
envied the affluent and the powerful and aspired to their stations, not just for himself but for his family as well\.
Excellence was still his hallmark and it was not remote that with his acumen and drive, Art could attain his ambitions for prosperity and influence\. He continued applying his best to the practice and teaching of law\. He took on additional load, working in the evenings as a professor in two law schools: one in the Sampaloc university belt and the other in an exclusive convent school for privileged students\. The experience gave him insight into the differences in thinking and lifestyle of the affluent in the private school from those of the poor students in Manila’s university belt\.

He also engaged in business and vowed to himself that travel and education would never be a problem for his children\. That was how he got involved in the travel industry\. He organized Baron Travel Corporation in 1967 with a ₱5,000 participation\. The additional ₱100,000 was provided by friends who wanted to help him\. His father\-in\-law, Joe Carpio, put in P20,000, and one of his wedding sponsors also infused several thousands more to set up the travel company with a starting capital of ₱105,000\. Every one of his benefactor\-investors later sold their shares back to him at book value, but never less than par\.
Baron Travel had a slow start and initially lost money\. The tourism business was not as good as Art had anticipated\. Forestalling the embarrassment of a losing proposition, he devoted more time to the corporation\. He didn’t want to face his family and friends, who were now his stakeholders, empty\-handed\.

The hard work and extra hours paid off\. The business venture became a successful enterprise\. As his agency grew, so too did his reputation\. Art came to be known not just as leader among travel agents but as a pioneering spirit in the tourism industry\. It positioned him to connect with major investors in tourism– the likes of Benigno Toda, chairman of Philippine Airlines; Alfredo Montelibano, chairman of the Sheraton hotel; Antonio Delgado, chairman of the Hilton; Enrique Zobel, chairman of InterContinental; and John Gokongwei, who had
bought the property of Ateneo de Manila and Assumption in the Padre Faura/Pedro Gil area, which he later developed into what is now known as Robinsons Place Manila\. They were the directors of the Philippine Chamber of Tourism, of which Art was a part\-time Executive Director\.
	Art continued to expand his network and influence not just locally but abroad\. One of his major achievements came about on November 15, 1985, when he got voted as chairman of the International Division of the American Society of Travel Agents\. Though American in name and beginnings, it was the world’s largest travel organization then, with over 20,000 members in 128 countries\.

iety of Travel Agents\. Though American in name and beginnings, it was the world’s largest travel organization then, with over 20,000 members in 128 countries\. During the ASTA convention in Rome, delegates elected Art to the top post, making him the first and only Filipino, and the first Asian, to hold the position\. In his inaugural address, he said that the honor was given not just to him personally, but to his country and his people\. He went on to say, “I’d like to believe that my election is really a triumph of the American dream where everyone, even the lowliest in society,
can aspire for and be given the opportunity to lead, to serve and to succeed\.” It was a sentiment that harkened to his own beginnings\.
Art expanded Baron Travel Corporation and put up a branch in California\. It was this business that set him on track to fulfilling the objective of providing transportation and at the same time the means for his five children to pursue graduate degrees at some of the best schools abroad\. There were slips and slides but his legal practice managed to adequately sustain his family\. He had become a director in a commercial bank, The Continental Bank; an insurance company, Overseas Insurance Corporation; and a mining company, Pentagon Mines, Inc\. The controlling stockbroker of these three companies was Vicente Tan, a client of his law office\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
text:
Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace (cont.)

ance Corporation; and a mining company, Pentagon Mines, Inc\. The controlling stockbroker of these three companies was Vicente Tan, a client of his law office\. The company directorships, borne of his law practice, were eclipsed by his deep involvement in the high\-profile tourism industry\. However, during the martial law years, the law office, as well as many other professional firms and commercial companies, did not do well\.
The three companies on whose boards he sat were closed by General Fabian Ver in 1973 and 1974 and taken over by the government with neither due compensation nor due process\.
Vicente Tan was detained indefinitely on suspicion that he was a front for Communist China\. Though the suspicion was totally false, he was detained anyway and released only after several years\. He never recovered his company or his wealth\. The business climate in the country stagnated for years\. It was then that Art explored ventures in Hong Kong\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: The Hong Kong Opportunity
text:
The Hong Kong Opportunity

Mao Zedong’s Cultural Revolution in mainland China in the 1960s became the catalyst for the acceleration of the then British territory’s industrialization\. Hong Kong was not directly governed by the Chinese Communist Party, but the close proximity to and economic ties with mainland China impacted significantly on the city’s economy\. The  
closure of borders, as well as the severance of transportation and communication links, made it difficult for Hong Kong businesses to conduct trade with their counterparts in China\. It limited the flow of goods and people between the two regions\.
Mao’s political movement led to a shift in the structure of Hong Kong’s economy\. Hong Kong had traditionally been a manufacturing hub, producing low\-cost goods for export to the rest of the world\. The disruption brought about by the Cultural Revolution forced many manufacturers to look for new markets and diversify their products\.
This led to the emergence of new industries such as finance, tourism and services which became increasingly important to Hong Kong’s economy\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: The Hong Kong Opportunity
text:
The Hong Kong Opportunity (cont.)

their products\.
This led to the emergence of new industries such as finance, tourism and services which became increasingly important to Hong Kong’s economy\. During the 1980s and the 1990s, Hong Kong emerged as a major player in the global financial industry, with its stock market growing rapidly in size and importance\. This boom in the Hong Kong bourse was fueled by a range of factors, including the city’s strategic location and its role as a financial hub, the increasing openness and liberalization of China’s economy, and a surge of foreign investments into the city\. Geographically, it was ideally situated as a gateway between East and West, favorable for businesses looking to expand in Asia\. In particular, Hong Kong’s status as a free port with low taxes and few restrictions on trade made it an attractive destination for foreign investors\. The Crown Colony developed into a capitalists’ haven with remarkable growth that historians and economists marveled at\.
Art keenly observed the ultra\-rapid amassing of wealth in Hong Kong\. When he became counsel to one of its rising conglomerates, an opportunity to invest in the stock market opened up\. His client was involved in transactions worth billions of Hong Kong dollars and he benefited financially from those dealings\. He began to experience perks once unattainable, afforded by the principal who had engaged him\. He had to travel frequently to the United States and to Europe to evaluate the legal, political and financial impacts of the project the conglomerate was investing in or buying, the Philippines included\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: The Hong Kong Opportunity
text:
The Hong Kong Opportunity (cont.)

ates and to Europe to evaluate the legal, political and financial impacts of the project the conglomerate was investing in or buying, the Philippines included\. It was a quick study for the ways of the world\. He also had the growing means to live well\. The compensation for his legal services provided him the capital to procure shares in the Hong Kong stock exchange\. It was an auspicious move\. As the robust market continued its upward trend, the value of his shares reached as much as $2 million\. It was a considerable amount even then, the equivalent today is easily 10 times more or about $20 million\.
The poor boy became rich beyond his imaginings\. He had developed an acumen for business and looked to increase his investments beyond Hong Kong\. Art studied world trends and businesses on the upswing and saw the possibilities of profitable returns in real property developments\.
The 1990s was a period of significant growth in the global real estate market, with property values soaring in many countries around the world\. The upsurge was boosted by low interest rates, increased availability of credit and a general sense of optimism\.
Art studied the movements of prevailing tendencies before deciding on what would be most favorable for maximum returns and

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: The Hong Kong Opportunity
text:
The Hong Kong Opportunity (cont.)

dit and a general sense of optimism\.
Art studied the movements of prevailing tendencies before deciding on what would be most favorable for maximum returns and minimal risk\. He allocated earnings from his dividends for the acquisition of a 10\-acre property with 182 townhouses in Texas\. It was a source of pride to have been able to buy a prime development beside a flowing river in the second largest US state\. He calculated it was a sound investment, as the South Central region was experiencing significant growth\. The property was valued by an American appraisal company at over five million dollars\.
The late 1970s and early 1980s brought an influx of Mexican investors to Texas, attracted by the region’s favorable tax laws and growing economy\. It became even more enticing as developers constructed large\-scale projects, building commercial establishments, shopping centers and residential communities\. This was the time of a worldwide property boom as economies were on an upturn\. Service sectors were experiencing substantial growth, and liberalized financial systems made credit easily accessible\. Consumers were spending much more than previously\. Art was able to procure his investment by making a down payment of $800,000, with the rest covered by three mortgages, which was allowed in the US\. He invested an additional $500,000 for a total investment of $1,350,000\. The property was valued by an American appraisal company at over $5 million\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Man of the World
text:
Man of the World

Art began to live it up\. He was tasting the privileges of wealth and enjoying these immensely\. He traveled frequently to different continents, spending at least half a year abroad\. He could now afford first\-class plane tickets, accommodations in five\-star hotels and dinners  in celebrated restaurants\. He became accustomed to yachts and Rolls Royce limousine services, sporting Piaget and Patek Philippe watches, which were given by the conglomerate’s major owner who was a watch collector\. 

Art circulated with famous names and faces in society and was entertained in the mansions of the ultra\-rich\. He hankered to be famous himself, and it did happen\. His photos regularly appeared in pages covering social events, and he became fodder for high\-society gossip\. It seemed that he had finally achieved the pinnacle of his boyhood’s glory dreams\.

Meanwhile, the flipside to the dissipated life he was living was the absence of peace and quiet\. He felt dissatisfied, always wanting more but not finding satisfaction in the acquisition\. He felt no fulfillment in the overindulgence of his appetite and ego\. The pursuit of temporal gratifications fed a sense of meaninglessness and loss of purpose\. The greater price for the lifestyle he had taken up was alienation from his wife and children\. He was spiraling away from them but couldn’t get himself to disengage from the fast life he had coveted\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: The Shadow of Failure
text:
The Shadow of Failure

The heady days of high living came to an abrupt end when the Hong Kong stock market crashed in the early 1980s\. Suddenly, then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher announced the signing of the Sino\-British Joint Declaration that declared Hong Kong would be
returned to China in 1997, effectively ending the British colonial rule in the region\.
There was an immediate impact on the Hong Kong stock market\. The Hang Seng index, which tracks the largest companies listed in the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, fell by more than 20% as uncertainty loomed over the future under Chinese rule\. Worries were rife that the new government would not be able to maintain the economic stability that had been achieved under British rule\. It was a painful catastrophe that purportedly led several people to commit suicide\.
Art was heartbroken\. He lost more than two million U\.S\. dollars which he had earned from his Hong Kong business ventures\. The conglomerate he was counsel for, where he had heavily invested more than that amount, became insolvent because of heavy debt\.
His misfortunes continued when the Mexican dollar was devalued by the Mexican Central Bank\. The reduction of the currency’s value led to financial contagion beyond the country’s borders\. Many Mexican businesses and investors pulled out of the state, resulting in a sharp
drop in demand for Texas real estate\. Prices of properties plummeted and many people lost their homes in bank foreclosures\. Investors were unable to sell their land assets, which led to a surplus of unsold homes\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: The Shadow of Failure
text:
The Shadow of Failure (cont.)

ties plummeted and many people lost their homes in bank foreclosures\. Investors were unable to sell their land assets, which led to a surplus of unsold homes\. The majority of Art’s tenants who were renting his apartments were Mexicans\. They left, and the lost revenue from their rentals caused Art to default on his mortgage payments\. The bank automatically foreclosed the property after three consecutive months of unpaid installments\. There was no right to repurchase\.
It was a very low point in his life\. After having experienced what seemed like the heights of living well, Art felt the loss more acutely\. He felt dismally poor again\.
Such vagaries of life can bring to the fore qualities that define a person’s character\. It may be that the grim developments stirred the newsboy within, the one who had slept on sidewalks clutching dreams, hawked cigarettes, and cleaned shoes while tenaciously clinging to aspirations for a better life\. They were not phantoms of a distant past but part of who he was\.
Besides ambition, there, too, was a deeper hunger yet unrealized which he had not yet put a name to or acknowledged\. Failure was not part of his life plan but it would become part of a redirection towards that which he had yet to discover\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Service Above Self
text:
Service Above Self

Art was at a crossroads, and he weighed his options\. He could remain in the United States and explore other possibilities there with the hope of regaining his lost fortune from dollar\-generating investments\. The alternative was to make a go of his local business endeavors and his legal practice\. Leni tilted the decision for the latter\. She did not want to live abroad\. 
Consequently, Art reverted full time to the Philippines and applied himself to growing his practice and his other enterprises in the country\. He remembered that his father had told him to be a good lawyer, and once again his parent’s voice prodded him in that direction when all else seemed bleak and lost\. He focused on building up his practice, which had been relegated behind his business pursuits\.
Art joined the Rotary Club of Manila in 1983\. It was an association that brought out his civic\-mindedness and expanded his network\. That was where he met the then Chief of the Philippine Constabulary, General Fidel V\. Ramos, who joined the club at the same time as Art\. Ramos would become President of the Philippines nine years later and play a significant role in Art’s career\.
The Rotary Club of Manila was the oldest club in Asia and the largest outside the United States where it first began\. The organization promoted the ideals of service, contributing to the improvement and development of community and high standards in occupational and career practices\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Service Above Self
text:
Service Above Self (cont.)

anization promoted the ideals of service, contributing to the improvement and development of community and high standards in occupational and career practices\. The Manila Rotary was just the beginning of his business and professional resurrection\. Art’s acumen in navigating his métier gained the trust and respect of industry colleagues and associates, subsequently leading to his election as a major officer and director in leading organizations including the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Management Association of the Philippines\.
When the country regained its political and economic freedom in 1986 following the peaceful EDSA Revolution, his law practice picked up and flourished as many of his friends assumed top government posts during the presidency of Corazon C\. Aquino\.
By then, he was actively participating in the undertakings of the Manila Rotary\. Spending his time and energy on the meaningful projects of the club, Art rediscovered a sense of purpose in those programs benefiting the underserved\. He was, as he had been during his NUSP days, helping others who had so much less\. His concern then was for the rights and well\-being of the students; now it was for the marginalized sectors\. Rotary was into medico\-surgical missions, free eye operations, health and nutrition education for disadvantaged communities, street children, and deserving but financially challenged students\.
Refocusing his attention on others in need also became a remedy for the pain from the crushing devastation of his losses\. He knew the

Refocusing his attention on others in need also became a remedy for the pain from the crushing devastation of his losses\. He knew the poor man’s challenges, having been there himself, and understood what would be most helpful to them\. Members took note of the lawyer\-businessman and, not surprisingly, installed him as president in 1990\.
During his induction at the Manila Hotel Fiesta Pavilion he declared, “\[O\]ur most important commitment is for the Manila Rotary to be for the poor, the afflicted and the weak\. This is the base, the most important component, the driving force of our vision, our triad and our pyramid\. As your president, I vow to channel our major treasures, time and talent in helping our less fortunate brothers\. To me this is the *raison d’etre, *the reason for being, of Manila Rotary – to help those who cannot help themselves\.”

Indeed, when we, in our utter nakedness, face our Creator and Ultimate Judge on that inevitable day, He will not ask how many digits are in our bank accounts; or how many diplomas have been conferred on us; how many plaques were awarded; or even how many times we have gone to church\. Art was getting his groove back with an emerging sense of responsibility for others\. It may have been cultivated from exposure to persons like his father, who had supported the education of others besides his own children; and Fr\. Nolan, who took the time to provide him basic awareness of God and to teach him to pray\. Certainly, Dean Salonga’s principled conduct founded on a faith life deeply impressed him\. His own wife Leni was a powerhouse of prayer from the day they first met, and, with considerable certainty, was a spiritual stronghold in their home and constant intercessor for her husband\.
Undoubtedly the devastation of loss from failed ventures, the feeling of emptiness amidst worldly gain and recognition, the feeling of being stripped of attachments and reduced to humbler circumstances–all this could have factored in the palpable shift expressed in his induction speech\. All of the above and more were part of an inner transformation that was as dramatic as it was real\.

title: Chapter 7: Lawyer in the Marketplace
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 7 covers the twenty-three-year stretch (1963-1986) of Art's life as a private lawyer in the marketplace.
After three years apprenticing with Salonga, he opened his own firm with the dean's blessing, taught law at two schools (Sampaloc university-belt and an exclusive convent), and pursued worldly success driven by what the chapter names as 'the deprivations of poverty' as 'an unhealed wound': the explicit goal 'to become prosperous and be able to control the lives of other people,' to ensure his five children would never know the deprivations he had.
In 1967 he founded Baron Travel Corporation with 5,000 pesos of his own participation, 100,000 from friends, and 20,000 from his father-in-law Joe Carpio -- total ₱105,000 capital that he kept by buying back every benefactor's shares at book value 'but never less than par.' The travel agency, after a money-losing start, became successful, drawing Art into the Philippine tourism leadership network: Benigno Toda Jr.
(PAL), Alfredo Montelibano (Sheraton), Antonio Delgado (Hilton), Enrique Zobel (InterContinental), John Gokongwei (the Padre Faura/Pedro Gil land that became Robinsons Place Manila).

__*                          St\. Augustine, Confessions*__
__The Turning Point__
![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAID/AMDAwAAAACH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAICRAEAOw==)
![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAID/AMDAwAAAACH5BAEAAAAALAAAAAABAAEAAAICRAEAOw==)
1986 was a pivotal time in the Philippines\. Over twenty years of  dictatorship under President Ferdinand E\. Marcos came to a dramatic end with the People Power revolution\. It was that peaceful amassing of the citizenry on the major thoroughfare which precipitated a change of government in the country\. Also known as the EDSA revolution, it determined the change of government from Marcos’ military rule to democracy under President Corazon C\. Aquino, his political challenger in the presidential derby\.
EDSA is the acronym for Epifanio de los Santos, the name of a noted Filipino historian, writer and civil servant\. The highway, connecting several cities in Metropolitan Manila, was named after him\. When Marcos called a snap presidential elections and declared himself the winner amidst reports of widespread cheating and vote\-buying, supporters of Mrs\. Aquino amassed on EDSA in protest and threw their support behind then Defense Secretary Juan Ponce Enrile and General Fidel V\. Ramos, Art’s co\-Rotarian, who both had withdrawn their support from the dictator\.

title: Chapter 8: Turning Point
heading: Chapter 8: Turning Point
text:
Chapter 8: Turning Point (cont.)

upport behind then Defense Secretary Juan Ponce Enrile and General Fidel V\. Ramos, Art’s co\-Rotarian, who both had withdrawn their support from the dictator\. Epifanio de los Santos, which translates from Spanish to mean Highway of the Saints, became the stretch where people faced armed soldiers in tanks and full battle gear\. A cross section of society stood their ground for four days, sharing food and water donated by individuals, families, communities and companies who had hastily organized themselves in solidarity with the masses on the streets\. What made the situation astounding was the only arsenal of the unarmed people was prayer\.
It was widely held that the societal change brought about by the EDSA revolution was an intervention of a power greater than human effort\. Despite the absence of reference to a divine involvement in the accounts of civil resistance building up to a nonviolent revolution,
the astounding developments were attributed in different circles as a God\-action\. Sufficient historical accounts cover the February events of 1985 that led to the end of a 20\-year dictatorship and the restoration of democracy in the Philippines\. It is in the personal accounts of those who faced armored tanks and huddled together clutching rosaries and praying that the Presence of an Almighty God figured largely\. The Christian God is, after all, personal, possessing both supreme sovereignty over all history and nations while as much interested in the affairs of men as well as everyman\.

title: Chapter 8: Turning Point
heading: Chapter 8: Turning Point
text:
Chapter 8: Turning Point (cont.)

d is, after all, personal, possessing both supreme sovereignty over all history and nations while as much interested in the affairs of men as well as everyman\. It would not, therefore, be hard to imagine that what happened on the magnitude of a people’s collective life was also the experience of an individual\. His Presence, in Art’s life, though but an inkling through the years, would come to a dramatic turn which he himself did not foresee\. It was no less astonishing than a country’s bloodless revolution\. While 1986 would perpetually be inscribed in the annals of world history as the time of People Power triumph in the Philippines, it would also be forever etched in Art’s memory as the year of his own liberation from darkness to light\.
He had been a spectator with a modicum of spiritual awareness as the events of history unfolded\. Phenomenal as it was, he viewed the happenings as the consequence of people’s actions, a confluence of a collective discontent with the system, political motives and aspirations, plus a bandwagon response\. He had not, as yet, been able to go beyond the mindset that man was the master of his own destiny\.

__A Divine Appointment in Baguio  __ It was a day in May on that same year when Raul and Aurora Paredes invited Art and Leni to join them for what they described as a weekend of rest and relaxation\. These friends knew about the Panganiban’s mid\-life marital problems\. The decline of Art’s law practice in the late 1970s, the slump of his Philippine businesses and the diminished circumstances of his board memberships in the Continental Bank, the Overseas Insurance Company and the Pentagon Mines, Inc\. had made him a difficult person to live with\. Preoccupied with achieving that quality of living afforded by the affluent and those deemed successful by the world’s standards, he looked for gainful options outside of the country and traveled extensively\. He stayed abroad for extended periods of time\. More than half of the year, he was either in Hong Kong, the United States or Europe\.
Initially, he met with success following investments in the Hong Kong stock market and in the rapid rise of Texas real estate\. Everything, however, came to an abrupt end when British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher announced the cessation of Hong Kong to China and the sudden decline of the Mexican economy which resulted in the fall of Texas real estate prices\. Art lost everything\.

the cessation of Hong Kong to China and the sudden decline of the Mexican economy which resulted in the fall of Texas real estate prices\. Art lost everything\. Dejected and crestfallen, he returned to the Philippines and refocused efforts on his law practice and local businesses\. It was a time of mending, the scope of which would go beyond his professional life to significantly more than just financial recovery\. The prompt was that invitation from their friends for a weekend in Mirador Villa although years in search for meaning was the lead\-up to the point of their acceptance\.
The Mirador Villa was originally a meteorological observatory where Jesuit scientists measured rainfall, observed winds and recorded the movements of the earth\. The facility on the second highest peak in Baguio City evolved over the years to become a summer resting place for Jesuit educators, then a scholasticate for young Jesuits, and later a conference and retreat venue\. It was here that Art and Leni found themselves as participants in a Marriage Encounter conducted by the Bukas Loob sa Diyos\.

text:

r a conference and retreat venue\. It was here that Art and Leni found themselves as participants in a Marriage Encounter conducted by the Bukas Loob sa Diyos\. The trip up to the city of pines was not without challenges\. Less than an hour after leaving their residence in Quezon City, the car had a flat tire\. Art had to have it replaced with a spare\. He resumed driving but another tire blew out while they were going through Tarlac and it took  another hour to find a replacement\. When they finally reached their destination, they apologized profusely to their hosts who waved off their embarrassment with congratulations at having successfully overcome the obstacles\. They said that the couples attending the ME were usually beset with similar problems devised by the evil one to discourage them from getting to Mirador\.
The ME was a program that originated in the United States in 1967\. It was developed by founder Charles Gallagher who conceptualized a weekend designed to provide married couples time away from distractions and tensions of everyday living and improve their communications as husband and wife\. The Life in the Spirit Seminar was sponsored by the charismatic community Bukas Loob sa Diyos\. Fr\. Ado, as he was widely known, was active in the charismatic renewal movement when it first began in the Philippines\. Central to the movement was the enlivening of spiritual gifts through the power of the Holy Spirit\. Members of the movement met regularly in prayer meetings where the exercise of these spiritual gifts or charisms was encouraged\. The charisms had been part of the early church life since Pentecost and were acknowledged as a benefit to enrich the faith life of believers\. It saw a resurgence in the twentieth century through the charismatic renewal\. The worldwide movement was seen to restore the dynamism of the Christian way of life as Jesus Christ had taught it\.

__Movement of the Holy Spirit__ The LSS was designed as an introductory course on living according to the gospel, which essentially meant becoming a follower of Christ\. The talks aimed to establish or deepen a personal relationship with Jesus\. In the course of the seminar, facilitators lay hands on the participants, similar to early church traditions, as an act of conferring a blessing\. They ask God to bestow the gift of the Holy Spirit on the person being prayed over\.
Praying for the blessing of God’s Spirit draws from the biblical account of Pentecost, when God poured out His Holy Spirit on the apostles, empowering them to live as Christ did\. The New Testament account dramatized the transformation of men cowered by fear and doubt into bold and confident followers of Jesus Christ\. It happened after the crucifixion of the Christ and His resurrection from the dead\.
“When the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all together in one place\. Suddenly a sound like the blowing of a violent wind came and filled the house where they were sitting\. They saw what appeared to be tongues of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them\. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them\. \(Acts 2:1ff, NIV \)\.”

It was a turning point for the fledgling faith community who understood the occurrence as the fulfillment of an Old Testament prophecy\. The book of Joel declared that the Holy Spirit would be poured out on all people\. The account in the book of Acts 2:41 records that about 3,000 people joined the apostles on Pentecost as followers of Jesus Christ\. This was one of the strongest indications of the action of God’s Spirit at work in people’s lives\.
The living reality of Jesus in the Spirit is central in the charismatic renewal, which takes its name from the Greek word charisma, meaning a gift\. This gift, described in the New Testament, involves everything God gives as grace through Jesus Christ, palpable through the ways that the Spirit manifests himself in the lives of people\.

Summary

Chapter 8 is the central conversion narrative of the biography.
It opens with the macro turning point: February 1986, EDSA People Power Revolution ending the twenty-year Marcos dictatorship, Cory Aquino taking the presidency, Juan Ponce Enrile and Art's co-Rotarian General Fidel V.
Ramos defecting from the regime, and EDSA -- the 'Highway of the Saints' named for Epifanio de los Santos -- becoming the stretch where unarmed citizens faced armed soldiers in tanks for four days with rosaries and prayer as their only arsenal.

__Chapter 9__

__Catholic Lay Leader __
The ardor with which Art responded to God’s love found expression in civic and community engagements\. Outside of his responsibilities as personal adviser of Senator Salonga and chief legal counsel of the Liberal Party, he took on the duties of Special Minister of Holy Communion in his parish of San Antonio in Makati\.
He hungered to know more about God and read the Bible voraciously\. Art pored over Scriptures from cover to cover several times, from the Old Testament to the New Testament\. He had a burning desire to share about God and understood that it was necessary to learn more about Jesus if he was to speak to others about the Lord\. He went through volumes of commentaries and researched the teachings of the Holy Father, whose encyclicals became part of his vocabulary\. “In my practice of law, in my home and in my lifestyle, the Scriptures became my guide and my light\.”
 	Art was sharing the story of his life’s transformation with different audiences and was making an impact\. One of those who heard about him was Henrietta de Villa, who was then president of the Council of the Laity of the Philippines\. It was an association created by the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines for a consultative and collaborative engagement with the lay population of the Church\.

ssociation created by the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines for a consultative and collaborative engagement with the lay population of the Church\. Tita, as she was widely known, was preparing for the celebration of the Laity Week during the feast day of San Lorenzo Ruiz, the first Filipino martyr\. She was organizing an assembly of laypersons and priests, both secular and religious to raise an awareness that the Church was composed, not just of bishops, cardinals, clerics and members of religious communities, but included every church\-going member of the Catholic Church\. Tita had seen Art several times in various activities and events and knew he was the president of the Rotary Club of Manila\. “I invited him to give a testimonial to the assembly on how he was practicing his faith,” she said\. He accepted without hesitation\.
Came the day of his talk\. Tita was astounded to hear him unabashedly declaring himself for God\. “Here was a man of the world who openly proclaimed Jesus,” she said\. “I was listening to him declare boldly that we were all sinners and that our salvation was only through the mercy of God, that God used even sinners to carry out his saving work\.” He talked about how the programs of the Rotary Club were premised on God and about his work among the underserved of society\. Tita listened and was convinced that he should be included in the Council of the Laity\.

__Among Bishops and Cardinals __ The Second Plenary Council was Art’s first major encounter with the ecclesiastical hierarchy\. “For over a month, I had the opportunity to converse at length with Catholic Church leaders and learn from many of them,” Art recalls\.
Tita believed Art had the skills and competence to make valuable contributions to the work of the Church and enlisted him again when the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting \(PPCRV\) was organized in 1991\. The PPCRV was created after the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines \(PCP II\) had called for reforms in the electoral exercise in anticipation of the upcoming elections in 1992\. Together with the Archbishop of Manila Jaime Cardinal Sin, Commission on Elections Commissioner Haydee Yorac, Bishop Gabriel Reyes and Bayani Valenzuela, Tita and 30 other lay leaders conceived the idea of a non\-partisan, non\-sectarian, non\-profit volunteer organization
established for the sole purpose of ensuring fraud\-free, fair and free elections in the Philippines\.

The PPCRV would be affiliated to the Catholic Church as an advocate for electoral reforms engaged in manual auditing during automated elections, poll\-watching in coordination with parishes, reporting violations, and securing legal help as it pertained to the elections\. It was launched in October 1991 with the attendance of about a thousand members of the laity representing parishes in the Archdiocese of Manila\. The month after, participation expanded nationwide to more than 300,000 people, following the express support of the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines\. Tita was one of the founders together with Jaime Cardinal Sin, Commissioner Yorac, Bishop Reyes and Bayani Valenzuela\.
Art accepted Tita’s invitation to serve with her and became the national vice\-chairperson and chief legal counsel of the PPCRV\. When hackles were raised over the increasing role of the church in the affairs of the state, Art provided sound perspective based on objective facts\. He spoke in different fora addressing the question of why the Catholic Church was in politics\. He had effectively become a champion of the Church, applying his legal knowledge and understanding to respond to accusations that the church was meddling in government matters\. A summary of his points was turned into an article that saw print in the leading dailies, putting into perspective the issues raised\.

g in government matters\. A summary of his points was turned into an article that saw print in the leading dailies, putting into perspective the issues raised\. “Prior to 1965, Church involvement in politics was largely unheard of,” he wrote\. “Since then, however, the Philippine Church has increasingly become visible in the political sphere\. During the peaceful revolution of 1986 which saw the dismantling of the Marcos government and during the snap elections just before that, the Philippine Church, represented by the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines\. assumed a proactive role in a ‘Joint Pastoral Exhortation on the Snap Elections’ dated January 25, 1986\.
“The CBCP, through its then president Ricardo Cardinal Vidal, exhorted the faithful to ‘vote into office the persons you believe God wants you to put into office as president and vice president of this land’ and ‘to exercise unwavering vigilance in organized collaboration with others so that your votes are cast, counted, tallied and reported properly and honestly\.’ More strongly, in a post\-election statement, the CBCP condemned the snap elections as ‘unparalleled’ in its fraud as attested to by the ‘systematic disenfranchisement of voters \. \. \. widespread, massive vote\-buying \. \. \. deliberate tampering with election returns \. \. \. and intimidation, harassment, terrorism and murder\.

ters \. \. \. widespread, massive vote\-buying \. \. \. deliberate tampering with election returns \. \. \. and intimidation, harassment, terrorism and murder\. For the forthcoming 1992 elections, the Church had become even more involved in nonpartisan political activities\. Whereas in 1986, the CBCP merely endorsed the efforts of Namfrel, which was a civic organization, in this election the Church directly sponsored the PPCRV\. To be sure, the PPCRV was created out of a confluence of three major events: \(1\) the Second Vatican Council \(1962\-1965\), \(2\) the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines \(Jan\.20\-Feb\.17, 1991\) and \(3\) three pastoral letters issued recently by the CBCP\.”
It was unlikely for Art to have presumed that his legal career might be placed in the context of a greater plan beyond the practice of his profession\. By his willingness to serve in the PPCRV, he found himself in the company of Church leaders who were forthright in addressing electoral concerns\. While not in the forefront of the contentions, he was providing a solid basis for the position taken by the Philippine bishops\. His association with Tita de Villa and the prelates proved to be auspicious in the events that would unfold in the forthcoming months\.

__Adviser to the Pope __
Tita de Villa had earned the respect and confidence of the
Bishops and was consequently appointed by Pope John Paul II to the Pontifical Council of the Laity in the Vatican\. It was an unqualified honor to be part of the dicastery that “assists the Holy Father in the exercise of his supreme office for the good and the service of the universal Church and the particular Churches, as regards the promotion and coordination of the lay apostolate and, in general, the Christian life of lay people\.” \(Vatican\.va\)
Tita completed the five\-year term and was re\-appointed for another five years in 1995\. However, before she could complete her second term, she was appointed as Philippine ambassador to the Holy See in 1996\. Having worked well with Art, she thought of him as her replacement\. She asked Eduardo Francisco Cardinal Pironio, who was in charge of the Pontifical Council of the Laity, if she could nominate someone else to assume her place for the rest of her term\. He said she would have to get the approval of either the CBCP or the Archbishop of Manila, who at that time was Jaime Cardinal Sin\. Between having to talk with all the bishops or to call Cardinal Sin, Tita opted for the latter, who immediately approved\. “He knew Art by then, from his participation in the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines in 1991\.” This was Art’s entry ticket into the Pontifical Council of the Laity in the Vatican\. Tita lost no time in recruiting Art to also be part of the preparations for Pope John Paul II’s visit to the Philippines in

ouncil of the Laity in the Vatican\. He accepted at once\.” She continued, “Art became a member of the Pontifical Council of the Laity in the Vatican, adding the richness of his faith experience\. His legal know__\-__how was also helpful to the dicastery in Rome\.”
Tita lauded Art’s abilities as a coordinator in managing the Papal visit\. The World Youth Day was being held in Manila\. “It was a pastoral visit,” she said\. “Even if the government invites the Pope, like in a state visit, what takes precedence is the pastoral visit; and in a pastoral visit, it is the CBCP that takes the lead\. However, Jaime Cardinal Sin was the leader designated to manage the operations\.
“Many people were involved\. Delegations from all over the world were coming for the World Youth Day\. I had been making so many configurations for the organizational chart but felt it was not good enough so I called Art to help me\.” He astutely considered the requirements, the human resources, and the organizations before creating a structure that had a Central Committee led by the CBCP head and an Operations Committee under Jaime Cardinal Sin\. His model was the solution Tita needed for an organized and efficient system to
successfully manage an event of that magnitude\.

It was not just his legal know\-how but his ability to translate legalese into a language that laypersons could understand\. “Art explains the law in a way that is informative, educative and readable,” she says\. “He draws you into the conversation to enable you to participate and to make an informed judgment\.”
Her observation was validated when Art was appointed to the Pontifical Council for the Laity after he had completed Tita’s term\. From 1996 to 2002, he was the lone Filipino member assisting the Roman Catholic Curia in concerns pertaining to the lay people’s contribution to the life and mission of the Church\.
__A Prophecy __
When Art became a renewed Catholic, he embraced his role as a lay member of the faithful with an in\-depth understanding born of his readings and the teachings of his mentors\. When he was asked to address the National Convention of Dominican and Siena Schools in the Philippines, he talked about lay empowerment and defined the role of believers baptized into the Church with functions different from those of the ordained\.

he Philippines, he talked about lay empowerment and defined the role of believers baptized into the Church with functions different from those of the ordained\. He said, “The lay faithful are members of the Church as much as they are of the hierarchy\. For many decades, lay involvement in the Church was regarded only as a participation in the apostolate of the hierarchy\. But the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines or PCP II is clear: the lay faithful are not second\-class members\. They are not mere deputies or assistants or helpers of priests\. They are co\-workers and collaborators in the service of the Church\. In fact, they are equal to the clergy in dignity and mission\.
“This equality does not do away with the ecclesiastical hierarchy\. But this hierarchy is a hierarchy of service and not of excellence\. As the PCP II document says, ‘A person is not a better Christian simply because he is a bishop, presbyter or deacon\. The Christian dignity of the ordained is measured by the sincerity and genuineness of their service rather than by the office they hold\.’ \(PCP II, 96\)
“Because of this equality, lay people no longer need any specific mandate from the hierarchy in order to fulfill their mission as Christians – which is, to be evangelized and thereafter to evangelize others\. They are no longer merely the objects but are themselves the subjects or participants of evangelization\. \. \. \.”

elized and thereafter to evangelize others\. They are no longer merely the objects but are themselves the subjects or participants of evangelization\. \. \. \.” “The second fundamental aspect of the lay vocation is its secular character\. Lumen Gentium \(31\) and Christifideles Laici \(15\) require the lay faithful ‘to seek the Kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and ordering them according to the plan of God \. \. \. \(hence\) the world becomes the place and the means for the lay faithful to fulfill their Christian vocation\.’ There are many areas, particularly in the temporal sphere, where an empowered laity could do wonders and where, by their peculiar circumstances, the laity are restricted\. These areas include politics, government, business, industry and finance\. It is in these fields where Christ can more effectively be brought by the witness and fervor of lay people\. Because this is their world, this is their milieu\.”
