Because this is their world, this is their milieu\.” Art could not have known how prophetic those words would be for him when he spoke them to his audience\. His journey–from a boy with negligible knowledge of catechism, much less of Jesus Christ, to a student leader who came under the wing of a priest and later a Protestant pastor, went on to become a lawyer and successful businessman who lost his wealth but found God on a mountain retreat and became immersed in the service of the Lord–all this was about to take a dramatic turn\. He would find himself on a road leading to one of the most painful and purifying episodes of his life\. It would transpire through one person with whom he had crossed paths in a politically charged environment that he had steered away from, but which he nevertheless had to navigate in response to the God he had chosen to follow\.

text:
Summary

Chapter 9 traces how Art's renewed Catholic faith found expression in Church leadership through a chain of invitations from Henrietta 'Tita' de Villa, then president of the Council of the Laity of the Philippines.
Beginning as Special Minister of Holy Communion at his San Antonio parish in Makati, where his voracious Bible reading and study of papal encyclicals became part of his 'vocabulary,' Art was first invited to give a testimonial at the Laity Week assembly during the Feast of San Lorenzo Ruiz -- where his 'unabashed' declaration of Christ astonished Tita and convinced her he belonged in the Council.
Through Tita he became a lay participant in the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (PCP II, January-February 1991), called by CBCP President Archbishop Leonardo Zamora Legazpi as the first plenary council where lay faithful voted (consultatively) before the bishops voted (deliberatively), with both votes always concurring -- what Tita called 'a time of grace' and the chapter calls a 'historic breaking away from tradition.' For over a month Art conversed with Catholic Church leaders, including Cardinal Sin.
After PCP II, Tita recruited him as national vice-chairperson and chief legal counsel of the newly founded Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV), the non-partisan, non-sectarian, non-profit volunteer organization launched in October 1991 by Tita, Cardinal Sin, Comelec Commissioner Haydee Yorac, Bishop Gabriel Reyes, Bayani Valenzuela, and 30 other lay leaders, growing to 300,000+ members nationwide after CBCP endorsement.

Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court

__Chapter 10__
*“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “plans to *
*prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future*__*\.” Jeremiah 29:11*__
__Appointment to the Supreme Court __
One year after the transition of power from the dictatorship to the democratic government under President Corazon C\. Aquino, Art was invited by his mentor Jovito Salonga to serve as Counsel of the Senate\. Salonga had been elected as senator in the 1987 elections and topped the polls for the third time\. He had run twice before and in both times garnered the most votes among all the senatorial candidates\. This lawyer, lawmaker and defender of human rights was highly esteemed by his colleagues in the Upper House and voted him to the position of Senate President\. He, in turn, looked to his protégé to join him\. “It was indisputable evidence of my high regard for him,” Senator Salonga said\. “The work involved rendering written opinions on controversial legal issues before the Senate and handling cases in court\.”
Aside from his abilities as a lawyer, Salonga perceived what he described as “a radical change in Art in terms of outlook, his sense of
values, his insights, even his conversation\.” He wrote this observation in the Preface of “Love God, Serve Man,” a collection of Art’s speeches and papers published in 1994 by the *Philippine Daily Inquirer*\. “Evidently, he had undergone a profound transformation that I had not noticed

title: Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court
heading: Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court
text:
Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court (cont.)

f Art’s speeches and papers published in 1994 by the *Philippine Daily Inquirer*\. “Evidently, he had undergone a profound transformation that I had not noticed before\. This must have been one additional reason, entirely apart from his legal background, why I relied on him for advice on some legal and political problems that confronted us in the Senate, after my election to that body in 1987\.”
Salonga was not the first to extend an invitation to Art to join the government\. Then Executive Secretary Rafael Salas had asked him in the
late 1960s to serve as a technical assistant in Malacañang or a judge\. The offer was politely declined\. Art’s main consideration was financial\. Compensation of public officials was not sufficient to sustain the education of his children; much less, provide for his family’s needs\. He could not forget his own financial woes as a student and did not want to
put his children through the difficulties he went through\.

Art would repeatedly acknowledge his learnings from the man who had taken him under his wing\. “I can write volumes about him and speak endlessly of my gratitude, but let me sum up in one sentence his foremost teaching: While it is desirable to have some of the necessities that money can buy – like adequate food on the table, sufficient clothing, sports, and recreation for the body, and even a car and a house for the family – we should never ever forget that it is far more important to aspire even more ardently for things that money cannot buy, like honor, dignity, ethics, character and excellence\.”
Art became the personal legal counsel of Senate President Salonga and concurrently counsel of the Liberal Party, of which Salonga was president\. He served in these positions for four years from 1987 to 1991\. The following year, Salonga ran for the highest office in the land and intimated to his protégé to prepare for the possibility of becoming his executive secretary should he succeed in his bid to become president\. It was not meant to be, as Salonga lost to General Fidel V\. Ramos who became the 12th President of the Philippine Republic\.

__A President’s Offer __ While Art did not support the candidacy of Ramos, they were in fact friends\. Both had joined the Rotary Club of Manila \(RCM\) at the same time when then General Ramos was Chief of the Philippine Constabulary\. Their association and interaction in the RCM fostered a congenial relationship and, more importantly, engendered in Ramos an appreciation of Art’s capabilities as a leader\.
That appreciation became evident when FVR, as the President was widely known, extended an invitation to him to join the Cabinet\. It was during a dinner hosted by Ambassador Henrietta de Villa that FVR first broached the idea\. The newly elected Chief Executive was a Protestant and was hoping to enlist Catholic lay leaders like Art and Ambassador De Villa to help him run the government\.
A few weeks after FVR was declared winner of the electoral exercise, he called Art to ask him to meet with him in his private office in Makati City\. The hour\-long meeting between just the two of
4
them was a discussion of the efficacy of the rule of law in Philippine society, the role of the courts and the expectations of the people from their newly elected head of state\. It was the preamble to President\-elect Ramos’s primary agenda\. He again offered Art a seat on his Cabinet as Secretary of Justice\.

title: Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court

text:

ly elected head of state\. It was the preamble to President\-elect Ramos’s primary agenda\. He again offered Art a seat on his Cabinet as Secretary of Justice\. Art was definitive in his response and respectfully declined\. He explained that he had neither campaigned nor voted for him and forthrightly declared that his vote had been cast for Salonga\. He continued to say that since he did not support Ramos’s bid, he did not deserve to be part of the official family\. Besides, Art added, his wife Leni did not want him to be involved in a political job\.
Ramos countered with a characteristic retort, “I know you did not campaign for me\. You did not even vote for me\. You voted for your mentor, Jovy Salonga\. But that’s all right\. I do not want to be the president only of those who voted for me\. I want to be president of all Filipinos\. Anyway, I have known you a long time and I know you will serve with competence and integrity\.” He had seen firsthand how Art had conducted himself as president of their Rotary Club and as national vice\-chairman of the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting \(PPCRV\)\. Ramos gave Art two weeks to reconsider his refusal\.
He went into a period of prayer, reflection and consultation with,
5
among others, the leaders of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines\. They were also the spiritual advisers of the PPCRV\. Two different positions were taken by the membership\.

The group led by Archbishop Legazpi was concerned that Art’s  acceptance could adversely reflect on the PPCRV and the Catholic Church\. There was a possibility that certain quarters would cast suspicion on the political neutrality of PPCRV\. The appointment might give rise to the suspicion that the Commission on Elections’ citizens’ arm had been secretly working for erstwhile presidential candidate Ramos\.
Bishop Ted Bacani, however, felt that accepting FVR’s offer would be a good way to show the new Protestant president that the Catholic laity was ready to help him achieve his announced goal of promoting the welfare of the Filipino people\. It also strategically placed Art in proximity to the head of state to oppose any possible anti\-Catholic initiatives–an unfounded fear, given that FVR was above religious tugs\-of\-war\.
Ultimately, both groups agreed that the decision was his to make\. Art consulted Leni whose answer gave him the clarity to decide\. She said, “We already agreed when we got married many years ago that you
could become anything, anything at all, except a politician because I

He respectfully declined the unsolicited offer and explained that while the esteemed bishops were split in their opinions, his wife was absolutely against it\. The president smiled amusingly and replied, *“Ander de saya ka pala…dalawa na tayo\.*  \(I see you are henpecked\. That makes two of us\)\.” Ramos then countered and offered him a position Art could not refuse\. He said, “Please help me just the same by joining the Supreme Court\.” It was a nonpolitical position and an offer that set the lawyer on course to the highest court of the land without having to climb the judicial ladder\.
__The Arduous Journey to the Supreme Court __
Somewhere in most, if not all, lawyers’ minds is a vision of wearing the long, black robes as a sitting magistrate in the august halls of the Supreme Court\. The generous offer of President Ramos certainly appealed to Art\. However, it did not sit well with members of the judiciary\.  In 1987 the Judicial and Bar Council of the Philippines was constitutionally mandated to recommend appointees to the judiciary and the Office of the Ombudsman for the President’s consideration\. The JBC was conceived to attain and preserve the independence of
7

title: Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court
heading: Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court
text:
Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court (cont.)

pointees to the judiciary and the Office of the Ombudsman for the President’s consideration\. The JBC was conceived to attain and preserve the independence of
7 the judiciary, and no Philippine head of state could arbitrarily choose to fill any vacancy in the local courts\. The 1987 Philippine Constitution \(Article VIII Section 8\), which had created the Judicial and Bar Council, tasked the JBC to screen nominees for judicial appointments\. The council found it improper for President Ramos to express his choice before it had submitted their list of nominees to him\. Chief Justice Andres R\. Narvasa was the sitting JBC chairperson\. He vehemently opposed Art’s nomination to convey the independence of the Council to President Ramos\. The conservative jurist made it clear that the JBC could not be influenced\. He was adamant and uncompromising despite his personal friendship with Art, who he admitted was qualified for the post\.
It was a painful and overextended journey that spanned three years of being interviewed by the Council and then getting rejected\. There were seven vacancies created in the Supreme Court from 1992 to 1994 due to the retirement of the incumbents\. Each time there was a

hen getting rejected\. There were seven vacancies created in the Supreme Court from 1992 to 1994 due to the retirement of the incumbents\. Each time there was a vacancy, Art’s name was submitted for consideration and each time he was vetted\. Objections raised against him alleged insufficiency of professional competence and purported sins and wrongdoings\. A former client suddenly surfaced to lodge a complaint with the JBC about the supposed mishandling of a case that happened 25 years earlier\.  To his mind, Art had sufficiently responded to the charges
8
against him but he was still bypassed in favor of appellate justices\. It was pointed out that while he might be qualified, there were others more so\.
__The Humbling __
The practicing lawyer became increasingly discouraged\. Friends like Sonny and Bai stood by him in some of his darkest moments, praying with him and for him\. Once, after he had been rejected yet again, he broke down before them\. It was not the first time he had sobbed his pain\. He wept before God and directed his questions to Him\. “How long, O God, must I bear these frustrations and the embarrassment of being repeatedly rejected? Why must I suffer for charges and accusations that are absolutely baseless? I have repented for my sins and reformed my life; why do You still allow me to be chastised?”

I have repented for my sins and reformed my life; why do You still allow me to be chastised?” Yet, even as he felt defeated, Art held on to God, keeping faith in the Almighty’s wisdom and providence\. He took comfort in the Scripture verse from the book of Romans, Chapter 8: “God makes all things work together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose” \(v\.8\)\.
After three years of screening and being bypassed seven times, he concluded that becoming a member of the Supreme Court was not part

title: Chapter 10: Appointment to the Supreme Court
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 10 chronicles the arduous and ultimately providential road to Art's appointment as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines.
After the 1986 transition, Senator Jovito R.
Salonga -- Art's law-school dean turned three-time poll-topping Senate President -- asked his protégé to take over as personal counsel of the Upper House upon Justice Abraham Sarmiento's elevation to the Supreme Court.
Concurrently counsel of the Liberal Party, Art served Salonga from 1987 to 1991 and absorbed the motto that would become his own: things money cannot buy -- honor, dignity, ethics, character and excellence.
When Salonga lost the 1992 presidential race to General Fidel V.
Ramos, the new chief executive -- Art's Rotary Club of Manila co-member -- invited him to dinner at Ambassador Henrietta de Villa's home and at a subsequent one-hour private meeting in Makati offered him Secretary of Justice.
Art declined on three grounds: he had voted for Salonga, the PPCRV's political neutrality could be damaged, and Leni had made political office a marriage-contracted veto.
He consulted the CBCP, where Archbishop Legazpi feared reputational damage and Bishop Bacani saw strategic value, before Leni's clinching line -- 'we already agreed when we got married many years ago that you could become anything, anything at all, except a politician' -- decided the matter.
Ramos, amused ('Ander de saya ka pala...dalawa na tayo'), pivoted to offer the non-political Supreme Court seat instead.
But the road to the bench was not direct.

text:

But the road to the bench was not direct. Article VIII Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution had created the Judicial and Bar Council precisely to prevent arbitrary presidential picks, and Chief Justice Andres R.
Narvasa as JBC chair adamantly opposed Art's nomination -- defending the council's independence even while acknowledging Art's qualification.
Across seven Supreme Court vacancies from 1992 to 1994, Art's name was submitted to the JBC and seven times he was rejected: appellate justices were given priority, a former client surfaced with a 25-year-old complaint, and the 'others more qualified' rationale was repeatedly cited.
Art wept before God, asking 'How long, O God, must I bear these frustrations and the embarrassment of being repeatedly rejected?' but clung to Romans 8:28.

\(Chapter 11\)     
Associate Justice
*“Be of good courage and *

*2 Samuel 10:12*
The offices of the Supreme Court of the Philippines, located on Padre Faura Street in Ermita, Manila, was designed by Filipino architect Antonio Toledo\. He adhered to the 1905 Burnham Plan of Manila conceptualized by Daniel Burnham, who had intended it to be part of the University of the Philippines Manila\. Upon the invitation of the new colonial administration, urban designer and architect Burnham from Chicago was invited to the Philippines to draw up a master plan for modernizing the country’s capital\. Together with his associate Pierce Anderson, he included proposals for improvements, mapping out a detailed scheme with a nod to the Beaux\-Arts movement and the antique simplicity of neo\-classical architecture of which the prominent architect was a known proponent\.

title: Chapter 11: Associate Justice
heading: Chapter 11: Associate Justice
text:
Chapter 11: Associate Justice (cont.)

scheme with a nod to the Beaux\-Arts movement and the antique simplicity of neo\-classical architecture of which the prominent architect was a known proponent\. The neo\-classical building in the Supreme Court complex has four towering pillars representing the hierarchy of courts in the Philippine Judicial system\. Flanking the entrance are the bronze figures of Chief Justices Cayetano Arellano and José Abad Santos\. Inside, the Court’s seal prominently occupies the center of the main lobby\. Each element in the logo stands for the foundational values and principles of the highest court of the land\. The scales of justice, which universally represent balance and fairness when administering the law, correspond to the supreme duty of providing fair and decisive judgments\. Beneath the scales of justice are two tablets on which are supposedly inscribed the Ten Commandments given to Moses on Mount Sinai\. These symbols reflect the origins of the Philippine legal system which draws from Judeo\-Christian ethos\. The principle of Christian ethics reflects the Christ’s kindness, mercy and compassion and God’s love for all men\. A crown of laurel leaves encircling the Philippine flag represents the honor of upholding the rule of law for country and countrymen\.
 The tenets were not apart from Art’s own credo, and he embraced all these even more closely in his heart as he embarked on his mission to serve God in the Supreme Court\.
__Death to the Death Penalty__

__Death to the Death Penalty__ __	__The newest associate justice of the Supreme Court plunged into the task of unclogging court dockets\. His determination to serve the cause of justice was matched by seemingly boundless energy as he addressed himself to the task of writing decisions assigned to him\. He wrote coherent, intelligible, full\-length decisions and minute resolutions and left no case on his desk undecided\. By the end of his tenure that spanned more than a decade, Art had authored the most number of decisions, distinguishing him as the most prolific writer in the history of the Supreme Court\.
Even with the volumes of legal paperwork penned, he was mindful to resolve each dispute with fairness and equitability\. Foremost in Art’s work was the desire to align himself with the mind of God, as was apparent in his pro\-poor opinions\.  His opposition to the death penalty further underscored such resolve to adhere to the Divine statutes\. This he demonstrated vigorously in the case of Leo Echagaray, who had been charged with raping his ten\-year\-old stepdaughter\. The accused was meted out the death sentence, to be administered through lethal injection\.

title: Chapter 11: Associate Justice

text:
Chapter 11: Associate Justice (cont.)

, who had been charged with raping his ten\-year\-old stepdaughter\. The accused was meted out the death sentence, to be administered through lethal injection\. 	There was no doubt in Art’s mind that death was not the just course, being in direct opposition to the sixth commandment “Thou shall not kill\.” He stood in opposition to the Death Penalty Law \(RA 7659\), arguing that it was unconstitutional\. He quoted Pope John Paul II in his encyclical *Evangelium Vitae* \(A Hymn to Human Life\): “\[P\]unishment must be carefully evaluated and decided upon, and ought not to go to the extreme of executing the offender except in cases of absolute necessity; in other words, when it may otherwise not be possible to defend society \. \. \. \(which is\) very rare, if not practically nonexistent\.” \(Separate Opinion in *People v\. Echegaray*, G\.R\. No\. 117472, February 7, 1997\)
	He had earlier penned a Separate Opinion in *People v\. Esparas and Libed *\(G\.R\. No\. 12003, August 20, 1996, 260 SCRA 552\) underscoring the primacy of human life\. He wrote: “Life is too precious to be settled by legalisms, however exalted\. I believe that this court cannot abandon its sacred duty to God and country to see to it that a lower court judgment that takes away life is ERROR\-FREE and can stand THE MOST SEARCHING SCRUTINY\.”

Art was repeatedly outvoted when his fellow justices weighed in on the constitutionality of the death penalty\. Still, he remained relentless to the point that then Chief Justice Andres R\. Narvasa took him to task, raising the specter of his impeachment for his crusade against capital punishment even for heinous crimes\. The possible ousting or loss of position could not dissuade him\. After all, he believed that his ascent to the highest court of the land was a stroke of the Divine\. He was beholden to no one else but God who had commanded that nobody has the right to take another’s life\.
	His unrelenting contentions put him at odds with his colleagues who held that sufficient time had been given to dissents\. The continuous discussion on the death penalty was, to their mind, undermining the judicial process and confusing the lower courts\. He stood his ground and though the Court upheld the Death Penalty Law, new jurisprudence stipulated that imprisonment and not the death penalty was the recourse for cases up for review\. It was only when then President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo abolished the death penalty by repealing Republic Act 9346 on June 24, 2006, that Art rested his case\.

__Family Code Provision__ __	__Art adhered to the independence of Church and State\. He believed that these institutions, while separate and apart from each other, “walk together in synodal cadence towards the same goal of protecting and cherishing marriage and the family as the inviolable base of the nation\.”\(*Republic v\. Court of Appeals and Molina,* G\.R\. No\. 108763, February 13, 1997\)
	When President Corazon C\. Aquino approved the Family Code of the Philippines, the declaration of nullity of a marriage due to the “psychological incapacity” of one of the spouses, was included in Article 36\. This inclusion effectively gave the courts the power to void a marriage on the grounds of a mental condition existing when the marriage was contracted\. The law, which took effect on August 3, 1988, stated: “A marriage contracted by any party who, at the time of the celebration, was psychologically incapacitated to comply with the essential obligations of marriage shall likewise be void even if such incapacity becomes manifest only after the solemnization” of the union\.  This provision became subject to interpretation and application by law practitioners and the judiciary\. The Office of the Solicitor General sought to standardize the application and required clear guidelines, a task that fell on Art as the decision writer in *Republic v\. Molina* \(Feb\. 13, 1997\)\.

Cruz as an Amicus Curiae or a friend of the Court to provide a better understanding of “psychological incapacity\.” It would have seemed that his grounding in faith motivated such an action\.  But in truth, referencing Canon Law was academic and pertinent to the process, since the concept of “psychological incapacity” was sourced from the ecclesiastical law laid down by papal pronouncement\. Archbishop Oscar Cruz was head of the National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal of the Philippine Church\. The prelate was asked to explain the meaning of “psychological incapacity” to assist the court in creating the guidelines sought for a consistent and uniform application of the law\.
 	The Supreme Court’s earliest ruling on the matter \(*Santos v\. Court of Appeals,* January 1995\) declared that “psychological incapacity should refer to no less than a mental \(not physical\) incapacity, to confine \[its meaning\] to the most serious cases of personality disorders clearly demonstrative of an utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning and significance to the marriage\.” The condition “must be characterized by gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability\.”

Following the considerations and recommendations of Archbishop Cruz, Art crafted eight guidelines on the application of the law\. He included the parameters that Canon Law required\.
	While there were criticisms that the guidelines were too strict, Art remained unperturbed\. He maintained that “psychological incapacity as a ground to nullify a marriage was copied by the Family Code from Canon Law\. It had no prior constitutional, statutory or jurisprudential precedent\.”
__Separation of Church and State__
__	__He was not troubled by the aspersions on the sternness of the guidelines or the considerable weight that his ecclesiastical leanings might have been given\. He was uncompromising in upholding the separation of church and state\. Art held that the doctrine did not prohibit the clergy and the laity from advocating pro\-Christian tenets and opposing anti\-Christian policies and actions\. He maintained that separation of church and state meant that the government could not interfere in the church, and the church could not interfere in the affairs of the state\. The most fundamental principle holds that the state remains neutral, not favoring any religious denomination\. No public funds shall be appropriated to any church group, and no tenet or dogma shall be favored over the others\.

While there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God, he said\. Art explained that “the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic\. In fact, it is monotheistic; it worships one God\. __Praying Magistrates__
__	__Art was not alone in taking his cue from God\. Chief Justice Hilario G\. Davide was known to begin his day reading the Bible\. Art esteemed him for his integrity, wisdom, humility, patriotism and keen sense of righteousness\. He lauded the Chief Justice for his meticulous work accomplished with fastidious analysis and thoroughness\.
	Art admired the moral courage of Chief Justice Davide\. During the introduction of his colleague at a Kilosbayan Forum, he described the senior magistrate as a man with abundant moral courage who “was born with it and thrived on it\. To have moral courage means not only theoretical bravery in battle but, *a priori,* a purity of spirit and a clarity of conscience…\. He is pure of heart and clear of mind, possessed of integrity beyond suspicion and with no skeletons to hide…”

__21st Chief Justice of the Philippines__

__  							\(Isaiah 42: 6\-7\)__
It was almost eight o’clock in the evening\. Most people had gone home and the halls were empty, save for an occasional janitor\. Justice Art sat behind his desk\. It was quiet in his chamber\.  He had stayed on to review other tribunals’ decisions assigned to him\. The work was mainly affirming, modifying, or reversing orders of lower courts\. It was work that suited him and he did not mind the long hours, or the weekends spent reducing the backlog of the Court\.

or reversing orders of lower courts\. It was work that suited him and he did not mind the long hours, or the weekends spent reducing the backlog of the Court\. There were other adjustments he made upon his assumption of office\. He divested himself of all his interests in the law firm he had established and sold off, completely and absolutely, all shares he owned\. Art also resigned from his business involvements, barring none\. There were 15 organizations where he had been an active member but from which he disengaged following his appointment\. He no longer took part in any of these professional, civic, religious, charitable and nonjudicial associations, except for three\. Art remained a member of the Pontifical Council for the Laity, the Rotary Club of Manila, and Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation, all of which were allowed for incumbent justices\.
__The Lonely Perch__
The distancing from his circle of friends, relatives and associates was quite contrary to Art’s nature\. He was a people person who liked to engage and interact with others\. Removing himself from the company he enjoyed and found stimulating was one of the costs of his designation\. He severely limited his social life\. He only went to family get\-togethers, anniversary and birthday celebrations of close friends\. He likewise continued to take part in golf and tennis competitions with colleagues in the judiciary or friends with whom he had already been hitting the greens and the tennis courts prior to his appointment\. He was mindful to stay clear of those who had any known litigations before the Court\.

heading: Chapter 13: 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines
text:

been hitting the greens and the tennis courts prior to his appointment\. He was mindful to stay clear of those who had any known litigations before the Court\. It was not just about making himself physically scarce in normal social settings; he also refused non\-official visits and phone calls to his office\. Written instructions to the Supreme Court security force stipulated that no one was allowed into his chamber without his express permission\. Should any written material concerning Court matters be addressed and delivered to him, these were submitted for proper notation and included in the Court’s agenda\. No exceptions were made for those marked “personal\.” He held that there was nothing personal about matters pending before the Court\. He took the opportunity, during speaking engagements and whenever appropriate, to ask his audience the favor of not writing or calling him to discuss any matter pending before the Court\.  Strictly adhering to this code of conduct, he risked the alienation and disappointment of others\. It weighed on his heart, but his commitment to duty was ironclad\.
Remarks he delivered at the retirement of Justice Antonio Martinez included a quote from Anthony Lewis’ book *Gideon’s Trumpet,*__ __which intimated his understanding of what the position entailed__: “__\[A\] justice brings to the task only his character, his intellect, his education, his experience, his human understanding, his imagination\.”

Career jurists who ascended to the Supreme Court through well\-earned promotions in the judicial hierarchy are in a sense lucky, because their adjustments to the lonely perches on this tribunal were not sudden or unexpected, unlike those of us who were picked straight from private practice or from the academe or from the nonjudicial branches of government\.”
__The Good Judge et al\.__
__	__There was no sentimental attachment to or longing for the social whirl to which he had been accustomed\. Without reservation, he accepted the norm that went with his office\. He spoke of the attributes of a good judge in an inspirational message delivered during the closing ceremonies of a career development workshop for first\-level judges\.  “Those who wear the black robes are enrolled in a noble mission and become different persons\.  They forfeit their past activities, friends and even relatives and devote full time, attention and effort to the rather reclusive and exclusive world of decision\-making\.

	The conscientious application of his responsibilities produced 1,200 full\-length decisions over 10 years\. Justice Antonio T\. Carpio, who served in the Supreme Court together with Art, described him as “undoubtedly the most prolific writer in the Court, bar none\.”  It was an extraordinary  stint made even more remarkable by the publication of 10 books since he began his term in 1995\. There was a book every year written in a style lauded by his fellow justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez, who praised his “preeminent judicial craftsmanship, social philosophies and literary style\.” These volumes were Art’s way of reporting on his magistracy\.

Opinions he penned more than intimated a pro\-poor stance\. The deprivations of his past had widened the scope of his understanding\. Without prejudicing facts, he could contextualize cases to render decisions that resonated with President Ramon Magsaysay’s slogan: “Those who have less in life should have more in law\.”
	His faculties were not confined to the august chambers, sometimes referred to as the Olympus of the gods\. He was a good speaker and was often tasked to speak on behalf of the Supreme Court, covering diverse legal controversies over varied topics\. With knowledge that was extensive, he could tackle multiple subjects, from mathematics and economics to business and accounting; and, unsurprisingly, canon law–the legal system of the Catholic Church\.
 	Art was invited to speak on different occasions to address local and international audiences\. Speaking engagements brought him to different parts of the world to talk on various subjects other than law\. When he was invited to participate in two international fora held in Chile in 2005, he took to the podium to give five lectures on bioscience\. Chief Justice Davide would describe his colleague’s “mental dexterity” as an ability to “extricate the possible from the hypothetical, the emerging from the established, the literature in science and the law in art\.”

__Interrupted Speech__ 	Art was in a good place, grounded in an acknowledgement of being a steward for all that he now regarded as blessings from God\. He found satisfaction in his work and his family life\. There was nothing more to ask from his Supreme Benefactor\. Gratitude welled up when he considered the station he had not even imagined for himself\. It was so much more than his father’s dream or his own\. That God would continue to outdo the dream was something he did not foresee\.
	When Chief Justice Davide was due for retirement in the latter part of 2005, the Judicial and Bar Council was tasked to submit to President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo a list of names for his successor\. Art, being one of the senior members of the Court, was in the short list of three nominees from whom the chief executive would select the next chief justice\.  Unlike his experience with President Ramos, he had no interaction, much less any conversation, with the sitting head of state\. Prayer was his only course of action and it was a supplication for God’s will, and God’s will alone\. It would have been untrue to posture as if the inclusion did not stir some hope and aspiration in his heart\. That feeling, however, was tempered by his belief that the choice would be God’s own to make and administered by the powers that be\.

aspiration in his heart\. That feeling, however, was tempered by his belief that the choice would be God’s own to make and administered by the powers that be\. 	It was on the 7th of December, his 69th birthday, when the president’s decision reached Art\. He was behind a rostrum addressing employees of the Supreme Court at the Pan Pacific Hotel\.  The short speech to thank his audience for their support and cooperation during his terms as chair of several committees was interrupted when someone hastily slipped something into his hand\. He read the scribbled message and was thunderstruck\. The slip of paper with the handwritten line spelled out what would become the highest point of his career: “I heard on DZBB that the president had appointed you as chief justice\.”
	He blinked and read it again\. It was the only time in his life that Art was at a loss for words\. He stared at the people who had been listening to his remarks\. As he looked at them, they sensed that something was afoot\. The momentary pause in the middle of his address seemed a stretch to him as he took in the significance of the information\. He collected his thoughts and resumed speaking, apologizing that he would be unable to finish his speech, then excused himself and left the stage\.

Art looked for Leni who had been watching him quietly\. When he motioned her to join him, she left her seat and walked beside him\. His gait was a little quicker as he avoided media reporters waiting to interview him\.  The Panganiban couple headed to the hotel entrance where their driver pulled up\. When the couple settled inside the car, he told his wife the news and showed her the note\. Art was about to begin a new chapter in his storied life, and this time he knew who was the Author writing it\. Instructions were given to the driver to bring them to Santuario de San Antonio, their parish church\. Once there, they made their way to the prayer room within the church grounds\.  It was there in that quiet sanctuary, a few hundred meters away from the main church, where he thanked the Lord for what he regarded as a magnanimous blessing and offered himself once more to God\. He prayed on bended knees, with Leni by his side, for the grace to carry out the mandate of the office of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and to give all the glory to God\.

Had he pursued his business enterprises abroad in Hong Kong or the United States, he would most likely have been too preoccupied to give God any attention and consequently would never have taken the road that would lead to the Supreme Court\.
__Lobbying in the Church__
	Art succeeded Hilario G\. Davide Jr\. and became the 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines\. He had, by then, disengaged from his numerous civic, social and religious associations, save for his service as a Special Minister of Holy Communion\. Upon his assumption as Chief Magistrate, the parish priest Fr\. Antonio Rosales approached him as he had previously done years before when Art became a member of the high tribunal\. The priest asked if he would continue to distribute the consecrated Bread and Wine to the parishioners, and if special arrangements were needed to accommodate security and seating protocol\.

Expressing his desire to continue as a Eucharistic minister with the prelate’s permission, he dispelled the notion that extra arrangements or protocols were necessary\. Additionally, he assured Fr\. He concluded by saying that he, too, was a praying man who invoked God before rendering his decisions and was confident that the Almighty would grant him enlightenment to render a just judgment in her case\.
__The Role of the Chief Justice__
__	__The standard of conduct Art had set was not just for himself, but for the entirety of his colleagues in the profession\. He held himself to lead by example, steering judiciary by adhering to unquestionable behavior or speech\. As Chief Justice, he was the first among equals, *primus inter pares, *in the highest court of the land\.
He also stood as leader of a judiciary that counted an estimated 2,000 justices and judges, and an estimated 26,000 personnel serving the courts nationwide\. This amalgam of public servants needed an exemplar to emulate and to inspire them\.  It was not only before them that he upheld the bar of integrity but, as a public official, he was answerable to the people as a whole\. Public esteem factored into the credibility and success of the Supreme Court\.

integrity but, as a public official, he was answerable to the people as a whole\. Public esteem factored into the credibility and success of the Supreme Court\. Had he not already assimilated the values of his Christian faith, the task of being a model of upstandingness and probity would have been burdensome\. Art made no claims to possessing moral ascendancy\. He was aware of his finiteness and his need to stay connected to God, who he believed had brought him to the position of chief justice\.
 This consciousness exacted the best of what he could give in his dual roles of *primus inter pares* and head of the judiciary\. He was making a return for the good his Lord had given him\. There were no overt spiritual overtones in managing the flow of Court proceedings or shaping the Court’s agenda, opening the discussion of cases or summarizing arguments\. These were duties attendant to his position, but he performed them with deliberate mindfulness to honor God\. It was the same when he addressed administrative, management and financial concerns of the entire judicial department of government\. He saw himself as a steward accountable to and in service of the Master\. It was a position of privilege that demanded nothing less than excellence as a response to an excellent God\. That was the standard he held himself to and the standard that he likewise enjoined upon others\.

Summary

Chapter 13 narrates Art Panganiban's elevation as the 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines, succeeding Hilario G.
Davide Jr.
The chapter opens with Art alone in his chamber after eight in the evening, reviewing decisions of lower tribunals, and uses that quiet image to introduce the costs of the office: full divestment from his law firm, sale of all his shares, resignation from fifteen professional and civic associations (he retains only the Pontifical Council for the Laity, the Rotary Club of Manila, and the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation, all canonically permitted for incumbent justices), severely restricted social life, and a strict no-contact regime -- no visitors or calls into his chambers, no exceptions even for letters marked 'personal,' and public requests that audiences not lobby him about pending cases.

Thunderstruck, he apologizes that he cannot finish his remarks, finds Leni in the audience, and they slip past waiting reporters to drive to the prayer room at Santuario de San Antonio, where he kneels with her beside him and offers himself anew to God.

Chapter 14
			           __Liberty and Prosperity__
__*	            He has shown you, O mortal, what is good\.*__
__*		    And what does the Lord require of you?*__
__*		       To act justly and to love mercy and *__
__*                               to walk humbly with your God\.*__
__* \(Micah 6:8\)*__
	Chief Justice Artemio V\. Panganiban completed his term in the Supreme Court at midnight of his 69th year\.  It was a constitutionally mandated retirement which stipulated magistrates at all levels “shall hold office during good behavior until they reach the age of seventy years\.” He had served for over 11 years, the last of which was as primus inter pares of the highest court of the land\.
	Colleagues lauded him for an unsurpassed record of leaving no case undecided\. Upon his assumption as a member of the Supreme Court in October 1995, he immediately went to work on 700 pending cases that had accumulated in his predecessor’s chamber\. The 14 senior sitting members also “unloaded” 280 more cases for him to address, in addition to the 35 or more new cases raffled monthly to his chambers\.

title: Chapter 14: Liberty and Prosperity (Life after the Supreme Court)
heading: Chapter 14: Liberty and Prosperity (Life after the Supreme Court)
text:
Chapter 14: Liberty and Prosperity (Life after the Supreme Court) (cont.)

ber\. The 14 senior sitting members also “unloaded” 280 more cases for him to address, in addition to the 35 or more new cases raffled monthly to his chambers\. 	Unfazed by the tremendous responsibilities, Associate Justice Art Panganiban worked systematically to reduce the backlog, imposing upon himself a quota of 104 fully written decisions annually–or two per week–despite vacations, official travels, illnesses and other emergencies\. The 1987 Constitution directed that all cases in which the last pleading required by the Court had been submitted must be resolved within 24 months\. That was the guideline by which he measured his output\. He was serving the cause of justice, minding the Christian tenet to act justly as God required\.
	 Other tasks he had to accomplish included giving short shrift to thousands of petitions that lacked merit at sight by disposing them through “minute resolutions\.” These resolutions were signed by the clerk of court under the authority of the justices\. The pace he kept enabled him to finish the inherited, uncompleted work, as well as his own monthly load\. Eventually, just after a few years from his appointment, only current cases were on his desk\.

Not only did Chief Justice Art accomplish his judicial responsibilities, he published one book a year since he became a justice of the Supreme Court\. Each volume reported his activities as a magistrate covering the year from October 10 to October 10, which was the date he took his oath of office in 1995\. The number of books published corresponded to the number of years he had served in the Supreme Court\.
__Renaissance Jurist__
	When he assumed the position of chief magistrate, it would not have been humanly possible to maintain the quota he had previously set for himself\. Chief Justice Art had to contend with administrative functions attendant to his new designation\. Almost 70 percent of his waking hours was spent managing the entire judiciary and only 30 percent making decisions\. Without cutting his self\-imposed quota, he still produced an average of two full *ponencias* every week\.

tire judiciary and only 30 percent making decisions\. Without cutting his self\-imposed quota, he still produced an average of two full *ponencias* every week\. Applying skills honed in his previous occupation as a practicing lawyer, law professor, and business entrepreneur, he restructured processes following management principles in order to establish more efficient and productive systems\. While continuing to dispose of the cases assigned to him, he turned his attention to the many old cases pending in the Supreme Court, particularly those that had been assigned to other justices for more than two years\. He initiated a “Zero\-Backlog Program” upon his assumption as chief justice and led in complying with it through the expeditious completion of the work assigned to his chambers\. By the end of his term, there were 59 volumes of Resolutions, Decisions and Separate Opinions credited to him\. Each volume of about 600 pages was tantamount to an average of ten pages a day for seven days a week in a span of over 11 years\. A colleague in the Court, Justice Romeo Callejo Jr\., underscored the feat by declaring, “One book a year and no cases left undecided\. It was an unsurpassed record\.” His other peers led by Justice Angelina Sandoval\-Gutierrez lauded him “not just for being an outstanding jurist but also for his clarity of thought and clearness of prose\.” Justice Antonio T\. Carpio described him as "Undoubtedly the most prolific writer of the Court, bar none\.”

Carpio described him as "Undoubtedly the most prolific writer of the Court, bar none\.” He aimed to influence the direction and pace of the Court’s work following his judicial philosophy, which in his own words was “to safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of our people under the rule of law\.” He posited that liberty and prosperity are mutually inclusive and necessarily bound by the same legal structures\. Adherence to the rule of law promotes an environment conducive to “freedom for the spirit and food for the body\.”  To thrive, it was essential for the flourishing of human capabilities and man’s material wealth to impose no restriction to think, speak and act for as long as these were exercised within the bounds of jurisprudence\.
“Liberty becomes the guarantee that, free from all undue interference and suppression, we all can conceive of the good life and act according to those conceptions,” he explained\. “In litigations involving civil liberties, the scales should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the people – particularly the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak\. In conflicts affecting prosperity, development and the economy, deference must be accorded to the political branches of the government\.”
__Legacy__

They all became accomplished professionals, but none in the field that he had pursued\.

__Foundation for Liberty & Prosperity__
	The intent to promote and propagate “Liberty and Prosperity under the Rule of Law” set in motion an institution that would be known as the “Foundation for Liberty & Prosperity” \(FLP\)\. The Chief Justice envisioned a society that fully appreciated the necessity of freedom and of thriving well economically as essentially

The Chief Justice envisioned a society that fully appreciated the necessity of freedom and of thriving well economically as essentially  interdependent and mutually inclusive\. FLP stood to be the Chief Justice’s legacy as well as his contribution to nation\-building with programs supporting the country’s government and business sectors towards economic growth and expansion\. He believed that wealth generated through economic activity should benefit more people as prescribed under the social justice principle of giving more law to those who have less in life and to the encyclical Solicitudo Rei Socialis\. Beyond providing safeguards for the people to freely express their thoughts and actions, he felt it weighed just as much for the law to provide for freedom from poverty and hunger\.
	He expressed that “libertarianism of the mind, though extremely important, is not enough\. We must also have liberation from extreme poverty; we must have both freedom for the spirit and food for the body, freedom from fear and freedom from want\. We need and deserve justice and jobs, ethics and economics, peace and development, liberty and prosperity under the rule of law, not under the rule of dictators or authoritarians\.” Even as he acknowledged that the task to promote and develop the country’s economy was primarily the charge of the country’s political leadership, he wanted to make his own contribution towards achieving the Philippines’ full potential as a rapidly developing nation\.

	Chief Justice Art earlier imagined that his retirement years would be spent attending to the foundation, writing a weekly column for the nationally circulated broadsheet *Philippine Daily Inquirer* where he once sat as president, and generally pedaling down to a more relaxed pace\. He saw himself at the golf course, the tennis court, the gym and leisurely travelling with his family\. It was not to be\. Big business enterprises recognized the contributions he could make to their companies with his vast business experience, legal acumen and stature\. He began to receive invitations to join several leading conglomerates as an independent director or an independent advisor\. The offers came from persons who appreciated his work in the judiciary, people he had not previously known\.

	 It wasn’t just the corporate world that tapped the retired chief justice to assist their companies\. The Catholic Church also sought him for help\. He was appointed president of the Manila Cathedral\-Basilica Foundation, which had been tasked by the then Archbishop of Manila Gaudencio B\. Cardinal Rosales to restore, retrofit and enhance the basilica in Intramuros\. The good prelate felt it was necessary to strengthen the belfry of the cathedral dedicated to the Immaculate Concepcion\. The belfry moved from side to side whenever cargo trucks rumbled by on the street outside\. The possibility of its toppling over in the event of a major earthquake would incur considerable damage to the basilica\. The Foundation responded by hiring engineers who assessed that not only the belfry, but the entire church building, needed to be strengthened\.
	It became an even more daunting task when necessary documents \(“as\-completed plans”\) to start the work could not be found in the archives of the Archdiocese, the National Library, or the Manila City Engineer’s office\. It was crucial to know the pilings or rocks on which the Neo\-Romanesque cultural property stood\. Adding to these concerns was the fact that the cathedral was built on reclaimed land that could liquify and cause it to collapse\.

__Singing an Ageless Passion__ 	Chief Justice Art himself looked at the upturns and downturns of his life and could only attribute to the Lord his ascent from humble beginnings to where he now found himself\. He had spoken many times of how the Lord had been generous to him throughout his dire circumstances that had  given him no intimation of a station so far removed from that impoverished state\. It was a stretch of imagination that the newsboy\-sleeping\-on\-sidewalks would become the president of the largest\-circulated daily in the country\. What, too, was the likelihood that the applicant for a college education who was humiliated for his ignorance of the Catholic faith would become a lay member of the Vatican’s Pontifical Council of the Laity, the highest lay adviser of the Pope\.  And who would have thought that he–who had bitterly suffered the anguish of losing a scholarship in Yale for lack of money to buy a plane ticket, and whose visa application was unceremoniously rejected by the US Embassy due to his known student activism–would be able to send his five children abroad to obtain postgraduate degrees in top universities\. Most astonishing of all was how he, acquiescing to his father’s dream for him to become a lawyer, and forgoing his ambition to be an engineer, would occupy the highest judicial position in the country?

Whether we may have ten years
or ten days left,

heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 14 covers Art Panganiban's life from his constitutionally mandated retirement at midnight of his sixty-ninth year (December 2006) through his ongoing post-Supreme Court life as foundation founder, independent director, church benefactor, and elder statesman.
It opens with the discipline of his eleven-year tenure: inheriting seven hundred pending cases, being 'unloaded' two hundred and eighty more by senior colleagues, taking thirty-five fresh cases each month, and yet meeting a self-imposed quota of 104 decisions per year (two a week) calibrated to the 1987 Constitution's twenty-four-month deadline.
As Chief Justice, with seventy percent of his time going to administration, he still produces two ponencias a week, leaving fifty-nine volumes of Resolutions, Decisions and Separate Opinions -- averaging ten pages a day, seven days a week, for eleven years -- and no case left undecided.
The chapter articulates his judicial philosophy, 'to safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of our people under the rule of law,' with its two-track structure: in civil-liberties cases the scales tilt against the government and toward the poor and marginalized; in conflicts affecting prosperity and economic development, deference belongs to the political branches.
The chapter then turns to legacy.

title: Chapter 14: Liberty and Prosperity (Life after the Supreme Court)
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

On Day One as Associate Justice in October 1995, Art finds 700 pending cases in his predecessor's chamber and is 'unloaded' 280 more by the fourteen senior sitting members -- plus 35 raffled to him each month.

Anecdote 2

He imposes on himself a quota of 104 written decisions a year (two per week) and uses the 1987 Constitution's 24-month deadline as the measuring stick -- eventually clearing the inherited backlog and reaching only-current cases on his desk.

Anecdote 3

As Chief Justice, 70 percent of his waking hours go to administration and only 30 percent to writing -- yet he still produces two ponencias a week, ending with 59 volumes of Resolutions, Decisions and Separate Opinions, each about 600 pages: ten pages a day, seven days a week, for over eleven years.

Anecdote 4

The Manila Cathedral's belfry sways whenever cargo trucks rumble past; the 'as-completed' plans cannot be found in the Archdiocese, the National Library, or the Manila City Engineer's office; the cathedral sits on reclaimed land that could liquify. Art, as foundation president, advises Archbishop Tagle of legal liability if a death follows the engineers' written warning -- Tagle closes the cathedral, and Art's business network funds a complete three-year retrofit (the eighth iteration of the basilica since 1571).

	The retired Chief Justice of the Philippines arrived at the Manila Cathedral early\. It was a momentous day\. He was going to be conferred the papal award Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice in recognition of his contribution as president of the Manila Cathedral Basilica Foundation in funding, retrofitting, restrengthening and updating with new technologies the “Mother Church of the Philippines\.” It was no small matter to receive the highest possible honor bestowed on laypersons by the Pope\. As much as the Chief Justice was elated, a part of him was quiet and reflective\. He had come to a point in his life where accolades were viewed from the perspective of eternity\. He counted his blessings daily, taking into account what had been and the unlikelihood of reaching his present station\.

He made his way inside the still empty Church, save for a few of the people preparing for the ceremony\. Kneeling before the altar, the man prayed\. His life story was a remarkable ascent from poverty to the comfortable life he was able to provide for his family\. He counted his blessings and remembered with gratitude the ironic turn of events throughout the years\. While he himself had been unable to enter the university of his first choice, as his family did not have the means to provide for the daily commute, he was able to send all his five children to pedigreed US institutions\. He, who had missed the opportunity to study in Yale on a full scholarship with board and lodging because he couldn’t raise the funds for an airplane ticket– and was later refused a visa by the US Embassy due to his student activism–now lived with the comforts of life that money could buy\.
	The boy who peddled newspapers early in the morning had become president of one the largest circulating broadsheets, a part\-time position he held for two years before he joined the Supreme Court\. Eventually, he returned as a columnist who held a soft spot for the newsboys to whom he donated his initial journalist fees when he joined the *Philippine Daily Inquirer\.* The ironies of his life were not lost to him and he could only acknowledge the God he had barely known as a boy\.

__A Presence Missed__ 	He sat on the pew, a sense of poignancy overcoming him\. Today was a highlight in his spiritual life but his Leni was no longer with him\. She had passed away almost a year before, a sudden departure on Easter Sunday that left him devastated\. She had been teaching graduate students for 39 years at AIM, patiently stroking traditional Chinese pastels on delicate rice paper and travelling occasionally when tragedy struck\. The night before her passing, Leni and the Chief were online with their children and grandchildren abroad\. They had a happy exchange and there was no indication of what was to happen within hours\. She had no heart condition, and her blood pressure was stable, so the heart attack that triggered her demise baffled the Chief Justice\.
	The memory of the ambulance ride played in his mind\. She had suddenly weakened in the early morning and broken into a cold sweat\. He held his wife’s hand as he held on to God\. He kept holding on to the Father as she slipped quietly away in the emergency room of the Makati Medical Center\. The finality brought an ache that remained and was deeply felt especially on occasions he so wanted to share with her such as that day of his awarding\. Faith that she was with the Lord tempered the sadness, but the grief was there nonetheless\.

A year before Leni’s death, they celebrated their diamond wedding anniversary in a quiet chapel tucked in the Tagaytay countryside\. The milestone occasion was an intimate affair with their immediate family, a handful of select friends, and 86 incumbent archbishops and bishops of the Philippines\. He remembered there was a gentle rain on that afternoon as they entered the private Carmelite Missionaries Center of Spirituality lit up by a thousand flickering lights\. The Manila Cathedral Choir sang the entrance march as they walked down the aisle, Leni resting her arm on her husband of sixty\-one years\.

Addressing the congregation, he said, “This award belongs to all of you, not just to unworthy me\.” He wanted to name everyone including the workers but exercised restraint knowing the list was lengthy\. In the end, he chose to acknowledge the one name that really mattered\. “…I reiterate the vow I delivered when I first entered the Supreme Court in 1995 without passing through the judicial hierarchy and without holding any prior public or quasi\-public office…\[I  vow to\] hold office by God’s grace, and I pledge to serve Him and our people…\. I pledge to serve Him and our people with fortitude, integrity, competence and prudence… I dedicate all that I am and all that I will ever be to Him who is the Source of everything…\.”
__A Second Wind at 89__
	Chief Justice Art was in high spirits throughout the evening\. He was much engaged at the reception following the solemnities\. The company and the conversations stimulated him, and he interacted with his guests, enjoying the presence of people who had been part of his journey\. He went home that night, tired but happy\. It had been a full day\.

The weeks and months following resumed a routine that kept him busy and active\. He had meetings, received visitors or spent time on the greens for a few rounds of golf\. It was in the latter part of the day that he faced aloneness in the sanctuary of his seven\-bedroom home\. His five children now had their families, and their own houses–three in the USA and two in Metro Manila\. If there were no dinner engagements, he would sit with his thoughts\. He still had many plans and things he wanted to do\. Living fully invigorated him\. He had picked up a second wind\.
	The Chief Justice pondered the events of life from the vantage view of 89 years\. Though he had not been schooled in catechesis, a confluence of events led him to the firm acknowledgement that Divinity charted his course\. He deemed that circumstances and encounters, people he met, opportunities, as well as failures and losses, were alliances of destiny\. These led to a faith life that he valued more than the successes of a career, material gain and the esteem of men\. He viewed all that had been as an orchestration for him to realize a plan greater than he had envisioned for himself\.

The days and months quickly passed, but there were markers that punctuated his progression to a relationship with God\. Some might have been perceptible, others not as apparent\. Yet when he reflected on his spiritual journey, the Chief Justice believed with certainty that the Christian God he had raged against had been with him from the moment of his conception\. It did not feel so to him then–growing up in humble circumstances, losing his parents early, hawking newspapers to pay for his studies, and sleeping on sidewalks\. Only by understanding with faith did he grasp that everything unique to him led to the ultimate purpose of his life\.
	When he graduated from the Court upon turning 70, he thought his chase for earthly glory was over\. He wanted to dedicate his remaining years in service to God\. He spurned offers to rejoin the government as a senior member of the President’s cabinet, or as head of a large government corporation, or to embark on a new diplomatic career as an ambassador\. But to help him financially contribute to charitable, philanthropic and spiritual causes, he accepted independent directorships and adviserships in conglomerates that enabled him to tap their resources towards worthy causes\.

Dusk was setting in, extending shadows before nightfall\. The man looked up at the sky, quietly watching the streaks of light fade into the darkness\. He sat in a room full of memorabilia, souvenirs from travels abroad, books he had written, a collection of local and international honors, accolades and honorary doctoral degrees reaped throughout a distinguished career\.  There were citations framed on the wall and photographs with men and women of history, leaders and kingmakers who counted him as their equal\. The accomplishments and regard had so mattered to him at the time that he commissioned this private museum to house such glory\. That was many years ago\.
	Without discounting the achievements of an extraordinary life, these no longer held his heart\. Something had happened that caused him to see the value of things in the light of eternity\. He watched the stars begin to flicker in the night sky\. Tomorrow would be another day, but he was content to sit under the celestial sphere bright with a constellation overhead\.
	Still robust, hale and healthy in body and mind at 89 going on 90, he was regularly and amazingly striking golf and tennis balls four times a week\. He walked the jogging oval at the Manila Polo Club twice a week and could see himself easily reaching 100 years and beyond\. His powerful mind and body were still happily functioning\.

Every night, he prayed that the Lord manifest His will for him\. It was an acknowledgement that he was a temporary resident of earth\. His goal was to someday take his place as a citizen of Heaven and rest in the bosom of the Heavenly Father\. Until then, he would continue to put his legal expertise at the disposal of the Lord\. Law had not been the path of his original intention, but the rise in a profession he had not chosen had the markings of a divinely ordained destiny\. After all the bends and curves, he could not dispute that his life had been guided by the hand of God\.  CJ Art had become a lawyer in the vineyard of the Lord, and it was a calling that he fully embraced with gratitude for the Holy Presence who had always been there through the valleys and peaks of his remarkable life journey\.

title: Chapter 15: Papal Award
heading: Summary
text:
Summary

Chapter 15, the closing chapter of the biography, opens with Art Panganiban arriving early and alone at the Manila Cathedral on the day he is to be conferred Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice -- the highest honor the Pope bestows on laypersons -- in recognition of his work as president of the Manila Cathedral-Basilica Foundation, which funded and led the engineering retrofit of the 'Mother Church of the Philippines.' Kneeling alone in the still-empty cathedral, he reads his life from the vantage of eighty-nine years and through a frame of eternity: the boy who slept on Sampaloc pavements selling newspapers has become president of the country's largest-circulating broadsheet and, later, its columnist; the lawyer denied a UP slot for a fifteen-centavo fare and Yale for an airplane ticket has sent all five children to top US universities; the one whose US visa was once denied for student activism has stood at the apex of the judiciary.
The brightest day, however, carries a quiet ache -- his Leni has died almost a year before, on Easter Sunday, from a sudden heart attack at the Makati Medical Center.
Art recalls the night before her passing, the ambulance ride, the eulogy column that became the most-read piece the Philippine Daily Inquirer has carried, and their 61st diamond wedding anniversary the year prior at the Carmelite Missionaries Center in Tagaytay, with Cardinal Advincula officiating, Archbishop Soc Villegas preaching, the Manila Cathedral Choir singing, and eighty-six incumbent archbishops and bishops attending.

The chapter ends with a meditation on what the long arc means: the Christian God he had once raged against was with him from his conception; the seeming failures were 'alliances of destiny'; the earthly identity is provisional and the citizen of Heaven is the permanent one.

title: Chapter 15: Papal Award
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 1

Art arrives early at the Manila Cathedral on the day of the Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice investiture, walks into a still-empty church, kneels before the altar, and prays -- counting blessings and reading the ironies of his life from the long view of eternity.

Anecdote 2

Leni's last night: she and Art are online with the children and grandchildren abroad with no indication of what is coming; in the early morning she suddenly weakens and breaks into a cold sweat; in the ambulance Art holds her hand and holds onto God; she slips quietly away in the emergency room of the Makati Medical Center.

Anecdote 3

The ninth-day eulogy column for Leni, published in the Philippine Daily Inquirer, becomes the most-read column the national broadsheet has carried -- capturing the marriage and Leni's quiet steadiness through six decades.

Anecdote 4

Recalled: their 61st diamond wedding anniversary the year before, at the Carmelite Missionaries Center in the Tagaytay countryside, with Cardinal Jose F. Advincula Jr. officiating, an inspired homily by Archbishop Soc Villegas, the Manila Cathedral Choir, eighty-six incumbent archbishops and bishops, and Leni resting her arm on her husband of sixty-one years as a gentle rain falls outside.

Anecdote 5

At his specific request, the cathedral pews on the day of his investiture include not only donors, contractors, and engineers, but the carpenters, masons, electricians, and other workers who physically toiled to fortify the basilica.

title: Chapter 15: Papal Award
heading: Notable Anecdotes
text:
Anecdote 6

Among the guests: the incumbent Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo foregoes a judicial conference abroad to attend; Tessie Sy Coson, Art's former student, now an industry leader, sits in the front row with her family; Ramon Ang and his daughter Cecile, the Zobels and Linas and Tys, and one major anonymous donor -- make time to be present.

Anecdote 7

Quivering at his own mention of Leni's name, Art breathes deeply, scans the faces, and concludes by reaffirming verbatim the vow he took in 1995 entering the Supreme Court: 'I hold office by God's grace, and I pledge to serve Him and our people with fortitude, integrity, competence and prudence... I dedicate all that I am and all that I will ever be to Him who is the Source of everything.'

Anecdote 8

At eighty-nine going on ninety, Art keeps a routine of golf and tennis four times a week, walks the jogging oval at the Manila Polo Club twice a week, and can imagine reaching a hundred -- describing himself, in the chapter's final lines, as a 'lawyer in the vineyard of the Lord' awaiting his place as a citizen of Heaven.
